Germans in the History of Russia: Documents of the Highest Organs of State Power and Military Command. 1652—1917 / Compiled by V.F. Diesendorf — Moscow:

MFD : Materik, 2006. — 784 pp. — (Russia. XX Century. Documents).

**ISBN 5-85646-165-7**

This collection of documents, prepared by the Public Academy of Sciences of Russian Germans, reflects the life and activity of the German population in the Russian state. The book contains the principal documents adopted on these matters by the highest organs of state power, as well as by the military command of Russia.

The chronological boundaries of the book (1652—1917) encompass the entire pre-revolutionary period of Russian history, during which the German population played a significant role in the life of the Russian state.

## INTRODUCTION

The history of Germans residing in the Russian state stretches back into the depths of centuries. With the development of Russia's foreign trade ties and the invitation of ever more foreign masters and military specialists into Russian service, visits to the country, and subsequently the settlement of foreigners here, became increasingly common phenomena. It is also natural that Germans always made up a significant portion of these settlers. After all, it was with the German lands that Russia had long maintained its closest ties. For people of the twentieth century, who lived through two horrifying military confrontations between our states, it is not easy to fully come to terms with the idea that Russia and Germany were, throughout history, far more often good neighbors and even allies than irreconcilable adversaries. But that is nonetheless the case — otherwise there could of course have been no talk of any mass settlement of Germans in Russia, and there would have been no occasion for publishing the present book.

It is noteworthy that it opens with a decree of Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich on the re-establishment in Moscow of the German Quarter, which had been destroyed almost half a century earlier. This is clear evidence that already by the mid-seventeenth century, immigrants from Europe — Germans above all — occupied a notable place in the life of the Russian capital. After this, over the course of more than two centuries, the role of Germans in the life of the Russian state grew almost steadily.

Domestic historiography, as well as popular journalism, long characterized this phenomenon exclusively as "German dominance," linking its origins above all to the so-called Bironovshchina. Bearing in mind the persistence of these historical stereotypes, the compilers of this book were prepared to publish any documents from the ten-year reign of Empress Anna Ioannovna and her favorite Biron that might shed light on the true attitude of Russia's rulers of the time toward the role of Germans in the life of the country. Alas, apart from a single decree of Anna's, nothing noteworthy in this respect could be found. Anna Ioannovna gave special preference not to Germans as such, but to her familiar Courland entourage. These people, German by origin, did indeed crowd around the empress's throne, but soon after her death not a trace of their influence remained. The same fate befell such well-known natives of Germany itself as Ostermann and Münnich. The political careers of these figures reached their zenith precisely during this period, yet their steady rise to the heights of power had begun long before the "Bironovshchina," and in the end it was not they but the Courlander Biron who came closest to Anna Ioannovna's throne. So the "dominance" of that time was more Courland than German in character, and, moreover, quite fleeting.

Incomparably more significant changes, from the standpoint of the role of Germans in the life of Russia, occurred during the reigns of Peter I and Catherine II. It was precisely under Peter that the influx of Germans, as well as of other Europeans, into the country sharply increased, and the documents we are publishing allow us to see why this happened. Moreover, in that period, as a result of the Northern War, the Baltic provinces, with their purely German nobility, passed to Russia. It was under Peter, not under his niece Anna Ioannovna, that the Baltic German nobles began to make ever more active inroads into the Russian ruling elite. Analogous processes during Catherine's reign were not as conspicuous to contemporaries and historians: she attracted to Russia not so much military or state figures who would later become famous, but colonists — peasants and artisans. Yet in time they played no less serious a role in the life of Russia, settling vast, sparsely populated, predominantly peripheral territories and creating prosperous farms on these lands. Under Catherine, Germans for the first time came to constitute a notable share of the population not only in the capital cities or the Baltic governorates, but across the country as a whole.

At the same time, neither Peter nor even the German-born Catherine can in any way be classed as fervent Germanophiles. With far greater justification they might be called Eurocentrists. Both of them, so different in origin and in the character of their rule, were possessed by the idea of Europeanizing Russia, and the question of what place Germans specifically should occupy in this process never seriously concerned them. It is quite telling that Catherine, having initiated the invitation of tens of thousands of German colonists into the country, thereafter took very little interest in their fate, and this of course could not have benefited the realization of her large-scale colonization plans.

Apart from the hapless Peter III, swiftly overthrown from the throne by that same Catherine, among all the Russian rulers only Paul I might perhaps be counted among the Germanophiles — he, unlike his mother, was not, as is well known, a pure-blooded German. Paul's reign lasted too briefly for this predilection of the emperor's to alter Russia's destiny, but his role in strengthening the position of Germans in the country was indeed very substantial. To be sure, he earned this role not because he introduced Prussian order into the army and state administration, as countless historians and publicists have emphasized. Far more significant, in our view, were other circumstances that have until now remained practically unnoticed.

Paul I, as readers of the book will see, devoted enormous attention to the German colonists, who at the time of his accession to the throne were in a very dire condition. Under no other Russian ruler were the foreign colonies subjected to such a serious and painstaking survey as under Paul, and no one strove as much as he did to help them. Had Paul not succeeded in setting the still very young and weak German colonies on a path of dynamic development, and had his sons — Alexander I and then Nicholas I — not continued this work, it is uncertain what fate might have befallen Catherine II's ambitious colonization project, and it is uncertain whether we would today have sufficiently weighty grounds to speak of the role of Germans in the history of Russia at all. Moreover, Paul exerted a decisive influence on the creation (or, more precisely, the restoration) of Dorpat University, which was of enormous INTRODUCTION_______________________________________________________________________________________ 7

importance for the German population of Russia (and, of course, not only for it). It is enough to note that almost 600 Lutheran pastors trained at the theological faculty in Dorpat, finding positions not only in the Baltic governorates but in the most varied regions of Russia far beyond their borders. I believe I would not be mistaken in supposing that it is precisely the documents of the Pauline period presented in this book that will arouse the greatest interest among historians and among all concerned readers alike.

Among Russian rulers there were practically no Germanophiles, but neither were there any outright Germanophobes. Nor can Alexander III be classed among the latter, still less Nicholas II, in whose reigns the Germans of Russia had to endure difficult trials, which are given broad coverage in our book. It is known, to be sure, that Empress Maria Fyodorovna, who played a far from minor role in that period, was noted for her demonstrative hostility toward all things German. But however this former Danish princess may have felt about Germans or Germany, it was not within her power, say, to induce Alexander III, her husband, to adopt in 1892 the first act in history to seriously infringe upon the rights of a considerable part of Russia's German population. Policy toward Germans, as toward any other peoples of the Russian Empire, was determined, of course, not so much by the personal sympathies and antipathies of members of the imperial family, or even of the emperors themselves, as by the general political line adhered to by those in power. For example, the policy of Alexander III and Nicholas II toward German subjects was inextricably linked to the system of foreign-policy alliances in which the Russian state was involved at the time.

Serious changes in this respect had already begun to take shape in 1871, with Prussia's triumph in the Franco-Prussian War and the subsequent formation of the German Empire, which was received with great wariness in Russia's ruling circles. These events are not without reason linked to the subsequent measures of the Russian authorities toward the country's German population — the abolition of colonist status in 1871 and the subjection of former colonists to the general Statute on Military Service in 1874. However, the existence of the League of the Three Emperors (the Russian, German, and Austro-Hungarian empires), concluded in 1873, protected the Germans of Russia from any overt infringement of their rights. As long as power in our two countries remained in the hands of adherents of the Russo-German alliance — Alexander II and Chancellor Gorchakov in Russia, Wilhelm I and Chancellor Bismarck in Germany — the German population of the Russian Empire could feel relatively secure.

Unfortunately, not only for the Germans of Russia but for the very destinies of our states, these men were succeeded by figures who preferred to seek allies far from their own borders, thereby breeding opponents and enemies in close proximity. This mad "geopolitics," which became firmly established under Nicholas II and Wilhelm II, despite all their ostentatious mutual amiability, could not fail to lead to mutual catastrophe.

Since the time of the First World War and the collapse, as a result of it, of the Russian and German empires, almost a century has now passed, yet our two states still feel the distant consequences of the fateful cataclysms of that time. In essence, neither Russia nor Germany has ever truly returned from that distant war. This can be said all the more of the Germans of Russia.

On the eve of that war there were about 2.5 million German inhabitants in the Russian Empire. Never again has such a number of Germans lived in Russia or the USSR. Today, across the entire post-Soviet space, there are not even a million of them, and in the last decade and a half their number has been dwindling with particular speed — this time not as a result of renewed repression, but because of mass departure to a historical homeland that had seemed long forgotten. This process has the most varied causes, but the roots of many of them go back to the beginning of the twentieth century, to the "liquidation legislation" of Nicholas II, which is reflected in our book in its full extent and unattractiveness. It was then that Russia's rulers first made it clear, plainly and unambiguously, to the country's German population that there was no longer a place for it on Russian soil.

The Germans of the Russian Empire consisted of several dissimilar groups, which never managed to coalesce into a single people, although both the preconditions and the tendencies toward this undoubtedly existed. This is attested to by the fact, so conspicuous throughout our book, that Russian officials of German origin were distinguished by especially active participation in receiving colonists, and subsequently in creating German colonies, arranging them, and administering them.

The various groups of Germans arrived on the territory of the Russian Empire in very different ways, and they left it, too, each in its own way. The former Kingdom of Poland fell away from Russia — and Polish Germans ceased to be Russian subjects; the Bolsheviks seized control of the country — and most of the urban Germans, who belonged to the propertied classes hated by the new rulers, went into emigration; Stalin and Hitler entered into collusion — and Germans were resettled to Germany from all the territories annexed by the Soviet Union in 1939—1940: from the Baltic states, Bessarabia, western Volhynia, and so on.

The most complex and tragic fate befell the most numerous group — the former German colonists, whose descendants make up today the overwhelming majority of the German population still remaining in the post-Soviet space. It is entirely fitting that the greater part of the documents published in this book is devoted to them. These people became the object of a centuries-long experiment unprecedented in history. First, for a century, the Russian authorities by every possible means attracted German colonists to the country, but several decades later their descendants began to be pushed out of it just as insistently and consistently (or, as happened under Stalin, simply destroyed).

What is the reason for this — perhaps the German colonists failed to live up to the hopes that Russia's rulers placed in them? This notion, set in circulation by the Russian authorities themselves, has a long pedigree, and traces of it can be found in some of the documents published in this book. Its most widespread version, translated into modern language, amounts to the following: the rulers of Russia, expending large sums of state funds to attract colonists, expected that they would not only establish advanced farms but would also induce the surrounding peasantry to follow their example, as a result of which the Russian agrarian sector would rise to a qualitatively new level — but in fact this did not happen.

This sounds quite logical, although such a goal for inviting foreign settlers to Russia cannot be traced in any of the numerous documents devoted to their recruitment. But whatever may have been declared, this historical legend has a simple and convincing refutation: right up until the second half of the nineteenth century, the Russian authorities made practically no effort to bring the colonists into contact with the Russian language. It is perfectly obvious that the complete linguistic (and not only linguistic) isolation of the colonies suited the rulers throughout an entire century. How, under these conditions, could the German colonists have passed on their experience to Russian peasants?

The documents we are publishing convincingly demonstrate that the purpose of bringing tens of thousands of colonists into Russia was not this at all, but rather that they and their descendants would settle the vast, largely empty territories on the country's periphery. And it is precisely this task that the Russian Germans accomplished with honor.

Basing ourselves not on legends but on facts reflected in the documents, it is difficult, in our view, not to arrive at the following disheartening conclusion: the centuries-long colonist saga was doomed to a sad end from the very outset — above all because even its initiators, the Russian authorities, gave no thought whatsoever to its probable long-term consequences. The point is not that it involved mass emigration — such historical phenomena have long been known, and they have often produced quite satisfactory results. In this case, the familiar problems of emigration processes were compounded many times over by the fact that people settled in Russia in large numbers who were, in their mentality, traditions, customs, and entire way of life, very far removed from native Russians. The only way for them and their descendants to establish themselves permanently in Russian society lay in the swiftest possible integration into it, as one would now put it. However, neither the Russian authorities nor the colonists themselves desired this.

The result was a situation with few analogues in history: on the territory of the Russian Empire there formed large, highly developed, closed and — to borrow the vocabulary of the fighters against "German dominance" — "alien" enclaves. No, their inhabitants as a rule did not gravitate toward Germany and remained loyal to the Russian crown, and in time they came to bring Russia tangible economic benefit. Yet this did not stop the authorities from continuing to regard them as a foreign body within the Russian state organism. On top of everything else, these were people descended from a state that, from the 1880s on, became Russia's principal rival, and later its adversary, on the world stage. It is precisely from this that the persistent striving of the Russian authorities arose to eliminate these enclaves of their own making, to assimilate their inhabitants, or to rid themselves of them by one means or another. The rulers of the Russian Empire were not granted enough time to accomplish these tasks, but their work was practically completed by their successors — the Soviet heralds of "proletarian internationalism."

Thus the German colonists and their descendants, having involuntarily become the object of a vast historical experiment, confirmed through their sad experience the German proverb that one can be a welcome guest for only one day. Who is to blame for this, and is it even appropriate to speak of blame here at all? Let the readers of the book, drawing on its contents, attempt to answer these questions for themselves.

Such, in the most general outline, is the historical path traveled by the German population of Russia. The documents we are publishing reflect many stages and turns of this path. Another, no less important problem — the concrete role played by Germans in the life of Russia — is, as one can readily see, touched upon by the documents only in passing. This is understandable: it plainly lies beyond the scope of any legislative acts. We shall therefore not attempt to analyze it either, especially since to do so within the confines of our brief introduction would be entirely impossible.

Whole volumes have already been written on the role of Germans in the history of Russia, and their number continues to grow — so multifaceted, ambiguous, and complex is this subject. So that the reader may at least form a general idea of the scale of the personalities and events in question here, we have appended to the book brief biographical information on approximately one hundred outstanding Germans who lived and worked in Russia before 1917. In doing so we sought, as far as possible, to encompass people of the most varied origins, spheres, and fields of activity. In reality, of course, there were far more Germans who left a notable mark on the history of Russia. Detailed articles on many of them are to be found in the three-volume encyclopedia "Germans of Russia," the publication of which is currently being completed by the Public Academy of Sciences of Russian Germans.

In the literature, attempts have often been made to portray the role of Germans in the life of Russia in a single color — now black, now white. One may write popular journalism in this manner (and, as a rule, journalism of no great quality), but certainly not history. In the present case one thing is absolutely clear: without the centuries-long efforts of hundreds of thousands and millions of its German inhabitants, Russia would have been an altogether different country.

---

The residence of Germans in Russia over the course of many centuries has left its mark in an enormous mass of documents. The most important place among them belongs, of course, to the documents of the highest organs of state power, above all the legislative acts that regulated every aspect of the life of Germans, as of the rest of the country's population. Many such documents devoted to the Germans of Russia (the USSR) have already been published, and more than once at that. In particular, a great deal of work has been done in this direction over the last 15 years, when, after a long period of total silence regarding the history and life of its German population, publications on this subject once again became possible in our country. Nevertheless, no one has until now set out to publish all the principal official documents concerning the Germans of Russia for an entire historical epoch.

The present book represents the first such attempt. Its chronological scope is not accidental: the pre-revolutionary period has been noticeably less studied in this respect than the Soviet one. On the other hand, the principal official documents issued before 1917 are more readily surveyable. Most of them are contained in three multi-volume official publications — the Complete Collection of Laws of the Russian Empire, the Digest of Laws of the Russian Empire, and the Collection of Statutes and Orders of the Government. These were taken as the basis for the preparation of this book. It is true that in doing so a very important subject was left aside — one concerning the fate of the Germans of Russia during the First World War: the deportation of the German population from the western regions of the country and the repression against it, which were carried out not by civil but by military authorities. Therefore, in addition to the aforementioned sources, corresponding documents from the Russian State Military-Historical Archive (RGVIA) were also drawn upon.

In Russia before 1917, numerous legislative acts were devoted to Germans (or predominantly to Germans) — among the peoples of the Russian Empire, Germans were second in this respect only to the Jews, though by a very wide margin. This is explained above all by the fact that the greater part of the German population belonged for a long time to a special peasant estate — that of the colonists. According to the calculations of the pre-revolutionary historian and jurist Ya. Ye. Dietz, a deputy of the First State Duma, various legal provisions concerning the colonists occupy almost 1,000 pages in the Complete Collection of Laws of the Russian Empire. It is telling that after the abolition of colonist status in 1871, the number of legislative acts devoted to Germans immediately decreased substantially. In addition, a considerable number of official acts regulated the religious affairs of the "foreign" confessions (Catholicism, Lutheranism, Reformed Christianity, etc.) professed by the Germans of Russia. From the end of the nineteenth century, especially during the years of the First World War, these were joined by numerous acts aimed at restricting and infringing upon the rights of the German population. Otherwise, Russian legislation did not accord Germans any particular preference. For instance, our book contains a fair number of documents devoted to individual German churches, educational institutions, charitable societies, and the like. However, analogous acts were also adopted with respect to other institutions of a similar kind — and, naturally, in far greater numbers.

The foregoing makes it possible to understand that identifying the principal legislative acts devoted to the German population of Russia before 1917 is a rather complex task. In this work we were guided by the following criteria.

First, we of course took into account the significance of the document, that is, the consequences of its implementation for the German population of Russia. Legislative acts that had a profound, long-term impact on all Germans of Russia, or at least on a significant portion of them, are, for the entire pre-revolutionary period, quite few in number, and all of them are naturally included in the book. There were far more acts that changed the fate of the German inhabitants of a particular region or locality — an example being documents on the resettlement of Germans, for one reason or another, to another place. We generally tried to publish such acts as well.

Second, it seemed of fundamental importance to cover, as far as possible, all the notable groups of the German population and the regions where they lived. This was achieved in most cases, but not always. Thus, the book contains no documents on the life of the numerous German population in the Polish governorates — such acts were simply not adopted at the central level. Aside from mentions in several "liquidation laws," the sources we used say nothing about the German population of the Don Cossack Host region, Ufa governorate, Orenburg, Siberia, the Steppe Territory, Turkestan, and certain other regions. The reason is that Germans settled there either on private lands or within the framework of the general resettlement policy, and the highest organs of power did not adopt separate documents concerning them. On the other hand, apart from two charters granted by Peter I and the plan for the creation of Dorpat University, we have not included in the book documents on the Baltic (Ostsee) Germans. The acts adopted concerning them, as a rule, dealt with quite specific matters — this group of Germans, predominantly nobles, had a history altogether different from that of the rest of the German population of Russia, which belonged mainly to other estates, above all the peasantry. The subject of the Baltic Germans therefore requires separate treatment, as is most often done in historiography. By contrast, we sought to cover as broadly as possible the life of the German population of Russian cities: this group of Germans has a very long history that is of great interest. Rather few legislative acts were adopted concerning it, and almost all of them are included in the book.

Third, legislative acts on the Germans of Russia were distributed very unevenly over time. Moreover, various periods have been studied to very different degrees. In light of these circumstances, we have, for example, omitted a number of documents from the Catherinian period, which has been studied better than others, especially since they were published quite recently, in 2004, by Ye. Ye. Lykova and M. I. Osekina (with the assistance of the Public Academy of Sciences of Russian Germans) in the collection "German Colonists in the Age of Catherine." By contrast, documents on the subsequent history of the Germans of Russia, especially from the mid-nineteenth century to the First World War, have been studied far less, and are therefore represented far more fully in the book. As for the period of the First World War, we have published without exception all the documents discovered from this time, although some of them have been known since 1993 from V.A. Auman and V.G. Chebotareva's collection "The History of the Russian Germans in Documents (1763—1992)." This period, with its "liquidation legislation," had enormous, pivotal significance in the history of the Germans of Russia, and any information about it deserves careful study.

Fourth, the thematic focus of the documents was taken into account. We published documents concerning entire groups of the German population, rather than individual persons of German origin, however well known they might be. Thus the book does not include, for example, the charters issued from the time of Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich onward to German merchants trading in Russia, nor documents on various enterprises whose owners were German but whose staff consisted mainly of people of other nationalities. Further, we gave preference to documents devoted to various aspects of the life of the German population over documents that concerned only its external conditions (an example being acts on the administrative bodies of the colonies). In addition, we tried to avoid unwarranted duplication of documents on one and the same subject. Thus, many Russian emperors issued charters to the inhabitants of the well-known Volga colony of Sarepta. Given that the subject of Sarepta is already represented quite fully elsewhere in our book, we have published only one of these charters. For similar reasons we have omitted the Instruction on Internal Order and Administration in the St. Petersburg Colonies, which practically duplicates the corresponding instruction for the New Russia colonies.

Fifth, we sought to publish as fully as possible two principal codes of law concerning the Germans of the Russian Empire — the Statute on the Religious Affairs of Foreign Confessions and the Statute on the Colonies. These codes are of very great interest, although, for instance, the main provisions of the Statute on the Colonies are contained in other documents published in the book. The point is that these codes of law contain information about all the corresponding legislative acts adopted up to the time of their issuance (1857). It is of fundamental importance, of course, that the codes also cover extremely significant subject matter: the first, the activity of those churches and religious communities that exerted the most profound influence on the life of the Germans of the Russian Empire; the second, the norms of life of the colonists, who constituted, over the course of a century beginning in the 1760s, a significant, and later the principal, part of the German population of Russia.

We were guided by essentially the same criteria in cases where it was necessary to abridge documents. Omitted passages are indicated by ellipses in angle brackets. Each document has an editorial heading indicating the year of issuance (if the date is not given in the original title). The peculiarities of punctuation, and in part of spelling, have been preserved (except for words sufficiently common in modern language, whose spelling has been brought into conformity with currently accepted norms). Minor misprints have been corrected without comment; for more substantial ones (for example, errors in dates or document numbers), corrections are given in square brackets. Obvious gaps in meaning are also reproduced in square brackets. After each officially published document, the source and publication data of its first appearance are indicated (except for official publications); after archival documents, the archival reference code, whether it is an original or a copy, and the method of text reproduction are indicated. The selection of archival documents, their preparation for publication, and the compilation of notes to them were carried out by I.V. Karpeev, a staff member of RGVIA. The compiler's notes to these documents are specially marked.

The notes to the content of the documents serve a variety of purposes — to clarify the meaning of the document, and where possible, the circumstances of its preparation (adoption); to provide necessary information about the principal publications addressing the issues raised in it, as well as about the German localities, persons of German nationality, other documents, and so forth, that are mentioned (or implied) in the document.

The collection is supplied with a name commentary and an index of names. The principal source used in compiling the name commentary was the corresponding articles in vols. 1–2, as well as the forthcoming vol. 3, of the three-volume publication "Germans of Russia: An Encyclopedia," issued by the Public Academy of Sciences of Russian Germans. ## No. 1. DECREE OF TSAR ALEKSEI MIKHAILOVICH ON THE ALLOTMENT OF LAND FOR THE GERMAN QUARTER IN MOSCOW (1652)

85. — October 4. On the allotment of land for building in the German Quarter.

By decree of the Great Sovereign, Tsar and Grand Prince Aleksei Mikhailovich of All Russia, Afonasy Ivanov son Nesterov, and the clerks Fyodor Ivanov and Bogdan Arefyev, built a new foreigners' quarter beyond the Pokrovsky Gate, beyond the Earthen City, alongside the Yauza River, where German houses had formerly stood, under previous Great Sovereigns, before the Moscow devastation, and they allotted land for house plots in that German Quarter, measuring it out according to the instructions given to them from the Zemsky prikaz [Land Office], by order of the Court Steward Bogdan Matveevich Khitrovo, countersigned by the clerk Maksim Likhachev. For Germans in military service, the first category [was] 40 fathoms in length by 20 in width; the second category 30 fathoms in length by 15 in width; the third category 15 fathoms in length by 10 in width; and for Doctors, [land] as in the first category; for Apothecaries, as in the middle category; for German masters of diamond-work, and gold-work, and silver-work, and gold-thread or lace work, according to a petition endorsed with the notation of the Duma clerk Mikhail Volosheninov, all as in the middle category; and for German merchants and widows, [land] was matched to their former Moscow house-plots; for Germans of the lesser categories: sergeants, and corporals, and regimental wagon-masters, and Germans in military service of all minor ranks, 10 fathoms in length by 8 in width, according to the memorandum sent from the Zemsky prikaz, countersigned by the clerk Maksim Likhachev. Plots for houses are to be given to German women, widows, and all manner of lesser German folk who have no houses of their own in Moscow, 8 fathoms in length by 6 in width; the names of who was given how much land in length and width for house plots, and of what rank, whether German men, women, or widows, and how many large streets and lanes were laid out, and of how many fathoms in width, is recorded by name in the construction registers.

*Complete Collection of Laws of the Russian Empire (PSZRI). Coll. 1. Vol. III. P. 273.*

## No. 2. DECREE OF IVAN V AND PETER I ON THE INVESTIGATION OF RUSSIAN ORES IN GERMANY AND ON THE INVITATION OF FOREIGN MINING SPECIALISTS INTO RUSSIAN SERVICE (1695)

1512. — May 7. By name. — On sending the foreigner Matvei Poppu to Germany with samples of lead and silver ore for testing, and on inviting into Russian service foreigners knowledgeable in the art of mining.

The Great Sovereigns have ordered that 10 pounds of lead and silver ore, sent from the Musketeers' Office, be sent from Moscow overseas to the German states and given to the foreign merchant Matvei Poppu, and that he, Matvei, be instructed to have a genuine assay made of that ore; and [to determine] how much lead and silver will come out of that ore, and whether, according to the assay, it would be profitable to work that ore on a large scale, and whether, in large-scale smelting, many additional materials and compounds will be needed, and how much of such compounds will be required per 100 poods, and what the price would be by the foreign rate, and whether, having regard to that ore, by comparison with such works and ores, it can be said whether the ore that was taken from near the surface, would be better and yield more silver if taken from deeper down — and concerning all of this those ore-smelting masters are to be instructed to set it down properly in writing; and if, according to their assay and inspection, they come to recognize that there will in future be profit from that ore and that profitable works can be established, then he, Matvei, having made inquiry, is to seek out and engage knowledgeable and needed ore-smelting masters, [determining] whether any of them will be willing to serve the Great Sovereigns in that work, and what monthly salary from the Great Sovereigns they will ask, and for how many years they will hire themselves out; and concerning all of this, having obtained it in writing from those masters, [he] is instructed to send to Moscow, to the Siberian prikaz, [a report of] how much silver and lead will result, together with those written inspection findings.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. III. P. 204.*

## No. 3. MANIFESTO OF PETER I ON THE INVITATION OF FOREIGNERS TO SETTLE IN RUSSIA (1702)

1910. — April 16. Manifesto. — On summoning foreigners to Russia, granting them freedom of religion.

It is well known in all the lands which the Almighty has subjected to Our rule, that from the time of Our accession to this throne, all Our efforts and intentions have been directed toward governing this State in such a manner that all Our subjects, through Our concern for the general good, might come more and more into a better and more prosperous condition; to this end We have taken great pains to preserve internal tranquility, to defend the State from external attack, and in every way to improve and expand trade. For this same purpose We were compelled, in the very administration [of the state], to make certain necessary changes serving the good of Our land, so that Our subjects might the more readily and conveniently learn skills hitherto unknown to them, and thereby become more proficient in all commercial matters. For which reason We have most graciously issued, and intend hereafter to issue, all orders, arrangements, and institutions especially necessary for the promotion of trade with foreigners; but inasmuch as We fear that these matters are not yet in such a state as We would wish, and that Our subjects cannot yet enjoy in complete tranquility the fruits of Our labors, We have therefore also considered other means by which to secure Our borders from enemy attack and to preserve the rights and prerogatives of Our State and the general peace of Christendom, as befits a Christian Monarch. To attain these good ends, We have taken particular care for the best organization of the Military Establishment, as the mainstay of Our State, so that Our troops might not only consist of well-trained men, but also live in good order and discipline; but in order to improve this the more, and to encourage foreigners who can contribute to this end and assist in such improvement, together with other craftsmen useful to the State, to come to Us, and to remain both in Our service and in Our land, We have ordered this Manifesto, with the points written below, to be proclaimed everywhere, and, once printed, to be published throughout Europe. 1). It is not unknown how long ago, already during Our reign, We abolished and did away with the ancient custom by which free entry into Russia was entirely forbidden to foreigners; wherefore We not only confirm this, but extend it, so that any and every person having the intention of coming here to enter into service in Our army, and who has beforehand obtained new certificates from Our General Commissar in Germany, whom We intend accordingly to maintain there, shall, upon presenting himself to the first frontier Governor or Viceroy, together with the retinue and baggage he has with him, be provided from there to Our capital with relay-horses at no charge, and shall likewise enjoy full safety along his way. Wherefore We shall, from this date, communicate to all Our Viceroys, Governors, and Commanders, both on the borders and along the roads leading here from Kiev, Smolensk, and Pskov, Our confirmatory decrees and instructions to that effect, so that henceforth no hindrance or trouble whatsoever shall be caused to arriving officers, but that, on the contrary, every voluntary readiness to be of service shall be shown them; likewise merchants and craftsmen intending to enter Russia are to be received with every kindness. 2). And whereas here in Our Capital free performance of worship has already been introduced for all other Christian sects, even those not in agreement with Our own Church; for this reason it is hereby newly confirmed as well, in such manner that We, by the power granted to Us by the Almighty, do not wish to compel the human conscience, and gladly leave it to every Christian, on his own responsibility, to care for the salvation of his soul. And thus We shall watch closely that, as by former custom, no one shall be troubled in his public or private performance of worship, but shall be maintained therein and protected against every hindrance. Should it happen that in some place of Our State, or with Our armies and garrisons, there be no proper clergyman or church of the appropriate confession, then it shall be permitted to everyone not only to perform divine service in his own house, himself together with his household, but also to receive into it those who wish to gather with him, so that, according to the general order of the Christian churches, they may with one voice praise God and thus conduct divine worship. And should there be, with Our armies, individual officers, or entire corps consisting of regiments and companies, with whom preachers are found, then they too shall without doubt enjoy all those benefits, privileges, and liberties which We have granted to such churches here in the Capital, in Arkhangelsk, and in other places; and which are customary not only in the performance of the actual preaching service, but also in the administration of the Holy Sacraments and other church rites; and We further permit, at the request of such fellow believers, that they build new churches in other places as well. 3). And so that foreigners may not be deterred from coming to Russia by fear of being subjected to institutions, judicial proceedings, or kinds of punishment incompatible with their own countries' laws and customs, We have therefore hereby and by virtue hereof ordered that a Secret Council of War Collegium be formed from among foreigners skilled in matters of the Military Establishment, to consist of a President, Councilors, Secretaries, and other chancery officials, inasmuch as We intend to incorporate it into Our Military Establishment, and have ordered this to be published in an order by means of the press; and upon this Collegium shall depend all and any matters concerning the foreign Military Establishment, of whatever kind and nature they may be, as well as the Foreign Kriegs-Commissariat, the military treasury, and their officials; and the aforementioned President is to render account of his administration to Us alone; and is likewise bound to await from Us alone instructions and orders in matters of necessity. As for judicial matters beyond this, the first instance shall remain with the regiments, over whose decisions review shall be exercised by the General Military Court, and further proceedings shall follow as is the practice in other foreign regular armies and as shall, among other things, be contained in the military articles; which military articles and other regulations and statutes serving the Military Establishment, the President of Our Secret Council of War, in general deliberation with the whole Secret Military Collegium, shall draw up, and shall first submit to Us for consideration, and thereafter, once printed, shall publish. Furthermore, not only shall all and any persons, of higher and lower rank, who are enrolled in Our Foreign Military Establishment, whether officers or other officials and rank-and-file, together with all their servants or those who in any manner belong to their retinue, pertain to them, or depend on them, be, in respect of military or other matters — whether of property or personal contracts or suits — subject to the court and judgment of Our Secret Council of War Collegium; but We also subject to that same court and judgment all other foreigners who, having entered Our service, shall in any way be dependent on the military department, so that they too need not fear being subjected to a court not corresponding to their own countries' laws, customs, and mores; in such cases We permit that Our Secret Council of War Collegium administer justice, first according to Divine law, and then according to Roman civil law and other customary law of nations, mercifully, relying on the fact that in doing so Our Tsarist prerogatives, rights, and appurtenances shall always be observed. 4). And so that all those who enter into Our service may be assured that they will not be deprived of the freedom to leave Our service, We hereby assure them that upon discharge from Our service they will always be treated in the manner customary among other European Monarchs; with which all and everyone whom it concerns shall comply. Given in Our Capital, Moscow.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. IV. P. 192–195.*

## No. 4. CHARTER OF PETER I TO THE LIVONIAN NOBILITY (1710)

2301. — September 30. Charter to the nobility of the Principality of Livonia — confirming their former rights, and especially the privilege granted by the Polish King Sigismund Augustus at Vilna in 1561, concerning their noble rights, statutes, liberties, dignities, and lawful estates, both those in their possession and those which, though hereditary, had been unlawfully taken from them.

We, Peter the First, by the Grace of God Tsar and Emperor of All Russia,

and so forth, and so forth, and so forth.

We hereby declare that whereas Our noble Knighthood and Landed Gentry of the Principality of Livonia, together with that whole Province, by God's merciful governance and Our just and victorious arms, in accordance with the capitulation previously granted by Us, have surrendered to Us and become Our subjects, and have taken a solemn oath of allegiance to Us and to Our lawful Heirs, and thereafter, through Our dear and faithful Privy Councilor Baron von Löwenwolde, most submissively petitioned that We might graciously confirm and grant to them and their heirs all their ancient privileges acquired and held down to the present time, especially the privilege of Sigismund Augustus granted at Vilna in 1561, their knightly rights, statutes, liberties, and appurtenances, their rightful possessions, and both those properties presently held by them and those unlawfully taken from them. Wherefore, taking into most gracious consideration that the aforesaid Knighthood and Landed Gentry of the Principality of Livonia have always shown to their former Sovereigns, to their great benefit and to their own everlasting glory, zealous loyalty and good service, and have faithfully promised, by virtue of the aforesaid oath, likewise to render the same to Us and to Our lawful Heirs on every occasion, and always to uphold with honor the duty of faithful subjects, We have justly resolved, in response to their most humble and just petition, to grant, by Imperial favor, that the said Knighthood and Landed Gentry and their posterity might thereby be all the more encouraged to confirm their sworn subject loyalty with zealous good service, and, as the times may require, with their blood and their lives; and We hereby, to the said faithful Knighthood and Landed Gentry of Ours in Livonia and to their heirs, most graciously confirm and establish, for Ourself and for Our lawful Heirs, by this and by virtue hereof, all their previously acquired privileges, under which they have already submitted to Us, and especially the privilege of Sigismund Augustus granted at Vilna in 1561, [their] statutes, knightly rights, liberties, appurtenances (insofar as these are compatible with the present Government and time), rightful possessions and properties, both those which they actually hold and enjoy, and those to which they have claim from their ancestors by their rights and appurtenances; and We promise that they and their heirs, as is right and just, shall in all this be fully and continually maintained and protected; reserving, however, without prejudice or harm, Our own Sovereign right and that of Our States, and their Highness and rights, according to which all and every stipulation is likewise to be upheld; and We hereby expressly command Our high and low officials holding command in those places, and those who are bound to Us by obedience and oath, that they shall cause no hindrance or prejudice whatsoever to Our faithful Knighthood and Landed Gentry in Livonia contrary to their privileges, knightly rights, statutes, liberties, and appurtenances, nor permit any to be caused, but rather, wherever occasion may require, shall defend and protect them therein. This original document We have, for greater security and confirmation, signed with Our own hand, and have ordered it to be strengthened with Our Imperial seal.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. IV. P. 575–577.*

## No. 5. CHARTER OF PETER I TO THE ESTONIAN NOBILITY (1712)

2495. — March 1. Charter to the Gentry and Landed Gentry of the Principality of Estonia — confirming their ancient privileges, rights, and Statutes.

We, Peter the First, Tsar and Autocrat of All Russia,

and so forth, and so forth, and so forth.

We hereby declare and make known. Whereas Our faithful subjects, the whole Gentry and Landed Gentry of the Principality of Estonia, through their dispatched noble, steadfast, and courageous Landrats, Reinhold Baron von Ungern-Sternberg and Bengt Heinrich von Bystrom, have most submissively petitioned Us for the confirmation and establishment, in due allegiance, of their ancient privileges, rights, courts, justice, recesses, Statutes, and praiseworthy provincial customs, which they received from their respective authorities — namely, from King to King, from Hochmeister to Hochmeister, from Hermeister to Hermeister, and from Sovereign to Sovereign — and have freely exercised down to the present time, We, by Imperial grace and favor, did not wish to refuse them; and inasmuch as We are Ourself fully assured of their constant and most loyal fidelity to Us and to Our Imperial Heirs, We do hereby, and by virtue of this Our open charter, confirm to them the free and open exercise of the Evangelical faith, and together with it all their ancient privileges, as well as agreements, concessions, rights, courts, recesses, statutes, Christian provincial customs and usages, in which We wish to defend, protect, and maintain them against all, as they received and held them from King to King, from Hochmeister to Hochmeister, from Hermeister to Hermeister, and from Sovereign to Sovereign. We likewise most graciously promise them that they and their descendants shall always be maintained and preserved in all of this; and to that end We do hereby strictly command all Our high and low Commanders of places, and all those bound to Us by dutiful subjection and obedience, that they shall themselves cause no hindrance or prejudice to them in this regard, nor permit it to be caused by others, but shall rather, in cases of need, defend and maintain them therein. In confirmation whereof We have signed this with Our own hand and have ordered Our Imperial seal to be affixed hereunto.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. IV. P. 810.*

## No. 6. MANIFESTO OF PETER I ON PERMITTING FOREIGNERS TO ENGAGE IN MINING (1720)

3621. — July 30. Manifesto. — On admitting foreigners to the building and expansion of mining works.

Whereas in Our States and lands there now appear, ever more abundantly, favorable signs of ores and useful minerals, which, by God's blessing, give genuine hope of great profit. Therefore We have graciously deemed it fit not only to instill, through the Mining Privilege published on the 10th day of December, a true love and eagerness for mining works in Our faithful subjects, but also to admit, by this Our open charter, all foreign enthusiasts, of whatever nation they may be, to the use of the aforementioned privilege for mining affairs, and We do invite them, and, equally with Our natural-born subjects, We grant them leave to build mining works, to form new companies, to join those already established, paying a tithe from the profit and ceding to Us the first right of purchase, and [otherwise to have] free and secure disposition to use, as their own true acquisition, for their own benefit; moreover, We do especially assure such foreigners and mining enthusiasts of Our gracious protection; and for greater confirmation We have signed this with Our own hand, and have ordered it to be confirmed with Our State seal.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. VI. P. 223.*

## No. 7. DECREE OF PETER II ON THE ALLOCATION OF A SITE FOR AN EVANGELICAL CHURCH, SCHOOL, AND PASTOR'S HOUSE IN ST. PETERSBURG (1727)

5215. — December 26. Nominal decree, announced by Baron Osterman to State Councillor Poznyakov. — On the allocation, on the Admiralty side, of a site for the construction of an Evangelical church, school, and pastor's house.

We have ordered, upon the petition of the foreigners and parishioners of the German Evangelical parish located on Admiralty Island, that for the construction of a church for the conduct of services according to their faith, as well as a school and a pastor's house, a site be allocated on the Admiralty side along the great Perspective Road, behind the courtyards of Major-General Lefort and Admiral Sievers, leaving a street for passage, of whatever width and length as is proper; and as to whatever building they must erect on that site, a plan is to be obtained from them.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. VII. P. 908.*

## No. 8. DECREE OF EMPRESS ANNA IOANNOVNA ON THE ACCEPTANCE INTO RUSSIAN SERVICE OF ENGINEER-OFFICERS FROM PRUSSIA AND OTHER COUNTRIES (1731)

5865. — November 2. Nominal decree, given to the Senate. — On the acceptance of foreign Engineer-Officers from Prussian and other services by capitulation.

Whereas it is known to Us that, owing to the many postings of engineers to various places by Our decrees, a great shortage exists, We have therefore ordered Our General-Feldzeugmeister Count von Münnich, in order to remedy such shortage to some degree, at his discretion, until such time as We establish the establishment of the Artillery and Fortification, to accept foreign Engineer-Officers from Prussian and other services, and to conclude capitulations with them himself, as Our General-Feldzeugmeister; of which Our Senate is to take notice.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. VIII. P. 550-551.*

## No. 9. DECREE OF EMPRESS ELIZABETH PETROVNA ON THE OATH OF FOREIGNERS TO ALLEGIANCE TO RUSSIA (1747)

9434. — August 27. Senate decree. — On the oath of allegiance for foreigners wishing to swear perpetual allegiance to Russia.

In session, the Governing Senate, upon signing the composed oath concerning perpetual allegiance for foreigners, Ordered: that of this oath, having printed up to 500 copies in German and in Russian at the Academy of Sciences, copies be sent to the Military, Admiralty, and Foreign Collegiums, to the Governorates of Riga, Reval, and Vyborg, and to the Provinces of those Governorates along with the decrees; and that if foreign persons should wish to enter into perpetual allegiance to Her Imperial Majesty, they are to swear thereto according to this oath, and those of them who are found to have no knowledge whatsoever of the Russian language are to take the oath in their own language, and both that oath and the oath printed in Russian are to be signed, and of these one copy is to be kept in the places where the oath is administered, and the other sent to the Governing Senate.

Oath of allegiance.

I, the undersigned, formerly a subject [of another power], do promise and swear to Almighty God that I will be a faithful, good, and obedient servant and perpetual subject, together with my family, to the Most Illustrious, Most Mighty Great Sovereign, the Empress Elizabeth Petrovna, Autocrat of All Russia, etc., etc., etc., and to Her Imperial Majesty's high and lawful Heir, His Imperial Highness the Right-Believing Sovereign, Grand Duke Peter Fedorovich, who has been appointed by the will and autocratic power of Her Imperial Majesty, and to those hereafter to be appointed by Her Imperial Majesty's autocratic power and deemed worthy High Heirs to the succession of the Throne; and that I will not depart abroad anywhere without the Most High permission and decree of Her Imperial Majesty, nor enter into foreign service; nor will I have any harmful understanding with the enemies of Her Imperial Majesty, nor maintain any forbidden correspondence within or outside the Russian State, nor in any way act against the duty of a faithful subject of Her Imperial Majesty; and that I will, to the utmost of my understanding, strength, and ability, safeguard and defend all the rights and prerogatives (or advantages), now established by law and hereafter to be established by law, belonging to Her Imperial Majesty's High Autocracy, power, and authority, and will spare not even my life in this, should the need arise; and moreover I will endeavor to the utmost to further everything that may pertain, in any circumstance, to the faithful service of Her Imperial Majesty and the good of the State. And as to any harm to Her Majesty's interest, damage, or loss, as soon as I learn of it, I will not only report it in timely fashion but will strive by every means to avert and prevent it. And when, for the service and benefit of Her Majesty, some secret matter, of whatever nature it may be, shall be entrusted to me to be kept secret, I will keep it in complete secrecy and will disclose it to no one who ought not to know of it and to whom I am not instructed to disclose it; this I must and will faithfully uphold, so help me Almighty God in soul and body. And in conclusion of this my oath, I kiss the Words and the Cross of my Savior. Amen.

Eydes-Formul.

Ich Endesbenannter gelobe und schwöre zu dem Allmächtigen Gott, daß ich will der Allerdurchlauchtigsten Großmächtigsten Grossen Frau und Kayserin Elisabeth Petrowna Selbstherrscherin aller Reussen, ic. ic. ic., und Ihro Kayserl[ichen] Majestät hohen rechtmäßigen Erbfolger S[eine]r Kayserlichen Hoheit des rechtgläubigen Herrn und Groß-Fürsten Petro Feodorowitsch, welcher nach dem Willen und Souverainen Macht Ihro Kayserl[ichen] Majestät dazu verordnet worden, auch derer inskünftige von Ihro Kayserl[ichen] Majestät zu verordnenden und zur Besitzung des Trohns würdig erachteten hohen Nachfolgern, getreuer redlicher und gehorsamer Diener, und ewiger Unterthan nebst meiner Familie seyn, und ohne Ihro Kayserlfichen] Majestät Allerhöchste Erlaubniß und Befehl nirgendshin über die Gräntze mich begeben, und in keine fremde Dienste treten, imgleichen mit Ihro Kayserlfichen] Majestät Feinden kein Verständniß hegen, auch keine verbothene Correspondence weder inn, noch ausserhalb dem Rußischen Reiche führen, und auf keinerlei Weise wieder die Pflichten eines getreuen Unterthanen Ihro Kayserlfichen] Majestät handeln, vielmehr alle zu Ihro Kayserlichen Majestät hohen Souverainität Macht und Gewalt gehörige, bereits festgestellte, und künftig festzustellende, Gerechtsahme und Prärogativen, nach äusserstem Verstände Kräften und Vermögen in Acht nehmen und vertheydigen, auch in allem dem erfordernden Falls meines Lebens selbst nicht schonen, sondern dabey mir aufs höchste angelegen seyn lassen, alles zu befördern, was zu Ihro Kayserl[ichen] Majestät getreuen Dienst und Nutzen des Reichs bey allen Gelegenheiten gereichen kan; Schaden und Nachtheil, aber an Ihro Kayserl[ichen] Majestät Interesse, so bald ich dergleichen vermercken solte, nicht allein bey Zeiten entdecken, sondern auf alle Art zu hindern und abzuwehren suchen, desgleichen wann zum Dienst und Nutzen Ihro Kayserlfichen] Majestät mir eine geheime Sache, selbige bestehe worinn sie wolle, sollte anbefohlen werden geheim zu halten, so soll solche vollkommen Geheim halten, und niemanden dem es zu wissen nicht gebühret und kund zu machen nicht befohlen wird offenbahren. Dieses soll und will ich getreulich halten; so wahr mir der Allmächtige Gott an Seel und Leib helffe, zur Bekräftigung dieses meines Eydes, küsse ich das Wort und Creutz meines Heylandes. Amen.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XII. P. 748-749.*

## No. 10. DECREE OF PETER III ON CEMETERIES IN THE GERMAN QUARTER OF MOSCOW (1762)

11,568. — June 13. Nominal decree, announced to the Senate by Procurator-General Glebov. — On the existence, in the German Quarter of Moscow, of Catholic, Lutheran, and Reformed cemeteries at their former sites next to their churches.

His Imperial Majesty, our Most Gracious Sovereign, has been most graciously pleased, upon the petition of the Moscow Lutheran Pastor Minau, to order: that the Catholic, Lutheran, and Reformed cemeteries in the German Quarter of Moscow be built at their former sites next to their churches, and that the burial of the dead of those confessions in those cemeteries be permitted.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XV. P. 1039.*

## No. 11. MANIFESTO OF CATHERINE II INVITING FOREIGN COLONISTS TO SETTLE IN RUSSIA (1763)

11,880. — July 22. Manifesto. — On permitting all foreigners entering Russia to settle in whichever Governorates they wish, and on the rights granted to them.

We, being aware of the vastness of the lands of Our Empire, observe among other things a considerable number of places, most advantageous for the settlement and habitation of mankind and most useful, that still remain vacant, many of which conceal within their depths an inexhaustible wealth of various metals; and as there are forests, rivers, lakes, and seas suitable for commerce in sufficient abundance, there is likewise great capacity for the multiplication of many manufactories, factories, and other works. This gave Us cause to issue, for the benefit of all Our loyal subjects, a Manifesto on December 4 of last year, 1762; but as in that Manifesto We only briefly declared Our consent regarding those of foreign nations wishing to settle in Our Empire, in supplement thereto We command that the following regulation be announced to all, which We most solemnly establish and command to be carried out:

1. We permit all foreigners to enter Our Empire and settle wherever they wish, in all Our Governorates.

2. Such foreigners may come and present themselves not only at Our Residence, at the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners established for that purpose, but also in other border towns of Our Empire, wherever is more convenient for anyone, before the Governors, and where there are none, before the chief town officials.

3. Among the number of foreigners wishing to settle in Russia there will be some who do not have sufficient means for their journey; such persons may present themselves to Our Ministers and Residents at foreign Courts, by whom they will not only be sent to Russia immediately at Our expense, but will also be provided with travel money.

4. As soon as foreigners arrive at Our Residence and present themselves at the Chancellery of Guardianship, or at any other border town of Ours, they must declare their firm intention as to what their wish consists of — whether to enroll in the merchantry or in the guilds and become townspeople, and in which town, or to settle in colonies and small towns on free and advantageous lands for agriculture and other many advantages. All such persons will, according to their wishes, receive an immediate determination concerning themselves; and where, and in exactly which places in Our Empire, free lands suitable for settlement are to be found, may be seen from the following register — although there is an incomparably greater quantity of vast lands and all manner of amenities than the number declared, on which We likewise permit settlement, by whomever, wherever among them, chooses for their own benefit.

5. As soon as any foreigner arrives in Our Empire for settlement, and presents himself at the Chancellery of Guardianship established for them, or at Our other border towns, he must first, as prescribed above in point 4, declare his wish, and thereafter every such person must take, according to his faith and its rites, the customary oath of allegiance to Us in fidelity.

6. But so that all foreigners wishing to settle in Our Empire may see how great is Our benevolence for their benefit and advantage, We are pleased to grant: 1. To all who arrive in Our Empire for settlement, free exercise of their religion according to their own statutes and rites without hindrance; and to those wishing to settle, not in towns, but separately on vacant lands, in colonies and small towns, permission to build churches and belfries, having the requisite number of Pastors and other clergy, excepting only the building of monasteries; noting, however, that none of those living in Russia under Christian confessions shall, under any pretext, induce or draw anyone into agreement with their own faith or community, under pain of the full severity of Our laws — excepting from this those of various ranks living under the Mohammedan faith adjacent to the borders of Our Empire, whom We permit not only to be suitably induced into the Christian faiths, but also permit anyone to make into their own serfs. 2. Such persons arriving from among foreigners for settlement in Russia shall not be obliged to pay any taxes to Our treasury, nor to perform any ordinary or extraordinary services, nor to provide billeting, and, in a word, shall be free from all levies and burdens, as follows, namely: those settling with many families and entire colonies on vacant lands, for 30 years; and those wishing to reside in towns, likewise to enroll in guilds and the merchantry, in Our Residence of St. Petersburg, or in the nearby places of Livonia and Estonia, Ingria, Karelia, and the Finnish towns, as well as in the capital city of Moscow, for five years; in other Governorate, Provincial, and other towns, for ten years; but in addition, every person arriving in Russia not for temporary residence but for settlement shall be given free lodging for half a year. 3. To all foreigners arriving in Russia for settlement, every assistance and satisfaction will be given to those inclined to agriculture or any other handicraft, and to the establishment of manufactories, factories, and works — not only will a sufficient quantity of suitable and advantageous lands be allotted for this purpose, but every necessary assistance will be provided, according to the means of each, with particular attention to the need and benefit of newly established factories and works, especially those not yet established in Russia to this day. 4. For the building of houses, for the acquisition of various livestock for household management, and for the instruments, supplies, and materials necessary for agriculture and handicraft, the necessary sum of money will be issued from Our treasury without any interest, but with a single repayment, and that after the lapse of ten years, over three years in equal installments. 5. To those settling in separate colonies and small towns, We leave their internal jurisdiction to their own good governance, on the condition that Our authorities will have no part in their internal arrangements, but in other respects they are obliged to obey Our civil law. If, however, they should at some time wish to have from Us a special person for their guardianship, or for their safety and protection, until they become acquainted with the neighboring inhabitants, together with a well-disciplined military safeguard, this will be given to them. 6. To every foreigner wishing to settle in Russia, We permit the import of his property, of whatever it may consist, without payment of any duties whatsoever, provided, however, that it is for his own use and needs, and not for sale. And if such a person, beyond his own use, brings something in the way of goods for sale, We permit the duty-free import of no more than goods to the value of 300 rubles per family, provided they remain in Russia not less than 10 years; otherwise, upon their return journey, the current import and export duties are to be collected on those goods. 7. Foreigners settled in Russia shall not, for the whole time of their residence, be assigned against their will either to military or to civil service, except for the ordinary local [zemstvo] service, and that only after the lapse of the prescribed years of exemption; but should anyone wish of his own free will to enter military service as a soldier, such a person will be given, upon assignment to a regiment, 30 rubles as a reward, in addition to the ordinary pay. 8. Foreigners who present themselves at the Chancellery of Guardianship established for them, or at Our other border towns, as soon as they declare their wish to travel into the interior of Russia for settlement, shall be given both provision money and carts free of charge, as far as their intended destination. 9. Should any of the foreigners settled in Russia establish such factories, manufactories, or works, and begin to produce thereon goods of a kind not previously made in Russia, We permit the sale and export of such goods from Our Empire for 10 years without payment of any internal, port, or border duty. 10. And should any foreign capitalists, at their own expense, establish factories, manufactories, and works in Russia, We permit such persons to purchase the requisite number of serfs and peasants for those manufactories, factories, and works. 11. To foreigners settled in Our Empire in colonies or small towns, We permit the establishment, at their own good discretion, of markets and fairs, without any levy or payment of duties to Our treasury.

7. All the aforesaid advantages and provisions shall be enjoyed not only by those who come to Our Empire for settlement, but also by their surviving children and descendants, even should the latter be born in Russia, the number of years being counted from the day of their ancestors' arrival in Russia.

8. After the lapse of the aforesaid years of exemption, all foreigners settled in Russia shall be obliged to pay the ordinary taxes without any burden, and to perform local [zemstvo] services, as do Our other subjects.

9. Finally, should any of those who have settled and entered into Our allegiance among the foreigners wish to leave Our Empire, We always grant them freedom to do so, with this explanation, however, that they are obliged to render to Our treasury a portion of all the property lawfully acquired in Our Empire, namely: those living from one year up to five years, a fifth part; and those from five up to ten years and beyond, a tenth part; and thereafter to depart, wherever they wish, without hindrance.

10. Should some of the foreigners wishing to settle in Russia, for whatever particular reasons, require yet other conditions and privileges beyond those prescribed, they may address themselves, in writing or in person, to Our established Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners, from which a detailed report will be made to Us on all matters, and We will then, according to the circumstances presented, render a decision all the more favorable, such as they may hope for from Our sense of justice.

Register of free lands in Russia suitable for settlement.

1) In the Tobolsk [Siberian] Governorate, near Tobolsk, on the Baraba steppe, where there are several hundred thousand desyatinas of fertile land advantageous for settlement, with forests, rivers, and fisheries.

2) In the same Governorate, in the lands under the jurisdiction of the Ust-Kamenogorsk fortress, along the rivers Uba, Ulba, Berezovka, Glubokaya, and other streams flowing into them and into the Irtysh River, where there are likewise places very advantageous for settlement.

3) In the Astrakhan Governorate, upstream from Saratov along the Volga River:

At the Razdory tract, where the Karaman River divides into two branches, on the Telyauzika River, there is sufficient arable land, with 5,478 desyatinas of hayfields and 4,467 desyatinas of firewood forest and timber suitable for building houses.

At the Zaumorsky Rvoyka tract, 810 desyatinas of hayfields, 1,131 desyatinas of forest.

At the Tishanka stream, 469 desyatinas of hayfields, 496 desyatinas of forest.

At the Vertuban stream, 2,979 desyatinas of hayfields, 3,607 desyatinas of forest suitable for building.

At the Irgiz stream, 5,418 desyatinas of hayfields, 2,575 desyatinas of forest.

At the Sanzalei stream, 2,979 [1,789] desyatinas of hayfields, 1,711 desyatinas of forest.

At the Berezovka stream, 1,325 desyatinas of hayfields, 1,606 desyatinas of forest.

At the Small Irgiz stream, 731 desyatinas of hayfields, 712 desyatinas of forest. DOCUMENTS__________________________________________________________________________________ 27

Downstream from Saratov along the Volga River, below the Mukhar-Tarlyk stream, there is likewise sufficient arable land, with 6,366 desyatinas for hayfields, and 94[3] desyatinas of firewood forest and timber suitable for building. Beside the Bezymyannaya stream, 962 desyatinas of hayfields, 609 desyatinas of forest.

Along the Lesser Tarlyk stream, 3,509 desyatinas of hayfields, 840 desyatinas of forest.

At the Greater Tarlyk stream, 4,122 desyatinas of hayfields, 2,118 desyatinas of forest.

Between the Greater Tarlyk stream and the Kamyshёv ravine, 3,433 desyatinas of hayfields, 1,828 desyatinas of forest.

At the Kamyshёv ravine stream, 1,751 desyatinas of hayfields, 2,254 desyatinas of forest.

Along the Eruslan stream, 1,744 desyatinas of meadow land, 523 desyatinas of forest.

At the mouth of the Lower Eruslan stream, 1,770 desyatinas of hayfields, 1,104 desyatinas of forest.

At the Yablonny ravine stream, 4,003 desyatinas of hayfields and forest.

In total, such convenient and suitable places for settlement extend to more than 70,000 desyatinas.

4) In the Orenburg Governorate, along the Sakmara River, forty versts from Orenburg, and downstream along the Samara River, three hundred versts further to the Kanel River, and below the town of Samara, along the Volga River to the mouth of the Irgiz stream, and upstream along the Irgiz, there are very fertile and advantageous lands for the settlement of several thousand families.

5) In the Belgorod Governorate, in Valuysky district, along the streams Zhuravka, Derkul, Bitka, and Oskol, for several hundred households, there are likewise free lands with a sufficient number of hay meadows, which may likewise be very suitable for new settlers.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XVI. P. 313-316.*

## No. 12. DECREE OF CATHERINE II PERMITTING MEMBERS OF THE HERRNHUT RELIGIOUS SOCIETY TO SETTLE IN RUSSIA (1764)

12.057. — February 25. (*) Nominal decree given to the Senate. — On permitting the society of the brotherhood of the Evangelical Augsburg confession to depart and settle in Russia.

(*) Announced from the Senate on March 10.

By Our manifesto promulgated on July 22 of the past year 1763, on permitting foreign peoples to enter into Our subjecthood and settle on lands within Our Empire, the society of the brotherhood of the Evangelical Augsburg confession desired to avail itself of that same Highest favor of Ours, and their general directorate sent to Us the deputies Paul Layritz and Johann Lorenz to petition Us most submissively on that matter. We, in view of the vastness of Our abundant lands and their fertility, and still more out of Our natural hospitality, did not wish to decline the petition of these brethren united among themselves into a society; but rather to show them the same benefaction which the other foreign peoples freely coming to Us enjoy, and who dwell under Our scepter in Our Empire and Our lands, just as is set forth in Our manifesto; wherefore We ordered Our Synod to examine, in accordance with their wish, the principal foundations of the rules and teaching of their Church; and it was reported to Us by the Synod that the teaching of this society resembles the Lutheran, and still more the Reformed, with only a small difference, and is called the Evangelical society: therefore hereby We most graciously permit it, as We do other people of the Christian faith, to enter into Our subjecthood and settle in Our Empire, with such privileges and freedoms as We have publicly declared in Our aforementioned manifesto, permitting them, according to their teaching and conscience, to practice their faith and creed, as they have set it forth to Our Synod, without hindrance. We command the Senate (*), however, that should any member of the brethren of this society happen to appear in court, whether on their own affairs or under Our civil laws, an oath from them is to be accepted in all Our courts as valid in the form which, according to their creed, consists solely of an oral affirmation on their part; on the other hand, as to fidelity to Us in their subjecthood, they must swear in the same manner as all Our subject peoples swear according to the custom adopted in Our Empire. (**)

(*) In the privilege granted to this Society, instead of the words "We command the Senate, however," it is written: "moreover."

(**) The privilege granted to this Society and forwarded to the Senate on February 11, 1764 for due execution, contains, besides what is set forth in the decree of February 25, the following addition: moreover, should the families of this society, upon coming to settle in Our Empire, most submissively request other conditions and privileges from Us, We promise to render a decision the more favorably disposed to them according to the circumstances of their needs, the more each of them may hope for from Our love of justice. And in this manner the entire brotherhood of this society, however many have now newly settled and shall in future settle throughout Our whole Empire, shall remain under Our Imperial protection and patronage.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XVI. Pp. 547-548.*

## No. 13. REPORT OF THE SENATE ON THE COMMUNICATION OF G.G. ORLOV CONCERNING THE ORGANIZATION OF GERMAN COLONIES IN THE VOLGA REGION, CONFIRMED BY CATHERINE II (1764)

12.095. — March 19. Highest confirmed report of the Senate. — On the surveying of lands designated for the settlement of departing foreigners.

Report. Your Imperial Majesty's Lieutenant General and President of the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners, Count Orlov, submitted to the Senate a communication presenting his opinion: 1. Which places are now recognized as the best and most useful for the settlement of departing foreigners, and by what districts a detailed description and survey of those places should be made through specially dispatched agents. 2. How much arable land and other amenities should be measured out to each family of those emigrants, and on what basis that land should be granted to them in possession. 3. In what manner to establish the law of inheritance for these plots of land distributed to each family, and on the composition of various regulations to which those who have now emigrated or shall in future emigrate may agree, or which may be accepted as proposed by them. 4. How much, after such allotment of DOCUMENTS__________________________________________________________________________________ 29

arable land and other amenities to each family, should be left at each colony in villages and hamlets as vacant homestead plots for craftsmen and for the future-multiplying inhabitants of that same settlement, and that fairs and markets, permitted under the manifesto, should be held only in the principal settlements of each district. 5. What number of surveyors and geodesists should be involved in this matter, as well as clerical officials and a military detachment with full equipment, and, for the performance of labor, from invalids or garrison soldiers. 6. From where all these ranks should be recruited and what salary should be paid to them and to the rank-and-file serving with them, and from what sources it should be disbursed, and on the selection of overseers of the surveyors according to competence, who shall at the same time see to the procurement of materials, and shall for a certain time serve as guardians of the foreigners, and on the payment to them for their labors of salary according to their ranks, on a par with full cavalry pay.
