The Senate, having duly considered the foregoing, most submissively reports to Your Imperial Majesty: that inasmuch as all the arrangements set forth in the communication of his Excellency Lieutenant General Count Orlov are chiefly directed toward the benefit which the increase of the influx of foreign peoples into Russia will bring to the State, and this cannot otherwise be achieved except by following the advantages permitted by Your Imperial Majesty's Highest manifesto, to make now a proper beginning for those who have already actually come here to settle, and to establish for them such regulations as, being generally known, might serve to arouse in others a greater inclination to emigrate to Russia and to settle therein — for which purpose the Senate recognizes the arrangements presented by the Lieutenant General as sufficient and useful, and therefore most submissively reports them herewith in the original for the Highest confirmation of Your Imperial Majesty.

In consequence thereof, having selected the surveyors and geodesists needed for the description of those places and the making of plans thereof, the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners is to report to the Senate, whereupon they, with the necessary instruments and on such basis as is set forth in the presentation, shall be immediately appointed, and clerical officials shall likewise be assigned in the same manner.

Overseers of the surveyors, who shall at the same time see to the procurement of materials and shall for a certain time serve as guardians of the foreigners, are likewise to be selected by the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners at its own discretion and reported to the Senate; for guard duty and errands, a military detachment with full equipment, when requested by the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners, is to be detailed by the Military Collegium from the regular and irregular troops stationed near those places where the surveying is to take place, and likewise, for the performance of labor, the prescribed number of soldiers is to be furnished from the garrisons nearest to those same places.

Most Gracious Sovereign! The Senate, most submissively presenting this, requests Your Imperial Majesty's Highest decree.

Resolution. Let it be according to the presentations herewith attached by Count Orlov.

Communication. In the instruction given to the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners, signed by Her Imperial Majesty's own hand, it is, among other things, commanded in the points: in the 2nd, that departing foreigners are to be persuaded, without compulsion, to settle on vacant lands; in the 6th, that those wishing to settle in separate colonies or small towns are to be allotted the requisite quantity of lands and amenities according to the number of their families; for which purpose it is, of course, necessary to have accurate plans, with a description, if not of all the lands suitable for settlement, then at least of those which are listed in the register attached to the Manifesto of July 22. But in what manner exactly this surveying is to be carried out, how much arable land and other amenities are to be given to each emigrant foreigner, and with what provision regarding inheritance that land is to be granted to them in possession — on this, neither the instruction nor the Manifesto gives a detailed account. The vacant lands shown in the register attached to that Manifesto lie in various Governorates, at a distance one from another, and whether all of them are suitable for settlement, especially for the initial emigrants, who must serve to arouse inclination in others, is unknown; moreover, many of the localities in which those lands are recorded are not marked on the map, and consequently there is good reason to doubt the number of desiatinas as well. As for persuading people to settle on vacant lands, I find no other means than to present to them all the advantages which those places chosen for settlement possess by virtue of their situation, both as to the quality of the land and as to the suitability for commerce, for the Chancellery cannot promise any privileges beyond the Manifesto, save for some vague assurance, itself still unknown even to the Chancellery, which it is now compelled to make haphazardly regarding the vacant lands, for want of accurate plans and a detailed description. In view of these circumstances, in order to establish a single order in this matter, I submit the following to the Governing Senate for consideration.

1) It is known that in the Russian Empire there are very many places suitable for settlement, both in vast steppes entirely remote from habitation, and likewise not a few such are to be found near old settlements as well, and I consider the latter to be the best and most useful for settlement at present, both for the convenience of transporting all sorts of materials and provisions, of finding laborers and other necessities, and for the safety of the colonists, quicker acquaintance with neighbors, and more convenient internal commerce. But in order that, in accordance with the Manifesto, it might be possible to present to the emigrating foreigners, with exact accuracy, the advantages of various places for their choice, and moreover that these settlements might expand according to a known plan, and not haphazardly, I select for this purpose the following district, namely: beginning from Cherdyn Island to Tsaritsyn, from Tsaritsyn to the small fortress of Don and further to the Bezymyannaya River, which flows into the Don, then to the Medveditsa River and further to the Khoper, and from the Khoper up the Don to the Bityug River, and up that river to its very source, and from the source to Novokhopersk, and from there up along the Khoper to the villages of Znamenskoye and Dolgorukovo; and then along the lands of Penza Province to Saratov District and through it along small rivers to the Bezymyannaya River, which flows into the Volga opposite Gordymsky Island, and down that river to the aforementioned island, which can be seen more clearly, marked in yellow, on the sample plan attached hereto under No. 1. And when it is ordered that special agents be sent, they, having gone around this district according to instructions, from various places, shall be able to inquire in detail both about the situation of those places and about other circumstances necessary to be known, according to the instructions given to them by the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners.

Explanation: This location, beyond the aforementioned conveniences, seems very advantageous also for the following reasons: 1. That when the number of colonists increases (as is desired), there will be no danger whatsoever from any harmful undertakings, because they will be enclosed on almost all sides by old settlements; DOCUMENTS___________________________________________________________________________________31

2. Should circumstances in future require some new arrangement to be made, this same location will considerably assist in that; 3. And finally, when settlements are established in several places within this district, then all such colonies, although settled in different places, yet not very far from one another, may the more conveniently establish trade among themselves, and thereby, in keeping with their intention, Russia will no longer appear as strange and wild as it has hitherto, and the entrenched prejudice against her will imperceptibly vanish.

2) When the specially dispatched agents, having inquired as much as possible into the situation and other circumstances of the places suitable for settlement located within this district, adjacent to inhabited lands, send in detailed reports with descriptions, according to which, for example, let the beginning of those lands be as shown on plan No. 2, under the lines marked with the letters A, A, A, with inhabited places marked with the sign Z; then in the following spring it will be possible, on the basis of that information, to send surveyors to make plans, carrying this out by districts, as marked by the lines B, B, B; and these districts should be occupied first near the inhabited places, extending afterward toward the centers Q. Should it also be necessary to establish settlements in other places, the occupation of districts is to be carried out on the same basis.

3) For the establishment of order in the occupation of districts, both in view of their extent and for the arrangement therein of dwellings of every kind and the allotment, according to the number of people, of arable land and other amenities, I consider it necessary to determine a fixed number of desiatinas for each family, in the following manner, namely: to give to each family, in accordance with Article 1 of Chapter 23 of the Surveying Instruction, in parity with odnodvortsy (of whom each household is counted at approximately four male souls) regardless of how many persons it may actually consist of, a total of 30 desiatinas, allotting 15 desiatinas for arable land, 5 for hay meadows, 5 for forest land, and of the remaining 5 desiatinas for homestead, threshing-floor, and garden land, 1½ desiatinas seems sufficient, for in other respects the settlements will be quite spacious; and the last 3½ desiatinas are to be measured out for pasture, marked separately for each family, which, should the inhabitants agree to graze their livestock on the fields, each peasant may use at his own discretion for arable land, hay meadows, or leave as forest land. Thus, according to this or another established arrangement, once a plan has been made for each district, it will not be difficult to know how many families may be settled therein, and in which places dwellings may most conveniently be located.

Explanation: I propose this equality in the allotment of plots to each family, rather than by the number of persons, for the following reasons: 1. In order thereby to remove any cause for quarrels, for when each family possesses an equal share, there can arise no confusion or disputes whatsoever, either in arable land or in other amenities; and even should a dispute occasionally arise, then, given the equal shares, each peasant may settle and measure it out himself, without a surveyor, for each will be given a plan with a detailed description; whereas, on the contrary, if the allotment were made according to the number of persons, then in view of the increases and decreases that may occur in their numbers, there would have to be a constant change in the division of land, from which confusion and disputes over land would inevitably always arise. 2. Should the inequality of families be taken into consideration, I answer to this that an excess of children or relatives already capable of working can be neither harmful nor unprofitable to that householder, because in such a case not only will his fieldwork proceed with greater success, but this very fact will serve as an incentive to all manner of handicrafts and trades, or at the very least such a surplus laborer in the family may work for another, less populous family for money, and thus easily find sustenance for himself; and therefore every married man should be regarded as a householder, even should he have no children. 3. For the anticipated increase of such settlements, it is necessary so to arrange the places chosen within the surveyed districts as suitable for settlement, that a certain portion, both of arable land and of other amenities, be left vacant for the future children of the settlers of that village, so that when they come of age and marry, they themselves may become householders. Wherefore even to those who have now come to settle unmarried, plots should not be given in exactly the same full possession, for the reason that an unmarried man cannot be a proper peasant, except for those who, being not younger than 25 years of age, are not accepted into any family; in which case it is indeed necessary to allot land to such a one individually and to build him a household, but on the condition that he must certainly marry within a year. 4. Should any settlement increase so greatly that the plots left aside for this purpose are insufficient, and the people are unwilling to move to another colony, then such persons may reside in their former places and support themselves by handicrafts and trades; for which reason it is necessary to leave, at every settlement, a certain number of homestead and garden plots alone.

4) Once this or some other quantity of land has been ordered to be given to each family, it will also be necessary to prescribe a law of inheritance, explaining at the same time under what conditions these plots shall be granted in possession, which in my opinion may be done as follows, namely: 1. To establish by law that the younger sons shall be the heirs, in consideration that every father, knowing this law, will be compelled to see to it that his children, from their very childhood, are taught various handicrafts. 2. Should his younger son, on account of his youth or some incapacity, be unable to manage that plot with due success, then not only will all the other persons of that family thereby be impoverished, but the very settlement in which such orphaned households multiply will fall into decline. In such a case, it must without fail be left to the father's discretion to choose, from among his elder sons or relatives, whom he shall appoint as heir or guardian and confirm this in writing; and should he fail to do so during his lifetime, then the government of that district in which this settlement is located is obliged to choose, from among the elder brothers or relatives, a guardian for the duration of the heir's minority (which lasts until the age of 20), who must afterward render an account of everything, and as a reward for good stewardship shall receive one fourth part of the movable property acquired by him during his administration of that household; and should the heir prove entirely incapable of managing it, then that plot shall be given, from among the nearest relatives, to those who possess no plots of their own. And should there be several persons having equal right, it is to be given by lot. Should brothers or relatives themselves agree to live in one household, this is not to be forbidden, provided only that one of them be reputed the head of that household, and not all of them. 3. As for movable property, this is to be left entirely to the will of the parents, and should no will be left before death, it is to be divided in equal shares among the brothers, leaving one fourth part to the mother as her own inheritance, notwithstanding that the children are obliged to support and feed her until her death, and the same share is to be left to all the daughters as dowry, to be divided among them in equal shares. Until marriage, the female offspring remain with the heir of the land, unless they choose of their own accord to leave. 4. Should there remain only a wife with daughters, they shall together hold that plot in common until such time as the mother herself remarries, or gives one of her daughters in marriage, and the first man who enters such a household by marriage shall have the right to hold that plot forever, but on the agreement that he keep his wife's stepdaughters and sisters in that household and feed them until they marry, or voluntarily leave, and moreover he is obliged to see, to the best of his ability, to their welfare, and to support his mother-in-law until her death, concerning which they must, before the marriage, conclude written agreements witnessed by the Pastor and their Elders. As for the rest, whatever arrangement regarding the inheritance of plots may be made, neither the householders themselves to whom the grant is made, nor their heirs, shall have the power to sell or mortgage those plots of theirs, nor to divide them into fractional parts, but they shall remain undivided in the possession of the inhabitants of that village, so that the lands of these new settlements may never, under any pretext whatsoever, fall into outside hands. 5. As for other land grants, such as for the building of churches, factories, works, vineyards, and the like, it is not possible to know and determine this in advance, but it can be done when the need arises, according to necessity and circumstances, or by agreements; only such lands are to be granted in possession on exactly the same basis as set forth above. Should it also be ordered that clergy be allotted arable land with amenities equal to several such peasant plots, then that land, being church land, is to be set apart separately from the peasants', to be held by the clergy of that colony in common, dividing it among themselves in strips according to their rank or in proportion to their salaries and income, and upon death their children shall not inherit these plots, but they are to be given over to their successors, and until there are such successors, the surviving wives and children may be permitted to make use of that land. Should others arrive to replace deceased clergy, then even in that case the orphaned family is not to be compelled to leave that settlement, but a small house is to be built for them at the expense of the parishioners, on the church homestead land, for which purpose two desiatinas are to be set aside specifically; and should they, on account of poverty and their children's youth, have no means of sustenance, then in such a case they are to be supported jointly by all the parishioners, at their discretion, until the children reach the age of 15, and the elderly until their death. 6. All other amenities, such as rivers, lakes, clay and sandy places, lime, and the like, are to be given over to the common possession of the entire village or hamlet, and fishing is to be permitted only in those rivers and lakes which lie within their boundaries, while those lying on the borders are to be shared equally; and where precious metals occur, such places are excluded from the grants, while swamps that can be reclaimed only with difficulty are to be given into common possession; for somewhat wet and low-lying places, for want of hay meadows, may be assigned to meadows, and those on which forest grows may be assigned to forest land. Should a swamp be recorded as an amenity of a village, and some of the inhabitants wish to drain it by ditches, or only a portion of it, then this may be done with the knowledge and permission of the entire colony, and whatever portion of it they render usable shall remain forever as the reward for their labor, and those who labored shall receive it in equal shares, or according to the number of those who worked. But should the other inhabitants neither wish to labor themselves, nor, out of obstinacy, permit others to do so; in such a case, the Chief Government over them may, at its own discretion, grant permission to those who request it, according to the circumstances. Should there remain, in any village or hamlet, several plots vacant without owners, then that colony to which those plots belong may make joint use only of the hay meadows, but shall not cut timber nor plow the arable land, under penalty. Fishing in rivers and lakes located in as-yet-uninhabited places may be freely enjoyed, while hunting is left to the colonists' own discretion. 7. Although, under the Manifesto, internal jurisdiction has been left to their own will, yet on condition that in all else they obey the general Civil law; consequently it is necessary first to know what regulations the foreigners emigrating to settle will establish among themselves, and whether these are not contrary to the principal intention, or on what basis the foreigners will agree to accept them from the Government; for without this, most prejudicial consequences to the State's benefit could easily arise from such arbitrary establishments, and finally, from the diversity of arrangements in each colony there would follow perpetual confusion and disagreement; and thus, instead of encouraging others to emigrate to Russia, this would cause the utmost aversion. Wherefore, in my opinion, it is necessary to compose in good time several different regulations, taking various circumstances into consideration, and whichever of these those who have now emigrated, or shall in future emigrate, agree to, or whichever proposed by them may be accepted, these, once confirmed in writing, are to be made the permanent law of that colony and of all the settlers of one district, and as to the observance of this law, each person, upon taking possession of the land, is to be bound by a signed undertaking; and before the final conclusion of agreements concerning internal jurisdiction, the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners is to submit them for approval to the Governing Senate by way of communications.

5) Once arable land and other amenities have thus been apportioned to each family, allotting the proportion, it is to be left at each colony, in villages, a sixth part of vacant homestead plots, relative to the total number of all peasant households, for craftsmen, and the same proportion, with arable land and other amenities, for the future-multiplying inhabitants of that same settlement; while in hamlets, homestead plots for craftsmen are to be left at half the proportion relative to villages, because there is not as much need for them there as there may be in villages, or in the main small towns. Fairs and markets, permitted under the Manifesto, are to be held only in the principal settlements of each district. Thus it will be possible to occupy, without significant error, such districts in which as many families may be settled as shall be deemed advisable, or as circumstances require, for example, should it be decided that up to 1,000 families in total might be settled in each district, then for such a number 30,000 desiatinas of suitable land would be required, not counting swamps, bogs, sands, and other places unfit for plowing and hay meadows, which I estimate at approximately a third part relative to good land, making 40,000 desiatinas. And so, if the districts are occupied in the shape of a circle, care should be taken that its circumference extend not less than 60 and not more than 70 versts.

Explanation: I propose occupying by districts for the following reasons: 1. In order thereby to establish a single order in the making of plans, and so that the surveyors, being at such a great distance, might carry out their work without interruption, without requiring further instruction. 2. By districts it will be possible in future, as the settlers increase in number, more conveniently to make whatever arrangement the circumstances may require; and in view of the diversity of different faiths, by settling people of each religion in a separate district, thereby to avert all enmity and hatred, which usually occur between persons of different faiths from excessive religious zeal. 3. Moreover, by districts it is more convenient to arrange settlements of every kind, and to establish such an equalization in amenities that no vacant space remains in them, and that all the settlements of one district, in respect of amenities, may have mutual need of one another; moreover, it will be known without the slightest error how many families, and with what purpose, may be settled where. And should this proposal be approved, then the surveyors, both in the conduct of the surveying business and in the taking of allotments and the establishment of boundary markers, shall be given detailed instructions by the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners; and on the plan attached hereto under No. 3 is shown, for illustration only, how households are to be arranged, arable land divided, pasture land allotted, and hay meadows with forest amenities measured out, in those places where households cannot be built in such a way that field land with amenities can be allotted contiguously to each.

<...> For the rest, I do not regard these proposals of mine as an irrefutable rule; but my intention was only, having gathered as many as possible of the circumstances that seemed to me suitable and necessary for this arrangement, to request from the Governing Senate Her Imperial Majesty's decree, which I await.

(The three plans mentioned in this report may be seen in the book of drawings and diagrams.)

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XVI. Pp. 648-655.*

Published in: German Colonists in the Age of Catherine / Comp.: E.E. Lykova, M.I. Osekina. Moscow, 2004. Pp. 37-55.

## No. 14. REPORT OF G.G. ORLOV ON EXPENSES FOR TRANSPORTING COLONISTS TO THE VOLGA REGION, ALLOTTING LAND TO THEM, AND PRIVILEGES FOR THEIR RECRUITING AGENTS, APPROVED BY CATHERINE II (1764)

12,109. — March 28. Most Highly approved report of the President of the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners, Count Orlov. — On allotting land for grain farming between Saratov and Astrakhan to the foreigners Ludwig Beneteau and Docourt and their associates.

Report. Some time before this, the foreigners Ludwig Beneteau and Docourt of Bellefort, arriving with two associates, represented to the said Chancellery that they wish to recruit various foreign people for settlement in Russia, both grain farmers and various craftsmen, and they ask that land be allotted to them between Saratov and Astrakhan for the settlement of these foreigners, the same allotment per family as is prescribed for others, while to themselves personally there be granted, in hereditary possession, three times that amount each, and in addition 4,000 rubles each, 12,000 rubles in total, as a loan for ten years without interest, from which sum is to be issued, for distribution to the colonists, travel expenses from their former place of residence to the harbor at which arrangements will be made to gather them and, putting them aboard seagoing vessels, send them to St. Petersburg — to the one of them sent to The Hague and Paris, as much as need may require from time to time — and for travel expenses, to the one of them traveling, over a six-month period, 6 rubles a day without repayment, such payment to be made from one place to another. Once all the people are gathered in Saratov, should no fewer than one hundred families appear, wooden houses are to be built for each of them at the Treasury's expense, in reward for their efforts, without charging money for them, each house having four rooms and one kitchen, with stables attached thereto, each stable for four horses, with sheds and cellars — which requirements, apart from the building of the houses and the travel money due at 6 rubles a day, would not, it is considered, cause the Treasury any further loss, provided they achieve the desired success in their undertaking; however, without a Most High decree of Your Imperial Majesty, the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners cannot carry out all of this on its own.

For which reason I most humbly report this to Your Imperial Majesty, and I await Your Imperial Majesty's Most High decree as to whether it be ordered that these requests be fulfilled now, and that the same practice be followed in future in similar cases.

Resolution. Let it be so.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XVI. Pp. 682-683.*

## No. 15. FORM OF CONTRACTS WITH RECRUITING AGENTS OF COLONISTS, APPROVED BY CATHERINE II (1764)

12,283. — November 17. Most Highly approved form according to which contracts are to be concluded with agents for the recruitment of foreigners for settlement in Russia.

Report. The foreigner Bene Paul Dacourt, together with two of his associates, was the first of all to submit to the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners a project for recruiting colonists to Russia; after many negotiations with them the Chancellery finally induced them to accept more moderate conditions than they had originally demanded, which conditions Your Imperial Majesty, upon the most humble report submitted by me on March 1 of this year, was Most Highly pleased to approve, with the following order: that in future the same practice be followed with any volunteers who might come forward; and although, owing to the said Dacourt's failure to provide the sureties for money previously required by the Chancellery, no contract was concluded with him, nevertheless, pursuant to Your Imperial Majesty's Most High confirmation, copies of that report were at that time sent, through the Foreign Collegium, to all Russian Ministers residing at European Courts, with instructions that they too should deal with such volunteers in the same manner; but since in my aforementioned most humble report I mentioned only very briefly those advantages requested by the recruiting agents which the Chancellery could not on its own promise them, while all other particulars pertaining thereto were passed over in silence, it came about that Your Imperial Majesty's Plenipotentiary Minister at the French Court, Prince Golitsyn, concluded with the Frenchmen Jean Debofe, Quentin, Benjamin, Coulnet, Dauterive, and Menier Deprecourt a contract that differs considerably from the actual arrangement on the main points; namely: instead of taking 100 families as the basis and promising, for the transport of these, loan money for the recruiting agents' own household-building jointly amounting to 4,000 rubles along with the building of one house at Treasury expense, it was promised to each of them the same amount for merely one group of 100 families, not to mention other irregularities of lesser importance; and although in fact no loss whatsoever to Your Imperial Majesty's interests resulted from this contract, because the said recruiting agents, upon having the matter explained to them by the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners strictly according to the terms of the aforementioned report, not only agreed to it, but, following the same explanation, voluntarily settled accounts with the Chancellery for the people they had already brought, both as to loan money and travel money, and annulled the contract concluded with Prince Golitsyn — nevertheless, in order to avoid similar confusion in future, and especially needless expenditures, I have deemed it necessary to establish a single procedure in this matter; wherefore, enclosing herewith a detailed form drawn up for such contracts, for Your Imperial Majesty's Most High approval, I await a Most Gracious decree.

Form of contract with recruiting agents, which is to be concluded on the basis that all promises made to them and all monetary payments shall be calculated according to the number of people being recruited for settlement, not according to the number of recruiting agents.

1. To allot to them, at the discretion of the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners, a suitable place for settlement from among uninhabited lands, and to give, for each family, the same fixed amount of land as is given to foreigners who emigrate on their own account, which land the recruiting agents may divide among the settlers they have recruited as they see fit.

2. Should several families of their settlers drop out for any reason, they are on no account to lure away or accept, for the vacated place, people who have not settled on their own account in other locations, nor those who have already presented themselves to Russian Ministers on their own and received advance payments, but must fill their colony with newly recruited people, in which case they are to demand nothing beyond travel and subsistence money calculated per the number of such people; and if within two years no new settlers are recruited for such vacated places, then land in an amount corresponding to the number of families that dropped out shall be taken back from them; while into their own possession shall be given, for every 100 families of recruited foreigners, three of the allotments prescribed per family, except that this land may not be sold, mortgaged, or exchanged by either the recruiting agents or the settlers.

3. A family is understood to consist of a husband and wife with children, of whom males are under 20 and females under 18 years of age; unmarried persons are counted as follows: two males not younger than the ages stated above, or four females not younger than 18, to constitute one family.

4. Should they have, apart from the colonists, their own laborers who are likewise foreigners, for whom they request land, then land shall be given for each family of such laborers on the same basis as for colonists, on condition that these laborers too shall be considered settlers; but if no vacant land is found nearby, then in such case the recruiting agent may make use of their labor on the land previously allotted to him.

5. Such contracts are to specify explicitly whether these volunteers have undertaken to recruit people at their own expense, or whether money has been advanced to them beforehand against reliable surety or sufficient collateral, and if so, how much; in the first case the sureties are to be informed that they cannot be released from their suretyship until authorized to do so by the Chancellery of Trusteeship, and in the second case the recruiting agents themselves are to be informed that their collateral will not be returned to them until such authorization is given; and should a recruiting agent die before fulfilling his undertaking, or fail to fulfill his obligation owing to some other impediment, then in the first case the surety must repay the money issued from the Treasury together with interest, and in the second case such money, together with interest, shall be taken from the collateral deposited.

6. The recruited people are to be brought to Hamburg or to Lübeck, where, in the former place the Envoy, and in the latter the appointed Commissioner, upon receiving these people, shall dispatch them to St. Petersburg; the said Envoy and Commissioner are to reimburse the recruiting agents or their attorneys, against the colonists' receipts, for the money they have spent on transporting the colonists, but no more than 40 rubles per family, plus, without repayment, 1,000 rubles for provisions for every 100 families, collecting receipts from the recruiting agents for this and issuing them acknowledgments in return, and these receipts, together with the colonists' receipts, are to be forwarded to the Chancellery of Trusteeship; upon the dispatch of the colonists from Hamburg or Lübeck, the said Envoy and Commissioner are to give the recruiting agents or their attorneys money for the maintenance of these people and for their transport, calculating the time they must spend en route according to the prevailing local prices of provisions, without excess, as well as freight money, for which the recruiting agents or their attorneys must, upon arrival in St. Petersburg, submit detailed accounts under their own signatures together with the colonists' receipts; and if the recruiting agents spend more than 40 rubles per family transporting their people to Hamburg, then, once they have established their households, they must themselves collect this money at the place of settlement from the colonists they have recruited, but without imposing hardship, in accordance with special contracts concluded with the colonists, which must be shown, before the contract is concluded, to the Ministers negotiating with them for approval; and upon arrival in St. Petersburg they must be submitted to the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners, where they shall be confirmed and kept on file, and a signed copy shall be given to them; and thus, if they wish to continue their business further, they must request permission to do so from the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners; for the first instance, they are to send their own attorneys along with those who proceed to the place of settlement; but if they no longer wish to recruit people and come to establish their colony on the allotted place of settlement mentioned above, then:

7. Once all the people have been gathered, the recruiting agents shall be given, for their own household-building, for every 100 families, 4,000 rubles as a loan for ten years without interest, to be repaid after that time in three installments as prescribed by manifesto; and, in addition, in reward for their labors, they shall be given, for house-building, for every hundred families, 350 rubles without any charge; and if the number of people recruited is more or fewer than one hundred families, then both the money for house-building and the land to be given into their own possession shall be proportioned accordingly to the number of people;

8. All colonists must in everything abide by the special contracts they conclude with the recruiting agents, in which, among other things, the following must be strictly observed, namely: 1) that the recruiting agents shall promise the colonists nothing contrary to Russian law and nothing beyond what is published in the manifesto on the settlement of foreigners; 2) that it be included therein that the colonists shall have no freedom to leave until all Treasury money spent on them has been repaid to the Treasury; 3) that in all matters they must abide by the laws in force and to be enacted in future in Russia; but as regards the recruiting agents' own income and other mutual obligations between them, they may agree upon these as they wish. DOCUMENTS___________________________________________________________________________________ 39

9. The recruiting agents are permitted to sell, duty-free, for a fixed [term of] 10 years, goods and any supplies prepared by the colonists, other than purchased goods.

10. They may freely make use, on their allotted lands, of hunting and fishing grounds that are not subject to quitrent or lease, and may manage forests and other lands as they see fit, except that, in order to verify that such management is consistent with State laws and the common good, they must submit it for the approval of the Chancellery of Trusteeship.

11. Should there be more than one recruiting agent jointly entering into the contract, then, to avoid any inconvenience, they must have full written powers of attorney from one another for receiving money and settling expenses, so that the Russian Ministers or the Chancellery of Trusteeship negotiating with them may resolve any matter with each of them individually just as with all of them collectively.

12. In conclusion of all this, the recruiting agents undertake to fulfill their contracts in every respect exactly according to this agreement, without contriving any pretexts or various interpretations; and the Chancellery, for its part, likewise undertakes to fulfill its promises unfailingly.

Resolution. Let it be so.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XVI. Pp. 965-968.*

Published in: German Colonists in the Age of Catherine / Comp.: E.E. Lykova, M.I. Osekina. Moscow, 2004. Pp. 65-72.

## No. 16. REPORT OF G.G. ORLOV ON THE ORGANIZATION OF CHURCHES FOR THE COLONISTS, APPROVED BY CATHERINE II (1765)

12,322. — January 31. Most Highly approved report of the President of the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners. — On the building of Lutheran and Catholic churches on vacant lands, in districts being settled by colonies; on the appointment of pastors to these churches and their maintenance.

Report. By Your Imperial Majesty's Most High Manifesto concerning foreigners, although, under point six of Article 1, those who have arrived in Russia and wish to settle not in towns but in separate colonies and settlements on vacant lands are permitted to build churches and bell towers — and, according to my most humble reports, the Priests and Pastors needed for the first instance, two Catholic and one each of the Lutheran and Calvinist confessions, have already been appointed, with a salary for the first two years of 180 rubles a year to each — nevertheless, since the foreigners who have arrived to date are, owing to their poverty, unable to build either churches or houses for the pastors at their own expense, the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners, having no explicit order on this matter, cannot on its own satisfy this need of theirs.

For which reason I most humbly report this to Your Imperial Majesty, and beg to ask whether Your Most Gracious Majesty might not be pleased, seeing that the foreigners who have arrived, owing to their poverty and their not yet being established, will for a long time to come be unable to build churches, to order Most Highly that one church be built in each district being settled, furnishing it with all necessary vestments and vessels, together with a suitable house for the Pastor, at Treasury expense on account of all the inhabitants of that district, recovering these expenses, after the years of exemption have passed, from each household in equal shares, while the appointment of Priests and Pastors is to be left to the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners itself, on the same basis as Your Majesty was Most Graciously pleased to direct previously, concerning which I await Your Imperial Majesty's Most High decree.

Resolution. Let it be so.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XVII. Pp. 17-18.*

Published in: German Colonists in the Age of Catherine / Comp.: E.E. Lykova, M.I. Osekina. Moscow, 2004. Pp. 73-74.

## No. 17. REPORT OF G.G. ORLOV ON THE RULES FOR THE SETTLEMENT OF HERRNHUTERS IN RUSSIA, APPROVED BY CATHERINE II (1765)

12,411. — June 7. Most Highly approved report of the President of the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners, Count Orlov. — On the rules for the settlement in Russia of the Fraternal Evangelical Society.

Report. On April 11 of this year, 1765, the Agent of the Fraternal Evangelical Society who arrived here in St. Petersburg, Peter Conrad Fries, submitted to the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners a petition, attaching to it a most humble petition of the same content addressed to Your Imperial Majesty's name, explaining in it how the Society of the Evangelical Brotherhood of the Augsburg Confession, having formed the intention of establishing a separate settlement in Astrakhan Governorate, sent here to St. Petersburg people who are to lay the foundation of this undertaking for the benefit of the new settlement, relying on Your Imperial Majesty's Most Gracious decree given to them on February 11 of last year, 1764, and above all on the permission received that they might settle in whatever provinces of Your Imperial Majesty's domains they wish, and enjoy complete freedom in their faith and in the public practice of their religion according to their own regulations, which they had the honor of presenting to Your Imperial Majesty; and that, in order to proceed with this matter in proper order, the said Agent was sent by their leadership, residing in Herrnhut, with a letter of credence, who, having submitted this credential to the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners, requests that a means be provided for those of the brethren of their society whom he is to present, to proceed to whatever place they themselves may choose from among the vacant and uninhabited lands, up to four thousand desyatinas, or more if needed, in Astrakhan Governorate between Tsaritsyn and Astrakhan, wherever they themselves may select, in order to establish their residence there; and further, that permission be given to have that land surveyed, measured, and mapped, of which plan one copy is to be submitted to the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners, another sent to their leadership, and a third retained by the leaders of the colony; and that a full legal grant of that land be made to all the inhabitants of that colony, and particularly and specifically to those whom the leadership of their society shall now choose and shall in future appoint whenever the need arises to change the leaders of that colony; and that they hold that land in perpetual and full possession, and make use of it as they see fit, on the basis set forth at length in the points of the petition submitted by the Agent, DOCUMENTS__________________________________________________________________________________ 41

which, having been extracted as a separate enclosure, together with the explanations obtained from the Agent by the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners regarding all his points, and combined with the tentative confirmation drawn up by the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners on all of his points, as well as a draft of a special article on taxes, quitrents, and excise duties, which the said Agent Fries, after many negotiations with the Chancellery, agreed to accept and confirm, I submit to Your Imperial Majesty with this my most humble report, for Your Most High favor, and I await a Most Gracious decree of Your Imperial Majesty.

Points of the petition of the Fraternal Evangelical Society, and the tentative resolution thereon.

Taking into consideration the future benefit to the State from the manufactories and factories which the Fraternal Evangelical Society intends to establish upon settling in Russia, and no less the anticipated improvement, thanks to these skilled people, of commerce across the Caspian Sea, seeing that they are choosing a suitable place for their settlement for this purpose, mentioning in one place journeys to Persia, and likewise that they request loan money only for building and for purchasing a few instruments, promising verbally to bring most of these with them, which indeed they have already begun to do — the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners, upon consideration, finds nothing prejudicial to other Russian subjects, provided the privileges requested by Agent Fries for the brethren of the Evangelical Society are granted on the following basis; and above all, submits the whole matter to the Most High favor of Your Imperial Majesty.

Points of the petition submitted by Peter Conrad Fries, the Agent sent by the Fraternal Evangelical Society of the Augsburg Confession:

1. That all the settlers of the aforementioned colony enjoy all rights, freedoms, and privileges in the same fullness as other free landowners enjoy on their lands in the provinces of Your Imperial Majesty, and that they remain always, in their possession, under the Most Gracious and Most High protection of Your Imperial Majesty.

In what manner, moreover, the said Agent answered questions put by the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners is shown under each point in the explanations as set out below.

Explanation. By full authority over the land granted to the Evangelical Brotherhood, he understands its division according to their own arrangement, solely among the Evangelical brethren who shall be accepted into their colony, on condition that when any of them departs, he may give his land allotment to other brethren of the Evangelical Society, but not to outsiders, while undertaking to pay land or poll money.

2. That they have the freedom and permission to build on their land towns, villages, and hamlets as they themselves see fit for their own best benefit, likewise churches with bell towers and bells for proper use, as well as public schools and such houses where, according to their spiritual custom, they may make suitable arrangements, and maintain not only young children but also grown unmarried persons, male and female, each sex separately in a common household, until the time of their marriage; and in addition that they have the freedom to lay roads through adjoining uninhabited areas bordering their land, for travel to neighboring settlements and to nearby rivers, as they themselves, according to their needs and convenience, may see fit.

Explanation. Not knowing whether they will be able to build towns, and unable to promise this, nevertheless, in order to avoid difficulty in future, he requests this permission now, as well as permission to engage in urban trades and enjoy all civic rights, undertaking to pay all taxes justly imposed, provided only that these be specified now, for they do not intend to commit themselves to anything unknown.

3. That each town, village, and hamlet within that colony be permitted to establish its own internal police and administration as it sees fit, on condition that Your Imperial Majesty's military and civil administrators shall in no way interfere in any of their arrangements, contracts, inheritances, wills, guardianships, and other similar matters, but that they themselves shall choose among themselves such persons as shall be entrusted with establishing police, maintaining good order, and administering justice according to the civil laws of the Russian State, under the sole oversight of the local Governor.

Explanation. The right of inheritance, once established, consists chiefly, among them, in a will; and if there is no will, it passes to the deceased's children and close relatives, wherever they may be; and when there are neither children nor relatives, the estate of the deceased remains within the colony, as such a society is equally obliged to answer for debts.

4. That each locality enjoy, without any exception, all civil rights, having full freedom to trade, to practice any craft and trade, to establish factories and manufactories at will, and likewise to conduct whatever trade they wish, to brew beer for their own use and distill spirits for their own needs, to build any mills on their lands, to engage in fishing, to make use of the large rivers and small streams flowing through their lands, to have hunting grounds under their own control, and to cut timber freely, as they wish.

Explanation. As regards the distilling of spirits and the brewing of beer, considering these very necessary for the settlement, they request permission, with the undertaking that they will not only pay the appropriate taxes for this, but also, in assurance that they request this freedom solely for their own use and not for sale, they do not intend to establish any markets or designate any fairs in their colony; however, by their own use they also understand the freedom to be allowed to supply spirits and beer both to those who may lodge with them while passing through their settlements, and to those who may reside for a time in their colonies for some reason; and as to trade, the Agent explained that they will not import any prohibited goods, nor trade in anything not permitted within Russia, but request only permission to import and trade in such goods as are permitted to all, undertaking to pay all taxes and duties on the same basis as other merchants, manufacturers, or craftsmen; finally, assuring that they request nothing that could be of harm to the high Crown, they ask that it be explained to them regarding the protected forests needed for shipbuilding, whether entire forests in certain places, which must be preserved, or certain species of trees, or merely trees of a certain known size, are to be understood by this. DOCUMENTS__________________________________________________________________________________ 43

5. That a prohibition be imposed on all others from erecting any building whatsoever on their lands, not excluding taverns, drinking houses, or salt warehouses, and from establishing anything or settling and residing there, while the colony alone shall have the authority to admit whomever it wishes and to dismiss whomever it deems fit, without being accountable to anyone for this; that all settlers, their heirs, and their distant descendants have always the freedom and right to dispose of their property as they wish and to leave the Russian provinces whenever they please, taking with them, wherever they may go, all their property, giving up to the Treasury such a portion thereof as is set forth below in point 10.

Explanation. Salt will be obtained from the Treasury by a special person appointed by them for this purpose, as with other inhabitants of Russia, not for sale but for the colony's own use; and as to the authority to admit into their colony whomever they wish, the Agent declared that they mean by this such free persons as are free both by birth and from any obligations, and that, notwithstanding this, they will always inform the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners of the admission of such persons, and until such persons are declared free, they will conclude nothing definitive with them; nor will they accept Russian subjects for work without passports.

6. That all settlers of the Evangelical Brotherhood be able to obtain, without hindrance, the necessary passports from the Governorates or from the State Collegium of Foreign Affairs whenever they wish, both for safe travel within the State and for departure abroad, should any need call them to another State.

Explanation. In consideration of the great distance of their future settlement from the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners, and the difficulties and loss of time connected therewith, they earnestly request that the passports required by the elders of their colony, including those for abroad, be issued from the nearest Governorate.

7. That none of the said Brotherhood, who now or in future settle in the provinces of Your Imperial Majesty, nor their children or descendants, ever be taken against their will into either military or civil service, and likewise that neither quartering of soldiers, nor recruits, nor carts, nor any other supply obligation ever be demanded from their towns, villages, hamlets, or any of their settlements.

Explanation. According to the Agent Fries's declaration, the regulations of their Society, which have already been submitted to Your Imperial Majesty, do not permit them under any circumstances to maintain any billeting whatsoever, from which they have been exempted by all the Powers under whose protection they have resided, and from which they were also released by the warring Sovereigns during the recent grievous war, by which favor they flatter themselves here too, as faithful subjects; as for the maintenance of post-stations, they do not intend to take this upon themselves at all, nor will their land be so extensive as to necessarily require post-stations upon it.

8. That every settler of that colony be permitted, counting from the day of his arrival at the place of settlement, to enjoy for a full 30 years complete exemption from all taxes, of whatever kind these may be, paying no dues whatsoever to the Treasury and performing no service, ordinary or extraordinary; but that, after the 30 years of exemption have passed, in place of all the taxes and services paid and performed by Your Imperial Majesty's other subjects, each male member of the Evangelical Brotherhood from the age of 20 shall pay per year, with none excepted, except those who hold public offices within the settlement, and except also the elderly and the sick, and further that nothing be demanded from any of the brethren of their society individually, but solely from their permanent elders, who shall pay all the dues at the proper time and place.

Explanation. In whatever manner the dues may be arranged, whether by persons, by land, or by trades and occupations, they agree to all of it, provided only that this be settled now.

9. That, for the founding and carrying out of this settlement, there be given them not only the necessary materials and craftsmen of all kinds from among Russian subjects for building houses, but also that a necessary sum of money be given them from the Treasury as an interest-free loan, taking an obligation from their elders for repayment of that principal sum after 10 years, in 3 years, in equal installments from the day of its receipt.

Explanation. By a loan they mean the money needed for the purchase of livestock and necessary instruments for various craftsmen for establishing manufactories and factories, as well as for paying laborers, precisely in accordance with points 3 and 4 of Section 6 of the manifesto, requesting nothing for the conduct of trade; as for materials, they wish to receive these in kind, taking them at their own expense at whatever price these cost the Saratov Voivodeship Chancellery; only that they be informed of the price as soon as possible; and as to how many materials they will need for building houses, they will inform the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners of this beforehand, and they request that the loan money be issued to their Elder himself, or to whomever he shall entrust with this, for whom they all vouch.

10. If anyone among the people of the aforementioned Brotherhood who have settled in the provinces of Your Imperial Majesty should intend to leave Russia, that he and his children and descendants have freedom to do so, but under the following condition: that of the estate he has acquired in Russia — not of what he brought with him — he shall render unto the treasury a portion, namely: for one who has lived in Russia from one to 5 years, one fifth part; from 5 to 10 years and beyond, one tenth part, after which everyone shall be free to depart wherever he wishes; on the same basis and with the same payment shall also be established the right of inheritance of those of the Evangelical Brotherhood who die in the Russian lands, so that the goods they acquired in Russia and left behind shall be given to their heirs residing in foreign lands.

Explanation. If some of the brethren of the Evangelical Society, availing themselves of the sixth point of Article 6, bring goods with them and, having lived less than 10 years, depart again from Russia, they are obliged upon their departure to pay to the treasury all the duties properly due, exactly in accordance with the content of that point.

11. Finally, if the Society of the Evangelical Brotherhood and its leadership, for the furtherance of the common benefit of this settlement, should see fit to maintain in St. Petersburg one of the Brethren in the rank of Agent, who shall be charged with receiving the departing colonists, taking care of them, providing them with everything necessary, and ensuring their prompt dispatch, and with attending to everything pertaining to the common welfare of their settlement, and accordingly with going to the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers or presenting personally to Your Imperial Majesty whatever is required — may Your Imperial Majesty be graciously pleased to decree that the house in which the said Agent shall live enjoy all the privileges granted to the houses of the other clergy of the Protestant faith, so that the colonists, upon their arrival, may immediately attend divine service, obtain free lodging and maintenance until their dispatch to the place of settlement, and so that this house of the Agent may serve as a refuge for the brethren of their colony and as a place through which uninterrupted communication is to be maintained between this settlement and the other churches of this Brotherhood Society.

Explanation. As for purchasing, with money loaned from the treasury, the house in which the Agent shall live here in St. Petersburg, and likewise providing for the Brethren belonging to their colony here with the same funds — he has no other instruction than to carry out all of this at his own expense.

Draft resolution on confiscation, according to the opinion of the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers.

To Point 1. The land which has been allotted for the settlement of the brethren of the Evangelical Society of the Augsburg Confession, and for which a grant shall be made, they are permitted to hold according to their own discretion with complete freedom therein, save for the one restriction that they shall not sell nor under any pretext cede the smallest part of that granted land to any outside persons not belonging to their colony and Society.

To Point 2. All that is requested is permitted on the following conditions:

1) That notice be given to the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers not only of the founding of the town, but of every settlement, together with their names, and that plans be attached with a detailed description of the layout both of the settlement itself and of the field lands and other lands belonging to it.

2) That, once built, lists concerning the arrangements for schools and for those houses in which even adults, prior to marriage, will be kept under communal household management, be sent to the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers for information only.

3) Full freedom is granted to lay roads through uninhabited places adjoining their land, meaning vacant State lands, and it will be confirmed by decrees from the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers to the proper places that the roads they have laid shall not be damaged; but the laying of roads through lands belonging to private owners shall depend on the will and consent of the neighboring owner to whom that vacant land belongs; as for the tax for burgher rights, that is set forth in the appropriate place.

To Point 3. This article may be approved on condition that the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers be informed in advance, with a description of all particulars, of all their arrangements concerning internal jurisdiction as well as their right of inheritance; the Chancellery will in turn not fail to communicate this to the Governor of Astrakhan, as their appointed special guardian; and as for escheated estates, although these are left for the common benefit of the whole colony, it is on condition that the head of their society is obliged to pay all debts of the deceased out of the communal fund established by them.

To Point 4. They are permitted to enjoy all civil rights, to trade in any permitted (not prohibited) goods, and to engage in any craft, art, or trade, to establish factories and manufactories, and to build any kind of mill, and also to distill spirits and brew beer for their own needs and use and for the provisioning of outside persons temporarily residing in their colony and of those who, passing through their lands, may stop and lodge there — provided that they pay the duties set forth further on in a special article, using grain spirit exclusively within their own settlements and not exporting any of it under any pretext beyond the borders of their granted land; as for grape wines, cherry liqueurs, and similar beverages not made by infusing grain spirit but distilled in a stamped still, for which excise shall be paid under Article 12, they may take these with them on journeys for their own use only; they may also engage in fishing in waters not under lease, as well as in hunting on their own granted land, freely and without any payment to the treasury; however, timber suitable and much needed for shipbuilding will not be granted to them as part of their allotment; but should it happen that within the land allotted to them there are found, in various places, a number of trees suitable for the aforesaid purpose, these shall be given over for the colony's own use, while otherwise they may deal freely with any other forests once granted to them as part of their allotment.

To Point 5. Except with the consent of the colony's leaders, no one shall be permitted to settle on their granted land or to erect any building there; likewise all other matters are confirmed exactly in accordance with the understanding and explanation of Agent Friese.

To Point 6. Passports for travel into Asia shall be issued by order of the Governor of Astrakhan or whoever performs his duties; and when they travel through St. Petersburg to other foreign European states, passports shall be issued to them without delay by the College of Foreign Affairs through the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers; within the interior of the state, the leaders of the colony shall themselves furnish passports to those departing.

To Point 7. All that is requested is granted, except that free lodgings must necessarily be provided by the colony's leaders, for the duration of their stay, to any persons occasionally sent from the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers or from the Governor of Astrakhan for the purpose of some inspection or examination in their colonies.

To Point 8. Since the Agent, in the name of the Evangelical Brotherhood Society, requests for all their future settlers not only civil rights but also, beyond that, such benefits and privileges as are not included among the State revenues collected in the form of taxes — in consideration of this they are exempted for 30 years solely from taxes, but not from the payment of excises and duties; consequently they are permitted to enjoy all the requested liberties and privileges on the basis set forth and explained in the points of the special article that follows.

To Point 9. For the founding of their settlement, not only shall materials for building houses be issued to the leaders of their settlements, or to others on trusted letters from the leaders, in whatever amount is required in proportion to the construction, together with money to pay the workers against their receipts, but further loans shall be made to them according to the number of people who have actually emigrated and settled and of the manufactories, factories, and other trades established, upon the request of the head of the colony, the principal being recovered over 10 years, in installments over 3 years from the date it was issued; it is hereby further made known that when a loan has been made for the establishment of manufactories or trades which are not brought into operation, the head of the colony is obliged to return the loaned money to the treasury without waiting for the ten-year term, as soon as it becomes clear that the promise will not be fulfilled.

To Point 10. This is granted without exception, with only the reminder that, even for those who die in the Russian provinces whose estates by right of inheritance will belong to relatives residing in foreign lands, the head of their settlement is obliged to pay all debts, both to the treasury and to private parties.

To Point 11. It is permitted to maintain an Agent and to have a special house for him for the lodging of people arriving to settle in their colony, the maintenance thereof being at their own expense, and they may be exempted from billeting; a privilege shall also be granted to him on the same basis as is given, in due course, to other clergy of the Protestant faith.

Draft of a special article, in continuation of Article 12, on taxes, duties, and excises, showing after how many years these are to be paid.

§ 1. Considering that the Brethren of the Evangelical Society intend to settle in separate townships, or colonies, then by force of Article 6, Point 2, of the published Manifesto concerning foreigners, they are exempted from all taxes, both peasant and burgher, for 30 years, counting from the time of their arrival at the place of settlement; and since these people designate only a certain quantity of land for all their settlers collectively, without declaring their number, and request moreover that everything be collected from the heads of the colony rather than from each person individually, the years of exemption are to be counted from the founding of their first settlement, and the time allotted for this, according to their petitions, is the remainder of the current year and the whole of the coming year 1766; consequently the years of exemption shall begin on January 1, 1767; the taxes in Russia, both peasant taxes shared with the burghers and burgher taxes specifically, are as follows:

1. Poll tax, from each male soul, 70 kopecks per year.

2. Quitrent tax, 1 ruble 50 kopecks per soul; but from this tax the brethren of the Evangelical Society, as burghers, are exempted in consideration of the duties they pay on trade and manufacturing and the benefit accruing therefrom.

3. For the provision of recruits, in money, this levy being reckoned, on an average basis of numbers and time, at 150 rubles per recruit for every 120 souls over 5 years, 45 rubles for a dragoon horse, and 30 rubles for a pack horse, and, in lieu of recruit clothing, footwear, provisions, fodder, and salt, 20 kopecks per soul per year — in total, these general taxes amount to 1 ruble 27¼ kopecks per male soul per year; and since by the Supreme decree of Your Imperial Majesty it has already once been ordered that foreigners be given suitable land for each family, on the same basis as single-homesteaders (odnodvortsy), namely 30 desyatinas in all; and since each single-homesteader household is reckoned to contain 4 male souls; consequently, from such an allotment, that is, from each 30 desyatinas of land, after the exemption years have passed, the colony of the Evangelical Brotherhood Society shall be obliged to pay into the treasury of Your Imperial Majesty 5 rubles 10 kopecks per year, and from the entire suitable land granted to them, whatever amount is calculated accordingly.

4. All Russian merchants pay into the treasury a poll tax of 1 ruble 20 kopecks per soul per year, whereas peasants pay only 70 kopecks; consequently the additional 50 kopecks is taken from them for the right of citizenship (burgher status); and since for each family, on average, for the sake of avoiding many difficulties, 4 souls have been designated, as stated above, then, in accordance with Article 8 of the well-known Manifesto concerning foreigners, the brethren of the Evangelical Society shall be obliged, after the exemption years have passed, to pay into the treasury of Your Imperial Majesty 2 rubles per year from each 30-desyatina allotment for the right of citizenship; but since Agent Friese, in petitioning the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers for a reduction of these taxes, represented verbally, as grounds, that a considerable portion of the inhabitants of the settlement to be founded will, in accordance with their principal intention, work in factories, without in fact enjoying civil rights, and that justice would be done them if their factory workers were exempted from taxes for a privilege they cannot actually enjoy — in consideration of this, they shall pay for the right of citizenship, from each allotment, instead of 2 rubles, 1 ruble 40 kopecks per year; and in addition, after the exemption years, they must pay 1 ruble for each 30 desyatinas for their exemption from all local services, billeting, the provision of post-station and district horses in lieu thereof, and all incidental deliveries and extraordinary assistance; and so, for both kinds of taxes together, the colony of the Evangelical Brotherhood Society shall be obliged, after the 30 exemption years have passed, to pay annually for each 30 desyatinas of suitable land 7 rubles 50 kopecks, which comes to 25 kopecks per desyatina; as for the port duty and the border duty on goods, that remains as set forth in the Manifesto, for these revenues are of an entirely different kind from the aforementioned taxes.

§ 2. By the Supreme Personal decree of Your Imperial Majesty of December 15 of last year, 1763, it was ordered that from all factories under the jurisdiction of the Manufacturing Collegium, 1 ruble be taken for each loom, and that for other factories which have no looms, 1 percent be levied on the capital employed; accordingly, the future colony of the Evangelical Brotherhood Society is likewise obliged, after the exemption years have passed, to pay into the treasury of Your Imperial Majesty 1 ruble per year for each loom, and for factories having no looms, 1 percent on the capital employed therein, the declaration of the capital employed being left to their own good faith; and if, in the meantime, anyone establishes such factories, manufactories, or works as produce goods of a kind not hitherto made in Russia, then it is permitted to sell and export these from the Russian Empire for 10 years without any payment of internal, port, or border duty; but notice of this must first be given to the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers, when this colony of the Evangelical Society intends to begin such export, so that the ten years of exemption may be counted consecutively from that very time.

§ 3. From all mills, except sawmills, which are exempted from all quitrents, the same quitrents are to be paid into the treasury, after the exemption years have passed, as are collected from mills belonging to other Russian subjects.

§ 4. As for fishing in waters that are leased out or subject to quitrent, nothing definite can be established in advance, because payment for these varies, and moreover certain sites in such waters have been given to entrepreneurs without re-leasing; consequently no outside persons may fish in such waters without the consent of those entrepreneurs; on the other hand, as for sites in rivers and lakes that are leased out annually or over several years to whoever offers the most, the brethren of the Evangelical Society, as soon as they settle in Russia, shall, as loyal subjects of Your Imperial Majesty, obtain the right to make use of fishing grounds on exactly the same basis as other loyal subjects, but without exemption years.

§ 5. It is known that the sale of spirits constitutes a considerable part of the State revenues; it therefore seems just that the foreigners emigrating to Russia to settle should likewise, through their consumption of spirits, bring profit to the treasury of Your Imperial Majesty, as do other Russian subjects; and although, in consideration of the particular benefit expected from them in the growth of manufactories, factories, and commerce, the settlements of the brethren of the Evangelical Society are granted permission to distill spirits for their own use, this is not to be entirely exempt from contributing to these State revenues, but with an intermediate concession between that granted to the nobility and to other persons of lower estate, namely: they may have as many stills as they wish, but these must be made to a uniform measure of 6 buckets, and cauldrons of 12 buckets, which shall be stamped every year, or at least every two years, at the Astrakhan Provincial Chancellery, and they shall pay into the treasury of Your Imperial Majesty for this privilege, from the time the stills and cauldrons are stamped, 75 rubles per still and 170 rubles per cauldron each year.

§ 6. By the decree of Your Imperial Majesty of the year [17]63, all persons living in towns, from the least to the greatest, are required to pay into the treasury for beer-brewing 20 kopecks for each chetvert of grain used; consequently the brethren of the Evangelical Society are likewise obliged to pay the same amount, declaring the quantity of grain used for the brewing of beer and small beer, at the end of each year, at the Astrakhan Provincial Chancellery, this too being left to their own conscience.

Resolution. Let it be so.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XVII. Pp. 151-160.*

## No. 18. REPORT OF G.G. ORLOV ON THE SETTLEMENT OF FOREIGNERS ON PRIVATE LANDS NEAR ST. PETERSBURG, CONFIRMED BY CATHERINE II (1765)

12,503. — November 1. Supremely confirmed report of the President of the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers, Count Orlov. — On the settlement of foreigners in Ingermanland on private lands, under agreements with their owners.

Report. Upon the announcement to the colonists residing in Oranienbaum of the Supreme consent of Your Imperial Majesty that those among them who wished might be settled near St. Petersburg, not only have many shown inclination to do so, but some, as is already known to Your Imperial Majesty, have in fact already concluded contracts with the Steward of Your Imperial Majesty's village of Tsarskoye Selo, Court Councillor Udalov. This inclination on their part gives sure hope that those arriving in future, following this example, will also be willing to settle in Ingermanland; and in order to give foreigners still greater inclination to settle in the areas near St. Petersburg, and thereby to bring the solicitous intention of Your Imperial Majesty for the welfare of her subjects more quickly to the desired conclusion in this matter as well, would Your Most Gracious Majesty be pleased to order the Supreme confirmation of the following provisions:

1. In order to bring agriculture in Ingermanland into a better condition than before, and especially in order to expand and establish it on those lands which either lie entirely vacant or are only leased out as hay-mowing grounds for a small rent, it is most graciously permitted to noblemen, as well as to merchants and free foreigners residing here, to induce foreigners arriving in Russia to settle, on their own or on the Sovereign's vacant lands situated in Ingermanland, on condition that those who agree to settle voluntarily be settled and established under separate agreements made between themselves, at their own expense, without requiring anything from the treasury.

2. And so that the colonists may not think that this permission seeks to limit their freedom, it is for that reason to be established by law that those very foreigners who agree voluntarily to settle on the lands of private persons, whether on their own lands or on Sovereign lands specially allotted to them for that purpose, shall always remain free people, on the same basis as the original colonists, under the guardianship of the Chancellery established for that purpose, whose authority and oversight in this case shall extend no further than to see that the contracts concluded by both sides — whether with private persons or with the Court Chancellery, or with other government offices, should the need arise — are observed inviolably, and that nothing harmful to the interests of the State or prejudicial to the published Manifesto concerning foreigners be included in them. For this reason such contracts are to be submitted to the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers for approval, where they shall also be kept; and the parties to those contracts shall be given exact copies, signed by those present, while private settlers shall also receive copies bearing the seal of that Chancellery. Consequently, all such foreigners who by special contracts undertake to settle in Ingermanland may bring their complaints, whether against government offices or in other districts, to the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers, as the place expressly established for their protection.

3. Excepting those lands which, at the last land survey, were separated from the manorial estates and are now leased out by the Chancellery of Road Construction, insofar as it shall be deemed proper to leave some of them for the settlement of foreigners under the Court Department, the remainder shall be distributed by the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers to those willing to take them, on the following conditions:

4. That on the lands given to them they settle solely emigrating foreigners and free persons already residing here, under voluntary agreements made with them, at their own expense, being permitted to build for their own arrival as each shall see fit; in connection with such building anyone may also employ his own hired Russian workers, provided only that these are not settled for the purpose of farming, because these lands, in consideration of the freedom of the foreigners settled upon them, cannot be granted on the same basis as to others; but on condition that they shall not be ceded to anyone under any pretext, though the whole of the land — not in parts — may freely be sold or mortgaged, provided the successor undertakes to observe all the conditions set forth in the contract.

5.
