When the settler himself, or his heir or successor, through purchase or borrowing, is for whatever reason unable to fulfill the concluded contract, he shall not be compelled to do so; instead, the land, together with the settlers, shall be taken into treasury administration, and the buildings (except the settler's own, which he is free to keep) shall, if the colonists have not paid for them, be reimbursed from the treasury at whatever cost they came to; and so that there be no doubt in these accounts, settlers must take receipts from their colonists for all expenses incurred on their behalf, for without this settlers may find themselves at a loss.

6. If, however, after the period for payment set forth in the Manifesto has elapsed, or as the settlers and colonists shall have agreed, the latter do not pay what is owed, and the settlers accordingly renounce ownership, the treasury shall satisfy them in the manner described above, and the colonists shall be obliged to pay as shall be prescribed to them. But if the colonists are unable to pay what is owed because the settlers have not fulfilled everything under the concluded contract, and this is proven, then in such a case nothing shall be paid to the settlers from the treasury as a penalty; instead, they must either be satisfied under the contract, with payment deferred at the discretion of the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers, or the matter shall be transferred to treasury administration. On the other hand, the colonists are likewise obliged to fulfill without exception the promise they made to the settlers, save in cases of misfortune, which must also be stipulated in the contracts; and if, moreover, they act contrary to their undertaking out of obstinacy or negligence, they shall not only be compelled, for the satisfaction of the settlers, to obedience and fulfillment of the agreement, but shall also be punished according to the degree of their fault and offense, since these contracts are to be concluded by the good will and consent of each party; consequently they must be observed inviolably by both sides.

7. Since land shall be distributed to those willing to take it free of charge, on condition that they settle upon it foreigners emigrating to Russia; but if, after 10 years have passed, colonists have not been settled on the lands given to them, such lands shall be taken back into the treasury, with recovery of a holding fee of 15 kopecks per desyatina of good land for each year; and as for woodland, if it is cleared, 10 rubles per desyatina shall be charged once for timber-quality wood and 3 rubles for firewood-quality wood, in addition to the 15 kopecks per desyatina payable generally for the whole land; and even if several families are settled but so much land nevertheless remains vacant, that surplus land shall be dealt with in the same manner as described above.

8. And if anyone, having taken land, fails within the first two years to build even a single homestead on it or to settle even a single family of foreigners, and another applicant is found who did not receive land in the original distribution and petitions for that unsettled land after the two years have passed, representing that he has several families of foreigners ready for settlement, and this representation proves true, then that land shall be taken from the first party, with recovery of the holding fee for the two years, or for however long he made use of it, and given to the one who has people ready for settlement — but not before a contract has been concluded; and if, however, at that same time the first settler produces a contract he has concluded with several foreigners, the land shall not be taken from him, and the latter applicant shall be refused.

9. After 10 years from the granting of the land into ownership, on which several families of foreigners have been settled and the whole of that land has been divided among them according to the settler's discretion, the settler shall recover from the colonists, in three equal annual installments, first the treasury money that was spent on them before their arrival in St. Petersburg, as well as the subsistence money issued to them before the conclusion of the contract with the settler; but apart from this, no further exactions whatsoever shall be required, for the remaining exemption years, either from the settler or from the settlers themselves.

10. When the settlers themselves or their heirs no longer wish to retain those settled lands in their possession, or when no successors remain to them, such lands shall be taken into treasury administration, but on condition that if the Crown, for whatever reason, cannot or does not see fit to enjoy the benefits which the settlers had stipulated for themselves, then the settlers (peasants) shall be obliged, in place of those benefits, after the exemption years have passed, to pay into the treasury solely 25 kopecks per desyatina of good land each year; in all other respects no taxes whatsoever shall be collected from them; for which reason, before concluding contracts with settlers, this provision must be made known to them and their signed acknowledgment obtained.

11. As for those foreigners who shall be settled by various landowners on their own lands situated in Ingermanland, such settlers must, immediately upon concluding the contracts, pay into the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers the full amount of money that was spent on them from the treasury; and beyond this, the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers shall have no further business with such foreigners, either during the exemption years or afterward, except to protect them from abuses by their landlords and from breaches of contract on either side.

12. Such landowners, on whose lands the said foreigners shall live in houses, are not obliged, apart from the ordinary taxes levied on their manors and villages, to pay anything into the treasury for them even after the exemption years have passed, since the benefit expected from this settlement, in my opinion, consists not in increasing revenues but in the advancement of agriculture. As for billeting, that shall remain at their discretion and shall depend chiefly on the contracts concluded with the foreigners; for which reason such settlers must state clearly and specifically in the contracts concluded with the colonists whether the colonists voluntarily agree, after the exemption years have passed, to bear any levies in aid of their landlords' serfs; for whatever is not precisely and specifically mentioned in such agreements, the landowners may in no way exact from them.

13. In the sale and inheritance of these lands on which foreigners shall be settled, action shall be taken exactly according to Point 4. For this reason they must be settled separately from other peasants, or at least the land allotments given to them under the concluded contracts must be surveyed and marked with boundaries, and plans, immediately after the survey, submitted to the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers, so that settlers may be able to sell such lands together with the settlers, or, should some impossibility prevent the owner from maintaining the contracts, to cede them to the Crown. In the event of an offense by colonists warranting corporal punishment, the landowners shall not deal with the matter themselves, but shall seek redress against them from the Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers. In all other respects, both settlers and colonists must act unfailingly according to the obligations mutually given to one another; for whichever of them first breaches these shall be deemed the principal cause, and guilty of all the ill consequences arising therefrom, and shall accordingly be compelled to bear alone the whole burden and losses.

Beyond the expansion of agriculture in Ingermanland, I consider the above-described provisions, Most Gracious Sovereign, to be beneficial also in that, by this means, the treasury may avoid no small expense. In all else I submit this to the Supreme goodwill of Your Imperial Majesty, and shall await the Most Gracious decree.

Resolution. Let it be so.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XVII. Pp. 373-377.*

## No. 19. DECREE OF CATHERINE II ON THE CREATION OF TWO GERMAN COLONIES IN LIVONIA (1766)

12,640. — May 10. Nominal [decree], given to Governor-General Browne. — On the granting of the two manors of Hirschenhof and Helfreichshof, located in Livonia, for the settlement of foreigners who had come into Russia.

Among the empty crown hides [land units] located in Livonia, We have observed that the manors of Hirschenhof and Helfreichshof, lying together, stand almost empty, and barely a quarter of them is populated by peasants, wherefore they cannot be worked by so small a number of people; for this reason We have found it useful to designate both these manors for the settlement of newly arrived colonists, agricultural people from the German lands, and We entrust the arrangement thereof and the settlement, under your overall direction, to Our General Director of Economy of Livonia, Stackelberg. In consequence of this We command the following to be done: 1. In the shortest possible time, first of all, to verify from the Swedish land-division maps how much arable land and other amenities exist in both said manors under the homesteads and under the empty and inhabited peasant households recorded at the last census, and, in that proportion, taking a known measure, in accordance with the force of Our manifesto and the regulations established by the Guardianship Chancellery, to determine what number of families should be sent for settlement, and to request this from the Guardianship Chancellery. 2. This settlement is to be carried out without departing in the least from the force of the said manifesto and from the regulations established pursuant thereto by the Guardianship Chancellery, and such contracts are to be concluded with the colonists as would give them no advantage whatsoever over the Saratov colonists; and if possible, in some respects even with a reduction; for which reason the proportion of land in Livonian measures is to be brought into exact equivalence with the land measures given to each family in Saratov. 3. The peasants presently located on these Livonian manors are to be transferred to empty lands, including those lying near other manors, and their resettlement is to be made as tolerable and easy for them as possible; wherefore the leaseholders of these same manors are to be given notice without delay, with the assurance that in exchange for these leases, for the term not yet expired, other hides [land units] will be given to them, and the improvements and seed-grain due to them by custom are to be paid out now from Our treasury. All this We command to be carried out in deed, without any loss of time, so that the colonists assigned there should not remain for long without a place, and might still make use of this year's farming season.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XVII. Pp. 686-687.*

## No. 20. REPORT OF G. G. ORLOV ON SUPPLYING THE COLONISTS WITH SUBSISTENCE MONEY, WITH THE RESOLUTION OF CATHERINE II (1766)

12,651. — May 19. Supreme resolution on the report of the President of the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners, Count Orlov. — On supplying the colonists with sustenance and everything necessary for their establishment, in kind or in money, whichever is more convenient.

Report. On May 4, 1766, the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners, considering that from the very beginning of the departure of foreigners to Russia for settlement, subsistence money has to this day been paid in St. Petersburg, in Oranienbaum, and also during their conveyance to the place of settlement, at the rate of 15 kopecks per day for men, 10 for women, 6 for their children of both sexes from 15 down to 2 years of age, and 2 kopecks for those aged 2 and under, and that this payment has been confirmed neither by the Supreme command of Your Imperial Majesty nor by a Chancellery decree, but only since the very first arrival of foreigners, at their urgent request that, following the example of the payment established by the Minister in Hamburg, in view of the high cost of provisions there, subsistence money should likewise be paid here, the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners was compelled to retain the arrangement established in Hamburg on that same basis, with only a very small reduction, chiefly so as not to cause dissatisfaction among these first arrivals nor create an obstacle to the future arrival of foreigners; wherefore their promises of frugal living and of saving the remainder of the subsistence money for future household establishment were taken into consideration. But as it has now been sufficiently observed that the colonists, notwithstanding the considerable cheapness of provisions here as compared with Hamburg, for the most part use the subsistence money not with such thrift as their own benefit would require, but squander it largely on wine and other excesses, whereby, apart from the disorders connected therewith, they fall into considerable debts, quite burdensome to themselves, for this reason, in order to put a stop to these abuses, the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners has, among other things, resolved: that for all foreigners actually present here and those expected in future, both during their stay here and en route to the place of settlement, subsistence money should henceforth be paid to men and women equally at 10 kopecks, and to their children of both sexes, counting those from 17 to 10 years old, at 6 kopecks, from 10 down to 2 years old at 4 kopecks, and to those 2 years old and infants at 2 kopecks per day, for the Chancellery considers this proportion, even given the present high cost of living here, quite sufficient for subsistence; and that this reduction is highly beneficial to the colonists themselves, so that, having the necessary maintenance here without excess, they should not indulge in luxury and thereby incur less debt, [the Chancellery] exhorting them with sound arguments to avoid idleness and apply themselves diligently to labor. But for my part, without the Supreme permission of Your Imperial Majesty, I could not agree to this — not because the reasons presented by the Members of that Chancellery are unjust or insufficiently grounded, but solely in order to forestall the complaints against the Chancellery that would inevitably follow from the colonists, or else to solicit Your Imperial Majesty's most gracious confirmation for its justification of the payment made hitherto; because the amount of subsistence money that has been paid here and en route to the place of settlement up to now was not determined by the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners, but was established, as mentioned above, by the Minister who was in Hamburg, Mr. Musin-Pushkin, and subsequent colonists, pointing to the first arrivals, have come to imagine they have the right to demand the same payment, notwithstanding the published Supreme Manifesto of Your Imperial Majesty, in which no specific amount whatsoever is set for either subsistence or loan money for establishment, but only the necessary sustenance and the assistance and comfort required according to each person's condition are promised; which indeed it is impossible to fix, not only in advance at the issuing of the Manifesto but even now for all time to come, because prices everywhere, both for provisions and for other items needed for the colonists' establishment, are subject to constant change, not to mention the variation in loans that must be made for almost every family depending on people's circumstances.

Wherefore, presenting this to Your Imperial Majesty, I most humbly request Your most gracious decree.

Resolution. Since the Chancellery has indeed observed the disadvantages set forth in its decree, not only for the treasury but also for the colonists themselves, We consent to this, and command that henceforth in similar cases both Our interest and the colonists' own benefit be observed, not allowing them to fall into harmful idleness and luxury, and providing them with food and everything necessary for their establishment, in kind or in money, whichever proves more convenient, cheaper, and more beneficial for the colonists as circumstances permit, according to necessary need, without excess or deficiency, without fixing for all time the amount of these expenditures, which are subject to constant change.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XVII. Pp. 699-700.*

Published in: *German Colonists in the Age of Catherine* / Compiled by E. E. Lykova, M. I. Osekina. Moscow, 2004. Pp. 127-130.

## No. 21. DECREE OF CATHERINE II ON THE CREATION OF THE BELOVEZH COLONIES NEAR CHERNIGOV (1766)

12,655. — May 22. Nominal [decree], given to the Senate. — On the transfer of the Belovezh Steppe, located in the Ivangorod company district, with all its amenities, to the department of the Governor-General of Little Russia, for the settlement of colonists thereon.

We most graciously command: that the Belovezh Steppe, located in the Ivangorod company district and belonging to the Little Russian General Artillery, together with all its forest and hay amenities, be transferred to the department of Our Governor-General of Little Russia, Count Rumyantsev, entrusting him with settling thereon up to one hundred colonist families; and that the empty little town called Belye Vezhi be revived by settling in it likewise up to 50 families of foreign townsmen, and that it be granted municipal rights, with all establishments proper to a town. As for how the said land is to be divided among them proportionally for homesteads and for plowland, what kind of buildings there are to be, and to what extent each settler and townsman, according to his means, should be furnished for establishment — all this, as well as the establishment in the town of a church, a school, and a town hall, We leave to the arrangement and care of the Governor-General; and according to an approximate calculation, with an addition for the church, school, and town hall of 5,000, We grant him in all 77,550 rubles from the Kiev customs revenues. And as the present maintenance of the Little Russian General Artillery, in view of many inconveniences, needs to be corrected and reconciled with the other portions of that land, We command the Governor-General to make suitable arrangements in place of the land taken from them for this settlement.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XVII. Pp. 701-702.*

## No. 22. ANNOUNCEMENT OF CATHERINE II ON THE TEMPORARY SUSPENSION OF THE ADMISSION OF FOREIGN COLONISTS (1766)

12,793. — November. Supremely confirmed announcement to foreigners wishing to emigrate to Russia for settlement.

Her Imperial Majesty has to this day taken no small satisfaction in seeing how the great benefits and advantages promised in Her Imperial Majesty's Supreme Manifesto published in the year [1]763 to all foreigners resettling in Russia, and especially the exact fulfillment thereof, have in actual fact produced equally great success; but as this summer such a multitude of foreigners emigrated to Russia for settlement as had not even been expected, not counting those people whom, owing to the lateness of the season, the Russian ministers and commissioners located in various foreign lands were compelled to refuse dispatch to Russia this year: consequently, effects quite contrary [to what was intended] have already resulted, which — to say nothing of the many other circumstances involving losses to the treasury — are especially displeasing to Her Imperial Majesty because they are highly burdensome to the colonists themselves, since it is not possible quickly to build houses for all of them nor to supply them with other necessities, and many of them, living for a considerable time in lodgings in idleness and receiving subsistence money, will be compelled to fall deeply into debt: and therefore Her Imperial Majesty, out of her innate magnanimity and love of humanity, being concerned that in future such persons desiring to settle in Russia should not, out of ignorance, emigrate all at once in excessive numbers and thereby subject themselves to an even greater burden of debt than those who emigrated this year, has been Supremely pleased to resolve to suspend for the future the emigration of foreigners to Russia for settlement, until such time as all the colonists who have emigrated hitherto, having received houses, the necessary implements, livestock, and all other requirements, shall actually have entered into work and shall have their own means of subsistence.

As soon as all the colonists already in Russia shall have been brought to such a state as described, the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners, by the Supreme command of Her Imperial Majesty, will not fail to notify the public in good time, describing in full detail on what basis the emigration of colonists, their conveyance to St. Petersburg and further to the place of settlement, as well as their maintenance en route and during their stay at every place until they begin their household and work, are to be arranged, so that in future no disputes, deceptions, or confusions, which have sometimes arisen up to now [DOCUMENTS 57]

from ignorance and misunderstanding of the true force of the Manifesto, but more from the deliberate misinterpretation thereof out of self-interest by certain well-known persons, shall be able to occur; and for the satisfaction and relief of the settlers expected in future, building will be carried out in advance, so that the settlers arriving in future will find at the place of their future dwelling, if not the full number of houses for everyone, then at least enough ready houses that all of them may not only freely lodge and live peacefully in them until the remaining ones are built, but may also be able to carry out farming and other household work.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XVII. Pp. 1067-1068.*

Published in: *German Colonists in the Age of Catherine* / Compiled by E. E. Lykova, M. I. Osekina. Moscow, 2004. Pp. 133-135.

## No. 23. DECREE OF CATHERINE II ON MEASURES TO IMPROVE THE SITUATION IN THE VOLGA COLONIES (1775)

14,302. — April 18. Nominal [decree], given to the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners. — On the sorting of colonists settled near Saratov and on granting them a loan.

Having examined the report submitted by Our Senate together with the report from the President of the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners, and the opinion of that Chancellery, concerning the colonies settled near the city of Saratov, We find that among the number of foreigners settled in those places, some, by their orderly conduct, diligence in rural husbandry, and praiseworthy industriousness in agriculture, have shown themselves worthy of Our Supreme favor toward them; while others, on the contrary, through laziness, negligence, and dissolute living, have not only failed to succeed in establishing an orderly household, but, despite all the assistance rendered to them and repeated exhortations from the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners and from the President himself, having incurred great debts, now have no means of subsistence, and thus, being supplied according to each one's condition with abundant loans over and above what was promised by Our Manifesto issued on July 22, 1763, there is no longer any hope for their improvement: wherefore We command: 1. That the first group be informed of Our Supreme favor, while the others, though it would be proper, as having failed to fulfill their obligations, to leave them without any care whatsoever, yet, out of Our innate mercy, We have not failed to give orders that these too be supplied one last time with what is necessary for farming and subsistence until the next harvest, on condition that if in the future they likewise prove negligent and given to idleness, no further loan whatsoever will be made to them. 2. And since, even after this Our most gracious concern, in view of the dissolute condition and extreme negligence of many settled colonists reported to Us, We cannot hope that this last act of mercy of Ours will bring all of them, accustomed to idleness, self-will, and negligence, into proper order, therefore, in order to spare the industrious settlers from comrades who corrupt them by bad example, and, on the other hand, so that these latter too might have occupation suited to their inclinations, and thus better supervision, a sorting is to be made of those fit and unfit for farming; for which purpose the senior Member of the Saratov Guardianship Office is to be entrusted with collecting, in each settlement, written recommendations concerning every settler from the whole community and its elders, and those designated for farming are to be supplied once and for all with a suitable loan according to the report submitted to Us by the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners, on condition that these settlers approved for farming shall maintain the aged and infirm at the expense of the community. 3. Those unfit and not approved to be farmers are to be informed — those for whom the terms for payment of treasury debts have already expired — that upon paying these debts they may freely leave Russia, and otherwise must occupy themselves in the towns with various work suited to their abilities, and with the money earned thereby repay their treasury debt, or else enter Our military service, in accordance with the issued Manifesto; and likewise, by force of the same [Manifesto], those whose terms for payment have not yet expired are not forbidden, upon paying their debt, to leave the state. 4. And since, according to the aforementioned Our Manifesto, their internal jurisdiction has been left to their own good governance, while granting to the farmers remaining after the sorting a voluntary choice of their own village elders, We nevertheless confirm that the strictest observance is to be maintained, that each one should strive by his own labor in agriculture to acquire sufficient means of subsistence, and should by no means place hope in treasury assistance: for, as stated above, all manner of assistance was rendered to them over and above what was promised, so that from now on no further loan whatsoever will be made to them. 5. Although for some settlers the terms for the collection of debts have arrived, and for others they will soon arrive, yet in view of the disorders that occurred in those places, out of Our innate mercy, We most graciously grant to all who do not wish to leave Russia a further five-year postponement, on condition that, upon the expiry of this period of grace, each and every one of the foreigners remaining in Russia shall without fail strive, in exact fulfillment of Our issued Manifesto, to pay off their debts, and if anyone, even after this Supreme mercy shown by Us, fails to make full payment within the appointed term, such a person shall be dealt with as a violator of his own voluntary obligation. 6. For the better observance of public order, for the adjudication of petitions arising from settlers, and for the resolution of matters pertaining to village elders, one Commissioner is to be appointed for each of the existing 13 districts from among retired Staff and Ober-Officers, to whom is to be allotted, or where needed built, one crown homestead each, and 60 desyatinas of land, only for such time as they shall remain in these positions, from the lands remaining after allotting the established proportion to the settlers actually present in the same settlements to which each such Commissioner's duties are assigned. As for the annual salary, allowing 250 rubles for each, it is left to the Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners to distribute it according to the measure of their labors and diligence. 7. But since among these foreigners there are also those recruited by contractors [vyzyvateli], with whom accounts under the concluded contracts have not yet been settled to this day, in order that the contractors should have no cause for future dissatisfaction on the grounds that the said sorting was made without consulting them as to the fitness or unfitness of such persons who were bound to them by special contracts, it is to be permitted that the contractors themselves or their attorneys be present at the ordered sorting, and that the recommendations collected concerning each settler be confirmed by their own signatures, with the further declaration that if, among those they have approved, any prove unable to pay at the arrival of the terms for payment of debts, then for such persons — who, beyond the community's certification for each settlement, remain so by the contractors' own approval — the contractors themselves shall be obligated to pay, when, upon examination of their affairs and their actual accounts with them, these persons remain under their management; and until that time, the foreigners recruited by them are to remain on the same basis on which they were managed according to the Chancellery's review.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XX. Pp. 125-126.*

Published in: *German Colonists in the Age of Catherine* / Compiled by E. E. Lykova, M. I. Osekina. Moscow, 2004. Pp. 138-142.

## No. 24. DECREE OF CATHERINE II ON THE TRANSFORMATION OF THE SCHOOL AT THE ST. PETERSBURG LUTHERAN CHURCH OF ST. PETER INTO THE CHIEF GERMAN SCHOOL (1783)

15,826. — August 29. Nominal [decree], given to the Senate. — On the school established in St. Petersburg at the Evangelical Church of St. Peter being the chief public normal school for those using the German language, and on the establishment thereat of a special directorate or board over all public schools of the German language.

Our Senate is aware that We, having resolved to establish public schools everywhere throughout Our Empire, set up for that purpose a special Commission under Our own supervision, entrusting it not only with composing a plan of instruction suited thereto, but also with devising a method of instruction, together with the publication of textbooks, so that perfect uniformity might be observed therein and the most convenient means devised. The said Commission, continuing its labors with success, has already achieved the actual founding of several Russian public schools and of the chief school itself; but as among the regions subject to Our scepter there are also those whose inhabitants use the German language, We have undertaken to extend Our concern for the establishment of public schools also for the benefit of these Our subjects. With this intention We turn Our attention to the school established in St. Petersburg at the Lutheran Church of St. Peter, and furnished with Our Imperial charter, which, to Our satisfaction, has already borne good fruit and considerable benefit to society, and from which We expect the same in the matter now at hand. We therefore command that it be the chief public normal school for Our subjects using the German language; and as its school assembly, preachers, and chief teachers have recognized that the methods of instruction devised for normal schools are the easiest and most reliable, these are to be adopted and used in all German schools in both Our capitals, in Riga, Reval, Vyborg, and in other Governorates wherever such schools are needed; and therefore the teachers to be appointed therein in future are obliged to be trained in that method, either at this chief normal German school of St. Peter, or at one being established under its administration on the same basis elsewhere, or at another similar one established under the supervision of the Commission on the Establishment of Public Schools. We do not forbid the local chief normal school to retain the classes already established in it beyond the general plan, or to add such others as circumstances may require, provided that for the teaching of all these classes no methods other than those proper to normal schools are adopted, and that all arrangements likewise be drawn from the same source. For better supervision and management We establish at the St. Petersburg chief German school a special directorate, or board, over all public schools of the German language in Our Empire, composed of the warden of the Lutheran Church of St. Peter, of its two preachers, and of the overseer of the normal school attached to this church, adding to them one further member of the same confession, and appointing to this position at present Our Active Chamberlain Count Munnich. This directorate, or board, is to be subordinate to the Commission on the Establishment of Public Schools, from which it is to receive special instructions concerning the details of that directorate's duties, to which it is to submit for resolution any doubtful cases, and through which, where necessary, to request Our commands. The chief efforts of this directorate, or board, must be directed toward the speediest composition and publication of school textbooks for use in all public schools of the German language. These books must, as far as possible, correspond to those introduced or to be published for the Russian public schools, differing only in language; the printing thereof We reserve exclusively to the said directorate, for its own benefit and that of the schools under its supervision. We hereby confirm anew, in its full force, the charter granted by Us to the Lutheran Church of St. Peter and to the school established thereat, commanding that to this directorate, or board, there be added, by the choice of the church assembly, one further member of that assembly, who, under the supervision of the school directorate, managing the treasury and economic affairs, shall report on everything pertaining to his portion and shall have a vote therein.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXI. Pp. 1006-1007.*

## No. 25. DECREE OF CATHERINE II ON THE ORGANIZATION OF THE VOLGA COLONISTS (1785)

16,223. — July 10. Nominal decree, given to the Acting Governor-General of Saratov and the Caucasus, Potemkin. — On various measures concerning the organization of the Saratov colonists.

Having examined your reports on the Saratov Namestnichestvo (Vicegerency), We command: <...> 2) The sum expended on supplying the colonists of Saratov Governorate is to be regarded as a debt owed by them; and as to the collection of it, the Director of Economy is, after inspecting their condition, to make an assessment through the Treasury Chamber of how much they may pay annually toward that debt without undue hardship, and you shall then submit this to Us with your opinion thereon for DOCUMENTS___________________________________________________________________________________<Я

Our final decision. 3) If, upon inspection by the Director of Husbandry, it is found that among the lands allotted to the colonists there are some unsuitable for tillage and farming, other, more suitable, vacant crown lands are to be designated for their resettlement in place of these; but no further loan of treasury funds whatsoever is to be made to them henceforth. 4) The treasury debt outstanding on the colony called Sarepta, amounting to 48,748 rubles and kopecks, is to be arranged for payment so that, by paying six percent from the beginning of the coming year 1786, they shall, through these very payments, return the principal to Our treasury. <...> We remain, moreover, ever graciously disposed toward you with Our Imperial favor.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXII. Pp. 426-427.*

Published in: Nemtsy-kolonisty v Vek Ekateriny [German Colonists in the Age of Catherine] / Compiled by E.E. Lykova, M.I. Osekina. Moscow, 2004. Pp. 148-151.

## No. 26. DECREE OF CATHERINE II ON THE RESETTLEMENT OF COLONISTS FROM YAMBURG DISTRICT TO EKATERINOSLAV GOVERNORATE, ON PRIVILEGES FOR THE YAMBURG COLONISTS, AND ON PAYMENTS BY THE SHLISSELBURG COLONISTS (1793)

17,147. — August 17. Nominal decree, given in St. Petersburg to the Vice-Governor. — On the resettlement of 270 souls of colonists from Yamburg District to Ekaterinoslav Governorate; on the addition of arable land for the colonists remaining in that district; on granting them a five-year exemption, and on placing them, after that time has passed, on the same footing as the Izhora colonists with respect to the payment of taxes.

Having examined the report submitted to Us by the St. Petersburg Treasury Chamber on the condition of the Shlisselburg and Yamburg colonists, We have deemed it proper to satisfy those wishing to resettle from Yamburg District, numbering 273 souls of male and female sex. We have entrusted to the care and direction of Our Lieutenant-General Count Zubov the task of sending them from their present dwellings in the spring of the coming year 1794, and settling them in Ekaterinoslav Governorate, providing him with the sums necessary for this; and We command you: 1. To permit these resettlers to sell for their own benefit the houses and other structures belonging to them in their present places of residence, as well as other property which they cannot take with them. 2. The thirty-six families of colonists remaining thereafter in Yamburg District, having been satisfied with the arable and hay-mowing land and forest lands they requested, amounting in all to five hundred and nine desyatinas, are to be given a five-year exemption; upon its expiration, they are to pay annually the same tax as the Izhora colonists, at 30¾ kopecks per desyatina. 3. The treasury arrears owed by the Yamburg colonists, now grown to 137,493 rubles 85 kopecks, are not to be collected from them, owing to their extreme poverty and the unsuitability of the land on which they had been settled. 4. From the Shlisselburg colonists, pursuant to an obligation voluntarily undertaken by them, taxes are to be collected annually into the treasury for the land at 918 rubles 75 kopecks, and in addition 300 rubles toward payment of arrears, from which, however, 3,871 rubles 18¾ kopecks attributable to unsuitable land are to be excluded.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXIII. P. 454.*

## No. 27. DECREE OF PAUL I ON THE SETTLEMENT OF MENNONITES IN NEW RUSSIA (1797)

17,813. — February 17. Nominal decree, announced by the Procurator-General. — On the settlement of Mennonites in New Russia Governorate.

His Imperial Majesty has been Most Highly pleased to command: that the Mennonites resettling in New Russia Governorate — both all those who have already crossed over, who are to be satisfied in full measure with the benefits promised them, and those who shall cross over in future, who are to receive the same reliably. These resettlers are also to be given to understand that it is His Imperial Majesty's pleasure that such people should go forth to settle in the aforementioned Governorate.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXIV. P. 339.*

## No. 28. REPORT ON THE ST. PETERSBURG COLONISTS, CONFIRMED BY PAUL I (1797)

18,006. — June 20. Most Highly confirmed report of the Expedition of State Economy, Guardianship of Foreigners and Rural Husbandry. On levies from the St. Petersburg colonists; on satisfying them with land at 30 desyatinas per tiaglo (household labor-unit); on establishing practical instruction in agriculture for the settlers; on the propagation of the potato in Russia; on the establishment of artificial meadows; and on the non-resettlement of colonists to other Governorates.

Report. In undertaking active care for the foreign resettlers, primary attention has been directed to the colonies situated in St. Petersburg Governorate, which, by virtue of their location, are subject to the direct observation of the Expedition, and are to serve as an example of good order and rural husbandry, so that, in accordance with the beneficent intentions of Your Imperial Majesty, all the foreign colonies settled in Russia may be brought into a better condition.

For the most reliable and detailed knowledge of the colonies of this Governorate, in addition to the notifications and inquiries received by the Expedition, one of its Members, Active State Councillor Khitrovo, was commissioned to make a personal inspection, to go into the particulars of their husbandry, to identify their shortcomings, and to compile a detailed description, which is hereby most humbly submitted to Your Imperial Majesty. In this Governorate there are four colonies: the first, in Sofia District on the great Tsarskoye Selo road, founded in 1765; at its settlement 19,335 rubles 14 kopecks were expended; it has 22 households, in which there are now 86 male and 93 female souls. By agreement, 660 desyatinas of land were to have been allotted to them; but only 524 desyatinas are in their possession, of which one and a half desyatinas per household are plowed in the field, and the same amount behind the households for potatoes, while the rest of the land is under a small pasture, forest, and meadows. By the agreement they were obliged, after the passage of 10 years, to pay 1 ruble 22½ kopecks for each desyatina, and to repay the debt, after the 15 exempt years, over the following five years; but owing to their insolvency, by the Nominal decree of November 13, 1793, it was ordered that 61 kopecks be collected from them for every desyatina of suitable land; and toward payment of the debt, 10 rubles per household; which payment they have made without arrears from DOCUMENTS___________________________________________________________________________________ 63

1792, that is, 322 rubles 26 kopecks for land, and 220 rubles for the loan, 542 rubles 26 kopecks in all. And by this reckoning, each colonist pays 6 rubles 30 kopecks per year.

The second colony, Izhora, was settled in two villages in 1765, the first with 12, the second with 16 households, and in both there are now 106 male and 810 [108?] female souls. 25,234 rubles 91¼ kopecks were expended on their establishment. They were to have been allotted 840 desyatinas of suitable land, but 1,340 desyatinas were surveyed for them under the designation "suitable," of which only a small part is fit for tillage; up to 1½ desyatinas per household in the field are allotted, after setting aside land for planting potatoes. By agreement they were obliged to pay the land tax and repay the debt on the same basis as the Tsarskoye Selo colonists, and, by reason of an equal insolvency, the same decree of 1793 prescribed that 30¾ kopecks be collected from them per desyatina in land tax, and 5 rubles per household toward repayment of the loan, which they have paid into the treasury without arrears since 1792; that is: from 840 desyatinas, 258 rubles 30 kopecks in land tax, and 140 rubles in debt payments, 398 rubles 30 kopecks in all; consequently each colonist owes 3 rubles 75 kopecks per year.

The third colony, called Saratovka, has existed since 1765 on the bank of the Neva River; it has 60 households, in which there are 227 male and 231 female souls. 78,297 rubles 86½ kopecks were expended on the settlement; they were to have been allotted 2,100 desyatinas of land, but they received into their possession only 1,656 desyatinas of suitable land, of which 1½ desyatinas per household are plowed in the field, and the same amount under potatoes. By the agreement they were obliged to pay, after the passage of 10 exempt years, land money at 1 ruble 22½ kopecks per desyatina per year; and to repay the sums issued as a loan, after those same 10 years, over the following 6 years; however, owing to their lack of means and the accumulation of arrears, in 1793, on August 17, by Nominal decree issued upon the report of the Treasury Chamber, the voluntary consent of these colonists was confirmed, whereby they would pay land money for 1,500 desyatinas deemed truly suitable at 61¼ kopecks per desyatina, and toward payment of the loan money and prior arrears, 5 rubles per household; in fulfillment of which, since 1792 they have paid into the treasury properly and without arrears 300 rubles, and 918 rubles 75 kopecks in land tax, so that per soul it comes to 5 rubles 37 kopecks per year, without small fractions. Active State Councillor Khitrovo notes that the resettlers of this colony are less prosperous than the others, and their households are in worse repair, a considerable cause of which may be regarded as the crown tavern situated there. The Expedition most humbly requests the Most High command of Your Imperial Majesty for its removal from the Saratovka colony, together with an instruction for the future that no crown taverns be established in any of the colonies in St. Petersburg Governorate.

The fourth colony, Yamburg, was founded in 1767 in three villages, in which there were 92½ families; of these, pursuant to the aforementioned decree of August 17, 1793, issued upon the report of the Treasury Chamber, owing to the scarcity of land suitable for tillage, 272 souls of both sexes were resettled to Ekaterinoslav Governorate, so that in all three villages there now remain 22 households, in which there are 81 male and 63 female souls; 81,970 rubles 38¾ kopecks were expended from the treasury on the establishment and transport of these settlers; they were to have been given 35 desyatinas per household, 3,237½ desyatinas in all, but they were allotted 2,927 desyatinas of land of various quality, and now, among those who remain, only 509 desyatinas are considered suitable. These colonists were obliged by agreement to pay, after the passage of 13 exempt years, 1 ruble 22½ kopecks per desyatina, and to repay within three years the money expended on them, after 10 exempt years; however, the complete impossibility of this given their condition prompted the instruction in the aforesaid decree that, following the resettlement to Ekaterinoslav Governorate, the colonists remaining behind should be satisfied with land, given a five-year exemption, after which they would pay a tax equal to that of the Izhora colonists, at 30¾ kopecks per desyatina, and that the treasury debt, together with arrears, amounting to 137,493 rubles 85 kopecks, should not be collected from them. Thus, at the proper time, they will pay 156 rubles 51¾ kopecks in land money, and each colonist will owe 1 ruble 93¾ kopecks per year.

There is a sufficient quantity of forest attached to these colonies, with the exception of Yamburg, where almost all of it has been destroyed. At the first, on the Tsarskoye Selo road, there is also timber forest divided into 22 plots according to the number of households, while the firewood forest is held in common by the whole colony, from which 8 sazhens per household are cut in the month of February. In the possession of the Izhora colony there is little timber forest, from which the necessary quantity is issued to each family by communal decision; from the firewood forest, 8 sazhens per household are cut in February. At Saratovka the firewood forest is divided into 60 plots, and each household is permitted to cut 4 sazhens of three-log firewood in February.

From all the circumstances most humbly described here for Your Imperial Majesty, the Expedition concludes, from the conduct of former matters relating to the St. Petersburg colonies, that if to this day they have not brought the State the benefit that was hoped for at their establishment, this arose chiefly from the failure at that time to examine in due detail both the actual needs and the means employed to that end. The very construction of the settlements now existing shows how little thought was given to their agricultural condition and to providing the means for rural husbandry. The unsuitability and insufficiency of the lands allotted to them are the cause of the non-return of treasury funds expended without due examination. The innocent settlers established here, laboring diligently by the strength of their hands in the sweat of their brow, are unable within a year's time to extract from the land a tax worthy of their Sovereign and provisions for their own subsistence. A single glance from Your Imperial Majesty, as Father of the Fatherland, will revive these toiling people.

On this unshakeable foundation the Expedition most humbly submits the following opinion: 1. Would it please Your Imperial Majesty, having Most Graciously confirmed the present tax payments of the St. Petersburg colonies according to the latest decrees, to permit the Expedition, at a time convenient for these colonists and upon a perceptible improvement of their condition, to endeavor to bring their land assessment, on the principles Most Highly confirmed by Your Imperial Majesty concerning appanage estates, first to a third, and then to a half, of the annual income from each desyatina of arable land, assuming an ordinary grain sowing, an ordinary harvest, and ordinary grain prices. 2. That the Expedition examine the accounts by which the treasury debts charged to those colonies have been calculated, debts known to it only from summary statements, and that, by force of Your Imperial Majesty's Most High confirmation, it might seek out and demand payment wherever traces of them are found. 3. Having regard to the proximity of the colonies to the Capital of Your Imperial Majesty, to arrange matters so that no less than 30 desyatinas of land fall to each tiaglo, distributing it as follows: 4 desyatinas for the homestead, vegetable garden, and potatoes; 3 desyatinas for plowing in each of the three fields; and 17 desyatinas for meadows, forest, pasture, and for the increase of families until the next census. Such an abundant quantity of land, if it cannot be worked by the colonists themselves for lack of hands in the colony, may afford the opportunity to establish practical instruction in agriculture for the settlers. Foreign resettlers, having brought the art of husbandry from their homeland and having learned by experience to apply it to our climate and the nature of our soil, could serve as instructors for laborers sent to them for training by landowners and dispatched from crown villages. A sufficient quantity of land would permit various experiments toward the further propagation of the potato in Russia and toward the establishment of artificial meadows hitherto unknown among us. In this the Expedition must without fail see to it that each tiaglo actually works its thirteen desyatinas. 4. A consequence of this may be the resettlement of some of these colonists to new lands, but only in accordance with their own voluntary wishes; for which purpose a statement received by the Expedition from the Department of the Surveying Senate is appended here. 5. Without this, the inconvenience already observed will arise, namely that not only those summoned and settled, but also the tillers newly born, will turn to trades or crafts unrelated to agriculture; of which there is evidence in the description of Active State Councillor Khitrovo appended here. 6. Although the resettlement of colonists who wish it is attended by expenses that will inevitably be required, which will not be recovered except from future revenues from them, the colonists remaining in St. Petersburg Governorate after the resettlers' departure will not reduce the treasury taxes by the number who have left, because they pay not per soul but according to the quantity of land in their use. 7. Having freed the St. Petersburg colonies from various present departments, for closer and more convenient oversight of them and for administration corresponding to their actual benefit, to appoint over them an overseer or manager dependent solely on the Expedition, who, overseeing rural policing, internal good order, and a faithful accounting of State taxes, could impart practical instruction in agriculture, animal husbandry, and rural economy, conducive to the enrichment of the settlers and proven by actual experiments. 8. The manager appointed to the St. Petersburg colonies, being answerable for everything, is obliged to remit all treasury dues without arrears to the District Treasuries or to other proper offices, so that the colonists need have no dealings whatsoever with the District Treasurer, the Rural Commissioner, or the Ispravnik (district police officer). 9. Concerning everything pertaining to his duties, and concerning various circumstances and incidents that occur, the manager must at all times report to the Member of the Expedition having special charge of the St. Petersburg colonies.

Such is the opinion which the Expedition most humbly submits for the Most High Sovereign consideration, and awaits the All-Highest decree of Your Imperial Majesty.

Resolution. The colonists are not to be resettled to other Governorates, but are to be satisfied with the proportion of land laid down, in the Expedition's opinion, out of the adjoining and nearby crown tracts; as for everything else set forth in this report, it is to be carried out and observed.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXIV. Pp. 666-669.*

## No. 29. CHARTER OF PAUL I TO THE SAREPTA COLONY IN THE VOLGA REGION (1797)

18,011. — June 20. Charter to the Sarepta colony. — On the confirmation of its former rights and privileges.

By the Grace of God. We, Paul the First, Emperor

and Autocrat of All Russia, and so forth, and so forth, and so forth.

Yielding to the petition of the colony of Sarepta, which has existed for 33 years on the Volga River near Tsaritsyn, settled by the Brethren of the Evangelical Society of the Augsburg Confession, distinguished by exceptional industry, careful husbandry, good conduct, and exemplary behavior, We have been Most Graciously pleased, by this Our Imperial charter, not only to confirm all their former rights and privileges, but also, in order to arouse in them yet greater zeal for industry and the continuation of the useful establishments they have begun, and to instill in other foreign settlers a desire to emulate them, to grant them further new benefits, set forth in the following points:

1. We confirm the freedom granted to that Brotherhood to practice their faith according to the statute, doctrine, and rites universally observed among the Evangelical Brethren, with Our Most Gracious permission that, in judicial places, an oath may be taken from members thereof, should need require it, according to their custom, consisting solely of a verbal affirmation, excepting only the oath of allegiance to citizenship, which they must render uniformly with all Our loyal subjects.

2. We confirm to this Society the indisputable and perpetually hereditary possession of the lands allotted for the Sarepta colony and confirmed in due course by survey, together with all appurtenances belonging to them, as well as the land newly granted by Our decree of December 30, 1796, situated between the Healing Spring and this colony, for which plans and the necessary documents are to be issued from the proper quarter, extending this right not only to the present and actual possession of all lands hitherto granted, but equally to those which shall in future be lawfully added, on the condition, as previously established, that from these lands, belonging not to any individual but to the whole Society, not the smallest portion, under whatever pretext, is to be ceded, sold, or made the subject of any deed of conveyance.

3. To establish, on lands belonging to the Brotherhood, towns, boroughs, and settlements of every kind; to build churches with bell towers and the use of bells; to establish public schools and such houses where, according to the spiritual rite of the Evangelical Brethren, they may make all arrangements corresponding thereto, and to maintain both young children and adults of both sexes, keeping the male and female sexes separate within the communal household until the time of their entry into marriage, on the basis of the rules observed by the Brethren; but of such newly undertaken establishments and institutions notice is to be given to the Expedition of State Economy, Guardianship of Foreigners, and Rural Husbandry. Herewith is also confirmed the freedom to lay roads through unpopulated places adjoining their lands, for travel to neighboring settlements and to nearby rivers, according to their own needs and discretion, provided, however, that the laying of roads through lands belonging to private owners depends on the will and consent of the owner of those lands, and We hereby most strictly enjoin that neither roads already laid nor those newly to be laid are to be damaged.

4. To conduct legal proceedings in accordance with their own jurisdiction and to enjoy their customary right of inheritance, having, as previously established, their own special assembly consisting of two chiefs elected by the Society, one Justiciary, and three Assessors, We Most Graciously granting to this body the dignity and authority of a court instituted by Us, under the name of the Administration of the Evangelical Brotherhood Society, which is permitted to have its own seal and, with respect to its relations with other government offices, is to be regarded on an equal footing with municipal Magistracies, save that it is not subordinate to any government office by virtue of its location, nor may any of the military or civil authorities appointed by Us appropriate to himself any personal authority over it or interfere in its affairs, but that Administration, together with the whole colony, shall remain under the authority of the Expedition of State Economy, Guardianship of Foreigners, and Rural Husbandry, and shall render an account of its affairs to it alone; and as an Office of Guardianship of Foreigners is now being established at Saratov for the closer care and oversight of all the foreign colonies situated in Saratov Governorate, near which the Sarepta colony also lies, that colony, being always kept separate from the other colonists by virtue of its special rights, is entrusted specially to the guardianship solely of the chief Judge of that Office, subordinate to the Expedition of State Economy, Guardianship of Foreigners, and Rural Husbandry. The Sarepta Administration is to exercise its jurisdiction in civil matters of every kind, excluding criminal matters; for although, on the basis of many years' experience of the good conduct and honesty of the Evangelical Brethren, it cannot be supposed that any of them might fall into a serious criminal offense, yet should this, contrary to expectation, occur, such an offender shall no longer be subject to the judgment of the Brotherhood, but, under secure guard, must be delivered up and brought to trial in the district nearest the colony, for proceeding against the guilty party according to the general laws of the State.

5. To all the Brethren now living in the colony, as well as to those who shall in future come to settle there, We Most Graciously grant all rights of citizenship, not only in their colony but throughout Our whole Empire, permitting them, jointly or each individually, to conduct internal and foreign trade, with payment of duties according to the tariff, and not compelling the Brethren to enroll in the Russian merchantry, as they are exempted from the taxes and service pertaining thereto and are free to engage in any crafts, trades, and occupations, to establish and maintain any factories, manufactories, and works; to build mills of every kind; by right of possession, to freely and unhindered enjoy in their tracts all appurtenances, fishing, hunting, and fowling; to brew beer and distill grain spirits, both for their own use and for sale to travelers and those temporarily residing in their colony, provided that neither wine nor beer is exported or sold outside the lands belonging to the Brotherhood; but grape wines, brandy made from them, and any fruits and beverages steeped in grape (not grain) wine, are permitted to be transported from the colony for free sale in all Russian towns.

6. On the lands belonging to the Brotherhood Society, We forbid the building of eating-houses, taverns, salt warehouses, and any crown or private structures, or the settling there of any outside persons without the Society's consent; but if the Brethren should wish to receive someone to live with them temporarily or permanently, this is permitted them, provided only that the persons received have lawful written documents; but should they receive persons from among other colonists, notice thereof is to be given to the Expedition of State Economy, Guardianship of Foreigners, and Rural Husbandry. As for the provisioning of the Brotherhood Society with salt, they may purchase it from the treasury and sell it as prescribed in the Salt Statute.

7. We confirm the former provision that the chiefs of the Brotherhood shall issue passports to the Brethren for travel within the State, but for travel abroad and for entry from abroad, passports shall be issued to them, upon application by their established Administration, from the same office from which such passports are issued to others leaving and entering Russia.

8. We assure them, upon Our Imperial word, that none of the Brethren now living in the aforementioned Society, nor those who shall settle there hereafter, nor their children and descendants, shall at any time be taken or enrolled into military or civil service without their own desire to that effect. We likewise exempt forever all their towns, villages, boroughs, hamlets, and houses throughout the entire State from every kind of billeting and quartering, from the maintenance of postal stations, the provision of relay horses, and from other similar obligations; but when someone is sent to their colony on some matter by the Expedition of State Economy, Guardianship of Foreigners, and Rural Husbandry, or when someone is sent from the place where they reside, or from a nearby Governorate, for a necessary inspection or some verification, the Brotherhood Society must provide such persons with temporary lodging free of charge.

9. We Most Graciously grant to all the Brethren of this Society and their posterity full freedom and authority to dispose of their own property at the will and discretion of each; but should anyone of the present Brotherhood or of future generations wish to leave Russia with all his property, he must pay a three-year tax on the capital acquired in Russia, in whatever amount is conscientiously declared by their chiefs. On this same basis is to be dealt with the property of deceased Brethren whose relatives and heirs reside in foreign lands, when it is to be sent there by right of their inheritance, provided that the chiefs of the Brotherhood first pay off the crown and private debts of the deceased. But should anyone die without leaving heirs and without having made a will, his property is to be given into the possession of the Brotherhood Society of the whole colony, without any exaction therefrom to the treasury, provided only that the Society pays off all debts left by the deceased.

10. We permit the Brotherhood Society to maintain at all times in St. Petersburg one of the Brethren in the capacity of Agent, for the conduct of business for the benefit of the Society, and the house granted to the Brotherhood in that city for the Agent's residence, and more particularly for divine worship and for lodging Brethren arriving temporarily from the colony, is exempted from billeting and other police duties, on an equal footing DOCUMENTS___________________________________________________________________________________69

with the houses of other clergy and church officials of the Protestant confession.

11. We confirm the exemption granted to that Brotherhood from the payment of taxes until January 1 of the coming year 1806; upon the expiration of this term, these are to be collected not from each of the Brethren individually, but from all of them collectively through their chiefs, on the basis of the arrangement previously made in this regard, at 25 kopecks per year for each desyatina of suitable land, not excluding from this the newly given land, situated between the Healing Spring and the Sarepta colony, which We have Most Graciously granted to the Brotherhood; the collection of the treasury debt remaining on the Brotherhood is to be arranged so that, paying six percent per year, five of these percent shall be credited toward payment of the principal, and the sixth percent toward the sum remaining in debt.

12. In conclusion of this Our Imperial charter granting Most Graciously the rights, privileges, and liberties to the Society of the united Evangelical Brethren, We command all Our military and civil Chiefs and government offices not only to leave this Brotherhood Society and their descendants undisturbed in the peaceful possession of the dwellings, lands, and appurtenances belonging to them, and to place no obstacle to their enjoyment of all the privileges granted by Us, but, should the need arise, to protect them from any losses and harm that might befall them, and, upon application by the Administration established among them, to render every assistance, defense, and protection.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXIV. Pp. 671-675.*

Published in: Sarepta / Compiled by I.R. Pleve. Saratov, 1995. Pp. 77-82.

## No. 30. DECREE OF PAUL I ON GRANTING THE VOLGA COLONISTS THEIR MISSING LAND (1797)

18,263. — December 4. Personal decree, given to the Senate. — On surveying out to the colonists settled in Saratov the missing quantity of land.

According to the proposal of the Expedition of State Economy, Guardianship of Foreigners and Rural Husbandry, that for each revision soul the colonists settled in Saratov be given 20 desyatinas of land, we command: the missing quantity of that land, amounting according to the general calculation of souls to 63,954 desyatinas, is to be surveyed out at the forthcoming land survey of Saratov Governorate from state unoccupied lands, which may most conveniently be attached to the colonies lacking land; and since some of these settlers have an excess quantity beyond this established proportion, whatever amount is cut off from them during this survey shall be placed under the direct department and disposal of the aforementioned Expedition, adding to this also, by surveying from unoccupied lands, 6,331 desyatinas, so that the Expedition, in accordance with Our will, may have land ready for a thousand families, in case similar foreigners should wish to resettle anew.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXIV. P. 815.*

## No. 31. REPORT ON GRANTING THE VOLGA COLONISTS ARABLE LANDS, CONFIRMED BY PAUL I (1798)

18,305. — January 4. Most highly confirmed report of the Expedition of State Economy, Guardianship of Foreigners and Rural Husbandry. — On satisfying the Saratov colonists with lands suitable for grain farming.

Report. Your Imperial Majesty has been most highly pleased to command this Expedition to examine a petition submitted in the All-August name of Your Majesty by the attorney Genz on behalf of the Saratov foreign colonies of Nizhnyaya Dobrinka, Ust-Kulalinka, Buydakov Buyerak, Krestovy Buyerak, Vodyanoy Buyerak, Verkhnyaya Kulalinka and Verkhnyaya Dobrinka, complaining against the Saratov Treasury Chamber for having taken from them and let out on lease a lake and fishing grounds that had been in their possession for more than 20 years.

To carry out this Most High will of Your Majesty, the Expedition instructed the Office of Guardianship of Foreigners to investigate this matter on the spot, and having clarified it, to present to the Expedition all the circumstances thereof. In consequence, the Guardianship Office requested from the Saratov Treasury Chamber the information needed for this matter and the contract by which the lake and fishing grounds requested by the colonists had been let out on lease. Then, upon examination of the documents and the explanations submitted by the aforementioned colonists, to whose petition two further colonies, Shcherbakovka and Gryaznukha, had also joined, it was found that this lake and these fishing grounds, located in Kamyshin district, indeed lie—according to the register of the former Guardianship Office's Overseer of Surveyors, Collegiate Councilor Reuss, of the wastelands surveyed out to the colonists from 1769 to 1774—within those wastelands which, over and above the lands assigned to the colonists, had been allotted to them for haymaking and timber-cutting for a term of ten years; upon the expiry of that time they were further extended for 5 years, and the colonists held them until 1791. Although by rescript given to the acting Governor-General of Saratov, then Lieutenant-General Potemkin, on June [July] 10, 1785, it had been prescribed to satisfy settlers in need of land from state unoccupied and quitrent lands as suitable, and in consequence it had been assigned to the aforementioned colonies—whose land, upon inspection by the Director of Economy, proved for the most part unsuitable for grain farming—to leave in their possession those ten-year wastelands in exchange for the unsuitable land, which was proposed to be cut off to the treasury; while the colonies of Shcherbakovka and Gryaznukha, which had no outlying wastelands, were to be given suitable state lands, the former along the Shcherbakovka River and the other from the environs of the town of Kamyshin—however, this was not only not carried out, but those very wastelands were assigned by the Saratov Treasury Chamber to other quitrent items, and in 1791 were let out on a four-year lease to Councilor Zetler, mentioned in the colonists' petition, from whom, for lack of their own land, those colonists rented both land for grain farming and the fishing grounds, at a quitrent. In 1795 those same wastelands were again let out for four years to the Volsk [Volskii?] merchant Epifanov, at a price of 311 rubles a year. And upon the proposal of the aforementioned former Governor-General Potemkin, 1,262 desyatinas from those same wastelands were assigned to be allotted to Zetler in perpetual possession; but these have not yet been surveyed out, and by the Most High decree of June 5, 1797, are to be taken back into the treasury.

Your Imperial Majesty has been most graciously pleased to look upon the long-defenseless condition of the foreign settlers established in Your Majesty's Empire, prescribing, upon the establishment of the Expedition of State Economy, Guardianship of Foreigners and Rural Husbandry, that it maintain observation and care over the foreign colonies: wherefore it considers it its duty to submit, regarding the circumstances set forth here, its most loyal opinion, which, if honored with All-August confirmation, ought to serve as a general rule for restoring the well-being of all the Saratov colonies and for the treasury benefit expected of them: 1) that, at the survey ordered in Saratov Governorate, the colonists be satisfied with the most suitable lands, on the basis of point 8 of the Instruction to the Office of Guardianship of Foreigners, most highly confirmed by Your Imperial Majesty on June 30 [1797], where it is prescribed that, as the Kursk Land Survey Office has been ordered transferred to Saratov Governorate for the general resurveying there, the Office must ensure not only that the lands presently belonging to the colonies be protected from any unlawful claims, but that for each soul according to the latest census 20 desyatinas be surveyed out, making up the shortfall from unoccupied state lands most suitable for those colonies. 2) To allot to them, as convenient, also from those lands which had been designated for distribution and which, by the decree of Your Imperial Majesty of June 5 of this year 1797, are to be taken back into the state department; for by that decree it was ordered: of the lands of the state department distributed in Saratov Governorate during the recent period up to 1788, those which have already been given to owners and surveyed out to them are to remain in their possession, while the remaining lands beyond these are to be taken back into the state department and their distribution halted. 3) Also to give the colonists, from the quitrent lands together with the fishing grounds located on them, those which prove suitable upon the expiry of the contract terms, provided there is no special provision in them for the return of the lands before term, on the basis of the report submitted by the Senate and most highly confirmed by Your Majesty on September 26 of this year 1797, in point 2 of which, among other things concerning quitrent items in estates most highly granted in hereditary possession and Commandery estates, it is established: that those (quitrent items) which are under lease, and in whose contracts concluded with the lessees there is no provision that the treasury may reclaim them even before the expiry of the term of those contracts, shall be left with the lessees until their completion; but where such a provision is included in the contracts, there the Treasury Chambers, having received the said quitrent items from the lessees, shall give them to the owners. 4) All such lands, once surveyed out to the colonies in the proportion assigned to them by the aforementioned Instruction, that is, 20 desyatinas for each revision soul, shall be excluded from quitrent. On which the Expedition most loyally requests the Most High Decree of Your Imperial Majesty.

Resolution. Let it be so.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXV. P. 5-7.*

## No. 32. DECREE OF PAUL I ON USING THE COLONISTS' DEBT FOR THE NEEDS OF THE COLONISTS (1798)

18,490. — April 21. Personal decree, given to the Senate. — On directing the state debt owed by the colonists toward the establishment of their own well-being.

The state debt owed by the colonists settled in the Governorates of St. Petersburg, Livland, Saratov, Sloboda Ukraine and Little Russia, incurred for loans made to them at the time of their settlement, We are most graciously pleased to direct toward the restoration of their own condition. And therefore, entrusting the collection thereof to the care of the Expedition of State Economy, Guardianship of Foreigners and Rural Husbandry, We command: that it, taking into its disposal the moneys received in the past year and those to be received hereafter, make appropriate use of them from the general fund at its discretion: by lending the necessary amount to needy settlers for useful undertakings in husbandry, by providing assistance in cases of misfortune befalling them from fires, cattle plague and other unforeseen and unavoidable calamities; and thereby, in accordance with its duty, contribute in every way to the establishment and organization of the colonies on the soundest and most orderly economic footing.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXV. P. 214.*

## No. 33. PLAN OF THE PROTESTANT UNIVERSITY IN DORPAT, CONFIRMED BY PAUL I (1799)

18,953. — May 4. Most highly confirmed plan of the Protestant University in Dorpat.

Personal decree, given to the Senate. — Returning for due execution the plan of the Protestant University submitted to Us together with the report of the 3rd Department of Our Senate, and confirming the Senate's opinion on its establishment in Dorpat, We most graciously command: that, in encouragement and furtherance of it, there be assigned and allotted, at the discretion of the Governor-General of Livland and Estland, for its benefit in Dorpat the requisite quantity of land and a state building. And upon its establishment and opening, when all its parts shall have taken effect and been brought into successful operation, then Our Senate, for the further support of this useful institution and in token of Our attention to it, having chosen as convenient 100 Livland hooves of land, shall submit to Us a report on their confirmation to this institution, on condition that they remain in its possession for as long as it continues in operation and prosperity.

Report. The Active Privy Councilor and Prosecutor-General Prince Lopukhin announced on November 30, 1798, that Your Imperial Majesty was pleased to command that various drafts relating to the establishment of a Protestant University in the Russian Empire, and the project on this same subject by Court Councilor Schubert, be examined together with the plan of the deputies of the Courland, Estland and Livland Knighthoods, and that, having made the appropriate determination thereon, a report be submitted to Your Imperial Majesty.

DOCUMENTS___________________________________________________________________________________73

In execution of this Most High will of Your Imperial Majesty, the Senate examined these, and found the plan of the deputies of the Courland, Estland and Livland Knighthoods to be more adequate, sound and advantageous than the others, though still requiring certain exceptions and additions; wherefore it made certain changes therein, and in this final form has the honor of now submitting it to Your Imperial Majesty with the following most loyal report appended thereto.

The Courland Knighthood designated the town of Mitau as the most convenient place for founding the University; but the Senate, in agreement with the submission of the Livland and Estland Knighthoods, gives preference to the town of Dorpat: for it lies almost in the middle of the three said Governorates; its location is on dry ground, whereas Mitau is surrounded by marshes; it uses Russian coin and assignats, and moreover surpasses Mitau in the cheapness of provisions: consequently it can better provide means for parents of modest means to place their children in the proposed institution.

For the maintenance of the University, at which a Theological Faculty is also to be established in place of those Seminaries whose foundation Your Imperial Majesty was pleased to command be left in abeyance until the establishment of the University, 56,050 rubles are required annually; the Senate, mindful of the considerable size of such a sum being placed upon the three Knighthoods, and having regard to the benefit which this institution, under the protection of Your Imperial Majesty, will bring not only to them but to the whole Empire, and being encouraged above all by the Most High decree of Your Imperial Majesty of April 9, 1798, in which You were pleased to promise Your Most Sovereign support for this University, takes the liberty of most loyally proposing whether Your Imperial Majesty might not be pleased to grant the University the requisite quantity of vacant land together with any building unneeded by the treasury, should such exist in the town of Dorpat, and in addition a further hundred state Livland hooves upon the expiry of their lease term, and until that time to direct to the benefit of the University all the revenues which the Crown now receives from them: these revenues, by approximate calculation, reckoning in assignats two rubles for a yefimok, one ruble 40 kopecks for a silver ruble, and 5 rubles per quarter of rye, will amount in all, with the fifth part added under the decree of December 18, 1797 upon leasehold estates, to 18,350 rubles, a sum incomparably smaller than what the maintenance of the Lutheran Theological Seminaries would cost.

The construction of buildings for the University, the collection of funds for its maintenance and the disposal thereof are left to the joint care of the Knighthood of the said Governorates, from their own capital.

Finally, the Senate considers it its duty to lay at the feet of Your Imperial Majesty the most loyal petition of the three Knighthoods for Your Most Gracious permission, in undying memory of Your Most Sovereign favor toward them, to name this University after its August Founder: the Imperial Pavlovian University. For the rest, the Senate, submitting all this to the discerning consideration of Your Imperial Majesty, will await the Most High decree.

Plan of the University.

Section I. — On the purpose of the establishment of the University.
