§ 1. The University is established for the whole Russian Empire, but especially for the Knighthood of Livland, Estland and Courland.

§ 2. It is permitted to admit to it also persons of other social ranks, on the basis of the practice of the Imperial University of Moscow, as well as foreigners.

Sect. II. — On the privileges of the University.

§ 3. Since this University is established by the Most Sovereign will of His Imperial Majesty, it is granted the right to be called the Imperial University.

§ 4. The University is subordinate to the Senate alone; while the Professors, students and all other University officials and servants shall be under the disposal of the University in all matters, except Police, Civil and Criminal ones.

§ 5. All University buildings and the private houses of Professors and other University officials in which they themselves reside are exempt from billeting.

§ 6. University Professors, Teachers and their children are exempted from all personal taxation.

§ 7. The Knighthood of Livland, Estland and Courland is permitted to form among themselves a Collegium of Curators for the selection and summoning of Professors and for particular care of the University.

§ 8. The Collegium of Curators is obliged, with the participation of the University Council, to compose rules for the order and good governance of the University, to submit them to the Senate for confirmation, and thereafter to take every care for their unfailing observance.

§ 9. The University Council consists of all the Professors of the University and a Secretary for keeping the minutes.

§ 10. The Council must meet twice a year for the mutual proposal of various measures serving the benefit of the University; for the scheduling of lectures, and shall report on all this afterward to the Collegium of Curators; extraordinary sessions it shall hold only at the invitation of the Curators and the Prorector.

§ 11. The University, in the event of correspondence with judicial places, shall communicate by means of official communications; while to the Senate the Collegium of Curators makes submissions and sends reports, and receives decrees from the Senate.

§ 12. The whole University and each of its Faculties is permitted to have its own seal.

§ 13. The University may confer Doctoral and Master's degrees.

§ 14. It shall have its own Printing House and a special Censorship Commission for its own writings, which shall act according to the same rules as are prescribed by the Government for other Censorship bodies.

§ 15. All Professors, Deans and the Prorector are to be considered, during the exercise of their office, in the same ranks as similar officials are placed in the Imperial Academy of Arts.

§ 16. For the honoring of superiors at public University ceremonies, the Prorector, Deans and Faculties are permitted to use the distinctions customary in German Universities.

§ 17. In order to avert luxury and division by nationality of origin, from which coldness and even discord not infrequently arise among pupils in foreign schools,

DOCUMENTS___________________________________________________________________________________ 75

it is prescribed that Professors, Teachers and students wear a special uniform, to be designated hereafter, with the exception of provincial officials.

§ 18. Students who have studied at this University are to be admitted to civil service upon recommendation and examination, on the basis of the decree of December 16, 1790, and appointed to the ranks of Registrar and the like.

§ 19. Professors and Teachers summoned from foreign lands are permitted, at their own discretion, to leave Russia, and to take their property with them without any duty; the same right is held for three years by the widows and children remaining after the death of Professors and Teachers; moreover, the former, that is, the widows, upon the death of their husbands, also receive from the University treasury a widow's year, meaning by this the annual income of their deceased husband.

§ 20. If anyone belonging to the University dies without heirs and leaves no will concerning his property, the University must give notice that heirs come forward to receive that property, and set them terms on the basis of the laws issued for such a case; and if by such notices no heir of the deceased comes forward within the term, then that property is to be added to the University's capital.

Sect. III. — On general University regulations.

Ch. I. — On the Collegium of Curators.

§ 21. The Collegium of Curators consists of three enlightened men. The Knighthood of Livland, Estland and Courland elects them, at the time appointed by them for their assemblies, one from each Governorate, and submits them for confirmation in that rank to the Senate.

§ 22. Each Curator has a Substitute from his Governorate, who takes his place when necessary.

§ 23. The Collegium of Curators always convenes two weeks before the end of the regular lectures, at the place where the University is located.

§ 24. The chairmanship of this Collegium changes annually by lot at the close of the sessions.

§ 25. The Collegium of Curators sends to the Senate the regular semi-annual and extraordinary notifications and the submissions concluded by the Assembly.

§ 26. The Collegium of Curators selects and summons Professors, Teachers and servants at its own discretion, regardless of anyone's intercession, and without failing to examine the moral qualities of those it appoints.

§ 27. Should disagreement arise among the Curators in choosing one of the candidates proposed by them for a vacant position of Professor or Teacher, then the Assembly permits the Faculty for which a Professor or Teacher is being chosen to exclude one, and of the remainder the Curators choose by majority vote, and in this manner proceeding also in other cases.

§ 28. Professors and students, though they freely make use of the library, do so under the disposal of the Curators.

§ 29. The Collegium of Curators watches over the manner, order and clarity of instruction, and each Curator is to answer personally that the Professors and Teachers, especially those of the Theological Faculty, do not depart in their teaching from the rules of the Augsburg Confession; it is also obliged to prevent and suppress the spread of principles contrary to State enactments.

§ 30. If any of the students should be found adhering to bad principles, ill-behaved or negligent in study, the Collegium, if it has no hope of correcting him by fatherly admonition, shall expel him.

§ 31. Likewise, upon prior resolution of the Council, the Collegium removes from office those Professors or Teachers who are found negligent in the duty of their calling and of scandalous conduct.

§ 32. It examines the schedule of lectures for the coming half-year and ensures, as far as possible, that all necessary subjects are taught.

§ 33. It assigns, for diligence, the distribution of Stipends (an institution maintained at Universities to support poor students) among poor students, should such Stipends be established at the University.

§ 34. The Curators are obliged to draw to the University, and to ease the path of further education for, those who have obtained degrees and distinguished themselves by talent.

§ 35. The Collegium of Curators supervises the management of the treasury and all University institutions.

§ 36. It examines proposals submitted by the Teachers for the augmentation of the library, cabinet, instruments and the like, and confirms decisions on supplying the University with these at the expense of its revenues.

§ 37. It also has principal charge of the University building, its repair and expansion.

§ 38. It appoints and designates, from among the various Faculties of the University, Censors for the University's own writings, and obliges them to the exact fulfillment of the instructions given them.

§ 39. At each semi-annual session, the Collegium convenes a general assembly of all the Teachers for the examination of various proposals relating to the good and benefit of the University.

§ 40. At each new election of a Curator, the outgoing one must inform his successor of all matters pertaining to his office; if the latter notices any omission on the part of his predecessor, he is obliged to report it immediately; otherwise he shall himself be held answerable.

§ 41. The Collegium of Curators, in difficulties arising within the University which it cannot resolve itself, refers them to the Senate.

§ 42. And during the recess of sessions, entrusts the administration to the Vice-Curator.

§ 43. In order that the regulations of the University be observed and executed with full exactness, all three Governorates are to send to the University, every six years, at an appointed time, one Deputy each, to form a Commission whose duty it shall be to examine the administration of the Curators and to look into the state of the whole University.

§ 44. And in the event of any complaints against the Curators, an extraordinary Commission is also to be appointed, which, upon conducting an inquiry, shall report to the Senate.

Ch. II. — On the Vice-Curator.

§ 45. The Collegium of Curators elects by majority vote one of its members as Vice-Curator, who is obliged to furnish a surety for the sum of 5,000 rubles; should disagreement arise among the Curators in this election,

DOCUMENTS___________________________________________________________________________________77

then one of the Candidates is excluded by lot, and of the remaining two the Vice-Curator is chosen by majority vote.

§ 46. The Vice-Curator is elected for no fixed term, and upon entering his office is obliged in writing to discharge it conscientiously and according to instructions, and if the Collegium of Curators is unanimously dissatisfied with him, he must relinquish his rank without bringing a complaint against the Collegium.

§ 47. He is always to remain at the University, and may not be absent anywhere without the permission of the Curators, and must carry out with full exactness the instructions given him by the Collegium.

§ 48. In the sessions of the Curators he has no vote, but only makes submissions and reports.

§ 49. He is entrusted by the Curators with one of the three keys to the treasury, the disbursement of all sums, and the oversight that these be entered in the account books.

§ 50. In case of illness or absence, he may, with the consent of the presiding Curator, entrust his office, on his own responsibility, to another.

Ch. III. — On the Prorector.

§ 51. The Prorector changes annually among the Professors in order of Faculties; and no one may discharge this office a second time until the turn has passed to all the Professors.

§ 52. Every Professor whose turn it is to become Prorector has the right to decline, provided only that he presents reasons that will be deemed valid by the Curators.

§ 53. The outgoing Prorector, upon relinquishing his rank, must deliver a speech before the assembly and describe in it the duties of his successor; and the latter, having given a solemn promise to observe them, concludes the ceremony, now in his new dignity, likewise with a speech.

§ 54. The Prorector presides over the University Council, enrolls all students and announces to them their duties, receives from them a promise to fulfill these, and gives them a matriculation certificate together with a printed copy of the University Statute.

§ 55. He ascertains from each student entering the University which Faculty he wishes to be enrolled in, and thereupon receives from them for the matriculation certificate: from students of Theology 10 rubles each, and from the rest 20 rubles each; of the sum collected from students entering the University, the Prorector receives only one-fifth, while four-fifths are credited to the University treasury.

§ 56. He is obliged to see that only the assigned lectures are given to enrolled students.

§ 57. For the augmentation of the library, instruments and the like, every newly enrolled student is permitted, but not required, to make a contribution at his discretion, and such a sum is to be entered in a special receipts book and kept by the Prorector himself.

§ 58. He keeps a monthly record of the sums received and enters them only upon receipt from the Curator.

§ 59. He holds one of the three keys to the treasury.

§ 60. He keeps the great seal of the University.

§ 61. He grants permission for disputations (debates) and may refuse it only until the next session of the Curators.

Ch. IV. — On the Secretary.

§ 62. There shall be at the University one Secretary and one Adjunct, chosen by the Curators.

Ch. V. — On the Faculties.

§ 63. The following Faculties are established at the University: Theological, Juridical, Medical and Philosophical: all the ordinary Professors of one Faculty together form a special Collegium of the Faculty.

§ 64. Theological lectures for the Lutheran confession are to be given in accordance with the Augsburg Confession, and the Professors must take an oath that all their lectures, in expounding Holy Scripture, will be based on the rules of the said Confession.

§ 65. Members of all the Collegia of the Faculties must hold a Doctoral or Teaching degree.

§ 66. In each Collegium of a Faculty the chair is held by a Dean; he is elected by seniority from among the ordinary Professors for one year.

§ 67. In case of a tie vote, he has the right of decision.

§ 68. Should a Professor, in the year when it falls to him to be Dean, be assigned the dignity of Prorector, and should he accept this office, in such case he shall not assume the post of Dean until after the passage of two years, so that he may, in the second year, like the Ex-Prorector, be a Member of the University Council.

§ 69. All Deans sit on the University Council.

§ 70. Every Dean has the right to convene the Members of his Faculty whenever he sees fit.

§ 71. Each Faculty, after a preliminary examination by disputation and after a public examination, confers, with the consent of the Collegium of Curators, Academic degrees and the right to give lectures.

§ 72. No one may become an extraordinary Professor without having obtained Academic degrees and having conducted a public disputation in Latin.

§ 73. Of the fees assigned by the Collegium of Curators, with the participation of the Faculties, for promotion, a third part belongs to the University treasury, and the other two-thirds are divided at the discretion of the Faculty.

§ 74. If in a given year there is no promotion, then, by agreement of the Faculties, a disputation is to be held.

§ 75. At all public disputations, others are permitted to be admitted to raise objections as well.

§ 76. The Dean keeps the accounts of the Faculty's revenues, holds its seal, and issues patents for University degrees.

§ 77. Every half-year the Faculties draw up the schedule of lectures and submit it, through their Dean, to the University Council.

§ 78. All Faculties are to endeavor that every half-year there be an assembly, and at that time to give instruction in practical compositions.

§ 79. Each Faculty is also to establish a lecture in Methodology (on the order of the science) for each subject, for the benefit of those students who enroll during the semi-annual vacations.

§ 80. The Medical Faculty is to see diligently that a member thereof give a special lecture annually, so that a student preparing himself in due course to become a rural Priest may be able to help his parishioners in illnesses and instruct them in the prevention thereof.

DOCUMENTS______________________________ ______________________________________________ 79

Ch. VI. — On the necessary Professors and Teachers.

§ 81. In the Theological Faculty there shall be three ordinary Professors and a fourth extraordinary Professor.

Ordinary Professors. 1) Dogmatics and Theological Moral Doctrine. 2) Exegetics and Oriental languages. 3) Church History and Theological Literature. 4) Extraordinary Professor of Homiletics and Pastoral Theology.

§ 82. In the Juridical Faculty there shall be 4 ordinary Professors. 1) Positive State and national law. 2) Civil and Criminal law. 3) The laws existing in the Provincial and Baltic Governorates, as well as Russian law. 4) Practical jurisprudence.

§ 83. In the Medical Faculty there shall be six Professors. The 1st, Physiology and Pathology. The 2nd, Therapeutics and Clinical medicine. The 3rd, Anatomy and Medical science. The 4th, Surgery and all branches of obstetric science. The 5th, Botany and Materia Medica. The 6th, Chemistry and Pharmaceutics.

§ 84. In the Philosophical Faculty there shall be eight Professors. The 1st, Theoretical and practical Philosophy. The 2nd, Pure and applied Mathematics. The 3rd, Mixed Mathematics and Military science. The 4th, Natural History. The 5th, Theoretical and Experimental Physics. The 6th, Economics, Cameral science, Statistics and forestry. The 7th, Aesthetics, Latin and Greek eloquence and antiquities. The 8th, Universal History and Geography, especially Russian.

§ 85. Besides the Professors, there are to be the following Teachers: of the Russian language. Of French. Of English. Of Italian. A Master of the Horse. A Teacher of Fencing and Vaulting. Of Drawing and Dancing.

Ch. VII. — On the appurtenances of the University.

§ 86. At the University there shall be: a library under the care of a librarian chosen from among the Professors and an assistant; a natural history cabinet under the care of the Professor of Natural History; an Observatory with astronomical instruments belonging to it, a collection of mathematical and physical instruments and models under the care of the Professor of Mixed Mathematics; a clinical institute of 14 beds, under the care of the Professor of Therapeutics; a Surgical hospital of 10 beds, under the care of the Professor of Surgery; an obstetric institute of 6 beds, under the care of the same Professor, to which afterward a school of obstetric science is to be added; for these last three institutions an Overseer, a Steward and the necessary number of male and female servants are to be appointed; a Botanical garden, with a gardener and an assistant and the necessary number of workers; an anatomical theater, at which there must be a Prosector with two servants; a chemical laboratory under the supervision of the Professor of Chemistry, and in addition a riding school, under the care of the Master of the Horse, at which the necessary number of grooms and 8 horses are to be kept.

§ 87. There shall also be at the University an Architect with a clerk and two servants.

Ch. VIII. — On the order of instruction.

§ 88. Every Professor is obliged, during the half-year, to deliver one lecture free of charge, and at least two private ones.

§ 89. All semi-annual lectures must be finished and concluded shortly before the beginning of the vacations.

§ 90. The University is to have two vacations; the Curators must determine, once and for all, when they are to occur and how long they are to last.

§ 91. Private instruction by Professors shall be given for one hour per day, following the practice of other Universities, four times a week, namely on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Friday, while on Wednesday and Saturday a Professor may teach without charge; as regards payment by the students, the following distinction is established: for Theological lectures, which usually have the greatest number of students, many of them without means, no more than 8 rubles is to be charged; for Philosophical theoretical lectures, which everyone wishing to study Theology must attend, 8 rubles; for practical lectures, among which Medical lectures are to be counted, 10 rubles is to be charged, and for Legal lectures, which for the most part only Noblemen attend, and consequently in smaller numbers than the others, 12 rubles for half a year.

§ 92. Professors and private Teachers are permitted to give lectures on any subject, following a preliminary disputation, without written permission and recommendation from a Member of the Faculty; provided, however, that lectures pertaining to matters of faith shall not be given until after the Professor has taken the oath prescribed in § 64, that in the teaching of the Lutheran faith he will adhere to the Augsburg Confession.

§ 93. Every practicing Physician may give clinical lectures, and any Physician who has been awarded a degree may, for the benefit of students of the other 3 Faculties, give medical lectures, without requiring anything for this beyond his salary.

§ 94. Professors are obliged to notify the Curators of those students who frequently fail to attend lectures.

§ 95. In delivering their lectures, Professors must observe order and clarity; they must not omit explanations even of the most basic foundations of the subject, and must not merely read from a book or dictate their lectures, but must strive to explain them from memory as well, so as to produce a greater impression.

§ 96. The Professors of the Theological Faculty are to select a certain number of the most capable young men who have dedicated themselves to Theology, after preliminary examination, and form from them a Theological Seminary; each of them must, in turn, weekly, at midday, deliver a sermon in church and teach the catechism to those studying at the University.

§ 97. Further provisions on this matter are to be made in due course by the Professors of Theology and submitted for the approval of the Curators, who must, funds permitting, provide the seminarians with some assistance as encouragement.

§ 98. The Professor of practical Philosophy and the Professor of Aesthetics, Roman and Greek Literature, must, from among the most capable and willing young men, after preliminary examination, form a Philosophical Seminary, and, following arrangements approved by the Curators, teach without charge to the young men of their Faculty instruction in the liberal arts and fine sciences in general, as well as the particular knowledge needed by a school Teacher.

§ 99. The purpose of this Seminary shall be to supply skilled school Teachers for instruction in the liberal arts and practical sciences; the Curators are therefore obliged to assist this institution as much as possible, and to provide assistance to these seminarians from surplus funds. DOCUMENTS___________________________________________________________________________________81^

§ 100. All books needed for the University that are ordered from foreign countries must first be submitted for review by the established Censors.

CH. IX. — On the University treasury.

§ 101. Income from all capital designated for the University, as well as other income assigned or to be assigned in the future, shall accrue to the University treasury.

§ 102. At the end of each half-year, salaries for the past period are to be paid out of this treasury.

§ 103. The treasury shall be under the supervision of the Vice-Curator, the Pro-Rector, and the Professor keeping the accounts; each of them shall have a separate key to the treasury, and none may withdraw money from it without the knowledge of the two others. The Curators are to appoint the Professor for this purpose, and for his additional labor in this regard, he is to be given a small share of the sum collected from students for entering them on the roll.

§ 104. These persons shall meet at least once a week to verify the accounts.

§ 105. Every receipt and expenditure is to be entered in the bound ledger and cleared with receipts.

§ 106. Disbursements are to be made either according to a schedule of payments designated and certified by the Curators, or by special allocations of the Curators, excepting minor needs for the maintenance of buildings, for which the Vice-Curator is authorized by the Curators.

§ 107. Every half-year the accounts are to be closed, signed by the three aforementioned Keepers of the treasury, and submitted to the Curators, who, upon review, issue receipts, verify the treasury, and make arrangements regarding the sum remaining after expenses.

Sect. IV. — On the establishment (staff and budget) of the University.

§ 108. Model schedule of the sum required annually for the maintenance of the established University.

(See the book of establishments.)

## No. 34. REPORT OF THE SENATE ON MEASURES TO IMPROVE THE CONDITION OF THE NEW RUSSIA COLONIES, CONFIRMED BY PAUL I (1800)

19,372. — April 6. Report of the Senate, confirmed by the Emperor. — On the proposed means for improving the condition of the New Russia foreign settlers and on the establishment, under the Department of State Economy, of the Office of Guardianship of New Russia Foreign Settlers.

Report. The Department of State Economy and Guardianship of Foreigners reported to the Senate that, in the course of its duty of looking into the condition of the foreign settlers, it had noted various omissions and disorders in the slow organization of the New Russia colonies, and therefore considered it necessary to send there a reliable person who would examine in detail the economy of these settlers, report on their exact condition, and present means for the speediest improvement of their state. Only by this means did the Department hope to arrive at the truth needed for a proper resolution regarding them, both as concerns their economy and the recovery of monies expended on them by the Treasury, since the information received about these foreigners up to that point had been unclear and insufficient, and time had been wasted on mere correspondence. Having chosen for the execution of this task the Counselor of the Geographic Department, Court Counselor Kontenius, it requested Your Imperial Majesty's Highest permission for his dispatch, pursuant to which, furnished with instructions, he traveled there, examined everything with due precision, brought the confused accounts into order, and presented an accurate description of the settlers' situation and plans of their settlements. From his description it is evident that the situation of the foreigners in New Russia Governorate began in 1787; as they arrived in Russia, according to their confession and way of life, they arranged their dwellings by establishing separate colonies. Some of them emigrated under contracts previously concluded with the Treasury, while others were placed on the same footing as other settlers of New Russia Governorate. They are located in various places and are now known under the name of Mennonites in general and the colonists of Josephstal, Danzig, Swedish, and Yamburg.

I. The Mennonites emigrated from Prussia and the environs of Danzig beginning in 1789, in 228 families. Through Deputies they had beforehand requested special privileges for themselves, which were confirmed by the Emperor as follows: 1) freedom of religion; 2) the grant of land to each family of 65 desyatinas opposite Beryslav [Berislav] along the Konka River, together with a part of the island of Tavan lying nearby for haymaking, and a part of the forest on Kairy Island; 3) ten years' exemption from all taxes; 4) after the expiry of this exemption, permanent payment of 15 kopecks per desyatina, with exemption from providing horses/carts, labor obligations, and billeting, except for the passage of troop detachments and the proper maintenance of roads and bridges within their holdings; 5) freedom to establish factories, trade, and enter guilds and corporations in accordance with the Municipal Statute; 6) payment of 500 rubles to each family for establishment, within 5 months of arrival in Riga, to be repaid after the expiry of a 3-year exemption; 7) the taking of an oath according to their own custom; 8) exemption from military service; 9) the grant to each family of 120 four-sazhen logs and the necessary quantity of timber for two mills, as well as six millstones; 10) payment of money for travel and maintenance en route; 11) the provision of horses and carts from the border to Beryslav, and payment from the day of arrival at the border until the end of the journey, for each person over 15 years of age, of 25 kopecks per day, and for those under, 12 kopecks per day; 12) payment of 10 kopecks per day per person from the day of arrival at the place of settlement until the first harvest, to be repaid over 3 years after the expiry of the exemption; 13) the issuance of various seeds for sowing, to be repaid in due time; 14) the issuance of orders that no offense be done to them. In addition, they requested exemption from repayment of the money to be spent on them en route under points 10 and 11; but the reply given was that this depended on the Sovereign's Highest will. Upon their arrival in New Russia Governorate, instead of the lands designated in the agreement along the Konka River, they were allotted for settlement the tract of Khortitsa, lying on the right bank of the Dnieper River together with the island of the same name, where they founded 8 villages. After that, on the same privileges, other Mennonites arrived in Russia at various times, and from 1793 to 1796 DOCUMENTS___________________________________________________________________________________83

118 more families arrived; 86 of these, having waited more than two years for the designation of a place for their settlement, were compelled to settle among the previously arrived Mennonites in the Khortitsa villages; the remaining 32 settled in two separate colonies, one of 17 families in Pavlograd uyezd under the name Schönwiese, and the other of 15 families in Novomoskovsk uyezd under the name Kronsgarten. The Mennonites are almost all, in general, orderly and tidy in their home life, sober and honest in morals, and diligent and industrious in husbandry; but those living in Khortitsa, despite all their industriousness, can hardly ever attain a good condition. The terrain of this tract consists for the most part of elevated ground, where, owing to the dryness of the soil, lack of moisture, and absence of rain, the grass burns up, the grain grows poorly, and often the ploughman tills and sows his field in vain, so that from agriculture he not only gains no benefit but very rarely can even feed himself with his own grain for a whole year. Livestock-raising alone brings them some benefit; they engage a great deal in this branch of husbandry, having brought with them a sufficient number of foreign-breed horses and cattle, but owing to a lack of pasture and hay they cannot expand this as they would wish and are accustomed to, and moreover lose in harsh winters a considerable part of what they are currently able to keep. The crowding of their settlement in a place that yields no proper benefit is the chief cause of these hardships, and, in addition, on the part of the Treasury, the excessively slow and piecemeal satisfaction of them, out of keeping with their privileges and conditions; for the sums, disbursed in very fragmentary and small portions, owing to the long delay in settlement, served them only for bare subsistence and to this day have deprived them of the means to establish themselves properly, so that many houses to this day are either poorly built or unfinished, while 38 families do not have any at all. Under these circumstances they will be unable either to pay the land dues or to repay, at the appointed time, the money lent to them. This description is consistent with the petition submitted in 1799 to Your Imperial Majesty by their representatives for the easing of their lot, which, by the Highest command, was forwarded to the Senate for consideration.

II. The colonists of Josephstal emigrated in 1789 together with the Mennonites of the first emigration, in 90 families, of the Lutheran confession. It is not evident from the records whether any conditions were made with them, but by the Highest rescript given to Major-General Kakhovsky on June 2, 1792, it was ordered that they be satisfied with a loan half that given to the Mennonites. They were settled in Novomoskovsk uyezd as a separate colony under the name Josephstal, whose location is very good, the land beneath it most fertile, and the pastures lush; in short, this colony is so situated that the Colonists have every means to live in abundance, but unfortunately only some of them are in a good or middling condition, while the rest, having formerly in their homeland been artisans and day-laborers, and not knowing how to engage in farming, pay little attention to it, are negligent in husbandry, and remain poor and poorly established.

III. The Danzig colonists were recruited by Collegiate Counselor Trappe in 1787 and 1788, numbering 510 male and 400 female souls. Of this considerable number, Court Counselor Kontenius found only 111 male and 97 female souls, scattered among the Swedish and German colonies in Crimea and in Kherson, the rest having either died or dispersed of their own accord. It is not known on what terms they were recruited, but in the Highest rescript given to Major-General Kakhovsky on June 2, 1792, it is stated among other things concerning them: that as regards the exemption they should enjoy the ten-year exemption granted in Ekaterinoslav Governorate (which had already expired in 1797); and that of the money spent on them, only that sum owed on those still present should be repaid. Those living in Crimea, 10 male souls, and in Kherson, 27 male souls, earn their living either by a trade or by hired service in private households. In Kherson only three families have their own houses; their owners, through good conduct, labor, and diligence, obtain adequate support; others, such as cloth-dyers and a paper-master, who were recruited under contracts for factories but were not taken on at them, and who did not receive the satisfaction stipulated in those contracts, suffer want owing to the difficulty of practicing their trades and subsist on day-labor, while the greater part, owing to bad conduct and intemperance, are often left without food or footwear. 21 families, consisting of 41 male souls, form a separate colony called the German colony, settled in Elisavetgrad uyezd. These colonists, except for seven heads of household who were formerly artisans, sailors, or servants in private households, diligently engage in farming and in rainy years gather sufficient grain, but in the droughts that commonly occur there they sometimes even lose their seed; the condition of these colonists is such that they obtain with difficulty only a meager subsistence, and some, through their own negligence, do not even have daily bread; to these hardships may be added the lack of good water: that found in the ponds fills with worms in summer and acquires a bad smell; although no manifest illnesses have been observed from its use, that it is unhealthy may be concluded from the fact that every year one or two more people die than are born. The 14 families settled in the Swedish colony consist of 28 male souls; although they have sufficient means to improve their condition, enjoying equal benefits with the Swedish settlers, only 2 families among them are prosperous and diligent, the rest being lazy, negligent in husbandry, and in poor condition. All these colonists, under the name of Danzig colonists, are subject to taxation on the same footing as all State peasants of New Russia Governorate.

IV. The Swedish colonists, or Swedish peasants, were transferred in 1787 from the island of Dagö. At the time of the transfer their number, according to the report of the New Russia Treasury Chamber, consisted of 904 souls of both sexes, who upon arrival founded, in Kherson uyezd not far from the town of Beryslav, a colony called the Swedish colony. Of this considerable number there now remain in the colony only 74 male and an equal number of female souls, forming 22 families, the rest having died either in the colony or on the road from illnesses arising partly from the change of climate and poor unaccustomed food, and partly from the lack of houses and shortage of other essential necessities. Subsequently, Swedish prisoners of war were settled in this colony, who, having declared their wish to remain subjects of Russia, were sent by Prince Potemkin in 1790, numbering 31 persons, of whom there now remain only 4 male and 5 female souls, forming two families, the rest having either died or fled. In this same colony there are also 14 families of Danzig colonists, explained above. The Swedish colonists and the Swedish prisoners of war are diligent and careful in farming and in husbandry generally. Their place of settlement is elevated, so that in dry years the grain burns up, so that often only the seed is recovered, and sometimes even that is lost; moreover, ground squirrels cause great damage to the fields; on the other hand, the pastures there are very good, and moreover these colonists engage successfully in fishing, from which they obtain a modest income. On what basis they were settled, the Treasury Chamber found nothing in its records; they are taxed on the same footing as all State peasants in that Governorate.

V. The Yamburg colonists were resettled in 1793 from those residing in Yamburg, in 57 families, numbering 273 souls of both sexes. At first they were placed among the inhabitants of the state settlement of Old Kaidak, where they lived for a year and eight months in complete want of everything needed, as a result of which, through illnesses that occurred, their number diminished to 239 souls. They now live as a separate colony under the name Yamburg, 17 versts from Novorossiysk [Ekaterinoslav]. Part of the land there is good and suitable, while another part is sandy and stony. But the condition of the colonists is very poor; their very clothing reveals their poverty and want. Not all of them engage in farming, for some have lost, through theft and disease, the livestock purchased for them from the Treasury, while others, reduced to poverty by illness, sold their livestock, so that 11 families, for lack of it, are unable to engage in farming; there are also many heads of household who, having previously earned their living by working at the Yamburg cloth factory and not being accustomed to farming, remain to this day poor farmers. An exemption of 10 years has been established for them for payment of the land tax, after which 5 kopecks per desyatina per year is to be collected until a further arrangement is made regarding the lands there; while repayment of the loan is spread over 30 years.

Most Gracious Sovereign! The Senate, having undertaken a precise examination and investigation of the condition of the New Russia foreign settlers, as well as of the conclusions drawn up by the Department of State Economy for the correction and improvement thereof, in agreement with that opinion, submits the following:

I. On the Mennonites. 1) Of the 314 families residing in the Khortitsa villages, 150 are to be resettled on other, more suitable land. But since, upon inspection of all the remaining vacant state lands in New Russia Governorate by representatives sent from the village of Kronsweide, which is situated in a very poor location, no lands suitable for settlement have been found anywhere, it will be necessary to purchase such land at the Treasury's expense; for the representatives of the Mennonites residing in St. Petersburg, when summoned before the Department of State Economy, declared that they were not able to make such a purchase at their own expense, which was also attested by Court Counselor Kontenius. The finding of lands to purchase is to be left to themselves; for experience has already shown that the selection of tracts for the settlement of foreigners without their consent is always a cause for complaints, however advantageous it may be. Once they have found suitable lands, the Department will be obliged to calculate the sum required, both for their purchase and for the loan absolutely necessary for the new establishment of the resettled Mennonites, for which the Senate proposes to use money collected from the colonists settled in St. Petersburg, Saratov, Livonia, Little Russia, and Sloboda Ukraine Governorates, in repayment of the debt which, by Your Imperial Majesty's Personal Highest decree given to the Senate on April 21, 1798, is to be placed at the disposal of the Department for the restoration of the colonists' own condition. And since, after the resettlement of the aforementioned 150 families, the tract currently held by the Khortitsa Mennonites will be in surplus for the remaining number of families, since each would then have as much as 120 desyatinas, it would have followed to satisfy the said Mennonites with the more suitable of it, allotting 65 desyatinas per family, and to take the remaining land into state administration; but since, after the better and more advantageous places have been allotted to the Mennonites, the worse lands would remain vacant, as no one would wish to take waterless steppe on lease, the Senate deems it more advantageous to leave the entire tract currently allotted to the Khortitsa Mennonites in their possession, on condition that they pay 15 kopecks for each of the 65 desyatinas allotted per family, according to their agreements, while for the remaining desyatinas, after the expiry of the exemption years, they pay 2 kopecks into the Treasury, following the example of the land tax paid by all State peasants of New Russia Governorate in general. To this arrangement the aforementioned representatives of the Mennonites have also given their consent. 2) Of the Mennonites to be resettled, should they so wish, 30 families are to be settled in the Swedish colony, where, according to the description, there is sufficient land for them, which, although likewise unsuitable for farming as at Khortitsa, has an abundance of hay on the low-lying land and fishing, which can provide the settlers with a good livelihood. 3) The village of Kronsgarten, situated in a very good location, needs only to be measured out an additional 561 desyatinas 270 sazhens of land, which it is proposed to cut from the district allotted to the Josephstal colonists, in which, after satisfying the latter with the proper proportion of land, there will still remain enough. 4) In view of the disadvantageous settlement of the greater part of the Mennonites, their insufficient means, and the precarious establishment resulting from the slow and untimely assistance rendered to them and the fragmentary disbursement of the necessary money, the Senate deems it necessary to request Your Imperial Majesty's Most Gracious permission for a Most Gracious postponement of the exemption years for those Mennonites who remain at their present place of settlement, for a further five years, and for those being transferred, for ten years, counting from the expiry of the first exemption periods, on condition that, after the expiry of this new exemption, they pay without arrears both the land dues, calculated at 15 kopecks per desyatina, and repay the loan by installments, those remaining in place over 10 years, and those being resettled over 20 years. 5) As regards the loan made by the Treasury to the Mennonites under the terms of the agreements concluded with them, relying on the accounting of Court Counselor Kontenius, the Senate reckons the Treasury funds expended on them to date, for the 228 families of the first emigration, at 238,203 rubles 93 kopecks, and for the 118 families of the later emigrations, at 142,771 rubles 18 kopecks. But since this debt includes the sum spent on travel expenses and maintenance en route, from payment of which the Mennonites requested exemption when presenting their conditions — to which it was then replied that this depended on the Sovereign's Highest will — taking into consideration the content of point 3 of the Highest Manifesto issued on July 22, 1763, concerning the summoning of foreign settlers, in which it is stated that, should "among the foreigners wishing to settle in Russia there happen to be some who do not have sufficient means for their journey, they may present themselves to Our Ministers and Residents at Foreign courts, by whom they will not only be immediately sent to Russia at Our expense, but will also be provided with travel money" — and although the Mennonites, recruited under special conditions, do not fall under this Manifesto, nevertheless, in view of their disordered condition and poverty, the Senate deems it necessary to submit, for Your Imperial Majesty's Most Gracious approval, the forgiveness of the aforesaid money spent en route, which, according to the report of the New Russia Treasury Chamber, amounts, for the Mennonites of the first emigration, to 1,202 rubles 27 kopecks, and for the second emigration, to 21,535 rubles 85 kopecks. 6) The representatives of the Mennonites, in the petition submitted in Your Imperial Majesty's name, requested the forgiveness of the debt to the Treasury reckoned against them in general; but since such a write-off would, on the one hand, cause the Treasury to lose irrevocably a considerable sum, and, on the other, might give the Mennonites being transferred to other places occasion to use the money due to them as a loan not for the useful and lasting establishment of their households, but for the satisfaction of temporary whims, in the hope that this money would not be recovered from them; therefore, to prevent such abuse, and in order to bring the Mennonites into a uniform position with all the other foreign settlers established in Russia, the Senate makes bold to most humbly request whether Your Imperial Majesty would deign to command that, upon collecting from the Mennonites, at the appointed terms, the sum owed, it be placed at the disposal of the Department of State Economy for the restoration of their own condition, on the basis of Your Majesty's Personal Highest decree given to the Senate on April 21, 1798, and that this be extended in general both to the Mennonites and to the colonists of New Russia Governorate. 7) In satisfaction of the Mennonites' petition, based on the promise made to their Deputies in 1787, that if their community were satisfied with the years and assistance set forth in the decision on the points they submitted, they would then also receive a charter of grant signed by His Imperial Majesty and bearing the State seal, the Senate makes bold to submit for Your Imperial Majesty's Most Gracious consideration a draft prepared for the composition of such a charter of grant, consistent with the conditions confirmed for them by the Highest authority, which contain their essential privileges, and with the Highest Manifesto issued in 1763 concerning the summoning of foreign settlers in general. 8) <...> For the better preservation among the settlers of good morals, order, and diligent attention to husbandry, the Senate deems it necessary to request Your Imperial Majesty's Highest command that taverns, drinking-houses, and the sale of spirits by the glass never be permitted in the Mennonite settlements, which, although they do not exist there at present, are, under the arrangement made by the New Russia Treasury Chamber, permitted to be established by tax-farmers in state settlements after the expiry of the exemption granted to the settlements; and such a prohibition, in satisfaction of the petition of the Mennonites' representatives, would be consistent with the similar measure enacted in a like case and confirmed by Your Imperial Majesty in the past year 1797 with regard to the St. Petersburg foreign colonies.

//. On the Josefsthal colonists. 1) From the surveyed usable land allotted to them, consisting of 3,970 desyatinas 1,558 sazhens, to satisfy each family with 32½ desyatinas, that is, half as much as the Mennonites, on the basis of the Highest rescript of 1792 given to Major-General Kakhovsky, which will make up 2,925 desyatinas for 90 families; from what remains thereafter to allot 561 desyatinas 270 sazhens to the Kronsgarten Mennonites, as stated above in the discussion of those Mennonites; 390 desyatinas for the Orel colonists, who will be discussed below, and 94 desyatinas 1,288 sazhens for the Pastorate. 2) Regarding the land tax that the Josefsthal colonists ought to pay, there is as yet no provision: for this reason the Senate, bearing in mind that they hold very good allotments, proposes to assess them at 15 kopecks per desyatina, following the example of how land money is set to be collected from the Mennonites. 3) Taking as a basis the calculation of Court Councilor Konteniуs regarding the money issued to the Josefsthal colonists, the Senate considers them to be in debt for 53,808 rubles 88¾ kopecks; but since this sum includes money spent on travel expenses and maintenance en route, then on the basis of the aforementioned reasoning on this same matter with respect to the Mennonites, the Senate deems it necessary to most humbly request the writing-off of the money spent on the Josefsthal colonists' journey as well, which the New Russia Treasury Chamber reckons at 1,721 rubles 53 kopecks. 4) In consideration of the same reasons for which the Senate proposed to most humbly request new years of exemption for the Mennonites, such should also be granted to the Josefsthal colonists, that is, for the payment of land money, upon expiration of the current exemption, five more years, and for the repayment by installments of the debt, after the new exemption expires, 10 years. 5) The construction of the church in the colony, though begun by the colonists, has not been brought to completion for lack of timber and money; but since, according to the report of Court Councilor Konteniуs, from the dilapidated buildings remaining from the government offices of the former town of Novomoskovsk, such a quantity of beams as is needed to complete that church can be obtained, the Senate proposes to request Your Imperial Majesty's Highest permission to grant, for the completion of that church, the necessary number of beams from those buildings, if they have not been designated for some other state use. 6) Regarding the craftsmen located in the said colony, who, according to the testimony of Court Councilor Konteniуs, since their arrival in Russia, having lived in towns and spent there all the money issued to them as a loan, appeared in the colony only recently: since these persons have never engaged in rural husbandry, and having neither the means nor the necessary knowledge to establish a household, their presence in the colony only increases disorder; and moreover the trades they practice pertain more to the needs of town dwellers than to the requirements of villagers, the Senate proposes, having expelled them from the colony, to furnish them with certificates with which they might register in whatever town and guild they wish. In the certificates issued by the colony elders, certified and sealed by the administrator of the colonies, it is necessary to specify how much state debt is reckoned against each of them, and when the new years of exemption are to end, so that after that time has passed it will be possible, in whatever town each is registered, to collect in due terms the payment by installments, as explained above regarding the debts of all the Josefsthal colonists in general. And since they are to be excluded from the jurisdiction of the Expedition of State Economy, the money collected from them must go to the district Treasury and the general state revenue. 7) Observing from the report of Court Councilor Konteniуs that a considerable cause of the poor condition of these colonists is the bad personal conduct of some of them, the depravity and idleness to which they give themselves over, the Senate considers it useful, in order to check such evil and to keep these colonists in better order henceforth, that four persons <...>, who by communal verdict of the best colonists have been found to be the most depraved and offering no hope of correction, having been excluded from the community and their property seized to cover the debt reckoned against them, being already convicted of depravity, be sent to the Court to be dealt with according to the laws. 8) In this colony there are 12 families of Orel colonists, who had been recruited by various landowners, and then moved to live with the landowner Naumann on the Orel River, whence they were named "Orel"; but in 1795 they were, at their petition, assigned by the New Russia Treasury Chamber to the Josefsthal colony and allotted 15 desyatinas per soul for their possession. Although these colonists received no assistance whatsoever from the treasury, they engage in farming in an excellent manner, and are soundly and well built up. At the last census they were placed under the same assessment as state peasants and pay taxes, both land taxes and others, not by family but by soul; they now request the granting of a ten-year exemption, exclusion from the poll tax, and the allotment of land equal to that of the Josefsthal colonists, at 32½ desyatinas per family. On the one hand, in reward for their diligence and industriousness in husbandry, to which Court Councilor Konteniуs testifies with high praise, and on the other for the greater benefit of the treasury from them, the Senate deems it necessary, having allotted them 32½ desyatinas per family, following the example of the Josefsthal colonists, to exclude them from the poll tax and assess them a land tax of 15 kopecks per desyatina, instead of the 2½ kopecks per desyatina that they currently pay, which will amount to a total of 390 desyatinas of land to be surveyed, as already stated above, from the surplus allotment of the Josefsthal colonists. As for granting them years of exemption, the Senate deems this unnecessary, both in view of their having long since been settled in place and because of their good condition. 9) For the Josefsthal colony, Pastor Kirchmann was recruited from Holland, to whom, according to the agreement made with him, confirmed by the Highest rescript of June 2, 1792, given to Major-General Kakhovsky, there was to be allotted land in perpetual and hereditary possession of 500 desyatinas, a loan from the treasury of 2,000 rubles without interest for ten years, and a salary of 400 rubles per year for the first 10 years, after which the colony and the villagers would be obliged to support the Pastor; but he was given neither the land nor the loan money at all, and even the payment of his salary was discontinued once the exemption years had expired. And since, meanwhile, on January 6 last, the said Pastor Kirchmann died, the Senate makes bold to most humbly present for Your Imperial Majesty's Highest Monarchical consideration its opinion: that since the aforesaid land, 500 desyatinas, had been designated for Pastor Kirchmann in perpetual and hereditary possession, it is necessary to grant it to his widow and children, now left without means of subsistence, leaving it to her to locate the designated number of desyatinas from state lands and to present this to the Expedition of State Economy in order to request Your Imperial Majesty's Highest command confirming it to her; as for the monetary loan of 2,000 rubles, the Senate does not consider it proper to issue it to her, because it was designated solely for her husband, and even then subject to repayment after ten years. 10) Since the colonists, owing to their poverty, are not yet able themselves to support a Pastor, the Senate makes bold to most humbly represent that, if it should please Your Imperial Majesty to confirm the granting of a further 5-year exemption to the colonists, it would be deemed just for the newly appointed Pastor to be paid from the treasury the former salary of 400 rubles per year until the expiration of the new exemption, after which all the settlements where he shall perform his duties will be obliged to support him.

///. On the Danzig colonists. 1) Taking as a rule the Highest rescript of June 2, 1792, that of the money spent on the Danzig colonists recruited in 1787 and 1788, only that sum should be collected which is due in respect of those actually present, out of the total spent, according to the accounting of Court Councilor Konteniуs, on all the colonists of 53,201 rubles 98¼ kopecks, it should be considered that the debt owed by the 111 souls found amounts to 11,579 rubles 24¼ kopecks, of which 104 rubles 31¾ kopecks falls to each; collection of this money ought properly to begin now, since the exemption years have ended; but since it is evident from the report made that these colonists are in an extremely poor condition and are by no means able to pay the sum owed by them within a short term, the Senate proposes to spread the collection of it from those located in Kherson, Crimea, and the Swedish colony over 30 years, counting from the time when this proposal shall be honored with Your Imperial Majesty's Highest confirmation. Thus, adding to this the ordinary taxes, there will accrue from each colonist per year a not inconsiderable levy, considering the indigence in which they find themselves. 2) Owing to the wholly unsuitable location of the German colony's settlement, it is recognized as absolutely necessary to move it to a more suitable place; but since no such state lands are available in the New Russia Governorate, land will need to be sought for purchase for these settlers as well, on the same basis as stated above regarding the Khortitsa Mennonites; and when this proposal is honored with Your Imperial Majesty's Highest Monarchical approval, then a decision will be made regarding the repayment of the state money spent on them and the collection of taxes. For now, the Senate proposes to exempt them from any payment whatsoever, since they cannot pay any state tax without utterly exhausting themselves. 3) Those located in the Swedish colony, having been provided 15 desyatinas of land per soul, should be assessed a land tax on the same basis as the Yamburg colonists, at five kopecks per desyatina. 4) Since those located in Crimea and in Kherson are for the most part either craftsmen or in service in private households, having no land, and cannot be considered settlers, they should be excluded from the jurisdiction of the Expedition of State Economy, which has the duty of caring for foreign agriculturalists settled in Russia and established in separate colonies. To these same foreigners the Senate proposes to grant the freedom to register in guilds in the towns; and in order that the state money spent on them may reliably be recovered from them, it should be affirmed that no one may hire them without passports; passports should be issued to them, valid for a year, from whatever town they wish to register in, with collection, together with the ordinary tax, of a portion of the state debt attributed to each of them of 104 rubles 31¾ kopecks, the repayment of which, as explained above, is to be spread over 30 years, and which is to be credited to the general state revenues. The same procedure should apply to those foreigners included among the number of Danzig colonists who had been recruited for the factories established in the New Russia Governorate but were not taken on at them. 5) Having proposed to collect from the Danzig colonists settled in the Swedish colony five kopecks per desyatina, on the same basis as the Yamburg colonists, exempting those of them settled in the German colony, owing to their indigence, from any payment, and finally granting the other foreigners, known under the name of Danzig colonists, the freedom to register in guilds in the towns, where the taxes due from them will also be collected, the Senate deems it necessary to exclude all these colonists from the poll tax pursuant to the Highest Manifesto of June [July] 22, 1763.

IV. On the Swedish colonists. Considering that, although before their resettlement to the New Russia Governorate they belonged to Russia, and therefore it would not be proper to consider them foreign settlers; yet since they were transferred from the island of Dagö to a region so far removed from their native land, and so different in climate; since they find themselves settled among a people differing from them in customs, religious law, and language, it is impossible not to regard them as colonists, to whom the care of the Expedition of State Economy ought to extend; the Senate proposes: 1) Following the example of the other colonists of the New Russia Governorate, to exclude them from the poll tax, from which they had also been free in their former place of residence, though they paid from the land; and to do likewise with the Swedish prisoners of war who declared their wish to remain Russian subjects and were settled together with the Swedish villagers. 2) Having allotted them 15 desyatinas per soul, to assess a land tax, as stated above regarding the Danzig colonists, of 5 kopecks per desyatina, the same as is ordered to be collected from the Yamburg colonists. 3) Taking as a basis the Highest rescript of June 2, 1792, given to Major-General Kakhovsky, regarding the collection of the state debt from the Danzig colonists, and in accordance with Your Imperial Majesty's Highest Personal decree of November 29, 1792, concerning the collection of arrears from the inhabitants of Astrakhan Governorate, out of the sum spent on this colony of 19,622 rubles 69¾ kopecks, and on the settlement of 31 Swedish prisoners of war of 352 rubles 1¼ kopecks, only the sum owed by those actually present should be collected, that is, from the colonists 3,006 rubles 37¼ kopecks, and from the prisoners 45 rubles 42 kopecks; payment of this debt should begin in 1800 in such a way that the Swedish transferees pay off the entire sum in twenty years, and the Swedish prisoners of war in ten years. 4) Although these colonists claim that they were granted a thirty-year exemption, since they were unable to produce any proof of this, and nothing conclusive can be found in the records of the Treasury Chamber, they must therefore make use of the ordinary ten-year exemption granted generally to all peasants transferred to the New Russia Governorate; wherefore, considering this exemption to have expired, the designated land money should be collected from them.

V. On the Yamburg colonists. 1) According to the accounting of the New Russia Treasury Chamber, 19,795 rubles are shown as spent on these colonists, but included in that sum are 100 rubles issued by Major Knoring, who was in charge of the construction of the colonists' houses, to the contractor Shadashnikov, and not used at all for the benefit of the colonists, and 124 rubles 85 kopecks passed to the contractor Borisenko, who built some houses and the church in the colony; these 224 rubles 85 kopecks, improperly passed on and not spent on the colonists, ought in justice to be written off the colonists and collected instead from those who, upon investigation, are found guilty of it. 2) Having thus excluded from the 19,795 rubles reckoned by the New Russia Treasury Chamber as owed by the said colonists the aforementioned 224 rubles 85 kopecks, there remains an actual debt owed by them of 19,570 rubles 15 kopecks, collection of which is to begin after the expiration of the ten years of exemption, collecting annually from each family 11 rubles 45 kopecks, whereby the entire debt, excluding the proposed new expenditures for the purchase of livestock and other items, will be paid off in 30 years, in accordance with the arrangement made on this matter at the time of this colony's resettlement. 3) Of the land held by the Yamburg colonists, having allotted 15 desyatinas per soul, the remainder should be given over to the possession of that colony's Pastorate; for after the expiration of the exemption years, the salary of 300 rubles per year currently received by the Pastor from the treasury will cease, and the colonists will have to support him themselves. 4) On account of the crop failures in 1794 and 1795, 377 chetverts of grain were issued to these colonists on loan from the Kaidak storehouse, for which the authorities of that Governorate subsequently ordered the collection of two parts in money, 1,700 rubles 35 kopecks, and the third part in grain, 125 chetverts 5 chetveriks and 2 garnets; but since these colonists, both owing to the newness of their settlement and because of the crop failures that occurred, are in a most dire condition, there is no hope that they will be able to pay the money assessed against them for this; wherefore the Senate makes bold to most humbly represent whether it might please Your Imperial Majesty to command, in the Highest degree, that the entire 377 chetverts issued to them on loan be collected from them in kind, spreading this collection over 10 years, which would be not burdensome for them and would make the recovery more assured for the treasury.

In view of all the foregoing proposals for the improvement of the New Russia settlers, the Senate, taking into consideration their disordered condition, in agreement with the conclusion of the Expedition of State Economy, deems it absolutely necessary that the designated resettlements and other arrangements, as well as their general administration—requiring, both because of the settlers' dispersal and because of their number, special attention and continual oversight in various places—be carried out by a separately established Office of Guardianship of the New Russia Foreign Settlers, under the jurisdiction of the Expedition of State Economy, which is to have its seat in Novorossiysk and enjoy equal privilege with Collegiate Offices; the Senate makes bold to submit herewith a sample staff establishment for it, for Your Imperial Majesty's Highest Monarchical consideration, reporting that it proceeds to this all the more for the following reasons: 1. That the Expedition of State Economy, in submitting last year, 1797, for Your Imperial Majesty's Highest Monarchical consideration the staff establishment and Instruction for the Saratov Office of Guardianship of Foreigners, most humbly reported that it considers it necessary, upon receipt of the expected information, to appoint, in proportion to the number of souls, special overseers of the colonies for other Governorates. 2. That for the maintenance of that Office the Expedition does not require a special sum from the treasury, but proposes that the 4,000 rubles designated for that purpose be set aside from the money accumulating from the collection of debts from the colonists, which, as mentioned above, has been directed by Personal Highest decree of Your Imperial Majesty toward the restoration of their own condition. As for the position of chief Judge of that Office, the Senate, upon the representation of the Expedition of State Economy, finds eminently capable and worthy the aforementioned Court Councilor Konteniуs, both because of his excellent qualities known to the Expedition and because of the detailed information about the New Russia settlers that he has already acquired; and as his associate, Director Brigonzi, currently serving with the New Russia colonies. In this connection, giving full credit to the boundless zeal and untiring diligence of Court Councilor Konteniуs, with which, adding labor to labor, he has carried into precise execution everything entrusted to him by the Instruction given by the Expedition of State Economy, and, continuing this work for an entire year amid constant travel from one colony to another, which caused him no small significant expense, has compiled a full, clear, and thoroughly sound description of them; and moreover, by two verifications of all the records, has brought into precise order, together with the Treasury Chamber, all the confused and laborious calculations concerning the sums of money spent on the foreign settlers in the New Russia and Little Russia Governorates, thereby assisting the Expedition in the drafting of the aforementioned regulation concerning them, for the purpose of making them henceforth useful to the State, the Senate considers it its duty to report this to Your Imperial Majesty, most humbly requesting the Most Gracious rewarding, both of him and of Titular Councilor Gavrilov, who served under him in handling the paperwork, with the next ranks; their service records are herewith submitted for Your Imperial Majesty's Highest Monarchical consideration.

For the rest, the Senate, submitting all of this to Your Imperial Majesty's Highest Monarchical gracious pleasure, most humbly requests Your Imperial Majesty's Most High Decree.

Resolution. Let it be so. <...>

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXVI. P. 115-128.*

## No. 35. INSTRUCTION FOR THE OFFICE OF GUARDIANSHIP OF THE NEW RUSSIA FOREIGN SETTLERS, CONFIRMED BY PAUL I (1800)

19,492. — July 26. Highest confirmed report of the Senate. — With the Instruction for the Office of Guardianship of the New Russia Foreign Settlers.

Report. In the most humbly submitted report of the Senate, confirmed by Your Imperial Majesty on April 6 of this year, concerning the proposed means for improving the condition of the New Russia foreign settlers, it was decreed, among other things: "The designated resettlements and other arrangements, as well as their general administration, are to be carried out by a separately established Office of Guardianship of the New Russia Foreign Settlers, under the jurisdiction of the Expedition of State Economy."

In fulfillment of this Highest Monarchical will of Your Imperial Majesty, the Expedition of State Economy composed a draft instruction for that Office, which it submitted to the Senate.

Most Gracious Sovereign! The Senate finds the said instruction to be in accordance both with the laws and with the instruction for the Saratov Office of Guardianship of Foreigners confirmed by Your Imperial Majesty on June 30, 1797, and with the establishment concerning the Imperial Family, and likewise consistent with the present condition of the New Russia foreign settlers; and therefore makes bold to most humbly submit it herewith for Your Imperial Majesty's Highest Monarchical confirmation.

<...>

Resolution. Let it be so.

Instruction for the Office of Guardianship

of the New Russia Foreign Settlers.

1. It shall administer all the colonies of foreigners located in the New Russia Governorate, shall exercise proper guardianship care and oversight, and shall attend to the economic arrangements pertaining to their present benefit and to rural economy.

2. The initial task of the Office's operation shall consist in bringing into precise and unfailing execution all the provisions contained in the report submitted by the Governing Senate, confirmed by His Imperial Majesty on the 6th day of April of this year 1800, concerning the proposed means for the correction and improvement of the condition of the New Russia foreign settlers, for which purpose it has been furnished with a copy of that report.

3. The Office, administering justice and settling disputes among the foreigners in the colonies according to the laws, must review and decide any matters arising between them and native Russian subjects of various estates jointly with the government offices established in the Governorate capital, dispatching, according to the nature of the case, the associate of the chief Judge to the District Court or Municipal Magistracy; but when a case comes up in the normal course, or by appeal, to the Chamber of Court and Settlement, then the Office shall form a joint session with that Chamber and decide the case by joint verdict; and in case of dissatisfaction, both sides may appeal to the Governing Senate on the basis of the laws issued, the foreign settlers, however, only with the permission of the Expedition of State Economy after duly recording their dissatisfaction in the case file: for which purpose the Office must, in every such case, without the least delay, report to the Expedition, setting out all the circumstances of the case and attaching the petition of the dissatisfied foreigners.

4. If criminal offenses are committed by any of the foreigners, the Office shall send such a person, through the Provincial Government, to the District Court, under proper guard, for proceedings against him according to the general state laws.

5. It shall demand from the Treasury Chamber and from other bodies that had authority over the foreigners all papers and documents that were received there and processed concerning them, for consideration in necessary cases and for precise information about everything pertaining to them.

6. Since the sums spent on the New Russia foreign settlers have already been ascertained and precisely stated in the aforementioned report confirmed by His Imperial Majesty, excluding new disbursements to them, the Office's care must henceforth extend solely to sorting out, more precisely and thoroughly, how much of the total debt sum is attributable to each family.

7. The Office is responsible for everything pertaining to the colonies, and therefore the timely collection of payments due to the treasury by the Zemstvo Police, and the inquiries and investigations occurring in the settlements, remain within its accountability. It is therefore obliged, as soon as the appointed time arrives for any of the foreigners, to collect all state levies on land, pursuant to the Personal decree of May 4, 1769, in two installments per year, and deliver them to the Treasury Chamber, so that the settlers need have no dealings whatsoever with the district Treasurer or the zemstvo administration. As for the money that is to go toward the debt reckoned against them, which, on the basis of His Imperial Majesty's Personal decree of April 21, 1798, and the aforementioned report confirmed on the 6th day of April of this year, is likewise to be collected upon the arrival of the legally appointed time, it shall be kept at the Office until special instruction concerning it is received from the Expedition of State Economy, and the entire sum so held is to be verified monthly in accordance with the law, sending also, every month, statements of the receipt and expenditure of money to the Expedition.

8. The Office must endeavor to encourage the foreign settlers toward the cultivation of artificial meadows, the planting of mulberry trees, grapevines, sesame seed, and other useful plants, toward the increase of better breeds of sheep, and the establishment of linen, woolen, leather, and other factories, which, given the local climate and the occupations and knowledge of the foreigners, may be set up there.

9. The chief Judge of the Office is obliged to travel around all the colonies once every year, and, in case he is unable to do so himself, to dispatch his associate, or one of the other subordinates, to inspect them. In the course of such an inspection, his duty, or that of the person sent by him, shall be to examine in detail whether all the regulations and orders of the authorities are being carried out with due precision, and whether the order established for their proper conduct is being observed, endeavoring, if otherwise, by all means to put a stop to any discord and disorder by fining, or even punishing according to communal verdict, the guilty parties, and to seek means of bringing the colonies into a better condition.

10. For the clearer and more thorough understanding by the foreigners of all orders sent to the colonies by the Office, these should be written in the German language, so that they cannot excuse themselves on grounds of either ignorance or misunderstanding.

11. In the various particulars pertaining to the administration of the colonies, in the conduct of business, and in the keeping of account books, it shall conform to the duties of the Appanage Expeditions, as set forth in the Establishment concerning appanage estates.

11 [12]. It shall likewise introduce and observe, insofar as it is proper and fitting, in each colony, such order of internal rural administration as pertains to those settlements which are to be included in the appanage estates designated for the Imperial Family.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXVI. P. 243-245.*

## No. 36. RESOLUTION OF PAUL I ON THE SENATE REPORT CONCERNING THE SURVEYING OF LAND FOR THE CHERNIGOV COLONISTS (1800)

19,523. — August 21. Highest resolution on a Senate report. — On surveying the requisite quantity of land for the Little Russian colonists.

Report. The Expedition of State Economy and Guardianship of Foreigners presents to the Senate that, having received notification from the Little Russian Provincial Board concerning the colonists settled in that governorate on the Belovezh steppe, it observed that with respect to husbandry only a few of them are in moderate circumstances, while the greater part are in a poor state, the cause of which was the crop failures of past years, the loss of livestock, and the misfortunes suffered during the epidemic. The Treasury Chamber, under whose jurisdiction the colonists were placed, taking this as its basis, and knowing their genuine exhaustion, represented to the Senate the impossibility of collecting the money expended on them by the Treasury. This matter, as pertained to it, came before the Expedition of State Economy for consideration, which, having noted certain contradictions and deficiencies therein, corresponded with the Provincial Board and the Treasury Chamber. But since even so the information received could not fully satisfy the Expedition's need to determine an accurate resolution regarding those colonists, it instructed Collegiate Councillor Konteniuz — who by Your Imperial Majesty's Highest pleasure had been sent to inspect the foreign colonies settled in New Russia Governorate — to stop on his return journey from there to St. Petersburg at the Belovezh colony, and, having examined the colonists' condition in detail in every respect, to present a report on how most reliably and without undue burden to recover from them the money expended by the Crown, improve their condition, and establish economic administration over them. From the description he compiled, as well as from all the papers previously submitted to the Expedition, it appears that these colonists departed in 1765 and 1766 from places lying near Frankfurt am Main, and in 1768 from the environs of Danzig and Elbing; their number at that time consisted of 742 souls of both sexes. In the early years of their settlement many died, but in 1785 the Director of Economy found 469 males alone; according to the 1795 census there were 565 of them, and now there are reckoned to be 639 male and 588 female souls. They were of two kinds: farmers and craftsmen. Upon their departure from St. Petersburg for the place of settlement they concluded contracts with the Treasury, in which, among other things, it was stated: 1. That each family be given in kind a dwelling house with a barn and stable, grain for sowing and subsistence for the first year, the requisite number of livestock and poultry, and everything necessary for husbandry. 2. That churches be built for Catholics and Lutherans with all their appurtenances, and houses for the clergy, with their maintenance at Treasury expense for two years. 3. That they have the freedom, upon repayment of the money expended on them by the Treasury, to leave Russia. 4. That until they repay it, neither they themselves nor their heirs may abandon their dwelling and household, but must in all things act according to the contract without further recourse to the issued Manifesto. 5. That they not be charged for what was required for their travel and maintenance from St. Petersburg all the way to the place of settlement. 6.
