That of the sum expended in aid of their settlement, the farmers, apart from the first two years, pay in subsequent years six percent annually until the capital is fully repaid, and for fields and meadows, apart from the first year, according to their assessed value, 5 percent, or 25 percent of profit annually; while the craftsmen were to pay everything, after the ten years of exemption had passed, within three years, with the stipulation that thereafter they pay taxes on an equal footing with other subjects. As a result of this the colonists were provided for in full, except that no church was built for the Lutherans, nor houses for the craftsmen. The entire sum expended on them amounts to 71,219 rubles 83½ kopecks, the deadline for repayment of which, under their contracts, though it has passed — for the farmers in 1769, and for the craftsmen in 1777 — nevertheless, owing to the insolvency and poverty of all of them, it has to this day been possible to collect no more than 8,437 rubles 35¾ kopecks; after this collection there remains owing from them 62,782 rubles 48¾ kopecks, which sum, however, includes 20,708 rubles 57½ kopecks expended on their travel costs, from payment of which, by force of the contracts, they ought to be exempt. The craftsmen, among whom were various manufacturers, while awaiting the construction of the small town which was intended to be built on the site designated for their settlement, not having received the houses promised them under the contract, built themselves huts at their own expense, in which they still live in a state of hardship. The manufacturers, over the course of 30 years, have for the most part died out; the survivors, as well as the children of the deceased, for lack of means to practice their trade, have become tillers of the soil; but having only a very small quantity of land, some are compelled to rent plowland and hayfields from their neighbors, while others seek subsistence through wage labor. The farmers, meanwhile, are settled on the Belovezh steppe in five villages, built well and properly by the Treasury. The land held by both groups together is reckoned at 2,985 desyatinas, a quantity that was sufficient for them at the time of their initial settlement; but now, when their numbers have considerably increased, this quantity is quite insufficient, for it comes to no more than four and a half desyatinas per soul. Reckoning 4 souls per family, according to the number of souls presently on hand there would be a total of 160 families, and allotting to each 30 desyatinas, as designated by the former Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners, 4,800 desyatinas of land would be required; but since they now have only 2,985, and of this, moreover, 47 desyatinas, under the name of the Kilchinovsky and Smolovoy hamlets, situated in the very midst of their allotments, are being taken from them by state peasants who formerly served the overseers previously placed over this colony and who were settled there by them, they are thus short 1,815 desyatinas. On this account the Expedition applied to the Little Russian Treasury Chamber as to whether such a quantity of land might be found in that governorate to satisfy the colonists, and also whether it might be possible to allot to that amount the state hamlet lying near the colony, called Chernechy, consisting, according to the statement of Collegiate Councillor Konteniuz, of 250 desyatinas held under quitrent, and to grant 50 desyatinas of state land lying near the village of Khvastovtsy, and further requested that the Chamber remove the peasants from the Kilchinovsky and Smolovoy hamlets, which belong solely to the colony, to another location. To which the Treasury Chamber replied that, since there is a very considerable shortage of land needed to satisfy the 15-desyatina allotment for the state department's peasants, it could not, without a special order, either resettle the peasants from the Kilchinovsky and Smolovoy hamlets, or assign to the satisfaction of the colonists the quitrent land situated at the Buromsky hamlet and the village of Khvastovtsy; but since those colonists are listed in the register sent to the Senate as among the state peasants, then upon receipt of a final determination on the division of the quitrent lands, they too would not be left unsatisfied. These colonists, the thirty-year exemption granted by the Highest Manifesto of July 22, 1763, having expired, were registered by the Treasury Chamber as state peasants, and accordingly for the year 1799 each colonist soul was assessed taxes of 3 rubles 40 kopecks, and, following the example of other state settlers, the sale of spirits was established in the colony, from which the colonists themselves had previously benefited, deriving profit from it. According to the testimony of Collegiate Councillor Konteniuz, these colonists, through their industry and diligence in farming and household management generally, deserve regard; but owing to the lack of pastureland and hayfields, they cannot expand their husbandry as they would wish; for however much attention they devote to livestock breeding, they do not succeed at it for want of fodder. Their income, judging by the small amount of land and the low prices of their produce, must be modest; for although in fruitful years they sell various surplus household products and livestock, on the other hand they are compelled to purchase hay, firewood, and timber for house repairs, and after such necessary household expenses little profit remains to them from their labors; and so Collegiate Councillor Konteniuz found in the whole colony only 12 households of good means, 80 of moderate means, 116 with a sufficient livelihood, and 13 poor through their own negligence. To recover the money expended on them by the Treasury, according to the aforementioned Collegiate Councillor's report, cannot be done without hardship except by improving their condition through an increase of land; whereas if it were collected under their present circumstances, many would become destitute. The colonists themselves have declared that if enough land is added to what they already have so that every family receives 30 desyatinas, they will be able to pay annually to the Treasury 20 rubles for it, provided they are thereby freed from all other taxes.

The Senate, having examined in detail the Expedition of State Economy's proposals for improving the condition of the Little Russian colonists, and noting that, having suffered crop failures and losses of livestock from the very time of their settlement, they fell from the first years into an inability to fulfill their obligation to the Treasury; that thereafter, however many measures were undertaken to improve their situation, these were never put into effect, so that neither the taxes due from them nor the repayment of the money expended on their establishment could be collected by the appointed deadlines; and that now, given the changed circumstances and the considerable increase of families, those measures can no longer be usefully applied, for although the said colonists are more in a moderate than in a poor state, the shortage of land is the chief reason it is impossible to collect, without utterly exhausting them, the debt to the Treasury reckoned against them — the Senate, in accordance with the Expedition's conclusion, in order to reconcile the Treasury's interest with the genuine welfare of the colonists, ventures most humbly to submit for Your Imperial Majesty's Highest Monarchical consideration the following opinion: 1. Since the craftsmen, upon their arrival in Russia, finding no opportunity at their place of settlement to practice their trade or craft, abandoned it and for the most part turned to farming, they should be placed on the same footing as the farmers and all provided with land at 30 desyatinas per family, reckoning 4 male souls per family. By this reckoning, for 160 families there ought to be allotted 4,800 desyatinas; but since they hold only 2,985 desyatinas, it is necessary to survey and allot to them an additional 1,815 desyatinas of suitable land. Into this number should be included the nearby Chernechy hamlet, consisting of 250 desyatinas, and the state land near the village of Khvastovtsy amounting to 50 desyatinas, while the remaining quantity should be allotted to them, as far as possible, not at any great distance, so that it may be convenient and without great expense to transfer a certain number of families there. And although it is evident from the statement of the Little Russian Treasury Chamber that there is a considerable shortage of land for satisfying the fifteen-desyatina allotment for state settlers, pursuant to Your Imperial Majesty's Highest decree of November 11 (27), 1797, nevertheless, in view of the fact that it is proposed to grant the said colonists, according to the arrangement of the former Chancellery of Guardianship of Foreigners, 30 desyatinas per family, that is, half again more than the allotment set for state settlers, the Senate proposes to satisfy them in preference to the state peasants. 2. That the peasants settled in the Kilchinovsky and Smolovoy hamlets, situated within the plan of the Belovezh colony, placed there through the actions of the former overseers of the colony, be removed to other locations, in order to prevent disorders and disputes that might arise from joint ownership. 3. That of the 62,782 rubles 48¾ kopecks reckoned as the state debt owed by the colonists, 20,708 rubles 5½ kopecks expended on travel costs be excluded, since, both under the terms of point 3 of the Highest Manifesto of July 22, 1763, and by force of the conditions specially concluded with these settlers, this amount ought to be written off; after which the actual debt owed by them will be reckoned at 42,074 rubles 42¾ kopecks. 4. Under the contracts concluded with the Treasury, these colonists undertook to repay the loaned money, after the expiration of the known period of exemption, by an annual payment of 6 percent, and to pay as tax 25 percent of the profit they earn; but since they are unable to pay the former, and the payment of the latter is very difficult to determine, requiring a new calculation to be made every year, and since, moreover, the payment deadlines have passed, then, in order to avoid misunderstanding and further difficulties in calculation, the Senate deems it most convenient, rescinding the former arrangement, to substitute for it, with the colonists' own consent, having surveyed for them the above-mentioned quantity of land, to collect thereafter from each 30 desyatinas allotted per family 20 rubles annually, with the stipulation that 10 rubles of this be paid in as a land tax to the District Treasury and credited to the general State revenues, while the other 10 rubles be applied to the repayment of the debt reckoned against them, at the disposal of the Expedition of State Economy, for the restoration of the colonists' own condition, pursuant to the Highest Personal decree of Your Imperial Majesty given to the Senate on April 21, 1798, until such time as the entire aforesaid debt sum of 42,074 rubles 42¾ kopecks shall have been repaid, after which the full 20-ruble assessment will be collected from them as land tax into the general State revenue, on the same basis as has been established with regard to the Ostrogozhsk colonists; this will amount to 66⅔ kopecks of land tax per desyatina, which, in comparison with the tax paid by the St. Petersburg colonists, is deemed quite sufficient. 5. Having set an annual tax for the Little Russian colonists commensurate with their circumstances and therefore reliably payable to the Treasury, they should be freed from any other tax and excluded from the poll-tax assessment. 6. For the maintenance of proper order in this colony, the Senate deems it necessary to entrust it to the care and administration of the Office of Guardianship of the New Russian Foreign Settlers, established by Your Imperial Majesty's Highest command following the Senate's most humble report of April 6 of this year 1800, which, owing to the colony's not being far distant from Novorossiysk [Yekaterinoslav], may conveniently take charge of all arrangements concerning these colonists according to the instructions and directives of the Expedition of State Economy.

For the rest, the Senate, submitting all of this to Your Imperial Majesty's Highest Monarchical pleasure, requests Your Majesty's Highest decree.

Resolution. Begin by surveying the necessary quantity of land, as is done in the German lands; then sort this land into three kinds, and then, according to their custom there, establish the labor and form of tax, exactly as is customary in their lands.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXVI. P. 268-272.*

## No. 37. CHARTER OF PAUL I TO THE MENNONITE COLONISTS (1800)

19,546. — September 6. Highest charter to the Mennonites. — On confirming the freedom promised to them in the practice of their faith according to their ecclesiastical institutions and customs.

By the Grace of God, We, Paul the First,

Emperor and Autocrat of All the Russias, etc., etc., etc.

Yielding to the petition of the Mennonites settled in New Russia Governorate, who, according to the testimony of the Authorities, by their exceptional industry and good conduct may be held up as an example to the other foreigners settled there, and who thereby deserve special attention, We have most graciously resolved by this Our Imperial charter not only to confirm all their rights and privileges, set forth in the conditions previously concluded with them, but also, in order to arouse in them greater zeal for labor and diligence in household management, to grant them other benefits as well, contained in the following points:

1. We confirm the freedom promised to them and their descendants to practice their faith without hindrance according to their ecclesiastical institutions and customs, with Our most gracious permission that, should the need arise, the courts may accept from them, in place of an oath, their own custom, consisting of a single verbal affirmation.

2. The sixty-five desyatinas of suitable land designated for each family we confirm to them in indisputable and hereditary possession forever, provided, however, that no portion of it, under any pretext whatsoever, be ceded, sold, or made the subject of any deed to outside parties without the will of the Authority established over them.

3. To all Mennonites presently residing in Russia, as well as to those who shall come hereafter, We most graciously permit the establishment, both in their settlements and in the cities of Our Empire, of factories and other trades needed by them, to engage in commerce, to join guilds and corporations, and to sell the products of their labor without hindrance, in accordance with the State's laws on the matter.

4. By right of possession of the Mennonites' allotments, We permit them to make use of all lands and fishing grounds, to brew beer and vinegar, and to distill grain spirits, both for their own use and for retail sale, on the lands allotted to them.

5. On the lands belonging to the Mennonites We forbid outside persons to build taverns and drinking houses, and likewise forbid tax-farmers to sell spirits or keep public houses without their consent.

6. We assure them, on Our Imperial word, that none of the Mennonites, whether now settled or settling hereafter, nor their children and descendants, shall at any time be taken or enrolled into military or civil service without their own desire to do so.

7. We exempt all their settlements and houses from every kind of billeting and quartering, except at such times as troops shall be passing through, in which case they are to act according to the billeting rules; likewise We exempt them from all state labor obligations, provided, however, that the bridges, ferries, and roads situated on their lands be kept in proper order, and that, in accordance with the general arrangement, they participate in the maintenance of the postal service.

8. We most graciously grant to all Mennonites and their posterity full freedom and authority to dispose of their own property at each one's own discretion and invention, with the exception, however, of the land allotted to them by the Treasury; but if any of them, having paid off the entire debt reckoned against him, should wish to leave Russia with all his property, he must pay a three-year tax on the capital acquired in Russia, in whatever amount shall be declared in good conscience by himself and the authorities of the settlement in which he resides. On this same basis is to be handled the property left after the deceased, whose relatives and heirs reside in foreign lands, when it is to be sent there by right of inheritance as established among them. We hereby also grant the settlements freedom to choose, according to their own rules, guardians over the property of minor children left after the deceased.

9. We confirm the ten-year exemption from the payment of taxes previously granted to them, extending this also to those who shall hereafter wish to settle in New Russia Governorate. But since, according to the inspection carried out, they have now been found not to be in sufficient circumstances owing to the crop failures and livestock losses of certain years, and since, moreover, owing to overcrowding in the Khortitsa area it is proposed to resettle some families to other lands, then, in consideration of their poverty and want, We most graciously extend the ten-year exemption previously granted them for those who remain in their present places of settlement by a further five years, and for those being relocated by ten years, and We command that, once this time has elapsed, they pay, from the land allotted to them at sixty-five desyatinas per family, 15 kopecks per desyatina per year, exempting them otherwise from all taxes of any other kind. But the money given to them as a loan is to be collected, after the expiration of the said exemption, from those remaining in place over ten years, and from those being resettled over twenty years, in equal installments.

10. In conclusion of this Our Imperial charter, granting most graciously to the Mennonites the rights and privileges herein, We command all Our Military and Civil authorities and government offices not only to leave these Mennonites and their descendants in peaceful possession of the dwellings, lands, and lands granted to them, and not to hinder them in enjoying all the privileges given by Us, but to render them in all circumstances every assistance, protection, and patronage.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXVI. P. 286-287.*

## No. 38. INSTRUCTION ON THE INTERNAL ORDER AND ADMINISTRATION OF THE VOLGA COLONIES (1800)

19,562. — September 17. Instruction on the internal order and administration of the Saratov colonies.

1. The foremost duty of all settlers is to obey the law of their church: for this, each of them must, on Sundays and on holidays appointed by the priests, come to the church, pray with all reverence, attentively listen to the word of God, and, upon being found worthy, partake of the Holy Sacraments. If anyone absents himself from this, not for any lawful reason, but solely out of laziness and negligence, then such a person is to be admonished the first and second time; thereafter a fine of 10 kopecks is to be taken, and if this is taken three times within a single year and the guilty party does not desist, then in addition the monetary fine is to be doubled each time, and he is to be put to a full day of public labor, with the money collected going into the general fund.

2. The pastors, priests, and schoolmasters are to be maintained at the common expense of the colonists, for which the necessary sum of money is to be levied on them according to the number of souls composing the parish, apportioned not by the number of families but by the number of workers, counting as such those from 16 to 60 years of age. This collection is to take place three times a year, in the months of January, May, and September: for this purpose special church elders are to be elected annually, who, having collected the money assessed by common consent of the community for this purpose, must hand over one third each time to the district head and receive receipts from him. The forsteher [village elder] are obliged to render every assistance to such a church elder, so that nothing may fall into arrears; and whoever fails to pay his share by the appointed date shall, the first time, be charged 10 kopecks in addition by way of penalty, the second time 15 kopecks, and the third time shall be kept at public labor (concerning which labor more is said below in its place) until he pays, and shall be reported through the district head to the Office, with a description of the circumstances and the reasons that prompted such disobedience.

On the duties of priests and pastors.

3. Priests and pastors are to discharge the duty of their calling according to the instructions and directives given to them by their ecclesiastical superiors; they are in no way to meddle in secular affairs or other matters unbecoming to the priestly rank. But since it is indispensable to their office that they make constant rounds of the colonies of their parish, this is to be arranged so that every settlement may equally benefit from their teaching, for which purpose the parishioners must, in turn, convey them by their own carts from one settlement to another, without demanding payment for this; nor may the pastor demand from the colonists any compensation for these journeys beyond his appointed salary; but should the parishioners wish, by common consent of the whole parish confirmed in a joint signed statement attested by the head, to add something toward the maintenance of his own horses, beyond what is appointed in his salary, or to help with other needs, this is left to their discretion; the head must report this to the Office, and is not to proceed to execution until an order has been received from it. During such travels the priests and pastors must keep vigilant watch over the schoolmasters, so that they perform their duties with due exactness. If any offense is committed against these clergymen by their parishioners, this is to be reported immediately to the Office. But should the pastor agree to forgive the offender, the matter is dropped from the fine and the report; likewise the parishioners have the right, in cases of dissatisfaction with their pastor, to petition the Office through their chief. Accurate records, or registers, of marriages, births, and deaths are to be kept in chronological order and drawn up according to the special forms sent out from the Office of Guardianship for Foreign Settlers together with the decrees addressed to them, without any deviation whatsoever from those forms; these registers are to be submitted to the Office within the time limits specified in those decrees, that is, without fail after the close of each half-year.

On the election of village authorities and the internal

village administration in the colonies, as well as on fines

and punishments for offenses.

4. In the colonies, following the former internal arrangements and designations of the former Office of Guardianship for Foreign Settlers, special prikazy [district offices] are to be established; and in every such prikaz an elected district official, or head, is to be appointed, to whose assistance the whole prikaz shall elect two beisitzer, or assessors, and one clerk; and in the settlement where the head resides, one of the residents' houses shall be assigned annually in rotation for his residence, or else it shall be established permanently in one fixed place with the voluntary consent and monetary contribution of all the settlements composing that prikaz; and there, in a chest and coffer under the lock and seal of the head, together with the elders of that settlement, are to be kept the ledgers of income and expenditure, the money collected by that prikaz for various communal needs, all written documents, and the orders sent down from the authorities. As elected district officials, or heads, and likewise as beisitzer and clerks, colonists are to be elected for two years from among all the colonies belonging to that district, and their confirmation is to be submitted to the Office of Guardianship for Foreign Settlers; in the remaining colonies, where there is no head, one forsteher or schulz is to be elected, together with two beisitzer to assist him annually, under the special supervision of the heads, from among colonists of good conduct chosen by the community of each colony, exemplary in husbandry, and especially skilled in agriculture and animal husbandry, so that they may by their own example set an example for others; the district head, with an endorsement of their conduct, must submit their confirmation in these offices to the Office as well. For the conduct of judicial proceedings they are to assemble once or twice a week, as need requires and at the summons of the forsteher; from every 10 households one desyatsky [tithing-man] is to be elected, to be replaced monthly.

5. All village authorities are subordinate to the elected district official, or district head, of the prikaz to which they belong; accordingly, subordinate forsteher or schulzen, together with their beisitzer, must, if unable themselves to settle or reconcile minor quarrels and claims among the settlers, report them immediately to the head; and he, if he cannot bring the disputants to reconciliation, or if any of them proves stubborn and disobedient against his lawful demand, must report this to the Office, with a description of the circumstances of the matter and the offenses of those who are obstinate. As for criminal offenses in general, these are to be reported to the Office as promptly as possible, with the offenders themselves delivered under guard.

6. Excluded from the jurisdiction of the village authorities are all manner of misdeeds: forcible seizure of another's property, theft, cruel beatings inflicted with intent, offenses against the appointed village authorities, and especially beatings and any form of malicious abuse. For this reason, offenders in such cases, and thieves caught with stolen goods — whatever has been stolen or seized by whom — are to be reported to the Office in detail, with reports explaining the offenses.

7. Heads, forsteher, and beisitzer, as well as persons for other particular offices, are to be elected in each settlement by majority vote from among adults who have their own household, possess sufficient knowledge of rural economy, are sober and beyond suspicion, solicitous of the common good, and sufficiently reliable, each casting his vote in turn for whomever he chooses for whatever office, without any servility, following neither friendship nor enmity; and those who receive the greater number of votes are to be confirmed by the joint signature of all, with the results of the election submitted to the Office for approval. When a chief so elected has been confirmed, he must immediately demand from his predecessor a proper accounting, both of communal affairs and of the sum of money, and upon receiving all of it, record it in a ledger, attested by the former chief that it has indeed been handed over to him and that the new official has entered into administration. For this purpose every chief must keep a separate notebook and maintain an accurate record both of those who have been fined and of everything else done during his administration, from which it should always be possible, at the end of the year, to distinguish orderly settlers from disorderly ones, and to ascertain the growth or decline of each household.

8. The district head, in every prikaz, at a communal assembly, and the individual colonist's forsteher or schulz, in the colony, must:

1) Promulgate the enacted laws that concern the settlers, and read both these and this instruction given by the Office for the edification of the inhabitants, in installments, after the celebration of Divine service at the churches, or in the prayer houses, and at gatherings that occur.

2) Explain, instruct, and teach what pertains to good morals and to the benefit of communal life among the settlers, so that the young may be respectful and obedient toward parents and elders, and that these, by their own example, may teach them diligence, honesty, temperance, and peaceful cohabitation in the settlements and families.

3) Instruct on church decorum, on everyone's duty to devote Sundays, holidays, and solemn days to the service of God, and also, according to the traditions of each religion, on confession and, upon being found worthy, on partaking of the Holy Sacraments.

4) The district head is especially charged with taking precautions against contagious diseases, cattle plague, and fire, and with instructing the village authorities subordinate to him in this regard; he must see that weights and measures everywhere conform to the prescribed standard, and that disorderly conduct and suspicious persons are not tolerated; moreover DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 105

he must in every way ensure that nowhere, under any pretext, may harmful illicit liquor trade take place.

9. In every settlement, in order to guard against the occurrence of fire and any theft, there are to be day and night watchmen posted at appropriate points, according to the extent of the settlement, and barrels are always to be kept ready, together with two horses, taken in turn, for hauling water in them, which must always stand ready; and in the middle of settlements that have no church, there are to be bells or iron plates, so that if a fire or thieves are noticed in any house, the watchmen may strike the alarm on those plates, and the inhabitants of both sexes of full age must immediately gather to help at that place; for which reason every settlement must also have firefighting equipment, such as: a number of special large iron hooks and pitchforks, while every householder must have a ladder, and every household must always keep ready water in special tubs; for such an occasion all the settlers are to be assigned by household as to who is to go to the fire with what, under penalty of a fine of 1 ruble to the communal fund for each person absent from the fire.

10. The forsteher, and likewise the beisitzer, must, if an extraordinary disease appears among the people in any colony, give notice of this to the district head, who is obliged immediately to report it to the Office of Guardianship for Foreign Settlers; likewise, no persons without written documents are to be tolerated in the colonies under any circumstances, and if unknown, suspicious, or fugitive persons are noticed anywhere, this too must be reported in detail to the district head; unknown and suspicious persons found in the colonies, and persons engaged in acts contrary to decrees, are to be sought out, apprehended, and sent to him, and he, upon such reports, must immediately submit a detailed report to the Office of Guardianship for Foreign Settlers, and those apprehended, after being interrogated, together with everything found on them, as well as those who harbored them, are likewise to be sent to that Office; with regard to cattle plague and the precautions to be taken against it, in such a case the heads and other village authorities must act entirely in accordance with the special instruction sent out to the colonies for such an occasion, and at the same time, whenever such a plague breaks out anywhere, they must report to the Office, both on its continuation, diminution, or cessation, and also on the progress made in carrying out the measures prescribed by that instruction, reporting to the Office weekly; infected cattle are to be separated into a place set apart, remote from other places, special communal enclosures being made for this at each settlement in places remote from dwellings and from pastures, and contact of such infected cattle with neighboring areas is to be cut off, and notice is to be given to all neighboring foreign settlements; and when it happens that there are settlements in which infection appears along watercourses and streams, and there are other settlements below it not more than 10 versts away, then, so as not to cause the same harm to the neighbors through the watering place, the sick cattle are not to be watered at those sources, but water is to be carried by hand to the enclosures made for that purpose above, which should therefore be built closer to the water; likewise, if it becomes known that a similar occurrence has taken place among settlements on the same watercourses even if more than 10 versts away, the same precaution is to be observed. For failure to comply with this exactly, the head and other village authorities are to be fined.

11. Since it has come to the notice of this Office that in some colonies stoves have been built without chimneys, with their mouths opening into entryways covered only with straw, and moreover that grain and hay are stacked close to the houses, the inhabitants are therefore to be compelled, in order to avoid fire, to build stoves in their houses with chimneys and to fire them not from the entryway but from small kitchens specially built onto them, which are to be lined with brick or coated with clay, so that they may be safe; and for the stacking of grain and hay, in accordance with the orders previously sent out by the Office, threshing floors are to be made in places remote from the houses.

12. The district heads must take special care that the debt money assessed per worker, and the state taxes on the land, as shall be established for all the colonies under their jurisdiction, are paid into the Office of Guardianship for Foreign Settlers punctually and without arrears, within the appointed time limits; and in the assignment of carts, both for postal relay service and according to the published schedule, and in all lawful village duties or obligations, they must act with complete fairness, without the slightest burden to the settlers, observing carefully in every case equality and a genuine rotation established by the settlers themselves, on pain of strict and unremitting exaction for failure to observe this.

13. It is most strictly confirmed to all village authorities that nowhere, under any pretext, by anyone, shall any unlawful monetary or grain levies be made upon the colonists; and since all the colonies located in Saratov Governorate are entrusted to the administration of the Office of Guardianship for Foreign Settlers, which, being obliged to exercise proper guardianship care and oversight, must answer for everything relating both to the internal arrangement and organization of the colonies and to their provision with all necessary supplies; wherefore the very supervision of the general land survey, so that not only the lands presently belonging to the colonies be protected from any unlawful claims, but that 20 desyatinas be allotted per soul, is likewise entrusted to this Office; in view of which, no colony and no village authority may, without reporting to the Office and obtaining its permission, establish anew any levies whatsoever upon the colonists for any purpose, for anyone, anywhere, nor may it on its own authority incur monetary expenses of any sum whatsoever; nor may there be any such levies upon the colonists for any purpose other than the sole one of maintaining the churches, pastors, and schoolmasters; and in addition, fine money may go into the economic funds, to be used for communal public burdens, such as the repair of bridges and the upkeep of roads; wherefore both the district head and the other village authorities must receive annually from the Office bound and sealed ledgers, in which both the fine money and the monetary levies established for other needs — namely, for pastors, churches, and schoolmasters — are to be entered clearly and in detail without any concealment, showing from whom exactly how much was taken and where or for what and exactly when it was spent; and at the end of each year, the district head and the forsteher throughout the colonies are to be held to account by the colonists themselves for the money that was collected from them during the year for various needs, and then, any shortfall or deficiency being disclosed in those same ledgers, whatever is found owing from the head or forsteher is, after first reporting it to the Office, to be recovered with its permission, and the ledgers, signed by the village authorities and the leading members of the community, are to be submitted annually to the Office for review and audit; and in order that this provision be carried out with complete exactness by the village authorities in all the colonies, special oversight of this is entrusted to the district head; otherwise, should the slightest unauthorized DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 107

levy ever be discovered anywhere and come to the knowledge of the Office, then not only the village authority of that colony but also the district head, for failing to detect it, shall be subject to trial and the strictest punishment according to law.

14. When a chief decides some matter unjustly, and this is proven upon the bringing of a complaint to the Office, such a person must suffer a fine twice that imposed upon the person he wrongly accused; and if the accused person suffers any loss as a result, this too must be repaid to him by the chief in addition to the fine; conversely, for false denunciations against their superiors, each person shall suffer merciless punishment from the government as a slanderer.

15. It is most strictly forbidden to all colonists living in the colonies, as well as to heads and other village authorities, that no one, either on his own or with the consent of only a few persons, shall dare to submit petitions of his own accord anywhere concerning their common lawful needs, whatever these may consist of; but for all such needs there must be a general assembly with the head and the forsteher together with the beisitzer, at which communal resolutions are to be drawn up with the consent of all the settlers, with a detailed and clear description therein of their needs or deficiencies, and also of the representative to whom, from among themselves, all the colonists entrust the matter, so that, in accordance with their written resolution, the complaint or petition may be brought or submitted; and these resolutions, signed by all the settlers and by the forsteher together with the beisitzer, and attested by the head, are to be submitted to the Office; otherwise, should anyone dare to violate this order, he shall be dealt with according to law.

16. The district head must: 1) settle and reconcile minor quarrels and claims among the settlers, and in the event of disagreement or dissatisfaction, allow them the freedom to have the matter looked into at the Office; 2) exercise guardianship over widows and orphans, and likewise over those who are lazy and negligent in their husbandry, over whom he must also exercise supervision, personally inspecting monthly all aspects of their households and observing everything that may constitute the settlers' benefit; he is also entrusted with overseeing and observing the forsteher, schulzen, and likewise the beisitzer, so that each of them discharges what has been assigned to him and diligently performs his duty.

17. The district head, the prikaz beisitzer, clerks, and village elected officials, in consideration of the fact that they are obliged to devote their time to the public benefit, are to receive as remuneration from the community: the district head 20 rubles, the prikaz beisitzer and clerk 15 rubles each, and the forsteher or schulz 10 rubles a year, and are thereby personally exempted from all labor assignments and duties, but are not exempted from the monetary payment of state taxes. The village beisitzer and desyatskys, however, since the former are not always appointed to be continuously in office, and the latter are elected monthly and in rotation, must discharge their duties without remuneration and without any exemption from taxes and all other obligations. District heads, beisitzer, clerks, forsteher, or schulzen must be held in great respect by subordinate settlers of every rank; and in the event of disobedience, or of anyone daring to insult them by word, the offender shall pay a fine of one ruble to the former and half a ruble to all the others; and if anyone dares to lay hands on them, a triple monetary payment is to be exacted from him, and he is to be sent to prison for a time or put to various labors; and should peaceful possession be disturbed by anyone, contrary to expectation, the village elected officials must, without loss of time, report to the head, describing the localities in which, by whom, and exactly what occurred, and the head is to report this to the Office, which, in the discharge of its duty, must take the matter up and initiate proceedings in the manner prescribed by law.

18. Forsteher alone, without the heads, are not to impose any fines on their own authority, unless the heads are absent, and even then only with the general consent of the beisitzer and the leading men; the heads, however, have the authority to impose fines themselves, whether by labor or by monetary deduction, with the general consent of the forsteher; no chief individually has the right to impose fines on his own account, that is, the forsteher and beisitzer must apply to the head, while the others must seek their satisfaction from the Office, or, during its visits, from its Members.

19. Although it is set forth in the following points of this instruction for what each fine is to be imposed, naming the offenses, yet since offenses can never be of equal gravity, nor can offenders be of equal standing, in such deliberations one must proceed with the utmost prudence and caution; for example, if someone offends against the established rules deliberately or out of obstinacy, and some harm or loss to the settlement or to a neighbor results from it, such a person must be punished more severely, or more perceptibly, than one who transgresses unintentionally, or, though out of laziness, yet not out of obstinacy, and has caused no harm to anyone; and who, moreover, has never before been guilty of any vice — namely, the second offender is to be punished one third or even one half less than the first, this being left to the discretion of the chiefs.

20. It is forbidden that anyone at night, either in his own house or in the streets, should go about with splinters or candles without lanterns, or with lit pipes; those who disobey this are to be punished with a monetary fine of 5 kopecks each time.

21. From those householders who, notwithstanding all the admonitions of their chiefs, are found keeping their house and the gardens around it, as well as their stables and barns, in poor condition, a monetary fine of 20 kopecks is to be taken, and in addition they are to be compelled to put everything right immediately, under the supervision of a beisitzer specially assigned for that purpose.

22. It must be strictly observed that no one gives shelter in his house to disreputable women or men, and if anyone is noticed doing so, both the householder and those engaged in such disorderly conduct are to be reported immediately to the Office through the district head.

23. The hiring of laborers is not to be forbidden, especially for those with small families, the sick, and the well-off, but the chiefs must nevertheless keep unremitting watch to ensure that the householders themselves, who are able to work, are without fail engaged in agriculture and diligently occupied with their husbandry.

24. If anyone happens to find a lost item on the road or in a settlement, he must immediately declare it to his chief, keep it carefully in the meantime, and report it to the district head; and when the owner is found, it is to be handed over in the presence of witnesses, whereupon the finder is permitted to demand payment for his trouble, but by no means more than the lawful share of the value of the found item as assessed by the village authorities; and whoever chooses to return it without payment, such disinterestedness will be all the more praiseworthy.

25. Frequent inspections are to be made to ensure that the boundary markers that have been set up remain undamaged, and if any posts decay or any pyramids [boundary mounds] crumble, this is to be reported immediately to the district head, and such markers are to be repaired at once on his order, and for neglect of this a fine is to be exacted from the forsteher into the general fund DOCUMENTS_______________________________________________ _________________________________ 109

of 1 ruble 50 kopecks, and from the beisitzer 50 kopecks; and if such markers are found deliberately damaged by any of the inhabitants, this is to be reported through the district head to the Office for the imposition of punishment according to the general laws.

26. In every colony, upon notice given by the district head, or by the elected official through the beisitzer, the inhabitants, one from each household, or as many as ordered, must hasten immediately to the assembly on every occasion, and there, in complete quiet, must attend to and exactly carry out what is ordered of them, under penalty for disobedience or absence from the assembly upon summons of 50 kopecks, and for disorderly conduct and noise, four times that amount.

27. The district head, together with the elected officials, must diligently see to it, and are responsible for ensuring, that the main roads and the bridges and dams upon them are repaired and maintained according to the division of sections, on the basis of the instructions sent out from the Office, and that there be no filth in the streets of any colony; and, for protection against storms and winds in case of fire, orders are to be given to plant, along the streets around the yards and threshing floors, wherever suitable according to the nature of the climate and soil, various trees capable of growing there; and in some colonies, where ordinary willows are commonly used for such planting, mulberry trees are without fail to be planted instead, which can bring the settlers particular benefit easily obtained from silk cultivation; the heads and other colony authorities must also see to it that all the settlers behave kindly and amicably toward their neighbors, and politely and hospitably toward visitors, avoiding quarrels with the former over matters of land, in view of their proximity, and avoiding even the slightest rudeness with others.

28. The district heads and forsteher are obliged to make observations in their respective localities of whatever appears necessary for the common good of their places, and to report this to the Office; moreover, they are to explain to and impress upon the settlers the benefits contained therein, and to strive for the multiplication of every kind of handicraft and manufacture, and to encourage them toward these.

29. Since, in order to guard against a shortage of grain that might arise from crop failure or other extraordinary occurrences, and for the benefit of all the settlers themselves, grain storehouses must be maintained, it is hereby prescribed: 1) to fill these storehouses, after the completion of the harvest, there is to be collected annually from all the settlers, per revision soul — including in this number those who, having paid off their debts, make use of land plots — half a chetverik of rye, and half a garnets of spring grain, whichever kind grows in a given place; wherefore each head, after collecting this, must without fail send to the Office annually, in the month of November, detailed statements of how much grain has gone into which storehouse. 2) In order that these reserves may serve to the greater benefit of the settlers and be issued to them in case of shortage and genuine need, both for food and for sowing, it is absolutely necessary that the reserve grain be collected and kept as whole grain, and that, in case of need, it be issued by common communal resolution, with the permission of the Government established over the colonies, with an entry made in a ledger, which is to be kept at every storehouse for both income and expenditure. 3) In order to keep the reserve grain fit for use and to protect it in future from spoilage, at the time of the ordinary collection into the storehouses, the grain held there is to be exchanged annually by the same settlers for fresh grain, which is to be done only under the direction of the Office, and it is forbidden to do this on one's own authority without permission. 4) Since in every colony elders have been established, together with two beisitzer for each, it is entrusted to one of the beisitzer to keep the ledgers of income and expenditure, with the provision that this latter person shall keep the key to the storehouse, while the elder or elected official keeps the seal, both being responsible for its safekeeping.

30. The district heads, forsteher, and beisitzer, being distinguished and respected above all the other settlers, are mutually obliged to promote the benefit of the settlers in every way, and to warn everyone concerning it; in the discharge of their office they must exact compliance strictly but in an orderly manner, and otherwise treat the settlers with leniency and friendliness; they must receive all their requests patiently, attend to all their needs, be their honest advocates, and have nothing whatsoever to do with bribes, since they will be subject to equal prosecution and legal punishment both for neglect of their duties and for oppression of their subordinates.

31. It is confirmed to the district head that he must see to it that the colonists never enter into written obligations among themselves, without the knowledge and permission of the authorities, with anyone whomsoever; and moreover, that all written obligations or contracts, powers of attorney, wills, monetary accounts, agreements — in a word, all documents, whether among the colonists themselves or, should it happen, with others as well — be written without fail not on plain paper but on stamped paper, and without this no government office or authority is to accept them or act upon them; wherefore all such transactions must without fail be lawfully declared and recorded at the Office; moreover, promissory notes must also be written on stamped paper specially prepared for that purpose, the price of the sheets for promissory notes being fixed, according to the decree of December 18, 1797, as follows: from 10 to 1,000 rubles, 1 ruble per sheet; above 1,000 up to 5,000 rubles, 3 rubles; above 5,000 rubles up to 10,000 rubles, 5 rubles; above 10,000 up to 25,000 rubles, 12 rubles; above 25,000 up to 50,000 rubles, 20 rubles; above 50,000 up to 75,000 rubles, 30 rubles; above 75,000 up to 100,000 rubles, 45 rubles.

32. District Heads are to keep strict watch that village elders report to the Office immediately, with a detailed description, any strayed or additional livestock that has joined their settlements or herds, for publication, and that the livestock itself be kept in the settlement where it strayed to, but in a place separate from their own, under threat of penalty. When the owner is found, the animal is to be returned to him in the presence of the Vorsteher, with payment collected for the feeding of it for the time it was in someone's keeping. Horses purchased by colonists are to be recorded by each in the established offices, specifying exactly when purchased from whom, at what price, brand, and other identifying marks; otherwise, and in a suspicious case, one who has not declared and not recorded a horse bought or exchanged from someone shall not only lose it but shall also be brought to trial, for which purpose the Heads shall establish special books for this in their offices.

33. It is most strictly confirmed that nowhere, in accordance with previous instructions of this Office, are horses and carts to be given to anyone, whoever he may be, without payment of the toll fees and without a travel warrant, nor in excess of the number indicated therein. Therefore District Heads, exercising unrelaxed oversight so that no burden may occur anywhere, are to establish special registers in the colonies, into which are certainly to be entered the names of travelers, by whom the travel warrant was issued, or whether there was a special instruction of this Office, for exactly how many horses and whether that number was given, likewise who did the driving and whether the travelers paid the prescribed toll fees. DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 1 1 1

34. From petitions and complaints reaching the Office from colonists it is known that many settlers, accustomed previously to living in idleness and negligence of household management and farming, gathering often in drinking houses, engage in quarrels and fights among themselves, beat village elders, while others have squandered and continue to squander their property, caring not at all for their household, whereby their plots have fallen into neglect and their households suffer extreme poverty and exhaustion in every respect; to the further disorder, some colonists in the settlements sell drink in their own homes; in view of which village elders, often within the settlements, and District Heads, throughout entire districts, must most strictly observe that colonists in no way sell drink in their homes, whether by the cup or glass, nor under any other pretexts whatsoever, and that any abuse in this regard be without fail suppressed and forever prevented; for the sale of drink in the colonies is to be conducted in drinking houses and established outposts under the management of the holder of the drink-tax concessions, and moreover close watch is to be kept that colonists not be permitted to fall into idleness, drunkenness, profligacy, and rowdiness, and that, living a sober and quiet life, they always occupy themselves with work proper to their condition in farming, animal husbandry, and rural economy; and so that the settlers may see that diligence and good conduct secure their common good, village elders, under the special oversight of the District Head, must compile registers of those who excel in husbandry, as well as of the negligent, which are to be submitted annually, signed by the District Head and the village elders subordinate to him, to the Office, to the end that the diligent and honest may enjoy preference in trust, while the negligent, on the contrary, may be shown that they can not only not have a good opinion held of themselves and expect reward in benefits, but moreover the village elders, under the special observation of the District Heads, are to punish them with fines or confinement on bread and water, and compel them to work by assigning it in set tasks; and if among the colonists anyone should still be found not caring for household management, he is to be compelled to proceed without fail to the cultivation and sowing of his plot; and for better success in this, Beisitzers are to be assigned to them, and if, even after this, upon the urging of the village elder and Head, anyone should prove stubborn and lazy, such persons, with a description of their offenses, are to be reported for the Office's consideration.

35. It is prescribed that the strictest watch be kept that none of the colonists absent themselves without business from the residence where each was last recorded in the census, nor wander idly about the colonies. But since absences for the sale of produce, for trade and crafts, may be of use to them, these are by no means forbidden under the force of the Statute on Appanage Estates, provided, however, that farming does not suffer thereby, and that the settlement undertakes responsibility for the absentee and for the working of his land plot; those who have need to absent themselves to some settlement, or to the Governorate or district town for the sale of produce, are to be granted leave; but as for those colonists who must go to distant places and for periods requiring considerable time, even if to nearby settlements for work, such persons must, having received leave from the Vorstehers and Schulzes attested by the District Head that there are no obstacles to their absence for that length of time, and that neither their farming nor their livestock will suffer any harm thereby, appear at this Office, where, having received passports, they are obliged to return by the appointed date, with the further requirement that the passports issued be returned to the Office.

36. Village Elders or Heads of Offices are most strictly instructed, pursuant to the orders sent from the Office of Guardianship of Foreign Settlers to the Vorstehers and Schulzes of all colonies jointly, to observe the following: 1) the propagation of forests on the colony lands where none exist, and the sowing, on lands allotted to the colonies, of tree seeds suited to the soil, especially soft woods, such as: alder, birch, willow, aspen, sallow, and osier, and preferably above all the seeds of acacias and other similar species; the seeds of these trees are to be gathered when ripe, and sown on well-plowed land, and efforts are also to be made to plant mulberry trees, in accordance with the special instructions given to the village elders. 2) To observe that poor and destitute colonists in no way wander about the world nor beg alms in a beggarly manner, but are to be compelled to seek their sustenance through diligence, while the aged and infirm are to be maintained by relatives, and in the absence of such, are to be maintained by public charity, and moreover, for the aged who have neither relatives nor strength for work, and the infirm, two huts are to be built by public effort near the church, under the name of almshouse, for their dwelling, one for females and the other for males, where they are also to be provided with food, warmth, and clothing necessary to cover their nakedness, for which expense there is to be kept at the almshouse, under the seal and key of the church warden, a box, and in the churches a purse, into which the money collected on feast days and Sundays from alms is to be placed, and this box is to be emptied at the end of every month, and by this means the almshouse is to be maintained; in case of shortfall, the colony is to make up the difference. For better order in these almshouses, the priests of those churches are to have chief oversight; and finally, 3) On the establishment in the colonies, following the example of Russian peasants, of threshing floors and drying barns for the harvesting and drying of grain, under threat of the strictest and unfailing penalty for non-compliance.

37. District Heads are to see that strict watch is kept over prisoners of various ranks being conveyed through the colonies, so that none may manage to escape from custody, and for this purpose village elders in every colony are to establish special registers, in which are to be recorded precisely the names of the prisoners being conveyed, by whom and to which colony they were brought, with whom and when they were sent onward, and in which settlement to whom they were handed over.

38. Settlers are by no means to divide their households on their own without the permission of the Office, and, in the event such a wish should arise, the Heads are to observe very closely that such divisions truly serve the common good of the settlers and do not sometimes serve to their household's detriment, and to this end, in reporting such cases to the Office, they are specifically to explain the good will of the parents or relatives toward it, whether the one being separated will have sufficient land, farming implements, and livestock to establish a household — in short, under such circumstances it must without fail be observed that the household of the first is preserved intact, and that of the latter is established with success.

39. It is most strictly forbidden that anyone hand over or sell his household to anyone under any pretext whatsoever, except only in the case when someone, having no children or heirs, is, by reason of old age and utter infirmity and illness, wholly unable to manage it himself, and even then it is to be handed over only with the permission of this Office, and not left to communal arbitrariness on their own; the one who receives it must also assume together with it all the state debts reckoned against it, DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 113

and must moreover see to providing sustenance for the one who has proven unable to manage the household.

40. It is most strictly confirmed to the District Heads that all orders or instructions sent and hereafter to be sent by the Office are to be carried out in all the colonies with the utmost exactness, without delay or omission, and that letters sent from the Government are to be forwarded everywhere in turn, wherever required, from one settlement to another, without argument, with the utmost haste, under threat of punishment; and if anyone should prove disobedient in this, he is to be punished with three days of communal labor, and dispatched out of turn against his fellows twice. In view of this, District Heads and individual village elders are to keep a daily protocol or record of all matters whatsoever, for which purpose books are to be kept everywhere, into which are also to be entered the verbal orders and adjudications of the village elders among the settlers, so that, in the event of complaints reaching the Office, justice may more readily be found accordingly.

41. All enmity among inhabitants, private quarrels, and slanderous reproaches are to be suppressed by the elders, first by admonitions and public works, and, in case of recurrence, by fining such persons in money as well, into the common fund, exacting it only from whoever is the instigator of the quarrel, at 25 kopecks for each occasion.

42. Luxury, and above all profligacy, the elders must with all their strength eradicate among the colonists, bringing offenders to obedience by assigning them the heaviest tasks in various works for the commune, so that they may never have time for themselves or the colony for such harmful conduct, until they come to acknowledge their fault; and if they do not reform by this means, such persons are to be sent to the Office with reports.

Explanation.

Luxury is understood to mean it if someone has immoderate expenses in his household, frequent gatherings of guests, and the like, giving occasion for the squandering of property; profligacy, meanwhile, is card-playing and other games for money and goods, the sale of one's own livestock or other property, without the knowledge of one's authorities and without any need, for drunkenness, or to satisfy other passions.

43. Whoever sows someone else's land or plot, the grain thus sown is to be given to the one to whom that land belongs, taking from it a tenth part into the common fund; and if that other's land lay fallow and the owner, for some reason, was unable to plow it, and consequently no loss was caused to him thereby, then in such a case, for the impudence alone, 12 kopecks per desyatina is to be exacted into the common treasury, and the same amount again is to be exacted and given to the owner of that land; but if anyone under such circumstances plowed virgin land, nothing is to be given to the owner, because the plowing of virgin land will serve to the owner's benefit.

44. If anyone, on another's land, whether at his own place of residence or elsewhere, picks hops or other fruits, or spoils bait for animals or birds, then for the damage and loss he is to make restitution to the plaintiff in money according to valuation, and moreover a fine of 15 kopecks is to be exacted into the common fund.

45. If anyone, having seized someone's horse, keeps it for no more than two days without reporting it to his elder, then even if he performed no work on it at all, he must pay the owner 25 kopecks for each day; and if it should be injured during that time and this can be directly proven, then he must pay the owner the value as stated above in § 44.

46. Whoever kills someone's cow, or some other livestock, or fowl, is to be made to pay, to the satisfaction of the injured party, for every animal or fowl according to valuation, and moreover, for such an offense, is to be fined with imprisonment on bread and water — for the killing of a horse or cow, four days, and for small livestock half of that, excepting fowl and dogs.

47. If, however, anyone kills or injures someone's livestock without intent, and this is clearly proven, then in such a case only two-thirds of the valuation is to be exacted for the killing and no fine is to be imposed at all, and he is to be ordered to have the unintentionally injured animal treated; and if he fails to cure it, he is to be compelled to pay as stated for animals killed.

48. For the forcible seizure of livestock, fowl, and any goods, even if the one from whom some item was seized owed the other a debt, it is to be deducted from that debt at the price of the livestock, and for other goods, at what they are worth according to valuation, so that no one shall be tempted to commit such disorders willfully; and if anyone, under the pretense merely of a debt, forcibly seizes livestock or some item, such a person is to be regarded as a robber; consequently this offense does not fall within the internal court and adjudication of the colonists, but is to be reported to the Office.

49. Whoever, notwithstanding the announced fines and punishments, does not desist from impudent conduct, such persons, with a description of their offenses, are to be handed over to the Office under guard, with reports, for proceeding according to the laws.

50. Since it is impossible to enumerate all offenses and crimes in this instruction, which mentions only those that occur more often than others, it remains to say that if in future anyone should commit some offense not specifically indicated here, such cases are to be reported through the District Heads to the Office, and a new instruction from it is to be awaited, and no one is to impose fines or take monetary penalties on his own authority; punishment by labor, however, by majority vote, is permitted, but not more than 7 days, and the Office is nevertheless to be notified in the meantime.

On Rural Economy.

51. The District Head is instructed to see and endeavor that everywhere in the colonies the lands are and continue to be divided into three fields; and as soon as the snow melts and the ground thaws, every elder must urge his settlers that each settler, during the winter, stock up on and have plows, wooden plows, harrows, carts, and other items needed for field work, and that the livestock, namely oxen and horses, be in good condition for work; and if any should be deficient in this not through negligence but for other reasons or unfortunate accidents, such persons are to be given possible assistance by the combined effort of all the inhabitants.

52. As soon as the prescribed time for plowing arrives, every elder, together with his Beisitzers, must announce that all inhabitants of the settlement, at one and the same time, go out to the fields in the very earliest morning hours and work with the utmost diligence, for which purpose each of the elders is to ride about and oversee his own group of people, whether everyone has plowed enough land; and that the plowing not be shallow; above all the Vorstehers must observe still more closely that the sowing of the spring grain be, without fail, completed by the 20th of May at the very latest; likewise it is to be observed in the preparation of the winter fallow field and its sowing, that it be finished no later than the middle of September, and during the hay-DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 1 15

making season, to see to a sufficient store of hay for the livestock for winter and to the harvesting of grain from the fields in the autumn season. In the harvesting of grain and hay, conduct is to be governed by the harvest, the ripeness, and the custom observed in such cases, which is already well known to all; and as soon as the grain ripens, it is to be reaped without delay; the grass, meanwhile, is to be mowed as the harvest and occasion permit; after the passing of autumn and the harvesting of grain, diligent effort must be made to thresh it in good weather, and for this purpose, wattle-and-daub sheds are to be built for storage.

53. In settlements which are rich in forests allotted to their lands, every excess use is to be cut off and limited, so that colonists, apart from necessary household needs, do not profit by selling it elsewhere, and make no income for themselves from it whatsoever; and further, so that it may more readily be preserved, the forest is to be divided into different sections for cutting, and cutting of another section is not to be permitted until one is finished; and thus, wherever such divisions are made, the Head is to report in detail to the Office for consideration. If anyone, apart from the section designated for that year, should cut timber, a fine is to be exacted from him into the common fund, double the value of what he cut according to price; and in case of inability to make such payment, he is to be assigned to public labor until he works off that amount.

54. In wintertime it is to be seen that none of the inhabitants remain idle, but that each labor at keeping good watch over and properly feeding and maintaining his livestock, look after cleanliness, especially of the horses, after the repair of buildings, of fencing around yards and gardens, and endeavor to prepare all necessary supplies; no less is it to be observed that everyone stock up for sowing spring grain and other seeds and have all this in readiness, while the women likewise should be occupied in spinning wool and flax and in weaving linen and woolen cloth, in raising various fowl, in collecting butter, and the like — in a word, it is to be watched most strictly that no one remain idle during the winter season.

55. In every colony there is to be a smithy and a smith for various works and public needs, so that everyone may have on hand the material needed for his craft and may always render assistance with his necessary work. If any craftsman should be disobedient toward his elder, such persons are to be punished by assigned tasks and brought to fulfill what is ordered, and in case they refuse to do so, a fine of 50 kopecks is to be exacted into the public fund for each occasion; above all it is to be observed that craftsmen not demand excessive and immoderate prices for their labor from their fellows, but always be content with the prices established by common consent for their work; likewise, if during the working season some family, on account of illness, is unable to work its plot, to harvest ripened grain, or to mow hay, assistance is to be rendered to them communally, or those condemned for offenses to various labors for the common benefit are to be assigned to such work.

56. So that the sown winter and spring grain not be choked by weeds, every effort is to be made to harrow the plowed land as well as possible, so that no unbroken clods remain, and afterward, once it has sprouted, if grass should appear anywhere, such fields are always to be diligently weeded, employing for this purpose children from the age of 10.

57. Similarly it must be observed that the haymaking, too, be carried out in order, two [fields] at once, and not piecemeal, and that hay by no means be allowed to be carried home until it has been properly gathered into orderly cocks and stacks; those disobedient in this are to be compelled accordingly, not letting them leave the fields, until this is done.

The District Head, as well as the village elected representatives, are obliged to attend to all matters of rural economy in general, and to accustom the inhabitants: 1) that, in keeping with the people's custom, in the arrangement of buildings in the colonies, due order be observed, and that houses be built in such a way that they may be more quickly and readily protected in case of fire; and that no new houses be built on one's own initiative without the permission of the Office. 2) That lands not be left unused, and livestock not be left without proper care, encouraging better cultivation of the land and the propagation of better breeds of livestock. 3) That, in keeping with the climate of each place, seeds suited to the nature of the soil be sown, and those which more conveniently and profitably bring the settler income through sale. 4) With regard to kitchen gardens and orchards, to encourage colonists toward the propagation of various needed fruits and plants, especially where it is convenient to cultivate potatoes ["earth apples"], and to see that settlers become accustomed to their use, so that they may also sow their fields with them. 5) To observe most strictly, and to accustom everyone, that in caring for his own household he consider it necessary to keep in reserve what is needed for all his own use, having on hand double seed for everything he is accustomed to sow in his fields and gardens, so that in case of a new sowing he may not feel any shortage.

All the articles set forth in this instruction are to be carried out by all Heads and other village Elders with the utmost exactness, without omission, under threat of the strictest and unfailing penalty.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXVI. P. 299-313.*

## No. 39. INSTRUCTION ON THE INTERNAL ORDER AND ADMINISTRATION OF THE NEW RUSSIA COLONIES (1801)

19,873. — May 16. Instruction for the internal order and administration of the New Russia foreign colonies.

Article I. On the obedience of settlers to the church; on the maintenance of Pastors

and the duties of the latter both toward parishioners and toward the authorities.

§ 1. The foremost duty of all settlers is to obey the law of their church: for this purpose each of them must, on Sundays and holy days appointed by the Priests, come to the church, pray with all reverence, listen attentively to the Word of God, and, when deemed worthy, partake of the Holy Sacraments. If someone absents himself not for lawful reasons but solely out of laziness and negligence, he is to be admonished the first and second time, then a fine of 10 kopecks is to be taken from him; and if this is exacted three times in one year and the guilty party does not desist, then in addition the monetary fine is to be doubled each time, and he is to be employed for a whole day in public labor, the money collected being placed into the common fund.

Note. Public works may consist of the repair of bridges and roads, the digging of ditches, the planting, clearing, and preservation of forests and mulberry trees, the establishment of vineyards, the improvement of meadows, and so forth, as may arise according to the local situation of the colony and the economic establishments therein.
