For the most part, the cause of these householders' insufficiency lies in the fact that their fathers were negligent toward their farms, either through a dissolute way of life or through illness, and they, having come of age and having no means with which to restore the farm, hired themselves out as laborers to the well-off, and thereby accumulated money to purchase the livestock and agricultural implements needed for their fathers' household.

Many colonies could be considerably better off, if they occupied themselves in useful crafts during time free from field work, and if they followed the example of certain colonies where the inhabitants, in their spare time, engage in spinning cotton for Sarepta and for various merchants. But in general they spend such time in idleness, for the reason that most of them are in a condition that is not poor and have sufficient sustenance. DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 163

To encourage them to industriousness and to occupation with work during the autumn and winter, the sole means, in the opinion of the Chief Judge, is to assess each worker from 16 to 60 years of age toward repayment of the debt:

On the meadow side, at.................. 5 rubles

And on the hilly side, at............................ 3 —

Such a levy can be burdensome to no one: for every worker who has farming implements and the necessary livestock cultivates and sows, with a single plow, enough land that the harvest is sufficient for his carefree sustenance and for payment of the tax. Workers who do not have their own draft animals receive, by way of hire, such wages that they can save half of it each year toward payment of the debt sum. And although among the workers there may occasionally be some afflicted with chronic illnesses or disabled, the community of each colony is obligated to care for and feed such persons.

The number of workers cannot be the same every year, since some die while others come of age, and therefore, applying the figure current in 1807, it may be reckoned that up to 42,923 rubles can be received annually toward repayment of the debt.

Finding the proposal and calculation of Chief Judge Rogenbuk regarding the land levy to be well-founded, and considering the increase of the tax on the colonists to be just and absolutely necessary, I take the liberty of laying before the Highest consideration of Your Imperial Majesty the following provision:

1. That 124,249 rubles 80 kopecks, calculated in proportion to the tax paid by the treasury peasants of Saratov Governorate, and apportioned according to the amount of land plowed in the colonies, be collected annually from the colonists, until further review, allotted, in accordance with the calculation made by the said Chief Judge and appended hereto, to those living

on the meadow side of the Volga.............. 74,549 rubles 88 kopecks

And on the hilly side.................................. 49,699 — 92 —

124,249 - 80 -

2. That this collection, adhering to the aforementioned calculation made by district, be apportioned among the colonies, and that the colonists of each colony be allowed to arrange it among themselves according to their own disposition; and as this tax is established as a fixed one, laid upon all and each, they shall have the right to apportion it not only according to the land they plow, but also according to other resources, not excluding those who, being occupied in crafts, rent out their plots, provided only that the entire assessed sum from the colony and district reaches the treasury.

3. As regards the payment of the debt money, in order that the increase thereof, in accordance with the Chief Judge's conclusion, together with the increase of the land tax, should not overburden certain families too greatly, I consider it, for the present, quite sufficient to leave the collection of it on the former basis, from each worker aged 16 to 60, on both the meadow and the hilly side, at one ruble.

4. Each colony must contribute its assessed portion to the District Office, and the latter is then obligated to submit, on behalf of the whole district, the money due under the provision to the Board of Trustees, which will forward it to the Saratov Treasury Chamber, for inclusion in the general State revenues.

Thus, instead of the amounts these colonists currently pay each year,

## No. 55. MEMORANDUM OF THE MINISTER OF INTERNAL AFFAIRS ON THE SETTLEMENT OF COLONISTS NEAR ORANIENBAUM, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER I (1809)

23,440a. — January 9. Most Highly confirmed memorandum of the Minister of Internal Affairs. — On the settlement of colonists on the lands of Oranienbaum.

Your Imperial Majesty, having permitted last year the admission of foreign colonists who, owing to the disastrous events of war, seek resettlement in Russia, was most graciously pleased to remark that for this purpose, and for other useful establishments, there might be placed at my disposal up to 20,000 desiatinas of Your Imperial Majesty's own land, situated between Oranienbaum and Krasnaya Gorka.

Taking into consideration that although there are marshy places here, they may easily be brought into proper order for economic advantage; and that the proximity to the Capital, and especially to Kronstadt, the foremost port in Russia, to which nearly all provisions are for the most part brought from St. Petersburg, could furnish to people intending to settle here for farming, and capable thereof, every means of quickly bringing themselves into a good condition. I communicated this intention to some of our Missions, so that they might inform those willing to resettle in this place; but from almost all I received replies that no such persons were to be found, since all emigrants, having been forewarned of the advantages of the Southern region of Russia, direct their wishes there exclusively.

Now, however, the Chargé d'Affaires, State Councillor Anstett, writes to me from Vienna that the German émigrés who settled in Inowłódz on the river Pilica, 16 families numbering 55 souls, having suffered no small ruin from the war, wish to resettle together in Russia, and having obtained permission to leave their place of residence, are now ready to go wherever they might be invited. As they know nothing DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 165

about the Southern Governorates of Russia, in his opinion they will willingly agree to settle on the lands of Oranienbaum. And to that end he considers it necessary only to correspond from here with our embassy in Prussia; and, for the most reliable and economical execution of this undertaking as regards expenses, he considers it the best means to send an official to them from here, who would conduct them directly to St. Petersburg.

Recognizing that the settlement of these colonists in this region corresponds to Your Imperial Majesty's Most Highest intentions, and considering the opinion of State Councillor Anstett to be well founded, I propose that, to carry out this undertaking, it will be necessary to dispatch a reliable official who could escort them with proper care to these places and provide them with every convenience along the way.

I intend to entrust this Commission to Titular Councillor Spiegelberg, who is presently engaged in receiving colonists in the Volhynia Governorate, since he has almost no duties in winter, and by spring, when the departure of the people may begin, he will return there. And if it should please Your Majesty to confirm this my proposal, I make bold to request Most Highest command for the disbursement, both for his travel and for foreign expenses for the colonists, of 500 chervontsy; and for their provisioning and travel within Russia, I shall instruct the Governor of Grodno to issue him the requisite sum.

The settlement of these people here may be entrusted to State Councillor Kankrin, who serves in the Department entrusted to me, as a most diligent and zealous official. And meanwhile, might it not please you to allow me to request from the Ober-Hofmarschall a plan of the entire Oranienbaum land, so that upon it, with Your Imperial Majesty's consent, the plot of 20,000 desiatinas designated for the settlement of colonists might be marked out, and thereafter one might proceed in good time to clear the sites for settlement and to prepare materials for building houses and everything necessary for the household.

Written on the original: Most Highly approved; wherefore one is to proceed not only to conveying these colonists here, but to preparing their lodging pending the construction of houses for them, for their actual settlement, and for preparing land for their gardens, vegetable plots, and arable fields.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XL. Suppl. Pp. 57–58.*

## No. 56. DECREE OF ALEXANDER I ON THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE CHERNIGOV COLONIES (1809)

23,737. — July 2. Personal decree, given to the Minister of Internal Affairs, Prince Kurakin. — On placing the Belovezh foreign colony under the jurisdiction of the Chernigov Civil Governor, and on the appointment of a special Overseer to it.

Prince Aleksei Borisovich! Having examined the information and considerations you presented concerning the Belovezh colony, situated in the Little Russian Chernigov Governorate, and noting from them that the Novorossiysk Office of Guardianship of Foreigners, to which this colony is subordinate, has, owing to its remoteness, no convenient means of exercising proper oversight over it or maintaining order among the colonists, many of whom have become negligent in husbandry and dissolute, I, in accordance with your opinion, Command:

1. To place this colony under the jurisdiction of the Chernigov Civil Governor, who, in administering it according to the laws generally issued concerning colonists, is to keep strict watch over it.

2. For closer supervision of internal order therein, for restraining the colonists from bad conduct, and for encouraging them to better diligence in their husbandry, to appoint, under the Governor's authority and at their expense, a special Overseer chosen from officials of proven honesty, with a salary fixed at 300 rubles a year, and with a residence assigned to him in the colony.

I charge you to make the proper arrangements for the transfer of all matters relating to this colony from the Guardianship Office to the Chernigov Civil Governor, and to give him full instruction regarding its administration.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXX. Pp. 1028–1029.*

## No. 57. DECREE OF ALEXANDER I ON THE SETTLEMENT OF COLONISTS NEAR ORANIENBAUM (1809)

23,885. — October 1. Personal decree, given to the Senate. — On settling near Oranienbaum several families of newly arrived colonists, and on installing them on the land that had belonged to Treasurer Kliuchinsky, lying on the left side of the road from Oranienbaum to Krasnaya Gorka.

On the occasion of the arrival of new colonists for settlement in this Governorate, having found it necessary to settle several families of them near Oranienbaum, and finding that of the estate formerly belonging to the former Treasurer Kliuchinsky, and transferred by Our decree of December 9, 1808 to the jurisdiction of the Admiralty, the part lying on the left side of the road from Oranienbaum to Krasnaya Gorka is very well suited to this purpose, while according to information gathered from the Ministry of the Naval Forces, only that part lying from the shore of the Gulf of Finland to the said road is needed for the Admiralty — We command: leaving this part under the jurisdiction of the Admiralty, to transfer the remaining land, with everything belonging to it, to the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Internal Affairs for the settlement of colonists. Of which the Governing Senate shall not fail to make the proper arrangement.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXX. Pp. 1193–1194.*

## No. 58. DECREE OF ALEXANDER I ON THE DISCONTINUATION OF THE ISSUANCE OF MONETARY LOANS TO COLONISTS (1810)

24,131. — February 25. Personal decree, given to the Minister of Internal Affairs, with the journal of the Committee established for the reduction of expenditures for the year 1810 appended. — On discontinuing the issuance of monetary loans to colonists.

From the accompanying journal of the Committee established for the reduction of expenditures for the current year, you will observe the reductions in expenses DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 167

in the part entrusted to you, presented on the basis of its preliminary correspondence with you.

<…>

Extract from the journal of the Committee established for the reduction of expenditures for the year 1810.

<…>

In the part of the Expedition of State Economy: 1. To halt the 10,000 rubles allotted for 1810 for the establishment of various economic institutions in the Saratov colonies. 2. Of the 2,500,000 rubles requested for the settlement and recruitment of colonists, to reduce 500,000 rubles. And to have in view a disbursement from the Treasury of 2,000,000 rubles.

The Committee had initially proposed to make a significant reduction in this item and to limit its disbursement to no more than one million rubles; but upon the assurance of the Minister of Internal Affairs that he could by no means reduce this expenditure in 1810, owing to the actual arrival of colonists already under way, or expected, the Committee had to agree to the disbursement of the aforementioned sum, deeming it its duty to represent to His Imperial Majesty that, given the straitened condition of the Treasury, no possibility is foreseen of meeting henceforth, until our finances are set right, expenditures so considerable and moreover entailing no pressing necessity, and therefore deems it necessary to adopt the following measures:

1. To hasten to inform Our Missions and Consulates that henceforth the Government will grant no loan whatsoever to colonists, and that they, in announcing this to those foreigners who shall apply to them for passports, shall at the same time forewarn them that all those who wish to come and settle in Russia at their own expense will find full protection from the Government, will receive land, and will be treated exactly as their fellows have been treated heretofore, with the exception of the monetary assistance, which no one shall be able to receive henceforth.

2. To exclude from this rule the cloth-weavers, who, owing to the pressing need for their products, may be invited in a certain number, on the basis of those rules which, upon the representation of the Minister of Internal Affairs, have been Most Highly confirmed.

Thus, only for these people alone, in 1811, shall even a quite small sum be disbursed.

The Committee deems these measures necessary, both in view of the reduction of expenses so needful, and owing to the excessive costliness of settling colonists. From the reports of the Minister of Internal Affairs it appears that a single colonist family settling near the Capital costs the treasury, for initial establishment alone, upwards of 5,000 rubles, whereas peasants, natural subjects, resettling from populous Governorates to unpopulated places and forming colonies most useful to the State, receive almost no loan at all, so that the assistance given to a German family — exempt from recruit service and other obligations — could probably instead be applied to the resettlement of 50 Russian peasant families, to the substantial benefit of both themselves and the State.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXI. Pp. 68–69.*

## No. 59. MEMORANDUM OF THE MINISTER OF INTERNAL AFFAIRS ON THE ARRANGEMENT OF FUGITIVE NOVOROSSIYSK COLONISTS, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER I (1811)

24,745. — August 15. — Most Highly confirmed memorandum of the Minister of Internal Affairs. — On the means for settling in the Novorossiysk region colonists who will be unable to establish their own households.

I had the good fortune to bring to Your Imperial Majesty's attention in due time the flight of 50 families from among the German colonists being settled near Odessa.

Upon my communicating with the Kherson Military Governor about measures to be taken to stop such flight, he reports to me:

That indeed many of the newly arrived colonists had fled in entire parties, but most of them, through the efforts of Collegiate Councillor Rosenkampf, who is engaged in their settlement, have been caught and returned to their place of settlement, while the rest, as he supposes, are hiding in the neighborhood, in the former Polish territories.

That the reason for their flight is only that they never engaged in, and are incapable of, field labor, having become accustomed to living on ready-made bread; for not one of the actual farmers among them has fled, and the sowing of grain they have done this spring pleases him greatly, in that they seemingly will not be in want of sustenance in the future.

That as regards stopping the flight of colonists, having on his part taken every possible measure, he finds it necessary that instructions be given to the Governors of the Governorates neighboring the Novorossiysk ones, to see to it that no one, under any pretext whatsoever, harbor colonists without lawful documents from the authority established over them, since many of them have overstayed their passports, do not appear for new ones, and he sees no trace by which to find them — the same applying also to colonists who may newly arrive from abroad, lest, under the guise of the latter, those who have received treasury loans might conceal themselves.

Considering that the release of colonists from farming for other occupations, and moreover to distant Governorates, is as incompatible with the Government's aims in recruiting them to populate a sparsely inhabited region as it is harmful owing to various abuses that might occur thereby, and owing to the ease with which colonists could thereby evade repayment of the treasury debt owed by them and even flee back abroad, I propose to inform the Kherson Military Governor that he should order that those of them who are unable to establish their own households owing to unfamiliarity with rural pursuits be attached, as laborers, to the households of settlers who know their trade, in order to acquire skill therein, since they were accepted solely into the class of farmers; or else that they themselves be permitted to seek work, but nowhere except within the three Novorossiysk Governorates, where they will always be within view of their authorities, and where, owing to the shortage of hands in this region, they may receive good pay, thereby rendering benefit to the region through their labor; and he should report how many such people there are, and how many previously released have not appeared in the colonies.

I have made it my duty to report to Your Imperial Majesty's Most Highest consideration on the outcome of this matter and on my proposals. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 169

As for tracing those who have not returned from leave, as well as fugitive colonists, I shall not fail to apply to the Minister of Police for instructions to the Governors of neighboring Governorates to assist in this.

Written on the original memorandum, in the hand of the Minister of Internal Affairs: My proposal has been Most Highly confirmed.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXI. Pp. 823–824.*

## No. 60. DECREE OF ALEXANDER I ON THE RESETTLEMENT OF COLONISTS OF TSARSKOYE SELO DISTRICT (1811)

24,766. — September 12. Personal decree, given to the Minister of Internal Affairs Kozodavlev. — On the resettlement of colonists of Tsarskoye Selo District settled in the Izvara tract to other, more suitable places.

Osip Petrovich! From the information you presented on the condition of the colonists of Tsarskoye Selo District settled in the Izvara tract, and on the inconveniences of their present settlement, I find, in agreement with you, that under it they will be unable to attain that stable prosperity which could fully correspond to the Government's concern for them.

However considerable the sums that might be expended on clearing the land and on assisting the husbandry of these colonists, given the very poor soil and the unfavorable location, all efforts of labor and expenditure must inevitably remain fruitless. Meanwhile, this very place, owing to its abundance of timber forest, may serve some other purpose with greater advantage.

For these considerations, having decided to transfer all these colonists to other, more suitable places, I have agreed with pleasure to the wish expressed by Her Imperial Majesty, My Most Beloved Mother, and by His Imperial Highness, My most beloved brother, the Tsesarevich and Grand Duke Konstantin Pavlovich, for the allotment of land for the settlement of six families on the estates of the town of Pavlovsk, and of up to 20 families on the lands of the Strelna manor, at 35 desiatinas for each family. Accordingly, I charge you:

1. To carry out the resettlement of these families now, in consultation with the Administrators of the said places. 2. Of the remaining colonists, to resettle, on the same basis, into the treasury estates of the Ropsha and Oranienbaum departments, insofar as free land may be found there, allotting likewise 35 desiatinas for each family. 3. Finally, those families for whom, after all this, no more suitable lands can be found for placement, to be sent for settlement to the Novorossiysk region. 4. All expenses necessary for such resettlement, namely: for building houses, for clearing land, for supplementary provisioning and feeding of the colonists, both in the Pavlovsk and Strelna estates and in other places, to be drawn from the sum designated for the settlement of colonists for this year 1811. 5. As regards the rights of these colonists and their obligations, both remain on the general terms issued in 1804. As for the land taxes, upon the expiration of the years of exemption, they are to pay them to those departments to which the lands they settle belong. 6. It is left to your discretion, upon mutual consideration of both the colonists' advantage and the Treasury's benefit, whether to build new houses for the colonists settled in the environs of this capital, or to move them from the Izvara tract, bringing from there also the requisite quantity of timber materials. 7. Thereupon, the 15,000 desiatinas of land that had been designated for colonists in the Izvara tract are to be returned as before to the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Finance. For the rest, I remain well disposed toward you.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXI. Pp. 836–837.*

## No. 61. DECISION OF THE STATE COUNCIL ON RAISING TAXES ON COLONISTS, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER I (1812)

25,031. — March 12. — Most Highly confirmed opinion of the State Council. — On raising the taxes paid by the colonies settled in various Governorates.

The State Council, in General Assembly, having examined the journal of the Department of State Economy upon the representation of the Minister of Internal Affairs, concerning the raising of taxes paid by the colonies settled in the Governorates of St. Petersburg, Saratov, Voronezh, and Chernigov, and finding the conclusion of the Department of Economy on this subject to be correct, opines, in agreement therewith:

1. Instead of the taxes now paid by those colonies, to levy from them henceforth:

In St. Petersburg Governorate: a) From Srednyaya Rogatka, 2 rubles 50 kopecks per each desiatina of suitable land. b) From Izhora, 1 ruble 50 kopecks per desiatina. c) From Novo-Saratovka, 2 rubles per desiatina. d) From Yamburg, 1 ruble 23 kopecks per desiatina.

In Chernigov Governorate: from the Belovezh colony, one ruble per desiatina.

In Voronezh Governorate: from Riebensdorf, 75 kopecks per desiatina, without however exempting it from payment for the right of distilling and from the contribution of 18 kopecks per soul for the maintenance of Government offices.

2. In Saratov Governorate, to equalize the colonists in taxation with the state peasants there, while retaining, however, the apportionment of taxes by land on the former basis; but in consideration of the losses they have sustained from crop failure and cattle plague, to levy the tax under this new provision according to the number of souls of the previous census, not including in this obligation those who prove to be additional according to the new one, and to be guided by this rule until such time as those colonies, in the judgment of the local authorities, come into better condition. Moreover, to equalize the colonies there of the upland and the meadow side in the payment of this tax in such a way that its apportionment, equally by the quantity of land and likewise by the number of souls, be made uniformly, while nevertheless allowing each district, among the colonies composing it, to make a computation proportionate to their particular advantages.

3. The levying of the said taxes to begin with the year 1812.

4. The repayments of the capital sums issued to colonists as loans, while leaving the collection thereof on the former basis, to be directed, as they are received, to the Commission for the Redemption of Debts. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 171

5. The revenues from the two St. Petersburg colonies, Srednyaya Rogatka and Izhora, settled on lands belonging to the Tsarskoye Selo Palace, to be remitted as before to the jurisdiction of that Palace.

6. To take the proper measures for the speediest completion of the survey of the colonists' lands in Saratov Governorate and for allotting the colonists the quantity thereof still lacking.

Resolution. Let it be so.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXII. P. 219.*

## No. 62. DECISION OF THE STATE COUNCIL ON THE TRANSFER OF COLONISTS TO OTHER ESTATES, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER I (1812)

25,276. — November 27. Most Highly confirmed opinion of the State Council. — On the rules for the discharge of colonists into other estates.

Opinion. The State Council, in General Assembly, having examined the journal of the combined Departments of Laws and of State Economy upon the representation of the Minister of Internal Affairs, concerning the rules he proposed for the discharge of foreign colonists into other estates, and finding the conclusion of the combined Departments correct in every respect, on the basis thereof opines:

1. Foreign colonists are not to be discharged into other estates as whole settlements, or in such numbers from a single settlement that it might thereby be disrupted.

2. To permit colonists to pass into other estates only either with the written consent of the entire community composing the colony, or on condition that the one wishing to pass into another status presents someone else in his place to take over and continue his household.

3. Likewise, no one among the settlers may be discharged before definitively choosing another way of life, and until he pays off the portion of the treasury debt lying upon him for his establishment and provisioning at the place of settlement.

4. One requesting discharge must, upon petition, present a receipt from the overseer that he has cleared his entire debt, and the overseer who issued such a receipt assumes responsibility should it turn out that the reckoning of the debt was made incorrectly; but once all accounting matters have been put in order, responsibility passes to the Office of Guardianship.

5. One who has received discharge, upon entering another estate, enjoys, equally with others, all the rights and privileges granted to that estate.

6. To permit one discharged into another estate to remain, if he so wishes, also in the status of colonist, provided, however, that he perform all the obligations that will lie upon him under both statuses. Under such conditions of bearing obligations and paying taxes under both statuses, colonists are not forbidden to enroll in other estates even as whole settlements, and in any number without limitation.

7. From those colonists discharged by the Kherson Military Governor into the merchant estate who have not yet repaid the provisioning money expended on them by the treasury, the same is to be collected.

8. The discharge of colonists into other estates, on the basis of this Statute, is to be left to the local authorities without prior communication on the matter with the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

9. To repeal the effect of the provision contained in the report of the Governing Senate, Most Highly confirmed on October 10, 1799, requiring a personal report on each colonist passing into the merchantry.

Resolution. Let it be so.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXII. Pp. 464–465.*

## No. 63. DECREE OF ALEXANDER I ON THE RESETTLEMENT OF GERMAN COLONISTS FROM POLAND TO BESSARABIA (1814)

25,522. — January 22. Personal decree given to the Minister of Internal Affairs. — On permitting German colonists to resettle from the Duchy of Warsaw to Bessarabia.

The German colonists in the Duchy of Warsaw, seeking a peaceful refuge in the Russian Empire given its present situation, have expressed a wish to resettle to Bessarabia at their own expense. In deference to this wish of theirs, I have found it well to permit them to carry it out on the same basis as that on which the Bulgarians and Serbs settled in Bessarabia. Taking into consideration, however, that they have suffered many misfortunes owing to various circumstances, and that some of them may prove unable to accomplish this at their own expense without any outside assistance, I leave it to your judgment, in carrying out this resettlement, to determine whether it will be necessary to provide them with some assistance from the treasury, both for subsistence and for setting up their households. You are to determine the measure of this assistance with due regard for the benefit of the treasury, bearing in mind that this settlement in general is intended to be arranged not at the expense of the treasury but at the colonists' own expense, and that temporary assistance is to be rendered to them only in cases of the most extreme necessity. In cases of necessity on this subject, I authorize you to address representations to the Committee of Ministers. The local authorities shall be obliged to assist you in this matter. Entrusting this to your special care, I expect assured success in it; you are to report to Me on this from time to time, bringing to the attention of the Committee of Ministers all measures that you undertake.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXII. P. 734.*

## No. 64. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON ADMINISTERING THE OATH TO THE BESSARABIAN COLONISTS AND APPOINTING CLERGY TO THEM (1814)

25,622. — July 17. Resolution of the Committee of Ministers. — Concerning the Warsaw colonists who refuse to take the oath, and on granting the clergy in the Bessarabian colonies the same benefits enjoyed by the clergy in the colonies of the Novorossiysk territory.

The Committee, having heard the attached memorandum of the Minister of Internal Affairs concerning the Warsaw colonists who refuse to take the oath, having confirmed DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 173

the opinion of the Minister of Internal Affairs, authorized him to make the appropriate arrangements for its implementation.

Memorandum of the Minister of Internal Affairs.

The Military and Civil Chief of Bessarabia, Engineer-Major-General Harting, reports that the Warsaw colonists who have already arrived at the place of settlement, numbering 31 families, have refused to take the oath of citizenship.

Those colonists give as the reason for this that they did not receive in Bessarabia the 270 rubles in silver, the pair of oxen, the two horses, and the two cows per family that had allegedly been promised to them in Warsaw by the Governor-General there.

Engineer-Major-General Harting, recognizing that exhortation through the clergy of their respective confessions may have the greatest effect on them, has already applied to the Kherson Military Governor requesting that a Catholic priest and a Lutheran pastor be sent there temporarily for this purpose. Meanwhile, he requests the appointment of permanent clergy for the colonists resettling to Bessarabia.

He further requests instructions as to how he should proceed if the colonists persist in their obstinacy and do not take the oath.

Reference. I. By the privileges most graciously granted to the Warsaw colonists, which were communicated to me by the Warsaw Governor-General, it was promised that indigent families would receive a loan, in addition to subsistence money, of 270 rubles each; other families would receive, according to their means, whatever was needed for initial establishment. But it was not stated in the privileges that this money should be designated in silver, or that any further assistance beyond this had been promised them, and the Warsaw Governor-General wrote nothing to me on this matter.

By the Imperial decree given in my name on January 22 of this year, it was confirmed that assistance to the Warsaw colonists should be rendered only in cases of the most extreme necessity.

II. By the Imperial Manifesto of July 22, 1763, it was ordained that every foreigner arriving to settle in Russia should take an oath of citizenship.

However, both by this Manifesto and by the special rules issued pursuant to the report of the Ministry of Internal Affairs on the reception of colonists for settlement in the Novorossiysk territory, most graciously confirmed on February 23, 1804, all emigrants are permitted to leave Russia upon paying their debts and the prescribed dues.

These rules further provide that if any of those who have arrived for settlement proves disobedient and unsubmissive to the established authorities, such a person, after collection from him of what is owed to the treasury, is to be expelled abroad.

III. By the journals of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers of August 25, 1809, and March 23, 1810, most graciously confirmed, the following benefits have been granted to the clergy appointed to the colonists in the Novorossiysk territory:

1. Salary is paid from the treasury: to the Protestant pastor, 400 rubles, and to the Catholic priest, 300 rubles per year, for 10 years, which are granted to the colonists as a grace period exempting them from payment of taxes.

2. A loan is also given from the treasury for setting up a household:

To Catholic clergy, as they have no families, 300 rubles, and to Lutheran clergy, 600 rubles.

3. Land is allotted: to pastors, 120 desyatinas of arable and hay land, and to priests half that amount, plus 3 desyatinas for a house and garden.

In addition to this, 4) Imperial orders were given for the construction in the colonies of houses for the clergy and their assistants to live in. For travel there they are provided by the treasury with post-horse money, and to many of them a special relocation allowance was most graciously granted, namely 600 rubles each.

Opinion of the Minister. Given the significant number of colonists emigrating to Bessarabia, whose number already amounts to 1,072 families and about 5,500 souls of both sexes, the appointment to them of clergy of their own confessions is in any case absolutely necessary for the maintenance of their morals.

I propose that these clergy should be granted the same benefits as have been granted, by the most graciously confirmed resolutions of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers, to the clergy attached to the colonies in the Novorossiysk territory, with assistance to be given according to their needs, not exceeding what was previously allotted.

For the present, it will be necessary to appoint one priest and one pastor.

As for the colonists' refusal to take the oath of citizenship, by which they probably hope to obtain the excessive assistance they demand, taking into consideration: 1) that there has been no precedent for such a refusal in previous resettlements, and 2) that these people, without taking the oath, cannot be either loyal subjects or genuine inhabitants of state lands, — I consider it necessary, in order to avoid further disturbances, and especially useless expenditures from the treasury, to authorize the Civil and Military Chief in Bessarabia, should exhortation prove ineffective, to expel abroad the instigators of such obstinacy, after taking back from them everything that may have been given to them by the treasury for their establishment; and should this example fail to affect the rest, to proceed in the same manner with all who refuse to take the oath.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXII. Pp. 841-843.*

## No. 65. DECISION OF THE STATE COUNCIL ON EQUALIZING THE VOLGA COLONISTS WITH STATE PEASANTS IN THE PAYMENT OF TAXES (1815)

26,013. — December 8. Opinion of the State Council. — On equalizing the Saratov colonists with state peasants in the payment of taxes.

The State Council, in General Assembly, having examined the journal of the combined Departments of Laws and State Economy, upon the representation of the Minister of Internal Affairs, concerning the equalization of the Saratov colonists with state peasants in the payment of taxes, in agreement with the conclusion of the combined Departments, resolves as its opinion: that the Saratov colonists be equalized with state peasants in the matter of taxes, and that on this basis the collection thereof begin from the second half of the coming year 1816, according to the number of male souls that shall be found in the census now being conducted.

Signed on the original: to be executed. Chairman of the State Council.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXIII. P. 398.*

## No. 66. DECREE OF ALEXANDER I ON THE RECEPTION OF FOREIGN COLONISTS ON PRIVATE LANDS (1817)

27,022. — August 25. Personal decree given to the Senate. — On permitting landowners and proprietors of land to receive and recruit foreign colonists for settlement on their lands.

Contributing in every way to the spread of agriculture and industry in Russia, as the most abundant sources of national wealth, and thereby providing Our loyal subjects with the most convenient and easiest means both of settling vacant lands and of establishing various branches of husbandry, We already, back in 1804, expressed Our consent that landowners might receive and recruit foreign colonists for settlement on their lands. We confirmed the initial rules for such settlement, set forth in the report submitted to Us by the Minister of Internal Affairs, on April 12 of that same year, 1804.

However advantageous these rules may be both for the landowners and for the settlers, certain deficiencies in them have nonetheless been revealed in their application to present circumstances and in their actual implementation. For this reason, and especially in view of the newly expressed wish of foreign emigrants to resettle to Russia in great numbers, and taking into consideration that much of the land distributed for settlement still remains vacant and yields no desired benefit, We have found it well, for the greater advantage of landowners and to facilitate the more rapid settlement of lands, in confirmation and clarification of the rules set forth above, to establish the following: 1) Landowners, both nobles and all those who, on the basis of the decree of December 12, 1801, have the right to acquire land into their own ownership by purchase or other lawful means and to possess it, are permitted to receive and recruit colonists for settlement on their lands. 2) So that the colonists, through ignorance of Our laws and language, may not subject themselves, in concluding agreements with landowners, to burdens exceeding due measure, nor, on the other hand, that landowners be subjected to any excessive demands from the new settlers, We command that all contracts concluded with them, on the basis of the previous and the now-established rules, after being presented and examined in the government office where such agreements are required by law to be presented, be submitted for confirmation to the Minister of Internal Affairs, who, being the guardian of all colonists in general, is obliged to protect also those colonists resettled onto landowners' estates from any oppressions that might befall them. Such an arrangement is furthermore necessary in order thereby to eliminate, in the principal articles of the agreements, any variance which subsequently inevitably gives rise to disputes and litigation. 3) Such agreements must in each case be concluded for no longer than 20 years. In them, in particular, the obligations of the settled colonists must be clearly specified, namely: quitrent, payable in money or in produce in kind, by mutual agreement between them and the landowners. Although the obligation for colonists to perform personal labor on the landowner's estate is subject to misunderstanding and subsequently gives rise to disputes and litigation, it may nevertheless happen that both the landowners and the colonists settled on their lands will agree to such an obligation and wish to conclude a voluntary agreement to that effect; in that case this too is not to be forbidden them, only observing that this entire obligation be clearly specified in the agreement, namely: the types of work, the number of working days, and the like. 4) Likewise, the mutual payments that may be established by voluntary agreement of the contracting parties, upon expiration of the term of the agreement, in the event the colonists leave the land, or in the event the landowner does not consent for the colonists to remain on his land beyond the term, must be precisely and clearly defined in the agreement. 5) If the landowner to whom the land given to the colonists for settlement belongs should die, or should wish to sell or mortgage it, then in such case all the articles of the mutual obligations must remain inviolable, and the heirs or acquirers may not alter the terms of the agreement except with the full consent of the colonists, and are to notify the local authorities thereof for submission to the Minister of Internal Affairs.

The Governing Senate shall not fail to make the appropriate arrangements in this matter by promulgating this decree accordingly, and by announcing through public gazettes both this decree and the rules contained in the report of the Minister of Internal Affairs and confirmed by Us on April 12, 1804.

The rules contained in the report of the Minister of Internal Affairs, most graciously confirmed on April 12, 1804, concerning the rights and benefits for colonists settled on landowners' estates, are as follows: 1) Colonists settling on landowners' estates, on the basis of the Manifesto of 1763, must have freedom of religion and be exempt from military and civil service for the entire period of their residence in Russia, unless someone should voluntarily wish otherwise. 2) In order to provide landowners with greater conveniences and advantages in this form of settlement, the general rule of a 10-year grace period for state colonists is extended also to colonists settled on landowners' estates, it being established that upon expiration of this term the landowners shall pay into the treasury on their behalf the ordinary taxes paid by landowners' peasants. 3) Colonists must bear zemstvo obligations, from the time of their settlement, on an equal footing with the other inhabitants of the governorate in which they are settled. 4) Colonists settled on landowners' estates must be free from any personal bondage; and although at the census they will be recorded on the lands where they are settled, they do not thereby lose their rights, and no government office may effect any personal bondage over them. 5) Landowners may make agreements with colonists concerning their obligations for fixed terms of years, and present these agreements in the government offices for recording, and, in necessary cases, for the resolution of disputes according to the laws on contracts. 6) Colonists, having fulfilled the obligations made with a landowner, may move from one landowner to another. 7) On these general grounds, all landowners are permitted not only to receive but also to recruit colonists from abroad and settle them on landowners' lands by mutual and voluntary agreement as to obligations and labor.

Announcement made on September 17, 1818, by the Ministry of Internal Affairs, concerning the settlement of foreign colonists on proprietary lands.

The Minister of Internal Affairs, Active Privy Councillor Kozodavlev, announces the following concerning the settlement of foreign colonists on the lands of private proprietors: DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 127

It is already known that by the Imperial decree of His Imperial Majesty, given to the Governing Senate on August 25, 1817, and promulgated everywhere at that time by public decrees, all landowners and proprietors of land are permitted to recruit and settle foreign colonists on their lands.

In execution of this, in the past year 1817 the Minister of Internal Affairs made appropriate arrangements, set forth in his circular communications to all Governorate chiefs and in announcements printed in all gazettes.

It has now been received here that many foreign families from the domains of Württemberg and Baden, from Switzerland, and from other places situated along the Rhine River, intending to move to Russia, have expressed a wish, by virtue of the aforementioned Imperial decree, to settle on the lands of private proprietors and landowners.

Being assured that these foreign settlers are distinguished by honesty, good morals, and industriousness, the Minister of Internal Affairs announces to Messrs. landowners and all proprietors of land that should anyone wish to receive and settle foreign colonists on their lands, such persons, in addition to their representations to the Governorate chiefs, may also apply directly to him, and he will without delay enter into correspondence on this matter with persons who have information about those foreigners.

In this connection, the Minister of Internal Affairs requests Messrs. landowners wishing to settle colonists on their estates, when notifying him of such an intention, to inform him, in accordance with the arrangements set forth in his previous announcements, of the following:

I. What number of families is required, how many desyatinas of land will be given to each of them, and in what locations — jointly or separately — their settlement will be arranged.

II. What precisely will be the principal terms of the agreement on which it is proposed to settle the colonists, namely: concerning the construction of houses and establishment of households, for how many years, and what their obligations will be; that is, for the plot of land that will be given into the colonists' possession, is it proposed that they perform labor for the landowner for the number of days specified in the agreement, or that they pay the landowner quitrent in money, or in grain and other produce in kind? It is understood that these latter two types of obligation are far more convenient and less burdensome than the first.

III. At whose expense is the resettlement of the colonists and the travel costs to be carried out — at the landowner's expense, or at the expense of the colonists themselves? In the first case, the sum intended for this purpose must be specified, and the term by which it is to be repaid to the landowner, whether at once or in installments, in accordance with the agreement.

IV. Since it is not possible for the colonists, from the very first day of their settlement, to perform any obligation for the landowner or to pay quitrent under the agreement, it is also necessary to specify in the concluded agreement the period of grace granted by the landowner to the colonists settled on his land.

V. Likewise, concerning state obligations, taxes, and the grace periods granted to colonists under the general statutes concerning them, this must be stipulated precisely and clearly in the concluded agreements.

The advantages and benefits that landowners may expect from the settlement of foreign colonists on their lands are innumerable. This will increase the number of working hands: lands lying vacant will be cultivated with excellent skill; the quantity of produce will be doubled, and, most advantageous of all, agriculture, practiced by skilled and knowledgeable workers, will spread from the colonists to the other inhabitants as well.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXIV. Pp. 501-504.*

## No. 67. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE SETTLEMENT OF COLONISTS IN BESSARABIA (1817)

27,029. — August 28. Resolution of the Committee of Ministers. — On the settlement of colonists newly arriving in Bessarabia.

The Committee, having heard the attached memorandum of the Minister of Internal Affairs concerning the settlement of colonists newly arriving in Bessarabia, resolved: to confirm this representation, and to communicate to the Minister of Internal Affairs, for execution, an extract from this journal.

Memorandum. In the month of May of this year I had the honor to bring to the attention of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers that the Plenipotentiary Governor of the Bessarabian Region, Lieutenant-General Bakhmetev, on the basis of the instructions most graciously given to him for the administration of that territory, had designated a special sum from the Regional revenues, amounting to two hundred ten thousand two hundred lei, as a loan for the foreign settlers newly arriving there.

Now the Plenipotentiary Governor, in a communication received by me on the 7th of this August, reports that the foreign emigrants are arriving there for the most part from the Kingdom of Württemberg, and partly also from Bavaria; and that, having discussed with them their needs and demands, he has drawn up special privileges for them, a copy of which he has forwarded for information.

These privileges or terms are drawn up in every respect in conformity with those most graciously granted to the Warsaw colonists settling there, except that the entire treasury loan for one indigent family is limited to five hundred lei for subsistence and for household establishment in general on-site. Likewise the grace period is limited to 7 years, by the expiration of which they are obliged to repay their debts as well. Upon expiration of this term it is proposed to place them on an equal footing with the other inhabitants of a similar class.

Mr. Bakhmetev added that of the 67 families of the first party of Württemberg settlers, only 10 decline the monetary assistance, while the rest request the loan; land has already been allotted to all of them, and settlement is being carried out through the Colonist Office established in Bessarabia.

Reference. 1. By the journal of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers of May 26, 1816, an Imperial order was issued, among other things, that only the Ministry of Internal Affairs should continue correspondence with the Plenipotentiary Governor of Bessarabia concerning the settlement of foreign emigrants in that region, and the disbursement of funds for this purpose, DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 179

unless this disbursement is discontinued by the finding of the Region's own means for the purpose.

2. In the memorandum most graciously confirmed on May 21 of this year, serving as a guide for the Plenipotentiary Governor in organizing the Administration of Bessarabia, it is established, among other things, that the general statutes of the Russian Empire should be followed in providing the Bessarabian colonies with various advantages and privileges.

3. By the privileges most graciously granted to the Warsaw settlers, it is established, among other things, that indigent families are to be given a loan from the treasury for household establishment of two hundred seventy rubles each, and for subsistence until the first harvest, five kopecks per day per soul, with a grace period from payment of taxes and debts set at 10 years.

Subsequently the loan was increased to three hundred seventy rubles, and subsistence for the indigent was set at up to 20 kopecks per soul.

Opinion of the Minister. Finding, for my part, nothing in the terms drawn up by the Plenipotentiary Governor for the foreign emigrants newly arriving in Bessarabia contrary to the general rules established for the reception and settlement of colonists in Russia — for the reduction in the years of grace may serve as a means to greater diligence on their part in establishing themselves more quickly, so as to repay the loan money to the treasury without undue burden — I consider these terms advantageous both for the treasury and for the colonists; and I propose to express my consent to putting them into effect, only confirming to him that all the other privileges granted to colonists in Russia, by virtue of the instructions given to him referred to above, should be extended to these foreigners as well.

To this I consider it my duty to add that although it was established by the most graciously confirmed journal of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers that settlers leaving the Kingdom of Württemberg should be sent to the Novorossiysk territory and settled there at their own expense in the Kherson and Tavrida Governorates, whither, as is known to the Committee, a considerable number of them have arrived; yet as it may well happen that some of these people, and other similar emigrants, may in particular wish to settle in the Bessarabian Region — it having been stated above that the Plenipotentiary Governor of that Region has been authorized, by the instructions most graciously given to him, to establish and organize foreign colonies there, for the arrangement of which he has been ordered to allocate a special sum from the Region's revenues there — for these reasons I find no obstacle to establishing settlements in that territory of both other foreigners and Württemberg emigrants, on the terms set forth and drawn up by Mr. Bakhmetev.

Privileges granted by the Sovereign Emperor to the Warsaw colonists coming to Russia for settlement.

1. The Russian Government takes the settlers of the Duchy of Warsaw under its special protection, granting them the right to enjoy all the advantages, privileges, and protection of the laws prescribed for natural-born Russian subjects.

2. It is required of these settlers that they occupy themselves chiefly with the improvement of grain farming, the cultivation of fruit orchards, vineyards, and in particular mulberry trees, for those capable of it, and in general with everything befitting a good farmer and a new settler favored by the Monarch's grace.

To assist them in their establishment, the following privileges are granted to them.

1. Exemption from all taxes and zemstvo obligations from the time of arrival in Russia for the next 10 years, excepting payment of a certain sum of money in favor of the Bessarabian tax-farmer.

2. Indigent families are given a loan from the treasury, repayable over 10 years, of 270 rubles each; other families receive, according to their means, whatever is needed for initial establishment.

3. Each complete family is allotted 60 desyatinas of land in perpetual and hereditary possession.

4. In addition, a subsistence allowance in money is given to all in general who are in need of sustenance, from the day of arrival in Russia, of 5 kopecks per soul per day, until the first harvest or grain crop.

5. The new settlers, and their descendants as well, are exempted once and for all from conscription, as well as from the billeting of military units, except in extraordinary cases during the unavoidable passage of troops through these settlements, and then only for the shortest time, such as for a night's lodging or rest.

6. Colonists are granted the right to build churches according to their religion, to have their own clergy, and, in general, complete freedom of religion.

7. Upon expiration of the 10 years of grace from arrival in Russia, another 10 years is designated for the repayment of the money that each has received on loan from the treasury.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXIV. Pp. 747-749.*

## No. 68. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE RESETTLEMENT OF GERMAN COLONISTS FROM THE CAUCASUS COLONY OF KARRAS (1817)

27,070. — September 29. Resolution of the Committee of Ministers. — On the resettlement of German colonists from the Scottish colony to the town of Svyatoy Krest (Holy Cross).

The Committee, having heard the attached memorandum of the Minister of Internal Affairs on the resettlement of German colonists from the Scottish colony, and having confirmed the report of the Minister of Internal Affairs, resolved: to authorize him to instruct whom it concerns that colonists are not to be permitted to resettle arbitrarily from one place to another, and to communicate to the Minister of Internal Affairs an extract from this journal for execution.

Memorandum. In 1810 the Saratov Office of Guardianship for Foreign Settlers, at the request of 25 colonist families, sought permission for them to resettle from the Saratov colonies to the colony of Scottish Missionaries, settled at the foot of the Caucasus Mountains, acknowledging for its part that there were no obstacles to such resettlement.

While certain information was being requested from the Office on this matter, the Ministry of Internal Affairs received a report that the aforementioned colonists, numbering 30 families, had already resettled to the Scottish colony.

Since most of these colonists had, within a short time, managed to build homes there and establish households, there was nothing left to do but determine in what relation these settlers should stand to the Scots, inasmuch as the latter, under the charter graciously granted to them on December 25, 1806, DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 181

enjoy many privileges: whether they would be accepted by them into their society and what obligations should be imposed on them, since while in the Saratov colonies they had performed the same duties as state peasants. Correspondence on this matter accordingly began with the Caucasus Civil Governor.

In 1816 he reported that some of the Saratov colonists who had resettled to the Scottish colony had left it and returned to their former place of residence; while those who remained there, owing to disagreements that had arisen between them and the Missionaries, urgently requested to be resettled elsewhere, namely to the town of Svyatoy Krest, where they hoped to establish themselves to greater advantage both for themselves and for the treasury, citing as the reason for resettlement that the Scots excluded them from enjoying rights equal to their own, and although they offered them a plot of land for settlement on condition that they separate from them, the colonists would in no way agree to remain with them.

Not finding such a resettlement advantageous for them on my part, I instructed the Governor to look into this matter more closely and to obtain a definitive response from both parties, so that it might be submitted for the approval of higher authority.

At the beginning of this year the colonists themselves came to me with a request for permission to move to reside in the town of Svyatoy Krest; in support of which they presented a written certification from the town's inhabitants that they willingly agreed to accept them for settlement; and following this the Caucasus Civil Governor reported that the colonists in no way wished to remain with the Missionaries, reporting that 13 families among them, without any permission from the authorities and without his knowledge, had resettled to the town of Svyatoy Krest, where they had already managed to establish homes and households. For this reason he considers that the remaining colonists in the Scottish colony might also be permitted to settle in the said town.

Meanwhile, before I had even received the response of the Caucasus Civil Governor, the Chief Administrator of Georgia and the Astrakhan and Caucasus Governorates, Lieutenant-General Yermolov, wrote to me proposing to invite foreigners to settle in Georgia for the spread of agriculture and other branches of husbandry, having in mind the aforementioned German colonists living in the Scottish colony who were requesting resettlement elsewhere: I informed Mr. Yermolov of their agreement to resettle to Georgia.

Now the Caucasus Civil Governor, in a report received by me on July 29 of this year, explains that he proposed this to the colonists, and that although not all of them expressed a wish for such resettlement, they nevertheless sent two representatives there for a preliminary inspection of the lands.

The Governor considers that should the colonists not agree to resettle there, they might be permitted to move to reside in the town of Svyatoy Krest instead, with the rights granted to the Saratov colonists, but on condition that they participate in all obligations throughout the governorate generally, as state peasants do.

As for the privileges of the said town, he explains that these are set out in the charter of October 28, 1799, granted to the Armenians of Derbent and Mushkur, whereby, among other things, they were permitted to found the town, ordered to be allotted 12,000 desyatinas of usable land for pasture, and to establish their own Armenian court for the administration of the inhabitants both within and outside the town, subject to appeal to the Provincial Board and the Administrator of the Governorate; the town was granted exemption from all taxes and services, under the Highest decree of April 15, 1799, for 10 years, after which the inhabitants are obliged to pay into the treasury in perpetuity: merchants one percent per ruble of capital, townsmen and guild members 2 rubles per household, and district settlers, to whom 30 desyatinas of land each are allotted, 5 kopecks per desyatina per year; they are exempt from billeting, except in cases of troops passing through, and permanently from the provision of recruits.

To this the Governor adds that to date only 112 male souls of Armenians together with Georgians have settled in the town of Svyatoy Krest, and that therefore, if the colonists, numbering 88 souls, were permitted to move there from the Scottish colony, along with those already numbering 37 souls who have moved there, the present inhabitants of the town, having a great deal of land, could not suffer any shortage of it, and that among the colonists there the craftsmen would join the guilds and the farmers would become district settlers.

He further finds, however, that the residence of these colonists on the land of the Scottish colony would be incomparably more advantageous for them, both owing to the proximity to the town of Georgievsk and to the mineral springs, and owing to the very quality of the soil there, which is far better than in the town of Svyatoy Krest.

At the same time I received notice from the Kherson Military Governor that the Württemberg settlers, who had expressed a wish to settle in Georgia, and about whom I had the honor to report to the Committee of Messrs. Ministers, have already set off there, numbering 31 families.

Reference. I. The exemption from taxes and duties granted to the Saratov colonists under the Highest Manifesto of July 22, 1763, ended in 1798. Under the report confirmed by the Highest authority on December 18, 1808, they were made equal in taxation to the state peasants of Saratov Governorate.

II. By the opinion of the State Council, confirmed by the Highest authority on November 27, 1812, concerning the release of colonists into other estates, it was decreed that a colonist who receives release to enter another estate enjoys, equally with others, all the rights and advantages granted to that estate. By the same opinion it is permitted for a colonist released into another estate to remain also in colonist status, should he wish it, provided, however, that he perform all the duties that will lie upon him under both statuses.

III. In the charter graciously granted on December 25, 1806, to the Scottish colony, it is decreed, among other things:

In point 3: We confirm to them the indisputable and hereditary possession of the lands that shall be allotted to them, provided, however, that of these lands belonging to the whole community, not the smallest portion, under any pretext whatsoever, is to be ceded, mortgaged, sold to outside parties, or made subject to any deeds to that effect. In point 4: Members of this colony are to be free from all taxes and duties for 30 years, counting from their receipt of the land. In point 19: We permit all persons purchased [into freedom] by them and given their freedom, and all foreigners who, having left foreign lands, might wish, with their consent, to settle together with them, to enjoy the same privileges as We grant to them.

IV. According to the census record now submitted by the Caucasus Civil Governor, the Missionaries living in the Scottish colony, who arrived from Scotland and were, on the basis of the said charter, accepted by them as members of their community, number altogether 23 male souls. DOCUMENTS___________________________________________________________________ ________ 183

The land allotted for the possession of the Scottish colony amounts to about 6,500 desyatinas.

Opinion of the Minister. Taking into consideration, first, that in the Scottish colony, given the number of missionaries settled there, there is a significant amount of surplus land, which must remain entirely unused, and second, that the Scots themselves agree to allot the necessary amount of it to the colonists, I find that it would be quite beneficial if the latter were to remain residing in that colony, both because of their long residence there and because of the households they have already established, where it would also be possible, with the consent expressed by the former, to settle them with their own rights and with free exercise of their faith.

But since they in no way agree to remain there any longer, citing as the main reason that the Scots allegedly exclude them from enjoying rights equal to their own — which, under the aforementioned charter graciously granted to the Scots, cannot be demanded without the Scots' own consent — while the Caucasus Civil Governor reports that in the town of Svyatoy Krest there is likewise much surplus land, to which about half of the said German colonists from the Scottish colony have already resettled, and have received from the town's inhabitants a written certification that they willingly accept them for residence: I therefore propose to permit them such resettlement, and hereby to instruct the Caucasus Civil Governor: 1) to allot them, on the basis of the general rules for colonists, 60 desyatinas per family. 2) To equalize them in taxes and duties with the state peasants there, excepting the recruit levy, from which all foreign colonists are permanently exempt; and 3) With regard to their administration, they are to have a special overseer at their own expense, following the example of the Chernigov Belovezh colonists, and otherwise to remain under the direct authority of the Governor himself.

Should any of them wish to enter some other estate, each is to be left free to do so, acting on the basis of the rules issued for the release of colonists.

All of which I submit for the gracious consideration of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXIV. P. 781-784.*

## No. 69. DECREE OF ALEXANDER I ON SUPPLEMENTARY RULES FOR THE SETTLEMENT OF COLONISTS ON LANDOWNERS' LANDS (1817)

27,072. — October 1. Imperial decree, announced by the Minister of Internal Affairs to the Civil Governors. — Supplementary rules on the acceptance and settlement of colonists on landowners' lands.

His Imperial Majesty, by decree given to the Governing Senate on the 25th day of August of this year, for the greater benefit of landowners and for the more advantageous and speedy settlement of their lands, has graciously deigned, in confirmation and clarification of the rules issued in 1804 concerning the acceptance and settlement of foreign colonists on landowners' lands, to decree, among other things: 1) that colonists may be accepted and recruited for settlement both by the Nobility and by all who, under the law, have the right to acquire land. 2) That all contracts concluded with such colonists be submitted, after review by the relevant office, for confirmation by the Minister of Internal Affairs; and 3) That such agreements be concluded each time for no longer than 20 years, with a detailed statement of all circumstances, both on the part of the landowners and of the colonists being settled.

The said Highest decree, together with the rules issued in 1804 on the same subject, was promulgated by the Governing Senate by public decrees on September 10 of this year.

Meanwhile, the Sovereign Emperor, in consideration of the difficulties that landowners themselves might encounter in recruiting colonists, has graciously been pleased to command that such landowners as may wish, on the basis of that decree, to recruit and settle colonists on their lands, should apply in this matter to the Minister of Internal Affairs, who will use his good offices to persuade and recruit such people for settlement on landowners' lands, in accordance with the amount of land and the means proposed by the landowners; concerning which I have been instructed to make the appropriate arrangements.

In fulfillment of this Highest will of the Sovereign Emperor, I consider it essential that all such landowners and other owners of land who wish to settle foreign colonists on their lands should, when notifying the Minister of Internal Affairs of such an intention, communicate to him, through the mediation of Messrs. Civil Governors: first, on how many desyatinas of free land, in what places, whether together or separately, the landowners intend to establish the settlement of foreign immigrants, and how many families; second, what will constitute, at least in its main points, the terms on the basis of which it is proposed to settle the colonists, such as: regarding the construction of houses and establishment of households, for how many years, and what duties; and third, at whose expense their resettlement and travel costs are to be met, whether the landowner's or the colonists' own: in the first case the sum intended for that purpose must also be indicated.

To this I consider it not superfluous to add that, since the opinion of the State Council, confirmed by the Highest authority on the 27th day of November 1812, does not forbid foreign colonists settled on state lands in various governorates from passing, under certain rules, into another way of life, then should any landowner wish to accept such colonists for settlement on his land, he is likewise to notify the Minister of Internal Affairs of his wish as stated above, and colonists of this kind, as soon as they fulfill the obligations imposed upon them to the treasury and to the community, will receive permission for this without hindrance.

In communicating these arrangements, I request that you bring all of this, through whomever it may concern, to the attention of the landowners and owners of land within the governorate entrusted to your administration, and that you impress upon them meanwhile the very considerable benefit that they will derive from such settlement through better cultivation of the land, through the establishment of various foreign handicrafts, and through the reliable receipt of quitrent or other income.

As soon as there appear to be those wishing to accept colonists on the aforementioned terms, please inform me of this in detail, adding your own opinion as well.

I further trust that you will not fail to have the decree of the Governing Senate of September 10 of this year, published for general public information, in which DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 185

both the aforementioned Highest decree of August 25 and the earlier rules are set forth, distributed, as widely as possible, in as many copies as feasible throughout all the districts of the governorate entrusted to you.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXIV. P. 785-786.*

## No. 70. CHARTER OF ALEXANDER I TO THE BALTIC HERRNHUTERS (MORAVIAN BRETHREN) (1817)

27,113. — October 27. Charter — granting privileges and advantages to the Members of the Evangelical Brethren's Society in the Baltic Governorates.

By the Grace of God, We, Alexander I, Emperor and Autocrat of All Russia, etc., etc., etc.

The brethren of the Evangelical Society of the Augsburg Confession, who have long dwelt in Russia in the colony of Sarepta near Tsaritsyn, and who, living a quiet and humble Christian life, have always distinguished themselves by their industry, careful household management, good conduct, and exemplary behavior, received from Our ancestors and from Us at various times privileges which, by confirming their civil status, provide them the means to continue their commendable occupations and make them useful citizens of the State.

But the rights of status of the brethren of the same Evangelical Society in Livland, Estland, and Courland had not hitherto been determined. Yet their pious life, their zealous activity carried out quietly and in good order, each attending to his own work, and their successful instruction, by word and example, especially of the peasantry, to conform their deeds and conduct to the precepts of Christ's teaching, render the members of this Society worthy of every attention and protection.

In consequence of this We have deemed it good and just to grant and confirm to the brethren of the Evangelical Society of the Augsburg Confession living in the said three Baltic Governorates the rights and privileges of their co-religionists residing in the Sarepta colony, on the following basis:

1. We confirm the freedom granted to the brotherhood of this Society in the exercise of their faith according to the statute, doctrine, and rites existing among the Evangelical Brethren, permitting the courts, in cases of necessity, to accept from members of this brotherhood an oath according to their custom, consisting solely of a verbal affirmation, with the exception only of the oath of allegiance of subjecthood, which they, should any of them wish to take it, must render in the same manner as all Our other loyal subjects.

2. We permit the said members of the Brethren's Society to build, establish, and maintain under their own supervision, as has been the case hitherto, for the spiritual benefit and edification of Latvians, Estonians, and other willing persons, houses of prayer or meetings in towns, settlements, and villages, with the consent of the landowner and with the knowledge of the town authorities, without any hindrance otherwise. In these houses of prayer or meetings all who wish may freely gather, as has been the established practice to this day, except during the hours designated for the usual church services, and during time free from work. These edifying prayer meetings, established for the reading of the Word of God, prayers, and appropriate instruction, shall remain under the guidance and administration of the elders and members of the Evangelical Brethren's Society.

3. The small plots of land, together with the household establishments upon them, presently belonging to the Evangelical Society in the said three governorates, or such as may hereafter be lawfully acquired and established by them, as well as the houses and dwellings of the elders and members of the Society, are confirmed in their unhindered and lawful possession according to law and rights, provided that, since these plots of land, household establishments, and houses belong not to any individual but to their whole Society, nothing therefrom is to be ceded, sold, or made subject to any deeds, under any pretext whatsoever.

4. Since on the plots of land belonging to this Society there are now establishments for the upbringing and education of children of both sexes, these may not only continue as before, but new ones of the kind may be established at the discretion of the Elders of the Society. These establishments shall remain under the direct and sole guidance and supervision of the said Elders; the spiritual and secular authorities concerned, however, are not at any time prohibited from viewing these establishments and being informed about them.

5. Granting the members of the Brethren's Society free exercise of divine worship and prayer according to their own institutions and rites in all their dwellings and houses, We likewise permit that priests, ordained by the Bishops of that Society, may, among their brethren of German origin who are actual members of the Evangelical Brethren's Society, perform in their capacity all the spiritual rites which they are, under the statutes of the Society, called upon to perform.

6. We take under Our especially gracious protection all members of the Evangelical Brethren's Society now residing in the said three governorates, as well as those who may in future arrive and settle there, and We further decree, on the basis of the privileges granted to the Sarepta Society, that all of them living in towns, settlements, and villages who engage in some trade or craft shall be free from enrollment in guilds and corporations.

7. We assure them, upon Our Imperial word, that none of the brethren of the Society now living in those governorates, or who may hereafter arrive there, being actual members of the said Society, nor their children or descendants, shall at any time be taken or enrolled into military or civil service without their own wish to that effect. We likewise exempt forever their possessions and dwellings everywhere from all manner of billeting and quartering, from the maintenance of post stations, the provision of relay horses, and other similar duties. And since, moreover, their possessions in the said three governorates are of little extent, and the number of Society members is quite small, We, in consideration of their generally useful labors and occupations, exempt them from the poll tax and from all other communal, regular, and extraordinary levies. Should, however, the possessions of the Brethren's Society in time multiply and expand significantly in other governorates, the Government will then consider what moderate taxes might be imposed upon their lands, similar to those paid by the Sarepta Society.

8. The members of the Brethren's Society in these three governorates are permitted to have their own administration among themselves, composed of Elders, which shall be under the authority of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. These Elders are granted the right to have their own seal, and to issue to the members of the Society living in those governorates DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 187

passports of their own for travel and residence anywhere within the State; for travel abroad and entry into Russia, however, passports shall be supplied, upon communication from the Elders of the Society, by those offices from which such passports are issued to others leaving Russia and entering it.

9.
