We most graciously grant to all Members of this Society in these governorates, and to their descendants, full freedom and authority to dispose of their own property at each one's discretion; but should any of the brethren now living there, or of their future descendants, at any time wish to leave Russia together with all their property, he shall be obliged to pay a three-year tax on the capital acquired within the State, in whatever amount shall be declared in good conscience by the Elders of the Society. On the same basis shall be treated the property remaining after the death of members of the Society whose relatives and heirs reside in foreign states, when it must, by right of inheritance, be sent there; but the Elders of the Society are first obliged to pay the debts of the deceased, both to the treasury and to private persons. Should anyone die without leaving heirs and without having made a will, his property shall be given over into the possession of this Society, without any exaction from it by the treasury, save only for the payment of debts remaining after the deceased.

10. We permit the Agent residing in St. Petersburg on behalf of the Sarepta Brethren's Society, who, with the knowledge and confirmation of the Minister of Internal Affairs, conducts the affairs and commissions of that Society, to be likewise employed by the Society in the Baltic Governorates, in the same capacity and for the same purpose. Thus all members generally of the Brethren's Society of the Baltic Governorates shall, in all matters, be subject solely to the Minister of Internal Affairs, on the same basis as the members of the Sarepta Society.

11. In conclusion of this Our Imperial charter granting rights and privileges most graciously to the Evangelical Brethren's Society in Livland, Estland, and Courland, We command all authorities and government offices not only to leave the members of this Society and their descendants in peaceful possession of the lands, houses, and other property belonging to them, and to allow them to enjoy the privileges granted by Us, but also, should the need arise, to protect them from all harm and, upon the representations of their Elders, to render them every assistance, defense, and protection.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXIV. P. 843—845.*

## No. 71. DECISION OF THE STATE COUNCIL ON INCREASING THE PAYMENT FROM THE MENNONITES AND ON EQUALIZING THE FIRST NEW RUSSIAN COLONISTS WITH STATE PEASANTS, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER I (1817)

27,149. — November 19. Highest Confirmed Opinion of the State Council. — On increasing the payment of the debt sum from the Mennonites and on equating the old New Russian Colonists with state peasants. With the report of the Minister of Internal Affairs to the Senate on this subject appended.

The State Council, in the Department of State Economy and in the General Assembly, having examined the report of the Minister of Internal Affairs on increasing the payment of the debt sum from the Mennonites and on equating the New Russian colonists with state peasants, and finding, in agreement with the Minister of Internal Affairs, that the proposal of his Ministry's Council on this subject is well founded, gives the opinion: that it be confirmed in all its parts.

Resolution. His Imperial Majesty was pleased to confirm as Highest authority the opinion rendered by the General Assembly of the State Council on increasing the payment of the debt sum from the Mennonites and on equating the old New Russian colonists with state peasants, and ordered it to be carried out. Chairman of the State Council.

Report of the Minister of Internal Affairs to the Governing Senate, December 7, 1817.

By the report of the Governing Senate confirmed as Highest on the 6th day of April 1800, for the purpose of improving the condition of the New Russian foreign settlers, of whom there were then counted up to 560 families, it was ordered: 1. That of the Mennonites who settled in 1789 and subsequent years in the Ekaterinoslav Governorate at the Khortitsa tract, some be transferred to other land, and that those remaining in place, having been allotted 65 desyatinas per family, retain in their possession the surplus land beyond that, on condition that they pay 15 kopecks for each of the 65 desyatinas; and from the remaining surplus quantity, after the expiration of the grace years, they contribute to the treasury 2½ kopecks per desyatina. For those remaining in place the grace period is to be deferred for 5 years, and for those transferred for 10 years, after which they are obliged to pay both the assessed land dues and the loan installments, the former over 10 years and the latter over 10 years. 2) The colonists known under the names of Josephstal, Danzig, Swedish, and Jamburg, settled in the same Governorate from 1787 to 1793, are to be allotted land — the former at 32½ desyatinas per family, and the rest at 15 desyatinas per male soul — and the grace period for payment of taxes for the Josephstal colonists is deferred for 5 years, after which 15 kopecks are to be collected from each desyatina, and the repayment of debts in installments is to be arranged over 10 years. The rest are to be assessed a land tax of 5 kopecks per desyatina, and repayment of the debt is to be arranged over 20 and 30 years.

Later, when the grace period for payment of taxes expired for some of the Mennonites and Josephstal colonists, some of them were obliged to pay more than 100 rubles per family in land tax and debt repayment combined. Upon the representation of the Office of Trusteeship of Foreign Settlers that they would be excessively burdened by such collection, it was ordered by the report of the Ministry of Internal Affairs confirmed as Highest on September 9, 1805: that the Mennonites, in accordance with their petition, be assessed 25 rubles per family, with one part of this to be credited toward the land tax and the other toward debt repayment; and that when they improve their condition, the sum allotted toward debt repayment be doubled. From the Josephstal colonists, who received half the amount of land compared with the Mennonites, at 32½ desyatinas, 12 rubles 50 kopecks per year are to be collected, including in that sum both the land dues and the debt payments.

On this basis they have paid the debt and land dues up to the present time. Meanwhile, seeing that other colonists, settled also 15 years after them, on the basis of rules confirmed as Highest by the report of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of February 20, 1804, after the expiration of the first 10 grace years, pay, in respect of taxes and duties, land dues alone DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 1_89

exceeding 12 rubles, in addition to performing other duties, and taking into consideration that the indulgence granted to the above-mentioned old Mennonites and colonists in the deferral of grace years and in the repayment of debt under the report of September 9, 1805, was made only until the improvement of their condition, and receiving information about their now-settled position, I instructed the local colonial Administration in 1816 to consider to what extent the collections to the treasury from these Mennonites and colonists could be increased.

To this the New Russian Trusteeship Office reported that these Mennonites and colonists are now in good condition, and submitted a proposal on increasing the payment of the debt sum from the Mennonites and on equating the colonists in taxation with state peasants, on the following basis:

First. That from the Mennonites, numbering 346 families, who have hitherto paid 14 rubles 57 kopecks toward debt repayment, plus 10 rubles 43 kopecks in land dues, making a total of 25 rubles per family, the payment toward debt repayment be increased to 35 rubles per family, and that for all the surplus good land they hold beyond the established allotment, for which they now pay 2½ kopecks per desyatina on the basis of the report of the Governing Senate of April 6, 1800, they be charged 15 kopecks in accordance with the charter Highest granted to them on September 6 of that same year, since their community may allot such surplus land anew to families newly formed through marriage and to their brethren who have since arrived from abroad and joined them.

By this calculation each Mennonite family will owe annually, in both debt and land payments, from 48 to 53 rubles.

Second. That the above-mentioned old colonists, comprising 161 families, be equated in taxation, on the basis of the general regulations concerning colonists, with the local state peasants there, who pay 3 rubles in poll tax and 8 rubles in quitrent per soul; and that, instead of the debt payment hitherto made by the colonists of from 7 to 12 rubles, each family be charged equally 5 rubles, out of consideration that since the payment of the aforementioned poll and quitrent monies is in itself fairly substantial, an increase in the debt payment might render them unable to pay these in full.

By this calculation each family will be obliged to contribute from 21 to 43 rubles per year.

This report was examined in the Council of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, which, finding the opinion of the Office well founded, proposed to confirm it, adding thereto that the colonists mentioned by the Office be assessed a land tax in accordance with the regulation concerning the Saratov colonists confirmed as Highest by the report of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of December 18, 1808, so that they pay as much, by the number of souls of the last census and by the quantity of land, as the New Russian state peasants pay in quitrent and poll tax per year per soul, apart from the zemstvo duties they now also perform, and that the collection of this land tax be left to each colony to arrange among itself according to its own disposition.

Likewise, the Council of the Ministry of Internal Affairs found correct the Office's proposal that, upon equating these colonists in taxation with the peasants, each family be charged in repayment of the state debt owed by them no more than 5 rubles per household, since some of them have a smaller quantity of land than the Mennonites, and others even half as much, that is, 32½ desyatinas.

On this basis I submitted a report to the State Council, which by its opinion, per the minutes of the Department of State Economy of September 28 and of the General Assembly of October 8 of this year, confirmed all of this.

I have the honor of presenting to the Governing Senate a copy of this Highest-confirmed opinion, in case it may be found proper to instruct whomever is appropriate to carry it into execution. As for announcing this to the Mennonites and colonists, I shall not fail to issue the appropriate instruction to the colonial Administration.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXIV. P. 879-881.*

## No. 72. REGULATION ON THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE COLONIES OF SOUTHERN RUSSIA, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER I (1818)

27,312. — March 22. Highest Confirmed Regulation. — On the chief administration of the colonists of the southern territory of Russia.

Personal decree, given to the Senate. In view of the increased number of foreign settlers in the three New Russian Governorates and in the Bessarabian Region, We have deemed it proper that these settlers, instead of the various Authorities to which they have hitherto, according to various circumstances, been subordinated at their places of settlement, henceforth be administered by a single Authority, both in their administration and with regard to concern for their welfare. To this end, by Our command, a special regulation has been composed concerning the chief administration of the colonists of the southern territory of Russia. Having now confirmed this regulation and the staff establishments belonging to it, and forwarding them herewith, We command the Governing Senate to make the appropriate arrangements in this regard. The sums calculated in the appended staff establishments for the Trusteeship Committee and the three Offices, We command to be disbursed from the State Treasury beginning January 1 of the coming year 1819; for their maintenance until that time, during the course of the present year 1818, these sums are to be borrowed, for the New Russian Governorates from the sums assigned this year for colonists and officials attached to them, and in the Bessarabian Region from the revenues there.

Regulation. For the administration, in the three New Russian Governorates and in the Bessarabian Region, of foreign colonists, both those previously settled and those now being settled and that may hereafter come to settle, a Trusteeship Committee for the colonists of the southern territory of Russia is hereby established. This Committee, being under the direct authority of the Minister of Internal Affairs, shall have charge of all the offices and Authorities established for the administration of the colonies in the Governorates of Ekaterinoslav, Kherson, and Tavrida, and in the Bessarabian Region.

I. Composition of the Trusteeship Committee.

1. The Trusteeship Committee consists of a Chairman, two Members, and the requisite number of chancery officials and servants. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 191

2. The Chairman, under the title of Chief Trustee, must be of no lower than the fourth class. He is confirmed by the Sovereign Emperor.

3. Members of the Committee are appointed by the Minister of Internal Affairs, with the confirmation of the Committee of Ministers.

4. The Head of Chancery is appointed by the Minister of Internal Affairs, upon the recommendation of the Chief Trustee. The other Chancery officials and servants are appointed by the Trusteeship Committee, upon the proposals of the Chief Trustee.

The staff establishment of the Trusteeship Committee and its Chancery is appended hereto under letter A.

5. The Trusteeship Committee is the Chief authority governing all matters relating to the settlement and protection of migrants in the three New Russian Governorates and in the Bessarabian Region.

6. The chief subject of this administration shall be the foreign settlers or colonists, of whatever nation they may be, who have to this day settled in those places, are now being settled there, and may hereafter come to settle there.

7. The purpose of this administration is: the reception of such settlers, their settlement on the basis of established rules, the preservation of all the benefits, rights, and privileges granted and to be granted to them hereafter, and oversight of the fulfillment of the obligations they have undertaken.

8. This administration pertains only to those foreigners who settle on state lands as farmers, or as craftsmen needed in an agricultural community; but foreigners arriving singly or in families for trade purposes, or for enrollment into the townsman estate, merchantry, or another status within towns, do not belong to it at all.

9. Foreign settlers settling on lands belonging to landowners or private proprietors, on the basis of the decree of August 25, 1817, likewise belong to the charge of the Trusteeship Committee, but only with regard to oversight, so that mutual obligations are not violated.

10. Settlers from among Russian subjects, settled according to the rules issued for colonists, are subject to the administration of the Committee in the same manner as foreigners, only until such time as they are transferred into the general Governorate administration.

11. Subordinate to the Committee are the Offices of Trusteeship of Foreigners within the bounds of its jurisdiction, and those to be established hereafter; likewise all officials dependent, whether from those Offices or from the Governorate Authorities, on the colonial branch.

12. The Committee is obliged in all its affairs to be guided by those laws and instructions which have hitherto been given by the Government to the Offices and Governorate Authorities in the colonial branch, and to observe them precisely, until such time as, on the basis of the present regulation, a new draft of rules is submitted by the Chief Trustee and approved by the Government.

13. To this end the Committee must obtain from the Kherson Military Governor, and also from the Plenipotentiary Viceroy of Bessarabia, all cases hitherto conducted under their jurisdiction in the colonial branch; and likewise demand from the Offices and the Odessa Chancery everything that may pertain to the substance of the chief administration.

14. Together with this, all lands which have been, are, or shall hereafter be allotted or designated for the settlement of colonists in the three New Russian Governorates and in Bessarabia pass into the direct jurisdiction of the Committee.

15. The conduct of affairs in the Committee shall follow the same rules and order as prescribed in the Instruction to the Office of Trusteeship of New Russian Foreign Settlers confirmed as Highest on July 26, 1800. But this is to be understood only until such time as the Committee, based on local considerations, submits more convenient and suitable methods for this purpose.

16. The permanent seat of the Committee is fixed in the Governorate town of Kherson, where, by arrangement of the Civil Authority, separate houses are to be set aside both for the sittings of the Committee and for the residence of the Chief Trustee, and of two or three Chancery officials of his choosing, pending a special report from him on this matter.

II. Relations of the Trusteeship Committee to higher,

equal, and subordinate authorities.

1. The Committee is under the direct authority of the Minister of Internal Affairs.

2. The Committee receives the instructions and proposals of the Minister of Internal Affairs and carries them out precisely.

3. In all matters for which there is no precise law or instruction from the Minister, the Committee seeks his authorization.

4. In matters admitting no delay, the Committee is guided by the benefit of the treasury or the necessity of the settlers, reporting, however, everything to the Minister immediately.

5. The instructions of the Minister and the representations of the Committee are written according to the forms established in the General Institution of Ministries.

6. The Committee sends to the Ministry weekly brief memoranda on the conduct of affairs, and monthly registers, both of matters decided and undecided, and of the sums under its administration.

7. The annual report on sums the Committee sends directly on its own behalf, on the basis of the laws, to the State Expedition for the Audit of Accounts, and at the same time delivers a copy of that report to the Minister of Internal Affairs.

8. The Committee has no direct relations with other Ministries, except for reports to the Governing Senate on the receipt of decrees, which must be sent to the Committee every time they are dispatched to other higher government offices. But in all cases requiring communication with other Ministries, the Committee submits to the Minister of Internal Affairs.

9. Since the Kherson Military Governor is the Chief Authority in civil matters in the three New Russian Governorates, and the Plenipotentiary Viceroy in Bessarabia, relations between the Committee and them are necessary.

10. These relations may be either directly from the Committee, according to the form employed in the Ministries, or, by its decision, in the name of the Chief Trustee.

11. The Committee applies to the Kherson Military Governor and to the Plenipotentiary Viceroy of Bessarabia in all those cases where the assistance of the Chief Governorate Authority is necessary by law; and these Authorities, by virtue of their office, are obliged to satisfy all lawful requirements of the Committee in matters concerning colonists, and to notify the Committee at the same time of their own dispositions. DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 193

12. Likewise the Committee communicates with the military Authority stationed in that territory, whenever a matter touches upon its jurisdiction.

13. In matters depending on the Civil Governors and government offices of those Governorates where the subordinate colonies are located, the Committee communicates on a footing of equality, and requests assistance or necessary information; and if it does not receive these in due time, it applies to the Chief Authorities; and in necessary cases reports to the Minister of Internal Affairs. The lower officials of these Governorates, such as Town Governors, Zemstvo Commissioners of Police, and others, are obliged to carry out immediately the demands of the Committee or the Chief Trustee in all cases where those demands pertain to their duties.

14. In respect of other Governorates the Committee, when necessary, communicates with the Civil Governors and with the higher government offices likewise on a footing of equality; and if it does not receive a satisfactory answer in due time, it reports to the Minister of Internal Affairs.

15. To the subordinate Offices of foreign settlers the Committee gives instructions according to the Ministerial form, requires reports from them on affairs and sums, and resolves their submissions in everything that lies within its power.

16. The Chief Trustee is obliged to inspect the colonies from time to time; if, owing to illness, he is unable to do so himself, one of the Members of the Committee performs this duty on his behalf.

17. The Chief Trustee, or, on his behalf, a Member of the Committee, during the inspection of the colonies, receives the petitions and complaints of the colonists; and if anything is not contrary to the general regulations concerning colonists, he resolves their requests and gives instructions to the local colonial Authorities and proposals to the Offices, with the sole proviso that such instructions and proposals remain in force only until his return to the Committee, upon whose confirmation their further effect depends.

III. Composition of the Offices of Administration of Foreign Settlers.

1. Since, with the establishment of the Trusteeship Committee, the relations and functions of the Offices of Trusteeship of Foreigners and other Authorities now existing in that territory necessarily undergo change in many respects, their very composition requires a corresponding alteration, although the course of business in them is nevertheless to remain as before, pending the submission by the Chief Trustee of a draft of new rules for the settlement and administration of the colonies.

2. Therefore the Office of Trusteeship of New Russian Foreign Settlers shall henceforth be called the Ekaterinoslav Office of Foreign Settlers; or, should it be found necessary to transfer it to the Tavrida Governorate, it shall be called the Tavrida Office; in Odessa, or, better still, somewhere in a colony near Odessa, as the Trusteeship Committee shall determine, an Odessa Office of Foreign Settlers is to be established in place of the Chancery of Odessa Settlement; in Bessarabia the Bessarabian Office of Foreign Settlers shall remain.

3. Which particular districts of colonies are to belong to each Office, the Trusteeship Committee shall make arrangements for and submit for confirmation to the Minister of Internal Affairs. At the same time the Committee shall determine whether it would not be better, both for the benefit of the service and to avoid the high cost of living in Governorate towns, to place all the Offices within the colonies themselves, choosing a suitable colony for each.

4. Each Office consists of one senior Member and two junior ones. At least one Member must know German well. In addition, for the settlement of judicial and litigious matters among the colonists, two Deputies from the colonies are chosen to sit in the Office, who are to have a voice in the said matters, without otherwise interfering in governmental affairs.

The manner of election, the term of service at the Offices, and the maintenance of these Deputies, which is to be at the expense of the colonists, shall be determined by the Trusteeship Committee and submitted to the Minister of Internal Affairs.

5. The Chancery of the Office consists of a fixed number of officials, and of clerks, as needed.

The staff establishment of one Office is appended hereto under letter B, according to which all three are to be organized.

6. The senior Members of the Offices are appointed by the Minister of Internal Affairs with the confirmation of the Committee of Ministers. The junior ones are appointed by the Minister upon the recommendations of the Trusteeship Committee.

7. Chancery officials are appointed by the Trusteeship Committee upon the recommendations of the Offices; clerks are appointed at the discretion of the Offices.

8. All Offices make their submissions to the Trusteeship Committee, and receive authorizations from it. These submissions must follow the Ministerial forms.

9. The Offices conduct all colonial affairs pertaining to their districts in the same manner and with the same force as has hitherto been done according to the Instructions and special orders, and this shall continue until special rules on this matter are confirmed upon the submission of the Chief Trustee. It goes without saying that the authority of the Offices is in every respect limited by the authority of the Trusteeship Committee.

10. The Offices communicate only on a footing of equality with the Town Police, with the Zemstvo and District Courts, and with other similar Authorities; and therefore, in the event of judicial proceedings between colonists and other inhabitants, as well as in criminal cases involving colonists, the junior Members of the Offices have the right to be present at the said Courts, in accordance with the Instruction confirmed as Highest on June [July] 26, 1800. But when a case reaches the Civil or Criminal Chamber, then, with the authorization of the Trusteeship Committee, the senior Members of the Offices are present there, by virtue of the same Instruction.

11. The Offices, in cases admitting no delay, may make their submissions to the Civil Governors of those Governorates in which their colonial districts are located, reporting on this at the same time to the Trusteeship Committee.

12. The Overseers in the colonies are appointed by the Trusteeship Committee upon the recommendation of the Offices, and are under the direct authority of the latter.

Their duties and remuneration shall be determined by the submission of new rules by the Chief Trustee; until then they remain in their present position, in accordance with the provision made for them in the staff establishments of the Offices.

Staff establishments: 1. Of the Trusteeship Committee for the colonists of the southern territory of Russia, and 2. Of the Office of Foreign Settlers. (See the book of staff establishments.)

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXV. P. 154-159. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 195*

## No. 73. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE SETTLEMENT OF COLONISTS FROM WÜRTTEMBERG IN TRANSCAUCASIA (1818)

27,530. — September 7. Regulation of the Committee of Ministers. — On the settlement of Württembergers in Georgia.

The report of the Minister of Internal Affairs was heard, stating that, according to the reports of General Yermolov concerning the settlement of Württembergers in Georgia, His Imperial Majesty had been pleased to order that two Deputies first be sent from among them to Georgia, so that these Deputies might verify on the spot the difficulties of resettling there at present, and, upon their return, might more forcefully convince their fellow countrymen of this. Subsequently, when Lieutenant-General Inzov reported that no persuasion had been strong enough to dissuade the Württembergers from resettling to Georgia immediately, His Imperial Majesty was pleased to consent to this wish of theirs, on condition that Deputies from among them be sent ahead first, so that, upon meeting the colonists on the road on their way back from there, they might present to them accurately all the unpleasant things awaiting them there, and thereby dissuade them from continuing further. Finally, according to a new report from General Yermolov, which was presented to His Imperial Majesty by General of Artillery Count Arakcheyev on the day of the Sovereign's departure from the Capital, His Majesty was pleased to remark that, given the shortness of time, he saw no other means of resolving the difficulties of the Württembergers' resettlement than to send these people to Georgia in the smallest possible parties, so that only a few of them could be sent during the present autumn, leaving it, moreover, to the Minister of Internal Affairs to take such other measures as might help with the difficulties described by General Yermolov. Meanwhile, however, all 500 Württemberger families, as Lieutenant-General Inzov reports, divided into 10 parties, had already been sent from Odessa to Georgia. Their Deputies, who had arrived in Georgia beforehand, chose for settlement, from among the lands shown to them there, four plots totaling up to 18,000 desyatinas, of which, however, the greater part belongs to the ecclesiastical department and to various owners. The officer performing the duties of Georgian Civil Governor, Major-General Stahl, and General Yermolov consider the Muganli land, comprising approximately 5,000 desyatinas and belonging to Colonel Prince Chavchavadze, to be the most convenient for settlement and the safest from the raids of predatory peoples among those plots; 46 households are settled on it belonging to him, and he agrees to cede it to the treasury together with the peasants, on condition that in exchange he be given half of the crown village of Uriatubani, that very village on which he had previously had a claim, and for which, together with another village, Zelistsikhe, he has been assigned 19,167 rubles in silver from the treasury. In this half-village there are 45 families, but disputes still exist regarding the Muganli land, and its exact extent has not been ascertained; Major-General Stahl has promised to report on this separately. Pending this, the Minister of Internal Affairs has so far been unable to undertake anything regarding the exchange of that land. According to the rules on the settlement of colonists, each family ought to be given 60 desyatinas; but General Yermolov, given the fertility of the land there, considers 35 desyatinas per family sufficient, to which the Württemberg Deputies have also expressed agreement, provided only that they be allowed unhindered use of the forests and pasturelands used by the local inhabitants. In addition, General Yermolov, in his last two reports communicated to the Minister of Internal Affairs by General of Artillery Count Arakcheyev concerning the resettlement of the Württembergers, sets out the following difficulties: in the first, that the lands chosen by the Württemberg Deputies must for the most part still be obtained by exchange, for which Highest authorization is needed, and that even if the chosen lands are given to them, there are no means to fence in 500 families and protect them from raids, since troops are insufficient even for other no less important uses; that, in his opinion, it might be possible for the time being to settle the Württembergers near the very city of Tiflis and on the Muganli land belonging to Prince Chavchavadze, once it has been obtained by exchange, since the other lands they have chosen are exposed to raids by predators; in the second, that the Württembergers, contrary to his expectation, are already proceeding to Georgia, and, the parties being close to one another, are having difficulty obtaining food for themselves; that provisions must be stockpiled along the Georgian Military Road for their sustenance, which will require considerable time and large expenditures; that last year an extraordinary snow avalanche made the road impassable for heavy loads, and it is impossible to convey such a number of people together with their belongings on pack animals; that this would require halting them for settlement in the Caucasus Governorate, but they are already proceeding through that Governorate and will converge at Georgievsk or Mozdok, to their own extreme inconvenience and to the crowding of the inhabitants; that a request has already been sent to him from along the road, in which they complain of a lack of provisions and demand his assistance, but he has no special funds for that purpose. He therefore asks that some guardian be appointed and that a special sum be placed at his disposal for the maintenance of the colonists. Having examined these reports, the Minister of Internal Affairs first of all communicated by special courier to General Yermolov and the Caucasus Civil Governor that, if the colonists have not yet left the Caucasus Governorate, and if it is not possible to place all of them in towns and villages in Georgia, then halting some number of them in the Caucasus Governorate, quartering them for the winter in towns and villages there, would cost no more than doing so in Georgia, and they would be safer there from predatory raids. The Minister of Internal Affairs then presents the following opinion to the Committee: 1) to authorize General Yermolov now to carry out the exchange with Prince Chavchavadze for his Muganli land together with the peasants, giving him in return half of the crown village of Uriatubani, provided, however, that in carrying out such an exchange he obtain more detailed information regarding the Muganli land, which is not presently available, as well as documents establishing the landowner's title to it, preserving as far as possible the benefit and advantage of the treasury. On this same basis, General Yermolov is to be authorized, if he deems it necessary, to obtain land by exchange from other landowners as well. 2) Given the convenience and abundance of the lands chosen by the Württembergers in Georgia, to allot to them 35 desyatinas per family instead of the 60 desyatinas prescribed by the rules, allowing them to use the forests and pasturelands. 3) In order to prevent the colonists from suffering want in their maintenance, to assign forthwith up to 100,000 rubles from the Georgian Crown Expedition to the disposal of General Yermolov. And 4) for the administration and settlement of the colonists, and especially for the maintenance of order and accurate accounting of crown funds, to authorize General Yermolov to establish DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 197

there, for the time being, even if only a temporary Committee or Office, under his general supervision, which would manage their settlement according to the rules established for similar Offices in other colonies; and, so that the colonists might know of all expenditures made on their behalf, it is necessary that 1 or 2 Deputies elected by their community be present at the Office.

The Committee resolved to confirm the opinion of the Minister of Internal Affairs with the following addition: 1) to inform General Yermolov that, upon obtaining the lands from Prince Chavchavadze or from other landowners by exchange, he should hasten to submit detailed information here both on the lands obtained from the landowners and on the crown estates designated in exchange for them, on the basis of which a draft decree confirming those exchanges will then be submitted for the Highest signature; and 2) that the 100,000 rubles proposed by the Minister of Internal Affairs be released to the disposal of General Yermolov from the Georgian Crown Expedition, charged against the colonist funds of the current and coming year; and, since the present case requires haste, this resolution is to be put into effect forthwith, with a report thereon to His Imperial Majesty, and for execution, extracts from this journal are to be communicated to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Internal Affairs.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXV. Pp. 561-563.*

## No. 74. DECREE OF ALEXANDER I ON IMPROVING THE CONDITION OF FOREIGN CLOTHIERS SETTLED IN POLTAVA GOVERNORATE (1818)

27,598. — December 27. Personal decree, given to the Minister of Internal Affairs. — On measures to improve the condition of the foreign clothiers settled in Poltava Governorate.

From your report and the information provided by the Little Russian Military Governor, I have ascertained that the foreign clothiers settled, on the basis of the report of June 30, 1808, in Poltava Governorate, are in a disordered condition, resulting from a confluence of various circumstances.

In consideration of this, and in order to provide them with the means to secure their condition through a stable economic establishment, I command the following to be done:

1) The crown debt owed by them, both for their transport from abroad to Russia and that accumulated in the course of their settlement in their present locations, of whatever designation it may be, is to be written off and not collected from them.

2) The crown houses in which they are settled are to be given to them as their property, with the necessary plot of land attached to each such house for a kitchen garden and hay meadow. The acquisition of the necessary quantity of land for this purpose from the townspeople, whether by purchase or by such other means as may be found most convenient and advantageous for the treasury, is entrusted to the Little Russian Military Governor, in consultation with the Minister of Finance.

3) The crown instruments for cloth-making hitherto in the possession of these clothiers are to be given to them as their property.

4) To assist them in their economic establishment, one hundred rubles are to be issued to each family currently present, as a loan from the treasury, under joint surety, for three years.

5) These clothiers are to be left free to choose whether all of them will remain in their present place of residence, or whether some of them, namely the Lutherans, will resettle in Poltava, and others, namely the Catholics, in Konstantinograd, without, however, requiring any monetary assistance from the treasury for this purpose.

6) These communities are to be authorized to establish their own Court and civil administration, following the example of other foreign colonists in Russia, and under the direction of the Little Russian Military Governor, with exemption from the administration that has hitherto governed them.

7) The cloth and unfinished fabric produced by them under the former arrangement from crown wool, if not yet sold, as well as other items and materials remaining after they have been provided with everything necessary, are to be sold for the benefit of the treasury; the Little Russian Military Governor is authorized to make arrangements in this regard.

8) Furthermore, while leaving them free to practice their craft independently of the authorities' direction, the Little Russian Military Governor is charged with the particular responsibility both of bringing them now into a better order, and of overseeing them in future and managing economically the buildings left vacant by those who have departed and that may in future fall vacant. You will not fail to communicate on this matter with whom it concerns, and to make the remaining arrangements on this subject.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXV. Pp. 650-651.*

## No. 75. SENATE DECREE ON THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE TRANSCAUCASIAN COLONIES (1819)

27,822. — May 29. Senate decree. — On the Highest-confirmed establishment of the Temporary Office for the administration of the colonists settled in Georgia.

The Governing Senate heard the report of the Minister of Internal Affairs, in which he explained: that, in consequence of the Highest consent of the Sovereign Emperor to the resettlement from the New Russia territory to Georgia of up to 500 families of Württemberg settlers who had arrived in Russia in 1817, according to the journal of the Committee of Ministers of September 7, 1818, the Chief Administrator in Georgia, General of Infantry Yermolov, was authorized to establish there, for the administration and settlement of the colonists, and especially for the maintenance of order and accurate accounting in the use of crown funds, for the time being even if only a temporary Committee or Office under his general supervision, on condition that one or two deputies elected by the colonists from their communities be present at that Office, so that the colonists might know of all expenditures made on their behalf. In consequence of this, General of Infantry Yermolov forwarded to the Minister the establishment schedule (shtat) of the temporary Office he had set up in Georgia for the administration of the colonists settled there, which, upon the Minister's submission through the Committee of Ministers, was honored with the Highest confirmation of His Imperial Majesty on the 17th day of April of this year, on condition that the said Office be guided in all respects by the same rules as those established for such Offices set up in the Southern territory of Russia; the appointment and dismissal of officials, however, is left to the discretion of General Yermolov himself, as Chief Administrator in Georgia, at least until such time DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 199

as the colonists are fully settled; salaries for the officials already appointed to them, in accordance with his submission, are to be paid from November 1, 1818, since they had begun handling colonist affairs from that time, disbursing the money for this from the general funds allocated for the settlement of colonists. The Minister submitted this establishment schedule to the Governing Senate in the original, requesting that it be pleased to direct whomever it concerns regarding due execution thereof. The said Highest-confirmed establishment schedule, attached to the aforementioned report, was also heard. Ordered: that a copy of the said Highest-confirmed establishment schedule of the temporary Office for the administration of the colonists settled in Georgia be forwarded to the Chief Administrator in Georgia, General of Infantry Yermolov, and that he be authorized to make arrangements, both regarding the execution thereof and regarding the Highest-confirmed resolution of the Committee of Ministers that the Office established in Georgia for the administration and settlement of the colonists there be guided by the same rules as those established for such Offices in the Southern territory of Russia, as well as regarding the appointment and dismissal of the officials of the said Office; and that the Minister of Internal Affairs be instructed to make arrangements, through whomever it concerns, for the payment of salary to the already-appointed officials, according to the pay scale set in the establishment schedule, from November 1, 1818, through the May trimester of this year, as well as for its further payment from the general funds allocated for the settlement of colonists; and that decrees be sent to the Chief Administrator in Georgia and the Minister of Internal Affairs concerning this; <...>

Establishment schedule of the temporary Office for the administration of the colonists settled in Georgia. (See the book of establishment schedules.)

## No. 76. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON HALTING THE RESETTLEMENT OF FOREIGNERS TO RUSSIA (1819)

27,912. — August 5. Regulation of the Committee of Ministers. — On stopping the further resettlement of foreign émigrés to Russia.

The report of the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs of August 3, No. 126, from the Department of State Economy and Public Buildings, entered in the Committee's journal under No. 1447, concerning foreign settlers, was heard.

The Committee resolved: 1) to confirm the opinion of the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs, and, given the urgency of the matter requiring immediate resolution, to put it into effect forthwith. 2) At the same time, to authorize the Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs to make arrangements so that the further resettlement of foreign émigrés to Russia be completely stopped, placing responsibility for this on our Missions and Consulates; and 3) to bring all of this to the Highest attention; and, for due execution of this regulation, to communicate extracts from the journal to the Acting Ministers of Internal and Foreign Affairs.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXVI. P. 325.*

## No. 77. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE PROHIBITION OF ISSUING PASSPORTS FOR RESETTLEMENT TO RUSSIA, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER I (1819)

27,954. — October 25. Highest-confirmed regulation of the Committee of Ministers. — On the prohibition of Russian Missions issuing passports to foreigners resettling to Russia and to the Kingdom of Poland.

It was announced to the Committee, in the memorandum of August 5 on the item entered in the journal under No. 1447 and put into execution, concerning foreign émigrés resettling to Russia, that the Sovereign Emperor consents that it now be decisively forbidden for our Missions to issue passports to foreigners resettling either to Russia or to the Kingdom of Poland.

The Committee resolved: to communicate this to the Acting Ministers of Foreign and Internal Affairs for execution, by extracts from the journal.

## No. 78. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE ORAL OATH OF THE TRANSCAUCASIAN COLONISTS, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER I (1819)

28,012. — December 2. Highest-confirmed regulation of the Committee of Ministers. — On exempting the Württemberg colonists who arrived in Georgia in 1818 from the ordinary oath.

At the session of November 22, the report of the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs of November 18, No. 213 (from the Department of State Economy and Public Buildings), entered in the Committee's journal under No. 2164, concerning the exemption of the Württemberg colonists who arrived in Georgia in 1818 from the ordinary oath, was heard.

The Committee resolved: to confirm this submission, having first sought the Highest consent thereto.

At the session of December 2, it was announced to the Committee that the Sovereign Emperor consents to this.

The Committee resolved: to communicate this to the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs for execution, by an extract from the journal.

Report. In the absence of the Chief Administrator in Georgia, General of Infantry Yermolov, who was on the Caucasus Line, the Commander of the Independent Georgian Corps, Lieutenant-General Velyaminov 1st, reported to the Ministry of Internal Affairs that the Georgian Office for the administration of the colonists settled there had made arrangements for preparing the Württemberg colonists, who had arrived in Georgia from Odessa in 1818 by special Highest command, to take the oath of allegiance as subjects.

Some of the village councils of these colonies replied that, according to the rules of their religion, it is forbidden for them to swear oaths; they therefore requested that they not be compelled to take such an oath. Lieutenant-General Velyaminov requests authorization as to whether these settlers should be compelled to take the oath, or exempted from it, DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 201

and, in the latter case, how to proceed in judicial matters, particularly criminal cases, where by law witness testimony must be confirmed by oath.

He also forwarded, in translation, two reports of the village councils of the Württemberg colonists, submitted to the Georgian Office.

From these it is evident that, according to their faith, the oath consists in their having to say: asking God to help them be loyal subjects of the Sovereign Emperor, and that anything beyond this is considered a sin.

Reference. 1. By the Highest manifesto of July 22, 1763, and by the rules Highest-confirmed in 1804 concerning the settlement of colonists in Russia, they are granted free exercise of their faith according to their statutes and rites, without hindrance.

2. In the charter Highest-granted on September 6, 1800 to the Mennonites, it is stated in point 1: "We confirm the freedom promised to them and their descendants in the unhindered exercise of their faith according to their church institutions and customs, with Most Gracious permission for judicial bodies, should the need arise, to accept from them an oath according to their custom, consisting solely of a verbal affirmation."

Taking the above-mentioned provisions into consideration, I propose not to require of the Württemberg colonists, of the sect called Separatists, the customary oath known to us, but to allow them to perform it in accordance with the rules of their faith, consisting solely of a verbal affirmation.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXVI. Pp. 405-406.*

## No. 79. DECREE OF ALEXANDER I ON THE COLLECTION OF DEBT FROM THE ST. PETERSBURG COLONISTS (1820)

28,124. — February 2. Personal decree, announced to the State Council by its Chairman. — On the measure for collecting the repayable and non-repayable debt of the St. Petersburg colonists.

His Imperial Majesty, upon the opinion rendered in the General Assembly of the State Council concerning the debts of the new St. Petersburg colonists, was Highest pleased to command:

1) That the measure for collecting debts from the new St. Petersburg colonists, whereby no more than 50 and no less than 20 rubles is to be collected from each household, not be fixed, but rather be adjusted in proportion to the debtor's means; for it may easily happen that a payment of 50 rubles would be imperceptible to one, while another would be unable to pay even 20 rubles. In consideration of this, uniform payment from all households of a single colony is abolished, and this same rule is to be extended to the 48 families transferred from St. Petersburg to the New Russia territory.

2) That the measure of the land tax not be fixed, but that its assignment always be left to the Guardianship Committee, since it must be better acquainted with the quality of the land occupied by the colonists.

As for the remaining resolution of the State Council on this matter (confirming the proposal of the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs in all respects), the Sovereign Emperor confirms it and has ordered it to be carried out.

Report of the Acting Minister of Internal Affairs, Count Kochubey.

In 1809, by Highest command, German colonists were summoned from the former Duchy of Warsaw for settlement in St. Petersburg Governorate, numbering 91 families.

Part of them were settled near Oranienbaum, Peterhof, and in Strelna, and a larger number in Tsarskoye Selo district, in the so-called Izvarsky tract; but later, owing to significant inconveniences discovered at this latter location, pursuant to a Highest decree, in 1811, 31 families were transferred from there, some to Strelna and some to Kipen; and 48 families were sent for settlement to the New Russia territory.

All these colonists were settled on the basis of the rules on the settlement of colonists in Russia, confirmed pursuant to the Highest-confirmed report of the Minister of Internal Affairs of February 20, 1804.

For their settlement here — that is, for their departure from abroad, their subsistence en route, their settlement, the establishment of their households, resettlement anew, and other purposes related thereto — a total of 574,303 rubles 39¾ kopecks in assignat currency and 371 chervontsy have been expended from the treasury.

Upon review of all these expenditures, the Council of the Ministry of Internal Affairs found that, on the basis of the statutes issued regarding the collection of crown debts from colonists settled in Russia and the imposition of taxes upon them, and of prior precedents, of the said sum: a) 367,442 rubles 16¼ kopecks are to be converted into repayable debt to be collected from the colonists, which sum they are obliged, by statute, to repay, after the expiration of the years of exemption, in 10 equal annual installments thereafter. b) 33,359 rubles 86 kopecks are to be classed as non-repayable debt, which money is to be collected, insofar as it falls due from each, only if any of them should wish to leave Russia altogether. c) 173,501 rubles 37½ kopecks in assignat currency and 371 chervontsy are to be left entirely uncollected, as not properly pertaining to the settlement of the colonists, and d) the end of the 10-year exemption period for these colonists, on the basis of the general rules on this matter and the decree of the Governing Senate of September 27, 1806, is set at the expiration of this year, 1820.

Having examined all the circumstances of this matter, and taking into consideration that, although according to the rules on the settlement of colonists they are obliged to repay the repayable debt within 10 years, yet, as it appears from previous precedents, no colonists settled in Russia have ever been able to pay off their debts within the appointed time without utterly ruining themselves, I submitted all of this to the State Council in my opinion, which was as follows: 1). That the collection of the repayable and non-repayable debts from the colonists here be arranged so that the debts owed by each colony be apportioned equally among each household. 2). Having examined, through trusted officials, the condition of all the new colonists here, to impose upon them such an annual collection of debt that the colonists' obligation to repay remains firm while still allowing the colonists to improve their condition, collecting from each household from 50 to 20 rubles per year, provided that all households of one colony be assessed equally. 3). To proceed in the same manner in collecting the debt owed to the treasury from those transferred to the New Russia territory, leaving the examination of this matter to the Guardianship Committee for the colonists of the southern territory of Russia, on condition that it submit its conclusion thereon for confirmation by the MinisDOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 203

try of Internal Affairs. 4). As regards the collection of land tax from the colonists here, although, according to the rules on the settlement of colonists in Russia, they ought to pay from 15 to 20 kopecks per desyatina of land held per year; yet, since it is proposed to grant them an installment plan for the repayment of their debts to the treasury, they should be brought at least somewhat into line, in the payment of this tax, with the old colonists here, who pay from 1 ruble 50 kopecks to 2 rubles 50 kopecks per desyatina per year. 5). Wherefore, judging by the quality of the land they occupy and, in general, by the advantageous location of their settlements, to assess them a land tax of from 1 ruble 50 kopecks to 2 rubles per desyatina, paying it, on the basis of the Highest decree of September 12, 1811, into those departments to which the lands settled by the colonists belong. 6). That such an arrangement regarding payment of the land levy not be adopted as an invariable rule, but that the Government be authorized, as far as possible and as the condition of the colonists improves, to increase this tax in proportion to their advantages, and 7). that, as regards the imposition of such a tax upon the colonists transferred to the New Russia territory, it be collected from them equally, at no less a rate than that paid by the other colonists settled there, this too being entrusted to the Guardianship Committee, which, having made arrangements thereon, will not fail to submit a report here.

Such was the opinion that followed, upon my aforementioned submission, in the General Assembly of the State Council, Highest-confirmed on the 2nd day of this February, a copy of which I hereby submit to the Governing Senate, reporting at the same time that all necessary instructions and arrangements for its execution have been made by me to whomever it concerns.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXVII. Pp. 38-39.*

## No. 80. DECISION OF THE STATE COUNCIL ON RAISING THE PAYMENT FROM THE ORIGINAL ST. PETERSBURG COLONISTS, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER I (1823)

29,541. — July 13. Highest-confirmed opinion of the State Council. — On increasing the payment of debt monies to the treasury from the old St. Petersburg colonists.

The State Council, in the Department of State Economy and in the General Assembly, having examined the report of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs concerning an increase in the payment of debt monies owed to the treasury by the old St. Petersburg colonists, and finding the proposal of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs on this subject to be correct, resolves to confirm it.

Resolution. His Imperial Majesty was graciously pleased to confirm the opinion rendered in the General Assembly of the State Council concerning an increase in the payment of debt monies owed to the treasury by the old St. Petersburg colonists, and has ordered it to be carried out. For the Chairman of the State Council. Nikolai Mordvinov.

Report of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. The St. Petersburg colonists, who came to Russia in 1765 and 1767 and were at that time settled in four colonies — Srednyaya Rogatka, Izhora, Novosaratovka, and Yamburg — had, apart from the general benefits granted by the Highest Manifesto of 22 July 1763, various terms for exemption and payment of taxes according to the agreements concluded with them, namely:

The Srednyaya Rogatka and Izhora colonists were given a five-year exemption, and were required to repay their debt to the treasury after the expiry of 15 years, in five installments, that is, over two and a half years.

The debt recorded against them was: for the Srednyaya Rogatka colonists, 28,870 rubles 14 kopecks, and for the Izhora colonists, 25,234 rubles 91¼ kopecks.

The Novosaratovka colonists were given a five-year exemption, with repayment of the debt after 10 years set in six installments, that is, over three years. Their total recorded debt was 90,125 rubles 89 kopecks; and the Yamburg colonists were given a 13-year exemption, with repayment of the debt set for the last three years; their recorded debt was 137,493 rubles 50 kopecks, but it was forgiven them by Highest decree of 17 August 1793.

After the expiry of their exemption, the said colonists, contrary to their obligations and under various pretexts, paid nothing for more than 20 years, until finally in 1792 it was ordered that a land tax of from 30 to 60 kopecks per desiatina be collected from them, together with 5 to 10 rubles per household toward repayment of the debt.

These colonists are not subject to local (zemstvo) obligations except those relating to government offices, the construction of major roads, and waterways, since a special exception was made for them on this account under the terms agreed with them in 1765.

Thereafter, pursuant to the report of the Minister of Internal Affairs confirmed by the Highest authority on 18 July 1805, the said colonists were assessed a land tax per desiatina ranging from 30 kopecks to 1 ruble 23 kopecks.

Toward repayment of the debt, the following was paid annually per household: from the Srednyaya Rogatka colonists, 20 rubles; from the Novosaratovka colonists, 10 rubles; and from the Izhora colonists, 5 rubles.

On the basis of the opinion of the State Council confirmed by the Highest authority on 12 March 1812, the aforementioned colonists of the earlier arrival now pay land tax annually per desiatina of usable land as follows: a) Srednyaya Rogatka colonists, 2 rubles 50 kopecks; b) Novosaratovka colonists, 2 rubles; c) Izhora colonists, 1 ruble 50 kopecks; d) Yamburg colonists, 1 ruble 23 kopecks.

Repayment of debts to the treasury has been left as before, as set forth in the aforementioned report confirmed by the Highest authority on 18 July 1805.

By this reckoning, each family in total pays annually from 51 to 95 rubles.

The present condition of these colonies is as follows: 1) In the Srednyaya Rogatka colony, according to the last census, there are 136 male souls and 26 households; the usable land in its possession is 750 desiatinas, and the treasury debt recorded against this colony as of 1823 is 16,890 rubles 14 kopecks. 2) In the Novosaratovka colony there are 411 male souls, 60 households, 1,735 desiatinas of usable land, and a treasury debt of 76,325 rubles 89 kopecks. 3) In the Izhora colony there are 191 male souls, 29 households, 841 desiatinas of usable land, and a treasury debt of 20,894 rubles 91¼ kopecks; and 4) in the Yamburg colony there are 136 male souls, 32 households, 1,378 desiatinas of usable land; no treasury debt is recorded against it, since it was, as stated above, forgiven them.

The new colonists settled in 1810 in this same governorate, in the colonies of Strelna, Kipen, Peterhof, Oranienbaum, and Kronstadt, have, on the basis of the opinion of the State Council confirmed by the Highest authority on 2 February 1820 and the resolution of the Committee of Ministers of 24 April of that same year 1820, been assessed since 1821 with land tax and payment of the debt to the treasury standing against them, namely: 1) The Strelna colonists, 40 rubles per household toward repayment of the debt, and 2 rubles per desiatina annually as land tax. 2) The Kipen colonists, 40 rubles toward repayment of the debt, and 1 ruble 80 kopecks per desiatina as land tax. 3) The Peterhof colonists, 45 rubles toward repayment of the debt, and 2 rubles per desiatina as land tax. 4) The Oranienbaum colonists, 30 rubles toward repayment of the debt, and 1 ruble 60 kopecks per desiatina as land tax; and 5) The Kronstadt colonists, 35 rubles toward repayment of the debt, and 1 ruble 80 kopecks as land tax.

In addition, these new colonists are obliged to discharge all local (zemstvo) obligations according to the assessment of the Provincial Administration, on an equal footing with the treasury peasants here.

Including these obligations as well, the total comes to from 70 to 120 rubles annually per family.

Taking into consideration: 1) that the aforementioned colonists of the earlier arrival of the Srednyaya Rogatka, Novosaratovka, Izhora, and Yamburg colonies not only received sufficient assistance from the treasury, but also enjoyed a far greater exemption than others, and, contrary to the terms agreed with them, made no payment whatsoever for more than 80 [20] years toward the expenses incurred by the treasury for their settlement, while the other colonists settled in this governorate began repaying their debt after 10 years of arrival in Russia and pay twice as much as they do; and 2) that according to the annual reports submitted on their welfare, these colonists, especially those of Srednyaya Rogatka and Novosaratovka, are in a decidedly prosperous condition and could, without the slightest hardship, be brought into equal standing with the other colonists settled here in the payment of debt.

I consider it just, for the speedier recovery of the treasury debt recorded against them, amounting to more than 114,000 rubles, to collect from them per household as follows: from the Srednyaya Rogatka colonists, instead of the 20 rubles now paid, 40 rubles; from the Novosaratovka colonists, instead of 10 rubles, 30 rubles; and from the Izhora colonists, instead of 5 rubles, 20 rubles.

In submitting this for the consideration of the State Council, I have the honor to add that, once my opinion is confirmed, collection of the debt according to the above calculation may begin from the first half of the year following its confirmation.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXVIII. Pp. 1103–1105.*

## No. 81. DECISION OF THE STATE COUNCIL ON RAISING THE TAX FROM THE LIVONIAN COLONISTS, CONFIRMED BY ALEXANDER I (1824)

29,833. — March 10. Highest-confirmed opinion of the State Council. — On raising the land tax paid by the Livonian colonists.

The State Council, in the Department of State Economy and in the General Assembly, having examined the report of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs on raising the land tax paid by the Livonian colonists, in view of their having completed repayment of the treasury loan, and finding the opinion of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs on this subject to be correct, resolves to confirm it.

Resolution. His Imperial Majesty was graciously pleased to confirm the opinion rendered in the General Assembly of the State Council concerning the raising of the land tax paid by the Livonian colonists, and has ordered it to be carried out. Chairman of the State Council.

Report of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. In Wenden District of Livonia Governorate, on the treasury manors of Hirschenhof and Helfreichshof, German colonists were settled in 1766 and 1769 under a special contract concluded with them. That contract stipulated, among other things, that the land tax be collected from the colonists according to an assessment of their land.

These colonists, placed under the direct administration of the Livonian Civil Governor, have since 1797 paid to the treasury a land tax of 13 thalers, plus 2 thalers per household toward repayment of the loan made to them, on the basis of the decree of the Governing Senate to the Livonian Treasury Chamber of 5 September 1785, which also stated that, upon repayment of the debt, the land tax should be permanently increased to 15 thalers.

The treasury debt, which since 1815 has been collected in banknotes at rates set annually in the schedules of the Ministry of Finance, has been paid by the colonists in full and even with a surplus, amounting to 1,769 rubles 50 kopecks. The remainder of the debt was received from the colonists back in 1820.

On the occasion of this now fully completed repayment by the Livonian colonists of the treasury debt standing against them, the Livonian Treasury Chamber requested authorization last year: whether, on the basis of the decree of the Governing Senate of 5 September 1785, the quitrent monies from these colonists should be permanently raised to 15 thalers, and likewise whether, in future, the quitrent monies should continue to be collected at the rate previously set in the schedule, reckoning a 100 percent premium on the silver ruble; and in that case, whether the amounts overpaid by them to the treasury should be credited against the increased sums of 2 thalers per household still owed for 1821 and 1822.

The Ministry of Internal Affairs received a copy of this report of the Livonian Treasury Chamber from the Minister of Finance, and, taking into consideration, on the one hand, that the colonists, on the basis of the rules for their reception confirmed by the Highest authority on 20 February 1804, are, upon expiry of their exemption, placed on an equal footing in taxation with the treasury peasants of the same district or governorate, and, on the other hand, that under the contract concluded with the Livonian colonists it was stipulated that the land tax be collected from them according to an assessment of the land — that is, according to an assessment of the benefits which the colonists now derive from their land and holdings — sent to the place of settlement of those colonists one of the overseers of the St. Petersburg colonies, who, together with an official dispatched by the Livonian Civil Governor, inspected their condition and submitted detailed information on the whole matter, from which it emerged that the said settlers, without particular disruption to their circumstances, can pay from 15 to 17 thalers of land tax annually per household.

Having examined the information set forth, I found that although the Livonian colonists ought, on the basis of the rules for the reception of colonists confirmed by the Highest authority on 20 February 1804, and following the example of the Saratov colonists, to be placed on an equal footing in taxation with the local treasury peasants there, yet since the Livonian treasury peasants discharge their quitrent not in money but in labor, the colonists, who are not tenants, cannot be subjected to such a labor obligation, DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 207

and that a payment of 17 thalers annually per household will be, for the Livonian colonists, a land tax that is entirely not burdensome.

On this basis I proposed to collect from the Livonian colonists, who expect to improve their circumstances by that time, 15 thalers per household in annual land tax until 1826, reckoning from 1821, against which the 1,769 rubles 50 kopecks overpaid by them toward the debt are to be credited, and from 1826 to collect from them 17 thalers per household until a new regulation is issued.

I submitted this for the consideration of the State Council, adding that the authorization sought by the Livonian Treasury Chamber concerning the exchange rate at which it is to collect the land tax from the colonists would depend on the Ministry of Finance.

The State Council, having examined my aforementioned report on raising the land tax paid by the Livonian colonists, on the occasion of their having completed repayment of the treasury loan, in accordance with the minutes of the Department of State Economy of 30 November and of the General Assembly of 21 December 1823, confirmed it.

I have the honor to submit herewith to the Governing Senate a copy of this opinion of the State Council, confirmed by the Highest authority on 10 March of this year, requesting that it be pleased to instruct whomever is appropriate to carry it into due execution.

*PSZRI. Coll. 1. Vol. XXXIX. Pp. 211–212.*

## No. 82. SENATE DECREE ON THE TAXES AND OBLIGATIONS OF FOREIGN COLONISTS (1824)

30,172. — December 23. Senate decree, pursuant to the resolution of the Committee of Ministers confirmed by the Highest authority. — On the taxes and obligations of foreign immigrants belonging to the peasant estate.

The Governing Senate heard, firstly, the report of the Minister of Finance, to which he attached copies of a memorandum submitted by him to the Committee of Ministers and of an extract from its minutes, confirmed by the Highest authority on 11 March last, concerning treasury taxes and obligations owed by foreign immigrants; adding that particular cases giving rise to this new regulation would, strictly on the basis thereof, be resolved by instructions from the Ministry of Finance; but since these rules require universal notice and observance, would the Governing Senate be pleased to issue, to whomever it may concern, the necessary instructions for its execution? And secondly, the copies attached to this report of the memorandum of the Minister of Finance submitted to the Committee of Ministers on 31 August 1823, and of the extract from the minutes of that Committee, which state as follows. In the memorandum of the Minister of Finance: Last year the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, on the occasion of petitions received by him from foreign immigrants settled in Volhynia and Kiev Governorates on landlords' estates, corresponded with the former Minister of Finance regarding treasury taxes and obligations owed both by immigrants of this kind and by those who own land of their own in the Western Governorates. The laws on this subject state: <...> Regarding the taxes and obligations of immigrants settled on landlords' estates, Count Dmitry Alexandrovich [Guryev] held: 1) Mennonites and other foreigners who settled on landlords' estates in the Western Governorates, both before this territory's annexation to Russia and afterward, up until the issuance of the Highest decree of 9 May 1802, have no right to enjoy exemption from the payment of taxes, and must remain in the ranks and assessments in which they now stand; for prior to the issuance of the said decree, no legislation existed on this matter. Moreover, it would be extremely difficult, indeed impossible, to ascertain with due precision exactly when they arrived from abroad in the formerly Polish provinces, and whether they had not already availed themselves of some exemption. 2) Colonists who settled on landlords' estates after 9 May 1802, but before the promulgation of the report of the Minister of Internal Affairs confirmed by the Highest authority on 12 April 1804, ought, by the strict force of the Highest decree of 9 May 1802, to be granted exemption from the payment of taxes until the sixth census following that date. 3) Colonists who settled on landlords' estates after the promulgation of the report of the Minister of Internal Affairs confirmed by the Highest authority on 12 April 1804 should be reckoned a ten-year exemption from the payment of taxes from the time of their initial settlement on the landlords' estates. 4) After the expiry of the exemption period, treasury taxes are to be collected from all colonists settled on landlords' estates on an equal footing with the landlords' peasants; and they must discharge local (zemstvo) obligations from the time of their settlement. 5) Colonists who did not avail themselves of the legally established exemption in due time, or who were incorrectly assigned to a higher tax rate than the landlords' peasants, should be given due satisfaction by crediting all sums collected from them in excess against the taxes to be owed by them in future, at the rate applicable to landlords' peasants. 6) Colonists who have availed themselves of the ten-year exemption, or who, during the period of exemption, moved or shall move to other landlords' estates, or from one district to another, or from one governorate to another, are not to be granted a second exemption, and upon the expiry of 10 years from the time of their initial settlement, are to be assessed at the same rate as the landlords' peasants; to this end, the local authorities must ensure that colonists do not leave their settlements without their knowledge. 7) Landlords who have received foreigners onto their lands must, without delay, in accordance with the Highest decree of 9 May 1802, present the cordon certificates issued to them for registration with the District Court, which must at the same time report this to the Provincial Board; the latter, comparing the reports of the District Court with the notifications received from the border authorities, is obliged each time to inform the Treasury Chamber, as appropriate, of the number of such persons, the status they have chosen, and the time of their settlement, for its due action; without presentation of cordon certificates, no exemption may be granted to colonists, and landlords who fail to comply within three months, by force of the Highest decree of 9 May 1802, are deemed to be harboring fugitives. 8) The Treasury Chambers shall be obliged, having gathered the requisite information on all colonists under their jurisdiction on landlords' estates, to proceed, on the basis of the above rules, both in assessing their taxes and in satisfying their petitions. 9) Since existing legislation has granted colonists only exemption from military and civil service, and it is nowhere stated that they are entirely exempt from the recruit levy borne in Russia by all taxable estates DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 209

in kind or in money, and moreover, since complete exemption of colonists from the recruit levy for the future would result in an unwarranted burden on the rest of Russia's inhabitants, the obligation to pay the recruit commutation money of 500 rubles in lieu of a recruit should also be extended to colonists settled on landlords' estates, beginning with the forthcoming recruit levies. As for foreigners who own land of their own, the former Minister of Finance, taking into consideration that, by the report confirmed by the Highest authority on 1 March 1804, foreigners who have acquired land in ownership in the New Russia territory are ordered to pay such land dues as are levied on landlords' estates in that territory, and that peasants freed by their landlords to the status of free farmers pay taxes on the same footing as landlords' peasants, agreed with the conclusion of Count Viktor Pavlovich [Kochubei] that all foreigners who have hitherto come, and shall hereafter come, to Russia, who have purchased land in ownership and are not registered in any estate, should pay taxes on the same footing as landlords' peasants, and should discharge zemstvo obligations on the same basis as the treasury peasants living in the same governorate, subjecting them equally to payment of recruit money for the same reasons as those settled on landlords' estates. The Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, in the response now submitted to the Minister of Finance, finds that the question here raised regarding the recruit levy is not a matter for particular but for general consideration; for it must here be decided: are the colonists in general exempted forever solely from the provision of recruits in kind, or also from payment, after the expiry of the exemption period, of recruit commutation money? Although on this question the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs agrees with the opinion of the former Minister of Finance that the colonists are exempted forever only from the provision of recruits in kind, and not from the monetary levy that replaces this obligation, since the privileges granted to them speak only of military and civil service — exemption from which was probably prompted by the anticipated aversion of the colonists to military service among us, all the more so as it is contrary to the faith of some of them, namely the Mennonites, who, as is known, left their former dwellings and moved to us chiefly in order to avoid military service — yet, as he has made it a rule not to touch, during his temporary management of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, upon any general and important measures departing from the present order of things, he considers it best to leave the resolution of this question until the return of Count Kochubei; but in the present matter, which concerns only those colonists settled on landlords' lands, or on lands acquired by themselves, whose number is at present quite small, he considers it possible on this occasion, without touching upon the recruit tax, to resolve only the remaining questions relating to their other taxes and obligations, on which he, as well as the Department of State Economy and Public Buildings, agree with the opinion of the former Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance, finding for his part that if it should be deemed proper to postpone resolution of the question concerning the recruit levy on colonists until the return of Count Viktor Pavlovich [Kochubei], then in that case the local authorities of Volhynia and Kiev Governorates should nevertheless be instructed to cease all demands upon the colonists on this account, all the more so since subjecting them to the recruit levy cannot extend to past time, when no clear legislation existed on this matter — submitted this, together with the other proposals of his predecessor, for the further consideration of the Committee of Ministers. From the extract of the minutes of the Committee of Ministers of 3 November 1823 and 11 March 1824: at the session of 3 November, the memorandum of the Minister of Finance of 31 August, No. 3568 (of the Department of Various Taxes and Duties), submitted in the Committee's minutes under No. 18.95, concerning treasury taxes and obligations of foreign immigrants, was heard.
