In agreement with this opinion of mine, the Minister of Finance, in his communication to me of the 8th of this May, also holds that, since all foreigners are permitted, under the established rules, to come to Russia, nothing prevents the aforementioned craftsmen from availing themselves of this permission as well, without requiring any assistance from the Government.

All of which I have the honor to submit for the gracious decision of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. VI. Part 1. P. 425-427.*

## No. 90. DECREE OF NICHOLAS I ON THE SETTLEMENT OF COLONISTS NEAR PETERHOF (1833)

6307 a. — July 9. Personal decree, announced to the Chief Administrator of Peterhof by the Minister of the Imperial Court. — On the settlement of colonists on crown land near Peterhof.

Upon my most humble report of the memorandum submitted by Your Excellency from the Inspector of the St. Petersburg colonies, Bunin, concerning the wish of 4 colonist families to settle on crown land near Peterhof, His Imperial Majesty has deigned to command the following: 1) That these colonists be allotted, for arable land, hayfields, and pasture, the requested quantity of land; but first the site they have chosen, along the Samsonievsky Canal toward the reserve pond where stakes have now been placed, is to be shown on a general plan, which is to be delivered to me for presentation to His Majesty. 2) Since there are no crown forest tracts near Peterhof from which forest lands could be allotted to the said 4 families, you are to communicate with the Inspector of the St. Petersburg colonies as to whether they might be permitted to use the same forest from which the colonists of the Sobstvennaya (Crown's Own) tract draw their needs. 3) Information is to be obtained as to how much will need to be issued in aid to these colonists for clearing the land for sowing, for establishment, and for subsistence. 4) Copies are to be made of the plan and elevations shown in the portfolio being returned herewith, under Nos. 1, 2, and 9; but on the elevation under No. 2, the crossed-out weathervane and the ornaments on the gates, wicket-gates, and DOCUMENTS___________________________________________________________________________ 233

fence are to be removed, and in accordance with these designs an estimate is to be drawn up of the cost of building houses for the 4 colonist families, for each design separately,

In announcing this Supreme Will to Your Excellency for due execution, I propose that the said plans, elevations, and information be delivered to me for report to His Imperial Majesty. At the same time I inform you that His Imperial Majesty has been graciously pleased to confirm Bunin's submission concerning the granting to these colonists of a 10-year exemption, and of the same rights enjoyed by their brethren of the Novosaratovka and Srednyaya Rogatka colonies, as well as concerning the collection from them, after the 10 years have elapsed, of taxes and of payments toward their debt.

Memorandum of the Inspector of the St. Petersburg colonies.

In St. Petersburg Governorate nine colonies have been established for agriculture, of which four — Srednyaya Rogatka, Novosaratovka, Izhora, and Yamburg — were founded in 1765 and 1767, and the other five — Strelna, Peterhof, Oranienbaum, Kronstadt, and Kipen — in 1809.

The colonists of these colonies were settled as follows: the first four, on the basis of conditions specially concluded with them, with Supreme consent, at the time of their settlement, whereby they, in addition to the general rights granted to colonists, are exempt from payment of money toward zemstvo obligations; while the colonists of the other five colonies were settled on the basis of the report of the Minister of Internal Affairs, Highest confirmed on 20 February 1804 (21163), concerning the reception and settlement of colonists in Russia.

Under this decree the following was granted to those colonists: 1) Freedom from payment of taxes and from all obligations for 10 years. 2) Freedom of religion. 3) Freedom from military and civil service. 4) Freedom from military billeting, except for the passage of military detachments through their settlements. 5) Freedom to leave Russia should anyone so wish. 6) Permission to establish factories, engage in any trades, conduct trade, join guilds and crafts, and sell their products anywhere in the Empire.

The colonists of the four colonies of earlier settlement, on the basis of the opinion of the State Council, Highest confirmed on 4 June [13 July] 1823 (29541), pay land tax per year of from 1 ruble 23 kopecks to 2 rubles 50 kopecks for each desyatina of usable land they hold, while those of the five colonies of newer settlement, under the regulation of the Committee of Ministers Highest confirmed on 24 April 1820 (28252), pay from 1 ruble 60 kopecks to 2 rubles per desyatina.

Assistance was rendered to these colonists from the treasury, namely: 1) They were allotted crown lands of from 30 to 50 desyatinas per family, of which the necessary number of desyatinas was cleared for arable land for the first sowing. 2) Houses were built with yards and outbuildings. 3) They were supplied with horses and cattle. 4) Agricultural implements and other rural tools were purchased. 5) Subsistence money was paid until the first harvest.

All such expenses together then amounted to from 2,000 to 11,000 rubles per family. The colonists duly repay this treasury debt after the expiration of the exemption period, on the basis of Highest confirmed regulations, at from 20 to 45 rubles per year per family or household of the original settlement, and in addition pay state tax of 18 kopecks, and for land and water communications 30 kopecks, in total 48 kopecks per year per revision soul, and finally, the colonists of the new settlement also pay the sums assessed for zemstvo obligations.

The colonists who have declared their wish to resettle on the land situated near Peterhof most humbly request: 1) That they be allotted land in such quantity that its cultivation would cover their basic maintenance and crown taxes, considering that for arable land, hayfields, and pasture it will suffice to have the land they have chosen for 4 families along the Samsonovsky Canal, 700 sazhens in length and 300 sazhens in width toward the menagerie, forming a regular parallelogram, at those very points where they have placed stakes, and that, in addition, forest lands, even if at some distance, also be allotted to them. 2) That aid in money from the treasury be given them for clearing a certain amount of land for the initial sowing, for building houses, and for the necessary rural establishment and subsistence. 3) That an exemption of 10 years be granted to them, after the expiration of which they undertake to pay duly land tax of 3 rubles per desyatina, toward the crown debt 50 rubles per household, and the aforementioned taxes of 48 kopecks per revision soul per year, for which they have undertaken to give written pledges, and finally that they be granted the same rights enjoyed by their brethren of the Novosaratovka and Bessarabian [Srednyaya Rogatka] colonies.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Suppl. Vol. VIII. P. 18-20.*

## No. 91. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON SCHOOLS FOR TEACHING THE RUSSIAN LANGUAGE TO THE CHILDREN OF VOLGA COLONISTS, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS I (1833)

6551. — November 7. Highest confirmed Regulation of the Committee of Ministers. — On the establishment of schools for teaching the children of Saratov colonists the Russian language.

The memorandum of the Minister of Internal Affairs, of 12 October, on the establishment of schools for teaching the children of Saratov colonists the Russian language, was heard.

Upon the submission of the acting Governor of Saratov concerning the total ignorance of the Russian language among the colonists there and the necessity of teaching it to them, the Committee of Ministers, recognizing for its part the explanations of the local authorities as well founded, found that this proposal, requiring closer consideration, could in any case be carried out only gradually; and therefore, by journal entry of 14 February last, brought it to the attention of the Minister of Internal Affairs for his further arrangements, as far as possible and convenient.

The Saratov Office for Foreign Settlers, whose opinion was accordingly requested, proposes:

1. For teaching the children of colonists the Russian language, to establish one school for every two districts, which would make 5 schools for all 10 districts.

2. That these schools and their teachers be under the authority of the general School Administration.

3. That, for supervision of the pupils outside school, in addition to the teacher of Russian, a reliable overseer be selected from among the colonists with a modest salary. DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 235

4. That the expenses for maintaining the schools, estimated preliminarily as a one-time cost of up to 750 rubles for the purchase of textbooks and up to 7,500 rubles annually, be apportioned for payment among all the colonies in general.

The Minister of Internal Affairs acknowledges that the introduction of the Russian language among the foreign settlers is in every respect certainly beneficial and even necessary; but, taking into consideration the expenses for maintaining the proposed five schools, finds that up to 25 kopecks would fall on each revision soul, although the former number of revision souls, judging by their present actual numbers, will increase by more than a third after the new census; consequently the proposed levy will decrease proportionately; and although the Russian schools need not be established permanently, but only until teachers of their own can be prepared for the colonies, nevertheless the new levy, given the settlers' obligation to repay their crown debts within a shorter term than before, and moreover to maintain, under the new regulation, the Colonist Administrations, will be burdensome for them.

For these reasons he proposes: for the time being, to limit the measure to establishing in the Saratov colonies, for teaching Russian, only two schools, each for 25 pupils, at the most convenient locations, with the establishment of such schools in the other colonies, should this prove necessary, postponed until the settlers have paid off their crown debts, and with the selection of children for the schools left to the communities themselves, with the approval of the pastors, preferentially from the more populous colonies and from among orphans; the expenses required for this to be charged to all the colonies in general. In this way the levy calculated for maintaining the schools will be reduced by two-thirds and will be entirely imperceptible to the colonists; meanwhile, the 50 colonists so trained, each in his own colony, will be obliged, over the course of 6 years, to teach children in Russian in the very same schools where the Schulmeisters now teach in German, dividing the time between both languages in all classes. Subsequently, on this same basis, the best of the pupils may likewise be appointed teachers in the other colonies, and by this means knowledge of the Russian language will gradually spread among the colonists and in time achieve general use.

The Committee proposed: that this submission be confirmed.

His Imperial Majesty was Highest pleased to confirm the Committee's regulation.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. VIII. P. 643-644.*

## No. 92. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE ALLOTMENT OF LAND TO VOLGA COLONISTS, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS I (1835)

8146. — May 21. Highest confirmed regulation of the Committee of Ministers. — On the allotment of land to Saratov colonists from the tract set aside for the Elton salt-hauling route.

The memorandum of the Minister of Finance, of 22 April, concerning the satisfaction of the Saratov colonists with land from the 40-verst Elton salt-hauling route, was heard.

The Committee proposed: that the conclusion of the Minister of Finance in this matter be carried into execution.

His Imperial Majesty was Highest pleased to confirm the Committee's regulation.

Memorandum. The Governing Senate, by decree of 31 May 1828, forwarded for the opinion of the Minister of Finance a memorandum from a case that had long been proceeding in the Governing Senate and the Ministries of Finance and of Internal Affairs concerning the satisfaction with land of the colonists of Krasny Yar and Tarlyk districts of Saratov Governorate, toward the shortfall in their allotment of 20 desyatinas per soul assigned by the Highest decree of 4 December 1797 (18263), from lands designated according to the survey of the Land Survey Chancery, in execution of the report of the Governing Senate, Highest confirmed on 21 October 1806, for pasture for the settlements of Pokrovskaya and Uzmorye-Nikolaevskaya of the Saratov salt-haulers and for the main salt-hauling road to Lake Elton.

The Minister of Finance, having examined the said memorandum, took as his guide in this matter, first: that although, on the basis of the Highest decree given to the Governing Senate on 19 December 1802 (20556) concerning the allotment to colonists of the missing quantity of land, up to the amount assigned to them of 20 desyatinas per soul, allotments were made to them in 1811 and 1824 from the lands of the Elton salt works for their satisfaction, they, being entitled under the same decree to demand suitable land of their own choosing for their holdings, being dissatisfied with the allotments assigned to them, arbitrarily plow up, for sowing grain, a very considerable quantity of land belonging to the Elton salt-hauling route, thereby causing hardship both to the salt-haulers on the said route and great disorder and disputes among the former state peasants attached to Lake Elton; second: the Personal Highest decree issued to the Governing Senate on 23 November 1827 (1557), whereby, among other things, it was ordered: that the peasants attached to Lake Elton be converted into state peasants, retaining in their use the full allotments of surveyed lands, or at least those designated for them, with the settlement upon these lands, in addition to the 15-desyatina allotment per soul, of other state peasants from land-poor areas as well; while the salt-hauling routes from the reserve depots at Nikolaevsk and Pokrovsk to Lake Elton, and the pastures surveyed around the lake and around those depots, are to remain as at present pending further consideration; and any questions that might arise concerning those lands are to be left to the resolution of the Ministry of Finance; and third, that in the extensive pastures for the salt-haulers, such as exist within the forty-verst tract designated for the Elton salt-hauling route by the Land Survey Chancery, upon the report of the Governing Senate Highest confirmed on 21 October 1806, there is, according to local considerations, no particular need at present.

On the basis of such considerations, the Minister of Finance submitted a report to the Governing Senate, dated 31 August 1833, in which he proposed for his part: in order to satisfy the colonists and the salt-haulers and to put an end to the disputes and disorders existing between them, that instead of the forty-verst tract designated by the Land Survey Chancery for the Elton salt-hauling route, only a 10-verst strip be set aside for that route, with reserve areas, in addition to this strip, at the stations for pasturing the salt-hauling livestock; and that the colonists then be allotted, toward the shortfall in their assigned allotment, land remaining from that same 40-verst tract.

To this end, the Minister of Finance also submitted for the consideration of the Governing Senate his proposal for the establishment of a special Land Survey Commission consisting of deputies: one from the Saratov Treasury Chamber, one from the civil authorities of Saratov Governorate, and one from the authorities over the colonists, with surveyors from the Treasury Chamber and the provincial authorities attached to it.

This matter was submitted for consideration to the Minister of Internal Affairs, and finally the Governing Senate, having agreed to the establishment of the said Land Survey Commission, resolved to charge it with: 1) Limiting the salt-hauling routes between Lake Elton and the reserve depots at Pokrovsk and Nikolaevsk to a ten-verst width along their entire length. 2) Designating, on both sides of the ten-verst salt-hauling routes within the forty-verst tract, reserve areas for pasturing the salt-hauling livestock at 26 stations, in addition to the 10-verst strip, assigning to each area a space of three versts in length and two in width, which will amount to 6 square versts or 625 desyatinas. 3) In setting aside these areas, taking into consideration that along the left side of the salt-hauling road from Lake Elton to the Pokrovsk depots, for a distance of 70 versts, lie lands allotted to the colonists of Tarlyk district, and therefore, wherever, according to local judgment, such areas cannot be surveyed at stations lying near those lands, they may be designated on the right side of the road only, in the full 12-verst proportion. 4) Since, on the present forty-verst salt-hauling routes, peasants from among those formerly attached to Lake Elton have been settled at the watering wells, in order to protect the wells from plunder and to carry out other duties assigned to them, that in the places nearest to their dwellings, specifically within the ten-verst extent of the salt-hauling routes, the quantity of land necessary for them for grain-growing and their own hay-mowing be surveyed for them. 5) Of the lands remaining thereafter within the forty-verst extent of the salt-hauling routes: first, to satisfy the colonists with the lands necessary for them, of their choosing, or as the government deems fit; second, to lease out to those wishing it the lands not needed by the colonists, without touching the pastures designated for Lake Elton and for the reserve depots at Pokrovsk and Nikolaevsk, and the surveyed or merely designated lands of the peasants formerly attached to Lake Elton, which are to be dealt with in accordance with the Personal Highest decree of 23 November 1827 (1557); and finally, 6) That the Land Survey Commission be charged, after mapping all these designations — namely, the ten-verst salt-hauling routes with their areas, the allotments for the peasants settled at the watering wells, the pastures for Lake Elton and the reserve depots, and the lands of the colonists, as well as those allotments which, after these designations have been satisfied, remain free for leasing out or for other use useful to the treasury — with submitting the plans and field journals it has compiled for further consideration and decision by the Land Survey Chancery, which, having formed its own conclusion, shall be obliged to submit the whole matter to the Governing Senate for consideration.

The Governing Senate, by decree addressed to the Minister of Finance of 22 March of this year, gave notice that, since by the Personal Highest decree of 23 November 1827 it was ordered that the salt-hauling routes to Lake Elton remain in their present condition pending further consideration, the Senate proposes: without proceeding to arrange for the establishment of the aforementioned Commission for designating a ten-verst extent for those routes and other matters, to leave it to the Minister of Finance to request Highest authorization for this.

From this same decree of the Governing Senate it appears that the Minister of Internal Affairs also agreed with the said conclusion of the Senate.

In submitting all of this for the consideration and decision of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers, the Minister of Finance has the honor to add, for his part, that, in his opinion, since it is known from the proceedings of these cases that the colonists continuously and arbitrarily seize lands, but such lands could not have been designated for them on the former salt-hauling route, and these people, contrary to the purpose of their settlement — namely, to introduce improved agriculture — continuously only demand and occupy new lands; therefore, without now finally resolving the question of granting them additional land, final consideration of this matter should be undertaken when the conclusion of the Commission is submitted, all the more so since the Minister of Finance's proposal to reduce the salt-hauling route was aimed at obtaining land for the gradual settlement of land-poor state peasants, and not for the excessive endowment of colonists.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. X. Pt. 1. P. 435-438.*

## No. 93. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE REORGANIZATION OF THE CAUCASUS COLONY OF KARRAS, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS I (1835)

8271. — June 26. Highest confirmed regulation of the Committee of Ministers. — On measures for organizing the Scottish colony near the Caucasus Mountains.

The memorandum of the Minister of Internal Affairs of 27 April, on measures for organizing the Scottish colony near the Caucasus Mountains and concerning the right granted to the members of this colony and to the Basel missionaries residing in Shusha to convert Muhammadans and pagans to their faith, was heard.

The Committee, upon examining this matter, found that the principal circumstance contained in it is the right granted to the Scottish colonists to convert Muhammadans and pagans to their faith and thereby to increase the number of members of the colony.

On this subject the Committee could not fail to note that the actions of the colonists over more than 32 years, since the granting of this right to them, have been limited to the conversion of only nine mountaineers, and that since 1828, when the right was again confirmed to them, they have not converted a single person, whereas the preachers of the Ossetian mission, in the course of 17 years, have baptized 70,000 souls; such negligible success on the part of the colonists fully convinces one that they are not engaged in missionary work in the least, and consequently have not the slightest need of the right granted to them for increasing their colony.

As for the Basel missionaries settled in Shusha, it appears from the case that, since their establishment there, without having converted anyone to Christianity, DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 239

they have deviated from their true purpose, turning their attention instead to Armenian youth. Their conduct has provoked complaints on the part of the Armenian clergy which, according to the assurance of the local authorities, may have quite unpleasant consequences.

For this reason the Committee, fully sharing the opinion of the Chief Administrator in Georgia that the activities of all foreign-confession missionaries in general in the Transcaucasian territory should, for the reasons set out in detail in his explanation, be forever discontinued, and bearing in mind, moreover, the statement made in the presence of the Committee by the Synodal Chief Procurator, that the rules for the reorganization of the Caucasian ecclesiastical schools have already been honored with Highest confirmation, and that only the final considerations of Baron Rosen are awaited for the formation of a Greco-Russian missionary society beyond the Caucasus, which he, while here, promised to deliver immediately upon his arrival in Georgia — considered that there will then be no further need whatsoever to have foreign-confession missionaries in that territory.

Accordingly, the Committee proposed: 1) That the conclusion of the Minister of Internal Affairs regarding the measures he proposes for organizing the Scottish colony be confirmed. 2) That, having forbidden the members of this colony and the Basel missionaries settled in Shusha any missionary activity whatsoever, they be allowed henceforth to engage in agriculture, factories, and trades. 3) That the Basel missionaries, in order to remove any occasion for complaint on the part of the Armenian clergy, be further forbidden to accept Armenian youth into their schools. 4) That immediate oversight of this be entrusted to the Chief of the Caucasus Region, under the general supervision of the Chief Administrator of Georgia.

His Imperial Majesty was Highest pleased to confirm the Committee's regulation.

Conclusion of the Minister of Internal Affairs. — Having examined the details of this matter, I find in it two circumstances requiring resolution: 1) the organization of the Scottish colony; 2) the activities of the Basel missionaries, with respect to their influence on Armenian youth.

With regard to the Scottish colony, the investigation conducted on the spot and the report based on it by the Chief Administrator in Georgia, General of Infantry Baron Rosen, sufficiently establish that all the disorders that have occurred until now in the said colony arise from the colonist Paterson, who, retaining for himself without any right the title of elder, oppresses the colonists both in respect of land tenure and in the administration of communal affairs; wherefore the colony has for several years been subject to constant discord.

To put an end to such disorders and to bring order to the colony, I consider it necessary, in agreement with the opinion of General Rosen, to remove Paterson from the Scottish colony's community, and, on the basis of the Highest charter of 26 December 1806 (22410) and the Highest confirmed regulation of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers of 15 December 1828 (2517), to allot to the members of the colony a fixed proportion of land at 60 desyatinas per family, not excluding resettlers from the Saratov colonies, allowing them to establish an administration elected from among themselves consisting of an elder and two members, one from the Scottish and the other from the Saratov colonists, renewing this election every three years. The colonist Paterson is to be allotted the 1,000 desyatinas of land most graciously granted to him as a separate plot, set apart, as far as possible, from the colony's holdings, so as thereby to remove any occasion for new disputes.

As to the activities of the Basel missionaries, although the case contains certain remarks made in general against foreign missionaries by General Yermolov, later repeated by General of Infantry Baron Rosen, these remarks, having been considered by the Committee of Ministers in 1828, were left without action; and, on the other hand, taking into consideration that the conduct of Protestant missionaries in other states, and especially in Prussia, Sweden, and Denmark, has won the approval of their governments; that the Basel missionaries residing in the fortress of Shusha, during its siege by Abbas Mirza, likewise earned the approval both of the local military authorities and of the Commander-in-Chief of the Separate Caucasus Corps, Field Marshal Prince of Warsaw Count Paskevich-Erivansky; and finally, that in none of the documents concerning these missionaries is there anything definite to accuse them of any actions contrary to the interests of our Government — for these reasons I consider that the rights most graciously granted to them should remain inviolable. As for their influence specifically on the education of Armenian youth, in this case, basing myself on the assurance of the local civil and school authorities, who have recognized the missionaries' activities as very beneficial for the Armenian people, I would propose only, in accordance with the opinion of Prince of Warsaw Count Paskevich-Erivansky, to adopt certain measures to prevent, in future, disagreements arising between the missionaries and the Armenian clergy on account of the latter's apprehension regarding the drawing of Armenian youth into the Protestant faith. I would propose to limit these measures to those arrangements which the missionary society has already communicated for the preliminary consideration of General Rosen.

Accordingly, I propose: 1) That the colonist Alexander Paterson, for disorders and oppression of the colonists, be removed from the community of the Scottish colony of Karras. 2) That the members of this colony, on the basis of the Highest charter of 25 December 1806 and the Highest confirmed regulation of the Committee of Messrs. Ministers of 15 December 1828, be allotted from the tract situated at the Karras colony a fixed proportion of land at 60 desyatinas per family, not excluding resettlers from the Saratov colonies. 3) That the 1,000 desyatinas most graciously granted to the colonist Paterson be allotted to him as a separate plot, set apart as far as possible from the colony's holdings, so as thereby to remove any occasion for new disputes. 4) That, for the administration of the communal affairs of the Karras colony, the colonists be allowed to establish an Administration elected from among themselves, consisting of one elder and two members, with the election to be renewed every three years, and with the elder to be chosen in turn, once from among the Scottish and once from among the Saratov colonists. 5) That this colony be entrusted to the direct authority and protection of the District Chief of Pyatigorsk, who shall be obliged to watch over their welfare and to prevent any discord. 6) That, while leaving the Scottish and Basel missionaries in possession of the rights most graciously granted to them, the members of the Basel missionary society be permitted to accept into their schools not only Muhammadan but also Armenian youth, provided, however, that they, under pain of lawful prosecution, refrain from any DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 241

attempt to draw Armenians into their own faith, and that they select, with the confirmation of the local authorities, two honored trustees from among the Armenians for these schools, one from the laity and the other from the clergy.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. X. P. 767-769.*

## No. 94. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON RULES FOR THE INSTRUCTION OF CHILDREN IN THE VOLGA COLONIES, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS I (1840)

13233. — March 5. Imperially confirmed statute of the Committee of Ministers. — On rules for school and catechetical instruction in the colonies of the Saratov foreign settlers.

The memorandum of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, of February 9, on rules for school and catechetical instruction in the colonies of the Saratov foreign settlers, was heard.

The Committee decided: to confirm the said rules in accordance with the submission, with an increase of the fine proposed therein to three kopecks in silver.

His Imperial Majesty has Most Graciously deigned to approve the decision of the Committee.

Memorandum. Last year, 1839, the Evangelical Lutheran General Consistory submitted to the Ministry entrusted to me a draft of rules on school and catechetical instruction in the colonies of the Saratov foreign settlers, which it had received from the Moscow Provincial Consistory of the same confession. The impetus for drafting this project was the immorality of colonist youth noted by local pastors, which prompted the idea of establishing firm and permanent rules imposing a certain fine on those parents who fail to send their children properly to schools and church. The General Consistory, approving the Moscow Consistory's proposal for the introduction of such rules, and being in no doubt as to the beneficial consequences of this measure, being persuaded by the example of Livonia, where, under the Imperially confirmed statute on peasants, similarly modest monetary fines exist for negligent parents, requested further instructions.

Finding this proposal not without foundation, I referred it, as appropriate, to the consideration of the Minister of State Domains, requesting his opinion. As a result, Adjutant General Count Kiselev forwarded to me a newly drafted project of rules on school and catechetical instruction in the colonies there, prepared by the Office of the Saratov Foreign Settlers, which had been instructed to work out detailed considerations on this matter. This project, in drafting which the rules submitted to me by the Evangelical Lutheran General Consistory were taken as a guide, differs from the latter essentially only in that it has been extended also to settlers of the Roman Catholic confession, who make up a third of the population of the Saratov colonies. These rules comprise the following 12 paragraphs.

§ 1. Priests and pastors, at every convenient occasion, shall impress upon their parishioners the sanctity of their duty to raise children in the fear of God and to send them in good time to church schools, whose principal purpose consists in teaching the young the Law of God. (§ 181 of the Imperially confirmed Statute of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in Russia of December 28, 1832).

§ 2. Priests and pastors shall visit the schools of their parish in the colony where they themselves reside weekly; in the others at least once every two weeks. In addition to these mandatory visits, priests and pastors shall, at convenient times, make unannounced visits, unexpected to teachers and pupils alike. (Ibid., § 189).

§ 3. The visits of priests and pastors must have as their purpose not only general oversight of the proper instruction of children, but also the encouragement of diligence, both through praise for the diligent and through admonition for the idle.

§ 4. The mandatory and unannounced visits of priests and pastors shall be recorded, with an indication of the day and date on which they were made, by the schoolmasters in a special log kept by them, which, during visitations by the Superior and Provost of the parishes, is to be accepted as evidence of the extent to which the parish priest attends to his schools.

§ 5. Every head of household is obliged to send his children, wards, pupils, or servants of either sex who have reached the age of 7, daily, from the beginning of October to the end of March, to school, and each Sunday to attend the teaching of the catechism.

§ 6. Every schoolmaster shall keep an accurate name list of all children obliged to attend school, and, at the conclusion of both the morning and afternoon hours of instruction, as well as after every catechism lesson (Kathechisation oder Kinderlehre), shall take roll call from this list, entering the absentees in a special list, which he shall submit each day to the village authority of the colony.

§ 7. The village authority, upon receiving the list, shall immediately inquire of the families as to the reason for the pupil's absence from school; and if it finds the reason lawful, shall note it against his name, while from those absent without lawful reason it shall collect from the head of the family the fine established below.

§ 8. The following are recognized as lawful reasons for the absence of pupils: illness of the pupil himself, the necessity of caring for a sick member of the family, a death in the family, but only until the completion of the funeral, and inclement weather when the way to school is far.

Note. There may arise other, no less important reasons preventing a pupil from attending school. Therefore the village authority is obliged, in such cases, to determine at its own discretion whether these reasons should be considered sufficient grounds for exemption from the fine, or not.

§ 9. For every absence of a pupil from school without lawful cause, the parents, guardians, foster-parents, or, generally, heads of household, shall pay 5 kopecks in copper. (Digest of Laws, Vol. 12, Statute on Foreign Colonies, art. 983).

§ 10. The fine shall be collected, as stated above, by the village authority, and, together with the list, shall be handed over to the church elders, against their receipt, for allocation to the school fund.

§ 11. The school fund is administered on the same basis as any church property, and the money collected in fines is used for the purchase of necessary books for poor children and books for distribution at examinations to those distinguished for diligence.

§ 12. If persons liable to the fine are unable to pay it, they shall then be punished by the village authority, instead of the monetary fine, by being put to public labor, namely: for each absence of a pupil from school, half a day. (Ibid., art. 983).

In forwarding this project, Adjutant General Count Kiselev explains that, since it was drafted with reference to the way of life of the colonists and to the existing statutes for internal administration in the colonies belonging to the village and district authorities, he sees, in his opinion, no obstacle to the introduction of these rules, provided they receive proper confirmation. He finds it necessary only, in accordance with the earlier proposal of the Lutheran Consistories, General and Moscow, to increase the fine set in § 9 of the said rules for those guilty of failing to send colonist youth to school, from 5 kopecks in copper to 3 kopecks in silver, since a five-kopeck fine would already be entirely insignificant.

Since, under this new proposal, the rules on school and catechetical instruction of the children of foreign settlers in the colonies of the Saratov settlement are to be common to both Catholics and Protestants, I forwarded the draft of these rules to the Metropolitan of the Roman Catholic churches in Russia. Metropolitan Pavlovsky, finding the aforesaid draft to be in accordance with pure Christian teaching, considers that, owing to its brevity, precision, and clarity, it may be put into effect to the benefit of the children of foreign settlers.

Finding, for my part, the draft of rules on school and catechetical instruction in the Roman Catholic and Lutheran colonies of the Saratov settlement, drawn up by the Office of the Saratov Foreign Settlers, consistent with the proposals of the General and Moscow Evangelical Lutheran Consistories and approved by the Minister of State Domains and by the Metropolitan of the Roman Catholic churches in Russia, generally to correspond to its purpose and therefore to promise evident benefit for the youth there, and, in particular, sharing the opinion of Adjutant General Count Kiselev that, with the increase of the fine set for those guilty of irregular attendance by pupils at parish schools from 5 kopecks in copper to 3 kopecks in silver, still greater benefit may be expected from the present measure, — I have the honor to submit this for the consideration of the Committee of Ministers, proposing that the said draft be confirmed in its full force, with the sole amendment of setting the aforementioned fine at 3 kopecks in silver.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XV. Sec. 1. P. 108—111.*

## No. 95. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE ALLOTMENT OF LAND TO THE VOLGA COLONISTS, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS I (1840)

13255. — March 12. Imperially confirmed statute of the Committee of Ministers, announced by the Minister of State Domains. — On the allotment of land to the colonists of Saratov Governorate according to the number of souls of the 8th census.

The colonists of Saratov Governorate have still not fully received the 20-desiatina allotment per soul of the 5th census due to them under the Highest decree of December 4, 1797 (18263), while meanwhile the population in the Saratov colonies has greatly increased and these colonists suffer a palpable shortage of land, especially the settlers of the Tarlyk district, who, finding themselves in straitened circumstances, have repeatedly attempted to plough up land adjoining the leased sections of the Elton salt-hauling route, and although a monetary fine was collected from them for every desiatina they ploughed up without authorization, and although finally it was most strictly confirmed to them not to touch those lands which they had in fact left untouched for three years, nevertheless in the spring of last year they again violated the prohibition, driven to do so by extreme circumstances. The Governor immediately made the necessary arrangements to establish the exact amount of land they had ploughed up without authorization and the grain sown on it.

The Elton salt-hauling route, which originally extended to a width of 40 versts, was, by the Imperially confirmed statute of the Committee of Ministers of May 21, 1835 (8146), ordered to be limited to a width of 10 versts, with reserve areas in addition for grazing the salt-hauling livestock, on the condition that from the remaining lands pastures be allotted near Lake Elton and the salt depots, and that both the peasants settled at the watering wells and the colonists be provided allotments; the remaining lands, left over after these allocations, were to be kept in view for lease for quitrent or other useful purposes for the treasury. A special Commission was established at that time for the fulfillment of all these purposes, which was also charged with the duty, upon completion of the task assigned to it, of submitting the plans and field journals to the Surveying Chancellery, for the presentation of the whole matter, together with the Chancellery's opinion, to the Governing Senate.

When this Commission was transferred to the Ministry of State Domains, after it had completed the marking-out of land for the 10-verst salt-hauling route, what remained to be finished was the surveying of the lands released from the former, wider route, which were intended for lease for quitrent and for allotment to land-poor peasants and colonists; but since the performance of this work became part of the duties of the head of the survey of state lands of Saratov Governorate, there was no further need for the continued existence of the Commission, and accordingly, upon my submission, the Imperially confirmed statute of the Committee of Ministers of November 1, 1838 (11698) followed, on the closing of this Commission, which was indeed closed. As regards the actual designation made by it of the 10-verst width of the salt-hauling route, which came in due course before the Governing Senate for consideration, the Governing Senate requested my opinion. This matter was forwarded from the Ministry to the head of the Saratov survey, together with the plans drawn up by the former Commission for the demarcation of the Elton salt-hauling route, so that he might examine all the local circumstances and, having compared them with the plans drawn up by the Commission, report: 1) whether the given direction of the 10-verst salt-hauling route causes hardship to the state peasants, and 2) whether it would be convenient to compensate them, out of the land remaining from the former 40-verst width of the route, for the sections passing from them into the 10-verst width.

Meanwhile, during my personal inspection of the state domains in Saratov Governorate, the colonists there submitted a petition to me for an allotment of a 15-desiatina share of land per soul of the 8th census. To examine these petitions I established a special Commission consisting of the Managers of DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________ __________________ 245

the Office of the Saratov Foreign Settlers and the Saratov Chamber of State Domains and the head of the survey of state lands of Saratov Governorate. This Commission, having gathered the necessary information and having satisfied itself of the genuine need to grant the colonists' petition to remedy the land shortage they suffer, drew up a project for allotting them land per soul of the 8th census in accordance with local conditions, to which the Governor also agreed.

Upon consideration of the project of the aforesaid Commission, together with the circumstances reported by the Office of the Saratov Foreign Settlers concerning the renewed ploughing, in the spring of last year, by the colonists of the Tarlyk district of lands of the Elton salt-hauling route, having found it necessary to allot the Saratov colonists a sufficient quantity of land on the basis proposed by the Commission, I submitted this matter to the Committee of Ministers.

By the decision of the Committee of Ministers, His Imperial Majesty on the 12th day of this March Most Highly deigned to command: 1) That the grain harvested from the lands of the Elton salt-hauling route sown by the colonists of the Tarlyk district be left entirely at their disposal; but that, once the exact area they had sown is established, the same fine be collected from the colonists as was set for them for ploughing those lands in 1835, namely 43 kopecks in assignat notes per desiatina. 2) In view of the population of the colonies of Saratov Governorate having increased almost threefold compared with the number of souls of the 5th census, to confirm the proposal of the Commission established to examine the petitions submitted by the colonists for an allotment of land per soul of the 8th census, namely: that the former allotment, in which the quality of the land was determined by the colonists themselves, should remain untouched, and that, upon its being supplemented, on the same principle, with the number of desiatinas still owing to complete the 20-desiatina share per soul of the 5th census, the resulting quantity of land due under the new 15-desiatina share per soul of the 8th census should be surveyed for them, strictly on the basis of surveying rules, preferably from lands adjoining the colonies or close to them, while for the remainder such locations and such extensive tracts should be chosen as would allow several colonies to be founded, which would form a separate district. 3) Since the payment proposed by the Commission for this additional land, at 25 kopecks in assignat notes per desiatina, would amount in silver to about 7 1/7 kopecks, to set for the colonists a payment of exactly 8 kopecks in silver for each desiatina per year, until such time as the rules of cadastration are introduced, which are to be extended to the colonists as well. 4) Having in view with this allotment chiefly the colonists of the Tarlyk district, as being especially in need of land, to instruct the head of the survey of state lands of Saratov Governorate, upon the complete conclusion of the ongoing survey of free lands on the eastern side of the Elton salt-hauling route, to mark out on the plan, for the time being, only those lands which the Commission designated for allotment to the said colonists, that is, 6,174 desiatinas 586 sazhens per soul of the 5th census, and 44,305 desiatinas per soul of the 8th census, without touching such tracts as, in his judgment, may be needed to compensate the peasants for lands passing from them into the 10-verst width of the salt-hauling route, and to submit the plan with the marked-out sections to the Ministry of State Domains for preliminary examination and thereafter for submission for final examination and confirmation by the Governing Senate, once the reduction, actually designated, of the former 40-verst strip to 10 versts, with the corresponding compensation to the peasants, has already been confirmed by the Governing Senate. Having made the marking-out for the Tarlyk colonists, the head of the survey shall be obliged to proceed with designing the allotments of land to the colonists of the other districts as well, in the amount due to each of them, for the definitive assignment to them and confirmation to them, in the established manner, of the lands passing into allotment. 5) Meanwhile, so that the colonists of the Tarlyk district, while awaiting the formal allotment, should not be left again next spring in their former state of land shortage, they are to be permitted, with the onset of spring, to make sowings on the lands intended for them, with an indication to them of such an area or such sections as may without hindrance be temporarily occupied by them, for which they will be obliged to pay quitrent at 8 kopecks in silver for each desiatina. 6) Since, in allotting land to the colonists from tracts adjoining the colonies, difficulty may arise owing to a shortage of land, while the choice of distant tracts would require the resettlement of some colonies, the Minister of State Domains is authorized, after obtaining the most immediate information from the head of the Saratov survey, with whom the matter of the demarcation of the Elton salt-hauling route currently rests, and after communicating with the Minister of Finance, to consider whether it might be possible to limit the route to a width narrower than 10 versts, and to proceed with the further conduct of this matter in the established manner.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XV. Sec. 1. P. 138-140.*

## No. 96. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE APPOINTMENT OF AN OVERSEER FOR THE CHERNIGOV COLONY OF NOVYE MEZIRICHI, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS I (1841)

14368. — March 18. Imperially confirmed statute of the Committee of Ministers, announced by the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. — On the appointment of a special Overseer for the colony of Novye Mezirichi.

The Brest first-guild merchant Isaev founded, on land he had purchased in Mglin district of Chernigov Governorate, an extensive manufacturing establishment for the production of woolen goods, called the colony of Novye Mezirichi, where he has, among other things, built housing for the workers, among whom are more than 70 families of German factory workers whom Isaev summoned from the Kingdom of Poland. In 1834, at Isaev's request, the local authorities appointed a special official to the said colony, with the title of police Overseer and with salary and other maintenance to be provided by the founder of that colony. Upon the introduction into force of the statute on rural police, Imperially confirmed on June 3, 1837, the colony of Novye Mezirichi was to pass, on the general basis, into the jurisdiction of one of the District Police Officers; but the Chernigov provincial authorities petitioned for the retention of the special Overseer already present there. In consequence, upon the submission of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the decision of the Committee of Ministers, a Highest command followed on March 18, whereby it was ordained: 1) That a special police official, with the title of Overseer, be appointed to the colony of Novye Mezirichi, Mglin district, Chernigov Governorate, leaving it to the discretion of the local authorities either to retain in this post the official already serving in it, with the permission of the former Little Russian Military Governor, or to appoint another. 2) That the Overseer of the Mezirichi colony be granted, in his administration of the police branch in the colony, the same rights and duties generally vested in District Police Officers, his position being reckoned in Class X of the civil service, in the 9th category for length-of-service pension, and in the 10th category under the uniform schedule of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. 3) That the maintenance of this official be charged to the owner of the colony, in accordance with the wish expressed by him to that effect, the salary being set at not less than 180 rubles in silver per year, plus a suitable apartment with heating. 4) That the owner of the factory also assign to the Overseer one constable for errands and other commissions. Concerning this Highest command, the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs submitted it for execution to the Governing Senate, adding that His Imperial Majesty had also been pleased to command that this be put into effect as a temporary measure, until the benefit and necessity thereof should be assessed by actual experience, this to be left to the further consideration, in due course, of the Manager of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Minister of Finance.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XVI. Sec. 1. P. 191.*

## No. 97. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE ESTABLISHMENT OF AN ARTISAN COLONY OF THE MOLOCHNA MENNONITES, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS I (1841)

14703. — July 2. Imperially confirmed statute of the Committee of Ministers. — On permitting the Molochna Mennonites to establish a special colony of artisans.

The memorandum of the Minister of State Domains, of June 9, on permitting the Molochna Mennonites to establish a special colony of artisans, was heard.

The Committee decided: to confirm this submission.

His Imperial Majesty has Most Graciously deigned to approve the decision of the Committee.

Memorandum. To an official of the Ministry of State Domains, State Councillor Köppen, during his inspection of the state domains in Taurida Governorate, the Mennonites settled on the Molochna waters expressed a desire to establish, attached to the colony of Halbstadt, a special artisan settlement of 200 households, each to be allotted three desiatinas of land for a homestead and pasture, provided the settlers of Halbstadt were given, in exchange for these 600 desiatinas, an equal quantity of land from land adjoining their own tract. In addition, the inhabitants of the colony of Halbstadt requested that a certain further quantity of land be allotted to them for pasture grounds for visiting carters and chumaks [salt-and-fish haulers], since the industry of the colony, with the establishment of the new settlement, was bound to increase.

As a result of Köppen's report on the matter, in which he for his part found this proposal of the Mennonites to be beneficial, since of 539 artisans in the Mennonite colonies, 269 persons have no land, and their settlement together would give them the means to further mutual improvement through combined effort, an opinion on this subject was requested from the Guardianship Committee for Foreign Settlers of Southern Russia.

The Guardianship Committee reports that, in order to consider matters on the spot, it dispatched to the colony of Halbstadt one of its members, who found no inconvenience in separating from the colony's tract 600 desiatinas for the settlement of 200 families of artisans, replacing this land for the colony with adjoining land of the same kind, and additionally surveying to it a further 200 desiatinas for pasture for draft livestock. The Committee, in agreement with the opinion presented to it by the member who had returned from the colony, proposes to organize the settlement of artisans on the following rules: 1) They shall be obliged to build a house of prayer. 2) They shall also build a school for the instruction of youth. 3) Shops are to be designated for construction on the square. 4) When 20 families have settled, an Artisans' Board shall be appointed, under the administration of a Burgomaster and two Councilmen, to maintain order and settle disputes among the artisans. 5) This Board shall be subordinated to the jurisdiction of the Molochna District Board. 6) For police order in the market they shall have two hired constables chosen from free persons. 7) Houses are to be built exactly according to the model adopted in the Molochna colonies, of fired brick and of the same dimensions. 8) Gardens and vegetable plots are to be maintained at the houses, subject in this respect to the Commission for Horticulture and Forestry in the Mennonite colonies. 9) Settlement in the special colony shall be permitted to artisans only with the written permission of the Molochna Mennonite District Board jointly with the Commission for Horticulture, for which a protocol shall be drawn up on each occasion. 10) The members of the Board and Commission shall ensure that those admitted among the number of artisans are persons skilled in their craft, that building plots be allotted only to those who have already entered into marriage, and that persons not belonging to the Mennonite estate shall in no way enjoy the right to settle among them. 11) Artisans settled in the colony are permitted to take in young men for instruction and to hire workers from outside jurisdictions. 12) No artisan shall hold more than one plot of land, except in the case where he practices two crafts and his occupations require as much space as two designated plots together contain; in such a case, however, the permission of the chief local authority is to be sought. 13) Every artisan is obliged to build up his assigned plot within two years from the time of its assignment; should he fail to do so, the plot shall be taken from him without any compensation and given to another artisan not yet having a plot, while the materials stored there shall be left for the former owner to remove. If the material is not removed within two years, it shall be sold after two months at public auction, and the proceeds given to the owner of the material. 14) At the same time as building the house, and in no case later than two years from the day the plot is assigned, every artisan is obliged to enclose his plot with a solid fence and to prepare the land for the planting of trees. 15) Every homeowner is obliged, immediately upon building his house, to register with the fire insurance society existing in the colonies and insure his property; likewise to procure the fire-fighting equipment prescribed for each house. 16) On the plots designated for the artisan colony, owners must not engage in DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 249

grain farming and thereby divert themselves from their craft occupations. 17) Once up to 20 households have been established in the artisan colony, the householders must build a reserve grain store and deliver to it the grain allotment fixed per soul; until that time they shall remain subject to this obligation at their previous place of residence.

The Minister of State Domains, proposing to permit the Mennonites, in accordance with their petition, to organize an artisan colony, for the benefit both of themselves and of the region as a whole, brought this to the attention of His Imperial Majesty, on the understanding that, should Highest assent be given to this proposal, he would submit to the Committee of Ministers the basis on which the colony might be established.

His Imperial Majesty was Most Graciously pleased to approve this proposal.

The Minister of State Domains proposes: to permit the Mennonites settled in Taurida Governorate on the Molochna waters to establish a special colony of artisans, in the designated location, on the very basis reported by the Guardianship Committee for Foreign Settlers of Southern Russia, setting only, in place of the two-year term established by this Committee for the building-up of the plots to be assigned to the artisans, a three-year term for each householder, in order to afford them greater convenience in organizing the colony.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XVI. Sec. 1. P. 685-686.*

## No. 98. DECISION OF THE COMMITTEE OF MINISTERS ON THE RETURN OF THE RESIDENTS OF THE TRANSCAUCASIAN COLONY OF ANNENFELD TO THEIR COLONY, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS I (1842)

15913. — August 4. Imperially confirmed resolution of the Committee of Ministers. — On confirming the settlement of the Annenfeld colonists in the Transcaucasian territory at their former location in the colony of Annenfeld.

The memorandum of the Minister of State Domains, of July 16, on confirming the settlement of the Annenfeld colonists in the Transcaucasian territory at their former location in the colony of Annenfeld, was heard.

The Committee resolved: to confirm the settlement of the said colonists in Annenfeld in accordance with the submission.

The Sovereign Emperor was Most Graciously pleased to approve the Committee's resolution.

Memorandum. The Annenfeld colonists of the Transcaucasian territory, numbering 48 families, with the Most Gracious consent given in 1831, at the petition of the Field Marshal General Prince of Warsaw Count Paskevich-Erivansky and the submission of the former Minister of Internal Affairs Count Zakrevsky, were resettled in various Georgian colonies, owing to the poor climate in Annenfeld and the frequent cases of mortality resulting from it. In carrying out this resettlement, the government provided the colonists with assistance in the form of a payment of 2,832 rubles in silver, allocated for the arrangement of the affairs of the orphaned families of that colony. The lands and establishments remaining in it were leased out for 374 rubles in silver per year, with the stipulation that this money likewise be applied for the benefit of the resettled [colonists]. However, the leaseholder declined to maintain those lands and establishments. Meanwhile the colonists petitioned the former Georgian Civil Governor for permission to return to their former location, on the grounds that by their new settlement they had crowded other colonists and were themselves consequently unable to establish a settled, peaceful existence (which was subsequently confirmed also by Senator Baron Hahn, who personally inspected the Georgian colonies). The Governor reported on this to the Chief Administrator Baron Rosen, who requested from him a list of the colonists, but the instruction in this regard remained unfulfilled, while meanwhile the colonists themselves returned to Annenfeld.

The Chief Administrator of the Transcaucasian territory, having been assured of the means devised by these colonists to protect themselves from the effects of the poor climate — namely withdrawing to the mountains during the summer months — petitions, in accordance with the colonists' request, for confirmation of their settlement in Annenfeld.

In response to the question put to him by the Acting Minister of State Domains as to how successful the means devised by the colonists had been, he reported that, according to a report of the Georgian-Imeretian Chamber of State Domains, 427 souls had been settled in Annenfeld in 1819; of these, together with those subsequently born, 360 souls died before the resettlement to other colonies in 1832; in 1836, 185 souls again moved to Annenfeld, and from that time to the present, 77 souls, including those newly born, have died. He added that although it may be concluded from the figures cited that even now the climate of the colony of Annenfeld, despite the residents' migration to the mountains in summer, has a harmful effect on the colonists' health, nevertheless, taking into account the colonists' own earnest request for confirmation of their residence in Annenfeld, where they have already re-established their households, the Chamber finds it useful to grant their request, all the more so as mortality has recently decreased compared to before, and their resettlement elsewhere against their wishes would be burdensome for them.

Observing from this report that, although the said colonists withdraw to the mountains during the summer months to avoid the frequent cases of mortality from the poor climate, this does not fully eliminate the harmful effect of the climate on their health, I applied to the Chief Administrator of the Transcaucasian territory as to whether it might be possible to settle those colonists on some other state land.

In consequence of this, General of Infantry Golovin informed me that settling the Annenfeld colonists on some other land could bring substantial benefit, but since they have already established themselves in residence in the aforementioned colony, have set up their households, and themselves request permanent confirmation of their settlement there, their resettlement to other places against their wishes would be difficult for the government and ruinous for themselves. Therefore, also taking into account that mortality in the colony of Annenfeld has now decreased compared to before — since of the 185 souls who moved to this colony from 1836, only 77 souls, including those newly born, have died to date — he, General of Infantry Golovin, in agreement with the opinion of the Georgian-Imeretian Chamber of State Domains, finds it more expedient to confirm the settlement of the said colonists in the colony of Annenfeld.

I have the honor of submitting this petition of General of Infantry Golovin for the consideration of the Committee of Ministers, inasmuch as the resettlement of these colonists from Annenfeld to other Georgian colonies took place by Imperial decree, adding that, since the Annenfeld colonists have already returned to their former place of residence, the Ministry of State Domains sees no obstacle to confirming their settlement there.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XVII. P. 819-820.*

## No. 99. STATUTE ON THE WERNER SCHOOL IN THE BESSARABIAN COLONY OF SARATA, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS I (1842)

16117. — October 23. Imperially confirmed statute on the school in the colony of Sarata.

§ 1. The school being established in the Bessarabian colony of Sarata is intended for the training, from among colonist boys, of capable teachers for village schools and clerks for administrative offices, as well as surveyors and architects, with the further aim of thereby spreading knowledge of the Russian language in the colonies.

§ 2. This establishment is founded and maintained at the expense of a capital sum bequeathed by the Sarata colonist Werner for the benefit of the community of this colony, presently amounting to about 36,000 rubles in silver. Of this sum, 32,000 rubles in silver are set aside as an inviolable capital, the interest from which is used for the maintenance of the pupils and instructors, while the remaining 4,000 rubles in silver, together with any further accrued interest, are designated for the construction, according to a plan to be confirmed by the higher authorities, of a school building, for supplying it with the items needed for the educational establishment, and for the initial outfitting of the pupils. Any sum remaining thereafter is to be added to the inviolable capital.

§ 3. The Sarata school is under the direct authority of the Sarata District Office, while the present Ober-Schulze Feigel, as executor of the will of the late Werner, retains for life the title of Trustee. The District Office is responsible for the accounting and correspondence relating to the affairs of the establishment. It sends to the Committee a report on the condition of the school every four months, and a detailed report each January.

§ 4. The number of pupils shall not exceed 30; of these, 10 are maintained at the establishment's expense and are called, after the name of the founder, Werner pupils; the rest live with their parents or relatives and attend the establishment only during class hours.

§ 5. Boys maintained at the establishment may not, without especially valid reasons, leave it before completing the course of study, nor be diverted from regular class attendance by other occupations; but negligent and incapable boys are, upon submission to that effect by the District Office and with the permission of the Board of Trustees, expelled and immediately replaced by others.

§ 6. Only boys who have already studied in village schools and are distinguished by good moral conduct and diligence are admitted to the establishment, following a preliminary examination. However, preference for admission as Werner pupils is given to homeless orphans, whose fate is to be secured by the education granted them at the school. The admission of other boys at the establishment's expense is permitted only in the absence of such orphans.

§ 7. Since the school being opened in Sarata, in accordance with the will of the testator of the capital, is to serve chiefly for the benefit of this colony, the community thereof is granted the preferential right to allocate pupil vacancies in favor of its own orphans and boys, with the exception, however, of half of the Werner vacancies, which are always to be filled by orphans of the Lutheran confession from other colonies, at the direction of the colonial administration. But if no willing or capable candidates for admission to the establishment are found in Sarata, the colonial administration shall fill the deficiency with boys from other colonies, requiring those who cannot be included within the fixed number of Werner pupils to support themselves at their own expense.

§ 8. The District Office keeps a list of candidates for the colony of Sarata, from among whom, for the filling of each vacancy that opens, the community proposes three candidates; after they have been examined, the most capable is deemed worthy of admission. The selection of orphans placed in the establishment from other colonies is left to the immediate discretion of the colonial administration.

§ 9. In admitting boys to the establishment, care is taken that they be no older than sixteen, but by no means younger than fourteen years of age, so that upon completion of the course of study they may immediately be assigned to the colonies to take up teaching and clerical positions.

§ 10. Only one class is opened in the Sarata educational establishment; the course of study, however, continues for four years, divided into a preparatory and a final course.

§ 11. One year is allotted to the preparatory course, which is devoted to the thorough study of the subjects taught in village schools. These include: a) the Creed, the Commandments, and the principal prayers; b) reading in Russian and German; c) penmanship in both languages; d) the four basic operations of arithmetic; e) drawing.

§ 12. The subjects taught in the final course are: a) the Law of God and Sacred History; b) Russian and German grammar; c) rhetoric in Russian and German; d) translation from Russian into German and vice versa; e) a short general history; f) a short general geography; g) statistics of Russia and, in particular, of the New Russia territory; h) arithmetic, algebra, longimetry, planimetry, stereometry, and calculation on the abacus; i) surveying; j) short principles of rural architecture and the drawing up of plans and estimates.

The subjects listed in the last six points must be taught in Russian.

§ 13. The Law of God and the German language are taught by the local Pastor; the teaching of the other subjects is divided between two teachers, one of whom must without fail have a thorough knowledge of surveying and architecture. These teachers must also know German, in order to communicate with the pupils until the latter have become sufficiently familiar with the Russian language.

§ 14. Quarters are assigned to the teachers within the educational establishment itself, and it is their duty to maintain constant supervision over the boys kept at the establishment.

§ 15. The teachers enjoy the rights and privileges granted to teachers of district schools. They are to be paid a salary of 300 rubles in silver per year; the Pastor, for teaching the Law of God and the German language, is to be paid 150 rubles in silver per year.

§ 16. Class hours, excluding Sundays, holidays, and general vacation days, are set at five per day, namely: from 8 to 11 and from 2 to 4. The distribution of these hours among the teachers depends on the immediate discretion of the local authorities.

§ 17. Since the establishment is to be maintained from the interest on the capital of 32,000 rubles in silver set aside for this purpose, the annual income of the establishment amounts to 1,280 rubles in silver.

Of this sum the following are allotted: a) for the salaries of the teachers and the Pastor, 750 rubles; b) for the provisioning of 10 boys, at 7 kopecks in silver per day for each, 255 rubles 50 kopecks; c) for clothing and footwear for ten boys, at 10 rubles in silver per year for each, 100 rubles; d) for teaching aids, for the repair and heating of the building, for the maintenance of a female worker there, and for medicines, 274 rubles 50 kopecks. Total: 1,280 rubles in silver.

§ 18. Should experience show the above-calculated sum to be insufficient, it may be supplemented by the capital bequeathed by Active State Councillor Kontenius, presently amounting to more than 4,500 rubles in silver and designated by the testator for training teachers or pastors from among colonist boys. In that case, 12 pupils, instead of ten, may be maintained at the establishment.

§ 19. At the end of each year the pupils undergo an examination, at which a member of the higher colonial administration is always present. The most outstanding, as an encouragement, receive certificates of merit and gifts of books, and the best of the pupils holds the title of senior pupil and, under the guidance of the instructors, oversees the conduct of his fellow pupils. The corrective measures are as follows: entry into the black book at the discretion of the instructors, corporal punishment with the permission of the District Office, and finally expulsion from the establishment, upon confirmation by the chief colonial administration.

§ 20. Those educated at the establishment's expense are obliged to serve 10 years in a teaching or clerical position; during this time they receive maintenance of from 100 to 150 rubles in silver per year.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XVII. P. 42-44.*

**No. 100. STATUTE ON THE GERMAN CHARITABLE SOCIETY IN ODESSA, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS I (1846)**

20340. — August 23. Imperially confirmed statute on the charitable society for the benefit of Germans in Odessa.

1) A charitable society of Germans is established in the city of Odessa, having as its purpose the rendering of monetary assistance to their needy compatriots, without distinction of origin or religious confession. — Persons of other nationalities may also join the society. 2) The assistance rendered by the society to the needy shall consist of one-time or annual payments, or, finally, in the form of loans. 3) Persons who undertake to make voluntary monetary contributions to it annually are recognized as members of the society. 4) Members, by participating in the meetings of the society, provide it with information about persons in need of assistance. 5) From the contributions, both one-time and continuing, the capital of the society is formed, which, for the accrual of interest, is kept in a Bank and deposited there in the name of the society. For current expenses no more than 200 rubles in silver is to be left in the society's treasury. 6) The management of the society's affairs is entrusted to a Committee, consisting of a Chairman, a Treasurer, a Secretary, and four Assistant Members; for each of these positions one additional member is elected, in case of the need to fill the place of one who has left. 7) Members of the Committee are elected by majority vote and perform their duties without compensation. 8) The Secretary keeps the minutes and manages the correspondence of the society. All documents must bear the signature of the Chairman, the Secretary, and at least two members. 9) The Treasurer keeps the accounts, receives all contributions against receipts, and, by resolution of the Committee, makes payments and disbursements of money. 10) The Committee is charged with the duty of reviewing petitions for assistance addressed to the society. — Decisions on these are made by majority vote. 11) For the consideration of these petitions and for deciding other matters, the Committee meets once a week; in case of need, its meetings may be held more often. 12) In addition, a general meeting of members is held once a year, at the residence of the Chairman of the society, at which the Committee presents a report on the society's activities and the sums expended during the past year, and an election of members to Committee positions is held; in case of special need, extraordinary meetings of members may also be called. 13) A report on the society's activities is submitted annually, through the local authorities, to the Minister of Internal Affairs. 14) The general meeting of members is empowered to amend the rules of this statute by majority vote; but such amendments are permitted only with the confirmation of the government.

*PSZRI. Coll. 2. Vol. XXI. Pt. 2. P. 219-220.*

## No. 101. STATUTE ON THE MOSCOW BOARD OF GUARDIANS FOR THE POOR OF THE EVANGELICAL CONFESSION, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS I (1847)

20788. — January 10. Imperially confirmed statute for the Board of Guardians for the poor of the Evangelical confession in Moscow.

1. For the care of the poor of the three church parishes of the Evangelical confession in Moscow, a Board of Guardians is established.

2. This care is extended, besides the persons named in the preceding article who permanently reside in Moscow, also to those poor persons of the Evangelical confession who are temporarily present there, if, upon precise investigation, they are found to deserve it.

3. The Moscow Military Governor-General assumes the chief authority over the Board of Guardians.

4. The Board of Guardians is composed of: a) Guardians of the poor; b) Active Members; and c) benefactors.

Note. Ladies are also invited to assist in the work of charity.

5. Guardians engage in the care of the poor; Active Members support the purpose of the Board of Guardians through continuing annual contributions; benefactors through one-time donations.

6. The number of Guardians ranges from 20 to 30, as needed; the number of other members is not fixed.

7. Persons of all ranks may be Guardians. They undertake this duty of their own free will; subsequently their number is filled by election from among persons known for their charitable works.

8. Guardians are obliged to collect monetary contributions, visit the dwellings of the poor, look into their condition and needs, and, as circumstances require, render them the necessary assistance from the funds placed at their disposal by the Board of Guardians.

9. Guardians may render assistance to the poor in the following forms: a) for those capable of manual labor but without employment, to find work, supply tools and materials for carrying out work, and see to the sale of their products; or to place the poor in factories, plants, and with craftsmen; b) for those who have fallen into poverty owing to illness and lack the strength to work, to provide food supplies, clothing, linen, etc., and, if necessary, to provide them with medical assistance; c) for those impoverished as a result of dissolute living, carelessness, and laziness, besides providing needed assistance, to offer, with Christian forbearance, guidance which, by pointing out the causes of their unfortunate condition, might turn them onto the right path in life; d) to place the sick in medical institutions; and to place children for upbringing in schools, or with craftsmen for training in trades.

10. Guardians are elected from each district of the city, and take under their protection the poor living in the same district as themselves.

11. Guardians choose assistants for themselves, whom they charge with paying special attention to how the assistance given to the poor is used.

12. Each Guardian receives monthly from the Committee of the Board of Guardians the sum of money required for assistance to the poor, which he may spend at his own discretion; at the end of the month, together with detailed information on his activities, he submits to the Committee a report on the use of the disbursed sum.

13. The resources of the Board of Guardians for its charitable activities consist of: a) the annual monetary contributions of Active Members; b) the donations of benefactors; c) bequests under wills that have received legal confirmation, and the like.

14. The Board of Guardians is authorized to invite physicians and apothecaries to provide, free of charge, medical assistance to the poor cared for by the Board of Guardians.
