So that the villagers may see that diligence and good conduct establish their common good, the Village Schulzes, under the special supervision of the Head, must compile registers both of those who distinguish themselves in husbandry and of the negligent, which registers, signed by both, are to be submitted annually to the local administration, to the end that the well-ordered and the disorderly may be distinguished, and that the diligent and honest may enjoy advantages of trust.

*Ibid.*

395. The Head and the Schulzes see to it that poor and destitute colonists in no way wander about the world and beg alms in a mendicant manner. Such of them as are healthy are to be compelled, through labor, to earn their own sustenance, while the aged and infirm are to be maintained by their relatives. But if they have neither relatives nor strength for work, they are to be maintained at public expense, two almshouses being set up for them by common effort near the church, one for the female and the other for the male sex, where they are to be supplied with food and with warm clothing sufficient to cover their nakedness. For such expense there is to be kept at the almshouse, under the seal and lock of the Church Warden, a box, and in the churches a purse, by means of which the money collected on feast days and Sundays from alms is placed into the box, and at the end of each month is taken out and used to maintain the almshouses; in addition, fine money is likewise to be used for the same purpose, and in case of shortfall, a supplement is to be added from the colony. For the better order of these almshouses, the Priests of those churches must have chief oversight of them.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 36, p. 2; 1801 May 16 (19873) §§ 24 and 30; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) §28.

396. The Schulzes are strictly to observe that no one give shelter in their houses to disreputable women and men; and if anyone is noticed in this, then, both as to the householder and as to those found in such disorders, the Head must immediately report to the Office of the Saratov colonies, to the Guardianship Committee in the Novorossiya colonies, and to the Superintendent in the St. Petersburg colonies.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 22; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 44; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 44 [42]; 1833 Jul. 1 (6298).

397. Luxury, and still more profligacy, the Schulzes must eradicate among the colonists with all their power, bringing offenders to obedience by assigning them the heaviest tasks in various communal works, so that they may never find time for such harmful conduct, until they come to acknowledge their fault; and if they are not thereby reformed, such persons are to be sent, with reports, to the authorities.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 42; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 49; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 45.

398. By luxury is meant when someone has immoderate expenses in his household, frequent gatherings of guests and the like, giving occasion for the squandering of property; and profligacy is card-playing and other games for money and goods, the sale of one's own livestock or other property without the knowledge of the Schulze and without any need, for drunkenness or the satisfaction of other passions.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) note to art. 42; 1801 May 16 (19873) note to § 49; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) note to § 45.

399. The Village Heads and Schulzes are diligently to see to it that all villagers behave affably and amicably with their neighbors, and politely and hospitably with visitors, and that they avoid, with the former, quarrels over land in the neighborhood, and, with the latter, the slightest rudeness.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 27; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 53; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 48.

##### CHAPTER THREE.

On the protection of persons and property from harm and damage.

400. In the colonies, persons without written documents shall by no means be tolerated, and therefore, if anyone arrives in a settlement for any business for a considerable time, or for work or hire, and does not have a ticket or certificate, such a person shall not be received.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 10; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 43; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 41.

401. If unknown, suspicious, or fugitive persons are observed anywhere, they are to be sought out, caught, and sent to the Headman or Schulz, who, after conducting interrogations with a detailed description, immediately reports to his superior authority or the Overseer; in doing so he also presents those very persons together with everything found on them, as well as those who harbored them. Distant colonies shall send such persons directly to the District Court, as stated below in article 502 concerning criminal offenses.

*Ibid.*

402. In places where staging posts have not yet been established along the routes, and where criminals are transferred by means of the rural police, colonists are obliged, on an equal footing with other district inhabitants, to escort convoys of prisoners.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 37; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 45.

403. Headmen in particular must ensure that none of the prisoners of various ranks being escorted through the colonies can escape from guard; for this purpose, Schulzes in every colony shall keep special registers in which to record the names of the prisoners being escorted, from whom and to which colony they were brought, with whom and when they were sent onward, and in which settlement and to whom they were handed over; the receipts given upon receiving them are likewise to be kept.

*Ibid. DOCUMENTS_______________________________________________________________________________ 475*

404. If anyone should happen to find some lost item anywhere, he must immediately declare it to his Schulz, keeping it safely in the meantime, and the Schulz reports it to the Headman. When the owner is found, the found item is to be given to him in the presence of witnesses; in this case one may demand payment for one's trouble, but by no means more than the legally established third part of the value of the found item as appraised by the Schulz, and whoever wishes to return it without payment, such disinterestedness will be all the more praiseworthy.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 24; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 52; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 47.

405. Schulzes are strictly instructed that, regarding stray or additional livestock that has joined their settlements or herds, they report immediately, with a detailed description, through the Headman, to the Overseer or their local administration for publication, and that they keep the livestock itself in the settlement where it turned up, but in a place separate from their own, under threat of penalty. When the owner of the livestock is found, it is to be given to him in the presence of the Schulz, with payment taken for its feeding. In remote colonies the Schulz reports the stray livestock to the District Court of his uyezd.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 32; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 46; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 43.

406. When colonists purchase horses, each purchase must be recorded in the Office, indicating specifically when it was bought, from whom, at what price, the brand, and other distinguishing marks. Otherwise, and in suspicious cases, one who fails to declare and record a horse bought or exchanged from someone shall not only lose it but shall also be brought to trial; for this purpose Headmen are obliged to keep special books for this in the Offices.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 32; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 47.

407. The Headman in every Office, and the Schulz in every village, must take precautions against contagious and infectious diseases and livestock plague.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 8, item 4; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 16, item 4; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 14, item IV.

408. If an extraordinary disease among people should appear in any colony, the Schulzes must immediately notify the Headman of it, and he is obliged to report at once to the authorities or the Overseer.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 10; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 54; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 49.

409. As a precaution against livestock plague, Headmen and other rural authorities are to act in all respects in accordance with the special instruction sent out to the colonies for this purpose, and to be guided by it without fail, and when a plague breaks out anywhere, they must at once report it to their local administration, thereafter reporting weekly both on its continuation or diminution and on progress made under the measures prescribed by that instruction; in doing so, infected livestock is to be separated to a special place remote from the rest, special pens being built for this at every village, in places distant from dwellings and from grazing, and all contact with such infected livestock is to be cut off.

*Ibid.*

410. When it happens that settlements in which the infection appears are situated on streams and rivers, and there are other settlements no farther than ten versts downstream, then, so as not to cause the same harm to neighbors through their watering place, sick livestock must not be watered at those sources, but water must be carried by hand to pens built for that purpose (art. 409); therefore these should be built closer to the water. Likewise the utmost caution must be exercised if such a misfortune should occur in settlements situated on the same streams, even if more than ten versts away; for inexact compliance with this, the Headman and other Schulzes are to be fined.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 10; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 94 [54]; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 49.

411. Headmen and Schulzes must strictly observe that weights and measures are everywhere accurate, and that colonists do not denote the quantity of their produce using foreign measures and weights, from which only confusion and misunderstanding can arise; for this reason, every District Office, and where there is none, the Village Office, must keep a stamped official measure, namely: the garnets, chetverik, and chetvert, as well as a stamped weight in pounds and poods; based on these every householder must have the same made for himself and compare them with those kept stamped in the District Office, and when they are found to be entirely consistent, the District Office must then stamp them with its own seal.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 8, item 4; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 16, item 4; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 14, item IV; Jul. 7 (20841) § 12.

412. Headmen and Schulzes are to see to it that nowhere, under any pretext, may disorderly conduct, fights, or unauthorized gatherings occur.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 8, item 4, and art. 34.

413. Schulzes are to watch diligently that every householder keeps his house, threshing floor, stables, sheds, and fences in proper repair, tidiness, and cleanliness, and that in wintertime he attends to their repair.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 21, 51, 54; 1801 May 16 (19873) §§ 50, 72, 78; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) §§ 46, 68, 74; Jul. 7 (20841) § 5; 1845 Aug. 15 (19283) art. 1329.

414. Headmen and Schulzes are obliged to accustom the colonists, in keeping with the custom of the places from which they emigrated to Russia, to preserve in stone buildings the same style used there; to see that proper order is observed in the layout of houses in the colonies, so that they may be more quickly and conveniently protected in case of fire; and colonists are by no means to build new houses on their own without the permission of their local authority or the Overseers.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 57, item 1; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 80, item 1; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 75, item 1.

415. In every settlement, as protection against fire and any theft, there must be day and night watchmen specially assigned, in some places according to the extent of the settlement, and in the middle of settlements where there are no churches, bells or iron plates, so that if a fire or thieves are observed in some house, those watchmen may sound the alarm, and residents of both sexes of full age immediately gather to help at that place; for such an occasion, all villagers are to be assigned by household as to who is to go to the fire with what equipment.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 9; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 55; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 50.

416. In addition, every household must always keep ready water in special tubs, and for the whole settlement there must be kept in a designated place several special hooks, pitchforks, and barrels, with two horses always ready in turn for hauling water.

*Ibid. DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________ 477*

417. In case of fire, which sometimes occurs not from carelessness but from unforeseen causes, whereby a villager is brought to complete ruin, it would be necessary to establish in the colonies, by agreement of all the villagers, a rule that everyone render assistance to fire victims according to his means, if not with money then with labor or in some other way; to which the Headman and Schulzes are obliged to encourage them. This assistance must be provided through their mediation and under their direction.

1801 May 16 (19873) § 56; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 51.

418. Schulzes are to see that stoves in houses are built without fail with chimneys and are fired not from the entryway but from small kitchens specially built adjoining them, which are to be lined with brick and coated with clay for fire safety; in addition, chimneys must be cleaned every week, which the Tithingmen must strictly oversee. The Schulz or the Beisitzers oversee the fulfillment of this, ordering the Tithingmen to inspect the chimneys monthly.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 11; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 57; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 52.

419. As protection against fire, threshing barns are to be established as far as possible from the houses.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 11; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 80, item 2; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 75, item 2; 1845 Aug. 15 (19283) art. 1379.

420. At night, in houses and along the streets, no one whatsoever is to walk with a splint-torch or candles without lanterns, nor with lit pipes.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 20; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 58; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 53.

421. Schulzes are obliged to see that there is no filth in the streets of any colony; and for protection against storms and winds, and in case of fires, they are to order that various trees, whichever can grow there, be planted along the streets near households and threshing floors, wherever convenient given the nature of the climate and soil.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 27; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 15 [51]; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798); 1845 Aug. 15 (19283) art. 1329.

422. Schulzes must see that boundary markers that have been set up remain undamaged, and when posts become worn out or mounds crumble, they must immediately report this to their Headman and repair them at once upon his order.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 25; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 36; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 34; 1845 Aug. 15 (19283) art. 1337.

##### CHAPTER FOUR.

On absences of colonists, and their resettlement.

Section One.

On absences of colonists within the empire.

423. Colonists wishing to absent themselves to some settlement, or to the provincial and district towns to sell their produce, or generally on their own business, are granted leave by the Headmen, who issue them tickets for this from the Office.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 35; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 33; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 31.

424. Those who need to travel to distant places and for long periods, or even to nearby settlements but for some kind of work and for a considerable time, having received leave from the Schulzes with the Headman's certification that there is no obstacle to their absence for the requested period, and that neither their agriculture nor their livestock husbandry will suffer any harm from it, must appear as follows: Saratov colonists at the Office, where, upon receiving passports, they bind themselves by signed undertaking to return by the appointed date (a); St. Petersburg colonists receive such passports from the Treasury (b). The issuance of passports to colonists of the New Russia governorates and the Bessarabian oblast, upon presentation of leave certificates obtained from their rural authorities, is entrusted to the Overseers of the colonies and to the Administrator of the Trans-Danubian settlers, who also have the right to requisition passport blanks themselves from the District Treasuries (c).

Note. Temporarily, as an experiment, foreign settlers have been permitted to be issued passports from the District and Village Offices specifically in those places where, given the Elders' and Clerks' knowledge of the Russian language, this measure is found to be practicable, on condition that the passport forms, as needed, be sent to the Offices by the Board of Trustees, the Saratov Office, the Chambers of State Property, and the Administration of the Trans-Danubian settlers, and that the said institutions, upon receiving money and accounts from the Offices, settle accounts for the forms with the Treasury Chambers (d).

(a) 1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 35. - (b) 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 31. - (c) 1835 Jan. 14 (7761). - (d) 1850 Apr. 3 (24041).

425. The issuance of tickets and passports, under articles 423 and 424, is permitted only to those colonists who have no outstanding debts and are not under trial or investigation. Upon receiving permission for absence, colonists must pay in advance the taxes owed by them for one year; and upon the expiration of the year, those still absent are obliged either to appear in person to exchange their tickets, or else to send in the advance payment of taxes for the year in order to receive them.

1846 Dec. 9 (20685) item 2.

426. Leave for New Russia colonists to travel on passports for earnings is limited only to the three New Russia governorates.

1811 Aug. 15 (24745); 1812 Jan. 29, Highest command addressed to the Military Governor of Kherson.

427. The Saratov Office must issue passports to the colonists under its jurisdiction only in printed form, requesting the necessary quantity of these in good time from the Treasury Chamber, which is obliged to supply them without delay.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562); 1817 Apr. 30 (26823).

428. Members of the Evangelical community in Sarepta and in the Baltic governorates receive passports for absences within the Empire from the leaders of the brotherhood and the Elders (a); Scottish colonists, settled in Stavropol governorate, receive such passports from the Board (b).

(a) 1797 Jun. 20 (18011) item 7; 1817 Oct. 27 (27113) art. 8; 1856 Jan. 24 (30752[30252]). - (b) 1806 Dec. 25 (22410) art. 5.

<...>

430. Colonists, upon returning to their places of residence, are obliged to deliver the passports issued to them back to their authority.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 35; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 33; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 31.

Section Two.

On the departure of colonists abroad.

431. Colonists, in the event of leaving the state, are obliged to obtain passports through the communications of their authorities with those places and persons who, under the Passport Statute, are charged with the duty of issuing such passports.

1797 Jun. 20 (18011) item 7; 1806 Dec. 25 (22410) art. 5 and 20; 1817 Oct. 27 (27113) art. 8; 1856 Apr. 10 (30380).

432. A foreign passport is issued to a colonist only after collection from him, in a single payment to the treasury, of three years' tax, over and above payment of all debts owed by him, necessarily including therein the subsistence money paid to him from the day of his arrival at the border until the time he settled.

1797 Jun. 20 (18011) item 9; 1800 Sept. 6 (19546) item 8; 1802 Jan. 5 (20103); 1804 Feb. 20 (21163) art. 7, 11.

433. Every member of the Scottish colony wishing to leave the state is bound to pay into the treasury, out of all the wealth he has honestly acquired in Russia: if he has lived there from one to five years, a fifth part, and if from five to ten years or more, a tenth part, whichever the Board declares in good conscience.

1806 Dec. 25 (22410) art. 20.

434. In the event that any colonist owning land acquired by him in ownership through purchase should wish to leave the state altogether, he must, upon his departure, comply with the rules established in this regard in articles 508 and 509.

1804 Mar. 1 (21192) item 4.

Section Three.

On the resettlement of colonists.

435. The resettlement of colonists from one governorate to another may be permitted only with the prior authorization of the Ministry of State Property.

1797 Jun. 20 (18006); 1817 Sept. 29 (27070); 1828 Dec. 15 (2517); 1831 Jun. 2 (4616 and 4617); 1837 Dec. 26 (10834).

#### SECTION SEVEN. ON EXACTIONS AND PUNISHMENTS.

##### CHAPTER ONE.

General provisions.

436. Schulzes and Vorsteher shall not, on their own without the Headmen, subject anyone to punishment, unless the Headmen are absent, and even then only with the common consent of the Beisitzers and the best people; the Headmen have the authority to punish on their own with labor and monetary fines with the common consent of the Schulzes and Vorsteher; moreover, no Schulz individually has the right to impose fines on his own account; but Schulzes and Beisitzers apply to the Headman, while others seek satisfaction from their local authority or its members during their visits.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 18; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 25; 1803 Jun. 6[16] (20798) § 23; 1833 Jun.[Jul.] 1 (6298).

437. Monetary exactions are placed into the common fund, and are recorded together with other monetary collections in the bound ledgers, indicating precisely: for what offense whom was punished, how much was taken from whom, and to what it was applied.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 1, 9, 13; 1801 May 16 (19873) §§ 1, 40, 55; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) §§ 1, 38, 50.

438. Since it is impossible to enumerate all offenses and crimes, it is prescribed that if anyone commits an offense not mentioned in the articles below, it shall be reported in due order to the higher authority and a new instruction awaited from it, and it shall not be punished on one's own authority nor shall any monetary exaction be taken; however, sentencing to labor by majority vote is permitted, but for no more than seven days, with notification nonetheless to the local administration.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 50; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 60[66]; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 63; 1833 Jul. 1 (6298).

##### CHAPTER TWO.

On exactions for failure to perform duties

of public service.

439. For failure to appear when summoned to the Assembly, the guilty parties are held liable under article 1971 of the Code of Punishments, and for violation of due order at meetings of the colonist community, under article 1970 of the same Code.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 26; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 28; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 26; 1840 Aug. 31 (13750); 1845 Aug. 15 (19283) art. 1894, 1845.

440. Colonists, for disobedience, insubordination, obstinacy, and failure to carry out the orders of their authority, without, however, overt resistance to it, are subject to punishment on the basis of article 307 of the Code of Punishments.

1804 Feb. 20 (21163); 1845 Aug. 15 (19283) art. 295.

<...>

##### CHAPTER THREE.

On exactions for violation of civil rights.

Section One.

On exactions for insult and dishonor.

444. For insulting with unseemly words the Headman, Clerk, Schulz, Beisitzer, or in general a person belonging to the local administration of the colony, colonists guilty thereof are subject to punishments or exactions on the basis of the rules established in article 328 of the Code of Punishments, and in every case are obliged to ask forgiveness of the offended party at the general Assembly.

1845 Aug. 15 (19283) art. 316.

445. For insulting by actions the persons designated in the preceding article 444, colonists are subject to the punishments or exactions defined in article 328 of the Code of Punishments.

*Ibid.*

446. For unjust denunciations against their own Headmen and Schulzes, each shall suffer punishment from the authorities as a slanderer.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 14; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 19; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 17.

Section Two.

On exactions for violation of property rights.

447. Whoever knowingly builds upon, plows, or sows land belonging to another, or otherwise seizes it and turns it to his own use or benefit, without the consent and permission of its owner, shall, on the basis of article 2177 of the Code of Punishments, be subject to a monetary exaction in favor of the colonists' communal capital. Furthermore, upon the return of the land to its lawful owner together with all its produce, without any payment for it, the party guilty of seizure is obliged to compensate him for all losses he has suffered thereby.

1845 Aug. 15 (19283) art. 2098.

448. Whoever, without authorization, but not secretly and not in the manner of theft, reaps or gathers grain, oats, or other crops or vegetables found on another's land, or mows hay on another's meadows, shall, in addition to compensating the owner for the harm or loss caused, on the basis of the Civil Laws, be subject for this to the monetary exaction defined in article 2178 of the Code of Punishments. Whoever intentionally destroys or damages another's tools or gear for hunting animals or birds shall, in addition to compensating the owner for the losses thereby caused, be subject to a monetary exaction, on the basis of article 2182 of the same Code.

*Ibid., art. 2099, 2103.*

449. Whoever, by force or otherwise, or even accidentally, drives off to himself from another's land part of another's herd or drove or flock of birds or other domestic animals, or even a single horse or head of livestock or other domestic animal, and does not return them upon the owner's first demand, shall, in addition to the obligation to compensate him for losses, be subject to a monetary exaction, on the basis of article 2183 of the Code of Punishments.

*Ibid., art. 2104.*

450. For the slaughter of another's livestock, the guilty parties, in addition to compensation for the losses caused, are subject to a monetary exaction, on the basis of article 2181 of the Code of Punishments.

*Ibid., art. 2102.*

451. If, however, anyone kills or injures another's livestock without intent, and this is clearly proven, then in such a case only two thirds of the appraised value shall be collected for the killing, and no fine whatsoever shall be imposed, and he shall be ordered to have the unintentionally injured livestock treated; and if he does not have it cured, he shall be compelled as stated regarding livestock killed.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 47; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 63; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 60.

452. If anyone forcibly takes from another livestock, poultry, or any other item, even under the guise of a debt, the item taken is to be ordered returned to its owner, and the one who took it is to be reported to the authorities through the established procedure.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 48; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 64; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 61.

453. Whoever, notwithstanding the above-described exactions and punishments, will not desist from insolent conduct, such persons, with a description of their offenses, are to be delivered to the authorities under guard with a report, for proceedings according to the laws.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 49; 1801 May 16 (19873) § 65; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 62.

##### CHAPTER FOUR.

On penalties for failure to pay taxes

and to perform obligations.

454. Arrears from colonists are collected with a fine on the same basis as established for landlords' peasants.

1812 March 27 (25057) para. 3.

455. Should any of the Saratov, New Russia, or Bessarabia colonists fail to pay, within the appointed time, the sum assessed upon him for the maintenance of Patres, Pastors, and Schoolmasters, such person shall, the first time, be made to pay the debt with an addition, in lieu of a fine, of ten kopecks, the second time fifteen kopecks, and for a third failure shall be kept, until he pays, at public labor and reported to the authorities, with an explanation of his circumstances and the reason for his failure; in the St. Petersburg colonies, however, in such a case fifty kopecks are collected the first time, and double that the second time.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 2; 1801 May 16 (19873) §2; 1803 June 16 (20798) §2.

456. If any of the colonists proves disobedient and refuses to deliver, in his turn, to the next nearest colonist settlement the orders dispatched by the authorities, he shall be punished with three days' labor for the commune, and shall be assigned out of turn twice against the others.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 40; 1801 May 16 (19873) §34; 1803 June 16 (20798) §32.

457. If any of the colonists is convicted of not using a loan received from the treasury for the improvement of his household and the acquisition of the necessary farming implements, but squanders it in an unpardonable manner, and moreover does not possess property equal in value to the amount of his debt to the treasury, then in such a case the squanderer of the treasury loan shall be dealt with according to law.

1803 June [July] 7 (20841) §5.

##### CHAPTER FIVE.

On penalties and punishments

for violation of the rules of good order.

458. If any of the colonists of the southern territory, without particular reasons deserving of respect, fails to sow as much land as prescribed, he shall be dealt with on the basis of article 1395 of the Code of Punishments.

1803 July 7 (20841) §5; 1845 Aug. 15 (19283) art. 1338, para. 7.

<...>

461. If any of the colonists, apart from the portion assigned for that year, undertakes to cut timber, a fine double the value of what he has cut shall be collected from him for the common fund, and in the event of his inability to make such payment, he shall be assigned to public labor until he has earned that sum.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 53; 1801 May 16 (19873) §71; 1803 June 16 (20798) §67.

462. If any of the colonists of the southern territory damages, tears out, or otherwise destroys his own grapevines, or allows them to be damaged, or permits livestock to gnaw and trample them, he shall be subject for this to monetary penalty and punishment on the basis of article 1395 of the Code of Punishments.

1803 July 7 (20841) §6; 1845 Aug. 15 (19283) art. 1338, para. 6.

##### CHAPTER SIX.

On penalties and punishments

for violation of the rules of good conduct in the colonies.

Section One.

On penalties and punishments

for violation of the rules of church good conduct.

463. If anyone, not for any lawful reason, but solely out of laziness and negligence, withdraws from Christian duties, such as attending the house of God on feast days and Sundays and partaking of Holy Communion when deemed worthy, such person shall the first and second time be admonished, and thereafter shall be fined: three kopecks in the case of Saratov and New Russia colonists, and fifteen kopecks in the case of St. Petersburg colonists; if the guilty party, having been subjected to this penalty three times in a year, does not desist, the monetary fine shall in addition be doubled for each instance and he shall be put to public labor for a full day.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 1; 1801 May 16 (19873) §1; 1803 June 16 (20798) §1; 1840 Aug. 31 (13750).

Section Two.

On penalties and punishments

for violation of the rules of good order and morality.

464. Any enmity among the inhabitants, private quarrels, and reproaches must be stopped by the village Schulzes and elected officials, first through admonitions, then through public labor, and, in case of repetition, through a fine, collected only from whoever is found to be the instigator of the quarrel, thirty kopecks each time in the St. Petersburg colonies, and seven and a half kopecks in the colonies of the southern territory and in the Saratov colonies.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 41; 1801 May 16 (19873) §48; 1803 June 16 (20798) §44; 1840 Aug. 31 (13750).

465. If any craftsman proves disobedient before his Schulze, he shall be punished by being assigned tasks and made to carry out what has been ordered; and should he fail to carry it out, fifteen kopecks shall be collected for the public fund each time.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 55; 1801 May 16 (19873) §79; 1840 Aug. 31 (13750).

466. The Heads and Schulzes are obliged not only to remove from their position those negligent toward their household, idle, and unruly, but also to punish them with a fine, or with confinement on bread and water; moreover, they must compel them both to plow and sow their allotment and to perform other household tasks, assigning these as set tasks; and for greater success in this, Tithingmen [Desyatskys] are to be attached to them.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 34; 1801 May 16 (19873) §23; 1803 June 16 (20798) §21.

467. For manifest negligence toward agriculture, disorder in the household, or its ruin through drunkenness, laziness, or dissolute living, colonists are punished according to the rules established in article 1395 of the Code of Punishments.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 34; 1801 May 16 (19873) §23; 1803 June 16 (20798) §21; 1845 Aug. 15 (19283) art. 1338, para. 5.

468. With respect to colonists of dissolute conduct, the following measures are observed: 1) If a colonist, notwithstanding all measures taken to restrain him from dissoluteness, remains incorrigible in his conduct, the community may issue a communal verdict for his exclusion and removal from the colony. Such verdicts are considered lawful only when issued by at least two-thirds of the heads of families residing in the colony. Nevertheless, they are reviewed by the local colonist authorities, who, upon the most precise confirmation of the necessity of the measure proposed by the community, give it final approval (a). For the New Russia and Bessarabia colonies, such verdicts are reviewed and approved by the Board of Guardians; for the Saratov colonies, by the Office of Saratov Foreign Settlers (b); for the Livland (c), Chernigov, Voronezh, and St. Petersburg (d) colonies, by the local Chambers of State Domains; for the Transcaucasian colonies, by the local Expedition of State Domains there (d). 2) A colonist excluded from the community on the basis of the preceding point is handed over to the disposal of the civil authorities, which propose that he leave Russia forever and give, in the presence of the Provincial Board, a written undertaking that he will never, under any pretext, return within its borders. If he gives this undertaking, the provincial authorities issue him, for travel by a known route and through a known point abroad, the proper travel document, in which are stated both the reason for his expulsion and the undertaking he has given not to return to Russia. 3) At the same time, arrangements are made for publishing in the gazettes of both capitals, and in the local provincial gazettes where such are published, the name and surname of the person expelled and his description. 4) All expenses that may arise on this occasion are charged to the former community of the person expelled. 5) The family of the person expelled may, if it wishes, follow him; but the community is never entitled to issue a verdict for the removal of any of its members, on account of his personal vicious conduct, together with his family. 6) If the person excluded from the community is unable to leave the country abroad at his own expense, or is himself unwilling to do so, or, having given an undertaking to leave Russia, is found somewhere in hiding, or finally, in violation of the undertaking he has given, returns to Russia, then in all these cases he is subject to being handed over for military service, or, if unfit for it, to being sent into exile for settlement, under the laws concerning vagrants. His family, too, is subject to the operation of these same laws in the cases indicated, if it left the colony together with him (e).

(a) 1837 Jan. 11 (9859) para. 1. — (b) 1837 Jan. 11 (9851) para. 1. — (c) 1841 June 12 (14643). — (d) 1838 Apr. 30 (11189). — (d) 1841 Jan. 5 (14157); 1842 June 23 (15776). — (e) 1837 Jan. 11 (9851) paras. 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6.

Section Three.

On penalties and punishments

for causing harm and damage to property.

469. Any colonist who, notwithstanding the admonition of his authorities, and not out of necessity or unfortunate circumstances, but out of stubbornness, laziness, or negligence, instead of keeping his rural buildings in proper repair — such as his house, cottage, threshing barn, stable, cattle sheds, and kitchen gardens — allows them to fall into neglect and disrepair, shall, in addition to being compelled to make immediate repair of the damage, be subject to monetary penalty and punishment, on the basis of article 1396 of the Code of Punishments.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 21; 1803 June 16 (20798) §46; 1845 Aug. 15 (19283) art. 1338, para. 1. DOCUMENTS________________________________________________________________________ 485

470. Colonists who fail to appear at a fire with the fire-extinguishing equipment they are obliged to have for this purpose are held liable, on the basis of article 1471 of the Code of Punishments.

1845 Aug. 15 (19283) art. 1414.

471. Whoever walks at night in houses and in the streets with a splinter-torch or with candles, without lanterns, or likewise with lit pipes, shall be punished with a monetary fine each time — a kopeck and a half in the Saratov and New Russia colonies, and seven and a half kopecks in the St. Petersburg colonies.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 20; 1801 May 16 (19873) §58; 1803 June 16 (20798) §53; 1840 Aug. 31 (13750).

472. For failure to keep boundary markers that have been set up in proper repair, and for failure to repair dilapidated verst posts and other posts or pyramids, the Schulzes, elected officials, and Beisitzers in the St. Petersburg, Saratov, and New Russia colonies are subject to the monetary penalties set out in article 1395 of the Code of Punishments.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 25; 1801 May 16 (19873) §36; 1803 June 16 (20798) §34; 1845 Aug. 15 (19283) art. 1337.

473. Should boundary markers be damaged intentionally by any of the inhabitants, this is to be reported to the authorities, for punishment to be imposed according to the general laws.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 25; 1801 May 16 (19873) §36; 1803 June 16 (20798) §34.

Section Four.

On penalties and punishments

for unauthorized absences of colonists and for overstaying passports.

474. Colonists who absent themselves without authorization and without lawful passports, or who overstay them, are dealt with on the general basis applicable to persons without passports.

1821 Nov. 10; see also all the enactments cited in this section.

<...>

##### CHAPTER SEVEN.

On the employment of colonists in public works.

477. If anyone is sentenced by the District Office to a monetary fine and is unable to pay it, he shall be put to public labor for as long as it would take one hired laborer to earn that sum of money by performing the same work.

1803 July 7 (20841) §2.

478. Public works may consist of the repair of bridges and roads, the digging of ditches, the planting, clearing, and preservation of forests and mulberry trees, the establishment of vineyards, the improvement of meadows, and other such matters as may arise according to the local circumstances of the colonies and their economic establishments.

1801 May 16 (19873) note to §1; 1803 June 16 (20798) note to §1.

479. As it may happen that, at the time when someone ought to be punished by employment in public labor, no such work is available, the District Office must, at the beginning of each year, after general deliberation on the matter with the most far-sighted proprietors, designate public works, the performance of which might serve at once as punishment for the guilty and for the common good.

1803 July 7 (20841) §2.

480. If a guilty party has already been punished once or more by performance of public works, but nevertheless does not reform his conduct and is again found deserving of punishment, he shall, for a period fixed in proportion to the offense, be put to public works in stocks or a pillory-collar, and upon completion of the work shall sometimes be placed for the night in a jail as well, which, like the stocks and the pillory-collar with post, shall be built out of fine money, or, should such funds be insufficient, out of public revenues.

1803 June 16 (20798) §54; July 7 (20841) §3.

481. If any proprietor is, through his own offenses, subjected to frequent punishments by public labor, and is thereby drawn away from the performance of his own field work and household, or likewise if at that time no useful public works happen to be available in the colony, then in such a case the District Office, with the general agreement of several proprietors of good conduct, must impose upon him, in proportion to his guilt, corporal punishment, taking care that it in no way turns into an execution but serves rather as an instrument of fear through shame and reproach; but such sentences are to be carried into execution only with the approval of the authorities, in the usual manner.

1803 June 16 (20798) §55; July 7 (20841) §4.

#### SECTION EIGHT. ON THE CONDUCT OF COURT PROCEEDINGS AND ADJUDICATION.

##### CHAPTER ONE.

Jurisdiction and conduct of civil cases of colonists.

Section One.

Jurisdiction and conduct of cases between colonists.

482. In the colonies of the southern territory, as well as in the St. Petersburg and Saratov colonies, adjudication and reconciliation in minor quarrels and claims among colonists are the business of the Village Office.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 5 and 16; 1801 May 16 (19873) §18; 1803 June 16 (20798) §16.

483. Should a District Head or Schulze decide any case unjustly, and this be exposed upon complaint being lodged, such person must pay a fine twice that of the party he wrongly condemned; and if the condemned party suffers any loss as a result, this too must be repaid to him in addition to the fine.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 14; 1801 May 16 (19873) §19; 1803 June 16 (20798) §17; 1851 March 21 (25055).

484. Quarrels and claims not concluded by reconciliation in the Village Office are referred, in the colonies of the southern territory and in the Saratov colonies, to the District Office, and in the St. Petersburg colonies are submitted to the Superintendent.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 5 and 16; 1801 May 16 (19873) §18; 1803 June 16 (20798) §16.

485. The third level of court is constituted, in the colonies of the southern territory, by the Board of Guardians of Foreign Settlers, and in the Saratov colonies by their Office (a); while in the St. Petersburg (b) and Transcaucasian colonies (c), those dissatisfied with the Superintendent's decision lodge a complaint with the Chamber of State Domains or, DOCUMENTS_________________________________________________________________________________487

as appropriate, with the Expedition of State Domains under the Main Administration of the Transcaucasian Territory, under whose jurisdiction they fall.

(a) 1833 July 1 (6298). — (b) 1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 5 and 16; 1838 Apr. 30 (11189) pt. 1, para. 57. — (c) 1841 Jan. 5 (14157) §17.

486. The courts of these same places also have jurisdiction over cases involving offenses committed by parishioners against clergy; and likewise parishioners dissatisfied with a clergyman have the right to petition these local administrations through their Head or Schulze.

1801 May 16 (19873) §7; 1803 June 16 (20798) §7; 1833 July 1 (6298).

487. In the colonies of the southern territory, for the examination of litigious and contested cases among colonists, two deputies from the colonies are elected to sit in the Board of Guardians; they may have a voice only in the aforementioned cases, without however involving themselves in governmental matters. The manner of election and term of office of these deputies are determined by the Board of Guardians, with the approval of the Minister of State Domains.

1818 March 22 (27312) sec. III, para. 4; 1833 July 1 (6298); 1837 Dec. 26 (10834).

488. Cases arising between colonists are decided finally, in the New Russia and Bessarabia colonies, by the Board of Guardians; in the Saratov colonies, by their Office; and in the St. Petersburg and Transcaucasian colonies, by the Chamber or Expedition of State Domains.

Cf. the enactments cited under art. 487.

489. In the colony of Sarepta, a special body is established for court proceedings and adjudication in civil matters, under the name of the Administration of the Evangelical Brotherhood Society. It consists of two chiefs, one Justiciary, and three Assessors chosen by the community.

1797 June 20 (18011) para. 4.

490. The Administration of the Evangelical Brotherhood Society has its own seal, and in relation to other government offices is regarded on a par with Municipal Magistracies, with the difference that it is not subordinate to any government office, but is dependent upon the Ministry of State Domains, to which alone it renders a detailed account of its affairs.

*Ibid.; 1803 July 18 (20852); 1837 Dec. 26 (10834).*

491. Civil judicial cases of the Scottish colonists are conducted in the Uprava (administrative board).

1806 Dec. 25 (22410) para. 8.

492. Judicial cases of the Livland colonists are decided in the Village Office; cases not concluded in the Village Office are subject to examination by the Landgericht.

1830 Sept. 23 (3938) para. 3.

Section Two.

Jurisdiction and conduct of cases of colonists

with native inhabitants.

493. Cases of colonists with native Russian inhabitants are conducted in the general courts, to which, for the joint examination of such cases, a deputy is dispatched on behalf of the colonist authorities.

1797 June 30 (18022) para. 3; 1800 July 26 (19492) para. 3; 1827 June 9 (1162); 1828 Aug. 31 (2261).

494. If, in the colonies of the southern territory, none of the members of the Board of Guardians is able to absent himself owing to official duties, deputies are dispatched, as appropriate, from among the Superintendents or officials, chosen as those most capable and trustworthy, for which purpose they are furnished by the Board with the necessary information and instructions.

1828 Aug. 31 (2261); 1833 July 1 (6298).

495. When a case, in the ordinary course or by appeal, comes before a provincial judicial body, the Board of Guardians, or the Saratov Office, forms a Joint Presence with it; or, when this body is not located where the Board of Guardians or Office is situated, one of their members is likewise dispatched to it.

1797 June 30 (18022) para. 3; 1800 July 26 (19492) para. 3; 1828 Aug. 31 (2261); 1833 July 1 (6298).

496. In the adjudication of cases concerning St. Petersburg colonists, the Superintendent of Colonies is present in the district and provincial bodies.

1827 June 9 (1162); 1833 July 1 (6298) para. 5.

497. Colonists, in case of dissatisfaction with a decision of the Chamber, may appeal to the Senate, upon proper endorsement of their dissatisfaction on the case file, but only with the permission of the Minister of State Domains; for which purpose the local administrations must, in every such case, without the slightest delay, report to the Minister, setting out all the circumstances of the case and attaching the petition of the dissatisfied colonists.

1797 June 30 (18022) para. 3; 1800 July 26 (19492) para. 3; 1803 July 18 (20852); 1833 July 1 (6298); 1837 Dec. 26 (10834).

##### CHAPTER TWO.

Jurisdiction and conduct of cases involving police offenses.

498. The following offenses do not fall under the jurisdiction of the District and Village Offices: depravity, forcible seizure of another's property, theft, severe beatings and offenses committed against Heads and Schulzes, and especially beatings and other acts of malice. Persons accused of such offenses are, in the colonies of the southern territory, presented, with reports containing a detailed description of the incident, to the Board of Guardians; in the Saratov colonies, to the Office; and in the St. Petersburg and Transcaucasian colonies, to the Superintendent; from distant colonies, without presenting the offenders themselves, but having detained them under guard, a report is to be sent immediately, describing their offenses, and a decision awaited.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 6; 1801 May 16 (19873) §20; 1803 June 16 (20798) §18; 1833 July 1 (6298); 1841 Jan. 5 (14157).

499. In adjudicating offenses, the utmost prudence and caution are to be exercised; for example: if anyone commits an offense intentionally, and some harm or loss to the settlement or to a neighbor results from it, such person must be punished more severely, or more perceptibly, than one who offends unintentionally and causes no harm to anyone, and who, moreover, has not previously been guilty of any vice; namely, the second offender, as against the first, is to be punished one-third or one-half less, which is left to the discretion of the judges.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 19; 1801 May 16 (19873) §66, note; 1803 July [June] 16 (20798) §62, note.

##### CHAPTER THREE.

Department and conduct of criminal cases.

500. Criminal cases of colonists are handled in the general courts of law.

1797 Jun. 20 (18011) art. 4; 1800 Jul. 26 (19492) para. 4; Sept. 17 (19562) art. 5; 1801 May 16 (19873) §20; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 18; 1806 Dec. 25 (22410) para. 8; 1819 May 29 (27822).

501. In the event of a criminal offense, it is required to report to the authorities or to the Overseer as soon as possible, and to present the offenders themselves under guard, who are sent by way of the Governorate Board to the District Court.

1797 Jun. 20 (18011) art. 4; 1800 Jul. 26 (19492) para. 4; Sept. 17 (19562) art. 5; 1801 May 16 (19873) §20; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 18; 1806 Dec. 25 (22410) |para. 8|; 1819 May 29 (27822).

502. When colonies are situated at a distance, the Schulzen are obliged, with a clear and detailed description of the incident, to bring the offender directly to the Zemstvo Court and, at the same time, immediately report to their superior authority.

1800 Sept. 17 (19562) art. 5; 1801 May 26 (19373) § 20; 1803 Jun. 16 (20798) § 18; 1837 Jun. 3 (10305).

503. For the judgment and decision of criminal cases relating to colonists, deputies are appointed by the colony authorities to the District and Conscience Courts and to the Criminal Chambers, on the same basis as stated above, in articles 493–496, concerning civil cases.

1827 Jun. 9 (1162); 1833 Jul. 19 (6337).

#### SECTION NINE. ON COLONISTS SETTLED ON THEIR OWN LANDS AND ON THE LANDS OF PRIVATE LANDOWNERS.

##### CHAPTER ONE.

On colonists settled on their own lands.

504. Foreigners are permitted to acquire land in ownership from private persons and to settle on it.

1804 Mar. 1 (21192).

505. Foreigners who have settled on land they have purchased enjoy the following privileges.

506. Foreigners who have settled on land they have purchased are granted the general ten-year exemption from payment of taxes and performance of obligations established for all colonists; upon the expiration of which they are subject to taxation on an equal footing with landlords' peasants, according to the rate specified in the table appended to the Statute on Taxes.

1824 Dec. 23 (30179 [30172]); 1849 Mar. 23, information of the Ministries of Finance and State Domains; cf. Statute on Taxes.

507. Zemstvo obligations, in all respects, they must, from the time of their settlement, bear on an equal footing with the other native inhabitants of the region where they settle.

1804 Mar. 1 (21192) para. 3.

508. In the event that any of such settlers, owning land in ownership, should wish to leave the state entirely, he must, upon his departure, sell the land he has purchased to someone residing in Russia; otherwise it shall pass to the treasury without payment.

*Ibid., para. 4.*

509. This right extends not only to the original acquirers of the lands, but also to their heirs, in case they should wish to leave Russia.

*Ibid.*

##### CHAPTER TWO.

On colonists settled on the lands

of private landowners in general.

510. Colonists may be received for settlement by all persons in general who have the right to acquire and own land, without distinction of rank (a).

Note. The settlement of colonists on the lands of private landowners was first begun in 1765, when both noblemen and merchants residing in St. Petersburg were permitted to induce foreigners arriving in Russia to settle on their lands in Ingermanland, under special agreements concluded between them with the confirmation of the former Chancellery of Trusteeship for Foreigners; this was subsequently extended to the interior governorates as well (b).

(a) 1765 Nov. 1 (12503); 1767 May 19 (12897); 1803 Jul. 11 (20843); 1804 Apr. 12 (21254); 1817 Aug. 25 (27022) para. 1; Oct. 1 (27072) para. 1. — (b) 1765 Nov. 1 (12503); 1767 May 19 (12897).

511. The settlement of colonists on the lands of private landowners is accomplished by mutual agreements between them and the latter.

Cf. the same statutes.

512. Landlords and other landowners wishing to bring in and settle colonists on their property must notify the Minister of State Domains thereof through the Governors, informing him at the same time:

1) On what exact number of desyatinas of free land, in what locations, jointly or separately, and from how many families they intend to establish the settlement.

2) What exactly will constitute the main terms of the conditions on the basis of which it is proposed to settle the colonists, such as, for example: concerning the construction of houses, the establishment of farmsteads, the number of years, and the obligations involved.

3) At whose expense their resettlement and travel costs are to be carried out, whether at the landlord's or at the colonists' own expense; in the former case, the sum which it is proposed to allocate for this purpose must also be indicated.

1817 Oct. 1 (27072); 1837 Dec. 26 (10834).

513. Based on this information, the Minister of State Domains uses his good offices to induce and bring in such people, in accordance with the amount of land and the means proposed by the landowners.

The same statutes.

514. Agreements concluded with colonists, after being presented and examined at the appropriate government office, must be submitted for confirmation to the Minister of State Domains.

1804 Apr. 12 (21254); 1817 Aug. 25 (27022) para. 2; Oct. 1 (27072); 1837 Dec. 26 (10834). DOCUMENTS____________________________________________________________________________ 491

515. Such agreements must be concluded each time for a period of no more than twenty years, with a detailed statement of all circumstances, both on the part of the landlords and landowners and on the part of the colonists being settled.

1817 Oct. 1 (27072) para. 3.

516. Colonists are permitted to discharge their obligations on landlords' lands through personal labor, provided that the conditions clearly specify: the types of work, the number of working days, and the like.

1817 Aug. 25 (27022) para. 3.

517. Likewise, mutual payments, such as may be established by voluntary agreement of the contracting parties, upon the expiration of the term of the agreement, in the event of the colonists leaving the land, or in the event that the landlord does not agree for the colonists to remain on his land beyond the term, must be precisely and clearly defined in the agreement.

*Ibid., para. 4.*

518. Disputes arising under the agreements shall be resolved by the proper government offices in accordance with the statutes on contracts.

1804 Apr. 12 (21254) para. 5.

519. If the landlord to whom the land given to the colonists for settlement belongs should die, or should wish to sell or mortgage it, then in such case all the terms of the mutual obligations must remain inviolable, and the heirs or acquirers may not alter the conditions except with the consent of the colonists themselves, notifying the local authorities thereof for submission to the Minister of State Domains.

1817 Aug. 25 (27022) para. 5; 1837 Dec. 26 (10834).

520. A landlord who has taken colonists onto his land must immediately present the border-crossing certificates given to them by the border authorities for registration with the Zemstvo Court, which shall report thereon monthly to the Governorate Board; the latter, comparing these reports with the registers furnished by the border authorities, is obliged each time to notify the Treasury Chamber accordingly of the number of these people, the status they have chosen, and the time of their settlement, for the proper action on its part.

1802 May 9 (20259) para. 8; 1824 Dec. 2[3] (30172).

521. A landlord who has not presented the certificate for registration with the Zemstvo Court within three months shall be deemed to be harboring fugitives.

1802 May 9 (20259) para. 9.

522. Colonists, having fulfilled all the obligations made with the landowner, may move from him to another.

1804 Apr. 12 (21254) para. 6.

523. Colonists settled on the lands of private landowners have freedom of religion and are exempt for the entire duration of their residence in Russia from military and civil service.

1765 Nov. 1 (12503); 1767 May 19 (12897); 1803 Jul. 11 (20843); 1804 Apr. 12 (21254) para. 1; 1824 Dec. 23 (30172).

524. They forever retain their personal freedom, and landowners may under no circumstances bind them to themselves as property, even should these settlers themselves request it.

1765 Nov. 1 (12503); 1767 May 19 (12897); 1802 May 9 (20259) para. 7; 1803 Jul. 11 (20843); 1804 Apr. 12 (21254) |para. 4|; 1817 Aug. 25 (27022); 1824 Dec. 23 (30172).

525. The general rule of a ten-year exemption from payment of taxes extends to colonists settled on landlords' lands, provided that such exemption is to be reckoned from the time of their initial settlement with the landlords.

1804 Apr. 12 (21254) para. 2; 1824 Dec. 23 (30172).

526. Colonists who have availed themselves of the ten-year exemption, or who during the period of exemption have moved, or shall move, to other landlords' lands, or from one district to another, or from one governorate to another, are not to be granted the exemption a second time; for which purpose the local authorities must ensure that colonists do not leave their settlements without their knowledge.

1824 Dec. 23 (30172).

527. Upon the expiration of the exemption period, treasury taxes are collected from all colonists settled on landlords' lands on an equal footing with landlords' peasants.

1804 Apr. 12 (21254) para. 2; 1824 Dec. 23 (30172).

528. Colonists must bear zemstvo obligations from the time of their settlement, on an equal footing with the other villagers of the governorate in which they settle.

1804 Apr. 12 (21254) |para. 3|; 1824 Dec. 23 (30172).

529. Colonists settling on lands belonging to landlords or private landowners fall under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of State Domains, but only with regard to ensuring that mutual obligations are not violated.

1818 Mar. 22 (27312) art. 9; 1837 Dec. 26 (10834).
