Upon the passing to the Peasant Land Bank of lands alienated under the present rules, the structures and buildings specified in Article 2, together with their equipment, pass into the ownership of the Bank free of charge, and on the same basis are transferred by the Bank, by deeds of gift, together with the land plots occupied by the said structures and buildings, either to peasant societies newly formed on the said lands, or to the local zemstvo and other government or public institutions, according to local conveniences and needs, as well as other circumstances that have come to light.

14. Upon retaining for itself the real property of the societies specified in Article 1, the Peasant Land Bank informs the appropriate zemstvo chief or the official corresponding to him of the amount of the total compensation for the lands acquired, for announcement to the society and for apportionment by the latter of the said compensation among all the householders.

The said apportionment is carried out according to the following calculation: a) with respect to householders who hold, for their plots, deeds of confirmation, certification, or other instruments establishing right of ownership — in proportion to the area of the land holdings shown in these instruments as held in separate use, with the addition, in appropriate cases, for the right of participation in holdings of undivided use, of compensation calculated in proportion to that portion of such holdings which is due to each of the said householders according to the ratio of the area of holdings in separate use shown for him by instrument to the total area of holdings held in separate use by all members of the society, and b) with respect to the remaining householders — according to the extent of each householder's actual possession of holdings in separate use, while a householder participating in holdings of undivided use is assigned additional compensation calculated in proportion to that portion of such holdings which is due to the householder according to the ratio of the area of holdings in his separate use to the total area of holdings held in separate use by all members of the society.

Simultaneously with the conducting of the apportionment, lists of householders are compiled indicating how much is due to each out of the total sum of compensation, which of them are obligated to resettle and which are free of such obligation and wish to retain for themselves the right belonging to them in the alienated lands, whereby anyone who has not declared a wish to retain the said right is listed as resettling.

*SURP. 1916. First Section. 2nd half-year. No. 304. Pp. 3047–3049.*

## No. 192. DECISION OF THE COUNCIL OF MINISTERS ON THE LIQUIDATION OF INDUSTRIAL ENTERPRISES ON LANDS SUBJECT TO ALIENATION, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS II (1916)

2407. On the procedure for liquidating industrial enterprises located on lands of enemy subjects and immigrants subject to alienation.

By a decision of the Council of Ministers confirmed by His Imperial Majesty on 25 October 1916, it was resolved, on the basis of Article 87 of the Fundamental State Laws (Digest of Laws, vol. I, part 1, 1906 edition):

I. In amendment and supplement of the decisions of the Council of Ministers confirmed by His Imperial Majesty on 2 February and 13 December 1915 and on 19 August 1916 concerning the compulsory alienation of lands belonging to enemy subjects and immigrants (Collection of Enactments: 1915, art. 349, 351, and 2749, and 1916, art. 1869), to establish the following rules on the procedure for liquidating land plots subject to compulsory alienation on which more substantial industrial enterprises are located:

1. No later than one month from the day of promulgation of the present enactment, the governorate boards or the institutions corresponding to them shall communicate to the Minister of Trade and Industry and to the Peasant Land Bank special lists of plots subject to compulsory alienation, under the procedure of the enactments of 2 February and 13 December 1915 on measures to reduce foreign landholding and land use (Collection of Enactments, art. 349–351 and 2749), on which are located industrial enterprises of the first six categories with respect to payment of the basic trade tax (Digest of Laws, vol. V, Statute on Direct Taxes, 1914 edition, Art. 449, appendix).

2. For the affairs of the industrial enterprises specified in Article 1, liquidation boards are established, consisting of members appointed by the relevant Ministers, one each from the Ministries of Trade and Industry, Internal Affairs, Agriculture, and Finance (in respect of the Peasant Land Bank), under the chairmanship of a person appointed by the Minister of Trade and Industry, whereby a single liquidation board may, by order of the Minister of Trade and Industry, be charged with the management of several industrial enterprises.

Liquidation boards are established immediately upon receipt of the special lists specified in Article 1, if by that time the periods for voluntary alienation of the plots on which the industrial enterprises are located have expired, or, otherwise, upon the expiration of the periods for their voluntary alienation.

3. Within two months from the time of receipt of the lists mentioned above (Art. 1), if the liquidation boards have been established by that time, and otherwise immediately upon their establishment, the Peasant Land Bank is obligated to inform the relevant liquidation board of its wish to acquire the land plot together with the industrial enterprise located on it, or separately from such enterprise, or of its refusal to acquire the given land plot at all.

4. In the event the Peasant Land Bank expresses a wish to acquire a land plot together with the industrial enterprise located on it, the liquidation board, without proceeding to liquidate the enterprise, merely manages and administers it pending its alienation.

In the event, however, of a wish on the part of the Peasant Land Bank to acquire the land plot separately from the industrial enterprise located on it, the liquidation board determines the quantity and location of the land, out of the composition of the given holding, which is to be allotted to the industrial enterprise, taking into account both the land under factory and plant buildings and the land necessary for the continuation of the industrial enterprise's activity. The allotment proposed by the liquidation board is marked, by its order, on the plan of the estate subject to division.

5. Where the land allotted to the industrial enterprise is encumbered by a mortgage held in common with the entire estate, the liquidation board draws up a project for dividing the total sum for which the entire estate is mortgaged into two parts, in proportion to the value of the divided parts of the estate.

The division project is communicated to the mortgage holder, who is given a period of two weeks from the day of receipt of such communication to submit objections.

6. The proposals of the liquidation board regarding the quantity and location of the land allotted to the industrial enterprise, together with the estate plan attached (Art. 4), and the project for dividing the total sum of the mortgage encumbering the estate (Art. 5), together with the mortgage holder's objections, if any have been made, are submitted for confirmation to the relevant governorate board or the institution corresponding to it. The composition of the governorate boards or the institutions corresponding to them, in considering matters of this kind, includes representatives of the Ministries of Agriculture and of Trade and Industry, as well as a Member of the local District Court, elected by the general assembly of the Court, and a representative of the Peasant Land Bank.

7. Against the rulings of the governorate board or the institution corresponding to it specified in the preceding (6th) article, complaints may be lodged within two weeks from the day such rulings are announced, to the Governing Senate, First Department, where they are resolved according to the procedure specified in Article 94 of the Statute of the Governing Senate, 1915 edition.

8. Rulings of the governorate board or the institution corresponding to it, once they have entered into legal force, concerning the division of an estate and the mortgage encumbering it, and, in appropriate cases, rulings of the First Department of the Governing Senate on the same subject, are forwarded to the senior notary for the opening of a special sheet in the register of deeds and for the corresponding notation in the said register.

9. The liquidation of industrial enterprises together with the lands allotted to them, as well as of land plots with industrial enterprises located on them, the acquisition of which the Peasant Land Bank has declined, is carried out by liquidation boards in accordance with the rules of the decision of the Council of Ministers confirmed by His Imperial Majesty on 10 May 1915 on the liquidation of commercial enterprises belonging to enemy subjects (Collection of Enactments, art. 1113).

10. The procedure of action of the liquidation boards with regard to the allotment of land, the management and administration of industrial enterprises, and their sale as going concerns, as well as the compensation of members of the said boards, are determined by an instruction established by the Minister of Trade and Industry in agreement with the Ministers of Internal Affairs, Agriculture, Finance, and Justice.

11. Section II of the decision of the Council of Ministers confirmed by His Imperial Majesty on 19 August 1916 concerning certain amendments and supplements to the enactments of 2 February and 13 December 1915 on measures to reduce foreign landholding and land use in the Russian State (Collection of Enactments, art. 1869) is to be repealed, thereby terminating the effect of the deferrals of liquidation of land plots granted on the basis of Article 2 of the said section.

*SURP. 1916. First Section. 2nd half-year. No. 304. Pp. 3049–3051.*

## No. 193. DECISION ON THE SUSPENSION OF APPLICATION OF THE 1915 LIQUIDATION ENACTMENTS IN THE WESTERN REGIONS (1916)

2806. On the localities in which the running of the time limits established by the rules of 2 February and 13 December 1915 (Collection of Enactments, arts. 349, 351 and 2749) is deferred pending a corresponding new publication.

The Minister of Internal Affairs, in agreement with the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief, submitted to the Governing Senate on 3 December 1916, for publication, the following list of localities where the running of the time limits established by the rules of 2 February and 13 December 1915 (Collection of Enactments, arts. 349, 351 and 2749) is deferred pending a corresponding new publication.

Governorates: Warsaw, Grodno, Kalisz, Kovno, Courland, Kielce, Łomża, Lublin, Piotrków, Płock, Radom, Suwałki, Chełm.

Districts: Dvinsk, of Vitebsk Governorate; Vilna, Lida, Oshmyany, Sventsyany and Trakai, of Vilna Governorate; Vladimir-Volynsky, Dubno, Kovel and Lutsk, of Volhynia Governorate; Riga, of Livland Governorate; Novogrudok, Pinsk and Slutsk, of Minsk Governorate.

*SURP. 1917 [1916]. Part One. 2nd half-year. No. 356. P. 3841.*

## No. 194. DECISION OF THE COUNCIL OF MINISTERS ON THE PROCEDURE FOR APPEALING DECISIONS ON THE SEIZURE OF ALLOTMENT LANDS, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS II (1917)

196. On the procedure for appealing rulings on the termination of ownership of allotment lands by German, Austrian and Hungarian immigrants in Kainsk District, Tomsk Governorate, and in Tyukalinsk and Ishim Districts, Tobolsk Governorate.

By the enactment of the Council of Ministers Highest Confirmed on 28 January 1917, it was decreed: on the basis of article 87 of the Fundamental State Laws (Digest of Laws, vol. I, part 1, 1906 edition), to supplement the enactment of the Council of Ministers Highest Confirmed on 20 October 1916 concerning the special procedure for the termination of ownership of allotment lands by German, Austrian and Hungarian immigrants in Kainsk District, Tomsk Governorate, and in Tyukalinsk and Ishim Districts, Tobolsk Governorate (Collection of Enactments, art. 2361), with the following articles:

31. Concerning the termination of ownership of the lands allotted to the communities and individual householders specified in article 1, the resettlement official or the local peasant affairs commissioner, as applicable, shall draw up special rulings setting forth the lawful grounds therefor; such rulings shall be announced to the communities concerned, and, in appropriate cases, to individual householders, with an indication of the procedure and time limit for appeal.

The rulings are announced before the commencement of the inventory and valuation of the property subject to seizure from the communities and householders (art. 4).

32. Against the rulings of resettlement officials and peasant affairs commissioners specified in article 31, as well as against their rulings refusing petitions of individual householders for exemption from the effect of the enactments restricting the landownership and land use of enemy immigrants, complaints may be lodged, through these officials, as applicable, within a two-week period from the date of announcement of such rulings, to the general presence of the provincial administration, which shall examine them out of turn.

33. Against the rulings of the general presence of the provincial administration (art. 32), within a thirty-day period from the date of their announcement, complaints may be lodged with the Governing Senate, through the First Department, in which they shall be scheduled for hearing out of turn and shall be finally resolved in accordance with the rules set forth in article 94 of the Statute on the Governing Senate (Digest of Laws, vol. I, part 2, 1915 edition).

The lodging of a complaint does not halt the further progress of the case, except in cases where the general presence of the provincial administration or the Governing Senate deems it necessary to suspend the case pending final resolution of the complaint.

*SURP. 1917. Part One. No. 37. P. 377—378.*

## No. 195. DECISION OF THE COUNCIL OF MINISTERS ON EXTENDING THE LIQUIDATION ENACTMENTS TO THE CORE REGIONS OF THE COUNTRY, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS II (1917)

207. On extending to certain localities of the Empire the effect of the enactments restricting the landownership and land use of enemy immigrants.

The Council of Ministers resolved:

On the basis of article 87 of the Fundamental State Laws (Digest of Laws, vol. I, part 1, 1906 edition):

I. To replace article 1 of the enactment of the Council of Ministers Highest Confirmed on 2 February 1915 concerning the termination of landownership and land use by Austrian, Hungarian or German immigrants in border localities (Collection of Enactments, art. 351), as set forth in the enactment of the Council of Ministers Highest Confirmed on 13 December 1915 (Collection of Enactments, art. 2749), with the following article:

1. Russian subjects who are German, Austrian or Hungarian immigrants are granted, within the time limit established by these rules, the right to alienate, by voluntary agreements, their immovable property located outside urban settlements in the Governorates of Petrograd, Novgorod, Pskov, Vitebsk, Estland, Livland, Courland, Kovno, Grodno, Vilna, Minsk, Suwałki, Łomża, Płock, Warsaw, Kalisz, Piotrków, Kielce, Radom, Lublin, Chełm, Kiev, Volhynia, Podolia, Bessarabia, Kherson, Taurida, Yekaterinoslav, Kharkov, Samara, Saratov, Orenburg and Ufa, in the Don Cossack Host region, in all localities of the Caucasus territory, of the Grand Duchy of Finland and of the Amur Governor-Generalship, in the Akmolinsk and Semipalatinsk regions, in the Aktyubinsk and Kustanai Districts of Turgai Region, in the Ishim and Tyukalinsk Districts of Tobolsk Governorate and in the Barnaul, Zmeinogorsk, Kainsk and Tomsk Districts of Tomsk Governorate, and also within the lands of the Astrakhan, Orenburg and Siberian Cossack Hosts.

Non-urban properties subject to the effect of these rules, not alienated within the time allowed for that purpose by voluntary agreements with persons entitled to acquire such properties, shall be sold at public auction.

Note. Until special directions are issued, the effect of this (1) article does not extend to the lands allotted from the treasury to the community of the Sarepta colony, Tsaritsyn District, Saratov Governorate.

II. In addition to the enactments specified in Section I, and also to the enactment of the Council of Ministers Highest Confirmed on 2 February 1915 concerning the landownership and land use of certain categories of Austrian, Hungarian or German immigrants who are Russian subjects (Collection of Enactments, art. 350) and the enactment of the Council of Ministers Highest Confirmed on 20 October 1916 establishing a special procedure for the termination of ownership of allotment lands by German, Austrian and Hungarian immigrants in Kainsk District, Tomsk Governorate, and in Tyukalinsk and Ishim Districts, Tobolsk Governorate (Collection of Enactments, art. 2361), it is decreed:

1. In the Governorates of Samara, Saratov, Orenburg and Ufa, in the Akmolinsk and Semipalatinsk regions, in the Aktyubinsk and Kustanai Districts of Turgai Region and the Barnaul, Zmeinogorsk and Tomsk Districts of Tomsk Governorate, and also within the lands of the Astrakhan, Orenburg and Siberian Cossack Hosts, the two-month period for the publication of the nominal lists of owners of property subject to alienation in these localities [enactments of the Council of Ministers Highest Confirmed on 2 February and 13 December 1915 (Collection of Enactments, arts. 351 and 2749), art. 5], as well as the time limits specified in article 6 of the same enactment and in articles 1 and 5 of Section I of Part B of the enactment of 13 December 1915 (Collection of Enactments, art. 2749), shall be computed from the date of promulgation of this decision;

2. With respect to the localities enumerated in article 1 of this (II) Section, the effect of article 6 of Section IV of the enactment of 2 February 1915 (Collection of Enactments, art. 349) and of article 8 of the same section, as set forth in the enactment of 13 December 1915 (Collection of Enactments, art. 2749), extends to the claims of personal creditors arising before 1 January 1916, as well as to mortgage and other real encumbrances and rights arising from contracts of hire, lease or timber-cutting established after that date;

3. In the Akmolinsk and Semipalatinsk regions, as well as in the Aktyubinsk and Kustanai Districts of Turgai Region and the Barnaul, Zmeinogorsk and Tomsk Districts of Tomsk Governorate, the termination of ownership by rural communities formed from German, Austrian or Hungarian immigrants and their descendants, and likewise the ownership of individual householders among persons falling under the enactments specified in Section I who settled on vacant resettlement plots or joined other local rural or settlement communities, of lands allotted on the basis of the Rules on Resettlement (Digest of Laws, vol. IX, special appendix, book VIII, per the 1912 Continuation), as well as of lands held by the aforementioned householders on the basis of articles 1—111 of the Statute on Siberian Peasants (same volume, book VI) and the appendix to article 14 of the same Statute, per the 1912 Continuation, shall be carried out in accordance with the rules set forth in the enactment of the Council of Ministers Highest Confirmed on 20 October 1916 establishing a special procedure for the termination of ownership of allotment lands by German, Austrian and Hungarian immigrants in Kainsk District, Tomsk Governorate, and in Tyukalinsk and Ishim Districts, Tobolsk Governorate (Collection of Enactments, art. 2361), subject to the following changes and additions to the said rules:

a) compensation to owners for the lands alienated from them shall be computed, in the Akmolinsk and Semipalatinsk regions and in the Aktyubinsk and Kustanai Districts of Turgai Region, as follows: for homestead and arable lands, and also for flooded meadows, at the rate calculated, in accordance with articles 354, 357—359 and 361 of the Statute on Direct Taxes, 1914 edition, of the quitrent tax assessment established in the relevant rural community for the year 1914, multiplied by two hundred fifty, and for the remaining usable lands—at half that rate. The same compensation in the Barnaul, Zmeinogorsk and Tomsk Districts of Tomsk Governorate shall be computed at the rate of: in the first—thirty rubles, in the second—thirty-two rubles, and in the third—twenty-eight rubles per desiatina;

b) the general presence of the regional administration is authorized, in the Akmolinsk and Semipalatinsk regions and in the Aktyubinsk and Kustanai Districts of Turgai Region, to raise or lower the valuation made on the basis of the preceding point (a) of this article, in accordance with local conditions: in rural communities whose lands lie not more than fifty versts from a railway or navigable river—within twenty-five percent, and in the remaining communities—within forty percent of the total sum of the land valuation for each rural community;

c) concerning the termination of ownership by communities and individual householders of the lands allotted to them, the resettlement official or the local peasant affairs commissioner, as applicable, shall draw up special rulings setting forth the lawful grounds therefor; such rulings shall be announced to the communities concerned, and, in appropriate cases, to individual householders, with an indication of the time limit and procedure for appeal.

The rulings are announced before the commencement of the inventory and valuation of property alienated from communities and householders;

d) against the rulings of resettlement officials and peasant affairs commissioners specified in point (c) of this (3) article, as well as against their rulings refusing petitions of individual householders for exemption from the effect of the enactments restricting the landownership and land use of enemy immigrants, complaints may be lodged, through these officials, as applicable, within a two-week period from the date of announcement of such rulings to the complainants, to the general presence of the regional administration (provincial administration), which shall examine them out of turn;

e) against the rulings of the general presence of the regional administration (provincial administration), within a thirty-day period from the date of their announcement, complaints may be lodged with the Governing Senate, through the First Department, in which they shall be scheduled for hearing out of turn and shall be finally resolved in accordance with the rules set forth in article 94 of the Statute on the Governing Senate (Digest of Laws, vol. I, part 2, 1915 edition).

The lodging of a complaint does not halt the further progress of the case, except in cases where the general presence itself or the Governing Senate deems it necessary to suspend the case pending final resolution of the complaint;

4. The effect of point 3 of article 3 of the enactment of 2 February 1915 (Collection of Enactments, art. 350) does not extend to the localities enumerated in article 1 of this (II) Section;

5. The effect of point 2 of article 19 of Section II, Part A, of the enactment of 13 December 1915 (Collection of Enactments, art. 2749) extends to the localities enumerated in article 1 of this (II) Section, if the price specified in the said point of article 19 is less than the sum owed to the mortgagee under a mortgage deed executed before 1 January 1916;

6. The effect of the rule provided for in the second part of point 4 of Section I, Part B, of the enactment of 13 December 1915 (Collection of Enactments, art. 2749) extends to the localities enumerated in article 1 of this (II) Section, if the mortgage deeds specified in the said rule were executed after 1 January 1916;

7. The rules of article 9 of Section I and article 2 of Section II, Part D, of the enactment of 13 December 1915 (Collection of Enactments, art. 2749) apply in the localities enumerated in article 1 of this (II) Section in cases where the mortgage deeds mentioned in the said articles were executed after 1 January 1916 or belonged, prior to the promulgation of this decision, to the persons specified in the same articles, and where claims secured by other kinds of property are based on obligations arising after 1 January 1916.

The Sovereign Emperor, on the 6th day of February 1917, was pleased to confirm the aforesaid enactment of the Council of Ministers as Highest Confirmed.

*SURP. 1917. Part One. No. 39. P. 397-400.*

Published in part: The History of Russian Germans in Documents (1763—1992). / Compiled by: V.A. Auman, V.G. Chebotareva. Moscow, 1993. P. 52—54.

## No. 196. DECISION OF THE COUNCIL OF MINISTERS ON EXTENDING THE 1915 LIQUIDATION ENACTMENTS TO STAVROPOL GOVERNORATE, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS II (1917)

212. On confirming and clarifying the meaning of the enactments of 2 February and 13 December 1915 restricting the landownership and land use of the enemy.

The Council of Ministers resolved:

On the basis of article 87 of the Fundamental State Laws (Digest of Laws, vol. I, part 1, 1906 edition), in confirmation and clarification of the meaning of the enactments of the Council of Ministers Highest Confirmed on 2 February and 13 December 1915 concerning the landownership and land use in the Russian State of Austrian, Hungarian, German or Turkish subjects (Collection of Enactments, art. 349) and concerning certain changes and additions to the enactments of 2 February 1915 on the landownership and land use of subjects of the powers at war with Russia, as well as of Austrian, Hungarian or German immigrants (Collection of Enactments, art. 2749), it is decreed:

Among the localities of the Caucasus territory to which the effect of the enactments of 2 February and 13 December 1915 (Collection of Enactments, arts. 349 and 2749) restricting the landownership and land use of enemy subjects and immigrants extends, is also included Stavropol Governorate, which was removed, on the basis of the opinion of the State Council Highest Confirmed on 10 May 1899 (Complete Collection of Laws, No. 16841), from the administration of the aforesaid territory and placed under the relevant ministries.

The Sovereign Emperor, on the 8th day of February 1917, was pleased to confirm the aforesaid enactment of the Council of Ministers as Highest Confirmed.

*SURP. 1917. Part One. No. 39. P. 404-405.*

## No. 197. DECISION OF THE COUNCIL OF MINISTERS CLARIFYING THE AMOUNT OF COMPENSATION FOR ALLOTMENT LAND, CONFIRMED BY NICHOLAS II (1917)

213. On the amount of compensation for allotment lands of enemy immigrants in Kainsk District, Tomsk Governorate.

The Council of Ministers resolved:

On the basis of article 87 of the Fundamental State Laws (Digest of Laws, vol. I, part 1, 1906 edition), to set forth the first part of article 2 of the enactment of the Council of Ministers Highest Confirmed on 20 October 1916 establishing a special procedure for the termination of ownership of allotment lands by German, Austrian and Hungarian immigrants in Kainsk District, Tomsk Governorate, and in Tyukalinsk and Ishim Districts, Tobolsk Governorate (Collection of Enactments, art. 2361), as follows:

"2. Compensation to owners for the lands specified in the preceding (1) article shall be computed at the rate of twenty rubles in Ishim District, twenty-one rubles in Tyukalinsk District, and twenty-three rubles in Kainsk District per desiatina, and for buildings and equipment—according to their actual value."

The Sovereign Emperor, on the 8th day of February 1917, was pleased to confirm the aforesaid enactment of the Council of Ministers as Highest Confirmed.

*SURP. 1917. Part One. No. 39. P. 405.*

## No. 198. RESOLUTION OF THE PROVISIONAL GOVERNMENT ON THE SUSPENSION OF ENFORCEMENT OF THE LIQUIDATION ENACTMENTS (1917)

367. On the suspension of enforcement of the enactments concerning the landownership and land use of Austrian, Hungarian and German immigrants.

**RESOLUTION**

**OF THE PROVISIONAL GOVERNMENT.**

On the suspension of enforcement of the enactments

concerning the landownership and land use of Austrian,

Hungarian and German immigrants.

The Provisional Government has resolved: to suspend the enforcement of the following enactments pending their review by the Constituent Assembly or through the legislative procedure established by it:

1. Of 2 February 1915—concerning the landownership and land use of certain categories of Austrian, Hungarian or German immigrants who are Russian subjects (Collection of Enactments, 1915, art. 350);

2. Of 2 February 1915—concerning the termination of landownership and land use by Austrian, Hungarian or German immigrants in border localities (Collection of Enactments, 1915, art. 351);

3. Of 13 December 1915—concerning certain changes and additions to the enactments of 2 February 1915 on the landownership and land use of subjects of the powers at war with Russia, as well as of Austrian, Hungarian or German immigrants: Parts B and C, and also Part D (with respect to immigrants) (Collection of Enactments, 1915, art. 2749);

4. Of 10 July 1916—concerning certain measures to support farming on colonist lands subject to liquidation (Collection of Enactments, 1916, art. 1685);

5. Of 15 July 1916—concerning the supplementing of article 4 of the law of 2 February 1916 [1915] on the termination of landownership and land use by Austrian, Hungarian and German immigrants in border localities (Collection of Enactments, 1916, art. 1713);

6. Of 19 August 1916—concerning the amendment, supplementation and clarification of the enactments of 13 December 1915 on certain changes and additions to the enactments of 2 February 1915 on the landownership and land use of subjects of the powers at war with Russia, as well as of Austrian, Hungarian or German immigrants: art. 1, as well as arts. 2, 3 and 4 (with respect to immigrants) of Section II (Collection of Enactments, 1916, art. 1867);

7. Of 19 August 1916—concerning certain changes and additions to the enactments of 2 February and 13 December 1915 on measures to reduce foreign landownership and land use in the Russian State (Collection of Enactments, 1916, art. 1869);

8. Of 8 September 1916—concerning the extension of the effect of the enactments of 2 February and 13 December 1915 restricting the landownership and land use of the enemy to Kharkov Governorate, as well as to Kainsk District, Tomsk Governorate, and Tyukalinsk and Ishim Districts, Tobolsk Governorate: Sections III and IV, and also Section V (with respect to immigrants) (Collection of Enactments, 1916, art. 1955);

9. Of 20 October 1916—concerning the establishment of a special procedure for the termination of ownership of allotment lands by German, Austrian and Hungarian immigrants in Kainsk District, Tomsk Governorate, and in Tyukalinsk and Ishim Districts, Tobolsk Governorate (Collection of Enactments, 1916, art. 2361);

10. Of 25 October 1916—concerning certain changes and additions to the enactments in force restricting the landownership and land use of the enemy: Parts A (with respect to immigrants) and B (Collection of Enactments, 1916, art. 2406);

11. Of 25 October 1916—concerning the procedure for the liquidation of industrial enterprises located on lands subject to alienation belonging to enemy subjects and immigrants (with respect to immigrants) (Collection of Enactments, 1916, art. 2407);

12. Of 28 January 1917—concerning the procedure for appealing rulings on the termination of ownership of allotment lands by German, Austrian and Hungarian immigrants in Kainsk District, Tomsk Governorate, and in Tyukalinsk and Ishim Districts, Tobolsk Governorate (Collection of Enactments, 1917, art. 196);

13. Of 6 February 1917—concerning the extension to certain localities of the enactments restricting the landownership and land use of enemy immigrants (Collection of Enactments, 1917, art. 207);

14. Of 8 February 1917—concerning the confirmation and clarification of the meaning of the enactments of 2 February and 13 December 1915 restricting the landownership and land use of the enemy (with respect to immigrants) (Collection of Enactments, 1917, art. 212);

15. Of 8 February 1917—concerning the amount of compensation for allotment lands of enemy immigrants in Kainsk District, Tomsk Governorate (Collection of Enactments, 1917, art. 213).

## No. 199. REPORT OF S. BAZAROV, HEAD OF THE CHANCELLERY FOR CIVIL ADMINISTRATION UNDER THE COMMANDER OF THE SOUTHWESTERN FRONT, ON THE EXPULSION OF GERMAN COLONISTS (AUGUST 29, 1917)

## No. 1521.

Since the transfer of matters concerning colonists to the jurisdiction of the Civil Chancellery (from August 4, 1917), approximately 500 petitions (as of October 15) have been received from colonists requesting permission to reside in their colonies, with half of the petitioners having already returned without authorization, citing the Provisional Government's abolition of all national and religious [restrictions] and the pardon of all those administratively exiled.

In most cases these are petitions from persons whose fathers, husbands, or brothers are serving in the active army.

According to the journal of the Special Conference of June 23, 1915, on measures to be taken when troops clear certain localities of the Northern and Southwestern fronts, all German colonists without exception were subject to obligatory expulsion from the state border and further eastward.

But with the permission of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Commander, exemptions were allowed for: 1) the wives, children, and mothers of colonists serving in the active army; 2) the wives, widows, widowed mothers, orphaned children, and unmarried sisters of persons killed or deceased in the war or who have lost their capacity to work due to wounds and injuries; 3) fathers (over 60 years of age) of officers and soldiers serving in the active army; and 4) participants in the Turkish and other past campaigns who hold decorations of the Military Order and combat medals.

In addition, in response to individual petitions not covered by the above exemptions, permission was granted not to expel Mennonite colonists of Dutch, Danish, and Swiss origin, provided their loyalty was confirmed.

Furthermore, according to a clarification by the Commander-in-Chief of the armies of the Southwestern Front, in cases where the fathers and mothers of German colonists who were Russian subjects were permitted to remain, their grandfathers and grandmothers could likewise be permitted to remain, as could cripples, deaf-mutes, and the blind (upon confirmation by medical examination and with the permission of the governors).

But on October 20, 1915, following a telegram from the commander of the 8th Army, in view of the established, undoubtedly harmful activity of German colonists residing in the army's district — manifested in the damage of telegraph wires and espionage in favor of the enemy — the Commander-in-Chief of the armies of the Southwestern Front, with the consent of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Commander, ordered the expulsion of all German colonists from the district of Volhynia Governorate.

In actual practice the principle of wholesale expulsion of German colonists was not carried out in full, and in individual cases the Commander-in-Chief found it possible to permit certain colonists to remain in place — those whose sons were serving in the active army, had been wounded or killed — as well as elderly men who had served in the ranks of the army in past wars.

Taking into account that, according to the resolution of the Provisional Government of March 19, 1917, army commanders are authorized to order the removal from the theater of military operations only of persons of certain specified categories, namely: a) persons suspected of military espionage or of assisting enemy forces; b) persons agitating for the conclusion of a separate peace; c) persons secretly trading in spirits; and d) persons engaged in prostitution — and bearing in mind also that German colonists can be harmful only while located within the area occupied by the armies, it would seem just, in reviewing the petitions of colonists, to be guided by the following rules:

For each petition, a certificate is to be submitted to you, treating each individual case with particular caution, ascertaining through investigation by the provincial commissioner the undoubted loyalty of the petitioner, and also verifying through counterintelligence the absence in their past of any indications of espionage.

On the certificate I request permission to record my conclusion, being guided by the rule of allowing return to the area no closer than a 100-verst zone from the front for the families of those petitioners whose fathers, husbands, brothers, sons, and grandsons served or are serving in the active army, or were participants in the Turkish or previous campaigns, as well as for Mennonite colonists of Dutch, Danish, and Swiss origin.

All others are to be refused permission to return, and those who have returned without authorization are to be ordered to depart, by a stated deadline, eastward from the line of the Dnieper River.

I report the foregoing.

Signed: Active State Councillor                       Bazarov

Certified: Clerk, Provincial Secretary                Stegoshuk

Resolution: Agreed. Lieutenant General                  Volodchenko.

*RGVIA. Fond 2005. Inv. 1. File 28. Fol. 335—336. Certified copy.*

## No. 200. N.G. VOLODCHENKO, COMMANDER OF THE SOUTHWESTERN FRONT, TO SUPREME COMMANDER A.F. KERENSKY, ON THE EXPELLED GERMAN COLONISTS (OCTOBER 1, 1917)

## No. 1660.

According to the journal of the Special Conference of June 23, 1915, on measures to be taken when troops clear certain localities of the Northern and Southwestern fronts, all German colonists without exception were subject to obligatory expulsion from the state border and further eastward.

With the permission of the former Chief of Staff of the Supreme Commander, certain exemptions from this rule were allowed.

On October 20, 1915, following a telegram from the commander of the 8th Army, in view of the established, undoubtedly harmful activity of German colonists residing in the army's district, the Commander-in-Chief of the armies of the Southwestern Front, with the consent of the former Chief of Staff of the Supreme Commander, ordered the expulsion of all German colonists from the district of Volhynia Governorate.

Since the spring of this year the expelled colonists have begun returning to their colonies without authorization, at first in isolated cases, but at present their return movement has assumed a mass character.

Meanwhile their immovable property has been placed under sequestration and transferred to the jurisdiction of the Administration of Agriculture and State Properties, while refugees from Galicia and from the localities of Volhynia Governorate occupied by the enemy have been settled on their farmsteads; the unauthorized return of colonists to their farmsteads, now occupied by refugees, is therefore fraught with a whole series of serious complications threatening to become extremely acute, all the more so since the local native population is also hostile toward the Germans.

Both the former Commander-in-Chief, General Brusilov, and I myself, in view of these circumstances, have issued orders prohibiting the unauthorized return of colonists. As for those who have returned without permission, I propose to send them back eastward from the Dnieper River.

In reporting the foregoing, I request instructions as to where and by what means the colonists who are returning without authorization should be sent, and I consider it advisable to transport them by rail rather than by cart, since the latter method of expulsion is at present difficult to carry out.

Lieutenant General Volodchenko

Head of the Civil Chancellery, Active State Councillor S. Bazarov

*RGVIA. Fond 2005. Inv. 1. File 28. Fol. 323–323 verso. Original.*

## REFERENCE MATERIALS

## NOTES

### No. 1.

The first separate settlement of foreigners in Moscow appeared beyond the Yauza River in the second half of the 16th century. This Foreign, or German, Sloboda was burned in 1610 by the troops of False Dmitry II. After this, émigrés from Western Europe, a large proportion of them German, began to settle within the city itself; however, the Law Code (Sobornoye Ulozheniye) of 1649 forbade them to purchase houses within the Zemlyanoy Val (Earthen Rampart), that is, directly within the territory of Moscow at that time. In accordance with this decree of Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich, foreigners were resettled outside the city limits, on the site of the former German Sloboda. This settlement received the name of the New Foreign, New German, or simply German Sloboda. See: Kovrigina V.A. The German Sloboda of Moscow and Its Inhabitants at the End of the 17th — First Quarter of the 18th Century. Moscow, 1998. Pp. 25—28.

### No. 2.

During the Petrine period many German specialists in mining and metallurgy arrived in Russia. One of the first and most famous among them was Ivan Ivanovich (Johann Friedrich) Blüher, a mining master from Freiberg (Saxony), who was in Russian service from 1699 to 1728. In 1703 he founded the Petrovsky cast-iron and cannon works in Karelia, which gave rise to the town of Petrozavodsk; he subsequently worked on the construction of mining works in the Urals and the search for ore deposits in the south of Russia and the Caucasus. See: Zablotsky E. Mining // Germans of Russia: An Encyclopedia. Vol. 1. Moscow, 1999. P. 603; Korepanov N. Blüher // Ibid. Pp. 216—217.

Poppe, Matvei Lavrentyevich (Hans Matthias) (?—1711) — a Hamburg merchant, settled in Moscow in 1682, had a household there, and carried out various commissions for the Russian tsars, including the recruitment of foreign specialists.

### No. 3.

This manifesto is the most important state act on attracting foreigners to Russia adopted in the pre-Catherinian period. Its initiator is considered to be the Livonian nobleman Johann Reinhold von Patkul (1660—1707), a fierce opponent of Swedish rule in the Baltic region, who entered Russian service in 1702. After the severe defeat by the Swedes at Narva (1700), it was not difficult for him to persuade Peter I of the advisability of broadly attracting foreign specialists to Russia, above all in military affairs. The formation, provided for in Article 3 of the manifesto, of a special Secret Military Collegium composed of foreigners is an unprecedented phenomenon in the history of modern law, dictated by the urgent need to create a modern army in the country as quickly as possible. The manifesto was published in the West, above all in the German lands, and had great resonance, causing a powerful influx into Russia of specialists from various fields. See: Fleischhauer I. Die Deutschen im Zarenreich: Zwei Jahrhunderte deutsch-russische Kulturgemeinschaft. Stuttgart, 1991. Pp. 43—46.

### No. 4.

The charter was adopted after Russia's conquest of Livonia (1710) during the Great Northern War of 1700—1721.

Sigismund II Augustus (1520—1572) — King of Poland, participant in the Livonian War of 1558—1583, in the course of which (1561) he subordinated Livonia to Poland, guaranteeing the Livonian nobility the preservation of their rights and privileges.

Löwenwolde (Löwenwald), Gerhard Johann von (?—1723) — in Russian service from 1708; after the capitulation of Riga (1710) he was appointed Russian plenipotentiary in Livonia.

### No. 5.

The charter was adopted after Russia's conquest of Estland (1710) during the Great Northern War of 1700—1721.

Ungern-Sternberg, Reinhold (Reno) von (1656—1713) — Landrat (leader of the nobility) of Estland, president of the Landrat collegium. Bistram, Bengt Heinrich von (1667—1724) — Landrat of Estland. They formed the deputation of the Estland knighthood that received this charter of grant in St. Petersburg.

### No. 6.

The systematic development of mining in Russia began in the 18th century. Peter I extensively recruited foreign specialists for this purpose, above all from Saxony. Especially many of them arrived in the early 1720s, after the issuance of this manifesto.

Thus, in 1723 an entire group of 12 mining and smelting masters was sent to the Urals, having signed a contract to enter Russian service: A.G. Brandt, the brothers I.F. and I.Kh. Weidel, F.K. Kaiser, I.Kh. Leigsenring, I.G. Ostwurmann, I.Kh. Uhlspiegel, E.Kh. Schell, and others. See: Korepanov N. Weidel // Germans of Russia: An Encyclopedia. Vol. 1. P. 325; idem, Kaiser, Leigsenring, Ostwurmann // Ibid. Vol. 2. Moscow, 2004. Pp. 53–54, 292–293, 732.

### No. 7.

This concerns the oldest St. Petersburg Evangelical Lutheran church of St. Peter, founded almost simultaneously with the city itself, in 1704. The first church of this parish was built by Vice Admiral C. Cruys, a comrade-in-arms of Peter I, at his own expense and on his own land, in the settlement of foreigners near the Admiralty (see: Fleischhauer I. Op. cit. P. 55). The new Church of St. Peter was built, in accordance with this decree, along the "great perspective road" (the future Nevsky Prospekt). Its design was drawn up by the patron of the St. Peter's community, Kh.A. Münnich (see the Biographical Commentary); the church was consecrated in 1730. In 1833—1838 a new building of the Church of St. Peter was erected on this site to the design of the architect A.P. Bryullov (1798—1877) — the largest Evangelical Lutheran church by capacity in Russia.

Osterman, A.I. — at that time Vice-Chancellor, member of the Supreme Privy Council, and Ober-Hofmeister (tutor) of Emperor Peter II (see the Biographical Commentary).

### No. 8.

Contrary to the widespread notion of "German domination" under Empress Anna Ivanovna, during her reign there were, among the army's general officers, 68 Russians for every 10 Germans (see: Nelipovich S.G. Germans in Russian Military Service: A Historical and Historiographical Phenomenon // Germans of Russia in the Context of National History: General Problems and Regional Peculiarities. Moscow, 1999. P. 244). Peter I had brought far more European, including German, military specialists into Russia. This decree came about because by the time of Anna Ivanovna's accession to the throne most of them had already left Russian service.

Münnich, Kh.A. — at that time General-Feldzeugmeister, president of the Military Collegium, member of the Cabinet (see the Biographical Commentary).

### No. 9.

This act attests that the idea of inviting foreigners to Russia, actively pursued by Peter I, gained new impetus during the reign of his daughter, Elizabeth Petrovna. In time she went even further than Peter in her plans, intending to broadly attract European colonists to develop the country's vast, sparsely populated territories. The realization of these intentions was hindered by the Seven Years' War of 1756—1763, and they began to be implemented only after its conclusion, during the reign of Catherine II. A similar solemn oath to Catherine and to the heir to the throne, Paul Petrovich, introduced in 1763, was not confirmed by the highest organs of power, and is therefore absent from the Complete Collection of Laws of the Russian Empire. See: Pleve I.R. German Colonies on the Volga in the Second Half of the 18th Century. Moscow, 1998. Pp. 51—56, 104—105.

### No. 10.

In the 17th and early 18th centuries, in the German Sloboda, as everywhere else in Moscow, it was customary to bury the dead near churches. Empress Elizabeth Petrovna, who protected herself from reminders of death, forbade burials along the streets through which her carriage usually passed. This ban also affected the cemeteries near the churches of the German Sloboda, which were restored by this decree of Peter III, Elizabeth's successor. The present-day Vvedenskoye (German) Cemetery in Lefortovo arose after the plague epidemic of 1771, when Catherine II required that the dead be buried only outside the city limits. The remains from the destroyed churchyards of the German Sloboda's churches were transferred to this cemetery. See: Miklashevskaya E.P., Tseplyaeva M.S. Famous Germans of Lefortovo. History in Faces. Moscow, 2000. Pp. 197—198.

Minau, Karl Gottfried (1720—1775) — a native of Riga, pastor of the Church of Sts. Peter and Paul in Moscow from 1754 to 1775.

No. 11

This act was preceded by the manifesto of Catherine II permitting foreigners to settle in Russia, of December 4, 1762 (for the text see: German Colonists in the Age of Catherine / Comp.: E.E. Lykova, M.I. Osekina. Moscow, 2004. Pp. 10—11). Unlike the present manifesto, it was general in character and had no direct consequences.

It is difficult to find an analogue in history to the present manifesto, either in the scale of its conception or in the list of privileges promised to future settlers. Hence the unprecedented influx of colonists — more than 30,000 in just a few years. However, many of the manifesto's promises were never fulfilled. The most damaging consequences stemmed from the irresponsible assurances that in Russia a use would be found for settlers of the most diverse occupations, and that they would be free to choose their place of residence (Art. 1, 4, 6, para. 3). In reality, the overwhelming majority of settlers — among whom were people of all manner of professions who had believed Catherine's promises — were forced to take up agriculture in the arid steppes of the Volga region, where even experienced German peasants managed to establish themselves only decades later. Entirely unfamiliar conditions of life and labor, lack of proper arrangements, frequent raids by nomads, the ruin of the newly formed colonies during the rebellion of Ye.I. Pugachev, and the arbitrariness of recruiting agents and tsarist officials — this is far from a complete list of the causes that ultimately resulted in high mortality among the first Volga colonists. This is documented by the absolute decline in population between 1773 and 1788 in a whole series of colonies in the Volga region (see: Dizendorf V.F. Ten Years in "Renaissance." Moscow, 2000. Pp. 589—592).

The lack of forethought, and in many respects the reckless adventurism, of Catherine's colonization plans is vividly illustrated by the register of lands, allegedly set aside for settlement, appended to the manifesto. On one point it coincided with reality: many colonies did indeed form in the areas of the left bank of the Volga indicated here in paragraph 3. However, beyond that, the register names the Baraba steppes, the Ust-Kamenogorsk district, and the Orenburg region (paragraphs 1, 2, 4), where German settlements arose only at the end of the 19th century, as well as Valuysky Uyezd of Belgorod Governorate (paragraph 5), where they never appeared at all. On the other hand, the register is silent about the possibility of settling the first colonists on the right bank of the Volga, in Livonia, near St. Petersburg, Chernigov, and Voronezh, as actually occurred.

The permission granted in the manifesto (Art. 6, para. 1) for colonists to build churches with bell towers was of fundamental significance: at that time in Europe, having a bell tower meant that the church that built it possessed public rights; churches that did not have public rights had to locate their prayer houses in inner courtyards and could not equip them with bell towers. See: Suttner E. Catholics (German-speaking) in the Russian Empire and the USSR // Germans of Russia: An Encyclopedia. Vol. 2. P. 38.

The manifesto was translated into a number of languages and distributed in many European countries, but it was primarily the inhabitants of the German lands, ruined by the Seven Years' War of 1756—1763 and traditionally having closer ties with Russia, who responded to it.

### No. 12.

This decree is the first in an entire series of acts regulating the settlement and residence in Russia of members of the relatively small but influential Evangelical Brotherhood of the Augsburg (in this document, "Augustan") Confession. The Brotherhood, whose origins go back to the community of Czech (Bohemian, Moravian) Brethren that arose in the mid-15th century, established itself in Germany from the 18th century, with its center in the settlement of Herrnhut ("The Lord's Watch") near Dresden. Hence the most common name and self-designation of members of the Brotherhood — "Herrnhuters." See: Beznosova O. Herrnhuters // Germans of Russia: An Encyclopedia. Vol. 1. Pp. 537—538.

In the present act, unlike subsequent ones, the Herrnhuters were not granted special privileges compared to the other colonists. They were permitted only to give in court an oath consisting of a single affirmative statement. This was fundamentally important to the Herrnhuters: rejecting state service and the interference of the authorities in the affairs of their community, they considered the standard text of the judicial oath unacceptable for themselves.

The manifesto of July 22, 1763 — Doc. No. 11.

### No. 13.

Whereas the manifesto of Catherine II of July 22, 1763 (Doc. No. 11) was mainly declaratory and propagandistic in character, the present act regulated all the principal aspects of the actual process of establishing the first colonies and the system of landownership and land use among the colonists. For this reason it is often called the "agrarian law" of the colonies in the literature. It is notable that it quite candidly acknowledges the unsoundness of the register of lands appended to Catherine's manifesto (see note to Doc. No. 11). Although the document pertains to the Volga region, its key provisions were applied in the establishment of colonies in other regions as well, and were subsequently incorporated into the unified Statute on Colonies of 1857 (Doc. No. 115).

It was precisely in the Volga region that perhaps the most important points of the document found practically no application — namely, the household-based form of land use provided for in Articles 3 and 4, combined with the system of minorat (the transfer of the entire allotment by inheritance to the youngest son in the family). After Catherine II abolished the special administrative bodies governing the colonies in 1782, the Volga colonists came under the jurisdiction of the Saratov Chamber of State Domains, which replaced this form with the familiar system of per-capita (soul-based) land use.

Perhaps, at that time, this innovation, as is argued in the literature (see: Pleve I.R. Op. cit. P. 281), did make it possible, to some extent, to resolve the increasingly acute land problems of the colonies. However, in the long run the preservation of this arbitrarily established system undoubtedly played a negative role, leading to the rapid fragmentation of the allotments of colonists with large families, and moreover substantially hindering the socio-economic development of the Volga colonies. In these respects the Germans of the Volga region found themselves in a much worse position than colonists of other regions, where there was no per-capita land use. These consequences of the per-capita system could hardly have come as a surprise to the Russian authorities who introduced it: the same phenomena had long been observed in the Russian peasant commune (the "mir"), built on analogous principles.

It is noteworthy that Paul I, having abolished in 1797 the subordination of the colonies to the Saratov authorities, did not abolish the per-capita system introduced by them (perhaps out of fear that, under the conditions then prevailing, this might further aggravate the already dire situation of the colonists, who had already endured no small number of administrative innovations), but neither did he officially sanction it. As a result, having existed for more than a hundred years, it left no trace in colonial legislation, including in the Statute on Colonies of 1857.

The manifesto of July 22 — Doc. No. 11.

### No. 14.

This document is the first in our book to mention hired recruiters of the first colonists — the *vyzyvateli* (recruiting agents). In the 1760s the Russian government made extensive use of these foreign (mainly French) entrepreneurs to attract settlers, hoping thereby to save money, time, and effort. These calculations did not pay off: the activity of the *vyzyvateli* proved very costly to the treasury, provoking strong displeasure both among the governments of the European countries where the *vyzyvateli* were recruiting settlers and among the Russian authorities and the recruited colonists themselves. The colonies established in the Volga region by *vyzyvateli* ended up in the most dire situation and lagged in their development even decades later. Subsequently *vyzyvateli* were no longer used for recruiting colonists (the foreign commissioners later engaged for settling colonists in southern Russia possessed nowhere near the powers that the first *vyzyvateli* had). See: Pleve I.R. Op. cit. Pp. 77–94.

The present act gives a general picture of the conditions under which the *vyzyvateli* operated. The foreigners named in it, L. Benetaul and Docourt of Alsace ("Belefort" being the Alsatian city of Belfort), appear to be one and the same person. Bene Paul Dacourt (Docourt) is also mentioned in doc. No. 15 and in the report of G.G. Orlov to Catherine II of 3 October 1764 (see: German Colonists in the Age of Catherine. Pp. 62–63), while Benetaul does not appear in any other known document about colonists. Docourt, too, in the end never became a *vyzyvatel'*.

### No. 15.

This document details the terms of the agreements between the Russian government and foreign *vyzyvateli* of colonists, briefly set out in doc. No. 14. J. Debofe (Deboff, de Boffe) and M. Deprécourt (de Précourt), who settled colonists on the right bank of the Volga, belonged to the same company of *vyzyvateli*. Also belonging to it was Quentin Benjamin Coulet Dauterive (de Térive), who appears in this act under the names Quentinius, Benjamin, Coulnette, Dauterive.

### No. 16.

The most complete and reliable reference work on the history of the evangelical churches in Russia (Amburger E. Die Pastoren der evangelischen Kirchen Rußlands vom Ende des 16. Jahrhunderts bis 1937: ein biographisches Lexikon. Lüneburg, Erlangen, 1998) provides information on 10 evangelical pastors who headed parishes in the German colonies of Russia in the 1760s. Seven of them served in the Volga region — Johannes Janett (Ust-Zalikha), Ludwig Helm (Podstepnoye), Georg Christian Seyer (Talovka), Christian August Tornow (Lesnoy Karamysh), Ludwig Balthasar Wernborner (South Yekaterinenstadt), Johann Georg Herwig (North Yekaterinenstadt, Norka); three served outside it: Friedrich Asmus (the Voronezh colony of Riebensdorf), Georg Jakob Bobrik (the colony of Novosaratovka near St. Petersburg), Johann Wilhelm Schreiber (the Belovezh colonies near Chernigov). Herwig was the only one among them a pastor of the Reformed (Calvinist) confession; the rest were Lutherans. Janett was a native of Switzerland; the origins of Seyer and Asmus have not been established; the other seven pastors were natives of Germany. Only Tornow had been living in Russia since 1762, even before his service in the colonies. The others came to Russia specifically to become colonist pastors, and Helm (and possibly also Seyer and Asmus) arrived together with the colonists. There is also information that Wernborner arrived together with the colonists (see: Dietz Ya.E. History of the Volga German Colonists. Moscow, 1997. P. 61). His fate was tragic: having taken up his post in Yekaterinenstadt in 1768, in 1774 he led the pursuit of nomads (Kirghiz-Kaisaks) who had carried out another raid on the colonies, and was brutally killed by them. (Ibid. Pp. 114–115.)

Information about the first Catholic priests in the colonies is more fragmentary. The best-known reference work on the history of the religious life of the Russian-German Catholics (Schnurr J. Die Kirchen und das religiöse Leben der Russlanddeutschen. Katholischer Teil. Stuttgart, 1980) names only one priest heading a colonist parish in the 1760s — Johannes Müller (Kamenka, Volga region). According to other information, the first Catholic priests in the Volga colonies included the German and Czech Franciscan monks E. Müller, M. Trenker, A. Fuchs (probably referring to Leonhard Fuchs), as well as the Capuchin Corbinianus (see: Litsenberger O.A. The Roman Catholic Church in Russia: History and Legal Status. Saratov, 2001. Pp. 60–61). The latter arrived in Russia together with the colonists, performing rites along the way for both Catholics and Protestants (see: Dietz Ya.E. Op. cit. P. 61).

### No. 17.

The Herrnhuters were the only ones among the first colonists to take advantage of the opportunity, promised in Article 10 of Catherine II's manifesto of 22 July 1763 (doc. No. 11), to secure additional rights for themselves. It is clear that a major role in this was played by their energetic and enterprising agent and first preacher in St. Petersburg in 1765–1766, P.K. Friese (1721–1783), mentioned in the present act. Less clear are the reasons for the unprecedented favor shown by the Russian monarchs toward the Herrnhuters from the very outset and throughout an entire century: their special privileges were successively guaranteed by Catherine II (PSZRI. Coll. 1. No. 12852), Paul I (doc. No. 29), Alexander I (PSZRI. Coll. 1. No. 20013; doc. No. 70), and Nicholas I (PSZRI. Coll. 2. No. 611) (for the texts of these charters see: Sarepta / Compiled by I.R. Pleve. Saratov, 1995. Pp. 67–85).

The only Herrnhuter colony in Russia was Sarepta (later part of Tsaritsyn Uyezd, Saratov Governorate), whose settlement rules are set out in this document. It, of course, stood out sharply among the Volga colonies — if only because its inhabitants engaged not so much in agriculture (this was the principal task of the Sarepta farmstead of Schönbrunn) as in various crafts and even industries. Sarepta was the birthplace of the famous *sarpinka* — a fine cotton fabric whose production became widespread in the 19th century in the colonies of the right-bank Volga region. Sarepta mustard became famous throughout Russia. Sarepta had flour-milling, cloth-making, tobacco, candle-making, soap-making, confectionery, brewing, and other industries. Sarepta's schools were distinguished by a level of instruction high for the time; two academicians of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences at once came from Sarepta — the chemist-technologist I.Kh. Hamel (see Biographical Notes) and the orientalist Ya.I. Schmidt (1781–1847).

Nevertheless, one cannot speak of a steady, progressive development of Sarepta. Its population, comparable at first to that of other German colonies of the Volga region, subsequently grew much more slowly: 194 (1774), 384 (1843), 510 (1882). In later years growth was more noticeable, but it was driven not by Herrnhuters but by Lutheran colonists and people of other nationalities settling alongside them. Population growth and the development of Sarepta in general were hindered by a variety of factors: low birth rate, very high mortality due to unfavorable natural and climatic conditions, frequent destructive fires, the systematic departure of Sarepta residents to Herrnhut and other places for missionary work, which the Herrnhuters considered the chief business of their lives (in Sarepta itself and its surroundings there were practically no opportunities for missionary activity), the collective ownership established in the Herrnhuter community of the principal means of production and real property, the increasingly perceptible isolation from the surrounding world due to the religious separateness of the Herrnhuters, and so forth.

### No. 18.

The creation of German colonies in the environs of St. Petersburg (Ingria) was pure improvisation on the part of the Russian authorities — at first they intended neither to establish settlements in these places nor to settle colonists on private lands at all. The decision on this was made at a moment when the various and difficult-to-resolve problems connected with the simultaneous transport of thousands of colonists from St. Petersburg to the distant Volga region, and with providing them there with crown lands and everything necessary for life, had already become clear. On the other hand, the future colonists, having made the long, difficult journey to Oranienbaum, readily agreed to settle in Ingria. There is no doubt that far more of them would have remained here had there been enough free fertile land in these places and, of course, had the Russian authorities not obstructed this, stubbornly pursuing their original goal — to develop, by the hands of the colonists, the vast sparsely populated territories on the southern outskirts of the country. For these reasons the St. Petersburg colonies did not subsequently see any particular development. On the other hand, the settlement of foreigners on private lands became a widespread practice in the 19th century.

### No. 19.

The Livland colonies resulted from improvisation by the Russian authorities in exactly the same way as the St. Petersburg ones (see note to doc. No. 18). Aside from the settlement in Courland in 1904–1914 of about 5,000 colonists from Volhynia, from southern Russia, and from Germany (see: Katin-Yartsev M. Baltic Germans // Germans of Russia: Encyclopedia. Vol. 1. P. 102), Hirschenhof and Helfreichshof remained the only German colonies in the Baltic governorates. They formed a separate Hirschenhof volost in Wenden Uyezd (later Kreuzburg Uyezd) of Livland Governorate. The limited land resources hindered the development of these colonies: in 1897, 2,534 people lived in Hirschenhof — far fewer than in the large colonies of the Volga region.

Browne, George (1698–1792) — a Baltic-German nobleman, a native of Ireland, in Russian service from 1730, a full general, Governor-General of Livland in 1762–1775; in his second marriage he was wed to a Baltic-German woman, and over time his family became Germanized.

### No. 20.

The present act displays the evident duplicity characteristic of many documents about colonists from the period of Catherine II. Thus G.G. Orlov writes of "very burdensome debts" for the colonists arising from their uneconomical use of subsistence money, while Catherine, in her resolution, writes that the colonists should be supplied with both food and "everything necessary" for setting up their households "without excess."

In reality the position of the Russian authorities on these questions was far from unambiguous. Subsistence money was classified as a non-repayable expenditure — subsequently colonists were required to repay it only upon leaving Russia or moving to another social estate (see docs. No. 47 and 62). Therefore there simply could have been no particular concern on their part about "burdensome debts" in this case. Only the authorities had a direct interest in economizing on these funds, as is evident from the document.

By contrast, expenditures on setting up households, according to Article 6, point 4 of Catherine II's manifesto of 22 July 1763 (doc. No. 11), were repayable, and here the authorities indulged in quite evident "excesses" in the Volga colonies — at least at first. They issued colonists very large monetary loans, the colonists fell into debt bondage, and as a result the return of the great majority of them to their homeland became practically impossible. See: Pleve I.R. Op. cit. P. 136.

### No. 21.

This was the first act to speak of the creation of colonies near Chernigov, although there is evidence that agitation among potential settlers in this direction was carried out even before its issuance (see: Pleve I.R. Op. cit. P. 107). Nevertheless, the reception of the colonists was poorly prepared: the settlers were sent from St. Petersburg in January 1767, while construction of houses for them on site began only in 1768. Hence the not-infrequent cases of flight by Chernigov colonists in the first period. See: Brandes D., Pleve I. The Belovezh Colonies // Germans of Russia: Encyclopedia. Vol. 1. P. 155.

In all, seven colonies were founded here. Six of them — Belye Vezhi, Gross-Werder, Gorodok, Kalchinovka, Klein-Werder, Rundewiese (in the Russified form Rundeviziya) — were located close to one another and formed the Belovezh district, and in time became part of the separate Kalchinovka volost of Borzna Uyezd, Chernigov Governorate. One more colony — Kreshchatik (Chrishchatik) — was located further east, in Romny Uyezd, Poltava Governorate. Gross-Werder and Klein-Werder were Catholic colonies, the rest Lutheran. The colonies were fairly small: the largest of them, Rundewiese, numbered 1,011 inhabitants in 1897, including 925 Germans.

### No. 22.

By the time this act was adopted it had become finally clear to the Russian authorities that the settling-in of the tens of thousands of colonists who had already arrived would require much time and resources, and the reception of new settlers was prudently postponed to better times. Over the remaining 30 years of Catherine II's reign, those better times practically never came. Only in the last years of Catherine's reign was a small number of new colonists settled in southern Russia.

It did not prove possible to stop the reception of settlers immediately at the end of 1766 — the contract with the *vyzyvatel'* Beauregard had been concluded through 1768, and he, in defiance of the prohibition, sent another 100 families to Russia. In addition, the Chancellery for the Guardianship of Foreigners continued to accept settlers who presented themselves in St. Petersburg on their own. See: Dietz Ya.E. Op. cit. Pp. 55–56.

Information in the literature on Baron Cano de Beauregard, the largest *vyzyvatel'* of Volga colonists, is quite contradictory, and there is not even consistent data on his origin. Most likely he was French — there is a known locality called Beauregard near Paris.

The manifesto of 1763 — doc. No. 11.

### No. 23.

This was the first act in which Catherine II attempted to assess the situation of the colonists in the Volga region, although more than 10 years had already passed since their settlement there began. The assessment turned out to be entirely banal and typical of many who hold power: the whole blame for the plight of the subjects was placed on themselves. This condescending document contains not even an attempt to analyze state policy toward the Volga colonists or the objective reasons for their unenviable situation. Only "disturbances that occurred in those places" (Art. 5) are mentioned — a vague allusion either to the Pugachev rebellion or to the frequent nomad raids on the colonies. Also banal and offering little prospect are the remedies Catherine prescribed for correcting the situation. Among them one can note perhaps only the provision, in Articles 2 and 3, for identifying colonists "unfit for farming" and removing them from the colonies — an involuntary admission of the flawed nature of the policy of the Russian authorities, who had recruited, for what was almost exclusively peasant labor, people of the most varied occupations, some very far removed from agriculture. On the practical implementation of these measures see: Pleve I.R. Op. cit. Pp. 266–267.

The manifesto of 22 July 1763 — doc. No. 11.

### No. 24.

This decree is devoted to the famous Petrischule — the first evangelical parish school in St. Petersburg (founded in 1709), created under the city's oldest Evangelical Lutheran church, St. Peter's. The pastor of St. Peter's Church, who according to this decree was included in a special board overseeing all German schools in Russia, was, in 1783–1813, Johann Georg Lampe (1749–1813). Another member of this board mentioned in the decree was Christopher Sergeyevich (Burkhard Christoph) Münnich (1747–1824), grandson of Kh.A. Münnich (see Biographical Notes).

A great contribution to the establishment of the Petrischule was made by Johann Philipp Weisse (1753–1840), a native of Reval, director of the school in 1790–1818. Among those who studied at the school were such notable figures as the chemist F.F. Beilstein, the orientalist O.N. Böhtlingk, the polar explorer L.L. Breitfuss, the educator K.I. May, the physician K.A. Raukhfus, the sculptors R.R. Bach and G.R. Zaleman, the architects L.L. Bohnstedt, A.I. Krakau, M.E. Messmacher, K.A. Ton, and V.A. Schröter; the outstanding physicist E.Kh. Lenz taught here, and one of the school's directors was the prominent historian and educator F.K. Lorenz (see Biographical Notes). At the beginning of the 20th century the Petrischule was the largest school in Russia. See: Ulyanov N.P. The Petrischule — St. Petersburg's Oldest School // Germans and the Development of Education in Russia. St. Petersburg, 1998. Pp. 129–137.

### No. 25.

Ten years after the decree of 1775 (doc. No. 23), Catherine II again turned her attention to the Volga colonists. This was her last address to this category of subjects, although she was to reign for more than 11 more years, and throughout that time the situation of the tens of thousands of people whom she herself had drawn into the country remained dire. Despite the title of the decree, only 3 of its 15 articles are actually devoted to the colonists. Of these, two deal with the collection of the colonist debt, and only one (Art. 3) addresses a problem whose solution might somehow have eased the difficult lot of the first Volga colonists. True, the provision made here for allocating new land to them, should the land they had "upon inspection" prove "unsuitable for farming and husbandry," looks rather strange given that this concerned land that had been allotted two decades earlier and whose quality had long been known to anyone interested.

A partial explanation for this oddity may be the fact that the inspection of the land was to be carried out by the relatively new "master" of the colonists, whom they had acquired under the decree of 20 April 1782 (text in: German Colonists in the Age of Catherine. Pp. 146–148). By this act Catherine II abolished the Chancellery for the Guardianship of Foreigners in St. Petersburg and its office in Saratov, declaring them "unnecessary," and in their place entrusted the administration of the Volga colonies to the Saratov Treasury Chamber, through its Director of Husbandry (economy). Apart from a few lines in the preceding decree and in the present act, the Saratov authorities received no official instructions from the empress right up to the end of their activity in this sphere (1797), and could therefore do practically whatever they pleased in the colonies. It is no accident that both the colonists themselves and the overwhelming majority of researchers regarded the 15 years of the Saratov Treasury Chamber's management as a period of genuine calamity for the colonies.

### No. 26.

This decree mentions three of the first four groups of St. Petersburg colonists — the Yamburg, Shlisselburg, and Izhora colonists. The Yamburg colonists inhabited three small colonies southwest of St. Petersburg, near Yamburg (now the town of Kingisepp) — Lutskaya (Neu-Lutzk), Porkhovskaya (Neu-Porkhov), and Frankfurtskaya. All of them eventually became part of Gorka volost, Yamburg Uyezd. By the Shlisselburg colonists is meant the inhabitants of the largest St. Petersburg colony — Novosaratovka (Neu-Saratovka, Saratovka). It was located on the right bank of the Neva southeast of St. Petersburg, constituted a separate Novosaratovka volost of St. Petersburg Uyezd, and by 1797 already numbered 458 inhabitants. The Izhora colonists were the inhabitants of Izhora Colony No. 1 (the settlement of Verkhneye) and Izhora Colony No. 2. They were situated on the Izhora River south of Kolpino, formed part of Kolpino volost, Tsarskoye Selo Uyezd, and were fairly large by comparison with the other St. Petersburg colonies: 401 and 308 inhabitants respectively in 1862.

Settlers from Yamburg Uyezd were mostly Catholics — unlike all the other, Lutheran, St. Petersburg colonists. In their new location they founded a colony with the familiar name Yamburg, situated on the right bank of the Dnieper southeast of Yekaterinoslav. It formed a separate Yamburg volost of Yekaterinoslav Uyezd and numbered 1,135 inhabitants in 1897, including 1,062 Germans.

### No. 27.

This is the first imperial decree to mention the Mennonites, although they had begun settling in southern Russia as early as the 1780s (see doc. No. 34). Mennonitism is a branch of Protestantism professing adult baptism (Anabaptism), rejection of oaths, of bearing arms, and of violence; it arose as a movement in the 1530s and takes its name from Menno Simons, a well-known 16th-century religious figure who formulated its principles. The first Mennonites lived near the border of Germany and Holland, but as early as 1540–1560, for religious reasons, they moved to the region of Danzig (West Prussia), from where some of them later departed for Russia. See: Stricker G. Mennonites // Germans of Russia: Encyclopedia. Vol. 2. P. 471.

The Mennonites' decision to settle in Russia was prompted by the fact that the Russian authorities guaranteed them full freedom of worship and respect for their religious and moral principles. The Mennonites' language (Plautdietsch) has retained notable Dutch elements, yet its very name shows that it is a dialect of German rather than Dutch. Paul I, and later his sons Alexander I and Nicholas I, showed foresight in paying special attention to the Mennonites. Although they made up a relatively small proportion of the colonists, the Mennonites, thanks to their remarkable industriousness and enterprise, made a notable contribution to the development of the south and a number of other regions of Russia.

Novorossiysk Governorate — the name of Yekaterinoslav Governorate in 1796–1802, when Yekaterinoslav was called Novorossiysk.

### No. 28.

This is the first in a series of acts of Paul I in which a thorough analysis is given of the situation of the colonists in most of the regions where they were settled, and considered measures are proposed for a fundamental improvement of their situation. It is known that Paul was highly critical of the activities of Catherine II and, during the brief period of his reign, exerted great effort to overcome the omissions and vices that he considered inherent in his mother's rule. In this sphere he undoubtedly succeeded. This is largely explained by the fact that he was able to enlist very competent and conscientious people to solve the colonists' problems, among whom K.I. Gablitz and S.Kh. Contenius stood out (see the Biographical Commentary).

Along with the colonies mentioned in doc. No. 26, this act also describes another of the oldest St. Petersburg colonies — Srednyaya Rogatka, located south of St. Petersburg, "on the great Tsarskoye Selo road." The colony was fairly large — 737 inhabitants in 1897, including 498 Germans. It subsequently formed a separate Srednerogatskaya volost of St. Petersburg uyezd.

### No. 29.

By this charter Paul I confirmed the special rights of the Herrnhuters guaranteed by Catherine II (see doc. No. 17), and also granted them additional privileges.
