The most significant of these were: perpetual hereditary ownership of all lands that the colony of Sarepta would acquire in the future (Art. 2), the establishment of a special self-government body possessing administrative and judicial authority in the colony (Art. 4), the right to freely leave Russia upon payment of a three-year tax on accumulated capital (Art. 9), and the extension of the tax exemption until January 1, 1806 (Art. 11).

### No. 30.

This decree vividly illustrates the problem created in the 1780s by the decision of the Saratov Treasury Chamber to switch the Volga colonists from household-based to per-capita land use. Whereas initially a colonist family was allotted 30 desyatinas of land (see doc. No. 13), it was now prescribed that 20 desyatinas be allotted per male revision soul, which, given the large size of German families, was far more problematic. At that point the task set could still be resolved relatively easily, since in the first decades the Volga colonies experienced high mortality and the number of their inhabitants grew slowly. But later, as conditions normalized, the rate of population growth increased sharply, and the acuteness of the land-shortage problem began to grow rapidly.

### No. 31.

The document illustrates the particular problems that existed in the colonies of the Volga's right bank. Here the land question was most acute, since the colonists' plots directly bordered the lands of other landowners and the allotments of Russian villages that had existed even before the colonists' arrival. This act mentions all the colonies of the Ust-Kulalinsky district, located in a bend of the Volga northeast of Kamyshin: Nizhnyaya Dobrinka (Dobrinka, Moninger), Ust-Kulalinka (Galka, Meyerhöfer), Buydakov Buyerak (Shvab), Krestovy Buyerak (Miller), Vodyanoy Buyerak (Stefan), Verkhnyaya Kulalinka (Holstein), Verkhnyaya Dobrinka (Dreispitz), Shcherbakovka (Mühlberg), Gryaznukha (Verkhnyaya Gryaznukha, Kraft).

Reis (Rais) Ivan — captain of a dragoon regiment, was fluent in his native German as well as Russian and French, and knew engineering. In 1763, at the request of the Chancellery of Trusteeship of Foreign Settlers, he was included on the Senate's staff; on assignment from the Chancellery he directed the settlement of colonists in the Volga region until the establishment of the Saratov Office of Trusteeship of Foreign Settlers in 1766 (for documents on his activity during this period, see: German Colonists in the Age of Catherine. Pp. 193–195, 197–211, 220–221, 226–227, 230–231, 233–243, 266–267). He subsequently served in the Saratov Office.

Zetteler (Zetler) Fyodor Ivanovich — secretary in the Saratov Office of Trusteeship, and from 1782 under the Director of Economy of the Saratov Treasury Chamber.

Rescript of July 10, 1785 — doc. No. 25; instruction of June 30, 1797 — see: German Colonists in the Age of Catherine. Pp. 152–155.

### No. 32.

This unprecedented act confirms Paul I's determination to use every means to normalize the situation in the colonies. It remained in force until 1803 (see doc. No. 54) and undoubtedly played its part in resolving this task.

Sloboda-Ukraine governorate — subsequently renamed Kharkov governorate, but at that time it occupied a considerably larger territory than the latter. In particular, the Voronezh colony of Riebensdorf belonged to Sloboda-Ukraine governorate.

### No. 33.

Dorpat University was founded as early as 1632, during the period when Dorpat was under Swedish rule. After the city was captured by Russian troops during the Russo-Swedish War of 1656–1658, classes were moved to Reval, and in 1665 they ceased altogether. The university's activity resumed in 1690, when Dorpat once again belonged to Sweden. In 1699 the university was transferred to Pernau, where it functioned until the city was captured by Russian troops (1710) during the Great Northern War of 1700–1721. Despite repeated petitions by the Livonian nobility and promises from Peter I, and later Empress Anna Ivanovna, the question of restoring Dorpat University remained unresolved until the adoption of the present act by Paul I. In 1800 Paul leaned toward another option mentioned in this document — organizing a university in Mitau — and in the end Dorpat University opened only in 1802, already under Alexander I. The university's charter, adopted in 1803, essentially corresponded to the plan approved by Paul, but there was of course no longer any question of naming the university after the emperor who had been killed in 1801, its true patron. Dorpat University was distinguished both by a degree of university autonomy unheard of in Russia and by its adherence to German university traditions. Teaching there was conducted mainly in German, and up to 80% of the students were Germans. The university played a leading role in training Lutheran pastors for Russia and, more broadly, in shaping the Russian-German intelligentsia. Many world-famous scholars studied and taught there (see the Biographical Commentary). From the 1830s the authorities began a process of Russifying the university. This intensified especially after it was made subject to the university statute of 1884, which sharply restricted university autonomy. As a result, many German professors were forced to leave Russia. In 1893 Dorpat was renamed Yuryev, and Dorpat University became Yuryev University, finally losing its German character. See: Ulrich M. Dorpat University // Germans of Russia: An Encyclopedia. Vol. 1. Pp. 706–708.

### No. 34.

The eight original Mennonite villages in the Khortitsa area mentioned in the document were named: Khortitsa (Verkhnyaya Khortitsa), Rosental (Kantserovka), Ostrov Khortitsa (Insel Chortitza), Einlage (Kichkas), Kronsweide (Dneprovka, Vladimirovka), Neuenburg (Malashevka), Neuendorf (Shirokaya), Schönhorst (Vodyanaya). All of them belonged to the Khortitsa Mennonite district, and later to the Khortitsa volost of Ekaterinoslav uyezd. Between 1803 and 1824 other Mennonite villages appeared in the Khortitsa district. The largest of the original eight villages was Khortitsa — the center of the district and later of the uyezd; in 1897 it had 2,046 inhabitants, but only 1,134 of them were Germans. The colony of Schönwiese (Moevka) subsequently belonged to the Petrovo-Stroganovskaya (Petrovskaya) volost of Aleksandrovsk uyezd and had 999 inhabitants in 1897, including 507 Germans; the colony of Kronsgarten (Polovitsa) belonged to the Josephstal volost of Novomoskovsk uyezd, its maximum population being 212 in 1908. The Lutheran colony of Josephstal (Iosifovka, Dolgaya) eventually became the center of the volost of the same name and had 1,030 inhabitants in 1897, including 917 Germans. On the Catholic colony of Yamburg, see the note to doc. No. 26.

Unlike all these colonies, which were located in Ekaterinoslav governorate, the Danzig and Swedish colonists were settled in Kherson governorate. The Danzig colonists founded the colony of Old Danzig (Alt-Danzig, Danzig). It subsequently belonged to the Anninskaya volost of Elisavetgrad uyezd, with a maximum population of 504 (1887). The Swedish colonists, strictly speaking, were not foreigners: the island of Dagö (now the island of Hiiumaa, Estonia), from which they were resettled, had belonged to Russia since 1710. During the period in question the Swedes lived together with German colonists in the colony of Staroshvedskaya (Gammalsvenskby, Alt-Schwedendorf, Staro-Kostyrka). The colony belonged to the Swedish district, and later to the Staroshvedskaya volost of Kherson uyezd. In 1897 it had 630 inhabitants, including 584 Germans and Germanized Swedes. In 1804 three more colonies were established within the Swedish district.

Trappe Georg von — on behalf of Catherine II, was engaged in attracting to Russia both the Danzig colonists and the local Mennonites; from 1798, a member of the Expedition of State Economy.

Kirchmann Hiob Adolf (1752–1800) — a native of Germany, Evangelical Lutheran pastor in Josephstal from 1789 to 1799.

Decree of April 21, 1798 — doc. No. 32; manifesto of July 22, 1763 — doc. No. 11; ban on the operation of drinking establishments in the St. Petersburg colonies of 1797 — see doc. No. 28; the staff and instruction of the Saratov Office of Trusteeship of Foreign Settlers of 1797 — see: German Colonists in the Age of Catherine. Pp. 152–155.

### No. 35.

Just a few months after ascending the throne, Paul I, having ordered K.I. Gablitz to survey the Volga colonies and having become convinced of their dire condition, restored the Saratov Office of Trusteeship of Foreign Settlers by a decree of June 30, 1797, and on the same day approved an instruction on its activity (see: German Colonists in the Age of Catherine. Pp. 152–155). The subsequent survey of the Novorossiya colonies by S.Kh. Contenius resulted in a decision to establish a similar Office of Trusteeship in the south of Russia (see doc. No. 34).

Apart from reflecting certain local features, the instruction to the Office of Trusteeship of Novorossiya's Foreign Settlers approved by the present act differs from the previous one mainly in two additional articles: Art. 8 instructs the Office to carry out various economic functions, while Art. 9 obliges the Office to systematically monitor the situation in the colonies. These articles were addressed not only to the Novorossiya Office — as shown by the Instruction on Internal Order and Administration in the Saratov Colonies of September 17, 1800 (doc. No. 38), where they are set out in detail, the imposition of strict administration in the management of the colonies was a thoroughly typical idea of the Pauline period.

Report of April 6, 1800 — doc. No. 34; decree of April 21, 1798 — doc. No. 32.

### No. 36.

As this act shows, the situation in the Belovezh colonies at that time was quite typical of the early German colonies in general: problems with land allotment that worsened as the population grew, a shortage of pastures and hayfields, the unsettled state of artisans, and, as a result, low incomes and an inability to repay treasury debts on time. The measures proposed to remedy the situation are likewise fairly standard. One of them, however — placing the colonists under the newly established Office of Trusteeship of Novorossiya's Foreign Settlers — proved clearly unsuccessful, since the Belovezh colonies were too far from Novorossiya, and in 1809 this decision was rescinded (see doc. No. 56).

Ostrogozhsk colonists — inhabitants of the Voronezh colony of Riebensdorf, located in Ostrogozhsk uyezd.

Manifesto of July 22, 1763 — doc. No. 11; decree of April 21, 1798 — doc. No. 32; report of April 6, 1800 — doc. No. 34.

### No. 37.

The document vividly illustrates Paul I's special favor toward the Mennonites. Whereas many Russian emperors issued similar charters to the Herrnhuters (see the note to doc. No. 17), this Pauline charter remained unique of its kind. The privileges granted to the Mennonites were similar to those of the Herrnhuters, though they did not go quite as far. The principal purpose of Paul's charter was not to introduce new privileges but to confirm those received by the first Mennonites who had settled in Russia back under Catherine II. The charter was clearly intended to attract new Mennonite colonists to the country, and Paul's calculation was fully vindicated.

### No. 38.

In Art. 6, para. 5 of Catherine II's manifesto of July 22, 1763 (doc. No. 11), the internal jurisdiction of the colonies was left to the "good governance" of the colonists themselves, "with the proviso that Our authorities shall have no part whatsoever in their internal arrangements." However, as early as April 1769 the Chancellery of Trusteeship of Foreign Settlers approved an "Instruction according to which all newly settled foreigners must conduct themselves," which regulated every aspect of colony life in detail (see: Dietz Ya.E., op. cit., pp. 148–163). The instruction was declared "temporary," but it remained in force for a full 30 years. Catherine, it seems, was reluctant to publicize this flagrant violation of her own promises, and that instruction was never submitted to the Senate for approval. Under Paul I, who was not inclined to such blatant hypocrisy, a revised and expanded version of the instruction, set out in the present act, came to be regarded as a fully official document. Later, corresponding instructions were drawn up on its basis for the Novorossiya colonies (doc. No. 39) and the St. Petersburg colonies (PSZRI. Coll. 1. No. 20798); the main provisions of these three documents were incorporated into the Statute on Colonies of 1857 (doc. No. 115).

It is not easy for the modern reader to imagine why it was necessary to adopt these hyper-bureaucratic acts or how they could actually have been carried out. The answer to the first question is probably to be found in officials' perennial conviction that those in charge always know best, while the answer to the second lies in the well-known aphorisms: "If all the laws in Russia were obeyed, life there would become utterly impossible," and "The severity of Russian laws has always been compensated for by the non-obligatory nature of their enforcement." For such instructions to be carried out one hundred percent, it would at the very least have been necessary for the officials administering the colonies to understand peasant crafts and all the everyday affairs of the colonists far better than the colonists themselves. Nothing of the sort was, of course, actually observed. On the other hand, the Germans, as is well known, are themselves inclined toward order and regularity. This does not mean they needed every step of theirs to be regulated, and such instructions certainly made the colonists' lives worse, but apparently not too drastically — otherwise the quite successful subsequent development of the German colonies would simply have been impossible.

### No. 39.

Apart from a few points reflecting the specifics of Novorossiya, this document essentially coincides in content with the instruction for the Saratov colonies (doc. No. 38). The differences in form are far more significant: whereas the previous act was clearly prepared in haste, is poorly structured, is full of inaccuracies, and mechanically borrows the outdated vocabulary of the 1769 instruction, the present document is distinguished by a well-thought-out structure, clear style, and precise wording. It evidently bears the hand of an experienced official who was an expert on the matter. One may surmise that this was K.I. Gablitz, then a member of the Expedition of State Economy (see the Biographical Commentary).

### No. 40.

The document reflects the new methods of receiving colonists that became established during the reign of Alexander I. By this time a significant proportion of foreign settlers made their own way to Russia and settled on private (usually landowners') lands.

Bennigsen (Benigsen) Leontiy Leontyevich (Levin August Theophil) (1745–1826) — count (from 1813), general of cavalry, military governor of Vilna in 1801–1804.

Manifesto of [17]63 — doc. No. 11.

### No. 41.

The document attests to the rapid worsening of the land shortage among the Volga colonists, caused both by the onset of vigorous natural population growth and by the per-capita system of land use introduced in the Volga colonies. Under these conditions the authorities had to keep allotting new lands to the colonists.

Manifesto of December 8, 1765 — decree of Catherine II on the surveying of lands for the settlement of the Volga colonists (see: German Colonists in the Age of Catherine. Pp. 91–110); decree of December 4, 1797 — doc. No. 30.

### No. 42.

The document reveals the particular acuteness of the land problem on the Volga's right bank. In all, the Norka district comprised 10 colonies — 7 in Kamyshin uyezd of Saratov governorate (including Norka and Linevo Ozero) and 3 in Atkarsk uyezd. Even at that time these colonies were marked by rapid population growth: Norka (Weigand) — from 753 people in 1767 to 1,660 in 1798; Linevo Ozero (Hussenbach) — from 438 in 1769 to 907 in 1798.

Decree of September 4, 1802 — doc. No. 41; manifesto of July 22, 1763 — doc. No. 11.

### No. 43.

This concerns Mennonites who lived east of Danzig along the Baltic coast (West Prussia). They were settled in Berdyansk uyezd of Tavrida governorate, along the Molochnaya River. Between 1804 and 1805, 19 Mennonite colonies were established there, forming the Molochna Mennonite district.

### No. 44.

The very titles of the sections of this document reveal which problems of colony administration seemed most important to the Russian authorities of the time. The provision on the corporal punishment of colonists (§ 4) is especially notable. Under the "despot" Paul I, this provision, which had been included in the temporary instruction for the colonies (1769), was not incorporated into the instruction for the Saratov colonies (doc. No. 38); this omission was rectified in the present document, issued under the "liberal" Alexander I. Although the document formally concerns only the Novorossiya colonies, its provisions were extended to all colonies in Russia by the Statute on Colonies of 1857 (doc. No. 115). In particular, Art. 481 of the Statute reproduces the aforementioned § 4, albeit supplied with a bashful qualification: "taking care that this [corporal punishment] should by no means become an execution, but should serve rather as a fear of shame and disgrace."

### No. 45.

It is no accident that the document draws attention to the restoration of vineyards in Crimea — after Crimea's annexation to Russia (1783), many Tatars were forced to flee from there, and viticulture fell into decline. The first German colonies in Crimea arose in 1805 in Simferopol uyezd (the Neusatz district) and Feodosiya uyezd (the Zürichtal district) of Tavrida governorate.

Ziegler Franz — an agent who in 1803 was engaged in transporting colonists to Russia from southwestern Germany and Alsace; the settlers he transported founded all the first Crimean colonies except Zürichtal (see the note to doc. No. 47).

### No. 46.

The colonists who arrived in Odessa at that time were mostly settled in its environs. Between 1803 and 1806, 10 German colonies arose here, forming the Liebental district. The first Lutheran clergyman in these parts was Johann Christian Heinrich Pfersdorff (?–1819), a native of Thuringia, pastor in Odessa and the colony of Lustdorf (Olgino) in 1803–1806, and pastor in the colony of Gross-Liebental (Bolshoy Liebental, Bolshaya Akarzha) in 1806–1819.

### No. 47.

This principal colonization act of Alexander I is often referred to in the literature as a "manifesto." The document reflects a new, more pragmatic approach to the reception of colonists — admitting only a limited number of well-to-do, married, and highly moral settlers, and moreover ones with experience in those branches of agriculture and craft that seemed promising for the colonies of southern Russia. As a result, the new colonies here avoided many of the problems characteristic of the colonies of Catherine's time.

This act for the first time provided for the recovery from colonists, in the event of their leaving Russia, of the subsistence money expended on their settlement (Art. 7).

Escher Hans Kaspar — major of the Moscow Dragoon Regiment, a Swiss, who organized the resettlement of colonists from Switzerland; the colonists he resettled founded the Crimean colony of Zürichtal in 1808.

Manifesto of 1763 — doc. No. 11.

### No. 48.

This act specifies the places of settlement of colonists on the basis of the principles put forward in doc. No. 47. The provisions of the present document were subsequently implemented — alongside the colonies near Odessa, in Feodosiya uyezd, and in the Molochna Mennonite district, the following were established in subsequent years: the Molochna colonist district in Melitopol uyezd of Tavrida governorate (from 1804), and, in Kherson governorate, the Glückstal district in Tiraspol uyezd (from 1805), the Kuchurgan district in Odessa uyezd (from 1808), and the Berezan district in Odessa and Ananyev uyezds (from 1809).

### No. 49.

This is the first act permitting foreign colonists to purchase land. It acquired notable practical significance later on, once the colonists had accumulated the means necessary for this. It is worth noting that the acquisition of land by foreigners was excluded at the beginning of the 19th century in much the same way as in present-day Russia.

### No. 50.

Given the limited availability of free crown lands, the Russian authorities began to attach increasing importance to settling colonists on private (landowners') estates. This practice subsequently became widespread in New Russia, the South-Western governorates, and several other regions.

Decree of 9 May 1802 — doc. No. 40; manifesto of 1763 — doc. No. 11.

### No. 51.

Mire, Osip (Joseph) — a native of Strasbourg, staged performances in the theaters of Hamburg and Riga; in 1799 he founded a German theater in St. Petersburg, drawing German actors and singers into it. In 1800 he transferred the theater to the Theatrical Directorate, which paid off Mire's debts. In 1801 the directorship of the theater passed to the scholar-philologist Fyodor Pavlovich (Friedrich) Adelung (1768–1843), a corresponding member of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (from 1809), and the theater was once again handed over to Mire. He was an expert in stage effects and staged very lavish productions — operas and operettas. A number of his performances at the Hermitage Theater attracted the attention of Alexander I and secured state support for Mire. Despite this, Mire again found himself in a critical financial situation, and in 1805 was forced to hand the theater over to the actor, poet, and playwright Christlieb Georg Heinrich Aresto (1764–1818) and left St. Petersburg. See: Stöckl E. Musikgeschichte der Rußlanddeutschen. Dülmen, 1993. S. 98–100, 102.

### No. 52.

With the normalization of the economic situation in the St. Petersburg colonies, the authorities began to raise both the colonists' payments toward the crown debt and the land tax levied on them.

Manifesto of 22 July 1763 — doc. No. 11; decree of 1793 — doc. No. 26; report of 20 June 1797 — doc. No. 28.

### No. 53.

The document shows that the Khortitsa Mennonites and the Josephstal colonists, who had been in a difficult position from the outset, had still not fully established their farms even 16 years after settlement.

The Khortitsa Mennonites' intention to build a vessel for marketing their produce was realized: such a vessel was built in the colony of Kichkas (Einlage) in 1806, and the Mennonites sailed it down the Dnieper, carrying their goods to Kherson, Crimea, and Odessa. See: Meshkov D.Yu. Reporting registers and memoranda of the Office of Guardianship of New Russian Foreign Settlers as a source on the history of German colonization of southern Russia, 1800–1810 // Russian Germans: Historiography and Source Studies. Moscow, 1997. Pp. 319–320.

Report of 6 April 1800 — doc. No. 34.

### No. 54.

Alongside information about the increased prosperity of the Volga colonies, the document reflects several notable facts connected with the introduction of per-capita land use in the 1780s.

First, it emerges that a quarter of a century after that measure, the surveying of land holdings for allotting colonists 20 desyatinas of land per revision soul, as had been prescribed in 1797, had still not been completed. The authors, citing the Saratov Office of Guardianship, blame the colonists themselves for deliberately delaying this process, allegedly out of reluctance to pay the additional sums toward the land tax and repayment of the crown debt that would fall due from them once the survey was completed. This explanation puts everything upside down. These increased costs to the colonists were more than offset by the benefits of receiving the promised per-capita allotment. Nor did they have any real means of holding back the surveying process — that was within the power only of the colonial officials, if anyone.

Second, the document complains of the weak development of crafts in the colonies, again placing the blame on the colonists, although this phenomenon follows naturally from the per-capita system of land use itself. The example of cotton spinning, cited as an admonition to the "idle" colonists and which did develop in a number of colonies on the right bank, is hard to call convincing. This craft simply could not achieve the universal spread that the authors of the document desired: competition in this sphere was too great.

Roggenbuke (Rogenbuke) — chief judge of the Saratov Office of Guardianship of Foreigners in 1803–1814.

Manifesto of 1763 — doc. No. 11; rescript of 1785 — doc. No. 25; decree of 21 April 1798 — doc. No. 32; decree of 4 September 1802 — doc. No. 41; decree of 19 December 1802 — doc. No. 42.

### No. 55.

In fact the colonists were settled in the Izvara tract (see doc. No. 60) and in Peterhof District, where the colonies of Oranienbaum, Peterhof (Krasnenka), Strelna (Neudorf, Neuhausen), and Kronstadt (see doc. No. 57) were established. The Oranienbaum and Peterhof colonies were small and both became part of Oranienbaum volost; the Strelna colony belonged to Konstantinovka (Strelna) volost and, by the standards of the St. Petersburg colonies, was fairly large: 506 inhabitants in 1897, including 466 Germans. On the transport and settlement of these colonists, see: Bakhmutskaya E.V. The organization of the reception and settlement of German colonists in St. Petersburg Governorate during the reign of Emperor Alexander I // Migration processes among Russian Germans: a historical aspect. Moscow, 1998. Pp. 73–86.

Kankrin E.F. — shortly after this act, in 1809, appointed inspector of the foreign colonies of St. Petersburg Governorate (see Biographical Index).

### No. 56.

This act rescinded the ill-considered decision to subordinate the Belovezh colonies to the New Russia Office of Guardianship of Foreigners, adopted in 1800 (see doc. No. 36). It is noteworthy that in this instance the "remoteness" of the colonies from the office is cited, whereas nine years earlier, on the contrary, the "not-too-great" distance between them had been noted — a vivid example of how one and the same circumstance can be interpreted in diametrically opposite ways depending on "expediency."

### No. 57.

The document recounts the founding of the colony of Kronstadt (also known as Klyuchinsky, after the surname of a former landowner). The colony belonged to Oranienbaum (Strelna) volost of Peterhof District; its maximum population was 119 (in 1885).

### No. 58.

The sharp reduction in state expenditure amid an acute financial crisis and in the midst of a whole series of military campaigns (against France, Turkey, Sweden) is understandable and justified in itself. However, this apparently did not seem sufficient to the Committee of Ministers, and the supreme legislative-consultative body bolstered its proposals with reasoning that displays neither foresight nor elementary common sense.

Not only did the government decide to economize on all colonists except the cloth-makers, whose activity brought no appreciable benefit to the state either then or later (see docs. No. 74 and 89); nearly half a century after the active recruitment of foreign colonists had begun, the authorities suddenly realized that this undertaking was costing the treasury too much and that it would be far cheaper to use Russian peasants. The government seems to have forgotten that serfdom still existed in the country, and that Russian rulers, beginning with Catherine II, had had to resort to the services of foreign settlers precisely because of the shortage of serfs who could be relatively freely resettled from place to place. The only ones who belonged to such a category were the state peasants, but they were entirely insufficient to settle all the empty outlying territories of Russia. It was presumably they who were meant in the document by the phrase "natural subjects making up the colonies." Apart from the state peasants, this "most useful work for the State" was, among Russian subjects at that time, undertaken only by the small number of Swedes from the island of Hiiumaa (Dagö) (see note to doc. No. 34).

### No. 59.

The incident was caused by the fact that among the arriving colonists there turned out to be quite a few artisans who, naturally, had no intention of taking up farming. They began looking for work outside the colonies, since within them — still in their formative stage — no employment could be found for them. Alexander I, informed of this by the Minister of Internal Affairs, took the side of the fugitives: "Any free hands are needed!" The Emperor was concerned only that colonists leaving the colonies should remain within the bounds of New Russia. See: Fleischhauer I. Op. cit. S. 159.

Rosenkampf, Andrei Andreevich (Caspar Heinrich) von (1756–1814) — from 1808 to 1814 administrator of the colonies of the Odessa settlement, associate chief judge of the New Russia Office of Foreign Settlers; a trusted agent of the Governor-General of New Russia, A.E. (duc) de Richelieu, to whom he reported the colonists' flight.

### No. 60.

This concerns the colonies of Bolshaya, Srednyaya, and Nizhnyaya (known in the literature mainly under the collective name Izvara), founded from 1809 southwest of St. Petersburg, near the Gatchina–Yamburg road. Despite conditions entirely unsuited to farming, the authorities tried to force the colonists to live precisely there. This could not be achieved even by resorting to force, and as a result the present act had to be adopted. On these events, see: Bakhmutskaya E.V. Op. cit. Pp. 80–83.

In fact the inhabitants of Izvara were resettled to the colony of Strelna, to the newly founded colony of Kipen, and also to New Russia (see doc. No. 79). The colony of Kipen was part of Ropsha (Strelna) volost of Peterhof District and, by the standards of the St. Petersburg colonies, was medium-sized — 305 inhabitants in 1904.

### No. 61.

Two provisions concerning the Volga Germans are especially notable in this act. On the one hand, they were the first among the colonists to be placed on equal footing in tax obligations with the local crown peasants. Thus the principal differences between peasants of these two ranks with regard to payments to the state now consisted in the fact that the colonists continued to repay the crown debt but did not bear the recruitment levy even in monetary form. On the other hand, the survey of the colonists' lands in the Volga region had still not been completed, which precluded allotting colonists additional land in proportion to the growth in the number of revision souls, as had apparently been intended when they were transferred to the system of per-capita land use in the 1780s (see: Pleve I.R. Op. cit. P. 281).

### No. 62.

The transfer of colonists to other estates (mainly the merchantry or the petty-bourgeoisie/meshchanstvo) was most common among colonies located near major cities (St. Petersburg, Odessa, and others). This act mentions only the New Russia colonists, so it may be supposed that its appearance was prompted by increasingly frequent cases of their departure for the cities (see doc. No. 59).

This document for the first time prescribes that colonists who transfer to other estates be charged for the subsistence money expended on their settlement (Arts. 3, 7). Previously such a measure had been envisaged only in the case of colonists leaving Russia (see doc. No. 47, Art. 7).

### No. 63.

The appearance of this act is connected with the fact that, as a result of the Russo-Turkish War of 1806–1812, Turkey had to cede Bessarabia — the territory between the Dniester and Prut rivers — to Russia. Bessarabia was inhabited mainly by Romanians (Moldavians); its southern districts were sparsely settled, and part of the population had fled. This prompted the recruitment of foreign colonists, including Germans, to the region.

German colonists had been settled in a number of districts of the Duchy (Principality) of Warsaw at the beginning of the 19th century, when these districts belonged to Prussia. In 1812 the duchy, seized by Napoleon, served as a base for the French army's invasion of Russia; during the war years its inhabitants suffered from military operations. At the time this decree was issued, the future fate of the Duchy of Warsaw had not yet been determined. Following the outcome of the Congress of Vienna of 1814–1815, a substantial part of it passed to Russia, while Prussia once again received the districts that had previously belonged to it.

The Warsaw colonists, who resettled to the Bessarabia Region in 1814–1816, founded in Bendery District (later Akkerman District) 11 Lutheran colonies and one Catholic colony (Krasnoye), named in honor of the sites of battles of the Patriotic War of 1812 and the subsequent foreign campaigns of the Russian army. These colonies formed two districts: Maloyaroslavets — Maloyaroslavets I (Kirgiz, Wittenberg), Kulm (Madar, Paulsberg), Tarutino (Anchokrak), Krasnoye, Fère-Champenoise I (Alt-Fère-Champenoise, Old Champenoise); Klyastitsy — Klyastitsy (Chaga), Leipzig (Skinos), Berezina (Kagalnik, Rotunda), Borodino (Sak), Paris (Vesyoly Kut), Arciz I (Alt-Arciz, Old Arciz), Brienne (Peterwunsch).

### No. 64.

The Warsaw colonists were mainly Lutherans, partly Catholics, so that their refusal to take the oath could not have been prompted by religious motives, as was the case with the Herrnhuters or the Mennonites.

The first Lutheran pastor in the Bessarabian colonies (Tarutino parish) was, from 1815, Friedrich Wilhelm Schnabel (1772–1820). In 1815 he effectively led the uprising of the Bessarabian colonists against the arbitrary rule of local officials, was arrested as a "ringleader," and died in confinement five years later without ever having been brought to trial. See: Sheveleva T. The Bessarabian colonists' uprising // Germans of Russia: An Encyclopedia. Vol. 1. P. 191.

Harting, Ivan Markovich — administrator of the Bessarabia Region in 1814–1816.

Decree of 22 January 1814 — doc. No. 63; manifesto of 22 July 1763 — doc. No. 11; report of 23 February 1804 — doc. No. 48.

### No. 65.

The Volga colonists had already been placed on an equal footing in tax payments with the local crown peasants in 1812 (see doc. No. 61); however, at that time it had been decided to levy the tax on them according to the number of souls per the previous revision, rather than the new one, as is now the case. This refers respectively to the 6th (1798) and 7th (1816) revisions. Over this period the number of male souls in the Volga colonies grew from 20,021 to 30,953, i.e., by 54.6%. The tax payments were to increase correspondingly.

### No. 66.

The document attests to a strengthening tendency on the part of the Russian authorities to settle arriving colonists on private lands. However, the foreigners intending to move to Russia, mentioned in the announcement of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, were settled mainly on crown lands — in Bessarabia (see doc. No. 67) and Transcaucasia (see doc. No. 73).

Report of 12 April 1804 — doc. No. 50.

### No. 67.

The second group of Bessarabian colonists, referred to in the document, arrived directly from Germany from 1817 and founded the colonies of Teplitz and Katzbach (Alyaga) in Maloyaroslavets District. In addition, they formed the colony of Karlstal, whose inhabitants were later resettled to the newly founded colony of Hoffnungstal (Karaday) in Klyastitsy District. This second group of colonists also founded the colony of Sarata (Old Sarata), which became part of the new Sarata District of Akkerman District.

### No. 68.

The colony of Karras (Scottish, Inozemtsevo) near Zheleznovodsk, founded in 1804 by Scottish missionaries, subsequently became part of Karras (Pyatigorsk) volost of Pyatigorsk (Georgievsk) District of Terek Region. The Volga colonists who settled in Karras, despite the return of some of them to the Volga region and the resettlement of others to the town of Svyatoy Krest (present-day Budyonnovsk), together with their descendants made up the majority of the colony's inhabitants already by the mid-19th century. By the standards of the North Caucasus colonies it was fairly large, numbering 932 inhabitants in 1897, including 858 Germans and Germanized Scots.

Charter of 25 December 1806 — PSZRI. Coll. 1. No. 22410; manifesto of 22 July 1763 — doc. No. 11; report of 18 December 1808 — doc. No. 54; opinion of 27 November 1812 — doc. No. 62.

### No. 69.

This act shows that the authorities decided actively to involve the Ministry of Internal Affairs, which at that time was in charge of the foreign colonies, in the process — to which they attached ever greater importance — of settling colonists on private (landowners') lands.

Decree of 25 August 1817 — doc. No. 66; regulations of 1804 — doc. No. 50; opinion of 27 November 1812 — doc. No. 62.

### No. 70.

Followers of the Herrnhuters appeared in the Baltic governorates (Livonia) even earlier than in the Volga region; however, unlike Sarepta, they never established settlements of their own, confining their activity to the framework of individual religious communities. These maintained close ties chiefly with the German center at Herrnhut rather than with their brethren in Sarepta, St. Petersburg, or Moscow, and only a few Baltic Herrnhuters gained recognition among the latter. Among such exceptions were Christlieb Suter (1740–1811), a native of Livonia, agent in St. Petersburg in 1776–1781; and Johannes Scheuerle (1774–1855), a native of Sarepta who was active in Livonia and served as acting agent in St. Petersburg in 1812–1813. Under the influence of the Riga Herrnhuters, the future well-known religious figure Barbara Juliane von Krüdener-Vietinghoff (1764–1824) became attracted to pietist ideas at the beginning of the 19th century.

The privileges granted to the Baltic Herrnhuters by this act generally corresponded to the privileges of Sarepta (see doc. No. 29), with the natural exception of the points relating to the arrangement of that colony.

### No. 71.

In connection with the improvement of the economic situation, this act placed the first New Russia colonists on an equal footing with the local crown peasants in the payment of land tax, as had earlier been done with the Volga colonists (see docs. No. 61 and 65), and also raised the payments to the treasury owed by the Ekaterinoslav Mennonites. Per family, the Mennonites were required to pay more than the other colonists, but given their twice-as-large land allotment, their payments still remained lower.

Report of 6 April 1800 — doc. No. 34; report of 9 September 1805 — doc. No. 53; report of 20 February 1804 — doc. No. 47; charter of 6 September 1800 — doc. No. 37; report of 18 December 1808 — doc. No. 54.

### No. 72.

The proposal to establish a Guardianship Committee was put forward, after an inspection of the colonies of southern Russia, by P.D. Kiselev (1788–1872), aide-de-camp to Alexander I and future Minister of State Domains. The first chairman of the Committee (Chief Trustee of the Colonists) from 1818 to 1844 was General of Infantry Ivan Nikitich Inzov (1768–1845), during whose Kishinev exile (1820–1823) A.S. Pushkin served under him. The chairmanship was subsequently held by: E.F. von Hahn (see Biographical Index) in 1846–1848; Baron Fyodor Fyodorovich (Friedrich) Rosen (1808–1854) in 1849–1853; Baron Pavel Fyodorovich Mestmacher in 1853–1856; Vladimir Islavin in 1856–1858; Alexander Iosifovich von Hamm (1817–1888) in 1858–1866; F.S. von Dizander (see Biographical Index) in 1866–1867; and Vladimir Ivanovich von Oettinger in 1867–1871. See: Fleischhauer I. Op. cit. S. 170–174.

Decree of 25 August 1817 — doc. No. 66; instruction of 26 July 1800 — doc. No. 35.

### No. 73.

The Württemberg settlers founded 8 colonies in Transcaucasia (Georgia at that time): in the territory of the future Tiflis Governorate — Alexandersdorf (Aleksandrovskoye), Katharinenfeld (Ekaterinovka), Elisabethtal (Asureti), Marienfeld (Rosenfeld, Marino), Neu-Tiflis (New Tiflis, Michaelsdorf), Petersdorf (Petrovka); in the territory of the future Elisavetpol Governorate (present-day Azerbaijan) — Annenfeld (Annino, Shamkhor), Helenendorf (Elenino).

Staal, Karl Fyodorovich (Karl Gotthard) von (1774–1824) — civil governor of Georgia in 1815–1822.

### No. 74.

The first party of German weavers and cloth-makers from Saxony, as well as Alsace, Bohemia, and Moravia, arrived in Poltava in 1809 (see: Fleischhauer I. Op. cit. S. 163). The idea of attracting foreign artisans (workers) to Russia in order to establish separate craft (manufacturing) colonies practically never achieved the desired result. This time, too, it did not meet with success (see doc. No. 89). The country needed not so much workers (who were easier to find or train locally) as specialists and organizers of production. On the Poltava cloth-makers, see: Pavlov I.F. German colonies in Poltava Governorate in the 19th century. Poltava, 1913.

### No. 75.

The establishment in Georgia (Transcaucasia) of an Office for the settlement and administration of foreign colonists was proposed by the Minister of Internal Affairs in 1817 (see doc. No. 73, Art. 4). The Office, created in 1819, functioned under the civil governor of Georgia until 1841, after which the Transcaucasian colonies were subordinated to the local Expedition of State Domains. See: Tereshchenko A.G., Chernenko A.L. Russian Germans in the South of Russia and the Caucasus. Rostov-on-Don, 2000. Pp. 177–178.

### No. 76.

Scholarship has advanced the view that the sudden cessation of the admission of foreign settlers was caused by a reassessment on the part of the authorities of the entire half-century-long policy of foreign colonization of Russia, since the colonies had not brought the country the universal agricultural upsurge originally expected of them (see: Fleischhauer I. Op. cit. S. 174). If ruling circles indeed expected that the example of the German colonies would exert such a far-reaching beneficial influence on the Russian peasantry (and such hopes evidently did exist there), then the rulers were indulging in wholly groundless illusions. In reality, there were at that time no close contacts—nor could there have been—between the colonies and their neighbors, who farmed under entirely different conditions, if only because the German colonists had practically no knowledge of the local languages.

No known document from that period indicates that the authorities attempted to change this situation or even to introduce the colonists to the Russian language. The first tentative steps in this direction were taken only in the 1830s (see doc. No. 91), seventy years after the mass recruitment of colonists to Russia had begun. This, of course, can hardly be coincidental. Had the colonists mastered the local languages, they might well have tried, first and foremost, to impress upon their neighbors that serfdom, in whose grip those neighbors still had to live and farm, was hopelessly outdated and could in no way secure a "universal agricultural upsurge." The Russian authorities naturally sought to prevent the spread of such ideas at any cost, and it is entirely logical that the teaching of Russian to the colonists began to be seriously practiced only after the abolition of serfdom in 1861.

This act did not entail a complete halt to the influx of foreign colonists. In certain cases the authorities themselves introduced particular exceptions (an example being the settlement of Mennonites in the Volga region in the 1850s), and even more often those wishing to settle found ways to circumvent the restrictions imposed. In this connection, the mass influx of settlers into the South-Western governorates is especially notable, and it eventually gave rise to far-reaching consequences (see note to doc. No. 147).

### No. 77.

Along with a certain reassessment of values in matters concerning the colonists, it is difficult to find an exhaustive explanation for this document, as for the preceding one, unless one takes into account the general shift in policy during the final years of Alexander I's reign, when the emperor and his entourage moved ever further away from the markedly liberal "pro-European" course they had initially pursued.

Memorandum of August 5 — doc. No. 76.

### No. 78.

One of the principal reasons for the resettlement of the "Württemberg Separatists" to Russia was the conflict connected with their break from the Lutheran church. For them, unlike the Lutherans, the question of the form of the oath was just as fundamental as it was for the Herrnhuters or the Mennonites (see docs. No. 12 and 37). While living in Russia, the Transcaucasian religious separatists, though practically identical to the Lutherans in confession, never came under the jurisdiction of the Evangelical Lutheran General Consistory (see doc. No. 114, art. 869).

Manifesto of July 22, 1763 — doc. No. 11; regulations of 1804 — doc. No. 47; charter of September 6, 1800 — doc. No. 37.

### No. 79.

The document attests to the authorities' desire to move away from uniform norms for colonists' payments to the treasury, since such norms did not take into account the particular circumstances of the various colonies and, as a rule, proved unrealistic.

Decree of 1811 — doc. No. 60; report of February 20, 1804 — doc. No. 47; decree of September 27, 1806 — PSZRI. Coll. 1. No. 22293.

### No. 80.

The colonists settled near St. Petersburg in 1810 initially found themselves in a more favorable position than the first St. Petersburg colonists, since their settlement had been better planned and organized. By this point the condition of the first colonies had, at last, improved sufficiently for them to be placed on an equal footing with the later colonists in the repayment of the treasury debt.

Manifesto of July 22, 1763 — doc. No. 11; decree of August 17, 1793 — doc. No. 26; report of July 18, 1805 — doc. No. 52; opinion of March 12, 1812 — doc. No. 61; opinion of February 2, 1820 — doc. No. 79; statute of April 24, 1820 — PSZRI. Coll. 1. No. 28252.

### No. 81.

In effect, this act meant that the Livland colonists who had completed repayment of the treasury debt were placed on an equal footing, in terms of tax payments, with the state peasants of that area, as had earlier been prescribed with respect to the Saratov and the first Novorossiya colonists (see docs. No. 61, 65, and 71), although, given the local conditions of Livland mentioned in the document, this could not be carried out literally.

Regulations of February 20, 1804 — doc. No. 47.

### No. 82.

As is evident from the present act, the occasion for its adoption was the increasingly frequent settlement of foreign immigrants on landowners' and privately owned lands in the South-Western governorates. The decisions taken in this connection, as reflected in the document, undoubtedly reinforced this already noticeable process. Besides this important circumstance, the document is notable in that it raises, for the first time, the question of the justification for exempting colonists from conscription duty.

Decree of May 9, 1802 — doc. No. 40; report of April 12, 1804 — doc. No. 50; report of March 1, 1804 — doc. No. 49; manifesto of July 22, 1763 — doc. No. 11.

### No. 83.

The act established the procedure for repayment of the treasury debt by the Novorossiya colonists, and also provided for placing the second group of these colonists on an equal footing with the state peasants in the payment of taxes.

A.S. Pushkin, during his period of exile in the South, was among those called upon to combat the locust infestation of 1824 mentioned in the document (art. 2).

Rybalskaya (Fischersdorf) — a Lutheran colony east of Yekaterinoslav, founded in 1789 by immigrants from Germany as well as from the nearby colony of Josephstal; it was not mentioned in previous documents because its inhabitants were counted among the Josephstal colonists. It formed part of the Josephstal volost of Novomoskovsk district; in 1897 it had 474 inhabitants, including 412 Germans.

Miller (Miller von Rehfenstein), Georg — a colonist who, together with the colonists Vassal and Rouvier, concluded an agreement with the government in the early nineteenth century for the development of sheep-breeding in the south of Russia, under which fine-wooled merino sheep were imported from Spain. See: Fleischhauer I. Op. cit. S. 231.

Decree of March 22, 1818 — doc. No. 72; regulations of 1804 — doc. No. 47; report of December 18, 1808 — doc. No. 54.

### No. 84.

The present act in fact restored the institution of district commissioners, which had existed in the Volga colonies since 1768 and had been abolished together with the Saratov Office of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers in 1782. Both the overseers and the district commissioners reduced colonist self-government to a minimum and in practice held full authority in the colonies. See: Pleve I. Kreiskommissar // Germans of Russia: An Encyclopedia. Vol. 2. Pp. 218–219.

### No. 85.

The conflict between the Scottish missionaries and the German colonists had both objective roots (differences in social status and, correspondingly, in the value system) and subjective ones (the actions of the Scottish elder A. Paterson, referred to in the document as a pastor, although he had not officially been vested with that function in the colony). The measures prescribed in the present act did not lead to a normalization of the situation (see doc. No. 93).

Charter of December 25, 1806 — PSZRI. Coll. 1. No. 22410; statute of September 29, 1817 — doc. No. 68.

### No. 86.

Benckendorff, Alexander Khristoforovich (Konstantin Alexander Karl Wilhelm) von (1781–1844) — count, cavalry general; from 1826 to 1844, chief of the Corps of Gendarmes and head of the Third Section.

### No. 87.

The picture presented in the document—the unlawful deprivation of colonists of their lands, the arbitrary conduct of the overseer (in this case, one who had, moreover, been appointed illegally)—was highly typical not only of the Livland colonies but of all the foreign colonies.

Duhamel, Osip (Joseph) (1768–1840) — a Courland nobleman, civil governor of Livland from 1811 to 1827, later a senator.

Hagemeister, Ferdinand August Nikolaus Christoph von (1785–1869) — Wenden Ordnungsrichter from 1812 to 1839.

Decree of May 10, 1766 — doc. No. 18.

### No. 88.

Colonists from Chernigov who resettled in Yekaterinoslav governorate founded, in the Mariupol colonist district of Alexandrovsk county, five villages named after their mother colonies: Belye Vezhi, Gross-Werder (Great Werder, Marinovka), Kalchinovka, Klein-Werder (Yekaterinopol), and Rundewiese (Lugansk). These colonies were subsequently incorporated into the Alexandro-Nevskaya volost of Mariupol county. By the standards of the Novorossiya colonies they were of medium size: the population of Gross-Werder, the largest of them, was 502 in 1897, including 441 Germans.

Engel, Fyodor Ivanovich (1771–1837) — senator, member of the State Council.

Report of August 21, 1800 — doc. No. 36; opinion of March 12, 1812 — doc. No. 61; statute of December 15, 1828 — doc. No. 85; report of February 20, 1804 — doc. No. 47.

### No. 89.

The document attests to the desire of many colonists and artisans who had resettled from Prussia to the Kingdom of Poland, and who found themselves there in a difficult economic situation, to move on to the interior governorates of Russia. Whereas such colonists were often able to settle in the South-Western governorates, employment in Russia was frequently unavailable for the artisans (workers).

Dibich-Zabalkansky, I.I. — in 1830–1831, commander-in-chief of the army in Poland (see Biographical Notes).

Order of October 25, 1819 — doc. No. 76.

### No. 90.

This concerns the creation of the small colony of Samson (Peterhof county, Oranienbaum volost), named after the Samson Canal.

Report of February 20, 1804 — doc. No. 47; opinion of July 13, 1823 — doc. No. 80.

### No. 91.

It is notable that the initiative to create Russian schools in the Volga colonies came from the local authorities, evidently concerned about the isolation of the German colonists owing to their complete ignorance of the Russian language. The central authorities took little interest in this problem: they had no interest whatsoever in fostering contact between colonists—who sought to develop their farms according to the European models known to them from their forebears—and the surrounding serf peasantry. Tellingly, the Minister of Internal Affairs, concerned not with introducing the colonists to the Russian language but with their speedy repayment of treasury debts, reduced the proposed number of schools from five to two.

The schools, which in time came to be called central Russian schools, were ultimately established in the left-bank colony of Yekaterinenstadt, in the Yekaterinenstadt district, and in the right-bank colony of Lesnoy Karamysh (Grimm), in the Sosnovka district—the largest and most developed German villages on the Volga, which by 1834 already had 2,468 and 3,130 inhabitants respectively. These schools remained the only institutions of their kind in the German colonies of the Volga region. It is clear that two small schools (all the more so as they were conceived as temporary, as is evident from the document) could in no way train teachers with sufficient knowledge of Russian for the numerous colonist schools, let alone solve the problem of teaching this language to the hundreds of thousands of Volga colonists.

The first central schools in other regions were established in the Tavrida Mennonite colonies of Orlov (1829) and Halbstadt (1835), in the Yekaterinoslav Mennonite colony of Khortitsa (1842), in the Bessarabian Lutheran colony of Sarata (1844), and in the Tavrida Lutheran colony of Prishib (1846). See: Cherkazyanova I. Obrazovanie. Obrazovanie do 1917 // Germans of Russia: An Encyclopedia. Vol. 2. P. 673.

### No. 92.

The Elton salt-hauling route, running from Lake Elton westward to the Volga, arose even before the arrival of German colonists in the Volga region. Thus Pokrovskaya Sloboda (now the city of Engels) was founded by Ukrainian chumaks (salt haulers) in 1747. The lands of the left-bank German colonies bordered on the route both from the north (Krasny Yar district) and from the south (Tarlyk district).

This act attests that the problem of allotting the Volga colonists additional convenient land in proportion to the number of male souls registered in the census had still not been resolved by 1833, even as the number of colonists had grown rapidly since the end of the eighteenth century. This was what gave rise to instances of the colonists seizing land without authorization. There was no "excessive endowment of the colonists," as the document puts it—nothing of the sort; the colonists "constantly did nothing but demand and occupy new lands" precisely because these lands, in the promised amount, had never actually been allotted to them, despite a whole series of acts adopted in this connection by the very highest authorities.

Decree of December 4, 1797 — doc. No. 30; decree of December 19, 1802 — doc. No. 42.

### No. 93.

After an attempt at compromise in 1828 (see doc. No. 85), the authorities had to take radical measures to resolve the conflict between the Scottish missionaries and the German colonists who lived together in the North Caucasian colony of Karras.

Rosen, Roman Fyodorovich (Robert Fabian) von (1782–1848) — chief administrator in Georgia from 1832 to 1835.

Charter of December 25, 1806 — PSZRI. Coll. 1. No. 22410; statute of December 15, 1828 — doc. No. 85.

### No. 94.

The document attests that school education in the Volga (as in other) German colonies was at that time entirely under the control of the local clergy. Given the significance of this act, an account of it was included as a special appendix to the Statute on Colonies of 1857 (doc. No. 115). In the present edition that appendix has been omitted and the document is published in full. The Statute of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in Russia of December 28, 1832, cited in this act (§§ 1 and 2), was incorporated into the Statutes on the Spiritual Affairs of Foreign Confessions of 1857 (doc. No. 114, Book 2, Section I).

### No. 95.

The document shows that the previous decision on this matter, taken five years earlier (doc. No. 92), had still not been fully implemented. Meanwhile, the foreign colonies had been transferred from the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Internal Affairs to the newly created Ministry of State Domains, and the new minister in charge, P.D. Kiselyov, having visited the Volga region, personally saw for himself the severity of the problem. This is why the present act is far more realistic than the preceding one. It is noteworthy that provision was now made to allot the colonists additional land on the basis of 15 desiatinas per soul as counted in the most recent, 8th census, rather than 20 desiatinas per soul of the 5th census, as had been repeatedly promised earlier, beginning in 1797. According to the 5th census (1788), the Volga colonies had 15,607 male souls; according to the 8th (1834), 55,175. Thus, even allowing for the reduction in the per-soul allotment, the colonists were owed 2.7 times more land.

The resolution of the problem of the Elton salt-hauling route was of the greatest significance for the northern colonies of the Tarlyk district, whose lands directly bordered the route: Brabander (Kozitskoye), Deller (Beryozovka), Bangerdt (Zaumorye), Stahl (Stepnoye), and Kukkus (Volskoye).

Decree of December 4, 1797 — doc. No. 30; statute of May 21, 1835 — doc. No. 92.

### No. 96.

The colony of Novye Mezirichi (Neu-Meseritz), founded in 1833 and subsequently forming part of the Golubovka volost of Surazh county, Chernigov governorate, represents one of the few examples of the relatively successful creation in Russia of a purely artisanal (manufacturing) foreign colony. It is true, however, that the German colonists themselves made up only a small part of the colony's population: thus, in 1859 there were 348 inhabitants here, including 73 Germans.

### No. 97.

The proposal to establish, alongside the colony of Halbstadt (Molochansk) in the Molochna Mennonite district of Berdyansk county, a special settlement for landless peasants, allowing them to engage in crafts, was put forward by the well-known Mennonite figure I.I. Cornies (see Biographical Notes). The idea did not meet with support from all local Mennonites—many were unwilling to give up part of the land needed to settle the artisans. In addition, the settlers lacked sufficient means to set up craft workshops, and Cornies himself had to make substantial donations for this purpose. In the end, in 1842, 800 prospective artisans were settled on the eastern outskirts of Halbstadt, which gave impetus to the development of crafts among the Molochna Mennonites. See: Essays on the History of the Germans and Mennonites of Southern Ukraine (Late 18th–First Half of the 19th Century) / Ed. S.I. Bobyleva. Dnepropetrovsk, 1999. Pp. 119–120.

Nevertheless, it is rather difficult to speak of the complete success of this project. In the colony thus created, which was at first called "Halbstadt Artisanal" and later Neu-Halbstadt (Novo-Molochansk), there lived 150 people in 1864 and 185 in 1886. In other words, the bulk of the settled artisans evidently did not remain there for long. Indeed, the intention to create a settlement of 200 households looked quite problematic from the outset, considering that even Halbstadt, the largest colony in the area, had only 352 inhabitants in 1838. The idea that settling artisans together "would give them the means to jointly contribute to mutual improvement," as asserted in the present act, is likewise questionable. Experience shows that artisans need close contact not so much with one another as with their customers, and hence the settlement of artisans in ordinary, predominantly agrarian, colonies allowed crafts to develop quite successfully. It is another matter that the concentration of artisans in one place could, over time, contribute to the emergence of manufacturing and certain branches of industry. This is precisely what happened both in Neu-Halbstadt and in a number of other colonies.

Köppen, P.I. — from 1838, head of a division of the 3rd Department of the Ministry of State Domains (see Biographical Notes).

### No. 98.

The colony of Annenfeld (Shamkhor), founded in 1818, subsequently formed part of the Annenfeld volost of Yelisavetpol county, Yelisavetpol governorate. In time, the inhabitants of Annenfeld managed to adapt to the unfavorable natural and climatic conditions, and their numbers grew fairly rapidly—from 183 people in 1843 to 860, including 665 Germans, in 1897.

### No. 99.

The Werner Central School (later the Werner Teachers' Seminary) opened in the Bessarabian colony of Sarata in 1844. It was one of the first schools in southern Russia to train teachers for colonist schools from among the sons of colonists. A special building was constructed for it. By the beginning of the twentieth century the school had four grades. Among its graduates was Karl Adam Wilhelm (1849–1929), editor and publisher of the newspaper Odessaer Zeitung, one of the organizers of the movement among the German population of southern Russia for the preservation of its national identity. See: Plesskaya E. Vernerovskoye tsentralnoye uchilishche // Germans of Russia: An Encyclopedia. Vol. 1. P. 348.

### No. 100.

The organizers of the German Charitable Society in Odessa, founded in 1845, were subjects of various German states. In 1855 the society had 106 members. After German unification (1871), the society operated under the auspices of the German consulate, and in 1874 its new charter was confirmed. See: Plesskaya-Zebold E.G. Odessa Germans, 1803–1920. Odessa, 1999. Pp. 317–318.

### No. 101.

The board of trustees was created on the initiative of the Protestant communities of Moscow in 1845. In 1869 an almshouse was organized under its auspices, and from 1885 the society was under the patronage of Grand Duchess Maria Pavlovna. See: Germans of Russia: An Encyclopedia. Vol. 1. P. 207.

The three evangelical parishes of Moscow mentioned in the act (arts. 1, 16, 19) are the parishes of the Lutheran Church of St. Michael (in existence since 1575), the Lutheran Church of Sts. Peter and Paul (since 1626), and the Reformed church (since 1635).

### No. 102.

The question of whether the departure of colonists abroad required the permission of the Senate arose at that time in connection with the revolutions of 1848–1849 in a number of European countries, including Germany and Austria. Under these conditions the Russian authorities sought to eliminate any possibility of revolutionary ideas—let alone their bearers—penetrating the country. The present act confirmed the exception to the rules on departure that existed for colonists, in contrast to foreign immigrants of other estates: the Board of Trustees for Foreign Settlers of the Southern Region of Russia could, as before, grant permission to leave at its own discretion.

This decision applied only to colonists departing abroad permanently. However, as is evident from doc. No. 112, on May 24, 1849, measures were also adopted with respect to the temporary departure of colonists: in order to restrict it "until calm and order are restored in Europe," it was prescribed that "the Highest permission" be sought each time for such absences. This question appeared far more fundamental to the Russian authorities of the time, since the likelihood of undesirable ideas penetrating the country was much greater in the case of temporary absences.

### No. 103.

In fact, the Mennonites were settled at that time not in two districts of Saratov governorate, as had been envisaged in this act (Art. 8), but only in Novouzensk district. From 1854 several Mennonite colonies were established here, forming the Malyshinsky district (later Malyshinskaya volost): Gansau (Kamennoye), Köppental (Surki), Lindenau (Ovrazhnoye), Fresenheim (Sukhodolnoye). In the 1860s—1870s they were joined by the colonies of Hohendorf (Vysokoye), Lisandergei, Orlov, Ostenfeld (Porki), Medemtal (Gusevka), and Valuyevka. Almost all of these colonies were named in honor of specific figures — Academician P.I. Köppen, G.G. Orlov, Minister of State Domains P.A. Valuev, and colonial officials E.F. Hahn, A. Frese, F.S. Lisander, G.A. Osten-Sacken, and N.N. Medem. By the standards of the Volga colonies, these villages were very small. Even in Köppental, the largest of them, the maximum number of inhabitants was only 311 (1910). The development of these colonies was hindered above all by the lack of available land — they were situated in a narrow strip taken from the Elton salt-transport road (see docs. No. 92 and 95), and were therefore called the "Colonies along the road."

### No. 104.

By the time this act was adopted, the European revolutionary storms of 1848—1849 had long since subsided, and the authorities considered it possible to lift the restrictions then in force on the temporary travel of colonists abroad (see doc. No. 112). However, Nicholas I did not approve a complete lifting of the restrictions — an extremely rare case of a Russian emperor expressing his own particular opinion on a serious matter concerning the German colonists. This shows the importance Nicholas attached to this problem, despite the fact that temporary trips abroad by colonists were a rather infrequent occurrence.

### No. 105.

The colony of Riebensdorf (in Russian, Rybinskoye or Rybnoye) in Ostrogozhsk district of Voronezh governorate was a rare case of a completely isolated German settlement, surrounded on all sides by the lands of Russian villages. In the Riebensdorf volost, where the colony was located, only a small German offshoot settlement, Pavlovsky (82 inhabitants in 1905), eventually appeared, along with a few tiny hamlets (apiaries, a mill). Given the natural growth of the population and the absence of nearby available land, the inhabitants of Riebensdorf who wished to continue farming had to establish numerous daughter settlements in various regions of southern Russia. Hence the sharp decline in the population of Riebensdorf in the second half of the nineteenth century — from 2,285 people in 1868 to 1,056 in 1900.

This act concerns the establishment of the colony of Michelstal (Vorontsovskoye), which subsequently belonged to Yeisk district of Kuban Region. The colony was located southwest of Yeisk, at some distance from the Yeisk estuary. By the standards of its region, Michelstal was a fairly large colony — 713 inhabitants in 1897, including 488 Germans.

### No. 106.

The oldest colony in Transcaucasia, Marienfeld (Maryino), founded in 1817 east of Tiflis, was part of the Marienfeld volost of Tiflis district, Tiflis governorate, and was a medium-sized Transcaucasian colony — 412 inhabitants in 1886, including 396 Germans. Because the sites were unprepared for settlement, because of unfavorable natural and climatic conditions, raids by mountain tribesmen, and so on, the inhabitants of Marienfeld, like those of the other Transcaucasian colonies, remained in a difficult material situation right up until the second half of the nineteenth century.

### No. 107.

The drafting of a new plan for the best-known Volga colony, Yekaterinenstadt, in Yekaterinenstadt district (later Yekaterinenstadt volost) of Nikolayevsk district, Samara governorate, was prompted by the rapid growth of its population (from 720 people in 1798 to 3,669 in 1850), as well as by the construction of a stone Evangelical church. The church was erected on the central street leading to the Volga. For this occasion the street was widened, and on the site of the former wooden church a large public garden was laid out, in which a monument to Catherine II was erected at the same time. All this required the relocation of some houses, which is mentioned in the present act.

### No. 108.

The famous Annenschule (the school attached to the St. Petersburg Evangelical Lutheran Church of St. Anne) opened in 1736. Its first teacher and director was Johann Leonhard Schattner (1677—1741), the first pastor of the Church of St. Anne. In 1780 the parish school was transformed into a 6-grade municipal school. The Annenschule was maintained with funds from the parishioners of the Church of St. Anne. Children of various confessions were admitted to the school, which had both boys' and girls' divisions. From 1833, on the initiative of Director Alexander Eriksen, a transition to a gymnasium curriculum began, and education gradually acquired a classical orientation. By the end of the nineteenth century the Annenschule consisted of boys' and girls' gymnasiums, a Realschule division, and two elementary schools — for boys and for girls (1,800 pupils in total). Among those who studied here were the sculptor R.R. Bach, the artist A.K. Beggrov, the educator K.I. Lyugebil, the physician E.E. Eichwald, the philologist V.Ya. Propp, the director S.E. Raddov, the historian V.V. Struve, the jurist A.F. Koni, and the actor S.A. Martinson. See: Dedyulin, V. Annenschule // Germans of Russia: An Encyclopedia. Vol. 1. Pp. 59—60.

### No. 109.

Following the first groups of New Russian colonists (see docs. No. 71 and 83), this act equalized the tax payments of all German colonists of New Russia and Bessarabia with those of state peasants. The only exception was made for the Mennonites, who continued to retain special privileges.

### No. 110.

The document shows that the Ministry of State Domains, headed by P.D. Kiselyov, took a more active interest in the problem of teaching the Volga colonists the Russian language than did the Ministry of Internal Affairs, which had formally sanctioned the previous act on this matter (doc. No. 91). Evidently the Minister of State Domains, being a proponent of the abolition of serfdom in Russia, understood that afterward the isolation of the colonists caused by their ignorance of the Russian language would lose all basis and justification.

Graduates of the two central schools in the Volga colonies, having mastered the teaching of a number of subjects in Russian in accordance with the present act and the regulation of June 27, 1858 (doc. No. 116), made their contribution to teaching the colonists this language, but were of course unable to achieve a fundamental turnaround in this respect. This was impossible so long as the colonists' economy remained largely self-contained, not requiring them to communicate systematically in Russian.

The regulation of November 7, 1833 — doc. No. 91.

### No. 111.

The document reflects the considerable attention paid by the new emperor Alexander II and his entourage to various spheres of economic activity.

Tobacco growing was very widely developed in the German colonies of the Volga's left bank, especially in their northern part, which belonged to Nikolayevsk district. As a result, a tobacco factory had already appeared in the colony of Yekaterinenstadt in the 1790s, and colonists' tobacco achieved distribution throughout all Russia.

Solothurn (Wittmann) was one of the largest colonies of Panino district (later Panino volost); as early as 1850, 1,416 people were living here. This circumstance, combined with the growing shortage of land and the prevalence of tobacco growing in the district, prompted the colonists to organize the "Volga Tobacco Factory" on a cooperative basis, which is discussed in this act. It supplied various regions of the Volga area and Orenburg territory with large quantities of smoking tobacco, cigars, and cigarettes. See: Dietz, Ya.E. Op. cit. P. 266.

### No. 112.

The document finally abolished the restrictions on the temporary travel of colonists abroad that had been introduced in 1849 and partially retained in 1852 at the insistence of Nicholas I (see doc. No. 104). By this point these restrictions had become an obvious anachronism, all the more so since the new emperor, unlike his "late" father, sought to pursue a liberal policy.

### No. 113.

The educational institution for poor boys attached to the St. Petersburg Evangelical Lutheran Church of St. Peter, opened in 1856, was given the name of the Alexander School and was designed for 38 pupils. See: Ivanova, N.I. Germans in St. Petersburg and Its Environs. St. Petersburg, 1999. P. 16.

### No. 114.

This document contains complete information on the statutes of the Russian Empire issued up to its appearance (1857) concerning practically all the confessions that spread among the Russian Germans. The one notable exception is the Baptists, officially legalized in Russia in 1879, that is, after this act was issued, and who numbered 19,900 adherents among the country's German population in 1897 (1.1% of that population).

The present edition omits fragments of the document that have no bearing on the Germans, as well as the articles devoted to the Catholic monastic clergy (Arts. 78—88) and the administration of monastic properties (Arts. 126—128), since colonists in Russia were forbidden to establish monasteries.

It is worth noting that the portion of the document devoted to Catholicism is considerably smaller in volume than the Evangelical Lutheran portion. This is due above all to the fact that many aspects of the Catholic Church's activity were regulated not by Russian legislation but directly by the Holy See (by agreement between it and the Russian government). It evidently also played a role that the Evangelical Lutheran Church was noticeably more influential in the Russian Empire than the Catholic Church: the Lutheran confession was not uncommon in the very highest strata of society and even among members of the imperial family.

In 1897 there were 242,200 Catholics (13.5%) among the German population of Russia. Russian Germans of the Catholic faith belonged for the most part to parishes attached either to the Archdiocese of Mogilev (mostly townspeople) or to the Diocese of Tiraspol (colonists, some townspeople). In the Diocese of Tiraspol they constituted the great majority of the parishioners. The Archdiocese of Mogilev was founded in 1782; the Diocese of Tiraspol (known until 1852 as the Diocese of Kherson) was created in 1847, and from 1856 its seat was located in Saratov (Arts. 12, 13).

The German colonists' parishes of the Diocese of Tiraspol belonged to the following deaneries: Saratov (Saratov and Samara governorates), Kamenka (Saratov governorate), Yekaterinenstadt, Marienthal, Zelman (all in Samara governorate), Berdyansk (Taurida and Yekaterinoslav governorates, Don Cossack Host Region), Yekaterinoslav (Yekaterinoslav, Taurida, and Kherson governorates), Simferopol (Taurida governorate), Nikolayev (Kherson and Yekaterinoslav governorates), Odessa (Kherson governorate), and Pyatigorsk (Kuban Region) (Art. 15).

The Archdiocese of Mogilev was headed until 1917 exclusively by Poles or Lithuanians. By contrast, among the heads of the Diocese of Tiraspol there was only one Pole — Wincenty Lipski (1795—1875), who administered the diocese in 1864—1872. All its other heads were German bishops: Ferdinand Helanus Kahn (1787—1864) — 1850—1864, Franz Xaver von Zottmann (1826—1901) — 1872—1889, Anton Johannes Zerr von Padua (1849—1934) — 1889—1901, Eduard Yulyevich (Eduard Michael Johann) von der Ropp (1851—1939) — 1902—1903, Joseph Aloysius Kessler (1862—1933) — 1904—1929. Kahn was born in Galicia, Zottmann in Germany, von der Ropp in Courland, while Zerr and Kessler came from Russian German colonist families (Art. 16).

The theological seminary of the Diocese of Tiraspol, founded in 1856, was located in Saratov. From 1865 all subjects, except the Russian language, Russian literature, and Russian history, were taught here in German. By 1882, 68 priests, including 49 Germans, had graduated from the seminary. The seminary was opened on the initiative and with the participation of Bishop Kahn. Among those who studied there and subsequently served as its professors and inspectors were the future bishops Zottmann (the first professor of German origin), Zerr, and Kessler; Zottmann was also rector of the seminary (Art. 102).

In 1897 there were 1,360,800 Lutherans (76.0%) among the German population of Russia. The basis of the Lutheran portion of the present document was the Statute of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Russia of December 28, 1832, together with the accompanying Instruction to the Lutheran Clergy (PSZRI. Coll. 2. Nos. 5870 and 5871).

The term "preachers" (проповедники) used in this document (as in many other Russian-language documents) with reference to Evangelical Lutheran pastors (Art. 136 and following) is incorrect. In German the word "preacher" (Prediger) was customarily used for Lutheran clergy who had not been ordained or who served military units, or for clergy of certain Protestant confessions (Mennonites, Baptists, etc.) that reject church hierarchy. In Russian (if one wishes to avoid using the foreign word "pastor") Lutheran pastors should be called parish priests, as is done in the Catholic portion of the present document, or simply priests.

The colonies had the following provostal districts: the Volga region (Moscow Evangelical Lutheran Consistory) — Right Bank (the upland side of the Volga; Saratov governorate) and Left Bank (the meadow side of the Volga; Samara governorate); the south of Russia (St. Petersburg Evangelical Lutheran Consistory) — 1st South Russian (Bessarabia Region, Kherson governorate) and 2nd South Russian (Yekaterinoslav, Taurida, and Kherson governorates, Don Cossack Host and Kuban Regions) (Art. 401).

The lay presidents of the Evangelical Lutheran General Consistory were: Pavel Ivanovich (Paul) von Tiesenhausen (1774—1864) — 1833—1845, Yegor Fyodorovich (Georg Otto Wilhelm) von Meyendorff (1794—1879) — 1845—1879, Theodor Bruhn — 1880—1888, Fyodor Karlovich (Theodor) Giers (1824—1891) — 1888—1891, Alexander Alexandrovich (Alexander Karl Abraham) von Uexküll-Gyllenband (1840—1912) — 1891—1896, Emil von Scholtz (1841—1913) — 1897—1913, Yuly Alexandrovich (Julius Karl) von Uexküll-Gyllenband (1852—1918), brother of A.A. von Uexküll-Gyllenband — 1914—1917. The spiritual vice-presidents and general superintendents of the Evangelical Lutheran General Consistory were: Johann Friedrich August Vollborth (1768—1840) — 1832—1840, Friedrich Nikolaus von Paucker (1778—1856) — 1840—1856, Karl Christian Ulmann (1793—1871) — 1856—1868, Yuly Ivanovich (Julius Wilhelm Theophil) von Richter (1808—1892) — 1868—1892, Konrad Reimund Freifeld (1847—1923) — 1892—1918. Vollborth was born in Germany, Paucker and Richter in Courland, Ulmann and Freifeld in Livonia. Vollborth became a Doctor of Theology at Dorpat; Ulmann, Richter, and Freifeld studied at the University of Dorpat, where Ulmann also served as professor of theology and rector (Art. 452).

In 1897 there were 64,000 persons (3.6%) of the Reformed faith among the German population of Russia. In addition to the Evangelical Reformed parishes mentioned in this document, such parishes also existed in Russia in Vologda and Yaroslavl (1670—1704), in Odessa (from 1844), in the Volga colonies — North Yekaterinenstadt (1768—1905), Kukkus (from 1767), and others, and in the colonies of southern Russia — Rohrbach-Worms (from 1861), Neudorf (from 1862), and Shabo (from 1846).
