Reformed sessions [committees] existed in the St. Petersburg, Moscow, Courland, and Livonia Evangelical Lutheran Consistories (Art. 790).

The French and German Evangelical Reformed communities in St. Petersburg formed a single body from 1775 to 1858 (Art. 798); the French community was founded in 1724, the German community in 1775 (Art. 799).

The Evangelical Reformed parish in Moscow existed from 1635 (Art. 812); the Reformed parish in Arkhangelsk existed from 1660 (the Lutheran one from 1686) (Art. 834).

The first Evangelical Lutheran parishes in the German colonies of Transcaucasia arose in 1825—1832 (Art. 859).

Until 1884 the chief pastors (Oberpastoren) of the Transcaucasian colonies were, as a rule, the pastors of the colonist community of Tiflis (the colony of Neu-Tiflis): Johannes Bernhard Saltet (1792—1830) — 1825—1830, August Heinrich Dittrich (1797—1855) — 1833—1838, Christoph Heinrich Bonwetsch (1804—1876) — 1838—1845, Johannes Huppenbauer (1816—1887) — 1845—1851, Christian Gottlieb Roth (1802—1872) — 1852—1853, 1858—1864, Alexander Martin Geyer (1820—?) — 1853—1858, Karl Rudolph Roos (1825—1910) — 1865—1884; in 1884—1905 — the pastor of the colony of Yelenendorf, Markus Miller (1847—1905), who was killed during the revolutionary disturbances; in 1905—1909 — the pastor from Yelenendorf, Oskar Georg Rudolph von Wiren (1866—1950); in 1910—1915 — Heinrich Heinzelmann (1865—?), a former pastor of the colonies of Alexandershilf (Alexandrovo), Elisabethtal, and Yekaterinenfeld, who was exiled to Siberia in 1915. Owing to the peculiarities of religious life in the Transcaucasian colonies, the origins of the chief pastors here differed considerably from what was usual at that time for the Evangelical Lutheran churches of Russia. Saltet, Dittrich, Bonwetsch, Huppenbauer, Roth, and Miller were graduates of the Basel Mission Society; all of them, except Miller, a native of Switzerland, were born in Germany. Only from the second half of the nineteenth century did natives of the Russian Empire, graduates of the University of Dorpat — Geyer, Roos, von Wiren (Heinzelmann's origin has not been established) — begin to occupy the post of chief pastor in Transcaucasia (Art. 874).

The five colonies near Tiflis are the colonies of Tiflis governorate: Neu-Tiflis, Elisabethtal, Yekaterinenfeld, Marienfeld, and Alexandersdorf (Art. 877).

The Evangelical Brethren community (Herrnhuter community) in Sarepta arose in 1765 and existed until 1894, when it merged into the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Russia (Art. 885).

The Evangelical community in the colony of Karras (Stavropol governorate, later Terek Region) arose in 1805; until 1825 it was served by Scottish clergy, and thereafter by German clergy; from 1866 it was served by the Pyatigorsk parish (Art. 899).

In 1897 there were 65,900 Mennonites (3.7%) among the German population of Russia (Art. 903).

### No. 115.

This document is not the first attempt to codify the numerous statutes on the colonies of foreigners in the Russian Empire. In a number of earlier acts published in the present edition, earlier codes of the corresponding laws are mentioned under various names. Thus doc. No. 112 refers to the Regulations on the Colonies of Foreigners of 1842.

The Statute of 1857 became the best known — it was the latest and most complete code of laws of this kind. Thereafter it was amended annually in accordance with newly adopted statutes, but no other such statute ever again appeared, and from 1871, when the colonist status was abolished, the need for one disappeared as well.

The present publication omits fragments not relating to the German colonies, as well as Arts. 543—577, devoted to German colonists whom it was planned to settle on landowners' estates in Transcaucasia (this measure produced no notable results), and the appendix to Art. 387, which sets out the content of the document we publish as No. 94.

The German colony in Stavropol governorate near the mineral waters is the German part of the colony of Karras, founded by Scottish missionaries. The German colony near the town of St. Cross (now the town of Budyonnovsk) and the colony of the Basel missionaries near the town of Shusha (Nagorno-Karabakh) are not, strictly speaking, separate colonies: these settlements were located within the territory of the towns named (Art. 2).

The Tsarskoye Selo colonist-manufacturers are the inhabitants of the small colony of Friedental in Tsarskoye Selo district. The colony of Alexandriyskaya (Alexandrovka) belonged to Oranienbaum volost, Peterhof district, and was, by the standards of the St. Petersburg colonies, of medium size — 700 inhabitants in 1897, including 348 Germans (Art. 84).

In 1852 the German colony near Tiflis (Neu-Tiflis) had not yet been definitively incorporated into the city — see doc. No. 122 (Art. 92).

On the presence of Germans in Jewish colonies, see: Feldman, D.Z. The Role of German Colonists in the Formation and Development of Jewish Agricultural Colonies in Southern Russia // The Germans of Russia in the Context of National History: General Problems and Regional Peculiarities. Moscow, 1999. Pp. 120—145 (Art. 108).

### No. 116.

The central school in Yekaterinenstadt was established in place of the Russian schools in Yekaterinenstadt and Lesnoy Karamysh (Grimm). Subsequently a central school was also established in Lesnoy Karamysh (doc. No. 125). The curriculum of the central schools differed from that of the earlier schools in that it provided for instruction in Russian not only in reading, writing, and the Law of God (see doc. No. 110), but also in a number of other subjects.

The regulation of November 7, 1833 — doc. No. 91.

### No. 117.

This concerns the daughter settlements established in 1834—1836 northeast of Novgorod by émigrés from Novosaratovka and other St. Petersburg colonies. The Novgorod settlements belonged to Novo-Nikolayevskaya and Vysokovskaya volosts of Novgorod district. The colony of Gorelovo was small, while Alexandrovskoye and Nikolayevskoye (Novo-Nikolayevka) were rather large by the standards of the St. Petersburg colonies: Alexandrovskoye had 486 inhabitants (1885), and Nikolayevskoye had 966 inhabitants in 1897, including 924 Germans.

### No. 118.

This act established the last settlement of foreign colonists on state lands in Russia. In 1859—1866 Prussian Mennonites, together with settlers from New Russia, established 7 villages in Samara district, forming the Mennonite district (later Alexandertal volost): Alexandertal (Alexandrodar), Neuhoffnung (Nadezhdino), Marienthal (Maryevka), Grossfeld (Krotovka), Muravyevka, Orlov, and Marienau (later incorporated into the village of Krasnovka). Alexandertal had 365 inhabitants in 1897; the other villages were even smaller.

At the same time, in the same district, the Lutheran villages of Konstantinovka district (later Konstantinovka volost) arose, established by settlers from Poland and the eastern regions of Germany: Kaiserstal, Strassburg, Hoffental, Gross-Konstantinovka (Bolshaya Konstantinovka), Gross-Peterhof (Bolshaya Petrovka), Gross-Romanov (Bolshaya Romanovka), Nikolayevka, Bergtal (Dolinovka), Reinischfeld, Rosental (Rozovka), Klein-Konstantinovka (Malaya Konstantinovka), Klein-Romanov (Malaya Romanovka), and Rettungstal (Georgiyevka). The largest among them was the village of Hoffental — 574 inhabitants in 1897, including 561 Germans.

### No. 119.

The auxiliary funds (Hilfskassen), which were established over time in all colonist districts, provided colonists with cheap credit and also managed orphans' money. The funds paid 4% annually on deposits and charged 6% on loans, building up reserve capital from the difference. Colonists who used the credit of the auxiliary funds accumulated growing debt. See: Brandes D. Colonist Landownership and Land Use // Germans of Russia: An Encyclopedia. Vol. 2. Pp. 149–150.

### No. 120.

The implementation of this act, which conformed to European legislative standards, substantially expanded the commercial activity of foreigners, chiefly Germans, in Russia. Many of the Europeans who came to the country, having joined merchant guilds, acquired real property or taken over its management, settled in Russia for a long time or permanently.

### No. 121.

This act shows that the problem of settling foreigners in Crimea, which had already been placed on the agenda at the beginning of the 19th century (see doc. No. 45), remained relevant in connection with the continued emigration of Tatars abroad. The document was aimed not only at temporary but also at permanent attraction of foreigners, and as a result, from the second half of the 19th century, many small German settlements appeared in Crimea, especially in its central and northern parts.

### No. 122.

The document completed the incorporation of the predominantly artisanal German colony of Nei-Tiflis (New Tiflis) into the city. This process had begun in 1852 (see doc. No. 115, art. 92, note). The colony of Nei-Tiflis was small — 257 inhabitants in 1843. Subsequently the population on its territory began to grow rapidly (to 2,500 people in 1900), but mainly not through Germans.

### No. 123.

The increase in dues under this document was intended to speed up the completion of the repayment of the treasury debt by the colonists of southern Russia.

Hoffnungstal (Tsebrikovo) — a colony of Hoffnungstal volost, Tiraspol district, located northeast of Tiraspol, founded in 1819, 1,145 inhabitants (1859).

Herzenberg (Kizilnik) — a colony of Zürichtal district (later Salyn volost, Feodosia district), located north of Feodosia, founded in 1804, 39 inhabitants (1858).

### No. 124.

By introducing strict sanctions, the authorities sought to curb the unauthorized resettlement of colonists from one governorate to another. Amid an increasingly acute shortage of land, especially in the Volga region, with its rapidly growing colonist population and archaic system of per-capita land use, this process had taken on wide proportions. The document had no appreciable effect: only a few years later, in 1871, colonist status was abolished (see doc. No. 129), and with it disappeared the main obstacle to the widespread resettlement of former colonists across the territory of Russia.

### No. 125.

The consolidation of two Russian schools for colonists into a single central school in Ekaterinstadt, undertaken in 1858 (see doc. No. 116), somewhat improved the quality of training for teachers with knowledge of Russian for colonist schools, but aggravated their shortage in the Volga colonies of the right bank, for which teachers had previously been trained mainly in Lesnoi Karamysh.

On the other hand, by this point the right-bank colonies had accumulated significant resettlement capital, which had been formed since 1854 from leasing out the additional allotment granted to them on the left bank. The initiative to create such capital for financing future resettlement came from the Saratov Office of Foreign Settlers. Initially it was spent by the colonists themselves, but from 1862 the Ministry of State Domains intervened in its distribution, and soon the colonists were not even informed about the use of the capital. Fearing they would lose it, they demanded the creation, at the expense of the resettlement capital, of a central school in Lesnoi Karamysh, in response to which this act appeared. See: Pleve I. Resettlement Capital // Germans of Russia: An Encyclopedia. Vol. 2. Pp. 30–31.

### No. 126.

The auxiliary fund of Evangelical Lutheran parishes, established in 1859, provided substantial support to the Lutheran churches of Russia and their clergy. In particular, the fund's resources significantly accelerated the establishment of new parishes. This can be seen in the example of Bessarabia, where after 1858 the parishes of Benkendorf, Eigenheim, Nei-Sarata, and Alboto were formed. Tarutino was not only the largest German colony in Bessarabia (1,938 inhabitants in 1859) but also the center of the oldest Bessarabian Evangelical Lutheran parish, founded in 1815.

Over the first 50 years of its activity, the fund provided significant assistance in the construction or repair of 206 churches, 318 schools and prayer houses, and 100 parsonages; it supported 200 parishes and 500 schools, and financed the training of 100 pastors and 350 kusters (sextons). See: Luther's Legacy in Russia. Moscow, 2003. P. 19.

### No. 127.

This act began the process of transferring the colonies to the jurisdiction of the general administrative bodies, completed in 1871 (see doc. No. 129). In Samara governorate it affected the colonists who had settled in Samara district since the late 1850s (see doc. No. 118). Now only the remaining colonies of the Volga region, the colonies of southern Russia, Transcaucasia, and Livonia remained under the jurisdiction of special administrative bodies.

### No. 128.

By removing the intermediate authorities (the Saratov Office, the Guardianship Committee, and the overseers of the colonies of southern Russia) from issuing passports to foreign settlers for travel from the colonies to other colonies or other settlements in the country, the authorities helped simplify this procedure. Along with administrative countermeasures against the increasingly intense migration of colonists (see doc. No. 124), this was another measure intended to bring order to this process.

### No. 129.

This document is among the most important state acts concerning Russian Germans. It determined the future fate of hundreds of thousands of former German colonists for decades to come. The Regulations of 1871 belong to a series of reform laws of the reign of Alexander II intended to modernize the entire system of agrarian relations, a process begun by the Peasant Reform of 1861.

Except for Sarepta, which is covered by a proviso in art. 1 of the Regulations, the document also did not apply to the Transcaucasian and Livonian colonies, although they had been established on state lands. Special acts were subsequently adopted for all these groups of colonists (see docs. No. 136, 161, 162).

The document was drafted over a number of years by a representative commission that included such an expert on colonist affairs as A.A. Klaus, a high-ranking official of the Ministry of State Domains and himself descended from the colonists of southern Russia, author of the book *Our Colonies: Experiments and Materials on the History and Statistics of Foreign Colonization in Russia* (St. Petersburg, 1869). After the commission presented the results of its work to this ministry, the Regulations were discussed and revised for several more years in the higher state bodies. See: Fleischhauer I. Op. cit. Pp. 281–284.

As often happens, such a lengthy process of preparation and coordination did not benefit the document. It is marked by neither clarity nor consistency. Even the new concept it introduces, "peasant-proprietors (former colonists)," is quite ambiguous, which had significant consequences later on (see doc. No. 149). Proceeding from the well-meaning intention to bring colonists as close as possible in legal status to Russian peasants of other estates, while at the same time preserving, as far as possible, the tried-and-tested system of organization and self-government of the colonies (insofar as it is even appropriate to speak of self-government under the extremely strict regulation prescribed by the Colony Statute of 1857), the authorities ultimately arrived at a number of highly questionable decisions.

Thus, the Regulations provide that all record-keeping at village and volost assemblies of the former colonies and in the corresponding volost courts be conducted only in Russian (art. 4, para. i), a language which at that time the overwhelming majority of German colonists did not know (in large part through the fault of the authorities themselves). The document states that the existing norms for performing recruit duty (from which all colonists settled on state lands, except for the Volga Mennonites, had been exempted) would be preserved only "until the issuance of a general law on military service" (art. 5, para. a, note), making it clear that with the adoption of this law a number of the most important conditions, guaranteed "in perpetuity," on which the colonists had at one time agreed to settle in Russia, would be abolished. The Regulations state that the transformation and organization of the village and volost administrations of the settlers would be handled by various officials, without any participation whatsoever by the former colonists themselves (art. 10). The document requires communities of settlers who have surplus land compared to the "established normal allotment" to admit into their midst those with insufficient land (art. 16), even though, for example, in the Volga colonies with their system of per-capita land use, the concept of a "normal allotment" had long since lost any real meaning. And to top it all off, while declaring the preservation of the former colonists' existing personal privileges (art. 2), the Regulations at the same time unambiguously show them the door, offering anyone who wishes to do so the right, within 10 years, to renounce Russian citizenship and leave Russia on favorable terms — without paying into the treasury a portion of the capital they had accumulated, as had previously been required of colonists (art. 9, para. b).

The German colonists themselves could not fail to notice such provisions, although, of course, few of them studied and absorbed from beginning to end this voluminous document, written in dry bureaucratic language. It is not surprising that in the very same Volga colonies the Regulations were met with considerable wariness. The matter evidently lay not only in a whole series of points in the document that provoked at the very least bewilderment, but also in the fact that unerring popular instinct told the colonists: it was not merely certain rules of their life that were changing, but that fundamental changes were coming in the very attitude of the authorities toward Russian Germans, or even toward Germans as such. In principle this conclusion was obvious, especially since the issuance of the Regulations practically coincided in time with the unification of Germany and the proclamation of the German Empire — events that were received in Russia, to put it mildly, without enthusiasm.

In accordance with this document (art. 3), the existing German colonist districts were reorganized into the following volosts. Saratov governorate: Yagodno-Polyansky — Yagodno-Polyanskaya (Saratov district), Ilovlinsky — Ilovlinskaya (Kamyshin district), Sosnovsky — Sosnovskaya, Oleshinskaya (both Kamyshin district), Kamensky — Kamenskaya (Kamyshin district), Ust-Kulalinsky — Ust-Kulalinskaya (Kamyshin district), Norsky — Norskaya, Linevo-Ozerskaya, Oleshinskaya (all Kamyshin district), Medveditsko-Krestovo-Buerakskaya (Atkarsk district); Samara governorate: Paninsky — Paninskaya (Nikolaevsk district), Ekaterinstadtsky — Ekaterinstadtskaya (Nikolaevsk district), Krasnoyarsky — Krasnoyarskaya (Novouzensk district), Tonkoshurovsky — Tonkoshurovskaya (Novouzensk district), Tarlytsky — Tarlytskaya, Stepnovskaya, Rovninskaya (all Novouzensk district), Eruslansky — Verkhne-Eruslanskaya, Nizhne-Eruslanskaya, Bizyukskaya (all Novouzensk district), Malyshinsky — Malyshinskaya (Novouzensk district), Torgunsky — Torgunskaya (Novouzensk district), Nizhne-Karamansky — Nizhne-Karamanskaya (Novouzensk district), Verkhne-Karamansky — Verkhne-Karamanskaya (Novouzensk district), Konstantinovsky — Konstantinovskaya (Samara district), Mennonitsky — Aleksandrtalskaya (Samara district); Chernigov governorate: Belovezhsky — Kalchinovskaya (Borzna district); Bessarabia oblast: Saratsky — Saratskaya (Akkerman district), Maloyaroslavetsky — Maloyaroslavetskaya, Kulmskaya, Tarutinskaya, Krasnyanskaya, Teplitskaya (all Bendery district), Klyastitsky — Klyastitskaya, Parizhskaya, Artsizskaya (all Bendery district); Kherson governorate: Libentalsky — Gross-Libentalskaya, Freidentalskaya, Gildendorfskaya (all Odessa district), Kuchurgansky — Zeltsskaya, Badenskaya, Mannheimskaya (all Odessa district), Berezansky — Landauskaya, Rohrbachskaya, Neifreidentalskaya (all Odessa district), Rashtatskaya (Ananyev district), Glikstalsky — Glikstalskaya, Kasselskaya (both Tiraspol district), Shvedsky — Staroshvedskaya (Kherson district); Ekaterinoslav governorate: Khortitsky — Khortitskaya (Ekaterinoslav district), Iozefstalskaya (Novomoskovsk district), Petrovskaya (Aleksandrovsk district), Mariupolsky Mennonitsky — Petropavlovskaya (Aleksandrovsk district), Mariupolsky Kolonistsky — Aleksandro-Nevskaya, Romanovskaya (both Aleksandrovsk district); Tavrida governorate: Berdyansky — Neihoffnungskaya (Berdyansk district), Molochansky Mennonitsky — Halbstadtskaya, Gnadenfeldskaya (both Berdyansk district), Iogannesruskaya (Melitopol district), Molochansky Kolonistsky — Prishibskaya, Eigenfeldskaya (both Melitopol district), Neizatsky — Neizatskaya, Bulganakskaya (both Simferopol district), Zürichtalsky — Zürichtalskaya, Taraktashskaya, Salynskaya (all Feodosia district).

### No. 130.

After the Regulations of 1871 (doc. No. 129), the "general law on military service" promised in them (art. 5, para. a, note) was not long in coming — the Statute on Military Service of January 1, 1874. The Regulations themselves may be regarded as a rather clumsy embodiment of fairly sound ideas. The Statute, in all likelihood, deserves a more critical assessment. The point is not that the German colonists in principle rejected performing military service on an equal footing with other Russian subjects. Only the Mennonites (for religious reasons) were its categorical opponents, and even then not all of them. However, Alexander II and his government had no right to forget that previous Russian emperors, beginning with Catherine II, had solemnly promised all colonists entering Russia, as well as their descendants, exemption from military service for all time. The Statute of 1874 struck down these highest assurances at a single stroke, and no intelligible explanations, let alone apologies, followed from the authorities.

This high-handed action profoundly undermined the trust of Russian Germans in the supreme authority, which over the eight decades since Catherine II had never once deceived them and which they had therefore long been accustomed to trust unconditionally. This distrust naturally extended not only to the issue of military service. If the government had carelessly violated the laws that existed with respect to colonists in this sphere, then who could guarantee that it would not do the same in any other matter? The result, which could easily have been foreseen had anyone wished to, was a sharp rise in emigration sentiment — above all among the Mennonites, but partly also among other groups of Russian Germans, including not only colonists.

This phenomenon is reflected in the present act, which appeared almost immediately after the adoption of the Statute of 1874. Judging by the surnames listed in the act, the persons in question are not colonists but Baltic German nobles. They had wished to renounce Russian citizenship as early as 1873, that is, under the influence not of the Statute on Military Service itself but, evidently, already of the announcement of its forthcoming adoption, contained in the Regulations of 1871. The authorities, as the document shows, used the Statute to counteract the emigration sentiment that it itself had provoked, but this could not, of course, reverse the general trend that had emerged.

### No. 131.

This act, by introducing sanctions against peasant-proprietors (former colonists) of conscription age who had declared their intention to leave Russia but had not done so in time (para. 3), in fact only fanned the emigration fever caused by the Statute on Military Service of 1874.

The Statute of June 4, 1871 — doc. No. 129.

### No. 132.

The Regulations of June 4, 1871 (doc. No. 129) did not apply to Kiev governorate, since the colonists there had been settled not on state lands but on private lands. The inhabitants of the colony of Mikhalin belonged to the so-called "Upper Mennonites" and, unlike the overwhelming majority of Russian Mennonites, who came from West Prussia, originated from the Palatinate, from where they had resettled to Galicia and then to Volhynia. This decree extended to them only one provision of the Regulations of 1871 (art. 9, para. b), which offered colonists the right to leave Russia within a 10-year period without paying into the treasury a portion of the capital they had accumulated. This privilege was not granted to the other Volhynian colonists — another example of the special treatment accorded by the Russian authorities to Mennonites. The "Upper Mennonites" left for America as early as 1874, leaving their farmsteads to German Lutherans (see: Kostyuk M., Neutatz D. Volhynian Germans // Germans of Russia: An Encyclopedia. Vol. 1. P. 395).

### No. 133.

The Statute on Military Service of 1874 provided for noncombatant military service for the Mennonites, but this did not satisfy them, and many Mennonite families in southern Russia immediately began selling their property, preparing to leave for America. For some reason this reaction came as a complete surprise to Alexander II, and upon learning of it he instructed Adjutant General E.I. Totleben, hero of the defense of Sevastopol in 1854–1855 (see the Biographical Commentary), to travel immediately to the Mennonite colonies to work out a compromise solution. In April 1874 Totleben visited the Molochna and Khortitsa colonies. It turned out that among the local Mennonites there was a small group of radicals, of Flemish origin, disinclined to any compromise whatsoever. However, Totleben managed to reach an agreement with the main body of Mennonites (of German-Frisian origin), and the result was the adoption of this act, which provided for forms of alternative service involving neither the bearing of arms nor subordination to the military department. See: Fleischhauer I. Op. cit. Pp. 311–314.

### No. 134.

The decision on the redemption by the St. Petersburg colonists of the crown lands on which they had been settled was made in accordance with the provisions of the Peasant Reform of 1861.

The small colony of Znamenskaya, founded in 1843 and part of Konstantinovskaya (Strelinskaya) volost, Peterhof district, has not previously been mentioned in the documents published in this edition.

### No. 135.

Lippert, Pyotr Ivanovich (?–1861) — grain merchant, owner of a farmstead in Verkhne-Kushumskaya volost, Novouzensk district, Samara governorate; in 1830 he initiated the writing of memoirs by a number of the first Volga colonists (published in the Volga Protestant journal *Friedensbote* in 1900–1901); in 1857 he was decorated for making donations toward the construction of the monument to Catherine II in Ekaterinstadt. From 1877, using donations from Lippert and certain other funds, the education and upbringing of colonist boys aged 12–16 was organized in private or trade schools for 5–8 years, after which they were required to work for at least 6 years in the area of the colonies in the trade they had learned. See: Dietz Ya.E. Op. cit. Pp. 11–12, 370.

### No. 136.

The document constitutes the special regulations for the colony of Sarepta, the issuance of which was envisaged by the note to art. 1 of the Regulations of June 4, 1871 (doc. No. 129). While retaining, under this act, some of its privileges, the colony lost what was perhaps the most significant of them — exemption from military service (art. 11), which had originally been of just as much importance to the Herrnhuters as to the Mennonites. The abolition of this privilege for the Herrnhuters (unlike for the Mennonites) is largely explained by the fact that by this time the influence of the church community in Sarepta had seriously weakened.

A fateful influence on the further course of events was exerted by an incorrect wording in art. 2 of this document ("Sarepta Society" instead of "Sarepta Community"), as a result of which the Lutheran inhabitants of Sarepta, whose numbers were steadily increasing, found themselves subordinated to a clergyman of a different confession and, ultimately, to the German center of the Herrnhuters in Berthelsdorf. The conflict that flared up on this basis led to the German center excommunicating Sarepta from the Herrnhuter community in 1890, and the colony joined the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Russia. See: Dietz Ya.E. Op. cit. Pp. 461–464.

### No. 137.

In 1877, in accordance with art. II, para. 4 of the preamble to the Regulations of 1871 (doc. No. 129), the Saratov Office of Foreign Settlers and the Guardianship Committee for Foreign Settlers of the Southern Territory ceased their activity. Prior to that, in accordance with the Statute on the Spiritual Affairs of Foreign Confessions (doc. No. 114), the administration of the property of churches in the Evangelical Lutheran colonies had been under the oversight of these bodies (art. 623), and the same bodies had served as intermediaries between the relevant Evangelical Lutheran consistory and the lay assembly of parishioners in the process of calling and appointing priests (art. 292). This act abolished these two special norms established for the colonist parishes.

It is notable in the document that the funds for the maintenance of the Evangelical Lutheran General Consistory, which were contributed by the former colonists, were administered by the Ministry of Internal Affairs (art. II). This circumstance, together with similar provisions of the Statute on Spiritual Affairs, vividly illustrates the degree to which church life in the Russian Empire had been brought under state control.

### No. 138.

The school at the Moscow Evangelical Lutheran Church of Sts. Peter and Paul was founded as early as 1626, at the same time as the parish itself. Already in the second half of the 19th century the church maintained 5 educational institutions: boys' and girls' gymnasiums, a real school for boys, and primary schools for boys and girls; by 1910 they had about 1,400 pupils. See: Kovrigina V., Petrov Yu. Moscow // Germans of Russia: An Encyclopedia. Vol. 2. P. 567.

### No. 139.

Under the Military Service Statute of 1874, sons of foreign colonists who had settled on private lands on the basis of the decree of 18 December 1861 and had accepted Russian citizenship, and who had been born before their arrival in Russia, were exempted for life from military service. Among the German colonists, this privilege applied chiefly to peasants who had moved to the southwestern governorates from Poland during the Polish uprising of 1863–1864. See: Fleischhauer I. Op. cit. S. 310.

Czechs who settled in Perekop uezd founded 4 colonies in 1863–1864: Tabor (Tabor-Kirei) — Dzhurchinskaia (Ishunskaia) volost, Bogemka (Dzhadra) — Bogemskaia (Burlaktaminskaia) volost, Tsarekvich (Kurman-Kemelchi) — Aleksandrovskaia volost, and Aleksandrovka 3rd (Kemelchi) — Aleksandrovskaia (Aibarskaia) volost. In time, Germans came to make up a significant part of their population (in the last two, the majority).

### No. 140.

The girls' school at the Moscow Lutheran Church of Sts. Peter and Paul opened in 1829. A major role in its founding was played by the Moscow merchant Wilhelm Kloster, a hereditary honorary citizen and commercial counselor. The school, later transformed into a gymnasium, was attended in the mid-1890s by 420 female pupils. During this same period a new building was erected next to the old school building. See: Keller A. Germans in Moscow from the 16th to the Early 20th Century: Their Cultural and Social Life // Germans of Moscow: A Historical Contribution to the Capital's Culture. Moscow, 1997. Pp. 68, 99.

### No. 141.

The term of service of Mennonites in the forestry work units was 4 years (from 1907, 3 years). As a rule, most conscripts from a given volost served in the same forestry district. Responsibility for ensuring the timely appearance of conscripts for service rested with the Mennonite communities. To provide material and financial support for the forestry units, all the male population of the Mennonite colonies was subject to a special tax. With these funds, 5 barracks, each for 80 conscripts, were built in the New Russia governorates in 1880–1882. Residential quarters for forestry district staff, outbuildings, and artesian wells were also constructed. See: Beresten Yu. The Forestry Service // Germans of Russia: Encyclopedia. Vol. 2. P. 314.

### No. 142.

The school at the St. Petersburg Evangelical Lutheran Church of St. Catherine was founded in 1864. The course of study there lasted 4 years; in 1880 a 5th grade was introduced. After that, graduates who wished to continue their education had to transfer to the Petrischule (the school at the Church of St. Peter), where they completed the full course of the gymnasium or the "real" school. Such a transfer created inconveniences (in particular, because of the considerable distance between these schools), which is what prompted the request of the church council of St. Catherine's Church that its school be granted gymnasium status. See: Chebotareva V. Education. Gymnasiums // Germans of Russia: Encyclopedia. Vol. 2. P. 675.

### No. 143.

Outside the governorates named in the document, Mennonite settlements existed at that time in the North Caucasus (the Kuban and Terek oblasts, Stavropol governorate) and in Turkestan (the Syr-Darya oblast).

The Rules of 25 May 1882 — doc. No. 141.

### No. 144.

The Alexander Evangelical School received its name in memory of the saving of Alexander II during an attempt on his life (apparently referring to the explosion at the Winter Palace in 1880, organized by S.N. Khalturin). According to another version, the name is connected with the 25th anniversary of the reign of Alexander II (1880). See: Keller A. Op. cit. Pp. 63–64, 98.

### No. 145.

The Kharkov Evangelical Lutheran Church of the Holy Ascension was founded in 1804, and the girls' school attached to it in 1831. In 1881 this five-grade school for orphaned children was transformed into a six-grade school. See: Chebotareva V. Education. The Russian Language in the German School // Germans of Russia: Encyclopedia. Vol. 2. P. 677.

### No. 146.

The duties of the overseers elected from among the members of the forestry work units (Art. I, para. 1) included: monitoring the performance of work, discipline, and the moral condition of personnel, and providing them with everything necessary for the work. An overseer had the right to impose disciplinary penalties on offenders (the barracks had a guardhouse). In turn, the forestry unit that had put forward a candidate for the post of overseer could demand that the forestry district administration remove him. See: Beresten Yu. Op. cit. P. 315.

### No. 147.

This document is the first act at the highest level aimed at combating "foreign domination" in the southwestern governorates. This campaign, begun under Alexander III, markedly poisoned the domestic political atmosphere in the final decades of the Russian Empire's existence and had far-reaching consequences, above all for the German population of Volhynia, and subsequently for the whole country.

The problem was created, in its time, by the Russian authorities themselves. Catherine II and her circle, having taken an active part in the partitions of Poland in the 1770s–1790s, apparently did not consider that they were acquiring not only extensive and comparatively developed territories far to the west, but also a large mass of non-Russian subjects (Poles, Jews, Germans) who, moreover, would by no means necessarily remain forever in the places where they were then settled.

The gradual migration of this population eastward, together with that of peasants who had moved to the Kingdom of Poland and Galicia from German territories, became a notable phenomenon as early as the 1820s. Under Alexander I the authorities not only made no attempt to hinder this process but, on the contrary, gave it substantial assistance (see doc. No. 82).

This migratory process sharply intensified after the Peasant Reform of 1861, which brought on a protracted crisis of noble landownership in Volhynia. The local landowners, suffering an acute shortage of labor, themselves initiated the influx of colonists. The latter readily responded to this initiative: the low population density, extensive undeveloped land, and low rents created far more favorable conditions for farming in Volhynia than in the places of their previous residence. The peak of this migration fell precisely at the end of the 1880s. In 1890 more than 200,000 foreign colonists lived in Volhynia, including (by estimate) 175,000–180,000 Germans. Moreover, the colonists, who established their settlements without state involvement, had fairly broad scope to regulate their own affairs independently. See: Kostiuk M., Neutatz D. Op. cit. P. 396.

The present act put an end to this independence: the colonies were incorporated into the general administrative system and attached to existing peasant volosts (Art. I, para. 6), which ruled out the creation of separate colonist volosts. It is especially notable that in mixed volosts the offices of volost elder and clerk could be filled "exclusively by persons belonging to the native Russian population" (Art. 1, para. 8) — that is, by Ukrainians or Russians, but in no case by Germans. This was one of the first precedents of Russian legislation infringing upon the rights of the German population on ethnic grounds — a practice that became extremely widespread during the First World War.

The restrictive measures of the Russian authorities at that time against the German colonists of the southwestern governorates, initiated above all by the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the military leadership, as well as by the nationalist and Slavophile press, became possible in part because they found understanding and even support in the ruling circles of Germany, above all on the part of Chancellor Otto von Bismarck. He and his circle had no sympathy for the Polish Germans, who made up most of the settlers in Volhynia, and moreover the German authorities were interested not in the resettlement of peasants from Germany to the territory of the Russian Empire, but, on the contrary, in preventing this emigration and in the return of colonists who had already left. See: Lincke H.G. The German Question in Russian-German Relations // Germans of Russia: Encyclopedia. Vol. 2. Pp. 640–641.

### No. 148.

The colony of Gnadenburg (Smekalovskaia, Vinogradnoe) was founded by religious separatists from various regions of Germany, and later formed part of Gnadenburg volost of Nalchik (Sunzha) okrug. Already in 1889 it had 290 inhabitants — quite a considerable number by the standards of North Caucasus colonies. The document once again attests that the Russian authorities showed particular favor toward various Protestant minorities and were inclined to support them even at a time when other German colonists no longer enjoyed their trust.

### No. 149.

The document clearly shows that the very vague concept of "settler-proprietors" ("poseliane-sobstvenniki"), introduced in 1871, allowed the local authorities to deny former colonists even the rights granted to former serfs. Of course, in this case the Odessa uezd congress of justices of the peace acted in a plainly biased manner, in the interests of local men of wealth to whom the settler-proprietors were in debt, but it was the authors of the Rules of 1871 themselves who created the possibility for such actions, by failing to provide adequately for the protection of former colonists' rights. It is also notable that the Senate did not hand down a final ruling on so straightforward a legal question for more than 10 years.

Freudenthal (Nikolaevskoe) — a village of Freudenthal volost; Kuban — a Bulgarian village; Kandel (Blagoslovennoe) — a village of Seltz volost.

The Rules on the Organization of Settler-Proprietors — doc. No. 129.

### No. 150.

This act applied to all Lutheran church schools outside the Baltic governorates. In doing so, the authorities took the first major step toward the nationalization (étatization) of the parish schools of the Russian Germans.

The adoption of this measure was accompanied by the introduction, in the schools, of the post of Russian-language teacher, paid as a rule by the zemstvo. As a result, friction arose between the state administration and the rural communities, which up to then had themselves paid the teachers and thus retained full control over the school and its teaching staff. See: Bobyleva S.I. The Education System of the German Colonies in the Early 20th Century and the "Liquidation Laws" (Based on Materials from the Southern Governorates of Russia) // Germans of Russia and the USSR: 1901–1941. Moscow, 2000. P. 101.

### No. 151.

The changes in the procedure for appointing the presidents of the Evangelical Lutheran consistories consisted in the fact that henceforth, in all consistories, they were to be appointed by the emperor on the recommendation of the Minister of Internal Affairs (previously such a procedure had existed only in the St. Petersburg and Moscow consistories) — another sign of the growing influence of the Ministry of Internal Affairs in church affairs (see doc. No. 137).

### No. 152.

This decision entirely disregarded the well-known fact that the parishioners of Lutheran churches, especially in rural areas, still had a poor command of Russian — unlike the pastors, who, under Art. 271 of the Statutes on the Religious Affairs of Foreign Confessions (doc. No. 114), were required to know it. With the translation of the church registers into Russian, parishioners were in practice deprived of any means of getting errors, frequently made in vital-records entries, corrected. Under these circumstances it would of course have been more sensible to keep the registers in two languages, but such a natural measure ran counter to the firm course toward the Russification of every aspect of the German population's life, adopted by the Russian authorities under Alexander III.

### No. 153.

The present decree continued and considerably strengthened the restrictive measures against foreign settlers (above all Germans) in the southwestern governorates that had been adopted in 1888 (see doc. No. 147). Unlike the earlier measures, it concerned only Volhynia governorate, which, according to the decree, was in a "special position": it was here that the bulk of these settlers had until then been heading. Now they were forbidden, regardless of citizenship, both to settle in the rural districts of the governorate and to expand their landownership and land use there. These measures, together with a number of the conditions attached to them — differentiation of rights not only by ethnicity but also by confession (Art. 2), and administrative deportation of violators (Art. 5) — directly anticipated the so-called "liquidation laws" of the First World War period (see doc. No. 171 and following).

### No. 154.

This act names the authors of the decree of Alexander III of 14 March 1892 (doc. No. 153) — the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Committee of Ministers. The same was true of the corresponding bill of P.A. Stolypin mentioned in the note to doc. No. 158, who headed both of these institutions. The document is also notable for revealing one of the mechanisms for prompting unwanted foreign settlers to return to their homeland — the issuance to them of free emigration certificates.

### No. 155.

This act essentially completed the process, begun in 1890 (see doc. No. 150), of bringing the Protestant church schools under state control. For the Transcaucasian colonies and Sarepta a separate decision was needed, since the local parishes were not subordinate to the St. Petersburg or Moscow consistory (the Sarepta parish was placed under the Moscow consistory only at the end of 1893).

### No. 156.

This act continued the transition, begun a year earlier, to keeping the vital-records registers of the Protestant confessions in Russian. Among the Russian Germans, this measure affected persons of the Evangelical Reformed, Mennonite, and Baptist confessions.

The Opinion of 3 June 1891 — doc. No. 152.

### No. 157.

This act practically completed the process, begun in 1890 (see docs. No. 150 and 155), of bringing under state control the church schools of all the main confessions to which the Russian Germans belonged.

### No. 158.

This is the first act on the problems of the Russian Germans adopted by Nicholas II, who in 1915–1917 tirelessly rubber-stamped anti-German "liquidation laws." The document reflects a style of governance quite unlike that of Alexander III. The new emperor, unlike his father, tried to avoid sharp public gestures without particular need, and to steer around the sharpest corners, but this did not, in the end, make his policy any more measured or considered.

It is telling that the present document, which replaced the Provisional Rules of 1892 (doc. No. 153), does not bear the earlier title. Its authors plainly did not wish to create the impression that this concerned emergency measures called forth by extraordinary circumstances. In fact, no such circumstances existed at that moment: by the mid-1890s, thanks to the efforts of the Russian authorities, the flow of settlers to Volhynia had noticeably subsided, and the number of colonists there had begun to decline owing to migration to other regions or emigration (see: Kostiuk M., Neutatz D. Op. cit. Pp. 396, 399). This is presumably why the present act does not even contain the actual prohibition on foreign nationals settling in the rural areas of Volhynia governorate. In any case, such a prohibition had been superfluous even in 1892: the ban on acquiring rights of ownership, possession, and use of land alone guaranteed that no new settlers of foreign origin would appear in these places. In other respects the revised rules differ from the earlier ones chiefly in that the prohibition on acquiring rights to land was not extended to persons who had settled in the "closed" area before 1895 (a kind of amnesty for those who had committed this unseemly act even before the new emperor's accession to the throne), and in that the document lacks the odious differentiation of settlers by confession.

From 1 May 1905 the force of the restrictions that had existed in the southwestern governorates since 1892 was considerably weakened: now, on the wave of revolutionary events, the local authorities lost the right, granted to them back under Alexander III by the law of 1 November 1886, to issue land-purchase permits at their own discretion. As a result, by 1910, according to official figures, more than 10% of the non-urban land in Volhynia governorate had come into the hands of German colonists. This was enough for the then head of government, P.A. Stolypin, to declare the situation undesirable and dangerous to state interests, since foreign settlers who had preserved their language, customs, and religion "could be considered Russian subjects only formally." Having made this discovery, and thereby found a pretext for placing foreign-origin settlers on the same footing as foreign subjects (an idea that found its full realization in the "liquidation legislation" of the First World War era), the prime minister, on 28 September 1910, introduced a bill considerably tightening the present act. It applied not only to Volhynia but also to Kiev and Podolia governorates. Stolypin proposed reinstating the differentiation of settlers by confession (and, at the same time, by ethnicity), extending the restrictions to the male-line descendants of undesirable settlers, abolishing the exemptions based on length of settlement, and partly abolishing the exemptions for successors by inheritance as well; he proposed imposing on heirs stripped of these exemptions an obligation to sell any real property they inherited within three years of acquiring rights to it, and, in case of non-compliance, a procedure for the sale of such property at public auction (another key idea of the future "liquidation laws"). Having found that these draconian measures did not gain the support even of the Octobrist faction, his closest political allies, the prime minister withdrew the bill from consideration in the State Duma on 18 May 1911. On 28 December 1912 the bill was reintroduced in the Duma by the Minister of Internal Affairs A.A. Makarov, formerly a close associate of the now-deceased Stolypin. This time it was proposed to extend the restrictions to Bessarabia as well, although there, unlike in the southwestern governorates, the German colonists had originally settled on the initiative of the Russian authorities themselves and on state lands. However, the Octobrists again refused to support the bill, and the matter went no further than this dress rehearsal for the "liquidation laws." See: Baakh S.V. P.A. Stolypin's Bill to Restrict Foreign Landownership in the Southwestern Region of the Russian Empire // Germans of Russia: Socioeconomic and Spiritual Development (1871–1941). Moscow, 2002. Pp. 59–70; idem. Government Bills of the Early 20th Century to Restrict Foreign Landownership in Russia // Germans of Siberia: History and Culture. Omsk, 2002. Pp. 5–6.

### No. 159.

The colony of Katharinenfeld (Ekaterinovka) was located southwest of Tiflis and formed part of Katharinenfeld volost of Borchalo uezd. It was the second-largest Transcaucasian colony: in 1897 it had 2,064 inhabitants, including 1,744 Germans.

On the wave of the anti-colonist campaign it suddenly emerged that the inhabitants of Katharinenfeld had been granted, almost 80 years earlier, land that was not in fact state land. Nicholas II did not resettle them elsewhere, as the newly emerged landowners may perhaps have hoped (nor did he do so even during the First World War, when tens of thousands of Germans were deported from the western governorates). The emperor, at the treasury's expense, found a solution that satisfied everyone.

### No. 160.

This act, too, may be considered typical of Nicholas II. The authorities of course knew that the former colonist schools were plainly unprepared for the transition to instruction in Russian. The colonies had only about a dozen central schools that trained teachers to teach in that language, and a significant proportion of such schools were found in the Mennonite colonies. Besides this, colonist teachers for the Russian schools were trained only at Russian teachers' seminaries, and even there in minuscule numbers. Moreover, many graduates of these institutions preferred not to work in schools at all, taking positions instead as clerks, minor officials, and the like. Nor were the pupils themselves prepared for Russian-language instruction, since outside school they communicated, as a rule, in their native language. On the other hand, the voices of nationalist circles, indignant over the "separateness of the German colonies from Russia," were growing ever louder in the country. So Nicholas made a Solomonic decision: instruction in Russian was to be introduced, but "as far as possible, gradually." At the same time the emperor reassured German religious circles, giving them his word that the number of hours allotted to teaching the Law of God in German would be sufficient "for the proper mastery" of the subject.

Alexander III had acted far more decisively in such cases. Thus, in the southwestern governorates, a system for training teachers for the German schools had been practically nonexistent at all, yet this did not in the least prevent the emperor from introducing compulsory instruction in Russian there fully 10 years before the present act, in 1887 (see: Kostiuk M., Neutatz D. Op. cit. P. 398).

### No. 161.

The Rules of 1871 (doc. No. 129), which brought almost all the German colonies founded on state lands under the authority of the general institutions, did not even mention the Transcaucasian colonists. More than three decades later, only Nicholas II gave them any thought. Yet the emperor did not offer them the option of renouncing Russian citizenship and leaving Russia on favorable terms within 10 years, as his less delicate grandfather Alexander II had done with respect to the other colonists.

### No. 162.

The last of the colonies on state lands to undergo administrative and judicial reorganization were the Livland colonies. This act differs from the Regulations of 1871 (doc. No. 129) primarily in that it temporarily permits the use of German, alongside Russian, in volost courts (Art. I, para. 4) and recognizes German as the "native" (mother) language of schoolchildren (Art. III, para. 2). The German language had become too deeply rooted in the Baltic governorates for it to be replaced by Russian as unceremoniously as the authorities had done in the rest of the Russian Empire.

### No. 163.

The present document is the only state act in the last half-century of the Russian Empire's existence that to some extent eased the steadily intensifying Russification of the German population. The appearance of this act cannot be explained without taking into account the time of its issuance. The Revolution of 1905–1907 had just come to an end, and the authorities decided it was time to make at least some concession to "the aspirations of the people." True, this was done in a rather ambiguous manner, again typical of the reign of Nicholas II: non-state elementary schools in the former German colonies were permitted to teach most subjects in the native language, but "on condition that the said educational institutions be granted no rights whatsoever" (Art. 1). In other words, it was impossible for their graduates to continue their education anywhere. But the colonists were glad even of this, since at the beginning of the twentieth century education beyond the elementary level remained a rare exception in the German villages of Russia.

It is notable that the Volga region is absent from the list of areas where this measure was introduced. Art. II makes clear that no corresponding petitions had been received from there. This is quite plausible: for a number of reasons the Volga colonists lagged behind their brethren in the south and west of Russia in terms of social activity.

### No. 164.

In the last pre-war years the higher authorities scarcely addressed the problems of the Russian Germans, being absorbed in far more sweeping matters — the grand celebration of the 300th anniversary of the House of Romanov (1913), the feverish restructuring of the armed forces after the catastrophic defeat in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905, the large-scale agrarian reform (from 1906), and so on. But then Russia entered the First World War, and less than a month later Nicholas II authorized the first wartime conscription of Mennonites for alternative service, a promise made 40 years earlier. This was one of the few promises made by the authorities to the Russian Germans that was, on the whole, kept until the very end of the Russian Empire's existence.

True, the corresponding provision of the Military Service Statute (see doc. No. 133) said nothing about performing sanitary [medical] service in the active army, as this act provided for. But this can logically be attributed to the exigencies of wartime, which could not have been fully foreseen in advance. What is harder to understand is why, in the course of the war, the authorities, as we shall see, so often changed their decisions on this not especially complicated matter.

These fluctuations were accompanied by significant changes in the actual situation: in 1914 more than 3,000 Mennonites were in sanitary service; in 1915 the same number served there as in forest labor units and naval workshops combined (5,400 and 5,421 respectively); in 1916 the ratio shifted in favor of the latter (4,988 and 6,548 respectively); while in 1917, by contrast, there were already 15,000 Mennonites in sanitary service. In 1916 the Minister of Internal Affairs A.N. Khvostov proposed abolishing the Mennonites' alternative service altogether, but Nicholas II did not support this idea. See: Fleischhauer I. Op. cit. P. 476–478.

With the outbreak of war the remaining Russian Germans liable for military service also began to be conscripted into the active army. Unlike the Mennonites, they were conscripted on the same basis as everyone else, and no special acts were adopted concerning them. At first many of them ended up on the main fronts — the Russo-German and Russo-Austrian fronts. But from the autumn of 1914 these "enemy-alien" soldiers ceased to be sent there, and in 1914–1915, 17,000 German servicemen were transferred from those fronts to the Caucasian front. See: German A., Shulga I. Military Service // Germans of Russia: Encyclopedia. Vol. 1. P. 391.

### No. 165.

During the First World War, General M.I. Ebelov became known in Odessa and its environs as the organizer of a wide variety of repressive measures against the German population. Thus, in November 1914 he banned the delivery of sermons in German in Lutheran churches and prayer houses of the German settlements. This brought religious services to a halt, and the burial of deceased settlers came to be entrusted to Russians. This ban was rescinded by an order from Petrograd, but was reintroduced in June 1916, with pastors and preachers being notified of the renewed prohibition not through the consistory but through the police. Sermons were also banned outside churches and prayer houses — at the bedsides of the dying, at christenings, and so on. By Ebelov's order, violation of the ban entailed exile. In February 1915 he also banned telephone conversations in German. See: Plesskaya-Zebold E.G. Op. cit. P. 196, 393. In May 1915 Ebelov ordered the immediate suspension of the sale of German colonists' lands into private hands and the annulment of already concluded transactions for the sale of these lands to Jews, although the "liquidation laws" granted the Germans the right to dispose of their real property by voluntary agreements. See: Shevchuk N.A. Land Ownership of the Black Sea Germans in Odessa Uezd (Second Half of the 19th Century – 1917) // Germans of Russia in the Context of National History: General Problems and Regional Features. Moscow, 1999. P. 59. — Compiler's note.

Ebelov, M.I. (1855–1919) — Infantry General, Commander of the Troops of the Odessa Military District (1914–1917).

### No. 166.

I.L. Goremykin, whose signature appears under the "liquidation laws" of February 2, 1915 (docs. No. 171–173), held an ambivalent position with regard to the anti-German and anti-Germanic legislative measures of the First World War period. Thus, on August 23, 1914, the Council of Ministers under his leadership spoke out against restricting the property rights of "enemy subjects" on Russian territory, and in November 1914 Goremykin told a delegation from Tauride Governorate, concerned by reports of the preparation of future "liquidation laws," that the concerns of the German settlers and their representatives were groundless (see: Fleischhauer I. Op. cit. P. 479–480, 498–499). On the other hand, as early as October 10, 1914, he mentioned in one of his telegrams the "liquidation of German land ownership." See: Nelipovich S.G. The Role of the Russian Military Leadership in the "German Question" during the First World War (1914–1917) // Russian Germans: Problems of History, Language, and the Present Situation. Moscow, 1996. P. 264. — Compiler's note.

Goremykin, I.L. (1839–1917) — Chairman of the Council of Ministers (1914–1916).

Yanushkevich, N.N. (1868–1918) — Infantry General, Chief of Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief (1914–1915).

### No. 167.

N.N. Yanushkevich was the chief driving force in the Russian military command behind the "struggle against German domination." In October 1914 he was among the first to speak of the "German question." His directives concerning the eviction of German colonists are well known: "Better that the Germans should be ruined than that they should spy," "All the German filth must be dismissed, and without any tenderness — on the contrary, they must be driven off like cattle." M.V. Alekseev, Yanushkevich's successor as Chief of Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief, paid no such attention to these matters. See: Nelipovich S.G. Sources on the History of the German Colonists of Russia during the First World War (a survey of documents from the Russian State Military-Historical Archive) // Russian Germans: Historiography and Source Studies. Moscow, 1997. P. 107. — Compiler's note.

### No. 168.

Grand Duke Nikolai Nikolaevich, like his closest associate N.N. Yanushkevich, whom he held in high regard, openly proclaimed himself a fighter against "German domination." On November 3, 1914, he expressed displeasure at the Council of Ministers' decision on the limited character of the deportation of Germans and demanded that authority in this matter be transferred to himself personally in the border governorates, and to the Ministry of Internal Affairs in other regions. At the end of December 1914 – beginning of January 1915 he ordered the eviction of all German colonists from the Polish governorates, extending the deportation to the urban population as well. See: Nelipovich S.G. The Role of the Military Leadership. P. 265–268. — Compiler's note.

Nikolai Nikolaevich (the Younger) (1856–1929) — Grand Duke, Adjutant General, Cavalry General, Supreme Commander-in-Chief (1914–1915).

Wilhelm II Hohenzollern (1859–1941) — German Emperor and King of Prussia (1888–1918).

### No. 169.

Whereas in August 1914 it had been intended to employ Mennonites conscripted into the army both in forest work and in military sanitary service (see doc. No. 164), by December 1914, as is evident from the present act, the first of these assignments was no longer mentioned. In this connection, oddly enough, the task of carrying out the conscription was entrusted to the Chief Administrator of Land Settlement and Agriculture, who was in charge of forestry matters but had nothing to do with military sanitary service.

### No. 170.

Already in the first months of the war the authorities returned to a question that had been decided back in 1897 and then softened in 1907 (see docs. No. 160 and 163) — the language of instruction in the schools of the former colonies. The new decision provided for none of the earlier qualifications such as "as far as possible, gradually," and prescribed that German elementary schools be switched to Russian as the language of instruction at once and everywhere, allowing exceptions only for first-year pupils.

In 1897, as already noted (see note to doc. No. 160), neither the German schools nor their pupils were ready for radical changes in this sphere. Since then no particular improvement had occurred. On the contrary, given the extreme conditions of wartime, it can be argued that the situation had actually worsened, and in 1914 this measure had even less chance of success than in 1897. Nor could it have been intended to succeed — if only because the document concerned not only the schools of the former colonies but also the Warsaw educational district, whose territory was at that time in the front-line zone, or even under occupation. The evident purpose of this act was something else entirely: using the language-of-instruction issue — hardly the most pressing matter under wartime conditions — as a pretext to further inflame the campaign of hatred, not only against the enemy but against everything German, which was already raging throughout the country.

Similar measures were undertaken by the Ministry of Public Education with regard to urban German schools, and indeed even earlier. Thus, on August 25, 1914, an order was issued for teaching all subjects in Russian in the German schools attached to Petrograd churches; on September 1 the Ministry proposed that the trustee of the Moscow educational district take similar measures with regard to the German church schools of Moscow (see: Cherkazyanova I.V. The Question of the Fate of the German School of the Russian Empire during the First World War // Germans of Russia and the USSR: 1901–1941. Moscow, 2000. P. 75). Expressions of discontent over this were noted among teachers, as well as among the parents of pupils, in a number of German schools in Petrograd (see: Fleischhauer I. Op. cit. P. 451–452).

The Ministry of Public Education responded to the present act with an order of June 3, 1915, which provided, among other things, for the replacement by July 1915 of colonist-school teachers insufficiently proficient in Russian, primarily with teachers of Russian origin, and, where such were unavailable, for the closure of the corresponding schools. In addition, it prescribed the dismissal of persons whose presence in German schools was "undesirable for wartime reasons." For these reasons, as well as for financial ones, numerous cases of dismissal of teachers from German schools and closure of such schools occurred in Saratov Governorate. See: Vashkau N.E. The School in the German Colonies of the Volga Region, 1764–1917. Volgograd, 1998. P. 126–129.

### No. 171.

The so-called "liquidation legislation" of the Russian authorities during the First World War, directed above all against persons of German origin regardless of citizenship, represents a striking example of discrimination and repression on national as well as confessional grounds. In their sheer numbers, scale, methodicalness, consistency, and steadily intensifying severity, the liquidation laws of that time can perhaps be ranked alongside only two comparable phenomena in modern history — the Stalinist decrees and resolutions on repression against the German population of the USSR during the Second World War, and the anti-Jewish laws of Nazi Germany.

At the same time, nowhere in the liquidation laws was it asserted that they were dictated by extraordinary wartime circumstances and were temporary in character — unlike, for example, the 1942 resolutions of the USSR State Defense Committee "for the duration of the war" concerning the formation of "labor columns" from Russian Germans. In the liquidation legislation there are in general very few provisions reflecting the realities of wartime; it was clearly conceived as the basis for a long-term repressive policy toward "enemy" subjects and enemy-aliens — extending as far as their complete exclusion from the economic (and, apparently, not only economic) life of the country.

Comparing the liquidation laws with the state acts concerning the Russian Germans adopted in the preceding two decades, it is hard to believe that all these documents were confirmed by one and the same person — Nicholas II. This political metamorphosis of his can be explained only by the fact that the liquidation legislation was adopted on a wave of a ferocious anti-German (and not merely anti-Germanic) campaign that swept Russia with the outbreak of the war, not without the participation of the emperor himself. And the last Russian monarch, as is well known, did not so much steer events as drift with their current. On the other hand, the liquidation laws did not appear out of nowhere. Some of their provisions, as has been noted, were already anticipated in the decree of Alexander III of March 14, 1892 (doc. No. 153), as well as in a number of other acts adopted or being prepared before 1914.

In October 1914 the Council of Ministers discussed for the first time the question of restricting German landownership in Russia and spoke out against measures of this kind. However, the opinions of the members of the government on this matter at the time did not fully coincide. Attitudes toward the idea of liquidating "enemy" landownership and land use were likewise not uniform in the State Duma: there were both zealous champions of liquidation legislation, headed by the leader of the extreme right and one of the leading Black Hundred figures, N.E. Markov (Markov II), and influential opponents of such measures, above all the Kadet leader P.N. Milyukov and the Trudovik leader A.F. Kerensky. For this reason the higher authorities preferred not to bring the matter before the Duma, and all the liquidation laws were adopted on the basis of Article 87 of the Fundamental State Laws during periods when the Duma was not in session — the Duma being dissolved by the Tsar repeatedly and for long periods during the war. Direct preparation of the liquidation laws was carried out by a commission headed by Senator I.E. Ilyashenko, specially created for this purpose in the autumn of 1914; the commission dealt with this matter jointly with the Ministries of Internal Affairs and Justice. See: Fleischhauer I. Op. cit. P. 498.

On February 2, 1915, Nicholas II confirmed three liquidation laws at once. Of these, only one (No. 349) concerned subjects of the powers at war with Russia, while the other two (No. 350 and 351) were devoted to Russian subjects who had had the misfortune of being enemy-aliens or descendants of enemy-aliens from states now hostile to Russia — Austrians, Hungarians, but above all, of course, Germans. The authors of the liquidation laws showed no less close attention to "enemy-aliens" than to "enemy subjects" going forward as well.

As far as Germans were concerned, the present act applied to the rather small number of inhabitants of the Russian Empire who had retained German citizenship. Apart from Finland and the Polish governorates, they lived mainly in Russia's two capitals and other large cities, and in the countryside — in certain districts of southern Russia and in Volhynia. Thus, in the latter region, by 1882, of 88,000 German inhabitants, 21.5% did not hold Russian citizenship (see: Kostyuk M., Neutatz D. Op. cit. P. 396).

Many German subjects, having lived in Russia for a long time, had long since lost any real connection with Germany, and for that very reason plainly did not deserve to have their rights curtailed because of the war with her. But the authors of the law were not concerned with this in the least. It is telling that Section VI postulates entirely identical treatment for subjects of the German Empire and of those states that became part of it upon the empire's formation in 1871. This meant, for example, that a German who had settled in Russia while still a Prussian rather than a German subject was placed on the same footing as German subjects who had arrived only very recently.

The law restricted the economic activity of "enemy subjects" in two main directions, everywhere curbing the growth of their real property (Section I) and, on the other hand, liquidating their landownership and land use (hence the unofficial term "liquidation legislation") in the border governorates (Section IV). The orientation of the first liquidation laws concerning "enemy-aliens" was exactly the same. Thus it became clear from the very outset that the grounds for the discrimination introduced by these laws was not close ties with the main military adversary — Germany — nor even German citizenship, but simply belonging to the German nationality.

### No. 172.

The main purpose of the present document was to halt the further growth of landownership and land use by Russian Germans, above all former colonists. With regard to Volhynia Governorate this task had in principle already been resolved in 1892 (doc. No. 153) and in 1895 (doc. No. 158). The law applied to the entire territory of the country, but it was of primary importance for southern Russia, Western Siberia, and the Steppe Territory, where in preceding years German landownership and land use had expanded most vigorously, chiefly through the Germans' own resources. The authorities assisted them only beyond the Urals, within the framework of the resettlement policy initiated by P.A. Stolypin, though this policy gave the Germans no preference whatsoever over settlers of other nationalities.

Thus the Russian Germans were being punished for having actively made use of the market mechanisms that existed in the country and of the economic policy pursued by the government. Whether or not the authors of the liquidation laws realized it, the logical implication was that these very mechanisms and this very policy, which had proved to work all too well in favor of undesirable elements — the "enemy-aliens" — had no right to further existence. It was precisely this conclusion that the Bolsheviks, who came to power a couple of years later, would draw.

### No. 173.

The present act, unlike doc. No. 172, concerned only part of the country's territory — the border strip from the Baltic to the Caspian Sea — but provided for far more radical measures in these areas. Here the matter was no longer one of curbing further growth, but of destroying "enemy" landownership and land use altogether, with the sole exception of the allotment lands belonging to former colonists.

Within the strip delineated by the law (the southwestern governorates, southern Russia, Transcaucasia) there were numerous German settlements, and a considerable proportion of their inhabitants were, by this act, deprived of all means of subsistence in these places. The law thereby directly predetermined a large-scale deportation of the German population to the East, even though not a word was said in it about the necessity or possibility of such an action. Here once again was displayed the favorite tactic of Nicholas II, who always tried to avoid personally sanctioning the most odious political decisions.

The procedure prescribed by the law for the liquidation of "enemy" landownership and land use — the "voluntary" alienation of real property in rural areas under threat of its sale at auction (Art. 1), the forcible termination of lease or rental agreements for such property (Art. 6) — was marked by a demonstrative disregard for the "sacred" right of property and constituted, in essence, a thinly disguised mass expropriation. Opponents of the liquidation legislation immediately warned of the fateful consequences of such measures for the fate of the Russian state itself. The initiators and authors of the liquidation laws paid no attention whatsoever to this, but within just a few years expropriation (carried out by the Bolsheviks not on national but on an equally arbitrary "class" basis) dealt a fatal blow to these very figures, and to all the propertied strata of Russian society.

### No. 174.

The new document on the military service of Mennonites revised the decision on this matter of 24 December 1914 (doc. No. 169) and in fact amounted to a return to the original version (doc. No. 164), except that now medical-sanitary service, rather than forestry service, was placed first.

### No. 175.

In the zone of the Southwestern Front (Volhynia, Podolia, and Kiev governorates), the expulsion of Germans was begun on 24 June 1915 by order of A.A. Mavrin. His order also suspended the operation of the liquidation law of 2 February 1915 (doc. No. 173) in this territory, owing to the impossibility of disposing of the confiscated land. In the zone of the Northwestern Front (the Warsaw Governor-Generalship, Kholm and Grodno governorates, the Minsk and Dvinsk military districts, etc.), N.A. Danilov issued an order for the expulsion of the colonists on 26 June. See: Nelipovich S.G. The Role of the Military Leadership. P. 275. — Compiler's note.

The Chancellery for Civil Administration was formed as part of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief in 1914. Through it, in particular, restrictions were imposed on the rights of subjects of states at war with Russia, and questions were resolved concerning the use of the population and of prisoners of war on defense works, as well as evacuation.

Mavrin, A.A. (1854—?) — General of Infantry, chief of supply for the armies of the Southwestern Front (1915—1916), member of the Military Council.

Danilov, N.A. (1867—1934) — General of Infantry, chief of supply for the armies of the Northwestern Front (1914—1916). — Compiler's note.

Engalychev, P.N. (1864—?) — prince, aide-de-camp general, lieutenant general, Warsaw Governor-General (1914—1917).

Kondzerovsky, P.K. (1869—1929) — lieutenant general, duty general to the Supreme Commander-in-Chief (1914—1917), member of the Military Council.

Ronzhin, S.A. (1869—?) — lieutenant general (1917), chief of military communications (1915—1917).

Obolensky, N.L. — prince, head of the Chancellery for Civil Administration. — Compiler's note.

### No. 176.

This was the only occasion during the entire First World War when the military service of Mennonites received treatment in a decree of Nicholas II. Owing to an ambiguous formulation in the preamble of the document, one might get the impression that the tsar intended not only to "strengthen the personnel of sanitary institutions" but also to "fill up the reserve battalions" with Mennonites. This, of course, was not the case: Mennonites, exempted from bearing arms, were never enrolled in reserve battalions; the latter were, in this instance, to be filled up by militia warriors subject to conscription under the same decree.

### No. 177.

Yet another document on the very same question of the military service of Mennonites. This time a formula was finally found that made it possible to avoid further proliferation of acts of this kind: the Chief Administrator of Land Settlement and Agriculture was granted the right to conscript Mennonites automatically at the same time as other second-category militia warriors were called up.

Thus, the logic of the five documents (if it is even appropriate to speak of logic here) adopted on this matter was as follows: in the acts by which conscription was directly carried out (docs. No. 169 and 176), Mennonites were ordered to be sent only to sanitary institutions, whereas in the resolutions adopted afterward (docs. No. 174 and 177), as in the first act on this question (doc. No. 164), assignment to forestry units was added to this. As a result of this convoluted lawmaking, the bulk of Mennonites performed sanitary service, while the Mennonites of Ekaterinoslav governorate were sent to forestry districts (see: Beresten, Yu. Op. cit. P. 316).

### No. 178.

By the autumn of 1915, some military commanders, having encountered serious difficulties in the deportation of colonists, began trying to curb the anti-German wave that had been raised in large part by the military leadership itself. Thus, on 4 December 1915, M.V. Alekseev telegraphed the commanders-in-chief of the fronts that the expulsion of the peaceful population and its transport into the interior of the country had thoroughly disorganized the railway system, and he urgently asked them to restrain their subordinates "from uprooting the population." Hence his rather restrained position on questions of expulsion, reflected in the present document. By contrast, M.D. Bonch-Bruevich, N.V. Ruzsky, N.I. Ivanov, and A.A. Brusilov never displayed such restraint in this regard. Among the other commanders, Brusilov stood out in particular, as the author of the most notorious denunciation of the German population, mentioned both in the present act and in docs. No. 181, 199, and 200. As commander of the 8th Army, in October 1915 he obtained the expulsion from Volhynia of those German colonists who had previously been left in place: old people over 60, widows and mothers of those killed at the front, invalids, cripples, even including the blind.
