The future organizer of the "Brusilov Offensive" justified his démarche by claiming that they "undoubtedly damage telegraph and telephone wires." As a result of this denunciation, 20,000 people were made subject to expulsion within a three-week period. See: Nelipovich S.G. The Role of the Military Leadership. Pp. 276—278. — Compiler's note.

Stavka of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief — the supreme administrative body of the active Russian army and the seat of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Russia during the First World War of 1914–1918.

Bonch-Bruevich, M.D. (1870—1956) — major general, attached to the commander-in-chief of the armies of the Northern Front (1916—1917).

Ruzsky, N.V. (1854—1918) — aide-de-camp general, General of Infantry, commander-in-chief of the armies of the Northwestern Front (1914—1915), commander of the 6th Army (1915), commander-in-chief of the armies of the Northern Front (1915, 1916—1917), member of the Military and State Councils.

Alekseev, M.V. (1857—1918) — aide-de-camp general, General of Infantry, chief of staff to the Supreme Commander-in-Chief (1915—1917).

Ivanov, N.I. (1851—1919) — aide-de-camp general, General of Artillery, commander-in-chief of the armies of the Southwestern Front (1914—1916), member of the State Council.

Brusilov, A.A. (1853—1926) — aide-de-camp general, General of Cavalry, commander of the 8th Army (1914—1916), commander-in-chief of the armies of the Southwestern Front (1916—1917).

### No. 179.

The occasion for the adoption of the present act was sharp criticism of government policy, which was being voiced ever more loudly during this period not only from the traditionally anti-government left-wing circles, but also from nationalists and national liberals. The latter, accusing the authorities of causing land hunger among Russian peasants, proposed using the liquidation legislation to alleviate it. P.N. Miliukov tried to cool these hotheads by declaring in the Duma that there would in any case not be enough colonist land for all those in need, and that whoever began the process of confiscating land from the colonists would end up finishing it off against supporters of such measures themselves. The warning had no effect, and A.V. Krivoshein, Chief Administrator of Land Settlement and Agriculture, formerly a close associate of P.A. Stolypin, an advocate of restricting German landownership in the Southwestern Territory (incidentally, in 1910 Krivoshein and Stolypin visited German settlements in the Kulunda steppes and expressed no negative judgments about what they saw there), prepared proposals for the corresponding bill. The law he proposed, adopted on 1 May 1915 (SURP. 1915. Section I. No. 1116), entrusted the purchase of land confiscated from "enemy subjects" to the Peasant Land Bank, which during the Stolypin agrarian reform had bought up landowners' estates and then sold them off in small plots to peasants. Krivoshein had in fact directed the conduct of that reform and had at one time himself administered the Peasant Bank, so his attachment to such ideas is entirely understandable. A commission headed by Senator I.E. Ilyashenko immediately embodied these ideas in a new draft law, which regulated in detail the procedure for transferring confiscated lands to the disposal of the Peasant Bank. However, the Council of Ministers rejected this draft, deeming it contrary to the principles of Russian legal order concerning property rights. The project was revived in the autumn of 1915 by the new Minister of Internal Affairs, A.N. Khvostov, a well-known right-wing figure. The decisive role in the adoption of this law on 13 December 1915 was evidently played by the personal support of Nicholas II, who warmly approved the idea of having the Peasant Bank buy up colonist lands. See: Fleischhauer, I. Op. cit. Pp. 497, 505, 506, 512.

However, the content of the present act is far from exhausted by this central idea. The document revised all the liquidation laws of 2 February 1915 in the direction of noticeably greater severity. Thus, in Law No. 350 (doc. No. 172) the circle of persons prohibited from acquiring rights to real property in rural areas was expanded to include rural inhabitants classified as "enemy émigrés" who did not belong to colonist communities (Section B, Part I, Art. 2, para. a). But the main change in this law consisted in the fact that "enemy émigrés" could henceforth not be employees of any rank in companies entitled to acquire real property in rural areas (Section B, Part II, Art. 3). In this respect, as in many others, Russian Germans were placed on the same footing as German subjects, for whom such a restriction had already been provided for in Part II of Law No. 349 (doc. No. 171).

Law No. 351 (doc. No. 173) underwent even more significant changes. Russian Germans were forbidden to manage real property in the rural localities of border districts; for violation of the prohibition on owning and managing real property, expulsion beyond the governorate was for the first time made mandatory (Section V, Part I, Arts. 1, 2). The previously introduced restricted border strip was abolished — henceforth the restricted zone extended to entire governorates (Section V, Part II, Art. 1), as had already been provided for German subjects. The lifetime rights of use and possession of real property previously held by Russian Germans were abolished (Section V, Part II, Art. 2). The circle of persons subject to the prohibitions was expanded by analogy with Law No. 350 (Section V, Part II, Art. 3, para. 2a). And, most importantly, expropriation was extended to allotment lands as well (Section V, Part II, Art. 3, para. 3). Thus, it was no longer merely a significant part of the colonists, as before, but their entire mass, that was left without means of subsistence in the border districts. In addition, the period established for the "voluntary" alienation of the property of Russian Germans was shortened (Section V, Part II, Art. 5).

The central place in the new law undoubtedly belonged to the most extensive Section D. It was for the sake of this section, as noted, that the law was adopted in the first place. In this section, the Peasant Bank was granted virtually unlimited rights to buy up lands confiscated from Russian Germans and German subjects in the border governorates. The Bank, which had earlier played a leading role in carrying out the Stolypin reform, was now transformed into a super-expropriator. The provisions of Section D, though formulated in the terminology of a market economy, in fact amounted to as thorough a trampling of its mechanisms as can be found perhaps only in Bolshevik decrees.

The Peasant Bank made full use of the monopoly position granted to it by the law. Thus, by the middle of 1916 the bank had received information on 630 confiscated land plots with a total area of 146,941 desyatinas; of these it retained for itself the largest plots, with an area of 132,222 desyatinas. By 1 January 1917 the bank had already acquired 431 estates with an area of 144,984 desyatinas (see: Shrader, T.A. Results of the Tsarist Government's Agrarian Policy in Petrograd Governorate during the First World War // Migration Processes among Russian Germans: A Historical Aspect. Moscow, 1998. P. 199). It is true that no one has ever produced convincing evidence that the law brought any tangible benefit to landless Russian peasants. However, the Russian press of the time repeatedly reported that large landowners and high-ranking officials, including A.V. Krivoshein himself, grew substantially richer by buying up German lands at bargain prices. See: Fleischhauer, I. Op. cit. Pp. 520—522.

It is noteworthy that the Bank was granted its monopoly rights until 1 January 1921 (Section D, Part I, Art. 1). The authors could hardly have imagined that by that date the liquidation laws, the Peasant Land Bank, and the Russian Empire itself would all long since have vanished. Nor did the chief champions of the law live to see that date: Nicholas II and A.N. Khvostov were shot by the Bolsheviks as early as 1918. A.V. Krivoshein outlived them by not much, dying in emigration in 1921.

### No. 180.

The decision to create the Special Committee for Combating German Domination fell on well-prepared ground. Already in the initial period of the First World War, nationalist circles in the capital (above all in Petrograd) had created the "Society of 1914" to coordinate active struggle against "German domination" in various spheres, paying particular attention to the land question. On 11 August 1915 the State Duma formed a temporary inter-factional Commission on Measures for Combating German Domination in All Spheres of Russian Life, headed by A.S. Stishinsky, officially confirmed on 1 January 1916. See: Fleischhauer, I. Op. cit. P. 506. At the beginning of 1916 a Special Conference on Foreign Subjects and Émigrés, headed by Privy Councillor V.G. Kondoidi, was established within the Ministry of Internal Affairs (see: Plokhotnyuk, T.N. The Operation of the "Liquidation Laws" in the North Caucasus in 1915—1917 // Germans of Russia in the Context of National History: General Problems and Regional Peculiarities. Moscow, 1999. P. 225).

The Special Committee for Combating German Domination was created on the initiative of the Chairman of the Council of Ministers, B.V. Stürmer, who also signed the present act. The idea was approved by the government, and the creation of the committee was supported by the State Duma. The regulation on the committee was drafted between March and May 1916. The committee's sessions were held once a week. After the February Revolution, from 17 March 1917, the committee dealt only with the landownership of "enemy subjects" — matters concerning "enemy émigrés" were transferred to the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Peasant Land Bank. See: Shrader, T.A. Op. cit. Pp. 198—199.

Initially the Special Committee was chaired by aide-de-camp general F.F. Trepov (brother of A.F. Trepov, Chairman of the Council of Ministers at the end of 1916; Governor-General of Kiev, Podolia, and Volhynia in 1908—1914), who was later succeeded by A.S. Stishinsky, member of the State Council, who had headed the corresponding Duma commission. The deputy chairman was I.E. Ilyashenko, Assistant Minister of Justice, who had directed the drafting of the "liquidation laws" since the autumn of 1914. See: Plokhotnyuk, T.N. Op. cit. P. 225.

It is a curious fact that both the initiator and the first head of the Special Committee for Combating German Domination were figures bearing German surnames (Trepov being a Russified version of the surname Trepphoff). To be sure, in the role of chief official fighter against "German domination" they were succeeded by a "person of native nationality," but the successor proved to be quite fitting for the part: Stishinsky was a well-known right-wing figure who, from 1899 to 1904, served as Assistant Minister of Internal Affairs, and in the last two of those years under his like-minded minister V.K. Plehve (during the same years Stürmer, another bearer of a German surname and an extreme reactionary, also held a leading post in that ministry).

Judging by its membership (Art. 3), the committee was, in effect, a miniature Council of Ministers. Yet in the subsequent discriminatory acts concerning "enemy" subjects and émigrés there are practically no mentions of its activity. All we know is that on 19 August 1916 the Council of Ministers somewhat softened the restrictive measures against enemy subjects of non-German origin and Christian confession, following discussion of the matter in the Special Committee (SURP. 1916. Section 1. No. 1868). It appears the Committee did not play a particularly prominent role, since there was simply no need for it: the government was in any case paying unremitting attention to the fight against "German domination." On the forms and character of the Committee's activity, see: Bobyleva, S. Materials of the Special Committee as a Source for the History of the Fate of the German Population during the First World War // Germans of Russia: Socio-Economic and Spiritual Development (1871–1941). Moscow, 2001. Pp. 495—505.

### No. 181.

This document attests both to yet another initiative by General A.A. Brusilov aimed at the deportation of the German population, and to the increasingly evident desire of the higher military command, in the person of M.V. Alekseev, to distance itself from punitive actions of this kind. — Compiler's note.

Stürmer, B.V. (1848—1917) — Chairman of the Council of Ministers (1916).

### No. 182.

The appearance of the present document was prompted by the catastrophic situation on the lands confiscated from the colonists. This was reported, for example, by the zemstvo assemblies of Tavrida governorate and its Simferopol district in 1916 (see: Fleischhauer, I. Op. cit. P. 513). The government had already been discussing measures to combat the failure to sow the colonist lands as early as March–May 1916 (see: Nelipovich S.G. Sources on the History of the German Colonists. P. 109). In March 1916 the State Duma also expressed alarm over the reduction of sown area and the ruin of economic life in certain localities (see: Shevchuk, N.A. Op. cit. P. 58).

The present act placed the burden of maintaining the economy on the confiscated colonist lands mainly upon their former owners, threatening them with economic sanctions from the Peasant Land Bank (Art. 1). Such a measure could not produce any appreciable effect: the land was being bought up by the bank at such low prices that a possible further reduction of 5–10%, as provided by the law, was not a serious incentive to maintain the farms. Even more hopeless was the measure provided for in Art. 2. It is difficult to imagine that the former owners could themselves have wished to remain for up to a year on land already taken from them; nor did the bank have any practical means of compelling them to do so.

### No. 183.

By this act the government and the emperor made sure that Russian Germans would have to confirm, no later than 2 April 1915, that they themselves or their closest relatives had taken part in the combat operations of the Russian army and navy — a fact that made it possible to avoid the "voluntary" alienation of land in border districts. By this date a considerable proportion of the Germans serving in the Armed Forces of Russia during the First World War had not yet even been called up. Moreover, the very confirmation of the conditions listed in Art. 4, para. 1v of Law No. 351 (doc. No. 173) required a certain amount of time. Thus the corresponding privilege declared by Law No. 351 was to a considerable extent rendered a fiction.

### No. 184.

The present act sharply tightened the restrictions on teaching in the German language introduced on 24 December 1914 (doc. No. 170). At that time the term "prohibition" had not been used, the restrictions had applied only to primary schools rather than to all educational institutions, and exemptions had been provided for first-year pupils, of which there was now no mention. This act also marked the final completion of the Russification of Yuriev (Dorpat) University, which had begun back in the 1830s (see note to doc. No. 33).

### No. 185.

The main purpose of the present act was to facilitate in every way possible the Peasant Land Bank's purchase of any part of the confiscated property that caught its fancy, by means of the corresponding judicial procedures. The devotion of a special government decision to this question underscores the importance that the highest echelons of power attached to the role of the Peasant Bank in the confiscation of German real property.

### No. 186.

After paragraph 3 of Article 3 of Part II of Section V of the law of 13 December 1915 (doc. No. 179) provided for the confiscation, in the border territories, of not only privately owned but also allotment lands of German colonists, entirely new problems arose for the lawmakers, connected with the liquidation of whole rural communities and volosts. It is to the resolution of these problems that the present act is devoted, and in terms of its significance it undoubtedly stands alongside the principal liquidation laws of 2 February and 13 December 1915.

It is noteworthy that the document dealt only with communal allotments and real property. In doing so, its authors demonstrated that priority in the struggle against "enemy émigrés" was given precisely to the liquidation of their compact settlements, without which any people is doomed to assimilation and disappearance.

It is also of fundamental importance that this document is the first act of the higher organs of Russian power to speak directly of the expulsion of "enemy émigrés" from the rural localities of the border governorates (Part I, Art. 14). Indeed, no other fate could have awaited such émigrés: if all the real property of a given rural community passed to other owners, the former proprietors had no choice but to depart, vacating the place for the newcomers. Nevertheless, Nicholas II avoided, for as long as possible, any mention of mass expulsion in documents bearing his signature. Having declared the alienation of land a voluntary act, he evidently realized that such an interpretation of expulsion would look altogether too strange, even when applied to a front-line area. In the end, the authorities invented an equally strange combination — voluntary alienation and mandatory expulsion.

There is evidence that, from September 1916, legislative acts on the mass deportation of the German population were being prepared, which were meant to crown the process of liquidating German landownership and land use (see: Plokhotnyuk, T.N. Op. cit. P. 234). It is true that by this time deportation was already in full swing. German peasants had been expelled from Volhynia, Kiev, Podolia, Chernigov, Livonia, and other western governorates, as well as from northern Bessarabia; the count ran into many tens of thousands of people (see: Fleischhauer, I. Op. cit. Pp. 508—509). However, the expulsion was carried out mainly from privately owned rather than from allotment lands. It was clear that once the turn came to the latter and the deportation of the numerous colonists of the Black Sea region began, the count would run into the hundreds of thousands. The authorities did not manage to reach these areas in time, but even so, in 1914–1916 about 200,000 Germans, including 150,000 Germans from Volhynia, were expelled eastward from the western districts.

Since the authors of the document bashfully avoided the pivotal question — the procedure for the planned expulsion — the actions prescribed by them in Part I seem almost routine and do not produce an overt impression of acts of lawlessness and violence: voluntary alienation of the allotments and real property of communities (Art. 1), the gratuitous confiscation of public structures, buildings, and monetary funds (Arts. 2–7), the official abolition of German communities and volosts (Art. 9), the transfer of confiscated public structures, buildings, and capital to new owners through the intermediary of the Peasant Land Bank (Arts. 11–12), the distribution of symbolic compensation for real property among householders in proportion to the area of the confiscated land, the drawing up of lists for expulsion (Arts. 14–21), and the payment by the Peasant Bank of monetary compensation to each householder (Art. 22).

### No. 187.

The present act appears, at first glance, quite absurd: Nicholas II and the Council of Ministers issued a special document merely to replace, in art. 8 of the regulation on the Special Committee for Combating German Domination (doc. No. 180), the phrase "a general measure adopted by resolution..." with another — "a resolution adopted...". In reality there was nonetheless some sense to this. The creators of the Special Committee had evidently realized that they had gone too far, forming something like a parallel government. The adoption of "general measures" on a problem so important from the standpoint of the Russian authorities of the time — "freeing the country from German influence in all areas of the national life of the Russian State," as prescribed in art. 1 of the regulation on the Special Committee — was, of course, a task for the Council of Ministers, not for some committee, even one created with the sanction of the emperor himself. In light of this act it becomes clear why the government tried not to publicize the activities of the Special Committee.

### No. 188.

The Instruction on the application of the liquidation laws of 1915 has a distinct "prosecutorial bias": the numerous doubts that could arise in implementing these acts — which were not always clearly or unambiguously formulated — are, as a rule, resolved by the authors not in favor of those whose rights were infringed by the liquidation laws. In their zeal, the authors sometimes go beyond the bounds of the law in force, which is entirely inconsistent with the intended purpose of any instruction. Thus, in art. 14, section I, Stavropol governorate is listed among the forbidden localities of the Caucasus territory, although it had already been removed from the administration of that territory in 1899 (see doc. No. 196). On the other hand, the authors considerably eased their task by arbitrarily avoiding any clarification of the fundamentally important changes introduced into the liquidation laws on August 19, 1916 (doc. No. 186).

### No. 189.

By the present act, the alienation of real property belonging to "enemy" subjects and émigrés, provided for by the liquidation laws for border localities, was for the first time extended to the interior governorates of Russia. The localities mentioned in section V of this document are the same as those referred to in its sections III and IV.

The main German settlements of Kharkov governorate were located in Izium and Starobelsk uyezds. In Kainsk uyezd of Tomsk governorate (Kupino and Tatarsk volosts) there were mainly Mennonite settlements. In Tyukalinsk uyezd of Tobolsk governorate there were numerous German settlements, mainly farmsteads; the only known German settlement in Ishim uyezd (Vedovo volost) was the village of Peterfeld (Rybalsk).

### No. 190.

The adoption of the present act was prompted by the fact that in the Siberian uyezds named in it, "enemy émigrés" had received allotment land not as colonists but under the general resettlement laws. The main difference in the procedure for alienating land in these districts was that the leading role in the process belonged not to the Peasant Land Bank but to the Resettlement Administration (art. 1, 9). Moreover, the law applied not only to rural communities of enemy émigrés but also to all individual enemy householders not belonging to such communities (art. 1). The approximate amount of compensation for the alienated land, as well as for the buildings and equipment on it, was stipulated in advance (art. 2, 7). Unlike the law of August 19, 1916 (doc. No. 186), the present document proposes that the Germans demolish their own houses with their own hands (art. 3), but is silent about the subsequent fate of their occupants. The initiators of this scheme did not have time to demonstrate how they envisioned the resettlement of Germans from Siberia to Siberia: the bodies charged with carrying it out had only a few months left to act.

### No. 191.

Until now, under art. 10 of section I and art. 31 of section III of the Instruction on the application of the liquidation laws (doc. No. 188), those directly engaged in "work on the alienation of the immovable property" of enemy subjects and émigrés received no special remuneration for their labors. The present act (art. 1, section 1, part A) placed the process of expropriation on a sound commercial footing, thereby giving local officials a material interest in maximizing its scope.

Moreover, the document is notable for extending the provisions of the law of August 19, 1916 (doc. No. 186) on the seizure of the allotments and real property of German rural communities to all their separately located plots as well, and also to the private real property of peasants united in German communities, including those not formally confirmed as such (art. 1, part B). In particular, many German peasants who had taken advantage of the Stolypin law of November 9, 1906 on withdrawal from communes onto individual farmsteads (khutors) and consolidated plots (otrubs) were now officially subject to expulsion as well (art. 14, part B).

### No. 192.

On the German lands subject to alienation, especially in the south of Russia, there were a considerable number of industrial enterprises. The present act is devoted to their liquidation. Under it, these enterprises, together with the corresponding parcels of land, were to be acquired by the Peasant Land Bank (art. 4, section I), or, should the Bank decline to do so, were to pass into the charge of specially created liquidation boards, which would liquidate these enterprises according to the rules established for the liquidation of the commercial enterprises of enemy subjects (art. 9, section I). No deferrals for defense-related enterprises, which had been introduced quite recently, under the law of August 19, 1916 (doc. No. 186), were any longer permitted in this connection (section II). It appears that over the intervening two months the authors of the liquidation laws had concluded that the swift liquidation of German enterprises was of greater importance than the needs of national defense.

### No. 193.

The implementation of the liquidation laws was at that time manifestly impossible in many of the western governorates of the Russian Empire, which were under occupation or in the front-line zone. This act shows that almost two years after the appearance of the first liquidation laws, the Russian authorities (and, notably, without the participation of the Council of Ministers and Nicholas II, to whom the final word in such matters invariably belonged) finally decided to take this circumstance into account. The document postponed the start of the liquidation campaign in the territories it listed "until a corresponding new publication," but no such publication ever followed.

### No. 194.

Under the liquidation laws of February 2, 1915, the right to appeal decisions concerning the termination of landownership and land use was provided only for enemy subjects, in art. 4, section IV of law No. 349 (doc. No. 171). The law of December 13, 1915 (doc. No. 179), in art. 5, section II, part B, extended this right to enemy émigrés as well. Under arts. 5–7 of the law of October 20, 1916 (doc. No. 190), German peasants of the Siberian uyezds likewise gained the possibility of appealing such decisions, but only up to the level of the governorate administration, and not directly to the Senate, as enemy subjects and other enemy émigrés could. The present act equalized the rights of the Siberian Germans in this respect, but established for them, unlike for others, not a direct but a two-tier procedure of appeal (governorate administration — Senate).

### No. 195.

In terms of significance, the present act stands alongside the liquidation laws of 1915 (docs. No. 171–173, 179) and the law of August 19, 1916 (doc. No. 186). Outside the regions listed in art. 1, section I of this law, there were at that time only small numbers of German settlements remaining within the Russian Empire — in Voronezh, Nizhny Novgorod, Oryol, Perm, Poltava, Tula, and Chernigov governorates (already subjected to expulsion), Siedlce governorate (under occupation), Yenisei and Irkutsk governorates, the Transcaspian, Syr-Darya, and Ural oblasts, and also in Tara uyezd of Tobolsk governorate — where, taken together, only a few percent of the country's German population resided. Out of old habit, the authorities did not extend the provisions of the law to the colony of Sarepta, although by that time no trace remained of its once-privileged status. Thus the implementation of this act meant the virtually complete liquidation of German landownership and land use and, as a consequence, the general deportation of the rural German population of Russia, which at that time numbered approximately 2 million people.

The rules for the termination of landownership and land use set forth in section II of the document essentially coincide with the provisions of the previously adopted liquidation laws, apart from bringing the deadlines specified there into conformity with the date of issue of the present law. At the same time, for German settlers from the Steppe territory and Western Siberia, the procedure for the liquidation of landownership and land use, as well as for appealing decisions made on this account, was established following the model of the laws governing these matters in the resettlement uyezds of Tobolsk and Tomsk governorates (docs. No. 190 and 194).

### No. 196.

The occasion for the adoption of the present act was an error by the authors of the Instruction on the application of the liquidation laws of 1915 (doc. No. 188), who in art. 14, section I, groundlessly included Stavropol governorate among the forbidden localities of the Caucasus territory, although it had earlier been removed from the administration of that territory.

Meanwhile, the local authorities began pressing for the liquidation laws of 1915 to be extended to their governorate as well, and the acting Stavropol governor proposed that it be declared, for this occasion, as temporarily forming part of the Caucasus territory. See: The German Population of the North Caucasus: Socioeconomic, Political, and Religious Life (Last Quarter of the 18th – Mid-20th Century): Collected Documents / Comp. T.N. Plokhotnyuk. Stavropol, 2002. P. 112.

The higher authorities were therefore obliged to concern themselves once again with "confirming and clarifying the meaning" of previously adopted laws.

### No. 197.

The present act was adopted because, in art. 2 of the law of October 20, 1916 (doc. No. 190), compensation per desyatina of alienated land in Kainsk uyezd of Tomsk governorate had been given as 73 rubles instead of 23 rubles. Thus the authors or publishers of the law had erred more than threefold in favor of the German peasants. One may surmise that had a comparable error occurred in favor of the state, the higher authorities would hardly have troubled themselves to intervene.

The acts of February 8, 1917 (docs. No. 196 and 197) proved to be the last in the long series of liquidation laws. Twenty-two days later, Nicholas II, who had confirmed them, abdicated the throne. Thus the last Russian emperor took his leave of his German subjects by correcting two blunders made in the acts of repression against them. The liquidation saga, which had begun on February 2, 1915 (docs. No. 171–173) and reached its apogee two years later, on February 6, 1917 (doc. No. 195), culminated, a mere two days after that, in outright farce.

### No. 198.

Only nine days after coming to power, the Provisional Government suspended the enforcement of the liquidation laws with respect to "enemy émigrés." These laws were never subsequently reviewed by the Constituent Assembly, as this act had envisaged, since that supreme representative institution, having begun its work on January 5, 1918, was dispersed by the Bolshevik authorities early the next day. Among the relevant liquidation acts, the resolution does not mention the Instruction on the application of the liquidation laws of 1915 (doc. No. 188) or the decision of December 3, 1916 (doc. No. 193). The first of these documents automatically lost force once the enforcement of the laws it explained was suspended, while the second itself provided for the suspension of the liquidation acts in a number of governorates and, moreover, had not been officially confirmed by the Council of Ministers. It is notable that among the ministers who signed the resolution were P.N. Milyukov and A.F. Kerensky — longstanding, committed opponents of the liquidation laws.

Following this resolution, on March 20, 1917, the Provisional Government proclaimed the abolition of all legislative restrictions on the rights of citizens of non-Orthodox faith and non-Russian nationality. For the German citizens of Russia, the most important provisions of this act were: the removal of all restrictions on place of settlement and freedom of movement; equal rights for representatives of all nationalities in the acquisition of movable and immovable property and the leasing of real estate; and the right to use one's own language and dialects alongside Russian in the courts and in educational institutions of all kinds (see: Fleischhauer I. Op. cit. P. 530). This also nullified the discriminatory acts prohibiting instruction in German (docs. No. 170 and 184).

As for the Special Committee for Combating German Domination (see docs. No. 180 and 187), after the February Revolution its meetings were no longer held, and its chairman, deputy chairman, and most of its members were removed from office. The Special Committee was finally abolished by decree of the Provisional Government of July 14, 1917. See: Plokhotnyuk T.N. Op. cit. P. 234–235.

### No. 199.

This is the first act of the military command concerning the removal of German colonists from the theater of military operations adopted after the fall of the autocracy. The document reflects a new approach to this problem, based on the corresponding resolution of the Provisional Government of March 19, 1917. — Compiler's note.

Participants of the Turkish and other past campaigns — participants of the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878 and the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905.

Volodchenko, N.G. (1862–?) — lieutenant general, commander of the 16th Cavalry Division (1915–1917), commander-in-chief of the armies of the Southwestern Front (1917).

### No. 200.

German colonists expelled from Volhynia governorate began arriving in the Lower Volga region from September 1915, mostly in the German colonies located there. By mid-1916, the number of these settlers in Saratov governorate alone had reached 6,680 people. The Volhynian Germans found themselves in a very difficult position in the Volga region, and once the discriminatory acts against the German population were repealed after the February Revolution, they naturally rushed to return to their native places. As is already evident from the present act, the military command did everything it could to hinder this process, although it was not unauthorized: permission to return had been granted by a circular of May 24, 1917, after the Provisional Government had considered the matter. See: Reshetov D.G. German Colonists of the Western Governorates of Russia Deported to the Volga Region during the First World War // Migration Processes among the Russian Germans: A Historical Perspective. Moscow, 1998. P. 186–192. — Compiler's note.

Kerensky, A.F. (1881–1970) — chairman of the Trudovik faction in the Fourth State Duma (1912–1917). In 1917, a member of the Provisional Government: Minister of Justice (March–May), Minister of War and the Navy (May–September), Minister-Chairman (July–October). Supreme Commander-in-Chief in August–November 1917.

GERMANS IN RUSSIA BEFORE 1917

**(BIOGRAPHICAL COMMENTARY)**

ARNOLD, Fyodor Karlovich (Theodor Karl) (1819–1902) was born in St. Petersburg. His father was the founder of the Practical Commercial Academy in Moscow. In 1838 he graduated from the Forestry Institute in St. Petersburg. He furthered his training in forestry science abroad, and upon returning to Russia (1842) worked as a forester and directed forest-survey work. From 1844 to 1857 he held administrative posts in the Forestry Department, while also teaching at the Forestry Institute and the School of Agriculture. In 1848 he compiled, for the Free Economic Society, a map of state forests in European Russia, which was awarded a gold medal. From 1855 he published the weekly "Gazette of Forestry and Hunting." Leaving administrative service, he devoted himself to scholarly and pedagogical work. From 1857 to 1869 and from 1873 to 1876 he taught at the Institute of Agriculture (St. Petersburg), becoming a professor in 1866. From 1876 to 1883 he was director of the Petrovsky Academy of Agriculture and Forestry in Moscow. He then returned to St. Petersburg, where he was appointed a member of the Council of the Minister of State Domains and a specialist member of the Forestry Committee (1894), and until 1898 repeatedly served as acting director of the Forestry Department. He was the author of numerous scholarly works, including the substantial three-volume study "Russian Forest" (1890–1891). He made a great contribution to the protection, cultivation, and rational use of Russia's forests, and trained a whole generation of forestry specialists. He held the rank of active privy councillor (1898), was decorated with Russian orders, and was an honorary member of a number of learned societies. His contemporaries called Arnold "the father of Russian forestry." His brothers also achieved renown: I.K. Arnold, founder of the first school for the deaf and mute in Moscow, and Yu.K. Arnold, a composer. He is buried at the Volkovo Lutheran Cemetery in St. Petersburg.

AUERBACH, Alexander Andreyevich (Heinrichovich) (1844–1916) was born in the town of Kashin, Tver governorate. His father was a physician and the grandson of a Saxon merchant; his paternal grandfather owned a well-known faience factory in the village of Kuznetsovo, Tver governorate. He graduated from the Institute of the Corps of Mining Engineers in St. Petersburg (1863). From 1867 to 1871, having defended a dissertation in mineralogy, he was an adjunct professor at that institute. He was the first in Russia to apply the method of microscopic examination of minerals. From 1870 to 1873 he conducted coal prospecting in the Moscow Basin and the Donbass. He was the initiator of the 1st Congress of Mining Industrialists of Southern Russia (1874), a participant in subsequent congresses, and from 1899 an honorary member of the Congress Council. From 1877 he engaged in prospecting for gold-bearing sites in the Urals, and from 1881 to 1896 administered the Bogoslovsk mining district. In this post he organized the extraction of iron ore and built the Nadezhdinsk metallurgical works, the largest in the Urals (1895). He organized a steamship line to transport out the rails produced at the works, which were used in building the Siberian railway. In 1884 he founded the Turyinsk mining school, the first in the Northern Urals. In 1885 he surveyed a mercury deposit near Gorlovka (Donbass), where he founded Russia's first mercury works, which from 1887 met the country's demand for mercury. In 1896 he organized the company "A. Auerbach and Co. Mercury Enterprise," in which he served as chairman of the board and managing director. He held the rank of active state councillor (1897), was a member of the Councils on Railway Affairs and on Tariffs under the Committee of Ministers, was the initiator of the establishment (1904) of the Council on Mining Industry Affairs under the Ministry of Agriculture and State Domains, and served as a member of it.

BARCLAY DE TOLLY, Mikhail Bogdanovich (Michael Andreas) (1761–1818) was born on the estate of Pamūšis in Courland governorate, near Šiauliai (now in Lithuania). He came from a Baltic-German family, whose founder, the son of a Scot, had settled in Riga in the mid-17th century. His father was a lieutenant in the Russian army and a nobleman. He entered military service in 1776. He took part in the Russo-Turkish War (1787–1791) and the Russo-Swedish War (1788–1790). In 1799, while commanding a jäger regiment, he was promoted to major general. He distinguished himself in the Russo-Prussian-French War of 1806–1807 at Pułtusk and Preussisch-Eylau, and was promoted to lieutenant general (1807). In the Russo-Swedish War of 1808–1809 he commanded a division and occupied the Savolax region of Finland; leading a detachment on a march across the ice, he captured the town of Umeå, and was promoted to general of infantry. From 1809 he was commander-in-chief of the army in Finland and Governor-General of Finland. From 1810 to 1812 he was Minister of War, and from 1810 a member of the State Council; in March 1812 he was appointed commander-in-chief of the 1st Western Army. At the start of the Patriotic War of 1812, facing superior enemy forces, he managed to unite with the 2nd Army near Smolensk, thwarting Napoleon's plan to defeat the Russian armies separately. The army's retreat during this period provoked sharp discontent with Barclay's actions, and the commander's merits in the war were fully recognized only after his death, an appreciation later expressed in Alexander Pushkin's poem "The Commander." At the Battle of Borodino he directed operations in the center and on the right flank. He personally led cavalry charges, appearing in the most dangerous sectors. In the foreign campaigns of the Russian army of 1813–1814 he commanded an army and served as commander-in-chief of the combined Russo-Prussian forces. For his successful actions in the "Battle of the Nations" near Leipzig (1813) he was raised to the rank of count. He became Field Marshal General (1814) and Prince (1815). He was decorated with all the highest Russian orders and the highest awards of many European states. A monument to him stands by Kazan Cathedral in St. Petersburg.

BEILSTEIN, Fyodor Fyodorovich (Friedrich Konrad) (1838–1906) was born in St. Petersburg. His paternal grandfather had emigrated to Russia from Darmstadt. In 1852 he graduated from the Petrischule (a school attached to the Evangelical Lutheran Church of St. Peter) in St. Petersburg. From 1853 he studied chemistry in Germany, earning his doctorate in philosophy (1858), and became extraordinary professor at the University of Göttingen (1865). From 1866 to 1896 he was professor of chemistry at the St. Petersburg Technological Institute, succeeding D.I. Mendeleev in that chair. In 1867, at the invitation of A.M. Butlerov, he became professor of organic chemistry at St. Petersburg University. For his scholarly achievements he was awarded the Lomonosov Prize of the Academy of Sciences (1876). His research on the chlorination of toluene and the synthesis of organic acids was of great importance for the chemical industry and, in particular, for the aniline-dye industry. In 1872 he proposed a reaction for the detection of halogens in organic compounds (the Beilstein test). He laid the foundation for establishing the precise composition of Caucasian petroleum (1880–1881). The chief work of his life was a unique, multivolume reference work on organic chemistry, which began to be published in Germany in 1881 and went through several editions. He devoted about 40 years to work on this reference work. From 1886 he was a full academician of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (corresponding member from 1883). He was a member of the Berlin Academy of Sciences (1888) and an honorary member of a number of Russian and foreign scholarly and technical societies. He was deeply devoted to music, was an accomplished pianist, and served as president of the St. Petersburg Society of Chamber Music Lovers. He is buried at the Volkovo Lutheran Cemetery in St. Petersburg.

BELLINGSHAUSEN, Faddei Faddeyevich (Fabian Gottlieb Benjamin) von (1778–1852) was born at Lahhentagge, his father's estate on the island of Ösel in Arensburg uyezd of Livonia governorate (now the island of Saaremaa, Estonia). He was a descendant of an ancient baronial family originating in Lübeck and known on the island of Ösel since the 16th century. He graduated from the Naval Cadet Corps in Kronstadt (1797). From 1803 to 1806 he took part in the first Russian circumnavigation of the globe under the command of I.F. Kruzenshtern. He then served in the Baltic Fleet, and in 1809 commanded the corvette "Melpomene." From 1810 he commanded frigates in the Black Sea Fleet. He engaged in hydrographic work and made astronomical observations that made it possible to compile the first reliable map of the eastern coast of the Black Sea. From 1819 to 1821, holding the rank of captain of the 2nd rank, he led the Southern Polar Expedition on the sloops "Vostok" and "Mirny." The expedition, having sailed from Kronstadt, reached the shores of Antarctica in January 1820, discovering a new continent. Making stops at Sydney, the sailors explored vast territories of the southern Pacific and Atlantic Oceans and discovered entire groups of new islands. After crossing the Atlantic, the expedition returned to Kronstadt. It carried out major research in the fields of oceanology and oceanography, providing a scientific explanation of the Canary Current and the origin of the algae of the Sargasso Sea, and outlining a general picture of the climatic features of the polar and tropical zones. From 1821 Bellingshausen commanded naval crews, then a naval division, and from 1827 was a member of the Naval Scientific Committee with the rank of rear admiral, and a participant in the Russo-Turkish War of 1828–1829. From 1839 to 1852 he was chief commander (commandant) of the port of Kronstadt and military governor of Kronstadt. In 1843 he was promoted to admiral, and from 1844 was a member of the Admiralty Council. He was decorated with Russian orders. A sea off the coast of Antarctica, a number of islands, and a cape in the south of Sakhalin are named after him. A monument to him stands in Kronstadt.

BERATZ, Gottlieb (1871–1921) was born in the colony of Göbel (Ust-Gryaznukha), Kamyshin uyezd, Saratov governorate. He graduated from the Saratov Roman Catholic Seminary and was ordained in 1894. From 1894 to 1909 he was a pastor in the newly created left-bank parish of Deller (Beryozovka) of the Saratov deanery; from 1909 to 1911 he was a confessor at the Saratov Catholic Seminary; from 1911 he was pastor in the left-bank parish of Herzog (Susly) of the Mariental deanery. From 1901 he was a curate. He was the author of one of the first comprehensive works on the history of the Volga Germans — the book "The German Colonies on the Lower Volga: Their Formation and Early Development" (1914), dedicated to the 150th anniversary of the arrival of the first colonists in the Volga region (published in 1917). This event was also marked by a play about the life of the first settlers, written at the same time by Beratz (under the pseudonym von Göbel) together with the teacher A. Hunger. In April 1917 he was a delegate to the 1st Congress of German Colonists of the Volga Region in Saratov, and in May 1917 he was the organizer of the People's Union of Volga German Catholics and was elected its vice-chairman. He was shot by the Soviet authorities on charges of organizing the Mariental peasant uprising of 1921.

BEHR (Beer, Beyer), Andrei Benediktovich (Andreas) (1696–1751), son of an émigré from Saxony who had settled in Russia in the 1670s as a master of hammer-mill and sheet-iron works, was a nobleman. Holding the rank of shtyk-yunker, he served at the Olonets-Petrovsky works (1722), and was head of arms production (1723). In 1727 he became a lieutenant and commander of a ship. From 1731 he was in charge of the Sestroretsk arms works, and became captain of naval artillery (1735). He proved himself an inventor, creating a design for a machine to produce thin iron strips and improving the fusil, the musket of the time. From 1738 he administered the Tula Arms Works. In 1744, holding the rank of brigadier, he was sent to head a commission to A. Demidov's Altai works, where Demidov had secretly been smelting silver. The silver discovered was sent to St. Petersburg, where it was used to cast a reliquary for the relics of St. Alexander Nevsky. In 1747, on the basis of Behr's report, the works were acquired as property of the Cabinet, forming the district of the Kolyvano-Voskresensk Works (later the Altai Mining District), of which he became the first head. Under his direction, a major center of silver smelting was created there; under him, active settlement of the region began, along with the exploitation of its ore and forest resources, the survey of sites for new works, and measures to strengthen the state border and organize postal communications. He was awarded the rank of major general.

BLUMENTROST, Lavrenty Lavrentyevich (Robert Laurence) (1692–1755) was born in Moscow. He was the son of an émigré from Saxony who had served as personal physician to Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich. He studied at Gluck's gymnasium in Moscow — the first educational institution of its kind in Russia — and from 1707 at the universities of Halle and Oxford, receiving his doctorate in medicine (1714). From 1714 he was personal physician to Tsarevna Natalia Alekseyevna, sister of Peter I. In 1715 he drew up a description of Peter's state of health for consultations with leading European physicians. In 1717 he acquired in Amsterdam the well-known anatomical collection of Ruysch, which laid the foundation for Peter's Kunstkamera — the first public state museum in Russia. On Peter's instructions, he carried out a chemical analysis of the Olonets mineral waters. In 1718 he was appointed personal physician to Peter, and simultaneously oversaw the Kunstkamera and the tsar's library. He was the first president of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (1725–1733). He played the leading role in drawing up the plan for the academy, organizing it, and inviting foreign scholars to Russia. In 1728 he was compelled to withdraw from the affairs of the Academy of Sciences and move to Moscow together with the court of Emperor Peter II, returning to St. Petersburg in 1730. In 1733, under Empress Anna Ivanovna, he was removed from all his posts and exiled to Moscow. There he engaged in private practice; from 1738 he was senior doctor of the Main Military Hospital and director of the hospital school, and made a great contribution to the training of military physicians. In 1754 he was engaged by Empress Elizabeth Petrovna and I.I. Shuvalov in discussing the plan for the first Russian university in Moscow, and became its curator. Blumentrost's brothers, I.L. and L.Kh. Blumentrost, were also personal physicians in Russian service.

BRYULLOV (Bryullo), Karl Pavlovich (1799–1852) was born in St. Petersburg. He came from a Germanized line of French Huguenots who had lived in northern Germany since at least the 17th century. His father was a sculptor and ornamental artist who had settled in Russia with his father and grandfather in 1773. He studied under his father, and from 1809 at the St. Petersburg Academy of Arts, which he completed in 1821 with the Great Gold Medal and a first-class certificate. In 1822, together with his brother Alexander, later a well-known architect, he was sent abroad to study and work. He visited Dresden and Munich, and from 1823 lived in Rome. Bryullov's greatest work of this period, which established his place in the history of Russian art as the leading painter of the Romantic movement, was the painting "The Last Day of Pompeii" (1830–1833), which brought him European fame. In 1835 he returned to Russia, living in Moscow, and from 1836 in St. Petersburg, where he taught at the Academy of Arts (becoming a first-class professor in 1846). During this time his talent as a portraitist flourished, and he became a master of creating psychologically nuanced images of figures of Russian culture (portraits of N.V. Kukolnik and I.A. Krylov, a self-portrait). He also painted icons for churches in St. Petersburg, and from 1843 to 1847 worked on the interior decoration of St. Isaac's Cathedral. Having begun the painting of the great dome, he was forced to break it off due to lung disease. In 1849 he went abroad for treatment, living on the island of Madeira, and from 1850 in Italy, where he died.

BULLA, Karl Karlovich (Karl Oswald) (1854–1929) was born in Germany. He came to St. Petersburg at the age of 10. He was placed with a firm selling photographic supplies, where he rose from laboratory assistant to photographer. In 1875 he opened his own photographic studio in the center of the city, on Sadovaya Street. In 1886 he received permission to conduct on-location photography and moved his studio to Nevsky Prospect. In 1908 he bought and outfitted a new, luxurious studio on Nevsky Prospect, which was visited by members of the imperial family, dignitaries, and the artistic intelligentsia. His photo reports from the late 19th and early 20th centuries captured the most important events in the life of the capital, along with views of palaces and public and residential buildings. He created genre and scenic artistic compositions. In 1908, together with his son, he produced a photo report on the life of Leo Tolstoy at Yasnaya Polyana. He actively collaborated with Russian illustrated magazines and with major foreign publications. He served as photographer to the Ministry of the Imperial Court and received the special insignia "Photographer of the City of St. Petersburg" (1896). He was a participant in and prize-winner of several all-Russian exhibitions. He engaged in charitable work under the Department of Institutions of Empress Maria. A hereditary honorary citizen, he entered the merchant estate in 1908 and later became a personal nobleman. In 1916, having handed over the business to his sons Alexander and Viktor, he settled on the island of Ösel (now Saaremaa, Estonia).

BUNGE Nikolai Khristianovich von (1823—1895) was born in Kiev. Grandson of a pharmacist from the East Prussian town of Stallupönen (now Nesterov, Kaliningrad Region), who settled in Kiev in the mid-18th century. His father was a doctor of medicine. He graduated from the law faculty of Kiev University in 1845. Doctor of political science (1852). He taught at Kiev educational institutions, including the university, where he was an extraordinary professor from 1852 and an ordinary professor in 1854—1880. He was rector of the university (with interruptions) in 1859—1880. In 1863—1864 and 1886—1889 he taught economic disciplines to the heirs to the throne. Founder of the Kiev school of economists, who rejected the labor theory of value and socialist doctrines and focused primarily on practical questions of economic policy. In 1862—1880 he concurrently managed the Kiev office of the State Bank. He participated in carrying out the economic reforms of Alexander II and in drafting the new university statute (1861). From 1880 he was deputy minister of finance, from 1881 managing the ministry, and in 1882—1886 minister of finance. Amid a severe budget deficit, he sought to increase revenues and limit state budget expenditures, and advocated a peaceful foreign policy. During his tenure as minister, state intervention in the economy increased. His policy met with resistance from the reactionary circle around Alexander III, and he was forced to resign. Afterward Bunge unsuccessfully tried to counter these circles' course toward preserving the peasant commune. In 1887—1895 he was chairman of the Committee of Ministers, and in 1892—1895 he simultaneously served as deputy chairman of the Committee of the Siberian Railway. In his "Posthumous Notes," addressed to the emperor, he called for economic and political reforms. From 1890 he was an ordinary academician of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (corresponding member from 1859, honorary member from 1881). Active Privy Councillor (1885), decorated with many Russian and foreign orders.

BUSCH Ivan Fedorovich (Johann Peter) (1771—1843) was born in Narva. From a family of innkeepers. In 1785 he entered the Kalinkin Medical-Surgical School in St. Petersburg. With the outbreak of the Russo-Swedish War of 1788—1790 he was sent as a physician to the fleet, and in 1790 was taken prisoner by the Swedes. After the war he served as a prosector, then as an operator, and from 1793 taught at the Kronstadt Medical-Surgical Hospital. In 1797 he became a docent at the Kalinkin School, and from 1798 a professor. In 1800 he was invited to the newly founded Medical-Surgical Academy in St. Petersburg as professor of the chair of surgery, which he headed until 1833. The most celebrated Russian surgeon of his time and the founder of Russian traumatology. He placed particular importance on preserving organs as much as possible during operations, on observing the patient, studying the patient's individual characteristics, and carefully testing new methods of diagnosis and treatment. Author of the first surgical textbook in Russia (1807—1808); under his guidance a new method of teaching surgery was developed based on the unity of theory and practice. First president of the German Medical Society of St. Petersburg (1819—1843). Active State Councillor (1828), member of the Medical Council (1830), honorary member of Russian and foreign scholarly societies. In 1838, in honor of the 50th anniversary of his medical and pedagogical career, a gold medal and prizes bearing his name were established. He is buried in the Smolensk Lutheran Cemetery in St. Petersburg.

BAER Karl Maksimovich (Karl Ernst) von (1792—1876) was born on the Piep estate in Weissenstein County, Estland Governorate. A descendant of a noble family originating from Westphalia and known in the Baltic region since the 18th century. His father was the marshal of the nobility of Estland Governorate. In 1814 he graduated from the medical faculty of Dorpat University, earning the degree of doctor of medicine. During the Patriotic War of 1812 he served as an assistant physician at the Riga military hospital. From 1814 he studied in Vienna and Germany. In 1817—1828 and 1830—1834 he worked in Königsberg, becoming an extraordinary (1819) and then ordinary (1822) professor of zoology and anatomy at the local university. He defended a dissertation on fossil mammal remains (1823). Having discovered the mammalian and human ovum (1827), he gained worldwide fame. In 1828—1830 and from 1834 he worked in Russia at the invitation of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences. He served as librarian of the foreign department of the Academy Library, engaged in anthropology and ichthyology, established the basic laws of vertebrate embryogenesis, and conducted biological and geological research on Novaya Zemlya, the islands of the Gulf of Finland, and the Kola Peninsula. In 1853—1857 he headed an expedition to the Caspian Sea, where he conducted hydrological, hydrobiological, and ichthyological research, determining the conditions for the existence of commercial fish in the Volga and Ural river basins. This work laid the foundation for the development of fishing and fish farming in Russia. In 1857 he established the pattern of erosion of the right banks of rivers in the Northern Hemisphere and the left banks in the Southern Hemisphere (Baer's law). He retired in 1862. He was an ordinary academician of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences in 1828—1830 and 1834—1862 (foreign corresponding member in 1826—1828, foreign honorary member in 1830—1834, honorary member from 1862). He was a founding member of the Russian Geographical Society (chairman of its ethnographic division in 1844—1848) and of the Russian Entomological Society (its first chairman in 1860—1861). In 1865 the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences issued a medal in honor of the 50th anniversary of Baer's scientific career. His name was given to a cape and an island, and entered the name of ridges in the Caspian Lowland (the Baer Hillocks).

WALBERG Karl Ferdinand Emanuel von (1847—1920) was born in the Volga colony of Katharinenstadt, where his father, a native of Finland, served as Lutheran pastor in 1821—1877. He was raised to noble rank. He received a medical education. His first literary efforts were stories about the life of soldiers of the Russian army during the Russo-Turkish War of 1877—1878. For the 150th anniversary of the German settlement of the Volga (1914) he wrote a work titled "The Origin of Love for the Homeland Among the Inhabitants of the Volga Steppes" (unpublished). He wrote novels about the Volga Germans and Mennonites. They are composed in the style of German romanticism and sentimentalism, but give a fairly realistic picture of colonist life and of the relations between the colonists and the surrounding Russian population. Author of memoirs published in 1923, which reflect his impressions of his childhood on the Volga.

WERNER Christian Friedrich (1759—1823) was born in Schorndorf (Württemberg). He grew up in Ludwigsburg and was engaged in trade. In 1779 he moved to Gingen, where he owned a textile factory. He became interested in the ideas of Pietism, and from 1791 held "Bible hours" ("Stunden") in his home. The death of close relatives and friends deepened his religiosity, and he gained a reputation as a model Christian and citizen. The Bible studies held in his home served as an example for the creation of similar religious societies in neighboring villages. In 1819 he became acquainted with the Catholic priest I. Lindl, whose sermons in Gundremmingen (Bavaria) drew large audiences. In 1822 Lindl founded the colony of Sarata in Akkerman County, Bessarabia Region. Werner organized the resettlement there of followers of Lindl's ideas on Christian community of property, and in 1823 he himself set out for Sarata. He died shortly after arriving, bequeathing 25,000 silver rubles to the local community for missionary purposes. The Russian government forbade such use of the funds, and the executor of the will used them to establish a school in Sarata (1844). In honor of the testator it was named the Werner Central School (later the Werner Teachers' Seminary).

VILLEVALDE Bogdan Pavlovich (Gottfried) (1818—1903) was born in the town of Pavlovsk, St. Petersburg Governorate. In 1838—1842 he studied at the St. Petersburg Academy of Arts under K.P. Bryullov and A.I. Sauerweid, graduating from the academy with the Grand Gold Medal. In 1843—1844 he was a pensioner of the Academy of Arts abroad. By the Highest command he was summoned to St. Petersburg to complete the battle paintings begun by Sauerweid, who had died in 1844. He contributed to the development of the battle-painting genre in Russian art. He strove for documentary accuracy of depiction and for characteristic chosen episodes. He skillfully combined dramatic tension of subject with an abundance of typical, genre, and sometimes humorously interpreted details. In working on a series of paintings devoted to the Patriotic War of 1812, he used documents and eyewitness accounts. He depicted the major military campaigns of his own time, gathering material for his paintings during the Hungarian campaign of Russian troops in 1849, the Crimean War of 1853—1856, the Caucasus War, and the Russo-Turkish War of 1877—1878. His paintings were exhibited at several World's Fairs. Academician of the St. Petersburg Academy of Arts (1845). He taught at the Academy of Arts in 1848—1894 (professor from 1848, honored professor from 1888).

WITTGENSTEIN (Sayn-Wittgenstein-Berleburg) Pyotr Khristianovich (Peter Ludwig Adolf) (1768—1843) was born in the town of Pereyaslav, Poltava Governorate. His father was a lieutenant colonel in the Prussian army; having been taken prisoner by the Russians during the Seven Years' War of 1756—1763, he entered Russian service and rose to the rank of lieutenant general. In 1781 he was enrolled in the Russian army as a sergeant. He took part in military operations in Poland (1792—1794) and in the Persian campaign of 1796. In 1797 he became a major general and chief of the Mariupol Hussar Regiment. During the Russo-Austro-French War of 1805 he commanded a hussar brigade, distinguishing himself at Amstetten and Austerlitz. He took part in the Russo-Turkish War (1806—1812) and the Russo-Prussian-French War (1806—1807). Lieutenant general and chief of the Life Guards Hussar Regiment (1807). During the Patriotic War of 1812 he commanded the 1st Separate Infantry Corps, which covered the approach to St. Petersburg. He halted the advance of French forces at Klyastitsy, after which he was called "the defender of Peter's city." During the retreat of Napoleon's forces he inflicted defeats on them near Polotsk, Chashniki, Vitebsk, and Smolyantsy. In the course of the foreign campaigns of the Russian army of 1813—1814 he occupied Königsberg and Berlin. After the death of M.I. Kutuzov (1813) he was appointed commander-in-chief of the Russo-Prussian army, but having suffered defeats at Lützen and Bautzen, at his own request he was replaced by M.B. Barclay de Tolly. Subsequently commanding a corps, he distinguished himself at Dresden and Leipzig and was severely wounded at Arcis-sur-Aube. In 1818 he became commander-in-chief of the 2nd Army and a member of the State Council. Field Marshal General (1826). An excellent corps commander, he could not manage larger forces, lacking the strategic thinking required for that. However, he was popular in the army and known for his personal bravery. In 1834 he received from the Prussian king the title of Serene Prince (confirmed in Russia in 1836).

WRANGEL Ferdinand Petrovich von (1796—1870) was born in Pskov. From an old Baltic German noble family. His father was a major in the Russian army. In 1810—1815 he studied at the Naval Cadet Corps in St. Petersburg. He took part in a circumnavigation under the command of V.M. Golovnin (1817—1819). In 1820—1824, holding the rank of naval lieutenant, he led an expedition to study the coasts of northeastern Siberia. The expedition mapped the coastline from the Indigirka River to Kolyuchin Bay and part of the Bear Islands, and conducted valuable navigational, hydrographic, geomagnetic, and climatic research, establishing that the polar sea is not covered by solid strong ice even in the severest frosts. Author of the book "A Journey Along the Northern Shores of Siberia and the Arctic Ocean" (1841). In 1825—1827 he led a round-the-world expedition on the ship Krotky, which observed currents and water temperature and conducted regular meteorological observations. From 1829 he was a captain of the first rank. In 1829—1835 he was chief manager of the Russian settlements in Alaska. In 1867, when the government sold Alaska to the United States, he strongly objected to this. From 1836 he was a rear admiral. In 1840—1849 he was director of the Russian-American Company. From 1847 he was a vice admiral, from 1856 an adjutant general and admiral, and from 1857 a member of the State Council. In 1855—1857 he was minister of the navy. As minister, he did much to reform the navy and the merchant fleet. In 1859—1864 he was president of the Auxiliary Fund of Evangelical Lutheran Parishes in Russia. Honorary member of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences from 1855 (corresponding member from 1827). Member of the Paris Academy of Sciences (1856) and of other scholarly societies. Co-founder of the Russian Geographical Society (1845). An island in the Arctic Ocean, and a mountain and cape in Alaska, are named in his honor.

HAAS Fyodor Petrovich (Friedrich Joseph) (1780—1853) was born in Münstereifel near Cologne. His father was an apothecary. He was educated at German universities (1801—1803). He worked as a physician in Vienna, doctor of medicine (1805). From 1806 he was in Moscow as a private physician, then chief physician of the Pavlovsk Hospital (1807—1812). He also engaged in private practice, becoming one of the most famous physicians in Moscow, which brought him considerable wealth (he had his own house in the center of the city, on Kuznetsky Most). He discovered mineral water springs in the Caucasus (1809—1810) and described their curative properties (1811), laying the foundations of Russian balneology. He took part in the foreign campaign of the Russian army of 1813—1814, reaching Paris. City physician (chief physician) of Moscow (1825—1826), State Councillor (1838). From 1828 a member of the Moscow Governorate Prison Committee, from 1829 chief physician of the Moscow prisons. In 1831 he sold all his real estate, donating the proceeds to the construction of medical institutions and aid to the needy, and went to live at the hospitals. He worked energetically and persistently to improve the condition of prisoners: he petitioned for the mitigation of their punishments, for improved conditions of confinement and transport, for the opening of prison and police hospitals, prison workshops, and schools for prisoners' children, and collected funds for feeding prisoners. In Moscow he was called "the holy doctor." He died alone and in poverty. Thousands of Muscovites accompanied him on his final journey. He is buried in the German (Vvedenskoye) Cemetery. In 1909 a bust of him was erected in Moscow, and a charitable society was established in memory of Doctor Haas.

HABLITZ (Tablitz) Karl Ivanovich (Carl Ludwig) (1752—1821) was born in Königsberg. In 1758 he came to Moscow with his father, who became inspector of the printing house at Moscow University. In 1768 he entered Moscow University. In 1769—1773, as part of an expedition led by Academician S.G. Gmelin, he explored the Don basin, the lower Volga, the Caucasus, and the shores of the Caspian Sea. In 1776—1781 he was assistant director of the Astrakhan Garden Office. He took part in M.I. Voinovich's Caspian expedition (1781—1782). In 1784 he compiled a "physical description" of the Tauride Region (Crimea). Director of the economy of the Tauride Region (1787), its vice-governor (1788—1796). From 1796 he served under the Procurator-General of the Senate. He was the principal adviser to Paul I on matters concerning foreign colonists. In 1797, at Paul's instruction, he examined the German colonies of the Volga region, as a result of which a decision was made to restore a special body for administering the colonies — the Saratov Office of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers. From 1797 he was a member of the Expedition of State Economy, Trusteeship of Foreigners, and Rural Husbandry, while also serving as deputy minister of the Department of Appanages. In 1802—1803 he was deputy administrator, and in 1803—1811 administrator of the Expedition of State Economy. President of the Manufacturing Collegium (1802—1811), chief director of the Forestry Department of the Ministry of Finance (1803—1809). On his initiative the first schools of forestry were opened in Russia. From 1796 he was an honorary member of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (corresponding member from 1776). Privy Councillor (1800), Senator (1808). A genus of plants is named after Hablitz. He is buried in the Volkovo Lutheran Cemetery in St. Petersburg.

GAMBS Heinrich (1765—1831) was born in Baden-Baden. He settled in Russia at the end of the 18th century. In 1795, together with the Austrian merchant I. Ott, he founded a furniture workshop in St. Petersburg, and at the same time opened his own furniture business on Nevsky Prospekt. He filled orders for the grand dukes and the capital's nobility. He supplied furniture to the Mikhailovsky Castle, the Pavlovsk Palace, and the Hermitage. From 1801 he was close to the imperial court, executing nearly all of its important commissions. He also repaired furniture in the Winter Palace and the Hermitage. In 1810 he received the title of "court mechanic." After 1812 the Gambs firm held a leading position in furniture production in St. Petersburg. In 1828—1830 Gambs's sons became co-owners. He and his sons produced highly artistic furniture from the designs and sketches of well-known architects, as well as their own designs. The firm existed until the mid-19th century, remaining the largest in St. Petersburg. He died during a cholera epidemic and is buried in the cholera cemetery.

HAMEL Iosif Khristianovich (1788—1862) was born in the colony of Sarepta near Tsaritsyn. His father was a police chief. He studied at the Medical-Surgical Academy in St. Petersburg (1807—1811). From 1811 he conducted galvano-chemical experiments at the academy. Doctor of medicine (1813). He was sent abroad to continue his education, where he studied applied sciences and chemical production, carried out technical experiments, and became acquainted with the Bell-Lancaster system of mutual instruction, then popular, about which he wrote a book. Upon returning to Russia, he studied manufacturing industry and defended a dissertation on iron production in Russia (1833). In 1834 he contributed to resolving the question of building Russia's first railway, the Tsarskoye Selo Railway. From 1839 he studied in Great Britain and France the process of producing the first photographs — daguerreotypes — and compiled a detailed description of it. He took part in organizing the manufacturing exhibition in St. Petersburg (1849), was appointed a member of the Manufacturing Council (1849) and a member for the 1850 London World's Fair. Having visited the London exhibition, he arranged for a complete description of inventions patented in Great Britain since 1617 to be sent to Russia. After returning to Russia (1856) he studied the history of the telegraph, the search for silver ores in the Caucasus, and the trade-political relations between England and Russia. From 1829 he was an ordinary academician of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (corresponding member from 1813) — the first in an entire line of Russian and Soviet academicians descended from German colonists. Member of many scholarly societies. He bequeathed a significant part of his estate to the Sarepta school.

HAHN Yevgeny Fyodorovich von (1807—1874) was born in St. Petersburg. His ancestor, director of the St. Petersburg post office, came to Russia at the invitation of Catherine II. In 1826 he graduated from the Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum. He served in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and from 1833 in the Department of Appanages. From 1839 he was senior member of the Guardianship Committee for Foreign Settlers of Southern Russia, and in 1846—1848 its chairman (chief trustee). In these posts he did much to promote the development of forestry and horticulture in the New Russia colonies. During his period of leadership the colonies flourished. From 1848 he was director of the 1st department of the Ministry of State Domains, and from 1859 a member of the minister's Council. In 1857 he was appointed a member of the Provisional Executive Committee for the Organization of the Southern Settlements. From 1862 he chaired a special commission to work out preparatory measures for introducing general administration of the rural estates. In 1864 he took part in drafting the judicial reform. Privy Councillor (1858), Senator (1860). Decorated with Russian orders. The Mennonite colony of Hahnsau in Novouzensk County, Samara Governorate, was named in his honor.

HEYM Ivan Andreyevich (Johann Christian) (1758—1821) was born in Braunschweig. His father was a physician. He was educated at German universities. He arrived in Russia in 1779 as a private tutor. From 1781 he taught German at Moscow University, where he became an extraordinary (1783) and then ordinary (1786) professor. At the same time he taught at the University Noble Boarding School and other Moscow educational institutions. From 1786 he lectured in Russian. He gained wide fame for his dictionaries and textbooks of German and Russian, and anthologies of German and Russian literature. Member of the School Committee (1803). From 1804 professor of statistics and commercial sciences, author of works on the geography and statistics of Russia and Western European countries. He published the newspaper "Moskowitische Zeitung" (1811—1812). He was rector of Moscow University in 1808—1818. During the Patriotic War of 1812 he directed the evacuation of the university's property, professors, and students to Nizhny Novgorod. After the liberation of Moscow he worked on restoring the university and constructing its new building. He played a special role in restoring the university library, which had burned down, and from 1814 held the post of its librarian. Under Heym's will, the main part of his personal book collection (more than 2,000 volumes) was given to the university. State Councillor, decorated with Russian orders. He is buried in the German (Vvedenskoye) Cemetery in Moscow.

GELTSER Vasily Fyodorovich (Friedrichovich) (1840—1908) was born in Moscow. His father, a native of Prussia, was a member of the Cooks' Guild of the Moscow Craft Board. In 1848—1856 he studied in the ballet division of the Moscow Theater School. In 1856—1907 he performed on the stage of the Moscow Bolshoi Theater. A character dancer with a subtle feel for the style of folk dances, and an actor of mime and plastic expression, he possessed a concise and expressive gesture. He had a remarkable gift for transformation. The range of his roles was extraordinarily wide — from genre, comic, and grotesque characters and villains to tragic ones. The pinnacle of Geltser's mimetic achievements was the role of the mute Malay servant in A.Yu. Simon's opera "The Song of Triumphant Love." Audiences came to this mediocre opera mainly to see his performance. In 1894—1901 he was concurrently the director of the Bolshoi Theater ballet troupe. In 1898—1908 he taught mime and plasticity in the ballet division of the Moscow Theater School and in the drama courses at the Maly Theater. At the invitation of K.S. Stanislavsky he taught dance and plasticity at the Society of Art and Literature (1880). He was one of the authors of the libretto of "Swan Lake" and composed the dances for the first production of P.I. Tchaikovsky's opera "Eugene Onegin." His daughter Ye.V. Geltser was a well-known ballet artist. He is buried in the Vagankovo Cemetery.

HAHN Ivan Ivanovich (Johann) (1854—1938) was born in the colony of Hoffnungstal, Akkerman County, Bessarabia Region. His father, a colonist and owner of a plow-making workshop, moved to Russia from Württemberg with his parents in 1812. He studied at St. Paul's Odessa Real School. In 1880 he inherited the workshop in Odessa founded by his father, and on its basis created the largest agricultural equipment factory in Russia. In 1881 he developed the "New Russia plow," which was in great demand among German colonists as well as among landowners and peasants. From 1889 he began producing winnowing machines, and later reapers, threshers, and straw cutters. In 1893 he built a second factory. He successfully competed with local as well as English, American, and German manufacturers. He was repeatedly awarded prizes at agricultural exhibitions. From 1898 all of Hahn's products bore a factory trademark approved by the government. Their high quality was ensured by the latest equipment and strict discipline. Hereditary Honorary Citizen (1904). In 1907 the enterprises were reorganized into a joint-stock company, and Hahn became its manager. In 1909 he bought an estate near Odessa, in whose fields new machines were tested. By 1912 the firm employed 1,200 workers and produced 80,000 plows, 30,000 harrows, 6,000 reapers, and 3,000 seed drills a year. During the First World War production declined owing to the conscription of workers into the army, and the enterprises switched to producing military goods. In 1918 Hahn sold the factories, which had become unprofitable, and moved to Germany, and then to Chișinău, which at that time belonged to Romania.

GEORGI Ivan Ivanovich (Johann Gottlieb) (1729—1802) was born in Wachholzhagen (Pomerania). From the family of an Evangelical Lutheran pastor.
