He worked in a pharmacy and studied medicine in Sweden, earning the degree of doctor of medicine. He opened his own pharmacy in the town of Stendal. He came to Russia in 1770 to take part in expeditions of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences. In 1770—1774, as part of the expeditions of I.P. Falck and P.S. Pallas, he explored a vast territory from the Arkhangelsk region to Transbaikalia, gathering a wealth of material on geography, nature, climate, flora and fauna, geology, mineralogy, and ethnography. On this basis he produced the first comprehensive work on the ethnography of Russia (1776—1777), compiled a map of Lake Baikal and its surroundings, described local plants, and processed and published the notes of Falck, who had died during the expedition. In his final multi-volume work he attempted to compile a list of the plants of Russian flora, indicating the medicinal use of many of them. He also described the sights of St. Petersburg and its surroundings and compiled a list of local plants. In 1773, while participating in the Academy's expeditions, he visited the German colonies of the Volga region and left a description of them. Author of one of the first original works on chemistry in Russian. He developed new chemical methods for analyzing plant, mineral, and animal raw materials, was the first to carry out a chemical analysis of Russian marble, clays, and peat, and studied sugar-bearing, dye-producing, and rubber-bearing plants. He investigated the composition of mineral waters and classified them. He worked on locating deposits and developing methods for purifying salts. He studied methods of separating gold and silver and of obtaining iron from ores. He took part in prospecting for coal deposits, discovered oil shale, and determined its significance. He received awards from the Academy of Sciences three times for his labors. From 1783 he was an ordinary academician of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (adjunct from 1776). He was a member of Russian and foreign scholarly societies. The plant genus originating from Mexico, the dahlia (georgina), is named after him in Russia.

GERDT Pavel Andreyevich (Paul Friedrich) (1844—1917) was born in the village of Volynkino, St. Petersburg Governorate. His father was a pin maker and a Saxon subject. He studied at the Theater School in St. Petersburg (1854—1865), graduating as a first-class dancer. In 1866—1916 he served at the Mariinsky Theater. From his first year on stage he performed leading roles. He possessed an impressive stage appearance, excellent training, natural grace, and a distinctively elegant, masculine plasticity. His performing manner became the model of male dance style for decades. He danced leading character roles, was a superb mime, and an excellent partner. The audience greeted every one of his appearances on stage with applause. In the troupe he was valued not only for his talent but also for his gentle, even temper and discipline. He was the first performer of the leading male roles in the ballets of P.I. Tchaikovsky and A.K. Glazunov. He took part in S.P. Diaghilev's "Ballets Russes" enterprise (1909—1910). He also painted, which helped him create expressive makeup. He worked as a choreographer as well. In 1880—1916 he taught at the St. Petersburg Theater School. Among his students were A. Vaganova, T. Karsavina, A. Pavlova, and M. Fokine. Hereditary Honorary Citizen (1890), "soloist of His Imperial Majesty" (1901). Decorated with Russian orders. His daughter Ye.P. Gerdt was a well-known ballet artist. He is buried in the Smolensk Lutheran Cemetery in St. Petersburg.

HESS Herman Ivanovich (Hermann Heinrich) (1802—1850) was born in Geneva. His father was an architect and artist who moved to Russia in the early 19th century. He graduated from the medical faculty of Dorpat University, and in 1825 defended a dissertation for the degree of doctor of medicine on the chemical composition and curative effects of Russian mineral waters. He trained in Stockholm under the famous chemist J. Berzelius. He began his career as a physician in Irkutsk, studying deposits of table salt and mineral waters near Lake Baikal. From 1830 he was professor at St. Petersburg University, and also taught at other educational institutions in the capital. He taught chemistry to the future Emperor Alexander II. In 1840 he discovered the law of the thermal effect of chemical reactions (the basic law of thermochemistry, named after him). In 1849 he was the first in Russia to propose a systematization of the chemical elements. He discovered saccharic acid and a number of minerals, studied the catalytic properties of platinum and the composition of Caucasian petroleum, proposed a method for extracting tellurium from Altai telluride silver, established the expediency of hot-blast in blast furnaces, and invented the alcoholometer. Author of the first chemistry textbook in Russia. He was among the first to introduce systematic laboratory instruction in analytical chemistry. From 1834 he was an ordinary academician of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (adjunct from 1828, extraordinary academician from 1830). He is buried in the Smolensk Lutheran Cemetery in St. Petersburg.

GIERS Nikolai Karlovich von (1820—1895) was born near the town of Radzivilov, Volhynia Governorate. His father was a postmaster, and his mother was the sister of the navigator F.P. Litke. After graduating from the Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum (1838) he served in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Envoy extraordinary in Tehran (1863), Bern (1867), and Stockholm (1872). From 1875 deputy minister of foreign affairs. In 1876—1882 he repeatedly ran the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in the absence of the elderly minister A.M. Gorchakov. In 1882—1895 he was minister of foreign affairs. In 1879—1885 he was present at four meetings of the emperors of Russia, Germany, and Austria-Hungary. The foreign policy he pursued was characterized by restraint and caution, a tendency toward compromise, and was aimed at securing peace and security for the country. The means for achieving this goal was the minister's orientation toward alliance with Germany. Giers strove in every way to prevent a war in Europe, prophetically believing that it could lead to revolution and the fall of the monarchy in Russia. In his efforts to preserve the "Alliance of the Three Emperors," he came under attack from anti-German-minded members of the ruling circles. Giers was not a supporter of an alliance with France, but recognition of the danger of foreign-policy isolation for the country amid the deterioration of relations between Russia and Germany forced him to take steps in that direction. However, not wishing to bind Russia to premature obligations, he moved toward the formation of a Russo-French alliance in stages — from a diplomatic agreement (1891) to a military convention (1893). Active Privy Councillor (1878), Secretary of State (1879), Senator (1875). Honorary member of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (from 1876), author of memoirs. His brother F.K. Giers was president of the Evangelical Lutheran General Consistory in St. Petersburg.

GMELIN Johann Georg (1709—1755) was born in Tübingen. From a family of a scholar-chemist. From 1722 he studied at the medical faculty of Tübingen University, doctor of medicine (1727). In 1727 he was invited to the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences, where he engaged in anatomical dissection and compiled a catalogue of the Kunstkamera collection. In 1729—1733 he took part in publishing the Academy's "Notes to the Gazette." In 1733—1743, together with Academician G.F. Müller, he headed the work of the land detachment of the Second Kamchatka Expedition. During the expedition he organized the collection of specimens, conducted meteorological observations, and inspected and described the factories of the Urals and the towns and forts of Siberia. Upon returning to St. Petersburg he worked on processing the collected materials and preparing for publication his multi-volume work "Flora of Siberia" (published 1747—1769). In 1747, owing to conflicts with the Academy secretary I.D. Schumacher, he returned to his homeland. In 1749—1755 he was professor of botany and chemistry at Tübingen University. He published, in German, a multi-volume diary, "Journey Through Siberia" (1751—1752), which contains information new for its time on the nature and population of Siberia (in particular, on the sharp change in natural conditions east of the Yenisei, and on the life, occupations, religious beliefs, and customs of the Siberian peoples), on the development of the region, on the state of mining affairs in the Urals and Siberia, and descriptions of state and private factories, fairs, and deposits of iron ore, table salt, coal, and mica. Gmelin bequeathed his botanical collections, mineral collection, and materials on the flora and fauna of Siberia, along with his drawings, to the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences, of which he had been a professor in 1731—1748 (adjunct from 1727).

GOLDBACH, Christian (1690—1764) was born in Königsberg. He graduated from the law faculty of the University of Königsberg and studied mathematics on his own. In his youth he traveled extensively through Europe, maintaining friendly ties and correspondence with many outstanding people of his time. In 1725 he was invited to the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences. During his time in St. Petersburg he published a number of articles on the integration of differential equations, on converting divergent series into convergent ones, and other topics. But he is known above all for posing the famous problem of number theory known as "Goldbach's conjecture," which he put forward in a letter to Leonhard Euler in 1742. Goldbach asserted that every integer can be represented as the sum of three prime numbers. This assertion was only partially proven (for sufficiently large odd numbers) in the twentieth century. In addition to his scholarly research, he supervised the education of the future Emperor Peter II. In 1742 he transferred to service in the Collegium of Foreign Affairs, where he was in charge of cipher work, and moved to Moscow. From 1725 to 1742 he was professor of mathematics at the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (conference secretary in 1725—1728 and 1734—1742, honorary member from 1742).

GREGORY (Grigoryev), Johann Gottfried (Ivan or Yagan) (1631—1675) was born in Merseburg (Saxony). He was the son of an apothecary. He studied at the University of Leipzig. In 1658 he came to Moscow, where he became a teacher at a parish school and assistant to the pastor of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of St. Michael in the German Quarter. In 1662 he was ordained a pastor in Dresden and received the academic degree of magister in Jena. From 1662 he was pastor of the Church of St. Michael, and in 1669—1675 pastor of the Evangelical Lutheran Church of Sts. Peter and Paul in the German Quarter. In 1672, by decree of Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich, he was ordered to "stage a comedy," performing it in a hall specially built for the purpose in the village of Preobrazhenskoye. The German text of the play "The Play of Artaxerxes," written by Gregory, was translated into Russian and learned by youths from the German Quarter and pupils of the Lutheran school. The first performance took place in October 1672 in Preobrazhenskoye. In winter the performances were held in the Kremlin. In 1672—1675, under Gregory's direction and with his participation, six more plays were staged. These were the first theatrical performances in Russia. Although his plays were written on biblical subjects, they were secular in character and distinguished by dynamic stage action. Gregory was rewarded for this activity with sables, and also received permission to brew beer duty-free for household consumption. In 1673 he and his actors were invited to a reception with the tsar and treated to food from the tsar's own table. Gregory's son is also known — I.I. Gregorius (Gregory), who in 1701 founded one of the first private pharmacies in Russia in the German Quarter.

GROT, Yakov Karlovich (1812—1893) was born in St. Petersburg. His paternal grandfather was an Evangelical Lutheran pastor, a native of Holstein, in Russian service from 1758. His father was an official of the Ministry of Finance and a nobleman. He studied at the Lyceum boarding school (1823—1826) and the Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum (1826—1832). From 1832 to 1841 he was a civil official. From 1841 he was professor of Russian literature and history at the University of Helsingfors. He studied the history of Swedish and Finnish literature, Scandinavian folklore and mythology, translated Scandinavian poets, and participated in compiling a Swedish-Russian dictionary. In 1852—1859 he tutored the grand dukes Nicholas and Alexander Alexandrovich (the future Emperor Alexander III). In 1853—1862 he was professor of literature at the Alexander (formerly Tsarskoye Selo) Lyceum. From 1862 he engaged in research on Russian literature: he prepared the works of G.R. Derzhavin for publication and studied the work of Russian writers of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. He is the author of works on Alexander Pushkin's Lyceum years and on the history of the Decembrist movement. He worked on publishing the papers of Catherine II and studying her activities. He studied etymology, lexicography, and the grammar of the Russian language. From 1890 he worked on preparing the academic "Dictionary of the Russian Language." He is the author of the book "Russian Orthography" (1885), a compendium of scientifically grounded spelling rules. Spelling "according to Grot" came into universal use and was preserved right up to the orthographic reform of 1918. He was chairman of the Literary Fund (from 1866). From 1858 he was a full academician of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (corresponding member from 1852, adjunct from 1855, extraordinary academician from 1856). He was vice-president of the Academy of Sciences (1889—1893) and a member of many Russian and foreign learned societies. His brother K.K. Grot was governor of Samara, and in his honor the Mennonite village of Grotsfeld in Samara uyezd was named. Ya.K. Grot's sons became well-known scholars: N.Ya. Grot was a philosopher and psychologist, and K.Ya. Grot was a historian specializing in Slavic studies.

HUBER, Eduard Ivanovich (Johannovich) (1814—1847) was born in the colony of Messer (Ust-Zalikha) in Kamyshin uyezd, Saratov governorate. His father was a pastor, later general superintendent and vice-president of the Moscow Evangelical Lutheran Consistory, a native of Baden, in Russia from 1807. He composed verses from the age of 7, and from the age of 9 studied Greek and Latin with his father. He graduated from the gymnasium in Saratov. He studied at the Institute of the Corps of Railway Engineers in St. Petersburg (1830—1834), after which he served as a military engineer. In 1838 he retired with the rank of captain, became a civil official, and retired again in 1842. From 1831 he published verse, verse translations, and critical articles on literature and philosophy in the capital's journals. From 1840, at the invitation of O.I. Senkovsky, he helped him edit the "Library for Reading." A. Varlamov and A. Gurilev wrote romances to Huber's verses. His lyric poetry was imbued with the ideas of Romanticism. He was patronized by V.A. Zhukovsky and was acquainted with Alexander Pushkin, I.A. Krylov, and other leading writers. A significant influence on Huber's worldview was exerted by his mentor, Bishop I.A. Fessler — a theologian, mystic philosopher, historian, and writer. Huber's chief literary work was the first complete translation into Russian of Part One of Goethe's "Faust." At first the censors did not permit the translation to be printed (1835), and the author destroyed the manuscript. However, on Pushkin's advice, he resumed the work, which he later dedicated to Pushkin's memory. The translation was published in 1838 with a preface and notes by Huber and was highly praised by his contemporaries, who called it exemplary. He is buried in the Volkovo Lutheran Cemetery in St. Petersburg.

DERFELDEN, Vidim Khristoforovich (Otto Wilhelm) von (1737—1819) was born in Estland. He came from a noble family known in Estland since the sixteenth century. His father was an Estland landrat (marshal of the nobility). He was in military service from 1754. Commanding a carabineer regiment, he took part in the Russo-Turkish War of 1768—1774. He became major general (1777) and lieutenant general (1784). In the Russo-Turkish War of 1787—1791 he commanded a division and distinguished himself at Maximeni, Galați, and Focșani. From 1792 he commanded a corps stationed in Lithuania. In 1794 he took part in suppressing the uprising in Poland and received the rank of general-in-chief. In 1796 he was appointed to the Horse Guards, inspector of cavalry of the St. Petersburg and Finland divisions. He was awarded the Order of St. Andrew the First-Called (1797). From 1797 he was in retirement. In March 1799 he was again placed in active service to take part in A.V. Suvorov's Italian campaign; Suvorov held him in high regard. He commanded the reserve of the Russian army at Novi and prevented an enemy attack on the left flank. During the Swiss campaign of 1799 he commanded a corps of 10,000 men, with orders to take command of the Russian forces should Suvorov die or fall ill. He took part in the battles for the St. Gotthard Pass and the Devil's Bridge. From October 1799 he was in retirement. He was awarded Russian and foreign orders.

DIEBITSCH-ZABALKANSKY (Diebitsch), Ivan Ivanovich (Johann Karl Friedrich Anton) von (1785—1831) was born on the estate of Groß-Leipe (Silesia). His father was a military man who in 1792 transferred from Prussian to Russian service and became a major general. He graduated from the cadet corps in Berlin, arrived in Russia in 1801, and was enrolled in the Russian army as an ensign. During the Russo-Austro-French War of 1805 he distinguished himself at Austerlitz. He was a participant in the Russo-Prussian-French War of 1806—1807, distinguishing himself at Preussisch-Eylau, Heilsberg, Guttstadt, and Friedland. During the Patriotic War of 1812 he was chief quartermaster of the 1st Separate Infantry Corps, which covered the approach to St. Petersburg. For distinction at Polotsk he was promoted to major general. He displayed remarkable diplomatic ability in signing the Tauroggen Convention of 1812, under which Prussian troops separated from the French and ceased hostilities against Russia. In the foreign campaigns of the Russian army of 1813—1814 he was quartermaster general of the allied armies, distinguished himself in the capture of Berlin and in the battles at Lützen, Bautzen, and Dresden, and in the Battle of Leipzig, and was promoted to lieutenant general. As chief of staff of the 1st Army he took part in the Russian army's foreign campaign of 1815. From 1824 he was chief of the Main Staff and head of the quartermaster department, and a member of the Committee of Ministers. He was general of infantry, an honorary member of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (1826), and a count (1827). He distinguished himself brilliantly in the Russo-Turkish War of 1828—1829, and in 1829 replaced P.Kh. Wittgenstein as commander-in-chief. He became field marshal general and received the honorific addition "Zabalkansky" to his surname (1829). He was commander-in-chief of the army during the suppression of the Polish uprising of 1830—1831. He died of cholera during the campaign. He is buried in the Volkovo Lutheran Cemetery in St. Petersburg.

DITZ, Yakov Egorovich (Jakob) (1864—1917) was born in the colony of Kratzke (Pochinnaya) in Kamyshin uyezd, Saratov governorate. He came from a family of colonists. In 1884 he graduated from the gymnasium in Saratov, then received a higher legal education. He engaged in legal practice and farming in the Don Cossack Host territory. From 1905 he was a lawyer in Kamyshin and published articles on the situation of the German colonists in Saratov newspapers. He was editor of the newspaper "Povolzhsky Krai" in Kamyshin (1906). He was a deputy of the 1st State Duma from Saratov governorate (1906); he was a left-wing Kadet, aligned in political views with the Trudoviks. He was a member of the Duma's Presidium and several of its commissions. In protest against the dissolution of the Duma, he signed the Vyborg Manifesto (1907) along with a group of deputies, for which he served a three-month prison sentence. He then settled in the village of Danilovka in Kamyshin uyezd, where he wrote a fundamental study — the book "History of the Volga German Colonists," dedicated to the 150th anniversary of the colonists' arrival in the Volga region (1914). The value of the book lies chiefly in the fact that the author was the first to analyze in detail the legal status of the Volga Germans. Individual fragments of it were published in the newspaper "Saratovsky Listok" (1914), but it was published in full only in 1997. He saw the future of the Volga Germans in the development of local self-government. He was a participant in the national movement of the Volga Germans in 1917.

SEEBERG, Friedrich Georgievich (1872—1902) was born in St. Petersburg. He came from a Courland family. His father, grandfather, and paternal uncle were Evangelical Lutheran pastors (his father was a pastor in St. Petersburg in 1869—1882). He studied at the Annenschule (the school attached to the Evangelical Lutheran Church of St. Anne) in St. Petersburg (1881—1882), then in Courland — at a private school in Doblen (1882—1886) and the Mitau gymnasium (1886—1889). He was a private tutor in Courland (1889—1891) and a volunteer sapper in Vilna (1891—1892). He studied mathematics and astronomy at the University of Dorpat (1892—1897), earning the candidate's degree in mathematics. He was a private tutor in Vologda, and in 1897—1899 senior teacher of mathematics and physics at the Reformed school in St. Petersburg. In 1900—1902 he was astronomer and meteorologist of the Russian polar expedition led by E.V. Toll. He went missing at the end of 1902 together with Toll and two of their companions on the way from Bennett Island to the New Siberian Islands. Geographic features on Taymyr and the New Siberian Islands are named after Seeberg.

JORDAN, Fyodor Ivanovich (Friedrich Ludwig) (1800—1883) was born in the town of Pavlovsk, St. Petersburg governorate. His father was a native of Württemberg who was attached to the retinue of Empress Maria Feodorovna. He studied at the St. Petersburg Academy of Arts, receiving a first-degree certificate in 1824. He was a pensioner of the Academy of Arts abroad (1829—1834), working in Paris and London, where he studied various techniques of metal engraving. He became a recognized master of reproductive engraving on copper and steel. He was in Italy in 1835—1850 and 1853—1855, maintaining ties with N.V. Gogol and the artists A.A. Ivanov and K.P. Bryullov. He created a series of engravings after works by Raphael. He executed portraits of outstanding actors, artists, and writers. Collected works of M.Yu. Lermontov, N.V. Gogol, and V.G. Belinsky appeared with portraits by him. He illustrated literary works and books on art. From 1850 he was professor at the St. Petersburg Academy of Arts, heading the engraving class (from 1856). In 1871 he became the first engraver to serve as rector of the painting and sculpture departments of the Academy of Arts. He chaired the commission for revising the Academy of Arts Charter (1872—1874). He took part in organizing and displaying the Russian section at the World Exhibition in London (1862). In 1875 he was awarded the gold medal of the Academy of Arts in connection with the 50th anniversary of his creative activity. He was a member of foreign academies of arts.

KANKRIN, Egor Frantsevich (Georg Ludwig Daniel) (1774—1845) was born in Hanau (Hesse). In 1783 his father moved to Russia and became head of the salt works in Staraya Russa. He studied at German universities and earned a doctorate in law (1794). From 1794 he was councillor to the Duke of Anhalt-Bernburg. In 1797 he came to Russia at his father's invitation, and in 1800 became his assistant in Staraya Russa. From 1803 he was councillor of the Expedition of State Economy, and from 1809 inspector of the foreign colonies of St. Petersburg governorate. He published a work on military art (1809) that drew the attention of the Minister of War, M.B. Barclay de Tolly. At his request Kankrin drew up a plan for provisioning the army (1810), which was approved by Alexander I. From 1811 he was assistant to the quartermaster general of the Military Department. During the Patriotic War of 1812 he was intendant-general of the 1st Western Army, and from 1813 intendant-general of the entire active army, participating in the foreign campaigns of 1813—1814. He ensured the timely supply of the troops and enjoyed the trust of M.I. Kutuzov. In 1815 he conducted successful negotiations with the allies and France on the payment of indemnity and reimbursement of expenses for maintaining Russian troops. In 1815—1820 he was attached to the Main Headquarters of the 1st Army. He was a member of the Military Council (1820), a member of the State Council (1821), and of the Commission for Drafting the Customs Tariff (1822). In 1821 he took part in the 2nd Congress of the Holy Alliance. In 1823—1844 he was Minister of Finance and a member of the Finance Committee (from 1823). As minister he sought to increase state revenues and eliminate the chronic budget deficit, for which he raised indirect taxes and floated new loans. Holding protectionist views, he pursued a policy of protecting domestic industry through the regulation of customs duties. In 1835, on his initiative, the first law regulating relations between capitalists and workers was adopted, and in 1836 a law on joint-stock companies, establishing a permissive procedure for their formation. In 1839—1843 he carried out a monetary reform that for the first time established in Russia a system of silver monometallism, based on the silver ruble with a fixed exchange rate. He promoted the development of trade, science, technology, and education. From 1818 he repeatedly proposed plans for the abolition of serfdom, and was a member of the Committee for the Improvement of Agriculture in Russia (1834). He is the author of works on technical subjects and architecture, articles on German theater, and literary works. He was a senator (1823), general of infantry (1828), and count (1829). He was a member of learned societies and an honorary member of the St. Petersburg (1824) and Paris (1844) Academies of Sciences. He was awarded many Russian and foreign orders. He is buried in the Smolensk Lutheran Cemetery in St. Petersburg.

KOEPPEN, Pyotr Ivanovich (1793—1864) was born in Kharkov. His father was a physician from Brandenburg who came to Russia in 1786. He graduated from Kharkov University with a master's degree in jurisprudence (1814). In 1814—1821 he was an official in St. Petersburg. Upon retiring, he traveled through Europe (1822—1824), visiting Vienna, scholarly centers of Germany, and Slavic lands, studying monuments of Slavic writing. In 1824—1829 he was again a capital official, and in 1825—1826 he published one of the first bibliographic journals in Russia, "Bibliographic Sheets" (a survey of monuments of Russian and Slavic writing). In 1829—1834 he lived in Crimea, studying the local natural environment and the composition of the population. In 1834—1835 he was editor of the German-language "St. Petersburg Gazette" and compiled the first address-calendar of Russia in German. In 1837 he carried out an inspection of the foreign colonies in Taurida governorate, and until 1860 served as an official in St. Petersburg. He was a co-founder of the Russian Geographical Society (1845), where he headed the statistics section. He was the first to organize systematic collection of statistical data on the national composition of Russia's population, publishing the first "Ethnographic Map of European Russia" (1851). He is the author of numerous scholarly works, including a study of Russia's population (1857) based on the results of the 9th census of 1851. He promoted the beginning of publication of the unified "Lists of Populated Places of the Russian Empire" for individual governorates and regions (from 1861). His materials formed the basis for the multivolume "Geographic-Statistical Dictionary of the Russian Empire" (from 1863). He published a number of surveys of archaeological monuments of Russia. From 1843 he was a full academician of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (corresponding member from 1826, adjunct from 1837, extraordinary academician from 1839). The Mennonite colonies of Koeppental in Novouzensk uyezd, Samara governorate, and in Auliye-Ata uyezd, Syr-Darya oblast (now Kyrgyzstan), a saltwater animal species, and two grape varieties were named after him. Two of his sons became well-known scholars: V.P. Koeppen was a meteorologist and climatologist, and F.P. Koeppen was an entomologist, botanist, and bibliographer.

KLEIN, Roman Ivanovich (Robert Julius) (1858—1924) was born in Moscow. He was the son of a merchant. He graduated from the Moscow School of Painting, Sculpture and Architecture (1879) and the St. Petersburg Academy of Arts (1882). In 1882—1884 he trained in Paris. From 1884 he worked in Moscow. Buildings constructed to his designs include the "Chinese" tea house on Myasnitskaya Street (1891), the Middle Trading Rows on Red Square (1894), the "Muir and Mirrielees" department store on Petrovka Street (1906—1908, now TsUM), the Museum of Fine Arts on Volkhonka Street (1898—1912, now the Pushkin Museum), the Borodino Bridge (1912), the "Coliseum" cinema on Chistoprudny Boulevard (1913—1914, later rebuilt, now the "Sovremennik" theater), the Institute of Mineralogy of Moscow University on Mokhovaya Street (1913—1916), as well as mansions, apartment buildings, industrial buildings, and medical institutions. He engaged in restoration work. Klein's designs are executed in the spirit of neoclassicism, neo-Gothic, Byzantine-Russian, and other styles. From 1916 he was professor at the Riga Polytechnic Institute, evacuated to Moscow, and later at the Moscow Higher Technical School. He was a member of the Moscow Architectural Society (from 1893). In 1906—1916 he was a councillor of the Moscow City Duma. He is buried in the German (Vvedenskoye) Cemetery.

KLODT (Klodt von Jürgensburg), Pyotr Karlovich (Peter Jakob) (1805—1867) was born in St. Petersburg. He came from an old German noble family known in the Baltic provinces since the sixteenth century. His father was a major general. From 1822 he studied at the artillery school in St. Petersburg, after which he served in the artillery. From 1828 he was in retirement. From 1829 he was a non-matriculated student at the St. Petersburg Academy of Arts. From 1838 he was professor and head of the foundry workshop at the Academy of Arts, and from 1858 emeritus professor of the Academy. He was one of the founders of the animalier genre in Russian sculpture, a master of monumental sculpture and small-scale plastic art. Among his monumental works in St. Petersburg are the "Chariot of Glory" on the attic of the Narva Triumphal Gate (1831—1834, together with S. Pimenov), the monument to I.A. Krylov in the Summer Garden (1848—1855), and the equestrian statue of the monument to Nicholas I on St. Isaac's Square (1856—1859); among his works of small-scale plastic art are "Horse at a Watering Place" and "Mare with Foal." The sculptor's principal work is the four groups of horse tamers on the Anichkov Bridge over the Fontanka in St. Petersburg (1830s—1840s, installed 1849—1850), which gained worldwide fame. In 1851—1854 he cast the monument to St. Prince Vladimir in Kiev, and in 1851 the monument to Catherine II for the Volga colony of Yekaterinenstadt. He executed several sculptural projects for the Cathedral of Christ the Savior in Moscow (late 1850s—early 1860s). From 1855 he was chief supervisor of the teaching of drawing arts

NAME COMMENTARY______________________________________________________________ 735

in military educational institutions. He was a member of foreign academies of arts. He was an actual state councillor (1859) and was awarded Russian and foreign orders. His son M.P. Klodt was a painter, draughtsman, and engraver. He is buried in the Smolensk Lutheran Cemetery in St. Petersburg. His remains were subsequently transferred to the necropolis of the Alexander Nevsky Lavra.

KNOOP, Lev Gerasimovich (Johann Ludwig) (1821—1894) was born in Bremen. His father was a small tobacco merchant. Having received a commercial education, in 1838 he entered the service of the firm "De Jersey" in Manchester, where his brother Julius worked. In 1839 he was sent to the firm's Moscow branch and settled in Moscow. With his brother's assistance he became a major intermediary between Russian textile manufacturers and English producers of equipment and machinery. His first client was the founder of the well-known industrial dynasty S.V. Morozov, who equipped his Nikolskaya manufactory with Knoop's help. He also began importing into Russia raw materials for cotton production from the USA and India and cotton yarn from England. In 1852, having registered as a merchant of the first guild, he opened his own firm in Moscow — the trading house "L. Knoop." The house became one of Russia's leading foreign-trade firms, and from 1858 its branches opened in New York, Bombay, and Alexandria. With the firm's assistance, textile enterprises in Central Russia were equipped with the latest technology and supplied with raw materials and semi-finished products, and English craftsmen were invited to work at them. The firm played a major role in the establishment of enterprises belonging to many of Russia's industrial dynasties. Knoop extended credit to his Russian partners, engaging in banking operations within the framework of his trading house. To guarantee himself a leading position in the Russian cotton market, in 1857, together with Russian partners, he founded the Krenholm manufactory near Narva. It used the cheap energy of a waterfall and was one of the most advanced in the world in terms of technical equipment. In 1861 he settled near Bremen, but spent two to three months each year in Russia, overseeing the work of his enterprises. As one of the founders and directors he took part in the Moscow Fire Insurance Society (1858) and the Moscow Discount Bank (1869). On the occasion of the 25th anniversary of the trading house (1877) Knoop was granted the title of baron in Russia. After his death a monument to him was erected in Krenholm.

KONRADI, Karl Friedrich Georg (1794—1857) was born in Dobičar (Moravia). He came from an official's family. He studied at the universities of Vienna and Rostock (1812—1815). He was ordained in 1820. He arrived in Russia in 1820 at the invitation and with the assistance of Bishop I.A. Fessler. In 1820—1857 he was the Evangelical Lutheran pastor of the Volga right-bank parish of Grimm in Kamyshin uyezd, Saratov governorate. In 1825, on behalf of the Volga German clergy, he put forward a program for reforming parish schools. It called for the opening in the colony of Grimm (Lesnoy Karamysh) of a secular school subordinate not to the Evangelical Lutheran consistory but to the Saratov Office of Trusteeship for Foreign Settlers, and for the teaching of Russian, which had not yet been taught at any colonist school. The Office of Trusteeship supported the idea, but its implementation was delayed. Finally in 1833 the Ministry of Internal Affairs authorized the opening of two district secular schools in the German colonies of the Volga region — in Lesnoy Karamysh (established under Konradi's direction, transformed in 1866 into the Lesnoy-Karamysh Central School) and in Yekaterinenstadt. In 1827—1857 he was provost of the Right-Bank Evangelical Lutheran district, directing the work of the synods of the Right Bank (1834—1857). In 1832 he petitioned the General Consistory to propose publishing a collection of religious hymns (Gesangbuch) for the Volga colonies.

KONTENIUS, Samuil Khristianovich (1748—1830) was born in Westphalia. He came from the family of a Protestant pastor. He graduated from a university in Germany (studying linguistics), after which he came to Russia as a private tutor. From 1785 he was in state service. In 1797—1800, as councillor of the Geographic Department of the Expedition of State Economy, he inspected the German colonies of Chernigov, Kherson, and Yekaterinoslav governorates on government assignment. He submitted thorough reports and put forward proposals for improving the colonists' lives. In 1800—1818 he was chief judge of the newly organized Yekaterinoslav Office of Trusteeship, the supreme administrative and judicial authority for foreign settlers in southern Russia. He frequently toured the colonies under his jurisdiction, advised their elders (Schulzen), settled disputes, and monitored colonists' observance of standards of conduct and the economic organization of the colonies. He was an advocate of developing self-government in the colonies. He took part in drafting instructions that were included in Russian collections of laws and regulated legal matters affecting the life of the colonies. He devoted great attention to the development of agriculture in the colonies: he organized the supply to them of the best varieties of grain and vegetable seeds, quality seedlings, necessary equipment, and draft animals; he ensured that in the steppe regions, where most of the colonies were located, drought-resistant and profitable grain crops were cultivated, and he introduced rye and flax; he promoted the breeding of new livestock breeds, especially in sheep farming. In 1819—1830 he was an extraordinary member of the Guardianship Committee for Foreign Settlers of the Southern Region of Russia. At the request of Alexander I he assisted General I.N. Inzov, who had been appointed chairman of the Guardianship Committee. He was an actual state councillor. He bequeathed a large sum to the Werner School in the Bessarabian colony of Sarata. In 1831 the Mennonite colony of Konteniusfeld in Berdyansk uyezd, Taurida governorate, was named in his honor. He is buried in the Yekaterinoslav colony of Josephstal.

CORNIES, Johann Johannovich (1789—1848) was born in Bärwalde near Danzig (West Prussia). His father was a peasant and healer, a Mennonite by confession. In 1804 the family moved to Russia, to the Khortitsa Mennonite district of Yekaterinoslav governorate, and in 1806 settled in the colony of Orlov in the Molochna Mennonite district of Taurida governorate. Here Cornies worked for a miller, then took up trade: he bought up produce from the colonists and sold it in the port cities of Crimea. In 1809 he set up a large sheep-farming operation on leased lands. He constantly improved the breed of sheep, acquiring Spanish merinos. In 1813 he established his own farm in Orlov and built an estate that caught the attention of Alexander I as he passed by. On his farmstead of Yushanly he conducted exemplary horse breeding and, in particular, sheep breeding, and built brick, tile, and lime-burning works. In 1832 he acquired the estate of Tashchenak, and in 1842 the neighboring estate of Verigin. He was actively engaged in public affairs. In 1817 he was appointed commissioner for selecting settlement sites for arriving Mennonites from West Prussia and separatist Protestants from Württemberg. In 1820, on his initiative, a society was organized that built a parish school in Orlov. In 1821 he became cashier and treasurer of the branch of the Russian Bible Society established by the Mennonites. In 1824 the Guardianship Committee for the Colonies of Southern Russia instructed Cornies to improve the breed in the communal flocks of the Molochna colonies. From 1830 he headed the Commission for the Speedy Development of Forestry, Sericulture, and Viticulture established by the Guardianship Committee (from 1836 the Union for the Encouragement of Agriculture and Industry). He carried out extensive educational work among the colonists: he fined them for violating community rules and forced idlers to work at the communal sheepfold, among other measures. With the support of the Guardianship Committee he managed to overcome the resistance of fellow believers who opposed his authoritarian style of leadership and the strong influence of the state in the colonies. In 1838 he was appointed corresponding member of the Learned Council under the Ministry of State Domains and was entrusted with overseeing the Mennonite colonies. From 1843, on government instructions, he supervised and directed all Mennonite schools, helping to draw up curricula for them and to introduce modern teaching methods. He published articles in the press.

KRONEBERG, Ivan Yakovlevich (Johann Christian) (1788—1838) was born in Moscow. His father was a Lutheran pastor and educator who moved from Germany to Moscow in 1788. From 1804 he studied at German universities, studying philosophy, literature, and ancient culture, earning a doctorate in philosophy (1807). On returning to Russia he served in the Expedition of State Taxes, and in 1814—1818 was director of the Moscow Commercial School. From 1819 he was adjunct, then extraordinary, and from 1821 full professor at Kharkov University in the department of classical philology. He taught philosophical disciplines, courses on Greek and Roman antiquities, and German literature, and was one of the first in Russia to teach aesthetics. He was dean of the literary division (1822—1826, 1831—1832), rector (1828—1829, 1833—1836), secretary of the council of Kharkov University, and chairman of the Learned Society at the university (1826—1828). He is the author of works on Roman history, Latin grammar, ancient classical literature, and aesthetics. Kroneberg's greatest fame came from his Latin-Russian dictionary, which went through many editions. He was one of the founders of the study of Shakespeare's work in Russia. He published the scholarly journal on classical antiquities "Minerva." He was a state councillor and was awarded Russian orders. He is buried in the Kharkov Lutheran Cemetery.

KRUG, Filipp Ivanovich (Johann Philipp) (1764—1844) was born in Halle. He graduated from the theological faculty of the University of Halle and worked as a private tutor. In 1795 he arrived in Moscow, where he obtained a position as a private tutor. From his youth he had been enthusiastic about numismatics, and by the time he arrived in Russia he had a collection of coins and medals (partly inherited from his father). In Moscow he took up the collecting of Russian coins, for which he studied the Russian and Church Slavonic languages. He soon gained fame as an expert in Russian numismatics. In 1804 he moved to St. Petersburg, becoming assistant keeper of the library and coin cabinet of the Hermitage. He is the author of a work on ancient Russian coins (1805), in which he touched on questions of ancient Russian chronology, which largely determined the direction of his subsequent scholarly activity. In 1806 he presented a report to the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences on the "sources of Nestor," and in 1807 the reports "A Verification of Certain Numbers in the Russian Chronicles" and "A Correction of the Chronology in the Russian Chronicles of the First Half of the Twelfth Century." In 1810 his principal work, "A Critical Essay on Byzantine Chronology in Connection with the Most Ancient History of Rus," was published in German. He subsequently devoted great attention to studying the origin of the "Varangian Rus." In 1848 his works were published in German in two volumes, edited by the future academician A.A. Kunik. From 1815 he was a full academician of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (adjunct from 1805, extraordinary academician from 1807). He was an actual state councillor. He is buried in the Smolensk Lutheran Cemetery in St. Petersburg.

KRUSENSTERN, Ivan Fyodorovich (Adam Johann) von (1770–1846) was born at Haggud, his father's estate near Reval (Estland Governorate). He came from a German noble family known in Estland since the 17th century. He completed the Wyszhorod School in Reval and the Naval Cadet Corps in St. Petersburg (1785–1788), from which he graduated early in connection with the outbreak of the Russo-Swedish War of 1788–1790. He took part in the battles of Hogland, Öland, Reval, and Vyborg. In 1793, as one of the best officers, he was sent to England to improve his skills in naval affairs. With the English fleet he took part in battles against the French and sailed in the Atlantic and Indian Oceans. In 1799 he submitted to the naval department a project for a circumnavigation, which was approved in 1802. The expedition, led by Captain-Lieutenant Krusenstern aboard the ships *Nadezhda* and *Neva*, left Kronstadt in July 1803. The ships crossed the Atlantic Ocean, rounded Cape Horn, but lost each other in dense fog and met again only in April 1804 near the Marquesas Islands. In July the *Nadezhda* under Krusenstern's command arrived at Kamchatka, in September at Nagasaki, and in May 1805 returned to Petropavlovsk. In September the *Nadezhda* headed for China, met the *Neva* at Macao, and in July–August 1806 both ships returned to Kronstadt. During the expedition, large-scale hydrographic and meteorological observations were carried out in three oceans, part of the Kuril Islands, the coast of Sakhalin, Kamchatka, and some islands of Japan were surveyed, and botanical, zoological, and ethnographic collections were assembled. In 1809–1812 Krusenstern published a three-volume account of the voyage in Russian and German, and in 1813 its atlas. From 1808 he was an honorary member of the

Admiralty Department. In 1809 he was appointed commander of the corvette *Blagodat* (Kronstadt). From 1811 he was inspector, and in 1827–1842 director, of the Naval Cadet Corps in St. Petersburg. On his initiative a circumnavigation expedition was fitted out aboard the corvette *Rurik* under the command of O.E. von Kotzebue (1815–1818), who had earlier sailed around the world together with Krusenstern. In 1815–1818 he compiled a two-volume "Atlas of the South Sea" with an appendix of his notes, for which he was awarded the Demidov Prize of the Academy of Sciences. From 1823 he was a member of the Admiralty Department and in charge of its library; from 1827 a member of the Admiralty Council and the Scientific Committee of the Naval Staff; admiral (1842). From 1806 he was an honorary member of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (corresponding member from 1803). He was a member of Russian and foreign scholarly societies. Islands, a cape, a strait, and a passage in the Pacific Ocean are named after Krusenstern. His son was the well-known traveler and Vice Admiral P.I. Krusenstern. He was buried at the Wyszhorod Lutheran church in Reval (Tallinn).

KULMAN, Elizaveta Borisovna (Elisabeth) (1808–1825) was born in St. Petersburg. Her father was a retired captain whose ancestors had come to Russia from Alsace at the end of the 17th century. From an early age she was distinguished by curiosity, sensitivity, and a phenomenal memory. A family friend, the tutor F.K. Grossheinrich, taught her Russian and German, followed by Latin, ancient Greek, Church Slavonic, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Modern Greek, and other languages. She began writing verse at the age of eight. Her literary tastes were largely shaped by Grossheinrich, an admirer of the German classics and ancient poets. Under his guidance she quickly achieved success in the art of versification and poetic translation. She translated Anacreon's "Odes" into German, Russian, and Italian, and wrote poems in the anacreontic style. Her efforts were noticed by the Imperial court, and she was awarded an annual stipend. Grossheinrich sent a selection of her poems in German, French, and Italian to J.W. Goethe and Jean Paul, who predicted a great poetic future for her. She wrote mainly in German, translating her own poems into Russian herself. She translated from Spanish into Russian, and from Russian, English, Portuguese, and Greek into German. Having caught a cold during a severe flood in St. Petersburg in 1824, she fell gravely ill and died of consumption. Her poems were published in Russia, and later in Germany and Italy, only after the young poetess's death. The publications were received with enthusiasm; V.K. Küchelbecker dedicated verses to her, and R. Schumann set Kulman's poems to music in two song cycles.

KÜCHELBECKER, Wilhelm Karlovich von (1797–1846) was born in St. Petersburg. His father, a Saxon nobleman and agronomist, had moved to Russia at the end of the 18th century. In 1808 he was placed in a private German boarding school in the town of Werro (Livland Governorate), and in 1811 in the Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum, where he became a lyceum friend of A.S. Pushkin. After finishing the lyceum (1817) he was enrolled in the Main Archive of the Collegium of Foreign Affairs while also teaching in St. Petersburg. From 1817 he published his literary works. His poem "The Poets" (1820), inspired by Pushkin's exile to the South and dealing with the prophetic mission and civic calling of poets and their bitter fate, was regarded by the authorities as a challenge. Forced to resign (1820), he went abroad, visiting France, Italy, and Germany, where he met J.W. Goethe (with whom Küchelbecker's father had studied) and L. Tieck. His travel impressions were reflected in a series of publicistic letters published in Russian journals (1824–1825). From 1821 he was in Tiflis, an official of the Caucasus Chancellery. In the Caucasus he became close to A.S. Griboedov, who became his literary mentor and kindred spirit, his confidant and friend. Under his influence Küchelbecker moved away from Russian Byronism in the elegiac style, turning instead to biblical themes and Old Russian literature. From 1822 he was retired, and in 1823 he moved to Moscow, where he engaged in literary and teaching work. In Tiflis and Moscow he worked on the tyrant-fighting tragedy "The Argives." Together with V.F. Odoevsky he published the almanac "Mnemosyne" (1824–1825), in which Pushkin, Griboedov, P.A. Vyazemsky, E.A. Baratynsky, and others took part. From 1825 he was in St. Petersburg. He became close to A.I. Odoevsky, who introduced him into the circle of the Northern Secret Society. He was admitted to the Society by K.F. Ryleev in late November 1825. He actively participated in the uprising on Senate Square on December 14, 1825. After the suppression of the uprising he fled St. Petersburg and was arrested. He was sentenced to death, commuted to solitary confinement and lifelong exile in Siberia. In 1835 he was released from the fortress and sent to settle in the town of Barguzin, Irkutsk Governorate. In 1840 he moved with his family to the border fortress of Aksha, and in 1844 to Kurgan. In 1846 he traveled to Tobolsk for treatment (consumption, blindness), and died there. In prison and exile he continued his literary work, but only a few of these writings were published.

LEER, Genrikh Antonovich (Heinrich August) (1829–1904) was born in Nizhny Novgorod. Son of an architect, of noble origin. He studied at a gymnasium in St. Petersburg. He began his service in 1844 at the Main Engineering School (St. Petersburg). He served in a sapper battalion in the Caucasus, took part in fighting against the mountain peoples (1851), and then studied at the Military Academy, which he completed in 1854. From 1855 he was enrolled on the Main Staff. He taught courses in strategy, tactics, and military history at the Nikolaev Academy of the Main Staff (adjunct professor from 1858, professor from 1864, distinguished professor from 1874, head of the academy in 1889–1898), while also teaching at other military educational institutions. From 1872 he was a member of the Military Scientific Committee of the Main Staff. In 1874 he took part in the Brussels International Conference on the laws and customs of war. He taught strategy and military history to the future Emperor Nicholas II. From the late 1850s he published articles on military-theoretical questions. He effectively reduced strategy to the doctrine of the operation and was the first to formulate its basic principles. He paid special attention to the selection of the operational concept. He was among the first military theorists to conclude that, under conditions of mass armies and the increased scale of armed struggle, the entire country becomes the base of war, and that victory can be achieved only through unity of command, thought, and will in leadership, and thorough preparation of both the army and the theater of military operations. His principal work, "Strategy (the Tactics of the Theater of Military Operations)," went through six editions and was translated into foreign languages; for more than 30 years it was the sole textbook on strategy in Russia's military educational institutions. He authored many works on questions of military history and military theory. His works and his military-pedagogical activity had a significant influence on the conduct of the military reforms in Russia in the 1860s–1870s. He was a corresponding member of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (from 1887) and an honorary member of Russian and foreign academies. From 1896 he was an infantry general and a member of the Military Council.

LENZ, Emily Khristianovich (Heinrich Friedrich Emil) von (1804–1865) was born in the town of Dorpat, Livland Governorate. He was a great-nephew of Ya.M.R. Lenz. His great-grandfather was a pastor, a native of Pomerania. His father was chief secretary of the town magistrate. He studied at a gymnasium (1817–1820), and in 1820 entered the University of Dorpat. In 1823–1826, as a physicist, he took part in a circumnavigation expedition under the command of O.E. von Kotzebue, and authored a work on physical observations made during the voyage. As a result of the voyage he created a circulation theory of ocean currents. After the expedition he studied in Germany, earning a doctorate in philosophy (1827). In 1829–1830 he took part in an expedition of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences to the Caucasus and the coasts of the Black and Caspian Seas. Together with Academician A.Ya. Kupffer he made an ascent of Mount Elbrus, which made it possible to determine the mountain's height and marked the beginning of mountain meteorology. He established the level of the Caspian Sea. From 1836 he headed the department of physics and physical geography at St. Petersburg University, was dean of the Faculty of Physics and Mathematics (1840–1860), and rector (from 1863). From 1830 he also taught at the school attached to the Evangelical Lutheran Church of St. Peter and other educational institutions in St. Petersburg; in 1848 he taught a course in physics to the grand dukes. He authored textbooks on physics (1839) and physical geography (1851). In the 1830s, in the physics laboratory of the Academy of Sciences, reorganized with his participation, he began his research on electricity and magnetism. He was one of the founders of the study of electricity and the originator of theoretical electrical engineering. He established the rule determining the direction of induced currents (Lenz's law), substantiated the law of the thermal effect of current (the Joule–Lenz law), and discovered the phenomenon of "armature reaction." Together with B.S. Jacobi he was the first to propose a method for calculating electromagnets in electrical machines. He is also known for works on geophysics. From 1834 he was a full academician of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (adjunct from 1828, extraordinary academician from 1830). He was a Privy Councillor and was awarded many Russian orders. A cape on Taymyr is named after Lenz. His brother R.Kh. Lenz was a Sanskritologist, and his son R.E. Lenz was a well-known physicist.

LENZ, Jakob Michael Reinhold (1751–1792) was born in Sesswegen, Livland Governorate. His father was an Evangelical Lutheran pastor, a native of Pomerania, who had come to Livland in 1740. In 1759–1768 he studied at the Latin school in Dorpat. From his youth he was drawn to poetry, writing a play at the age of 15. In 1768–1770 he studied theology at the University of Königsberg. In 1771 he traveled to Strasbourg as a tutor, where he worked as a private teacher and became acquainted with J.W. Goethe. In 1776 he was in Weimar, and then wandered through Switzerland, Germany, and Alsace. As an ardent admirer of William Shakespeare, he translated one of his comedies into German, accompanying it with his own "Notes on the Theater" (1774), which reflected the ideas of the literary movement "Storm and Stress" ("Sturm und Drang"). In 1773–1776 he wrote a number of plays. Critics regarded him as a reformer of drama, placing his name alongside Goethe's; along with Goethe he was the most significant figure of the "Sturm und Drang." His most striking works were written in the comedic genre. His lyric poems are characterized by emotionality, the intonations of passionate confession, and an enthusiastic tone. In 1775–1776 he advocated the creation of a unified German literary language as the most important instrument for the national-cultural unification of Germany. Under the influence of a tragic love affair he developed a mental illness. In 1779 he lived in Riga, and in 1780 he was a private tutor in Livland. From 1781 he was in St. Petersburg and Moscow. In Moscow, under the guidance of Academician G.F. Müller, he studied Russian history. He translated into German a work on Russia during the reign of Catherine II (1790). He worked on a tragedy about Boris Godunov. He became close to the circle of N.I. Novikov and made the acquaintance of N.M. Karamzin. Having no permanent occupation, he earned his living by giving private lessons and ended his days in poverty.

LESGAFT, Pyotr Frantsevich (1837–1909) was born in St. Petersburg. Son of a jeweler. He completed the Annenschule (the school attached to the Evangelical Lutheran Church of St. Anne), and then the Medical-Surgical Academy in St. Petersburg (1861), where he was retained for scholarly work. In 1865 he defended his dissertation for the degree of Doctor of Medicine. In 1866–1868 he worked as a physician in St. Petersburg; Doctor of Surgery (1868). From 1868 he headed the department of physiological anatomy at Kazan University. In 1871, for a published protest against the arbitrary conduct of the university administration, he was dismissed and barred from teaching. Returning to St. Petersburg, he engaged in scholarly work, serving as an official of the Medical Department (1872). Having again received permission to teach (1874), he worked in the Main Directorate of Military Educational Institutions (1875–1886), where he dealt with questions of physical education. In 1872 he opened at his own apartment the first courses in Russia on the physical education of young people. At the same time he worked at a private gymnastics establishment (from 1872) and conducted gymnastics with pupils of a military gymnasium (from 1874). During this period his original concept of physical education took shape, based on the unity of physical and mental development. He viewed a system of directed exercises as a means not only of physical but also of mental, moral, and aesthetic education. In 1886–1897 he lectured on anatomy at St. Petersburg University and at women's courses. He was one of the founders (1893) of the St. Petersburg Society for the Promotion of Physical Development (chairman from 1897). In 1893 he created a Biological Laboratory, and in 1896 he achieved the opening, attached to it, of courses for female instructors and directors of physical education. The revolutionary sentiments prevailing at the courses led to their closure by the government in January 1905. In 1905 he opened

in the premises of the former courses a Free Higher School, with evening courses for workers attached to it (closed by the government in 1907, existing illegally until 1912). From 1907 he was professor of the department of anatomy at the Psycho-Neurological Institute. He was a member of scholarly and medical societies, chairman of the society "Assistance in Reading for the Sick and the Poor" (1895), and chairman of the 1st Congress on Technical and Vocational Education (1897). The Institute of Physical Culture in St. Petersburg bears his name, and a monument to him has been erected on its grounds.

LYSANDER, Fyodor Stanislavovich von (1816–1897) was born in Courland. He came from the family of a cavalry captain. From 1832 he was in military service, rising to the rank of colonel. From 1858 he administered the Chamber of State Domains in Olonets Governorate. He was manager of the Saratov Office of Foreign Settlers (1863–1866) and chairman (chief trustee) of the Trusteeship Committee for Foreign Settlers of the Southern Region of Russia (1866–1867). In 1867–1868 he administered the Chamber of State Domains in the Baltic governorates, was governor of Livland (1868–1871), and then served in the Directorate of Railways. He was an Active State Councillor and Chamberlain, and was awarded Russian orders. In his honor were named the Mennonite colony of Lysanderhöh in Novouzensk Uyezd, Samara Governorate, which in 1935 gave its name to the identically named canton of the ASSR of the Volga Germans, and the Reformed-Lutheran colony of Lysanderdorf (Neu-Messer) in Kamyshin Uyezd, Saratov Governorate.

LINDEMANN, Karl Eduardovich (1844–1929) was born in Nizhny Novgorod. Son of a physician. After completing the Nizhny Novgorod gymnasium, he entered the medical faculty of Kazan University in 1859, transferring to Moscow University in 1860. He received the degree of Candidate of Natural Sciences at Dorpat (1865). He discovered a human parasite (1865) later named in his honor. In 1865 he received a post as assistant at the newly established Petrovsky Agricultural Academy in Moscow; extraordinary professor (1870), and from the 1880s full professor, heading the department of general zoology, agricultural pests, and comparative anatomy of vertebrates. Doctor of Sciences (1876). For 20 field seasons he studied agricultural pests in southern Russia, the Caucasus, Crimea, and Western Siberia, while also becoming acquainted with the life and economic problems of local German settlers. After the Revolution of 1905–1907 he was one of the organizers of the "Union of October 17" (the Octobrist party), co-chairman of the Moscow Central Committee, and a member of the Main Board. During the debates over the bills of Chairman of the Council of Ministers P.A. Stolypin (1909) and Minister of Internal Affairs A.A. Makarov (1912), which envisaged restrictions on the purchase and lease of land by Russian subjects of foreign origin in border regions, he spoke out against their main provisions. His position influenced the Octobrist faction in the State Duma, and the bills were withdrawn by the government even before being discussed in the Duma. During the First World War he criticized the "liquidation laws" aimed at expropriating land and sharply restricting the economic rights of German citizens of Russia, and authored the work "The Termination of Landownership and Land Use by Settler-Proprietors: The Decrees of February 2 and December 13, 1915 and July 10, July 15, and August 19, 1916, and Their Effect on the Economic Condition of Southern Russia" (1917). After the February Revolution of 1917 he played a leading role in attempts to organize the Germans of Russia into an independent political force. He initiated two congresses of Russian Germans in Moscow (April and September 1917) and was one of the representatives of the Russian Germans before the Provisional Government.

LITKE (Lütke), Fyodor Petrovich (Friedrich Benjamin) (1797–1882) was born in St. Petersburg. Grandson of an Evangelical Lutheran pastor, a native of Saxony who settled in Russia in 1735. His father was a customs official. From 1804 he studied at a private boarding school in St. Petersburg. In 1813 he entered naval service as a volunteer and took part in battles against the French. In 1817–1819 he participated in a circumnavigation under the command of V.M. Golovnin. In 1821, on Golovnin's recommendation, he was appointed head of a hydrographic expedition to study the North. Over four summer navigation seasons (1821–1824) the expedition explored the coasts of Novaya Zemlya, the Matochkin Shar Strait, the Kola Peninsula, and the islands of Vaygach and Kolguyev, made significant corrections to the charts of the White and Barents Seas, conducted hydrological, meteorological, and ice observations, and discovered a permanent current along the western shore of Novaya Zemlya, later named after Litke. The results of the expedition were set forth in his book (1828). In 1826–1829, with the rank of captain-lieutenant, he commanded a circumnavigation aboard the sloops *Senyavin* and *Moller*, during which extensive material on oceanography, ethnography, zoology, and botany was collected. Litke compiled accurate charts of the Caroline Islands and discovered many new islands and atolls in the archipelago. For his account of the expedition's results he was awarded the Demidov Prize of the Academy of Sciences (1829). In 1832–1852 he served as tutor, and later guardian, to Grand Duke Konstantin Nikolaevich, who was to head the Russian Navy, and undertook a number of training voyages with him. He was aide-de-camp general (1842), vice admiral (1843), and chairman of the Naval Scientific Committee (1846). He was chief commander of the port and military governor at Reval (1850–1853) and Kronstadt (1853–1857). During the Crimean War of 1853–1856 he secured the defense of Kronstadt and St. Petersburg against the Anglo-French squadron. He was promoted to admiral and appointed a member of the State Council (1855), and was raised to the rank of count (1866). He was one of the initiators of the founding of the Russian Geographical Society, its first vice-chairman (1845–1850 and 1857–1872) and its de facto leader. In 1873 the Society established the Great Gold Medal named after Litke. In 1864–1882 he was president of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (corresponding member from 1829, honorary member from 1855). He was an honorary member of a number of Russian educational institutions and foreign scholarly societies. He was awarded many Russian and foreign orders. A cape, a peninsula, a mountain, and a bay on Novaya Zemlya, islands in the Franz Josef Land archipelago, and other features are named after him. He was buried at the Volkovo Lutheran Cemetery in St. Petersburg.

LOWITZ, David Yegorovich (Georg Moritz) (1722–1774) was born in Fürth (Bavaria). In 1762 he took the chair of mathematics and astronomy at the University of Göttingen. He was engaged in the manufacture of physical and astronomical instruments and apparatus, was a map draftsman and astronomer. From 1768 he was in Russia, professor of astronomy at the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences. He headed the Astrakhan Astronomical Expedition (1769–1774), which carried out astronomical work to determine the precise coordinates of towns and other locations, conducted geographic observations, and leveled terrain. On government instructions, work was carried out to draw up a plan of the territory between the Volga and the Don to investigate the feasibility of building a Volga–Don canal. During the rebellion of Ye.I. Pugachev of 1773–1775, Lowitz was conducting astronomical observations on the right bank of the Volga. He was seized in the German colony of Nizhnyaya Dobrinka on Pugachev's orders, who commanded that he be impaled "so that he could better see the stars," and was then hanged. His son T.Ye. Lowitz was a chemist and pharmacist, an academician of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences.

LORENZ, Fyodor Karlovich (Friedrich) (1803–1861) was born in Kreuznach (Prussia). He received his higher education in Heidelberg and Berlin; he was a historian. In 1831 he was invited to a professorship at the Main Pedagogical Institute in St. Petersburg. At the same time he served as editor of the newspaper *St. Petersburger Zeitung* (1836–1838), and in 1840 was elected director of the Petrischule (the school attached to the Evangelical Lutheran Church of St. Peter). During his tenure as head of the school, preparatory courses were created for the women's division, the courses in ancient languages, history, and geography were expanded, gymnastics lessons were introduced, and a gymnasium hall was built. After 25 years of teaching at the Main Pedagogical Institute he retired (1856). In 1857 he left the Petrischule and returned to Germany. He lectured on Russian history at the University of Bonn. He authored works on world history and the history of the modern era. From 1840 he was a corresponding member of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences.

MÖRING, Fyodor Fyodorovich (Friedrich) (1822–1887) was born in the town of Döhna near Dresden. Son of a physician. He studied at the Dresden Medical Academy and completed the medical faculty of Leipzig University. He defended his dissertation for the degree of Doctor of Medicine and Surgery and received a diploma as an obstetrician (1845). In 1845 he was invited to take the post of physician at a sugar factory near Kiev and moved to Russia. He was in charge of a rural hospital in Poltava Governorate, and, under the guidance of N.I. Pirogov, worked as a prosector at the Land Forces Hospital (St. Petersburg). In 1851 he received the degree of Doctor of Medicine at the University of Dorpat. With Pirogov's assistance, from 1853 he lectured at Kiev University, becoming extraordinary professor in 1857 and full professor of the department of special pathology and therapy in 1858; from 1856 he was professor of the faculty therapeutic clinic. His principal works were published in the form of lectures and were devoted to the clinical treatment of internal diseases, questions of the history and methodology of medicine, and public hygiene. He was renowned for his diagnostic skill and had an enormous private practice. He treated the poor free of charge. Thousands of residents of Kiev accompanied him on his last journey. A street in Kiev is named after Möring.

MÜLLER, Fyodor Ivanovich (Gerhard Friedrich) (1705–1783) was born in Herford (Westphalia). Son of a gymnasium rector. He studied at the Herford gymnasium and, in 1721–1725, at German universities. In 1725 he came to Russia to serve at the newly established St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences. He taught at the Academic Gymnasium (1725–1728). In addition to his work at the Academy, in 1728 he became editor of the German-language newspaper *St. Petersburgische Zeitung*. He originated the idea of publishing a special monthly supplement to the newspaper, which in fact became Russia's first scholarly journal. In 1732 he published the first program for a comprehensive study of the history and geography of Russia, designed to run for 30 years. From 1732 he published a collection of materials on Russian history intended for a Western European audience, which for the first time allowed foreign readers to obtain reliable scholarly information in this field. In 1733–1743, as head of the overland detachment, he took part in the Second Kamchatka Expedition. As a result, he produced numerous works on history, geography, ethnography, archaeology, linguistics, astronomy, geodesy, and cartography, and assembled an extensive collection of historical sources. In 1747 he became the first rector of the Academic University. In 1749, on assignment from the Academy of Sciences, he prepared a work on the early period of Russian statehood. Basing himself on chronicle sources, he developed propositions later known as the "Normanist theory." The work was criticized by a number of Academy members and banned from publication (it was published only in 1768). In 1750 the first volume of his "History of Siberia" appeared — the first fundamental study on this subject. In 1753 he was the first Russian scholar to publish a work on the geographical discoveries of the Kamchatka Expedition. In 1755–1764 he published Russia's first popular-scientific and literary journal, in which he himself was the author of most of the historical and geographical material. In 1764, on assignment from Catherine II, he prepared a detailed project for school reform, envisaging an education system open to all estates. In 1765 he was appointed chief overseer of the Foundling Home in Moscow while remaining with the Academy of Sciences in the rank of historiographer. He became the first Russian academician to live and work in Moscow. From 1766 he was a member of the Collegium of Foreign Affairs attached to its Moscow Archive (from 1773 manager of the archive). He was the organizer of Russia's first historical archive and the founder of the Russian school of archivists. In 1767 he was the first Russian scholar elected a deputy to the Commission for the Drafting of a New Law Code. In this connection he prepared proposals for the academic mandate, containing a program for organizing education in Russia. During his Moscow period he devoted much effort to publishing historical sources and scholarly works, took part in preparing the first Russian geographical dictionary, drew the attention of most of its early researchers to the history of Moscow, and played a significant role in the development of Moscow University. In 1775, in connection with the 50th anniversary of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences, he was assigned to describe its history; he worked on this task until the end of his life. In 1778–1779 he conducted the first scholarly expedition through the Moscow region, resulting in his travel essays and descriptions of towns and monasteries. From 1730 he was a professor of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (adjunct from 1725, conference secretary in 1728–1730 and 1754–1765). He was an honorary member of foreign academies and scholarly societies. He held the rank of State Councillor, and in 1783 was awarded the newly established Order of St. Vladimir. He was buried at the German (Vvedenskoye) Cemetery.

MÜNNICH, Khristofor Antonovich (Burkhard Christoph) von (1683–1767) was born at the estate of Neuenhuntorf near Oldenburg. His father was a hydraulic engineer and nobleman. Under his father's guidance he received a thorough home education. From 1701 he was in military service in Germany and Poland, taking part in battles and engaging in engineering work. From 1721 he was in Russian service, lieutenant general (1722); under Peter I he directed the construction of the Ladoga and other canals. He became a full general (1726); under Peter II he was made a count and St. Petersburg governor-general (1728). Under Anna Ioannovna he was master general of ordnance, president of the Military Collegium, member of the Cabinet, chief of police, and field marshal (1732). He reorganized the army and the guards, equalizing the pay of Russian officers with that of foreign ones. He founded in St. Petersburg the Cadet Corps for the Nobility — Russia's first higher military educational institution — and became its head. He completed the construction of the Ladoga Canal. In 1734 he directed the siege by Russian forces of Danzig, where the French candidate for the Polish throne, S. Leszczyński, had taken refuge. During the Russo-Turkish War of 1735–1739 he commanded the Russian army, which took Azov, Ochakov, and Khotin, and occupied the Crimea twice. After the death of Anna Ioannovna (1740), at the head of the guards he directed the arrest of the regent E.I. Biron and became first minister, but under pressure from A.I. Osterman was forced to resign (1741). Under Elizabeth Petrovna (1742) he was exiled to Pelym, a minor town of Siberia Governorate. He was returned from exile by Peter III (1762). He was with the emperor at the time of his overthrow, vainly urging Peter to go to Prussia, where a significant part of the Russian army was stationed, in order to reclaim the throne with its help. He was appointed by Catherine II chief director of the harbors of Reval and Narva and of the Kronstadt and Ladoga canals, and was charged with completing the harbor at Rogervik. In 1766 he laid the sluice on the Ladoga Canal and, for the last time, inspected the works carried out under his direction. He had no political influence in his final years.

MOLLER, Fyodor Antonovich (Otto Friedrich Theodor) von (1812–1874) was born in Kronstadt. He came from an old German family originating in Thuringia and known on the island of Ösel (now Saaremaa, Estonia) since the 14th century. His father was a naval officer, later an admiral and Minister of the Navy. He spent his childhood in Reval and studied at a gymnasium. When his family moved to St. Petersburg (1821) he entered the Naval Cadet Corps, upon completion of which (1826) he was appointed adjutant at the Naval Ministry. In 1829 he was transferred to the Life Guards Izmailovsky Regiment. Having shown artistic talent already in childhood, from 1828 he attended, in his off-duty hours, drawing classes at the St. Petersburg Academy of Arts. At the same time he took a course in anatomy at the Medical-Surgical Academy, making anatomical drawings. In 1832 he took part in the Academy's exhibition with the painting "The Battle of Ostrołęka," in which he had himself taken part in 1831. In 1835, holding the rank of staff captain, he retired and devoted himself entirely to painting. Until 1838 he continued his studies at the Academy of Arts, and from 1837 worked in the studio of K.P. Bryullov. In 1837 he received the Academy's first gold medal and the title of academician-designate. In 1838–1856 he lived for extended periods in Italy and traveled throughout Europe. He was the author of portraits of N.V. Gogol and other figures of Russian culture. He executed a series of paintings on the life of Alexander Nevsky for the Alexander Hall of the Grand Kremlin Palace, paintings for the frescoes of the Cathedral of Christ the Savior in Moscow, and a number of paintings on biblical subjects. He was an Academician of Painting (1840) and professor of historical painting (1857) at the St. Petersburg Academy of Arts.

OLIGER, Nikolai Fyodorovich (Friedrichovich) (1882—1919) was born in Omsk. His father was a military apothecary, whose ancestor, a master craftsman from Solingen, had been brought to the Urals at the beginning of the 19th century to forge Zlatoust blades. He completed 6 years at the Omsk gymnasium (1899), then studied at a technical college in Saratov. He joined the RSDLP, engaged in agitation, and was expelled from the college for this without the right to enroll in educational institutions. In 1901–1902 he was imprisoned in Omsk, then placed under covert police surveillance. Until 1904 he lived mainly in Tomsk, serving as secretary of the editorial board of the newspaper "Sibirsky Vestnik." In 1904 he was arrested for party work in the Kuban and released under the general amnesty in 1905. He took up literary work early, publishing his works under pseudonyms from 1897 to 1904, mostly in newspapers. Suffering from tuberculosis, in 1906 he withdrew from revolutionary activity due to illness, moved to St. Petersburg, and devoted himself to literature. He published stories and novellas in many St. Petersburg and provincial publications.
