He depicted the hardships of clandestine existence, prison stories, and the monotonous, wearisome life of exiled settlers. However, revolution served only as a backdrop in his works; they presented a wide variety of subjects and social strata, reflecting the author's ideological wanderings, his dissatisfaction with himself, and his search for a new meaning in life after abandoning revolutionary activity. He also worked as a playwright; his play was staged in 1913 at the Suvorin Theatre (St. Petersburg) and the Korsh Theatre (Moscow). He found his readership, and in 1910–1914 a five-volume collection of his works was published in St. Petersburg. Naturalism was characteristic of Oliger's style, and some of his subjects were perceived as pornography. In 1911, due to a worsening of his illness, he moved to Odessa, and in 1912 went abroad. In 1913 he lived on the island of Capri, read his drama to Maxim Gorky, and met I.A. Bunin, F.I. Chaliapin, and others. During the First World War he published essays in M.A. Suvorin's weekly "Lukomorye." Despite his illness, in early 1915 he volunteered for the front, and in 1916 was shell-shocked. In his war essays he wrote about the everyday life of a front-line hospital in the Carpathians, about retreats and attacks, refugees, and the mood in the army. In 1918 he came to Harbin, became head of the intelligence department at the headquarters of ataman G.M. Semyonov, and edited the newspaper "Prizyv." At the end of 1918 he moved to Chita, publishing numerous anti-Bolshevik articles in the newspaper "Russky Vostok."

OLDENBURG, Peter Georgievich (Konstantin Friedrich Peter) (1812—1881) was born in Yaroslavl. He belonged to the family of the Princes of Oldenburg. His father was a Russian statesman, his mother the sister of Alexander I and Nicholas I. Having lost his father early, and then his mother, he lived in Stuttgart and Oldenburg. After Greece gained independence (1829), he was considered among the candidates for the Greek throne. In 1830 Nicholas I summoned his nephew to Russia and enrolled him in military service. In Russia the prince continued his education (Russian law, natural sciences). In 1834, holding the rank of lieutenant general, he left military service due to his disagreement with the practice of corporal punishment in the army. In 1834 he was appointed a senator, in 1836 a member of the State Council, and in 1842 chairman of the Department of Civil and Ecclesiastical Affairs. He had been an honorary member of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences since 1834. From 1841 to 1859 he was president of the Free Economic Society. From 1845 he chaired the newly established Main Council of Women's Educational Institutions, and in 1860 he headed the Department of Institutions of Empress Maria. He promoted the development of women's education and the mass opening of girls' gymnasiums in Russia. With the prince's assistance, and partly at his own expense, the following were opened in St. Petersburg: the women's institute of his wife, Princess Therese (1841); the P.G. Oldenburg children's shelter (1846); and the School of Jurisprudence (1835) — the first institution of higher legal education in Russia, of which he remained trustee until the end of his life. From 1843 he also served as trustee of the Alexander Lyceum. He was the initiator and first chairman of the "Russian Society of International Law" founded in St. Petersburg (1880). He was fond of writing verse and composing music. Among his papers was found a translation he made into French of Alexander Pushkin's novella "The Queen of Spades" (1834). In 1889 a monument to the prince was unveiled in St. Petersburg on Liteiny Prospekt, opposite the Mariinsky Hospital, bearing the inscription: "To the Enlightened Benefactor."

OSTERMANN, Andrei Ivanovich (Heinrich Johann Friedrich) (1686—1747) was born in Bochum (Westphalia). He was the son of an Evangelical Lutheran pastor. In 1702–1703 he studied at the University of Jena. Due to his involvement in a duel in which he killed his opponent, he was forced to flee. In 1704 he came to Russia. He quickly learned Russian, attracted the attention of Peter I, and entered Russian service. From 1708 he was a translator in the Ambassadorial Office (he knew several languages), secretary of the Ambassadorial Chancellery (1711), councilor of the chancellery (1716), and privy councilor of the chancellery (1720). During the Great Northern War of 1700–1721 he carried out important diplomatic assignments, and was a member of the Russian delegation at the Åland Congress of 1718–1719 and at the conclusion of the Peace of Nystad in 1721. In 1719–1720 he drafted the preliminary version of Peter's Table of Ranks of 1722. From 1723 he was vice president of the Collegium of Foreign Affairs. After the death of Peter I he was vice-chancellor (1725—1740), a member of the Supreme Privy Council (1726—1730), and a senator (1725—1726, 1730—1731). He was Ober-Hofmeister (tutor) to Emperor Peter II (1727—1730). He held the rank of Active Privy Councilor (1725) and was made a count (1730). He was regarded as one of the organizers of the removal from power of A.D. Menshikov (1727). In 1730–1731 he headed the personal chancellery of Empress Anna Ioannovna, which on his initiative was transformed into the Cabinet of Ministers. He was second (1731—1734), then first cabinet minister (1734—1740). After the death of Anna Ioannovna (1740) he supported the appointment of E.I. Biron as regent under Emperor Ivan Antonovich; after Biron's arrest he again became second cabinet minister, losing the post of vice-chancellor but gaining charge of the Navy (together with the rank of General-Admiral). In 1741 he obtained from the regent Anna Leopoldovna a substantial reduction in the powers of Kh.A. Münnich and the restoration to himself of overall direction of foreign affairs; he then regained the post of first cabinet minister, but, meeting resistance from the regent, was unable to become the effective head of the cabinet. During the palace coup of 1741 he was arrested by supporters of Elizabeth Petrovna; he was officially accused of having, since the death of Peter II (1730), deliberately sought to prevent her, the lawful heir, from ascending the throne. He was sentenced to be broken on the wheel, a sentence commuted to exile in Siberia. From 1742 he lived under strict guard in Berezov, in the Siberian Governorate, where he died.

PROVE, Ivan Karlovich (Johann) (1833—1901) was born in Thorn (Prussia). In the late 1830s his family moved to Moscow. He graduated from the Moscow gymnasium (1850). From the 1850s he worked with the merchant and industrialist L. Knoop, becoming manager of affairs and co-owner of the "L. Knoop" trading house (from 1865), and from 1869 managed its Moscow office. From 1865 he belonged to the Narva merchantry, and from 1869 to the Moscow merchantry. From 1883 he was director of the board of the Krenholm Manufacturing Company, and headed the work of the board in 1894—1901. He was a board member and shareholder of a number of manufacturing and other enterprises, and a member of the councils of the Moscow Merchant Bank and the Russo-Chinese Bank. He was an elected representative of the Moscow merchant estate (1876—1885) and of the Moscow Exchange Society (1873—1898), and a member of the Moscow City Duma (1881—1885). He was a member of the council of the Elizabeth Charitable Society and trustee of the Basmanny branch of the hospital for manual laborers. In 1897—1901 he was a founding member and donor of the Committee for the Establishment of the Alexander III Museum of Fine Arts in Moscow (now the Pushkin Museum), and the library hall of the museum was built with his funds. He was a hereditary honorary citizen (1887) and a councilor of commerce (1892). His business was continued by his sons R.I. and K.I. Prove. He is buried at the German (Vvedenskoye) Cemetery in Moscow.

RAUPACH, Hermann Friedrich (1728—1778) was born in Stralsund. His father was a composer and organist. He received his early musical education under his father's guidance. From 1755 he was in St. Petersburg as harpsichordist in the court orchestra. A brilliant improvising performer, he won the favor of Empress Elizabeth Petrovna and regularly performed at receptions in the palace, including in the empress's private chambers. In 1758 his opera "Alceste," set to a Russian text by A.P. Sumarokov, was first performed in Peterhof. From 1759 he was court kapellmeister. He was the author of choral pieces in honor of Russian military victories in the Seven Years' War of 1756—1763, of the opera seria "Siroe" for the 20th anniversary of the empress's accession to the throne (1760), and of choruses on texts of psalms translated by Sumarokov and M.V. Lomonosov. In 1762, after the death of Elizabeth, he was released from service and left Russia. He lived mainly in Paris, where he became close to the young W.A. Mozart. From 1768 he was again in St. Petersburg, serving until 1777 as second kapellmeister and composer of ballet music, and thereafter taught in the music classes of the Academy of Arts. He created a number of ballets and arranged ballet divertissements in operas. He was the author of the comic opera "The Good Soldiers," to a libretto by M.M. Kheraskov, which was staged only after the composer's death. Built on the skillful use of folk-song melodic elements, the opera enjoyed wide popularity and was performed in many Russian theaters up to the beginning of the 19th century.

RAUCHFUSS, Karl Andreyevich (1835—1915) was born in St. Petersburg. He graduated from the Petrischule (the school attached to the Evangelical Lutheran Church of St. Peter), then from the Medical-Surgical Academy in St. Petersburg (1857). He worked as a prosector at the St. Petersburg Foundling Home (later the Orphanage), and in 1869 defended his dissertation. Under his direction model children's hospitals were built: the Prince P.G. Oldenburg Hospital in St. Petersburg (1864—1869) and the Vladimir Hospital in Moscow (1872—1876). The St. Petersburg hospital had isolated infectious-disease and quarantine wards and small wards. In 1869—1909 Rauchfuss was its chief physician, and in the Soviet period the hospital was named after him. He introduced a staff of assistant physicians at the hospital, turning it into a center for training medical and scientific personnel for Russian pediatrics. At the same time he taught at the Clinical Institute for the Advanced Training of Physicians and in courses for "learned midwives." A champion of women's equality, at his hospital he granted graduates of the courses all the rights of physicians. He paid particular attention to the training of qualified mid-level medical personnel and to the organization of care for sick children. In his last years he created a model school for nannies in Tsarskoye Selo, training staff to care for young children. He worked on creating a system for the protection of motherhood and infancy, and on the problem of improving schoolchildren's health. He was one of the pioneers of Russian laryngology, the first to describe subglottic laryngitis, and he invented or improved a number of ENT instruments. A patriarch of Russian pediatrics, he was the author of works on pathological anatomy and clinical bacteriology. A symptom indicating mediastinal displacement in exudative pleurisy is named after him ("the Rauchfuss–Grocco triangle"). For many years he was chairman of the Scientific Society of Pediatricians of St. Petersburg, and was honorary chairman of the 1st All-Russian Congress of Pediatricians (1912), as well as an honorary member of scientific-medical societies of many countries. He is buried at the Volkovo Lutheran Cemetery in St. Petersburg.

REUTERN, Mikhail Khristoforovich (Michael) von (1820—1890) was born in the town of Porechye, Smolensk Governorate. He came from a noble family originating in Lübeck and known in the Baltic region since the 17th century. His father was a lieutenant general, his mother a lady-in-waiting at the imperial court and adopted daughter of M.B. Barclay de Tolly. He spent his childhood in Livonia, educated at a German boarding school in the town of Werro. In 1839 he graduated from the Tsarskoye Selo Lyceum. From 1840 he served in the Ministry of Finance, from 1843 in the Ministry of Justice, and in 1854—1858 in the Naval Ministry. In 1855—1858 he traveled abroad to study naval accounting. He was manager of affairs of the Railway Committee (1858—1859), a member of the Council of the Minister of Finance (1859—1860), manager of affairs of the Finance Committee (1860—1862), and a member of the Learned Committee of the Ministry of Finance (1861—1862). He took part in the reforms of the 1860s, serving on commissions dealing with preparations for the abolition of serfdom (1859—1860), the reform of the tax system (1859—1862) and of credit (1859—1860), the drafting of the charter for zemstvo mortgage banks (1859—1862), the abolition of the liquor tax-farming system (1860—1861), and the regularization of budgetary and estimate procedures (1862—1868). From 1862 he was manager of the Ministry of Finance, and in 1862—1878 minister of finance. He was a member of the State Council (from 1862) and of the Finance Committee (1862—1890), and chairman of the Mining Council (1862—1873). He held the rank of Secretary of State (1858) and Active Privy Councilor (1870), and was made a count (1890). He became minister during a period of acute financial crisis following the defeat in the Crimean War of 1853—1856. He favored a peaceable foreign policy course and reductions in military spending. He carried out a number of financial reforms, relying on the development of the country's productive forces by stimulating private initiative and attracting foreign capital. His policy led, from the late 1860s, to a boom in company formation, contributing to the emergence of industrial enterprises, the opening of private commercial banks, and the rapid growth of the railway network. However, under the influence of the stock market crash in Europe (1873), he judged unlimited freedom of incorporation to be inadvisable and abandoned the already-prepared fundamental joint-stock reform, evolving from free trade toward moderate protectionism. He opposed war with Turkey, stressing its danger to the state of finances and the national economy, especially given the economic crisis that had begun in 1875. The war of 1877—1878 led to financial disorder and disrupted all the plans of the Ministry of Finance. After the signing of peace the minister resigned. He was a member (1878—1882) and chairman (1881—1882) of the Main Committee on the Organization of the Rural Estate, and chairman of the Committee of Ministers (1881—1886) and of the Finance Committee (1885—1890). He was in many respects unfavorably disposed toward the conservative course of Alexander III, but he opposed any encroachment on the principle of autocracy. He was awarded the highest Russian orders. He was an honorary member of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (from 1863) and of many scientific and technical societies.

RICHMANN, Georg Wilhelm (1711—1753) was born in Pernau (Livonia). He came from the family of a treasurer. He graduated from the gymnasium in Reval. He studied at German universities, and from 1735 at the Academic University in St. Petersburg. From 1741 he was a professor at the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (adjunct from 1740). From 1744 he headed the physics office of the Academy of Sciences. He lectured on physics and mathematics at the Academic University. His main works were devoted to the study of heat and electricity. In 1744 he was the first to derive a formula for determining the temperature of a mixture of homogeneous liquids; he established the law of cooling of bodies, drawing attention to the peculiarities of heat exchange under non-stationary conditions; and he proposed new instruments for the needs of meteorology, hydrology, and thermometry. He laid the foundations for the study of electricity in Russia, introduced quantitative measurements into the science of electricity, and in 1745 invented an electrical measuring instrument — the "electric indicator." In 1746—1752 he conducted a large number of experiments studying the electrification and electrical conductivity of bodies, and clarifying the dependence of the electrical capacitance of bodies on their mass and shape. In 1748—1751 he discovered the phenomenon of electrostatic induction. In 1752—1753, together with M.V. Lomonosov, he conducted research on atmospheric electricity using special measuring devices called "thunder machines," and paid much attention to the design of lightning rods. He was killed by a lightning strike while conducting experiments with an ungrounded "thunder machine."

RICHTER, Wilhelm Mikhailovich (Wilhelm Michael) (1767—1822) was born in Moscow. He was the son of a Moscow Evangelical Lutheran pastor, a native of Prussia who had come to Russia in 1742. He graduated from the gymnasium in Reval (1779—1783), then from the medical faculty of Moscow University (1783—1786). In 1786—1790 he worked at foreign universities and trained at obstetric clinics in Germany. In 1788 he defended his doctoral dissertation in medicine at Erlangen; his work earned the praise of prominent Western scholars, and he was elected a member of several learned societies. From 1790 he was an extraordinary professor, and in 1795—1819 an ordinary professor, of the chair of midwifery at Moscow University. He was named Distinguished Ordinary Professor of Obstetrics (1819). In 1807, 1808, and 1812 he was elected dean of the medical faculty. In 1795—1805 he was chief obstetrician of Moscow, and in 1801—1807 director of the Midwifery Institute and Maternity Hospital at the Moscow Foundling Home, and a member of the Medical Council under the Ministry of Internal Affairs. In 1806 he founded the Midwifery Institute and Maternity Hospital for poor women in labor at Moscow University. In 1818 he was invited to the court, acting as godfather at the birth of the future Emperor Alexander II, and was granted the title of Physician-in-Ordinary. From 1819 he headed the obstetric hospital at the Medical Institute of Moscow University. He was the author of scholarly works and textbooks. He was one of the founders of the Physico-Medical Society (chairman in 1810—1822), on whose behalf he directed the creation of a three-volume work in German and Russian, "The History of Medicine in Russia" (1813—1820). From 1814 he was an honorary member of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences. He was an honorary member of the Medical-Surgical Academy in St. Petersburg, of several Russian universities, and a member of Russian and foreign scientific societies. He is buried at the German (Vvedenskoye) Cemetery in Moscow.

STELLER, Georg Wilhelm (1709—1746) was born in Windsheim (Franconia). His father was a cantor and organist. He studied the natural sciences, medicine, and theology at German universities, and passed his examinations in Berlin (1734). In 1734 he arrived in Russia, working as a private physician. In 1736 he was invited into the service of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences as adjunct in natural history (from 1737). He took part in preparing the catalogue of the botanical and zoological collections of the Kunstkamera. At the end of 1737 he left St. Petersburg to join the overland detachment of the Second Kamchatka Expedition, arriving in Kamchatka in 1740. In 1740—1741, undertaking several trips across the peninsula, he studied not only the nature of Kamchatka but also gathered information about neighboring territories, including America. In 1741 he took part in the voyage under the command of the expedition's leader, Vitus Bering, to the shores of America. In November Bering's packet boat was wrecked on the rocks of an island later named after him. There the expedition spent nine months under harsh conditions, and in December Bering died of scurvy. Steller did not cease his scientific research; he compiled a physical and topographical description of the island, described its flora and fauna, and assembled a large herbarium and extensive collections of fish, animals, and birds. During the wintering he wrote a description of the sea cow (Steller's sea cow), which was already extinct by 1768. His studies of mammals that had not previously encountered humans are of great value. In 1742 the surviving members of the voyage returned to Kamchatka. After this Steller devoted two more years to studying Kamchatka and the Kuril Islands, and the way of life and customs of the local inhabitants. He wrote "The History of Kamchatka" (1742—1743) and other works. He was the first in Russian natural science to show that changes in certain animal traits are caused by climatic conditions and food sources, and that such changes are not hereditary. In 1744, at the conclusion of the expedition, Steller set out for St. Petersburg, fell ill with a fever on the way, and died in Tyumen.

STRUVE, Vasily Yakovlevich (Friedrich Georg Wilhelm) (1793—1864) was born in Altona (Holstein). His father was the director of a gymnasium. He studied at the gymnasium in Altona, and in 1810 graduated from the University of Dorpat in philology, teaching ancient languages. From 1811 he studied astronomy and mathematics, earning a doctorate in philosophy (1813). From 1813 he was extraordinary professor (ordinary professor from 1820) at the University of Dorpat and observing astronomer at the Dorpat Observatory; in 1818—1838 he was director of the observatory, and thanks to him it was equipped with first-class instruments. From 1833 he was a member of the commission overseeing the construction of the Pulkovo Observatory, becoming its first director (1839—1862). He was the founder of the Pulkovo school of astronomy. Thanks to outstanding results in fundamental astrometry, the determination of the coordinates of celestial bodies, and the compilation of star catalogues, the observatory won worldwide recognition. Struve carried out extensive research on double stars. In 1837 he was the first to reliably establish stellar parallax. He made the classical determination of the constant of aberration using a transit instrument built according to his own design. He established the absorption of light in interstellar space and the increase in the number of stars per unit volume as one approaches the plane of the Milky Way. The results of his research are set out in his work "Studies of Stellar Astronomy" (1847) and other works. He also made a great contribution to geodesy and practical astronomy. In 1832—1861 he was an ordinary academician of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (corresponding member from 1822, honorary member in 1826—1832 and from 1861). He was an honorary member of Russian universities and of many foreign academies and scientific societies. He held the rank of Privy Councilor. As director of the Pulkovo Observatory he was succeeded by his son, academician of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences O.V. Struve. Other sons also became known: G.V. Struve, a chemist, and B.V. Struve, a governor; the latter's son was the well-known political figure P.B. Struve. He is buried at Pulkovo.

TOLL, Eduard Vasilyevich (Eduard Gustav) von (1858—1902) was born in Reval. He was a descendant of a noble family originating in Wittenberg and known in the Baltic region since the 16th century. His father was a cavalry captain and baron. He studied at the Vyshgorod School in Reval (1869—1870), then at a gymnasium (1872—1877). He graduated from the natural-history faculty of the University of Dorpat (1877—1882), studying mineralogy, medicine, and zoology. He took part as a naturalist in an expedition to Algeria and the Balearic Islands (1882). He defended his candidate's dissertation in zoology (1883), and from 1884 lived in St. Petersburg. In 1885—1886 he took part in A.A. Bunge's expedition to study the New Siberian Islands and the basins of the Yana, Indigirka, and Kolyma rivers. In 1886, from Kotelny Island, he saw the outlines of mountains that he took to be "Sannikov Land." In 1893—1894 he took part in a second Arctic expedition surveying the basins of the Lena and Khatanga rivers. North of Kotelny Island he again saw land. In 1898 he presented to a commission of the Russian Geographical Society his plan for the exploration of Sannikov Land that he had conceived, and in 1899 the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences commissioned him to organize such an expedition according to his plan. In the summer of 1900 the expedition departed from St. Petersburg aboard the schooner "Zarya." As planned, the "Zarya" was to pass through the Northern Sea Route into the Pacific Ocean, but it could not do so because of the ice and wintered near Bennett Island. By the autumn of 1901 the expedition had reached Cape Chelyuskin and set off in search of Sannikov Land. But the schooner became trapped in an ice field, and to avoid the loss of the ship the further search had to be abandoned. The second wintering took place at Kotelny Island. The coal supplies aboard the "Zarya" were running out, and it was decided to send the ship on to the mouth of the Lena. In June 1902 Toll and three companions (F.G. Seeberg, the Yakut V. Gorokhov, and the Evenk N. Dyakonov) set off in search of Sannikov Land toward Bennett Island, on the understanding that the "Zarya" would pick them up from the island in early autumn. However, the ship tried in vain to break through the ice and abandoned the search due to a shortage of coal. In November Toll and his companions set off back toward the New Siberian Islands amid the polar night and 30-degree frost. Later only traces of Toll's camps, his notes, and his collections were found, but he and his companions vanished without a trace. A special commission of the Academy of Sciences worked on processing the extensive and valuable materials of his expedition until 1919. A number of geographical features on the Taymyr Peninsula and on Kotelny, Stolbovoy, and Bennett Islands, as well as several species of flora and fauna, are named after Toll. A memorial plaque commemorating his work has been erected on Kotelny Island.

TOTLEBEN (Todleben), Eduard Ivanovich (Franz Eduard) von (1818—1884) was born in Mitau, Courland Governorate. He was the son of a merchant. He studied at a private school in Riga, and from 1832 at the Nicholas Engineering School (St. Petersburg), where he was unable to complete the full course due to heart disease. In 1836 he was enrolled in the Riga engineering unit, then transferred to the training sapper battalion. He attracted the attention of General K.A. Schilder, who assigned him to work on the tube mine system. In 1848 he took part in the Caucasian War, then served as Schilder's adjutant in Warsaw, and served in St. Petersburg. In 1854, during the Crimean War of 1853—1856, he was summoned to the headquarters of the Army of the Danube and carried out a number of important assignments for Schilder. When Schilder was wounded, Totleben took charge of all the engineering works in the army and blew up the line of forward Turkish fortifications. He was then sent to Sevastopol, where an enemy landing was expected. Due to delays by the command, defensive works began only after the landing had taken place. Totleben expanded the frontal position on the northern side and essentially rebuilt the defensive line on the southern side of Sevastopol from scratch, striving to ensure that all approaches to the city had continuous frontal and flanking defense. The work went on day and night. The enemy was forced to abandon a direct assault on the city, since the very first bombardment of Sevastopol revealed the strength of its fortifications and the advantageous positioning of its batteries' fire. The enemy turned to underground warfare, but encountered an unexpectedly skillfully prepared network of mine galleries. In July 1855 Totleben was wounded in the leg but continued to direct the defensive works, and only a sharp deterioration in his condition forced his evacuation from the city. He was awarded the ranks of Major General and Adjutant General (1855), and made an honorary citizen of Sevastopol, Riga, and Reval. Later, as one of the leaders of the heroic defense, a monument to him was erected in Sevastopol (sculptor I.N. Schröder, artist A.A. Bilderling). From 1859 he was director of the Engineering Department, and in 1863—1879 deputy inspector general for engineering affairs; he directed defensive works in Nikolayev, at the mouth of the Dnieper, on the Black Sea coast, on the western border, in Kronstadt, and elsewhere. He was made Engineer-General (1869). In 1874, on the instructions of Alexander II, he worked out the terms for alternative service by Mennonite colonists. In 1877, during the Russo-Turkish War of 1877—1878, he directed engineering works and commanded the blockading army during the siege of Plevna. In 1878 he was commander-in-chief of the Russian army beyond the Balkans, and after the conclusion of peace he became governor-general of Odessa. He was a member of the State Council, and was made a count (1879). From 1880 he was governor-general of the northwestern territory (Vilna, Kovno, and Grodno) and commander of the troops of the Vilna Military District. Under his direction the work "Description of the Defense of the City of Sevastopol" (1863—1872) was prepared, and he was the author of works on military engineering. He was an honorary member of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (from 1855), of several Russian universities, and of Russian and foreign military academies. He is buried in Sevastopol.

FABERGÉ, Karl Gustavovich (Peter Carl) (1846—1920) was born in St. Petersburg. He came from a Germanized family of French Huguenots who had fled to Prussia at the end of the 17th century and settled at the end of the 18th century in Pernau (Livonia Governorate). His father was a goldsmith. He studied at the Annenschule (the school attached to the Evangelical Lutheran Church of St. Anne) in St. Petersburg. He finished school in Dresden, where he moved with his parents in 1860. He trained under well-known European jewelers and gem-cutters. In 1870 he inherited a jewelry workshop in St. Petersburg that had been opened by his father in 1842. He transformed it into the largest jewelry firm in St. Petersburg, with branches in Moscow (1887), Odessa (1890), Kiev (1905), and London (1908). Numerous German, Finnish, and Russian craftsmen worked for him, some of whom had their own workshops. He attracted attention in 1885 by producing a gold copy of Scythian PERSONAL-NAME COMMENTARY______________________________________________________________ 757

treasures found at Kerch; he received the title of jeweler to the imperial court. During this same period he began producing his famous "Easter eggs" on commission for the imperial family. The firm's products (clocks, jewelry, opera glasses, cigarette cases, etc.) interpreted historical artistic styles (baroque, rococo, classicism) or were executed in the Art Nouveau style. They were distinguished by the uniqueness of their design solutions (Easter eggs with mechanical surprises), by their polychromy (precious and ornamental stones, gold in various textures and color combinations, multicolored enamel coatings), and by the care of their finishing. He left Russia in 1918.

FELTEN, Yuri Matveyevich (Georg Friedrich) (1730—1801) was born in St. Petersburg. His father was a native of Danzig and served as steward at the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences. He graduated from the gymnasium of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (1740—1745), then studied in Germany. From 1749 he trained under the architect I.Ya. Schumacher in St. Petersburg. From 1756 he served in the Chancellery of Buildings, was promoted to architect in 1760, and from 1762 was chief architect. In St. Petersburg he built: the southern wing of the Small Hermitage and the Hanging Garden wing (1765—1766), the side galleries of the Hermitage (1769—1775), the Old Hermitage (1771—1787), the covered gallery connecting the Old Hermitage to the Hermitage Theatre (1783), the Chesme Palace (1774—1777), and the Kamennoostrovsky Palace (1776—1781), and he directed construction of the railing of the Summer Garden (1772—1778). He designed and directed the construction of the Evangelical Lutheran churches of St. Catherine (1768—1771) and St. Anne (1775—1779), as well as other churches. He carried out the layout of Senate Square, created the granite embankment of the Neva (1764—1788), and designed several St. Petersburg bridges. In the 1770s he worked at the suburban residences, creating park pavilions at Tsarskoye Selo and ceremonial interiors in the Great Peterhof Palace. His works expressed the ideas of early classicism. From 1772 he was professor of architecture at the St. Petersburg Academy of Arts, from 1785 adjunct rector, and in 1789—1794 director. He was a corresponding member of the Paris Academy of Architecture (1783). He held the rank of State Councilor.

FERREIN, Karl Ivanovich (1802—1887) was born in Arnswalde (Prussia). He arrived in Russia in 1815, and in Moscow in 1824. From 1824 he was a pharmacist's assistant. In 1827, having passed examinations at the Moscow branch of the Medical-Surgical Academy, he received the title of apothecary. In 1827 he bought the Novo-Polyansky pharmacy from M. Rudolph. In 1832 he sold it to K. Freimuth and bought the oldest private pharmacy in Moscow and in Russia — the Staro-Nikolskaya pharmacy (founded in 1701; from 1750 it had been owned by Germans — I.F. Meyer, G.Kh. Hildebrand, and others). At the pharmacy run by Ferrein there worked a pharmacist's assistant, two journeymen (Gesellen), and five helpers. The number of prescriptions filled reached up to 3,000 a year. In 1832 he was a member of the Committee for the Introduction of a New Pharmacy Tariff. He was a hereditary honorary citizen (1847). In 1872 he handed over all his affairs to his son, V.K. Ferrein, who in 1902 created the partnership "V.K. Ferrein," which became one of the leading pharmaceutical firms not only in Russia but in Europe. 758____________________________________________________ GERMANS IN THE HISTORY OF RUSSIA. 1652-1917

FISCHER von WALDHEIM Grigory Ivanovich (Johann Gotthelf) (1771–1853) was born in Waldheim (Saxony). He completed a gymnasium and the Mining Academy in Freiberg, studied at German and other foreign universities, and received his doctorate in medicine (1797). From 1798 he was a professor at the University of Mainz. From 1804 he was in Russia, professor of the department of natural history at Moscow University. He lectured on zoology, comparative anatomy, and mineralogy, taught special courses, and gave public lectures on natural history. He was dean of the physics-and-mathematics faculty (1829) and director of the university's Museum of Natural History (from 1805), to which he donated his own collection of animal skeletons and minerals. During the Patriotic War of 1812 he managed to save part of the museum's collections from fire and plunder, sacrificing his personal belongings and library. From 1808 he was also professor of mineralogy and zoology at the Moscow branch of the Medical-Surgical Academy, and from 1817 vice-president of that academy. He authored more than 200 scholarly works, including the five-volume "Entomographia Rossica" (1820–1851), "Oryctographie du Gouvernement de Moscou" (1830–1837), and the first Russian textbooks on zoology (1808) and mineralogy (1818–1820). For his works on zoology he was called "the Russian Cuvier"; he was the first to introduce the term "paleontology" into Russian science. He was the initiator, director (from 1805), and later vice-president of the Moscow Society of Naturalists. He was also one of the founders, and from 1820 to 1835 director, of the Moscow Society of Agriculture. From 1819 he was an honorary member of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (corresponding member from 1805). He was an honorary member of Russian universities and scholarly societies, and of foreign academies. He was a member of the Medical Council under the Ministry of Internal Affairs (1820). He held the rank of Active State Councillor (1822) and was awarded Russian orders. His son A.G. Fischer von Waldheim was a botanist and professor at Moscow University. He is buried at the German (Vvedenskoye) Cemetery.

KHEMNITSER Ivan Ivanovich (1745–1784) was born at the Yenotayevskaya fortress in Astrakhan governorate. His father was a staff physician who came from Saxony. In 1757 he enlisted as a private in an infantry regiment and took part in the Seven Years' War of 1756–1763. From 1769, having left military service, he worked at the Mining School in St. Petersburg. He translated and edited books on mineralogy and took part in compiling a Mining dictionary. From 1782 he served as consul-general in Smyrna (Turkey). Besides his official service, he wrote and translated fables and tales in verse. He constructed his plots as instructive scenes and cunning allegories, and developed a comic verse of varying meter later brought to perfection by I.A. Krylov and A.S. Griboyedov. He followed the poetics of classicism but valued simplicity and fidelity to nature above all. His fables, which enjoyed great popularity, are strongly marked by moralizing tendencies. Khemnitser's works are distinguished by the conversational ease of their language, their folk quality, and democratic motifs. During his lifetime two anonymous editions of the book "Fables and Tales of N.N., in Verse" (1779–1782) were published. After this he essentially withdrew from literary activity. He was a member of the Russian Academy (1784).

SHEKHTEL Fyodor Osipovich (Franz Albert) (1859–1926) was born in Saratov. His ancestors were Volga colonists who came from Bavaria. His father was an engineer-technologist and the first impresario of the Saratov theater. He completed the preparatory school at the Saratov Roman Catholic seminary. In 1875 he moved to Moscow, studying at the School of Painting, Sculpture, and Architecture (1876–1877), where he later taught from 1898 to 1926. He began his creative career as an assistant architect. From the mid-1880s he designed estates and created interior designs for Moscow mansions. In 1888 he built the "Paradise" theater in Moscow (now the Mayakovsky Theater). He received the right to carry out construction work in 1893. At the beginning of the twentieth century Shekhtel was the leading representative of the Art Nouveau (moderne) style in Russia. His most programmatic works in this style are the S.P. Ryabushinsky mansion on Malaya Nikitskaya Street (1900) and the Derozhinskaya mansion in Shtatny/Kropotkinsky Lane (1901). Striking too are the buildings belonging to the neo-Gothic and national-romantic branches of his moderne style (the Z.G. Morozova mansion on Spiridonovka, 1893; the Yaroslavl Station, 1902). In his projects he managed to reconcile the spirit of national architecture with the architectural currents of the early twentieth century. His body of work encompasses all the stylistic trends of the period and all types of buildings. Moscow of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries is rightly called "Shekhtel's Moscow." Built to his designs were the "Boyarsky Dvor" trading house on Staraya Square (1901), the Ryabushinsky bank on Karuninskaya/Kuibyshev Square (1903), and the printing house of the newspaper "Utro Rossii" on Strastnoy Boulevard (1907). He built and decorated more than 20 apartment buildings in Moscow, and in 1902 rebuilt and refurbished the building of the Moscow Art Theater. He also built in Ryazan, Rostov-on-Don, Nizhny Novgorod, Saratov, Taganrog, and Samara governorate. One of his programmatic works is the Russian pavilion at the international exhibition in Glasgow (1901). He was involved in the restoration of churches, dacha construction, and worked as a theatrical designer. From 1896 to 1923 he taught at the Stroganov School of Applied Arts. He headed the Moscow Architectural Society (1906–1922). He was an academician of the St. Petersburg Academy of Arts (1902). He is buried at Vagankovo Cemetery.

SHILLING (Shilling von Canstadt) Pavel Lvovich (Paul Ludwigovich) (1786–1837) was born in Reval. His father was a colonel and baron who moved to Russia in 1730. In 1795 he was enrolled in a musketeer regiment, and from 1797 to 1802 studied at the 1st Cadet Corps in St. Petersburg. He graduated as a second lieutenant and studied geodesy and cartography. In 1803 he was transferred as a translator to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and attached to the embassy in Munich. In 1812 he proposed using electric current to detonate underwater mines, developed a special fuse for this purpose, and carried out the detonation of a mine on the Neva. Having voluntarily joined the army in 1812, he took part in the Foreign Campaign of 1813–1814 with the rank of staff captain of cavalry. He proposed using lithography to reproduce documents, including topographic maps. In 1816 the first lithography workshop was opened at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and in 1818 Shilling was appointed its manager. During these years he became interested in Oriental studies and was considered one of the strongest chess players in St. Petersburg. In 1827 he was appointed chairman of the committee for publishing the Complete Collection of Laws of the Russian Empire. In 1828 760____________________________________________________ GERMANS IN THE HISTORY OF RUSSIA. 1652-1917

he invented a binary telegraph code. In 1829 he developed a method of lithographic reproduction of Chinese texts. In 1830–1832 he took part in an expedition in southern Siberia, near the borders of China. He studied Asian languages and gathered a collection of rare oriental manuscripts, which became the foundation of the Asiatic Museum. He became a specialist in cryptography and invented a telegraphic alphabet for transmitting Chinese characters. In 1832 he invented an electric telegraph apparatus, then developed an insulated cable for transmitting electrical signals underwater, and proposed a design for overhead telegraph lines using poles. In 1833, in the presence of Nicholas I, he conducted tests of a tube system for installing electromagnetic mines. In 1837 he proposed a project for the first telegraph line in Russia, between St. Petersburg and Peterhof, using a cable laid along the bottom of the Gulf of Finland. From 1828 he was a corresponding member of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences in the category of Eastern literature and antiquities. He was a member of foreign academies and scholarly societies. He held the rank of Active State Councillor (1828). A memorial plaque has been placed on the house on Marsovo Pole where he lived. He is buried at the Smolensk Lutheran Cemetery in St. Petersburg.

SHRÖTER Viktor Aleksandrovich (Viktor Johann Gottlieb) (1839–1901) was born in St. Petersburg. He was the son of a merchant who came from Reval. From 1851 he studied at the Petrischule (a school attached to the Evangelical Lutheran Church of St. Peter) in St. Petersburg, and from 1856 to 1858 at the St. Petersburg Academy of Arts. From 1858 to 1861 he studied at the Berlin Building Academy, where he attended lectures on theater construction, and also took classes at the Berlin Academy of Arts. In 1862 he received from the St. Petersburg Academy of Arts the rank of class artist with the right "to carry out construction." In 1864 he was elected an academician of the Academy of Arts for his design of the City Duma building, and from 1892 was a professor at the Academy of Arts. From 1865 he was an instructor at the St. Petersburg Building School (the Institute of Civil Engineers), where he worked until the end of his life. He built the Lutheran Church of St. Mary in St. Petersburg (1872–1874, together with I.S. Kitner) and took part in the construction of the monument to Catherine II (1872). From 1882 he was chief architect of the Directorate of the Imperial Theaters. In St. Petersburg he rebuilt the following theaters: the Alexandrinsky (1883, together with A.R. Geschwend), the Bolshoi (1883–1886), and the Mariinsky (1885–1894). He was the creator of theater buildings in Rybinsk, Tiflis, Irkutsk, Nizhny Novgorod, and Kiev. Among Shröter's most significant St. Petersburg projects are the buildings of the City Credit Society on Ostrovsky Square (1876), the firm "Stoll and Schmidt" on Malaya Morskaya Street (1880–1881), the Russian Bank for Foreign Trade on Bolshaya Morskaya Street (1887–1888), the Hospital of the Exchange Merchantry on Vasilievsky Island (1887–1889), and the "Ludwig Nobel" plant on Bolshoy Sampsonievsky Prospekt (1896). His designs for public buildings are distinguished by a free planning composition and the use of rational structural methods. He was one of the creators of the "brick style" and contributed to the development of "rational architecture." In the construction of residential buildings he more often drew on motifs of the Renaissance and classical style. He built a number of apartment buildings in St. Petersburg; to his designs were built the railway station (1883) and the Reformed church (1896) in Odessa, as well as buildings in Dorpat, Astrakhan, Samara, near Penza, and in Kiev and Kharkov governorates. He was one of the founders of the St. Petersburg Society of Architects (1870) and a member of the Royal Institute of British Architects and the Berlin Society of Architects (1895). He is buried at the Smolensk Lutheran Cemetery in St. Petersburg.

STACKENSCHNEIDER Andrei Ivanovich (Heinrich Gustav Clemens) (1802–1865) was born on the Ivanovka estate near the town of Gatchina in St. Petersburg governorate. His father owned a mill near Gatchina; his paternal grandfather had come to Russia from Brunswick at the invitation of Paul I to set up tanneries. He studied at the St. Petersburg Academy of Arts (1815–1820). From 1825 he was a draftsman-architect during the construction of St. Isaac's Cathedral. In 1830–1831 he traveled through Europe. On his return he was recommended to Count A.Kh. Benckendorff for the rebuilding of his Fall estate near Reval, where he created a striking composition in the Gothic style. This drew the attention of Nicholas I, opening the way to a career as a court architect. In 1837 he developed a design for a palace in Kolomenskoye near Moscow. He was the author of designs for numerous palaces in St. Petersburg: the Mariinsky Palace on St. Isaac's Square (1839–1844), the Beloselsky-Belozersky Palace on Nevsky Prospekt (1847–1848), the Nikolaevsky Palace on Blagoveshchenskaya Square (1853–1861), and the New Mikhailovsky Palace on Palace Embankment (1857–1862). He decorated a number of rooms in the Winter, Marble, Anichkov, and Kamennoostrovsky Palaces, in the Small and Old Hermitage, and also in the Strelna and Grand Peterhof Palaces. He was the author of buildings in the Baltic provinces, in Novgorod (the Nobility Assembly), in Oreanda (the imperial palace), in Uman, and in Oryol governorate. He worked near St. Petersburg — in Oranienbaum, Pavlovsk, Gatchina, Strelna — and built especially extensively in Peterhof. Besides palaces and palace interiors, he created numerous landscaped park complexes and so-called "small architectural forms" — cast-iron fences, benches, lanterns, vases, and the like. His designs for the layout of villages near Peterhof are among the earliest attempts at standardized construction in Russia. By creatively reinterpreting the legacy of the Baroque and classicism and skillfully combining Renaissance-Gothic motifs with elements of the "Russian style," he did much to determine the paths of development of Russian architecture in the nineteenth century. From 1854 he taught at the St. Petersburg Academy of Arts; he was an academician (1834), professor of architecture (1844), and professor of the Academy of Arts (1854). From 1856 he was architect of the imperial court, and held the rank of Active State Councillor (1858). He is buried at the cemetery of the Trinity-Sergius Hermitage near Strelna, which was destroyed during the Soviet period. The graves of Stackenschneider and his family have recently been found and restored.

STÄHLIN (Stählin von Storcksburg) Yakov Yakovlevich (Jacob) (1709–1785) was born in Memmingen (Bavaria). In his youth he took music lessons, played the flute, and performed as a conductor. In 1735, upon completing his studies at the University of Leipzig, he was invited to the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences as an adjunct in eloquence and poetry. He lectured on history, literature, rhetoric, and criticism at the gymnasium and university of the Academy of Sciences, and took part in compiling the catalogue of the academic library and the numismatic cabinet of the Kunstkamera. From 1737 he was a professor at the Academy of Sciences, and served as its conference secretary (1765–1769), putting the Academy's archive in order and conducting the Academy's foreign correspondence. From 1748 he headed the weekly meetings at the Academy of Sciences on artistic matters, and in 1757–1768 he was director of the Academy of Arts under the Academy of Sciences. For many years (1735–1737, 1748–1760, 1783–1785) he edited the German-language newspaper "St. Petersburgische Zeitung," selecting material for publication and writing most of the articles himself. From 1765 he took part in the work of the newly established Free Economic Society (member from 1766, secretary of the Society from 1768), compiling for it surveys of economic works published in Europe. He was tutor to the future Emperor Peter III (1742–1745) and his librarian. He published, after forty years of collecting, accounts by eyewitnesses of Peter I, compiled the first detailed biography of M.V. Lomonosov, and acquainted Europe with the achievements of Russian literature and culture. As in his youth, he engaged in musical activity and was co-chairman of the St. Petersburg Music Club. From 1757 he effectively headed the medal-making business in Russia, and hundreds of medals were produced from his designs. His most important achievement over half a century of life in Russia was the creation of the first history of Russian art. He made the first descriptions of the significant painting collections of St. Petersburg and its environs. He left notes on painting, sculpture, architecture, the history of the Academy of Arts, engraving, mosaics, ballets and dance art, and also on the collecting of paintings in Russia. In its scope this activity has no parallel in the European art scholarship of the time. He was a member of a number of foreign academies and scholarly societies.

SHTILKE Vasily Konstantinovich (1850–1908) was born in Barnaul. His father was a district treasurer; his grandfather came from Germany and had been in Russian service since 1800. On completing the Tomsk gymnasium (1870) he enrolled in the Medical-Surgical Academy in St. Petersburg, was expelled for non-payment of tuition, and in 1876 was exiled to Barnaul for association with the Narodniks. He worked as a home tutor, taught at a district school, and then served as a supervisor of land-survey works. In 1884 he founded, and for more than 20 years effectively headed, the Society for the Care of Primary Education in Barnaul. With the active participation of the Society, two mixed (for boys and girls) free schools, two Sunday schools for adults, two free libraries, the first bookshop, an amateur theater, and a city garden were opened in the city (mostly through voluntary donations). With the Society's funds a People's House was built with a hall seating 1,000 (now the Regional Philharmonic). The Society's activity was recognized with a silver medal at the World Exhibition in Paris (1900), and with a diploma and certificate of merit in Russia. Shtilke drew political exiles into the Society's work, and from 1885 until the end of his life he was under covert police surveillance. In 1905, during the Black Hundred pogrom in Barnaul, Shtilke's house and the municipal public library housed in it were damaged; he was forced to leave for Tomsk. In 1906, on his return from there, he was ordered to leave Barnaul, being forbidden to remain within the bounds of Siberia and the Steppe Territory "for the duration of martial law." Having gone to St. Petersburg, he was attached "for work on land-survey matters," but soon retired due to illness. In 1907 he was elected a member of the State Duma from Tomsk governorate, and headed the commission on public education within the Siberian faction. Due to a worsening of his illness he set out for Barnaul, but died en route, at Ob station (now Novosibirsk). A street in Barnaul is named after Shtilke. He is buried in Barnaul; his grave was destroyed in the 1930s and has now been partially restored.

STORCH Andrei Karlovich (Heinrich Friedrich) von (1766–1835) was born in Riga. His father was a Livland provincial secretary who came from Königsberg. He completed the Dom School in Riga (1783) and studied at the universities of Jena and Heidelberg (1784–1787). From 1787 he was in St. Petersburg, where he taught history and literature at the Cadet Corps, and for 20 years was tutor to the grand duchesses and grand dukes (from 1799), and reader to Empress Maria Feodorovna (1801). In 1815 he published the first course of political economy in Russia, in 6 volumes, showing himself in many respects a follower of Adam Smith. He was the author of the fundamental 8-volume work "Historical-Statistical Sketch of the Russian Empire at the End of the Eighteenth Century," published in Riga and Leipzig in German (1797–1803) and translated into English and French. He did much to popularize scholarly information about Russia abroad. His first work was a bibliographic index of the most important literature on Russian history, geography, and law (1789). One of its sections constituted the first index of bibliographic reference works in Russia. He was the author of the work "Materials for the Study of the Russian Empire" (1796), published in Riga in German. From 1804 to 1811 he published in St. Petersburg and Leipzig, in German, the journal "Russland unter Alexander dem Ersten." From 1804 he was an ordinary academician of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (corresponding member for political economy and statistics from 1796), and from 1830 to 1835 he held the newly established post of vice-president of the Academy of Sciences. He held the rank of Privy Councillor (1828) and was awarded Russian orders. He is buried at the Smolensk Lutheran Cemetery in St. Petersburg.

EULER Leonhard (1707–1783) was born in Basel. His father was a Protestant pastor with an interest in mathematics. Euler received his first lessons in mathematics from his father. He studied at the University of Basel (1720–1723), where mathematics was taught by Johann Bernoulli. He received his Master of Arts (1724). He published his first mathematical papers in 1726. On the recommendation of his teacher's sons, Nicolaus and Daniel Bernoulli, who had become professors at the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences founded in 1725, he was elected an adjunct of the Academy in 1726. Arriving in St. Petersburg in 1727, he threw himself actively into mathematics and corresponded with almost all the leading mathematicians of his time. During his first St. Petersburg period he prepared about 80 works for publication and published more than 50, devoted not only to mathematics but also to mechanics and hydrodynamics. Having thoroughly learned the Russian language, he took an active part in many of the Academy's undertakings. However, owing to the unstable political situation and growing resentment of the influence of foreigners, in 1741 he accepted the invitation of the Prussian king Frederick II and became his active assistant in organizing the Berlin Academy of Sciences. While in Berlin he maintained close ties with the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences, through whose mediation several well-known German scholars were admitted to it. In his last years 764_________________________________________ GERMANS IN THE HISTORY OF RUSSIA. 1652-1917 in Berlin, Euler's relations with Frederick II deteriorated, and in 1766, at the invitation of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences, the scholar returned to Russia. In St. Petersburg he was received with honors and granted an audience with Catherine II. A large house was built for his numerous family on the embankment of the Neva. The almost complete loss of his eyesight had little effect on Euler's creative activity; he now simply prepared his works with the help of skilled secretaries. During this period of activity he prepared about 400 works, and fundamental works of Euler's were published in St. Petersburg: the three-volume "Institutionum calculi integralis" (1768–1770) and the three-volume "Dioptrica" (1769–1771). He was the most prolific mathematician of all time, having prepared about 850 scholarly works, including 20 large monographs. He was professor (1731–1741, 1766–1783) and foreign honorary member (1742–1766) of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences. He was a member of many foreign academies and scholarly societies. A memorial plaque has been placed on his house on Vasilievsky Island. Among his 13 children, the best known are his sons: I.A. Euler, professor and conference secretary of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences, and Kh. Euler, lieutenant-general of the Russian army. He is buried at the Smolensk Lutheran Cemetery in St. Petersburg; in 1956 his remains were transferred to the necropolis of the Alexander Nevsky Lavra.

AEPINUS Franz Ulrich Theodor (1724–1802) was born in Rostock. His father was rector of the University of Rostock. He studied at the universities of Rostock and Jena (1740–1746), receiving his doctorate in philosophy and mathematics (1747) and his doctorate in medicine (1748). Arriving in St. Petersburg in 1757, in that same year he presented to the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences a proof of Newton's theorem on raising a binomial to an arbitrary power, as well as reports on new experiments in electricity and on a new design for a pyrometer. At meetings of the Academy he put forward important conjectures about the existence of a flow of heat from the Earth into space and about a continent at the South Pole (1761), and argued for the possibility of long-range weather forecasting given a global network of meteorological stations (1763). His fundamental work "Tentamen theoriae electricitatis et magnetismi," published in 1769 in German and Russian, brought him worldwide fame. It set out the first mathematical theory of electrical and magnetic phenomena. Aepinus came close to the concepts of capacitance and potential, put forward the idea of the electrophorus, explained the phenomenon of electrical induction, discovered electrical polarization and the pyroelectric properties of tourmaline, and constructed the first achromatic microscope. In the 1780s he published his two last major scholarly works (on volcanoes on the Moon and on a zoom telescopic microscope), and wrote a study on aeronautics in which he developed the idea of a steerable balloon. He tutored the grand dukes and grand duchesses, including future rulers from Catherine II to Alexander I. A textbook of Aepinus's, published anonymously and used in the education of the future Emperor Paul I, was called the first Russian textbook of elementary natural science. From 1764 Aepinus, under the direction of Catherine II, worked on preparations for introducing a state system of public education in Russia. In 1765 he was enrolled in the College of Foreign Affairs, where he headed Russia's cipher service, working on the development of cipher systems and the decryption of texts. He retired due to illness in 1797. He was professor of physics at the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (1756–1798). From 1766 he was a member of the Free Economic Society. He was a member of many foreign academies and scholarly societies. He held the rank of Privy Councillor (1796) and was awarded Russian orders.

JACOBI Boris Semyonovich (Moritz Hermann) (1801–1874) was born in Potsdam. He studied at the universities of Berlin and Göttingen, receiving a diploma in architecture in 1829. He worked in his profession until moving to Königsberg (1834), where his elder brother, C.G.J. Jacobi, was professor of mathematics (foreign corresponding member of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences from 1830, foreign honorary member from 1833). There he became interested in electrical engineering, moved to Dorpat in 1835, and to St. Petersburg in 1837. In 1835 Jacobi gave the first detailed description of an electric motor. He constructed several electric motors, one of which was installed in 1838 on a boat that sailed on the Neva. This tested not only the new motor but also the first electric-powered boat on water. In 1838 Jacobi discovered electrotyping (galvanoplasty), which made his name famous. Having carried out numerous experiments with electrolytes, he found a way to obtain precise copper copies reproducing any image. For this invention he was awarded the Demidov Prize of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences and the Grand Gold Medal of the French Academy. He did much to introduce electrotyping into printing and coinage, as well as into the manufacture of art objects. In 1838–1844, together with E.Kh. Lenz, he studied electromagnets and proposed a method for calculating them. In 1850 he published a work presenting the first attempt at an analysis of the operation of the electric motor. He created a number of electrical instruments — a voltmeter, a wire standard of resistance, several designs of galvanometers, a resistance regulator, and others. He designed about ten types of telegraph apparatus, including the first letter-printing apparatus (1850). He directed the laying of the first cable lines in St. Petersburg and between St. Petersburg and Tsarskoye Selo (1841–1843). He developed galvanic batteries and new types of mine weapons, including galvanic-impact mines. He was the initiator of the creation of galvanic units within the sapper units of the Russian army. The electric mines he designed were used in the Crimean War of 1853–1856. His works accelerated the solution of many problems of metrology: the establishment of the metric system of measures, the development of standards, the selection of units of measurement, and others. Jacobi laid the foundation for electrical engineering education in Russia. From 1847 he was an ordinary academician of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences (corresponding member from 1838, adjunct from 1839, extraordinary academician from 1842). He is buried at the Smolensk Lutheran Cemetery in St. Petersburg.

- THE XX th CENTURY DOCUMENTS

- GERMANS IN RUSSIA'S HISTORY Documents of the Supreme Organs of State Power

- And of the Military Command,

- 1652-1917

- Included in the present collection prepared by the Public Academy of Sciences of the Russian Germans are documents pertaining to life and activities of the ethnic Germans in the Russian State. These are the basic documents on the subject passed by the supreme bodies of state power, as well as by the Military Command of Russia Chronologically the book spans the period from 1652 to 1917 — the entire pre-revolutionary part of Russia's history during which ethnic Germans played a significant role in the Russian State. Books in the series "RUSSIA. THE 20TH CENTURY. DOCUMENTS"
